input: Dawa Norbu argues that modern Chinese Communist historians tend to be in favor of the view that the Ming simply reappointed old Yuan dynasty officials in Tibet and perpetuated their rule of Tibet in this manner. Norbu writes that, although this would have been true for the eastern Tibetan regions of Amdo and Kham's "tribute-cum-trade" relations with the Ming, it was untrue if applied to the western Tibetan regions of Ü-Tsang and Ngari. After the Phagmodrupa Changchub Gyaltsen, these were ruled by "three successive nationalistic regimes," which Norbu writes "Communist historians prefer to ignore."
rewrite: According to Dawa Norbu, contemporary historians aligned with the Chinese Communist Party often promote the idea that the Ming dynasty continued to govern Tibet by reinstating the former officials of the Yuan. He contends that while this characterization fits the eastern areas of Amdo and Kham, which engaged in tributary trade with the Ming, it does not hold for western Ü-Tsang and Ngari. Following Phagmodrupa Changchub Gyaltsen, that region was controlled by three consecutive patriotic governments, a fact Norbu states these historians typically overlook.

input: The study of genocide has mainly been focused towards the legal aspect of the term. By formally recognizing the act of genocide as a crime, involves the undergoing prosecution that begins with not only seeing genocide as outrageous past any moral standpoint but also may be a legal liability within international relations. When genocide is looked at in a general aspect it is viewed as the deliberate killing of a certain group. Yet is commonly seen to escape the process of trial and prosecution due to the fact that genocide is more often than not committed by the officials in power of a state or area. In 1648 before the term genocide had been coined, the Peace of Westphalia was established to protect ethnic, national, racial and in some instances religious groups. During the 19th century humanitarian intervention was needed due to the fact of conflict and justification of some of the actions executed by the military.
rewrite: Research on genocide has traditionally emphasized its legal dimensions. Defining genocide as an international crime initiates judicial processes that treat it not merely as a profound moral violation but also as an actionable offense under global law. Broadly, genocide is understood as the intentional destruction of a specific population. However, perpetrators frequently avoid legal accountability, as such acts are typically carried out by state authorities themselves. Prior to the creation of the term "genocide" in the 20th century, the 1648 Peace of Westphalia laid early foundations for protecting ethnic, national, racial, and sometimes religious communities. Later, in the 1800s, military conflicts and the rationalization of certain wartime conduct necessitated the development of humanitarian intervention principles.

input: New Haven was the host of the 1995 Special Olympics World Summer Games; then-President Bill Clinton spoke at the opening ceremonies. The city is home to the Pilot Pen International tennis event, which takes place every August at the Connecticut Tennis Center, one of the largest tennis venues in the world. New Haven biannually hosts "The Game" between Yale and Harvard, the country's second-oldest college football rivalry. Numerous road races take place in New Haven, including the USA 20K Championship during the New Haven Road Race.
rewrite: In 1995, New Haven welcomed the Special Olympics World Summer Games, featuring an opening address by President Bill Clinton. Each August, the city stages the Pilot Pen International tennis tournament at the globally sizable Connecticut Tennis Center. It is also the site for the historic Yale-Harvard football contest, "The Game," held every other year. Additionally, New Haven's calendar includes various road races, such as the USA 20K Championship.

input: The conversion rate of omega-6 DGLA to AA largely determines the production of the prostaglandins PGE1 and PGE2. Omega-3 EPA prevents AA from being released from membranes, thereby skewing prostaglandin balance away from pro-inflammatory PGE2 (made from AA) toward anti-inflammatory PGE1 (made from DGLA). Moreover, the conversion (desaturation) of DGLA to AA is controlled by the enzyme delta-5-desaturase, which in turn is controlled by hormones such as insulin (up-regulation) and glucagon (down-regulation). The amount and type of carbohydrates consumed, along with some types of amino acid, can influence processes involving insulin, glucagon, and other hormones; therefore, the ratio of omega-3 versus omega-6 has wide effects on general health, and specific effects on immune function and inflammation, and mitosis (i.e., cell division).
rewrite: The synthesis of prostaglandins PGE1 and PGE2 depends significantly on how much DGLA, an omega-6 fatty acid, is transformed into arachidonic acid (AA). Omega-3 EPA inhibits the release of AA from cell membranes, shifting prostaglandin synthesis from the pro-inflammatory PGE2, derived from AA, toward the anti-inflammatory PGE1, which comes from DGLA. This conversion of DGLA to AA is regulated by the delta-5-desaturase enzyme, itself influenced by hormones like insulin, which promotes it, and glucagon, which suppresses it. Dietary intake of carbohydrates and certain amino acids affects these hormonal activities. Consequently, the balance between omega-3 and omega-6 fats broadly impacts overall wellness, particularly influencing immune response, inflammatory processes, and cell division.

input: The university first offered graduate degrees, in the form of a Master of Arts (MA), in the 1854–1855 academic year. The program expanded to include Master of Laws (LL.M.) and Master of Civil Engineering in its early stages of growth, before a formal graduate school education was developed with a thesis not required to receive the degrees. This changed in 1924 with formal requirements developed for graduate degrees, including offering Doctorate (PhD) degrees. Today each of the five colleges offer graduate education. Most of the departments from the College of Arts and Letters offer PhD programs, while a professional Master of Divinity (M.Div.) program also exists. All of the departments in the College of Science offer PhD programs, except for the Department of Pre-Professional Studies. The School of Architecture offers a Master of Architecture, while each of the departments of the College of Engineering offer PhD programs. The College of Business offers multiple professional programs including MBA and Master of Science in Accountancy programs. It also operates facilities in Chicago and Cincinnati for its executive MBA program. Additionally, the Alliance for Catholic Education program offers a Master of Education program where students study at the university during the summer and teach in Catholic elementary schools, middle schools, and high schools across the Southern United States for two school years.
rewrite:
The institution began awarding advanced degrees, starting with a Master of Arts, during the 1854-1855 school year. In its initial phase of development, the curriculum grew to encompass Master of Laws and Master of Civil Engineering degrees. At that time, these could be earned without completing a thesis, prior to the establishment of an organized graduate school. This structure was revised in 1924 with the introduction of formal criteria for advanced degrees, which included the creation of Doctor of Philosophy programs.

Currently, all five of the university's colleges provide graduate-level instruction. Nearly every department within the College of Arts and Letters grants doctoral degrees, alongside a professional Master of Divinity. Every department in the College of Science offers a PhD, with the sole exception of Pre-Professional Studies. The School of Architecture confers a Master of Architecture degree, and each engineering department provides doctoral programs. The College of Business administers several professional offerings, such as the MBA and a Master of Science in Accountancy, and runs executive MBA facilities in Chicago and Cincinnati.

Furthermore, through the Alliance for Catholic Education, a Master of Education is available. Participants in this program attend summer sessions on campus and fulfill two academic years teaching in Catholic K-12 schools throughout the Southern United States.

input: Illustrated humour periodicals were popular in 19th-century Britain, the earliest of which was the short-lived The Glasgow Looking Glass in 1825. The most popular was Punch, which popularized the term cartoon for its humorous caricatures. On occasion the cartoons in these magazines appeared in sequences; the character Ally Sloper featured in the earliest serialized comic strip when the character began to feature in its own weekly magazine in 1884.
rewrite: In 19th-century Britain, illustrated comedy magazines were widely enjoyed. The first, *The Glasgow Looking Glass*, emerged briefly in 1825. The most famous, *Punch*, coined the word "cartoon" for its satirical drawings. Sometimes these images were arranged in series; the figure Ally Sloper starred in the first recurring comic strip when it gained a dedicated weekly publication in 1884.

input: The Gold Standard Act of 1900 abandoned the bimetallic standard and defined the dollar as 23.22 grains (1.505 g) of gold, equivalent to setting the price of 1 troy ounce of gold at $20.67. Silver coins continued to be issued for circulation until 1964, when all silver was removed from dimes and quarters, and the half dollar was reduced to 40% silver. Silver half dollars were last issued for circulation in 1970. Gold coins were confiscated by Executive Order 6102 issued in 1933 by Franklin Roosevelt. The gold standard was changed to 13.71 grains (0.888 g), equivalent to setting the price of 1 troy ounce of gold at $35. This standard persisted until 1968.
rewrite: In 1900, the Gold Standard Act replaced the bimetallic system, legally pegging the U.S. dollar to a specific quantity of gold: 23.22 grains. This established a fixed value of $20.67 per troy ounce of gold. While silver coins remained in production for general use, their precious metal content was gradually eliminated, starting with dimes and quarters in 1964. Half dollars followed, being reduced to a 40% silver composition before their final circulation issue in 1970. Earlier, in 1933, President Roosevelt's executive order mandated the seizure of private gold coins. Subsequently, the gold standard was adjusted, redefining the dollar to 13.71 grains of gold and raising the official price to $35 per ounce, a valuation that remained until 1968.

input: Worldwide prosperity changed dramatically with the onset of the Great Depression in 1929. The Wall Street Crash of 1929 served to punctuate the end of the previous era, as The Great Depression set in. The Great Depression was a worldwide economic downturn starting in most places in 1929 and ending at different times in the 1930s or early 1940s for different countries. It was the largest and most important economic depression in the 20th century, and is used in the 21st century as an example of how far the world's economy can fall.
rewrite: The Great Depression, beginning in 1929, radically altered global economic conditions. Its onset was starkly marked by the Wall Street Crash, which signaled the conclusion of a prior age. This severe worldwide downturn commenced around 1929 and persisted through the 1930s, with varying end dates extending into the early 1940s across nations. As the most significant depression of the twentieth century, it remains a key historical benchmark for the potential depth of an international economic collapse.

input: Rawski writes that Altan Khan's conversion to the Gelug "can be interpreted as an attempt to expand his authority in his conflict with his nominal superior, Tümen Khan." To further cement the Mongol-Tibetan alliance, the great-grandson of Altan Khan—the 4th Dalai Lama (1589–1616)—was made the fourth Dalai Lama. In 1642, the 5th Dalai Lama (1617–1682) became the first to wield effective political control over Tibet.
rewrite: According to Rawski, Altan Khan adopted the Gelug faith partly to strengthen his position against Tümen Khan, his formal overlord. This Mongol-Tibetan partnership was solidified when his great-grandson was recognized as the fourth Dalai Lama. Later, in 1642, the fifth Dalai Lama became the initial figure to exercise genuine political authority across Tibet.

input: Aposematism, where organisms are brightly colored as a warning to predators, is the antithesis of camouflage. Some organisms pose a threat to their predators—for example they may be poisonous, or able to harm them physically. Aposematic coloring involves bright, easily recognizable and unique colors and patterns. For example, bright coloration in Variable Checkerspot butterflies leads to decreased predation attempts by avian predators. Upon being harmed (e.g., stung) by their prey, the appearance in such an organism will be remembered as something to avoid. While that particular prey organism may be killed, the coloring benefits the prey species as a whole.
rewrite: Aposematism is the opposite of camouflage, featuring vivid hues that signal danger to potential predators. These conspicuous markings indicate that an organism might be toxic or physically harmful. For instance, the bold patterns of Variable Checkerspot butterflies reduce attacks from birds. If a predator experiences a negative encounter, like a sting, it learns to associate that distinct appearance with harm. Although the individual prey might not survive, this warning strategy ultimately protects the broader species.

input: A sound generated on any instrument produces many modes of vibration that occur simultaneously. A listener hears numerous frequencies at once. The vibration with the lowest frequency is called the fundamental frequency; the other frequencies are overtones. Harmonics are an important class of overtones with frequencies that are integer multiples of the fundamental. Whether or not the higher frequencies are integer multiples, they are collectively called the partials, referring to the different parts that make up the total spectrum.
rewrite: When an instrument creates a tone, it initiates multiple vibrations at the same time. This results in the perception of many combined frequencies. The most basic, lowest frequency is known as the fundamental, while the rest are overtones. Among these, harmonics are key—their frequencies are whole-number multiples of the fundamental. All higher frequencies, regardless of being multiples, are termed partials, representing the individual components of the complete sound spectrum.

input: In response to these hardware flaws, "Nintendo Authorized Repair Centers" sprang up across the U.S. According to Nintendo, the authorization program was designed to ensure that the machines were properly repaired. Nintendo would ship the necessary replacement parts only to shops that had enrolled in the authorization program. In practice, the authorization process consisted of nothing more than paying a fee to Nintendo for the privilege. In a recent trend, many sites have sprung up to offer Nintendo repair parts, guides, and services that replace those formerly offered by the authorized repair centers.
rewrite: To address these device issues, "Nintendo Authorized Repair Centers" emerged throughout the United States. Nintendo stated the program aimed to guarantee correct fixes for the consoles. The company would supply required components solely to businesses that joined this initiative. However, becoming authorized essentially involved just submitting a payment to Nintendo. Lately, numerous online sources have appeared, providing repair components, instructions, and support that now substitute the services once given by these official centers.

input: On the next day, December 18, protests turned into civil unrest as clashes between troops, volunteers, militia units, and Kazakh students turned into a wide-scale confrontation. The clashes could only be controlled on the third day. The Almaty events were followed by smaller protests and demonstrations in Shymkent, Pavlodar, Karaganda, and Taldykorgan. Reports from Kazakh SSR authorities estimated that the riots drew 3,000 people. Other estimates are of at least 30,000 to 40,000 protestors with 5,000 arrested and jailed, and an unknown number of casualties. Jeltoqsan leaders say over 60,000 Kazakhs participated in the protests. According to the Kazakh SSR government, there were two deaths during the riots, including a volunteer police worker and a student. Both of them had died due to blows to the head. About 100 others were detained and several others were sentenced to terms in labor camps. Sources cited by the Library of Congress claimed that at least 200 people died or were summarily executed soon thereafter; some accounts estimate casualties at more than 1,000. The writer Mukhtar Shakhanov claimed that a KGB officer testified that 168 protesters were killed, but that figure remains unconfirmed.
rewrite: The following day, December 18, demonstrations escalated into widespread civil disorder. A broad confrontation erupted involving troops, volunteer forces, militias, and Kazakh students, which persisted for three days before being brought under control. After the unrest in Almaty, additional, though smaller, protests occurred in several other cities including Shymkent, Pavlodar, Karaganda, and Taldykorgan. Official reports from the Kazakh SSR government stated the riots involved approximately 3,000 individuals. However, alternative assessments indicate significantly higher numbers, suggesting between 30,000 and 40,000 participants, with around 5,000 arrests and an undetermined number of injuries or deaths. Organizers of the Jeltoqsan movement assert that over 60,000 Kazakhs took part. Authorities reported only two fatalities: a volunteer police officer and a student, both from head injuries. They also noted about 100 detentions and several labor camp sentences. In contrast, sources referenced by the Library of Congress state at least 200 individuals were killed or executed in the immediate aftermath, with some estimates exceeding 1,000 casualties. Author Mukhtar Shakhanov reported an unverified claim from a KGB officer that 168 protesters lost their lives.

input: Washington University supports four major student-run media outlets. The university's student newspaper, Student Life, is available for students. KWUR (90.3 FM) serves as the students' official radio station; the station also attracts an audience in the immediately surrounding community due to its eclectic and free-form musical programming. WUTV is the university's closed-circuit television channel. The university's main student-run political publication is the Washington University Political Review (nicknamed "WUPR"), a self-described "multipartisan" monthly magazine. Washington University undergraduates publish two literary and art journals, The Eliot Review and Spires Intercollegiate Arts and Literary Magazine. A variety of other publications also serve the university community, ranging from in-house academic journals to glossy alumni magazines to WUnderground, campus' student-run satirical newspaper.
rewrite: Washington University is home to several media organizations managed by its student body. The primary campus newspaper is Student Life. KWUR (90.3 FM), the official student radio station, reaches both the university and the nearby area with its diverse, unconstrained music format. WUTV operates as a closed-circuit television station. For political discourse, students produce the Washington University Political Review ("WUPR"), a monthly publication identifying as multipartisan. Undergraduate editors also release two literary and arts periodicals: The Eliot Review and Spires Intercollegiate Arts and Literary Magazine. Additional publications, from scholarly journals and polished alumni magazines to the humorous student satire paper WUnderground, further serve the campus community.

input: In the United States and elsewhere in the world, there has been a marked rise in the evangelical wing of Protestant denominations, especially those that are more exclusively evangelical, and a corresponding decline in the mainstream liberal churches. In the post–World War I era, Liberal Christianity was on the rise, and a considerable number of seminaries held and taught from a liberal perspective as well. In the post–World War II era, the trend began to swing back towards the conservative camp in America's seminaries and church structures.
rewrite: Globally, particularly in the U.S., the evangelical segment of Protestantism has grown significantly, while more liberal mainstream churches have seen a downturn. This contrasts with the period following World War I, when liberal theological views were expanding and commonly taught in many seminaries. After World War II, however, a shift toward conservatism emerged within American religious training institutions and congregations.

input: Utrecht is the centre of a densely populated area, which makes concise definitions of its agglomeration difficult, and somewhat arbitrary. The smaller Utrecht agglomeration of continuously built up areas counts some 420,000 inhabitants and includes Nieuwegein, IJsselstein and Maarssen. It is sometimes argued that the close by municipalities De Bilt, Zeist, Houten, Vianen, Driebergen-Rijsenburg (Utrechtse Heuvelrug), and Bunnik should also be counted towards the Utrecht agglomeration, bringing the total to 640,000 inhabitants. The larger region, including slightly more remote towns such as Woerden and Amersfoort counts up to 820,000 inhabitants.
rewrite: Utrecht lies at the heart of a heavily populated region, making precise descriptions of its urban area challenging and somewhat subjective. The core built-up zone, encompassing places like Nieuwegein, holds around 420,000 residents. Many contend that neighboring municipalities, including De Bilt and Zeist, should be part of this agglomeration, which would increase the population to approximately 640,000. A broader definition that incorporates towns like Amersfoort raises the total to about 820,000 inhabitants.

input: Turner Classic Movies is available in many other countries around the world. In Canada, TCM began to be carried on Shaw Cable and satellite provider Shaw Direct in 2005. Rogers Cable started offering TCM in December 2006 as a free preview for subscribers of its digital cable tier, and was added to its analogue tier in February 2007. While the schedule for the Canadian feed is generally the same as that of the U.S. network, some films are replaced for broadcast in Canada due to rights issues and other reasons. Other versions of TCM are available in Australia, France, Middle East, South Africa, Cyprus, Spain, Asia, Latin America, Scandinavia, the United Kingdom, Ireland and Malta. The UK version operates two channels, including a spinoff called TCM 2.
rewrite: Turner Classic Movies reaches audiences in numerous nations globally. Canadian viewers first gained access through Shaw Cable and Shaw Direct in 2005. Rogers Cable introduced the channel in December 2006 as a complimentary digital offering, later including it in analogue packages by February 2007. Although the Canadian programming largely mirrors the U.S. lineup, certain movies are substituted because of licensing restrictions. Separate TCM services are provided in regions such as Australia, France, the Middle East, South Africa, Spain, Asia, Latin America, Scandinavia, and several European nations including the UK, Ireland, Malta, and Cyprus. In the United Kingdom, an additional channel named TCM 2 is also broadcast.

input: A person's self-report is the most reliable measure of pain, with health care professionals tending to underestimate severity. A definition of pain widely employed in nursing, emphasizing its subjective nature and the importance of believing patient reports, was introduced by Margo McCaffery in 1968: "Pain is whatever the experiencing person says it is, existing whenever he says it does". To assess intensity, the patient may be asked to locate their pain on a scale of 0 to 10, with 0 being no pain at all, and 10 the worst pain they have ever felt. Quality can be established by having the patient complete the McGill Pain Questionnaire indicating which words best describe their pain.
rewrite: The most accurate way to gauge pain is through an individual's own account, as medical practitioners often judge it as less severe than it truly is. In nursing, a commonly accepted concept stresses that pain is inherently personal and that clinicians should trust a patient's description. This idea, formalized by Margo McCaffery in 1968, asserts that pain is defined solely by the person feeling it and occurs exactly when they report it. To quantify its strength, patients might rate their discomfort from zero, meaning none, to ten, representing the most intense pain imaginable. Describing its character often involves selecting appropriate terms from tools like the McGill Pain Questionnaire.

input: Though still predominantly green, post-2004 series incorporate other colors to better distinguish different denominations. As a result of a 2008 decision in an accessibility lawsuit filed by the American Council of the Blind, the Bureau of Engraving and Printing is planning to implement a raised tactile feature in the next redesign of each note, except the $1 and the version of the $100 bill already in process. It also plans larger, higher-contrast numerals, more color differences, and distribution of currency readers to assist the visually impaired during the transition period.
rewrite: While U.S. currency remains mostly green, bills printed after 2004 began using additional colors to help tell denominations apart. Following a 2008 legal ruling in a case brought by the American Council of the Blind, future redesigns for most notes will include a raised, touchable element. The changes also involve bigger, bolder numbers, greater color variation, and providing electronic readers to aid those with vision challenges as the new money is introduced.

input: In Sand Springs, an outdoor amphitheater called "Discoveryland!" is the official performance headquarters for the musical Oklahoma! Ridge Bond, native of McAlester, Oklahoma, starred in the Broadway and International touring productions of Oklahoma!, playing the role of "Curly McClain" in more than 2,600 performances. In 1953 he was featured along with the Oklahoma! cast on a CBS Omnibus television broadcast. Bond was instrumental in the title song becoming the Oklahoma state song and is also featured on the U.S. postage stamp commemorating the musical's 50th anniversary. Historically, the state has produced musical styles such as The Tulsa Sound and western swing, which was popularized at Cain's Ballroom in Tulsa. The building, known as the "Carnegie Hall of Western Swing", served as the performance headquarters of Bob Wills and the Texas Playboys during the 1930s. Stillwater is known as the epicenter of Red Dirt music, the best-known proponent of which is the late Bob Childers.
rewrite: In Sand Springs, the musical Oklahoma! is officially staged at an open-air venue named "Discoveryland!" Ridge Bond, originally from McAlester, Oklahoma, portrayed the character Curly McClain over 2,600 times in both Broadway and global touring versions of the show. He appeared with the cast in a 1953 CBS Omnibus television program. Bond played a key role in having the production's title track designated as the state anthem and is pictured on a U.S. postage stamp marking the musical's fiftieth year. Musically, Oklahoma has been the birthplace of genres like The Tulsa Sound and western swing, the latter famously associated with Cain's Ballroom in Tulsa. That venue, often called the "Carnegie Hall of Western Swing," was the 1930s home base for Bob Wills and his band, the Texas Playboys. Additionally, Stillwater is recognized as the heart of Red Dirt music, a style greatly advanced by the musician Bob Childers, who has since passed away.

input: But Hanover is not only one of the most important Exhibition Cities in the world, it is also one of the German capitals for marksmen. The Schützenfest Hannover is the largest Marksmen's Fun Fair in the world and takes place once a year (late June to early July) (2014 - July 4th to the 13th). It consists of more than 260 rides and inns, five large beer tents and a big entertainment programme. The highlight of this fun fair is the 12 kilometres (7 mi) long Parade of the Marksmen with more than 12.000 participants from all over the world, among them around 5.000 marksmen, 128 bands and more than 70 wagons, carriages and big festival vehicles. It is the longest procession in Europe. Around 2 million people visit this fun fair every year. The landmark of this Fun Fair is the biggest transportable Ferris Wheel in the world (60 m or 197 ft high). The origins of this fun fair is located in the year 1529.
rewrite: Hanover holds a dual distinction as both a leading global hub for exhibitions and a premier center for marksmanship in Germany. The city hosts the Hanover Schützenfest, the world's largest annual fair for marksmen, held each year from late June into early July. The event features over 260 attractions including rides and taverns, five major beer tents, and an extensive schedule of entertainment. Its most notable event is a marksmen's parade stretching 12 kilometers, which includes roughly 12,000 participants from across the globe. This procession, the longest of its kind in Europe, comprises about 5,000 shooters, 128 musical bands, and over 70 floats and ceremonial vehicles. Annual attendance reaches approximately two million visitors. A key symbol of the fair is the planet's tallest mobile Ferris wheel, standing 60 meters high. The festival traces its beginnings back to 1529.

input: In 1943, at the age of 16, Elizabeth undertook her first solo public appearance on a visit to the Grenadier Guards, of which she had been appointed colonel the previous year. As she approached her 18th birthday, parliament changed the law so that she could act as one of five Counsellors of State in the event of her father's incapacity or absence abroad, such as his visit to Italy in July 1944. In February 1945, she joined the Women's Auxiliary Territorial Service as an honorary second subaltern with the service number of 230873. She trained as a driver and mechanic and was promoted to honorary junior commander five months later.
rewrite: At sixteen in 1943, Elizabeth made her initial independent official visit to the Grenadier Guards, a regiment she had been named colonel for the prior year. Nearing her eighteenth birthday, legislation was amended to allow her to serve among five Counsellors of State during her father's potential inability to rule or trips overseas, like his 1944 journey to Italy. She entered the Women's Auxiliary Territorial Service in February 1945 as an honorary second subaltern, bearing the number 230873. There, she received instruction as a driver and mechanic, rising to the honorary rank of junior commander within five months.

input: By the early 1940s, the company was concentrating on lower-budget productions that were the company's main staple: westerns, melodramas, serials and sequels to the studio's horror pictures, the latter now solely B pictures. The studio fostered many series: The Dead End Kids and Little Tough Guys action features and serials (1938–43); the comic adventures of infant Baby Sandy (1938–41); comedies with Hugh Herbert (1938–42) and The Ritz Brothers (1940–43); musicals with Robert Paige, Jane Frazee, The Andrews Sisters, and The Merry Macs (1938–45); and westerns with Tom Mix (1932–33), Buck Jones (1933–36), Bob Baker (1938–39), Johnny Mack Brown (1938–43); Rod Cameron (1944–45), and Kirby Grant (1946–47).
rewrite: By the start of the 1940s, the studio had shifted its primary focus to more economical films, which formed the core of its output. These included westerns, emotional dramas, chapter plays, and follow-ups to its earlier horror movies, which were now produced as secondary features. The company cultivated numerous recurring film series. These encompassed action titles and serials featuring The Dead End Kids and Little Tough Guys, comedic tales centered on the toddler Baby Sandy, various comedy franchises, musicals starring several popular acts, and a long-running sequence of westerns with a rotating roster of leading actors.

input: A number of universities in London are outside the University of London system, including Brunel University, City University London, Imperial College London, Kingston University, London Metropolitan University, Middlesex University, University of East London, University of West London and University of Westminster, (with over 34,000 students, the largest unitary university in London), London South Bank University, Middlesex University, University of the Arts London (the largest university of art, design, fashion, communication and the performing arts in Europe), University of East London, the University of West London and the University of Westminster. In addition there are three international universities in London – Regent's University London, Richmond, The American International University in London and Schiller International University.
rewrite: Several higher education institutions in London operate independently from the University of London network. Among these are Brunel University, City University London, Imperial College London, Kingston University, London Metropolitan University, and Middlesex University. Also included are the University of East London, the University of West London, and the University of Westminster—the latter being London's largest single-site university with a student body exceeding 34,000. Others are London South Bank University and the University of the Arts London, Europe's premier institution for art, design, fashion, communication, and performing arts. Furthermore, London hosts three international universities: Regent's University London, Richmond (The American International University in London), and Schiller International University.

input: On 26 February 2012, The Sun on Sunday was launched to replace the closed News of the World, employing some of its former journalists. In late 2013, it was given a new look, with a new typeface. The average circulation for The Sun on Sunday in March 2014 was 1,686,840; but in May 2015 The Mail on Sunday sold more copies for the first time, an average of 28,650 over those of its rival: 1,497,855 to 1,469,195. Roy Greenslade issued some caveats over the May 2015 figures, but believes the weekday Daily Mail will overtake The Sun in circulation during 2016.
rewrite: The Sun on Sunday began publication on February 26, 2012, taking the place of the defunct News of the World and hiring several of its previous staff. It received a visual redesign, including updated typography, toward the end of 2013. While its March 2014 average circulation stood at 1,686,840, The Mail on Sunday surpassed it in May 2015 by roughly 28,650 copies, selling 1,497,855 compared to 1,469,195. Roy Greenslade noted certain cautions regarding those 2015 statistics but anticipates the daily edition of the Mail will exceed The Sun's readership within 2016.

input: Incandescent light bulbs consist of an air-tight glass enclosure (the envelope, or bulb) with a filament of tungsten wire inside the bulb, through which an electric current is passed. Contact wires and a base with two (or more) conductors provide electrical connections to the filament. Incandescent light bulbs usually contain a stem or glass mount anchored to the bulb's base that allows the electrical contacts to run through the envelope without air or gas leaks. Small wires embedded in the stem in turn support the filament and its lead wires.
rewrite: An incandescent bulb is a sealed glass container housing a tungsten wire filament. Electricity flows through this filament via contact wires connected to a base with multiple conductors. Typically, a glass stem fixed to the base secures the electrical contacts, preventing leaks. This mount also has fine wires that hold both the filament and its connecting leads in place within the bulb.

input: Compact Disc + Graphics is a special audio compact disc that contains graphics data in addition to the audio data on the disc. The disc can be played on a regular audio CD player, but when played on a special CD+G player, it can output a graphics signal (typically, the CD+G player is hooked up to a television set or a computer monitor); these graphics are almost exclusively used to display lyrics on a television set for karaoke performers to sing along with. The CD+G format takes advantage of the channels R through W. These six bits store the graphics information.
rewrite: A CD+G disc is an enhanced audio compact disc that includes both sound and visual content. While it functions normally in standard CD players, specialized CD+G equipment can decode and transmit graphical data, usually to a TV or monitor. This feature is primarily utilized in karaoke systems to show song lyrics for performers. The graphics data is encoded using six specific subcode bits, labeled R through W, within the disc's structure.

input: The term "Sumerian" is the common name given to the ancient non-Semitic inhabitants of Mesopotamia, Sumer, by the Semitic Akkadians. The Sumerians referred to themselves as ùĝ saĝ gíg-ga (cuneiform: 𒌦 𒊕 𒈪 𒂵), phonetically /uŋ saŋ giga/, literally meaning "the black-headed people", and to their land as ki-en-gi(-r) ('place' + 'lords' + 'noble'), meaning "place of the noble lords". The Akkadian word Shumer may represent the geographical name in dialect, but the phonological development leading to the Akkadian term šumerû is uncertain. Hebrew Shinar, Egyptian Sngr, and Hittite Šanhar(a), all referring to southern Mesopotamia, could be western variants of Shumer.
rewrite: The name "Sumerian" was applied by the Akkadians, a Semitic group, to describe the early non-Semitic people of Sumer in Mesopotamia. These individuals called themselves "the black-headed people" in their own language, and they named their homeland "the land of the noble lords." While the Akkadian term "Shumer" likely comes from a regional name, its exact linguistic origin is unclear. Related names found in Hebrew, Egyptian, and Hittite texts for southern Mesopotamia are probably western adaptations of this same word.

input: During the Franco-Prussian War and the Siege of Strasbourg, the city was heavily bombarded by the Prussian army. The bombardment of the city was meant to break the morale of the people of Strasbourg. On 24 and 26 August 1870, the Museum of Fine Arts was destroyed by fire, as was the Municipal Library housed in the Gothic former Dominican church, with its unique collection of medieval manuscripts (most famously the Hortus deliciarum), rare Renaissance books, archeological finds and historical artifacts. The gothic cathedral was damaged as well as the medieval church of Temple Neuf, the theatre, the city hall, the court of justice and many houses. At the end of the siege 10,000 inhabitants were left without shelter; over 600 died, including 261 civilians, and 3200 were injured, including 1,100 civilians.
rewrite: In the Franco-Prussian War, Prussian forces besieged and shelled Strasbourg extensively, aiming to crush the spirit of its defenders. Fires ignited by the bombardment on August 24 and 26, 1870, consumed the Museum of Fine Arts and the Municipal Library. That library, located in a former Dominican church, lost its unparalleled holdings, which included precious medieval manuscripts like the *Hortus deliciarum*, along with rare books from the Renaissance and numerous archaeological items. The city's Gothic cathedral, the Temple Neuf church, the theater, the town hall, the courthouse, and countless residences were also struck. When the siege concluded, 10,000 people were homeless. The casualties exceeded 600 dead, 261 of whom were non-combatants, and 3,200 wounded, including 1,100 civilians.

input: In Northern Germany, Netherlands, northern Poland, Denmark, and the Baltic countries local building stone was unavailable but there was a strong tradition of building in brick. The resultant style, Brick Gothic, is called "Backsteingotik" in Germany and Scandinavia and is associated with the Hanseatic League. In Italy, stone was used for fortifications, but brick was preferred for other buildings. Because of the extensive and varied deposits of marble, many buildings were faced in marble, or were left with undecorated façade so that this might be achieved at a later date.
rewrite: In regions like Northern Germany, the Netherlands, northern Poland, Denmark, and the Baltic states, builders turned to brick due to a lack of local stone, creating a style known as Brick Gothic (Backsteingotik), often linked to the Hanseatic League. Conversely, in Italy, brick was common for most structures, though stone was reserved for fortifications. Abundant marble supplies led many Italian buildings to be clad in this material, while others had plain exteriors intended for future marble facing.

input: Neptune's orbit has a profound impact on the region directly beyond it, known as the Kuiper belt. The Kuiper belt is a ring of small icy worlds, similar to the asteroid belt but far larger, extending from Neptune's orbit at 30 AU out to about 55 AU from the Sun. Much in the same way that Jupiter's gravity dominates the asteroid belt, shaping its structure, so Neptune's gravity dominates the Kuiper belt. Over the age of the Solar System, certain regions of the Kuiper belt became destabilised by Neptune's gravity, creating gaps in the Kuiper belt's structure. The region between 40 and 42 AU is an example.
rewrite: The gravitational influence of Neptune significantly shapes the distant Kuiper belt, a vast disk of icy bodies located just past the planet's path. This expansive ring, stretching from roughly 30 to 55 astronomical units from the Sun, is far bigger than the inner asteroid belt. Similar to Jupiter's effect on the asteroid belt, Neptune's gravity has sculpted the Kuiper belt's architecture over billions of years. This force has destabilized specific zones, clearing out objects and leaving structural voids, such as the notable gap found between 40 and 42 AU from the Sun.

input: The formal study of adolescent psychology began with the publication of G. Stanley Hall's "Adolescence in 1904." Hall, who was the first president of the American Psychological Association, viewed adolescence primarily as a time of internal turmoil and upheaval (sturm und drang). This understanding of youth was based on two then new ways of understanding human behavior: Darwin's evolutionary theory and Freud's psychodynamic theory. He believed that adolescence was a representation of our human ancestors' phylogenetic shift from being primitive to being civilized. Hall's assertions stood relatively uncontested until the 1950s when psychologists such as Erik Erikson and Anna Freud started to formulate their theories about adolescence. Freud believed that the psychological disturbances associated with youth were biologically based and culturally universal while Erikson focused on the dichotomy between identity formation and role fulfillment. Even with their different theories, these three psychologists agreed that adolescence was inherently a time of disturbance and psychological confusion. The less turbulent aspects of adolescence, such as peer relations and cultural influence, were left largely ignored until the 1980s. From the '50s until the '80s, the focus of the field was mainly on describing patterns of behavior as opposed to explaining them.
rewrite: The field of adolescent psychology was established with G. Stanley Hall's 1904 work, "Adolescence." As the inaugural leader of the American Psychological Association, Hall characterized this life stage chiefly as one of intense inner conflict and distress, a concept influenced by contemporary ideas from Darwin and Freud. He proposed that adolescence mirrored humanity's evolutionary journey from a primitive to a civilized state. For decades, this perspective remained dominant until mid-20th century researchers like Erik Erikson and Anna Freud introduced alternative views. Anna Freud emphasized the biological and universal roots of teenage psychological struggles, whereas Erikson examined the tension between forming a personal identity and assuming social roles. Despite their theoretical differences, all three pioneers concurred that adolescence was fundamentally a period of disruption and inner turmoil. Consequently, more stable elements like peer interactions and cultural impacts received little attention until the 1980s. During the intervening decades, the discipline prioritized cataloging behavioral trends over investigating their underlying causes.

input: Hunting big game typically requires a "tag" for each animal harvested. Tags must be purchased in addition to the hunting license, and the number of tags issued to an individual is typically limited. In cases where there are more prospective hunters than the quota for that species, tags are usually assigned by lottery. Tags may be further restricted to a specific area, or wildlife management unit. Hunting migratory waterfowl requires a duck stamp from the Fish and Wildlife Service in addition to the appropriate state hunting license.
rewrite: To legally hunt large animals, a hunter must obtain a special permit, or "tag," for each one taken. This tag is an extra purchase beyond the basic hunting license, and each person is usually allowed only a limited number. If demand exceeds the available permits, they are often distributed through a random drawing. These tags can also be designated for use in particular zones. For waterfowl hunting, a federal duck stamp is also mandatory alongside the state license.

input: West founded the record label and production company GOOD Music in 2004, in conjunction with Sony BMG, shortly after releasing his debut album, The College Dropout. John Legend, Common, and West were the label's inaugural artists. The label houses artists including West, Big Sean, Pusha T, Teyana Taylor, Yasiin Bey / Mos Def, D'banj and John Legend, and producers including Hudson Mohawke, Q-Tip, Travis Scott, No I.D., Jeff Bhasker, and S1. GOOD Music has released ten albums certified gold or higher by the Recording Industry Association of America (RIAA). In November 2015, West appointed Pusha T the new president of GOOD Music.
rewrite: Kanye West established his recording and production venture GOOD Music in 2004 with Sony BMG, following the launch of his first album, *The College Dropout*. The label initially featured West alongside John Legend and Common. Its roster has since grown to include acts such as Big Sean, Teyana Taylor, and Yasiin Bey, as well as producers like Q-Tip and Travis Scott. GOOD Music has issued at least ten RIAA gold-certified albums or better. Pusha T was named the label's president by West in late 2015.

input: Many early immigrant groups traveled to America to worship freely, particularly after the English Civil War and religious conflict in France and Germany. They included nonconformists like the Puritans, who were Protestant Christians fleeing religious persecution from the Anglican King of England. Despite a common background, the groups' views on religious toleration were mixed. While some such as Roger Williams of Rhode Island and William Penn of Pennsylvania ensured the protection of religious minorities within their colonies, others like the Plymouth Colony and Massachusetts Bay Colony had established churches. The Dutch colony of New Netherland established the Dutch Reformed Church and outlawed all other worship, though enforcement was sparse. Religious conformity was desired partly for financial reasons: the established Church was responsible for poverty relief, putting dissenting churches at a significant disadvantage.
rewrite: Numerous settlers arrived in America seeking religious liberty, especially following periods of strife such as the English Civil War and turmoil in parts of Europe. Among them were dissenting Protestants like the Puritans, who escaped oppression under England’s Anglican monarchy. Their approaches to tolerance varied widely. In certain colonies, such as those founded by Roger Williams and William Penn, minority faiths received legal safeguards. Conversely, places like Plymouth and Massachusetts Bay designated official churches. Similarly, New Netherland endorsed the Dutch Reformed Church and banned alternative practices, albeit loosely. A key motive for enforcing a single faith was economic: the sanctioned church managed aid for the poor, leaving rival congregations at a practical and financial deficit.

input: Persistent heavy rain and landslides in Wenchuan County and the nearby area badly affected rescue efforts. At the start of rescue operations on May 12, 20 helicopters were deployed for the delivery of food, water, and emergency aid, and also the evacuation of the injured and reconnaissance of quake-stricken areas. By 17:37 CST on May 13, a total of over 15,600 troops and militia reservists from the Chengdu Military Region had joined the rescue force in the heavily affected areas. A commander reported from Yingxiu Town, Wenchuan, that around 3,000 survivors were found, while the status of the other inhabitants (around 9,000) remained unclear. The 1,300 rescuers reached the epicenter, and 300 pioneer troops reached the seat of Wenchuan at about 23:30 CST. By 12:17 CST, May 14, 2008, communication in the seat of Wenchuan was partly revived. On the afternoon of May 14, 15 Special Operations Troops, along with relief supplies and communications gear, parachuted into inaccessible Mao County, northeast of Wenchuan.
rewrite: Continuous downpours and mudslides in Wenchuan County and surrounding regions severely hindered relief operations. When rescue work began on May 12, twenty helicopters were assigned to transport essential supplies like food and water, provide emergency assistance, evacuate casualties, and survey earthquake-damaged zones. By 5:37 PM CST on May 13, more than 15,600 military personnel and reservists from the Chengdu Military Region had been mobilized to assist in the worst-hit locations. From Yingxiu Town in Wenchuan, a commander indicated approximately 3,000 people had been located alive, but the condition of the remaining residents—about 9,000—was still unknown. Around 11:30 PM CST, 1,300 responders arrived at the epicenter, with an advance group of 300 reaching Wenchuan’s main administrative center. Communications there were partially restored by 12:17 PM CST on May 14, 2008. That same afternoon, fifteen Special Operations Troops parachuted into isolated Mao County, northeast of Wenchuan, carrying critical aid and communication equipment.

input: Following the defeat of the German empire in World War I and the abdication of the German Emperor, some revolutionary insurgents declared Alsace-Lorraine as an independent Republic, without preliminary referendum or vote. On 11 November 1918 (Armistice Day), communist insurgents proclaimed a "soviet government" in Strasbourg, following the example of Kurt Eisner in Munich as well as other German towns. French troops commanded by French general Henri Gouraud entered triumphantly in the city on 22 November. A major street of the city now bears the name of that date (Rue du 22 Novembre) which celebrates the entry of the French in the city. Viewing the massive cheering crowd gathered under the balcony of Strasbourg's town hall, French President Raymond Poincaré stated that "the plebiscite is done".
rewrite: After Germany's loss in World War I and the Kaiser's abdication, a faction of revolutionaries announced the independence of Alsace-Lorraine, doing so without any prior public vote. That same November 11th—Armistice Day—leftist rebels in Strasbourg declared a "soviet government," inspired by similar actions in Munich and elsewhere. Just days later, on November 22, French forces led by General Henri Gouraud marched victoriously into the city. This event is now commemorated by a major street named Rue du 22 Novembre. Witnessing the large, enthusiastic crowd from the city hall balcony, French President Raymond Poincaré remarked that the public's will had been clearly demonstrated.

input: Egyptian President Anwar Sadat had a mother who was a dark-skinned Nubian Sudanese woman and a father who was a lighter-skinned Egyptian. In response to an advertisement for an acting position, as a young man he said, "I am not white but I am not exactly black either. My blackness is tending to reddish".
rewrite: President Anwar Sadat of Egypt was born to a dark-skinned Sudanese Nubian mother and a lighter-skinned Egyptian father. Once, when applying for an acting role in his youth, he described his complexion by stating he was neither fully white nor black, but rather a reddish shade of dark.

input: Madonna released the Material Girl clothing line, which she designed with her daughter, Lourdes. The 1980s inspired clothing line, borrowed from Madonna's punk-girl style when she rose to fame in the 1980s, was released under the Macy's label. Madonna also opened a series of fitness centers around the world named Hard Candy Fitness. In November 2011, Madonna and MG Icon announced the release of a second fashion brand called Truth or Dare by Madonna to include footwear, underclothing, and accessories. She also directed her second feature film, W.E., a biographic about the affair between King Edward VIII and Wallis Simpson; it was co-written with Alek Keshishian. Critical and commercial response to the film was negative. Madonna contributed the ballad "Masterpiece" for the film's soundtrack, which won her a Golden Globe Award for Best Original Song.
rewrite: Madonna introduced a clothing collection called Material Girl, created in collaboration with her daughter Lourdes. This line, sold at Macy’s, draws inspiration from the punk-influenced fashion Madonna became known for in the 1980s. Separately, she launched a global chain of gyms under the name Hard Candy Fitness. Later, in November 2011, Madonna partnered with MG Icon to debut another brand, Truth or Dare by Madonna, offering items like shoes, lingerie, and accessories. That same year, she co-wrote and directed her second movie, W.E., a biographical drama focusing on King Edward VIII and Wallis Simpson. The film was poorly received by critics and audiences. However, her song “Masterpiece,” written for the soundtrack, earned her a Golden Globe for Best Original Song.

input: Operation Torch also served as a valuable training ground for Eisenhower's combat command skills; during the initial phase of Generalfeldmarschall Erwin Rommel's move into the Kasserine Pass, Eisenhower created some confusion in the ranks by some interference with the execution of battle plans by his subordinates. He also was initially indecisive in his removal of Lloyd Fredendall, commanding U.S. II Corps. He became more adroit in such matters in later campaigns. In February 1943, his authority was extended as commander of AFHQ across the Mediterranean basin to include the British Eighth Army, commanded by General Sir Bernard Montgomery. The Eighth Army had advanced across the Western Desert from the east and was ready for the start of the Tunisia Campaign. Eisenhower gained his fourth star and gave up command of ETOUSA to become commander of NATOUSA.
rewrite: Operation Torch provided Eisenhower with crucial experience in leading combat operations. Early on, when German forces advanced into the Kasserine Pass, his tendency to micromanage disrupted his officers' implementation of their plans, causing some disarray. He also hesitated before finally relieving General Lloyd Fredendall of command of the U.S. II Corps. These early missteps later gave way to greater skill in handling such command decisions. By February 1943, his role as head of the Allied Forces Headquarters was broadened to encompass the entire Mediterranean theater, which now included General Bernard Montgomery's British Eighth Army. This army had moved westward across the desert and was poised to begin the offensive in Tunisia. Eisenhower was promoted to the rank of full general, relinquishing his previous position to assume leadership of Allied forces in North Africa.

input: Both the vertical and dipole antennas are simple in construction and relatively inexpensive. The dipole antenna, which is the basis for most antenna designs, is a balanced component, with equal but opposite voltages and currents applied at its two terminals through a balanced transmission line (or to a coaxial transmission line through a so-called balun). The vertical antenna, on the other hand, is a monopole antenna. It is typically connected to the inner conductor of a coaxial transmission line (or a matching network); the shield of the transmission line is connected to ground. In this way, the ground (or any large conductive surface) plays the role of the second conductor of a dipole, thereby forming a complete circuit. Since monopole antennas rely on a conductive ground, a so-called grounding structure may be employed to provide a better ground contact to the earth or which itself acts as a ground plane to perform that function regardless of (or in absence of) an actual contact with the earth.
rewrite: Vertical and dipole antennas are straightforward to build and cost-effective. The dipole serves as a foundational model for many antennas, operating as a balanced system. It requires symmetrical voltages and currents at its two terminals, typically fed via a balanced transmission line or through a balun when using coaxial cable. In contrast, the vertical antenna is a monopole. It is usually linked to the center conductor of a coaxial line or a matching network, with the cable's outer shield grounded. This setup allows the ground or another large conducting surface to act as the missing half of a dipole, completing the electrical circuit. Because monopoles depend on a conductive ground, a grounding structure is often used. This structure ensures a reliable connection to the earth or functions as an artificial ground plane, even without direct soil contact.

input: In 2012, Madonna performed at Super Bowl XLVI halftime show, visualized by Cirque Du Soleil and Jamie King and featured special guests LMFAO, Nicki Minaj, M.I.A. and Cee Lo Green. It became the then most-watched Super Bowl halftime show in history with 114 million viewers, higher than the game itself. It was also revealed that the singer had signed a three-album deal with Interscope Records, who would act as the distributor in partnership with her 360 deal with Live Nation. Her twelfth studio album, MDNA, was released in March 2012 and saw collaboration with various producers, most notably with William Orbit again and Martin Solveig. The album was well received by music critics, with Priya Elan from NME calling it "a ridiculously enjoyable romp", citing its "psychotic, soul-bearing stuff" as "some of the most visceral stuff she's ever done." MDNA debuted at number one on the Billboard 200 and many other countries worldwide. Madonna surpassed Elvis Presley's record for the most number-one album by a solo artist in the UK. The lead single "Give Me All Your Luvin'", featuring guest vocals from Minaj and M.I.A., became Madonna's record-extending 38th top-ten hit on the Billboard Hot 100.
rewrite: During the 2012 Super Bowl halftime show, Madonna took the stage in a spectacle designed by Cirque Du Soleil and Jamie King, joined by performers LMFAO, Nicki Minaj, M.I.A., and Cee Lo Green. This event set a viewership record at the time, attracting 114 million spectators—more than the actual game. That same year, it was announced she entered a three-album agreement with Interscope Records, which would handle distribution as part of her broader 360 arrangement with Live Nation. March 2012 saw the release of her twelfth studio album, MDNA, created with producers including William Orbit and Martin Solveig. Critics praised the record; NME's Priya Elan described it as an exhilarating listen, noting its intense and personal moments as among her most powerful work. MDNA entered the Billboard 200 at the top spot and led charts globally, allowing Madonna to exceed Elvis Presley's UK record for most number-one albums by a solo act. Featuring Minaj and M.I.A., the first single "Give Me All Your Luvin'" marked her 38th top-ten entry on the Billboard Hot 100, extending her own achievement.

input: Genomes are more than the sum of an organism's genes and have traits that may be measured and studied without reference to the details of any particular genes and their products. Researchers compare traits such as chromosome number (karyotype), genome size, gene order, codon usage bias, and GC-content to determine what mechanisms could have produced the great variety of genomes that exist today (for recent overviews, see Brown 2002; Saccone and Pesole 2003; Benfey and Protopapas 2004; Gibson and Muse 2004; Reese 2004; Gregory 2005).
rewrite: An organism's genome encompasses more than just its total genes, possessing measurable characteristics that can be analyzed independently of specific genetic details. Scientists examine features like karyotype, overall size, gene arrangement, codon preference, and GC-content. By comparing these attributes, they aim to uncover the processes responsible for the vast diversity of genomes observed in modern organisms (as discussed in several contemporary reviews).

input: As of the census of 2000, there were 197,790 people, 84,549 households, and 43,627 families residing in the city. The population density was 3,292.6 people per square mile (1,271.3/km²). There were 92,282 housing units at an average density of 1,536.2 per square mile (593.1/km²). The racial makeup of the city was 38.3% White, 57.2% African American, 0.2% Native American, 1.3% Asian, 0.1% Pacific Islander, 1.5% from other races, and 1.5% from two or more races. Hispanic or Latino of any race were 2.6% of the population.
rewrite: According to the 2000 census, the city was home to 197,790 individuals, comprising 84,549 households and 43,627 families. Population density reached 3,292.6 per square mile. The 92,282 housing units averaged 1,536.2 per square mile. Racially, the population was 38.3% White, 57.2% African American, 1.3% Asian, 0.2% Native American, and 0.1% Pacific Islander, with 1.5% identifying as multiracial or from other races. Those of Hispanic or Latino origin accounted for 2.6% of residents.

input: The Times Magazine features columns touching on various subjects such as celebrities, fashion and beauty, food and drink, homes and gardens or simply writers' anecdotes. Notable contributors include Giles Coren, Food and Drink Writer of the Year in 2005 and Nadiya Hussain, winner of BBC's The Great British Bake Off.
rewrite: The Times Magazine includes diverse columns covering topics from celebrity culture and style to culinary arts and domestic life, with personal stories from writers. Prominent columnists feature Giles Coren, a top food writer, and Nadiya Hussain, a celebrated baking champion.

input: The unlicensed clone market has flourished following Nintendo's discontinuation of the NES. Some of the more exotic of these resulting systems have gone beyond the functionality of the original hardware and have included variations such as a portable system with a color LCD (e.g. PocketFami). Others have been produced with certain specialized markets in mind, such as an NES clone that functions as a rather primitive personal computer, which includes a keyboard and basic word processing software. These unauthorized clones have been helped by the invention of the so-called NES-on-a-chip.
rewrite: After Nintendo halted production of the NES, a market for unauthorized replica consoles emerged. Certain unusual models have expanded on the original console's capabilities, featuring designs like a handheld version with a color screen. Some clones target niche audiences, including one that operates as a simple computer, equipped with a keyboard and basic text editing programs. The development of integrated "NES-on-a-chip" technology has facilitated the creation of these unofficial systems.

input: Capacitors, especially ceramic capacitors, and older designs such as paper capacitors, can absorb sound waves resulting in a microphonic effect. Vibration moves the plates, causing the capacitance to vary, in turn inducing AC current. Some dielectrics also generate piezoelectricity. The resulting interference is especially problematic in audio applications, potentially causing feedback or unintended recording. In the reverse microphonic effect, the varying electric field between the capacitor plates exerts a physical force, moving them as a speaker. This can generate audible sound, but drains energy and stresses the dielectric and the electrolyte, if any.
rewrite: Capacitors, particularly ceramic types and vintage models like paper capacitors, can pick up acoustic vibrations, leading to microphonic behavior. This occurs as movement alters the distance between plates, changing capacitance and producing alternating current. Certain insulating materials may also create piezoelectric charges. Such interference is disruptive in sound equipment, risking feedback or unwanted noise capture. Conversely, applying an alternating voltage can make the plates vibrate like a speaker, producing sound. However, this consumes power and strains the internal materials, including any electrolyte present.

input: The early track record of the CIA was poor, with the agency unable to provide sufficient intelligence about the Soviet takeovers of Romania and Czechoslovakia, the Soviet blockade of Berlin, and the Soviet atomic bomb project. In particular, the agency failed to predict the Chinese entry into the Korean War with 300,000 troops. The famous double agent Kim Philby was the British liaison to American Central Intelligence. Through him the CIA coordinated hundreds of airdrops inside the iron curtain, all compromised by Philby. Arlington Hall, the nerve center of CIA cryptanalysisl was compromised by Bill Weisband, a Russian translator and Soviet spy. The CIA would reuse the tactic of dropping plant agents behind enemy lines by parachute again on China, and North Korea. This too would be fruitless.
rewrite: In its initial years, the CIA's performance was notably deficient. It did not gather adequate information regarding the Soviet Union's annexation of Romania and Czechoslovakia, its blockade of Berlin, or its development of nuclear weapons. A significant failure was its inability to foresee China's deployment of 300,000 soldiers into the Korean War. The agency's operations were severely undermined by infiltration. Kim Philby, a renowned British double agent serving as liaison to the CIA, betrayed hundreds of coordinated airdrops behind the Iron Curtain. Furthermore, Bill Weisband, a Soviet spy working as a Russian translator, compromised Arlington Hall, the central hub for codebreaking. Later attempts to parachute agents into China and North Korea proved similarly unsuccessful.

input: The terms used to define Greekness have varied throughout history but were never limited or completely identified with membership to a Greek state. By Western standards, the term Greeks has traditionally referred to any native speakers of the Greek language, whether Mycenaean, Byzantine or modern Greek. Byzantine Greeks called themselves Romioi and considered themselves the political heirs of Rome, but at least by the 12th century a growing number of those educated, deemed themselves the heirs of ancient Greece as well, although for most of the Greek speakers, "Hellene" still meant pagan. On the eve of the Fall of Constantinople the Last Emperor urged his soldiers to remember that they were the descendants of Greeks and Romans.
rewrite: The concept of Greek identity has shifted over time and has never been exclusively tied to citizenship in a Greek nation. From a Western perspective, "Greeks" has historically described those whose native language is Greek, spanning ancient to contemporary times. During the Byzantine era, these individuals identified as Romioi, viewing themselves as successors to the Roman Empire. However, by the 1100s, many educated Byzantines also began embracing their lineage from ancient Greece, even though most common Greek speakers still associated the term "Hellene" with pre-Christian beliefs. As Constantinople faced its final days, the final Emperor called upon his troops to recall their shared heritage from both Greek and Roman ancestors.

input: An exhibition game may also be used to settle a challenge, to provide professional entertainment, to promote the sport, or to raise money for charities. Several sports leagues hold all-star games to showcase their best players against each other, while other exhibitions games may pit participants from two different leagues or countries to unofficially determine who would be the best in the world. International competitions like the Olympic Games may also hold exhibition games as part of a demonstration sport.
rewrite: Exhibition matches serve various purposes, such as resolving a challenge, offering entertainment, promoting the sport, or fundraising for charity. All-star games highlight top athletes within a league, while other exhibitions feature competitors from different leagues or nations, offering an informal test of global supremacy. Events like the Olympics may also include demonstration sports as exhibition games.

input: If the data to be compressed is analog (such as a voltage that varies with time), quantization is employed to digitize it into numbers (normally integers). This is referred to as analog-to-digital (A/D) conversion. If the integers generated by quantization are 8 bits each, then the entire range of the analog signal is divided into 256 intervals and all the signal values within an interval are quantized to the same number. If 16-bit integers are generated, then the range of the analog signal is divided into 65,536 intervals.
rewrite: When compressing analog signals like fluctuating voltages, they must first be digitized through quantization, a process known as analog-to-digital conversion. This method assigns integer values to the continuous signal. With 8-bit quantization, the signal range is split into 256 segments, each represented by a single number. Using 16-bit integers increases the resolution, creating 65,536 distinct intervals for more precise representation.

input: Contract law covers obligations established by agreement (express or implied) between private parties. Generally, contract law in transactions involving the sale of goods has become highly standardized nationwide as a result of the widespread adoption of the Uniform Commercial Code. However, there is still significant diversity in the interpretation of other kinds of contracts, depending upon the extent to which a given state has codified its common law of contracts or adopted portions of the Restatement (Second) of Contracts.
rewrite: Contract law governs duties that arise from mutual agreements, whether stated or understood. While the sale of goods is largely consistent across the country due to the Uniform Commercial Code, other agreements vary widely in their legal treatment. This diversity stems from differences in how states have integrated common law principles or adopted guidelines from the Restatement (Second) of Contracts.

input: The console was first officially announced at E3 2005, and was released at the end of 2006. It was the first console to use Blu-ray Disc as its primary storage medium. The console was the first PlayStation to integrate social gaming services, included it being the first to introduce Sony's social gaming service, PlayStation Network, and its remote connectivity with PlayStation Portable and PlayStation Vita, being able to remote control the console from the devices. In September 2009, the Slim model of the PlayStation 3 was released, being lighter and thinner than the original version, which notably featured a redesigned logo and marketing design, as well as a minor start-up change in software. A Super Slim variation was then released in late 2012, further refining and redesigning the console. As of March 2016, PlayStation 3 has sold 85 million units worldwide. Its successor, the PlayStation 4, was released later in November 2013.
rewrite: Initially unveiled during E3 in 2005, this gaming system launched globally in late 2006. It pioneered the use of Blu-ray Disc technology for its main storage format. This model marked Sony's inaugural foray into integrated online social gaming, introducing the PlayStation Network. It also offered unique connectivity, allowing users to operate it remotely via the PlayStation Portable and Vita handhelds. A redesigned Slim iteration debuted in September 2009, notable for its reduced size and weight, an updated logo, altered marketing aesthetics, and slight software modifications upon booting. An even more compact Super Slim version followed in 2012. Global sales reached approximately 85 million units by March 2016. It was eventually succeeded by the PlayStation 4, which arrived in November 2013.

input: Estonia's land border with Latvia runs 267 kilometers; the Russian border runs 290 kilometers. From 1920 to 1945, Estonia's border with Russia, set by the 1920 Tartu Peace Treaty, extended beyond the Narva River in the northeast and beyond the town of Pechory (Petseri) in the southeast. This territory, amounting to some 2,300 square kilometres (888 sq mi), was incorporated into Russia by Stalin at the end of World War II. For this reason the borders between Estonia and Russia are still not defined.
rewrite: Estonia shares a 267-kilometer frontier with Latvia and a 290-kilometer one with Russia. Historically, under the 1920 Tartu Treaty, Estonia's eastern boundary included areas northeast of the Narva River and southeast of Pechory. This approximately 2,300-square-kilometer region was annexed by the Soviet Union under Stalin following WWII. Consequently, the formal demarcation between Estonia and Russia remains unresolved.

input: There is confusion currently as to the name of the eldest Vinaccia luthier who first ran the shop. His name has been put forth as Gennaro Vinaccia (active c. 1710 to c. 1788) and Nic. Vinaccia. His son Antonio Vinaccia was active c. 1734 to c. 1796. An early extant example of a mandolin is one built by Antonio Vinaccia in 1759, which resides at the University of Edinburgh. Another is by Giuseppe Vinaccia, built in 1893, is also at the University of Edinburgh. The earliest extant mandolin was built in 1744 by Antonio's son, Gaetano Vinaccia. It resides in the Conservatoire Royal de Musique in Brussels, Belgium.
rewrite: The identity of the senior Vinaccia luthier who originally managed the workshop remains unclear, with proposals including both Gennaro Vinaccia (working approximately 1710–1788) and Nic. Vinaccia. His successor, Antonio Vinaccia, was active from around 1734 to 1796. A mandolin he crafted in 1759, held at the University of Edinburgh, is an early surviving model. That institution also houses a later 1893 instrument by Giuseppe Vinaccia. However, the oldest known mandolin in existence was made in 1744 by Antonio's son, Gaetano Vinaccia, and is kept at the Conservatoire Royal de Musique in Brussels.

input: Within hours of the UK and France declaring war on Germany on 3 September 1939, the RAF bombed German warships along the German coast at Wilhelmshaven. Thereafter bombing operations were against ports and shipping and propaganda leaflet drops. Operations were planned to minimize civilian casualties. From 15 May 1940 – the day after the Luftwaffe destroyed the centre of Rotterdam – the RAF also carried out operations east of the Rhine, attacking industrial and transportation targets. Operations were carried out every night thereafter.
rewrite: Shortly after Britain and France entered the conflict with Germany on September 3, 1939, British aircraft struck German naval vessels near Wilhelmshaven. Initial actions focused on coastal targets and dispersing informational leaflets, with care taken to avoid harming non-combatants. Following the German bombing of Rotterdam's center on May 14, 1940, the RAF expanded its nightly campaign to include strategic sites such as factories and railways located east of the Rhine River.

input: John's position in France was considerably strengthened by the victory at Mirebeau, but John's treatment of his new prisoners and of his ally, William de Roches, quickly undermined these gains. De Roches was a powerful Anjou noble, but John largely ignored him, causing considerable offence, whilst the king kept the rebel leaders in such bad conditions that twenty-two of them died. At this time most of the regional nobility were closely linked through kinship, and this behaviour towards their relatives was regarded as unacceptable. William de Roches and other of John's regional allies in Anjou and Brittany deserted him in favour of Philip, and Brittany rose in fresh revolt. John's financial situation was tenuous: once factors such as the comparative military costs of materiel and soldiers were taken into account, Philip enjoyed a considerable, although not overwhelming, advantage of resources over John.[nb 6]
rewrite: John's standing in France was greatly improved following the success at Mirebeau. However, his subsequent actions rapidly eroded this advantage. He mistreated the captured rebel leaders so severely that many perished, and he snubbed his key ally, William de Roches, a prominent Anjou lord. Given the extensive familial connections among the local aristocracy, this cruel handling of their kin was seen as deeply dishonorable. Consequently, de Roches and other supporters from Anjou and Brittany abandoned John, aligning with King Philip instead, and Brittany erupted in new rebellion. Financially, John was also in a precarious state. After accounting for the expenses of warfare, Philip held a significant, though not absolute, resource superiority.

input: The Wagner tuba, a modified member of the horn family, appears in Richard Wagner's cycle Der Ring des Nibelungen and several other works by Strauss, Béla Bartók, and others; it has a prominent role in Anton Bruckner's Symphony No. 7 in E Major. Cornets appear in Pyotr Ilyich Tchaikovsky's ballet Swan Lake, Claude Debussy's La Mer, and several orchestral works by Hector Berlioz. Unless these instruments are played by members doubling on another instrument (for example, a trombone player changing to euphonium for a certain passage), orchestras will use freelance musicians to augment their regular rosters.
rewrite: The Wagner tuba, an adapted brass instrument related to the horn, features notably in Wagner's *Der Ring des Nibelungen*, as well as pieces by Strauss, Bartók, and especially in Bruckner's Seventh Symphony. Cornets are used in compositions such as Tchaikovsky's *Swan Lake*, Debussy's *La Mer*, and various works by Berlioz.
