If orchestra members do not switch to these from their primary instruments, outside specialists are often hired temporarily to fill these parts.

input: In the British West Indian islands (and also in the United States), the majority of enslaved blacks brought across the Atlantic came from West Africa (roughly between modern Senegal and Ghana). Very little of Bermuda's original black emigration came from this area. The first blacks to arrive in Bermuda in any numbers were free blacks from Spanish-speaking areas of the West Indies, and most of the remainder were recently enslaved Africans captured from the Spanish and Portuguese. As Spain and Portugal sourced most of their slaves from South-West Africa (the Portuguese through ports in modern-day Angola; the Spanish purchased most of their African slaves from Portuguese traders, and from Arabs whose slave trading was centred in Zanzibar). Genetic studies have consequently shown that the African ancestry of black Bermudians (other than those resulting from recent immigration from the British West Indian islands) is largely from the a band across southern Africa, from Angola to Mozambique, which is similar to what is revealed in Latin America, but distinctly different from the blacks of the West Indies and the United States.
rewrite: In the British Caribbean territories and the United States, most enslaved Africans transported during the Atlantic slave trade originated from West Africa, particularly the region spanning present-day Senegal to Ghana. Bermuda’s early black population, however, largely did not derive from this source. The initial significant group of black arrivals in Bermuda consisted of free individuals from Spanish-speaking Caribbean islands, with most others being recently enslaved Africans taken from Spanish and Portuguese vessels. Since Spain and Portugal primarily obtained enslaved people from South-West Africa—the Portuguese via ports in what is now Angola, and the Spanish mainly buying from Portuguese traders and Arab slavers based in Zanzibar—genetic research indicates that the African lineage of black Bermudians (excluding recent migrants from the British Caribbean) is predominantly drawn from a broad swath of southern Africa, from Angola to Mozambique. This genetic profile resembles patterns found in Latin America but stands in clear contrast to those of black communities in the Caribbean and the United States.

input: On October 25, 1989, the Supreme Soviet voted to eliminate special seats for the Communist Party and other official organizations in national and local elections, responding to sharp popular criticism that such reserved slots were undemocratic. After vigorous debate, the 542-member Supreme Soviet passed the measure 254-85 (with 36 abstentions). The decision required a constitutional amendment, ratified by the full congress, which met December 12–25. It also passed measures that would allow direct elections for presidents of each of the 15 constituent republics. Gorbachev strongly opposed such a move during debate but was defeated.
rewrite: On October 25, 1989, the Supreme Soviet responded to widespread public condemnation that reserved legislative positions were unfair by voting to remove them for the Communist Party and similar groups in future elections. Following intense discussion, the body approved the resolution with 254 votes in favor, 85 against, and 36 abstentions. This change necessitated a constitutional revision, later endorsed by the full congress in December. Additionally, it approved the establishment of direct presidential elections in all 15 republics, a proposal Gorbachev argued against during deliberations but failed to stop.

input: Social predation offers the possibility of predators to kill creatures larger than those that members of the species could overpower singly. Lions, hyenas, wolves, dholes, African wild dogs, and piranhas can kill large herbivores that single animals of the same species usually don't dispatch. Social predation allows some animals to organize hunts of creatures that would easily escape a single predator; thus chimpanzees can prey upon colobus monkeys, and Harris's hawks can cut off all possible escapes for a doomed rabbit. Extreme specialization of roles is evident in some hunting that requires co-operation between predators of very different species: humans with the aid of falcons or dogs, or fishing with cormorants. Social predation is often very complex behavior, and not all social creatures (for example, domestic cats) perform it. Even without complex intelligence but instinct alone, some ant species can destroy much larger creatures.
rewrite: Group hunting enables predators to take down prey that would be too formidable for an individual. Species such as lions, hyenas, wolves, dholes, African wild dogs, and piranhas can collectively overcome large herbivores that a solitary member could not. This collaborative approach also permits the capture of agile animals; for instance, chimpanzees can catch colobus monkeys, and Harris’s hawks can trap rabbits by blocking every escape route. Sometimes, cooperation extends across species, as seen when humans hunt alongside falcons or dogs, or use cormorants for fishing, demonstrating specialized roles. Not all social animals, like house cats, engage in such behavior. Even with simple instinct rather than advanced intellect, certain ants can overwhelm foes many times their size, showing that coordinated predation can range from intricate strategies to basic collective action.

input: The task of organizing the U.S. Army commenced in 1775. In the first one hundred years of its existence, the United States Army was maintained as a small peacetime force to man permanent forts and perform other non-wartime duties such as engineering and construction works. During times of war, the U.S. Army was augmented by the much larger United States Volunteers which were raised independently by various state governments. States also maintained full-time militias which could also be called into the service of the army.
rewrite: The U.S. Army began forming in 1775. For its initial century, it remained a compact force during peace, staffing forts and handling duties like engineering. In wartime, it was supplemented by the significantly larger U.S. Volunteers, enlisted separately by state governments. Additionally, states operated their own permanent militias that could be mobilized to support the army.

input: From January 18–20, 2010 a national conference on Tibet and areas inhabited by Tibetans in Sichuan, Yunnan, Gansu and Qinghai was held in China and a substantial plan to improve development of the areas was announced. The conference was attended by General secretary Hu Jintao, Wu Bangguo, Wen Jiabao, Jia Qinglin, Li Changchun, Xi Jinping, Li Keqiang, He Guoqiang and Zhou Yongkang, all members of CPC Politburo Standing Committee signaling the commitment of senior Chinese leaders to development of Tibet and ethnic Tibetan areas. The plan calls for improvement of rural Tibetan income to national standards by 2020 and free education for all rural Tibetan children. China has invested 310 billion yuan (about 45.6 billion U.S. dollars) in Tibet since 2001. "Tibet's GDP was expected to reach 43.7 billion yuan in 2009, up 170 percent from that in 2000 and posting an annual growth of 12.3 percent over the past nine years."
rewrite: A major national conference focusing on Tibet and Tibetan-populated regions within Sichuan, Yunnan, Gansu, and Qinghai provinces convened in China from January 18 to 20, 2010. During this meeting, a comprehensive strategy to advance progress in these areas was unveiled. Demonstrating high-level dedication, the entire Politburo Standing Committee of the Communist Party of China was present, including Hu Jintao, Wu Bangguo, Wen Jiabao, Jia Qinglin, Li Changchun, Xi Jinping, Li Keqiang, He Guoqiang, and Zhou Yongkang. Key objectives of the strategy include raising the average income of rural Tibetan residents to match national levels by the year 2020 and providing tuition-free schooling for all children in these rural areas. Since 2001, national investment in Tibet has totaled 310 billion yuan (approximately 45.6 billion U.S. dollars). Projections for 2009 indicated Tibet's gross domestic product would hit 43.7 billion yuan, reflecting a 170 percent increase since 2000 and an average yearly growth rate of 12.3 percent over that nine-year period.

input: The Saint Helena Constitution took effect in 1989 and provided that the island would be governed by a Governor and Commander-in-Chief, and an elected Executive and Legislative Council. In 2002, the British Overseas Territories Act 2002 granted full British citizenship to the islanders, and renamed the Dependent Territories (including Saint Helena) the British Overseas Territories. In 2009, Saint Helena and its two territories received equal status under a new constitution, and the British Overseas Territory was renamed Saint Helena, Ascension and Tristan da Cunha.
rewrite: The constitution of Saint Helena was enacted in 1989, establishing a government led by a Governor and Commander-in-Chief alongside elected councils. In 2002, the British Overseas Territories Act conferred full citizenship on its inhabitants and reclassified its dependent territories. By 2009, a revised constitution granted equivalent standing to Saint Helena and its associated islands, leading to the territory being officially designated as Saint Helena, Ascension and Tristan da Cunha.

input: About 98% of Antarctica is covered by the Antarctic ice sheet, a sheet of ice averaging at least 1.6 km (1.0 mi) thick. The continent has about 90% of the world's ice (and thereby about 70% of the world's fresh water). If all of this ice were melted, sea levels would rise about 60 m (200 ft). In most of the interior of the continent, precipitation is very low, down to 20 mm (0.8 in) per year; in a few "blue ice" areas precipitation is lower than mass loss by sublimation and so the local mass balance is negative. In the dry valleys, the same effect occurs over a rock base, leading to a desiccated landscape.
rewrite: Nearly the entire Antarctic landmass, roughly 98 percent, lies beneath a vast ice sheet with an average thickness exceeding 1.6 kilometers. This single sheet holds approximately 90% of the planet's glacial ice, equating to nearly 70% of all fresh water. Its complete melting would cause global sea levels to increase by an estimated 60 meters. Precipitation across the inland regions is extremely scarce, often less than 20 millimeters annually. Certain "blue ice" zones experience even greater net ice loss through sublimation than they gain from snowfall, creating a negative mass balance. Similarly, in the dry valleys, this sublimation process over bare ground results in an intensely arid and barren terrain.

input: A database management system (DBMS) is a computer software application that interacts with the user, other applications, and the database itself to capture and analyze data. A general-purpose DBMS is designed to allow the definition, creation, querying, update, and administration of databases. Well-known DBMSs include MySQL, PostgreSQL, Microsoft SQL Server, Oracle, Sybase, SAP HANA, and IBM DB2. A database is not generally portable across different DBMSs, but different DBMS can interoperate by using standards such as SQL and ODBC or JDBC to allow a single application to work with more than one DBMS. Database management systems are often classified according to the database model that they support; the most popular database systems since the 1980s have all supported the relational model as represented by the SQL language.[disputed – discuss] Sometimes a DBMS is loosely referred to as a 'database'.
rewrite: A database management system (DBMS) is a software tool that enables users and other programs to store and examine information within a database. This general-purpose software facilitates the setup, maintenance, querying, modification, and overall oversight of these data repositories. Common examples are MySQL, PostgreSQL, Microsoft SQL Server, Oracle, and IBM DB2. Typically, a database created in one system cannot be directly transferred to another. However, interoperability is possible through standardized interfaces like SQL, ODBC, or JDBC, letting one application connect to various DBMS platforms. These systems are frequently categorized by their underlying data structure, with the relational model—commonly accessed via SQL—being the dominant type since the 1980s. Informally, the term "database" is sometimes used to refer to the DBMS itself.

input: In 1961, writer-editor Stan Lee revolutionized superhero comics by introducing superheroes designed to appeal to more all-ages readers than the predominantly child audiences of the medium. Modern Marvel's first superhero team, the titular stars of The Fantastic Four #1 (Nov. 1961), broke convention with other comic book archetypes of the time by squabbling, holding grudges both deep and petty, and eschewing anonymity or secret identities in favor of celebrity status. Subsequently, Marvel comics developed a reputation for focusing on characterization and adult issues to a greater extent than most superhero comics before them, a quality which the new generation of older readers appreciated. This applied to The Amazing Spider-Man title in particular, which turned out to be Marvel's most successful book. Its young hero suffered from self-doubt and mundane problems like any other teenager, something readers could identify with.
rewrite: In 1961, Stan Lee, a writer and editor, transformed the landscape of superhero comics by creating characters intended to attract a broader, all-ages audience, moving beyond the genre's traditional focus on children. The debut of Marvel's initial superhero team in *The Fantastic Four* #1 that November defied the norms of contemporary comics. These characters argued, harbored significant and trivial resentments, and embraced public fame over hidden alter egos. This approach led Marvel to become known for emphasizing deeper character development and more mature themes compared to earlier superhero stories, a shift welcomed by an emerging cohort of older fans. This was especially true for *The Amazing Spider-Man*, Marvel's top-selling series, whose adolescent hero grappled with insecurity and everyday teenage troubles, allowing readers to see their own struggles reflected.

input: There are several other important art museums in Montevideo. The National Museum of Visual Arts in Parque Rodó has Uruguay's largest collection of paintings. The Juan Manuel Blanes Museum was founded in 1930, the 100th anniversary of the first Constitution of Uruguay, significant with regard to the fact that Juan Manuel Blanes painted Uruguayan patriotic themes. In back of the museum is a beautiful Japanese Garden with a pond where there are over a hundred carp. The Museo de Historia del Arte, located in the Palacio Municipal, features replicas of ancient monuments and exhibits a varied collection of artifacts from Egypt, Mesopotamia, Persia, Greece, Rome and Native American cultures including local finds of the pre-Columbian period. The Museo Municipal Precolombino y Colonial, in the Ciudad Vieja, has preserved collections of the archaeological finds from excavations carried out by Uruguayan archaeologist Antonio Taddei. These antiquaries are exhibits of pre-Columbian art of Latin America, painting and sculpture from the 17th and 18th century mostly from Mexico, Peru and Brazil. The Museo de Arte Contempo has small but impressive exhibits of modern Uruguayan painting and sculpture.
rewrite: Montevideo hosts numerous significant art institutions beyond its most famous ones. The nation's most extensive painting collection is housed at the National Museum of Visual Arts within Parque Rodó. Founded in 1930 to mark a century since Uruguay's inaugural constitution, the Juan Manuel Blanes Museum honors an artist renowned for nationalistic subjects. Behind this building lies a serene Japanese Garden containing a pond stocked with hundreds of carp. Housed in the Palacio Municipal, the Museo de Historia del Arte displays reproductions of ancient structures and original artifacts from early civilizations, including Egyptian, Mesopotamian, Greek, Roman, and pre-Columbian societies. In the Ciudad Vieja, the Museo Municipal Precolombino y Colonial safeguards archaeological materials recovered by scholar Antonio Taddei, showcasing ancient Latin American works alongside colonial-era art from several countries. For modern works, the Museo de Arte Contempo presents a concise yet striking selection of Uruguayan painting and sculpture.

input: It is common to classify wood as either softwood or hardwood. The wood from conifers (e.g. pine) is called softwood, and the wood from dicotyledons (usually broad-leaved trees, e.g. oak) is called hardwood. These names are a bit misleading, as hardwoods are not necessarily hard, and softwoods are not necessarily soft. The well-known balsa (a hardwood) is actually softer than any commercial softwood. Conversely, some softwoods (e.g. yew) are harder than many hardwoods.
rewrite: Wood is typically categorized as either softwood or hardwood. Softwoods come from coniferous trees like pine, while hardwoods originate from broad-leaved dicots such as oak. However, these labels can be deceptive, since not all hardwoods are hard, nor are all softwoods soft. For instance, balsa, a hardwood, is notably softer than any commercial softwood. Meanwhile, certain softwoods like yew are harder than many hardwoods.

input: Asthma as a result of (or worsened by) workplace exposures, is a commonly reported occupational disease. Many cases however are not reported or recognized as such. It is estimated that 5–25% of asthma cases in adults are work–related. A few hundred different agents have been implicated with the most common being: isocyanates, grain and wood dust, colophony, soldering flux, latex, animals, and aldehydes. The employment associated with the highest risk of problems include: those who spray paint, bakers and those who process food, nurses, chemical workers, those who work with animals, welders, hairdressers and timber workers.
rewrite: Asthma triggered or aggravated by conditions at work is a frequent occupational illness, yet it often goes unreported or undiagnosed. Experts believe between 5 and 25 percent of adult asthma cases are linked to job environments. Hundreds of substances can be responsible, with typical culprits including isocyanates, various dusts, latex, animal dander, and aldehydes. Professions at greatest risk encompass spray painters, food industry bakers, nurses, chemical industry employees, animal handlers, welders, hairdressers, and woodworkers.

input: The Victorian era of the United Kingdom was the period of Queen Victoria's reign from June 1837 to January 1901. This was a long period of prosperity for the British people, as profits gained from the overseas British Empire, as well as from industrial improvements at home, allowed a large, educated middle class to develop. Some scholars would extend the beginning of the period—as defined by a variety of sensibilities and political games that have come to be associated with the Victorians—back five years to the passage of the Reform Act 1832.
rewrite: Queen Victoria ruled the United Kingdom from 1837 until her death in 1901. This lengthy epoch was marked by significant national wealth, fueled by both the expansive British Empire abroad and domestic industrial progress. Such economic success fostered the growth of a sizable and educated middle class. Certain academics, however, date the start of this age to 1832, linking it to the cultural attitudes and political shifts symbolized by the Reform Act of that year.

input: Except for the five species of monotremes (egg-laying mammals), all modern mammals give birth to live young. Most mammals, including the six most species-rich orders, belong to the placental group. The three largest orders in numbers, are first Rodentia: mice, rats, porcupines, beavers, capybaras, and other gnawing mammals; then Chiroptera: bats; and then Soricomorpha: shrews, moles and solenodons. The next three orders, depending on the biological classification scheme used, are the Primates including the humans; the Cetartiodactyla including the whales and the even-toed hoofed mammals; and the Carnivora, that is, cats, dogs, weasels, bears, seals, and their relatives.
rewrite: All contemporary mammals, aside from the five monotreme species that lay eggs, are viviparous, delivering live offspring. The majority, encompassing the six most diverse orders, are placentals. The most populous orders are Rodentia (gnawing animals like rodents and beavers), followed by Chiroptera (bats), and Soricomorpha (shrews and moles). Subsequently, depending on the taxonomic system, come Primates (including humans), Cetartiodactyla (whales and even-toed ungulates), and Carnivora (such as cats, dogs, bears, and seals).

input: In the 17th century, the Somers Isles Company suppressed shipbuilding, as it needed Bermudians to farm to generate income from the land. Agricultural production met with limited success, however. The Bermuda cedar boxes used to ship tobacco to England were reportedly worth more than their contents.[citation needed] The colony of Virginia far surpassed Bermuda in both quality and quantity of tobacco produced. Bermudians began to turn to maritime trades relatively early in the 17th century, but the Somers Isles Company used all its authority to suppress turning away from agriculture. This interference led to the islanders demanding, and receiving, the revocation of the Company's charter in 1684, and the Company was dissolved.
rewrite: During the 1600s, the Somers Isles Company restricted boat construction in Bermuda, insisting locals focus on farming to profit from the land. This agricultural effort proved largely unsuccessful. Notably, the cedar containers that held Bermuda’s tobacco for export to England were said to have greater value than the tobacco itself. Virginia’s colony produced tobacco of higher quality and in larger amounts. Bermudians had started pursuing sea-based trades earlier that century, but the Company exerted its power to prevent any shift away from farming. Such control eventually prompted islanders to successfully demand the Company’s charter be withdrawn in 1684, leading to its termination.

input: In the mid-19th century, Serbian (led by self-taught writer and folklorist Vuk Stefanović Karadžić) and most Croatian writers and linguists (represented by the Illyrian movement and led by Ljudevit Gaj and Đuro Daničić), proposed the use of the most widespread dialect, Shtokavian, as the base for their common standard language. Karadžić standardised the Serbian Cyrillic alphabet, and Gaj and Daničić standardized the Croatian Latin alphabet, on the basis of vernacular speech phonemes and the principle of phonological spelling. In 1850 Serbian and Croatian writers and linguists signed the Vienna Literary Agreement, declaring their intention to create a unified standard. Thus a complex bi-variant language appeared, which the Serbs officially called "Serbo-Croatian" or "Serbian or Croatian" and the Croats "Croato-Serbian", or "Croatian or Serbian". Yet, in practice, the variants of the conceived common literary language served as different literary variants, chiefly differing in lexical inventory and stylistic devices. The common phrase describing this situation was that Serbo-Croatian or "Croatian or Serbian" was a single language. During the Austro-Hungarian occupation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the language of all three nations was called "Bosnian" until the death of administrator von Kállay in 1907, at which point the name was changed to "Serbo-Croatian".
rewrite: During the middle of the 1800s, Serbian intellectuals, most notably the autodidact Vuk Stefanović Karadžić, along with the majority of Croatian authors and language scholars from the Illyrian movement, spearheaded by Ljudevit Gaj and Đuro Daničić, advocated for adopting the most commonly spoken Shtokavian dialect as the foundation for a shared literary language. Karadžić reformed the Serbian Cyrillic script, while Gaj and Daničić codified the Croatian Latin alphabet, both grounding their work in the sounds of everyday speech and adhering to phonetic spelling rules. This cooperation culminated in the 1850 Vienna Literary Agreement, where figures from both groups pledged to forge a unified standard. The result was a intricate language with two main forms, officially termed "Serbo-Croatian" or "Serbian or Croatian" by Serbs, and "Croato-Serbian" or "Croatian or Serbian" by Croats. In actual usage, however, these envisioned common standards functioned as distinct literary versions, primarily varying in word choice and stylistic expression. It was often stated that Serbo-Croatian, or "Croatian or Serbian," constituted one language. Under Austro-Hungarian rule in Bosnia and Herzegovina, the tongue shared by the three peoples was designated "Bosnian" until 1907, following the passing of administrator von Kállay, when its official name shifted to "Serbo-Croatian."

input: One of the most important developments that the Enlightenment era brought to the discipline of science was its popularization. An increasingly literate population seeking knowledge and education in both the arts and the sciences drove the expansion of print culture and the dissemination of scientific learning. The new literate population was due to a high rise in the availability of food. This enabled many people to rise out of poverty, and instead of paying more for food, they had money for education. Popularization was generally part of an overarching Enlightenment ideal that endeavoured "to make information available to the greatest number of people." As public interest in natural philosophy grew during the 18th century, public lecture courses and the publication of popular texts opened up new roads to money and fame for amateurs and scientists who remained on the periphery of universities and academies. More formal works included explanations of scientific theories for individuals lacking the educational background to comprehend the original scientific text. Sir Isaac Newton's celebrated Philosophiae Naturalis Principia Mathematica was published in Latin and remained inaccessible to readers without education in the classics until Enlightenment writers began to translate and analyze the text in the vernacular.
rewrite: A key contribution of the Enlightenment to science was its widespread dissemination among the public. Growing literacy rates, fueled by a population eager to learn about both the arts and sciences, spurred a boom in printing and the circulation of scientific ideas. This rise in literacy was itself made possible by greater food security, which lifted many from poverty and freed up resources for schooling instead of mere survival. This drive to share knowledge aligned with a core Enlightenment principle: to spread information as broadly as possible. The 18th century saw surging public curiosity about natural philosophy, creating opportunities through public lectures and popular publications. These avenues offered both financial reward and recognition for independent scholars and scientists operating outside formal academic institutions. To reach eager but less-trained audiences, more formal works began to include clear explanations of complex theories. For instance, Isaac Newton's seminal *Principia Mathematica* was originally published in Latin, limiting its readership to the classically educated. It was only through the efforts of Enlightenment thinkers who translated and interpreted it into common languages that its ideas became widely accessible.

input: By design, it is difficult to insert a USB plug into its receptacle incorrectly. The USB specification states that the required USB icon must be embossed on the "topside" of the USB plug, which "...provides easy user recognition and facilitates alignment during the mating process." The specification also shows that the "recommended" "Manufacturer's logo" ("engraved" on the diagram but not specified in the text) is on the opposite side of the USB icon. The specification further states, "The USB Icon is also located adjacent to each receptacle. Receptacles should be oriented to allow the icon on the plug to be visible during the mating process." However, the specification does not consider the height of the device compared to the eye level height of the user, so the side of the cable that is "visible" when mated to a computer on a desk can depend on whether the user is standing or kneeling.
rewrite: USB connectors are intentionally designed to prevent incorrect insertion. According to the official standards, the USB symbol must be imprinted on the upper surface of the plug to help users identify the correct orientation and align it properly when connecting. Opposite this symbol, the manufacturer's logo is typically placed, as indicated in design diagrams. The guidelines also specify that the matching port should display the same icon nearby, positioned so it remains in view while plugging in the cable. Despite these instructions, the standard does not account for the user’s physical position relative to the device. Whether someone is standing or crouching can change which side of the cable is visible when connecting to a computer on a desk, potentially affecting ease of use.

input: Motorcycles are also commonly used, particularly in locations that a car may not be able to reach, to control potential public order situations involving meetings of motorcyclists and often in escort duties where motorcycle police officers can quickly clear a path for escorted vehicles. Bicycle patrols are used in some areas because they allow for more open interaction with the public. In addition, their quieter operation can facilitate approaching suspects unawares and can help in pursuing them attempting to escape on foot.
rewrite: Motorcycles are frequently employed in law enforcement, especially for accessing areas inaccessible to cars. They help manage gatherings of bikers and perform escort roles by swiftly creating routes for protected convoys. Bicycles serve in certain regions, enabling officers to engage more freely with communities. Their silent movement also allows for stealthy approaches to unsuspecting individuals and aids in chasing suspects fleeing on foot.

input: The exact causes for the development of a particular sexual orientation have yet to be established. To date, a lot of research has been conducted to determine the influence of genetics, hormonal action, development dynamics, social and cultural influences—which has led many to think that biology and environment factors play a complex role in forming it. It was once thought that homosexuality was the result of faulty psychological development, resulting from childhood experiences and troubled relationships, including childhood sexual abuse. It has been found that this was based on prejudice and misinformation.
rewrite: The specific origins of sexual orientation remain unclear. Extensive studies have explored potential genetic, hormonal, developmental, social, and cultural factors, leading to a prevailing view that it arises from intricate biological and environmental interactions. Earlier theories, which incorrectly attributed homosexuality to psychological disturbances caused by childhood experiences or abuse, have been discredited as rooted in bias and inaccurate information.

input: Director Sima Urale is an award-winning filmmaker. Urale's short film O Tamaiti won the prestigious Best Short Film at the Venice Film Festival in 1996. Her first feature film Apron Strings opened the 2008 NZ International Film Festival. The feature film Siones Wedding, co-written by Oscar Kightley, was financially successful following premieres in Auckland and Apia. The 2011 film The Orator was the first ever fully Samoan film, shot in Samoa in the Samoan language with a Samoan cast telling a uniquely Samoan story. Written and directed by Tusi Tamasese, it received much critical acclaim and attention at film festivals throughout the world.
rewrite: Sima Urale is an acclaimed director whose short film O Tamaiti earned top honors for short film at the Venice Film Festival in 1996. Her debut feature, Apron Strings, was the opening presentation at the 2008 New Zealand International Film Festival. She also co-wrote the commercially successful Siones Wedding. In 2011, The Orator, created by Tusi Tamasese, made history as the first complete Samoan-language feature. Filmed in Samoa with a local cast and narrative, it gained significant international praise at festivals worldwide.

input: Bell's patent 174,465, was issued to Bell on March 7, 1876, by the U.S. Patent Office. Bell's patent covered "the method of, and apparatus for, transmitting vocal or other sounds telegraphically ... by causing electrical undulations, similar in form to the vibrations of the air accompanying the said vocal or other sound" [N 16] Bell returned to Boston the same day and the next day resumed work, drawing in his notebook a diagram similar to that in Gray's patent caveat.
rewrite: On March 7, 1876, the U.S. Patent Office granted Alexander Bell patent number 174,465. This patent protected a technique and device for sending sounds like speech over telegraph lines. It achieved this by creating electrical waves that mirrored the air vibrations of the original sounds. Bell traveled back to Boston that day and continued his work the following day, sketching a design in his notebook comparable to one in Gray's earlier patent filing.

input: The phrase "[A] hedge or wall of separation between the garden of the church and the wilderness of the world" was first used by Baptist theologian Roger Williams, the founder of the colony of Rhode Island, in his 1644 book The Bloody Tenent of Persecution. The phrase was later used by Thomas Jefferson as a description of the First Amendment and its restriction on the legislative branch of the federal government, in an 1802 letter to the Danbury Baptists (a religious minority concerned about the dominant position of the Congregationalist church in Connecticut):
rewrite: Baptist theologian Roger Williams, who established Rhode Island, originally coined the expression "a hedge or wall of separation between the garden of the church and the wilderness of the world" in his 1644 work. Later, Thomas Jefferson referenced this metaphor in an 1802 letter. He employed it to characterize the First Amendment's limits on federal legislative power, addressing the Danbury Baptists, who were uneasy about the Congregationalist church's sway in Connecticut.

input: The City of Charleston Police Department, with a total of 452 sworn officers, 137 civilians, and 27 reserve police officers, is South Carolina's largest police department. Their procedures on cracking down on drug use and gang violence in the city are used as models to other cities to do the same.[citation needed] According to the final 2005 FBI Crime Reports, Charleston crime level is worse than the national average in almost every major category. Greg Mullen, the former Deputy Chief of the Virginia Beach, Virginia Police Department, serves as the current Chief of the Charleston Police Department. The former Charleston police chief was Reuben Greenberg, who resigned August 12, 2005. Greenberg was credited with creating a polite police force that kept police brutality well in check, even as it developed a visible presence in community policing and a significant reduction in crime rates.
rewrite: With 452 sworn personnel, 137 civilian staff, and 27 reserve officers, the Charleston Police Department is the largest such force in South Carolina. Its strategies for combating narcotics and gang activity are frequently cited as examples for other municipalities. However, FBI data from 2005 indicates the city's crime rates exceeded national averages in most major classifications. The department is currently led by Chief Greg Mullen, previously a deputy chief in Virginia Beach. His predecessor, Reuben Greenberg, stepped down in August 2005. Greenberg was recognized for fostering a respectful police culture that minimized excessive force while maintaining a strong community presence, which contributed to a notable decline in criminal activity.

input: According to some historians, Bismarck adroitly created a diplomatic crisis over the succession to the Spanish throne, then edited a dispatch about a meeting between King William of Prussia and the French ambassador, to make it appear that the French had been insulted. The French press and parliament demanded a war, which the generals of Napoleon III assured him that France would win. Napoleon and his Prime Minister, Émile Ollivier, for their parts sought war to solve their problems with political disunity in France. On 16 July 1870, the French parliament voted to declare war on the German Kingdom of Prussia and hostilities began three days later. The German coalition mobilised its troops much more quickly than the French and rapidly invaded northeastern France. The German forces were superior in numbers, had better training and leadership and made more effective use of modern technology, particularly railroads and artillery.
rewrite: Some historical accounts suggest that Bismarck skillfully manufactured a diplomatic dispute regarding who would inherit the Spanish crown. He subsequently altered an account of an encounter between Prussia's King William and a French ambassador, presenting it as a deliberate slight against France. This provoked calls for war from French media and lawmakers, with military advisors confidently promising Emperor Napoleon III a victory. Both Napoleon and his premier, Émile Ollivier, also viewed the conflict as a means to address domestic political divisions. Consequently, France's legislative body approved a declaration of war against Prussia on July 16, 1870, with fighting commencing three days later. The allied German states mobilized with far greater speed, promptly entering northeastern France. Their armies held advantages in troop strength, discipline, command, and the strategic application of contemporary innovations like railways and heavy guns.

input: Napoleon turned his focus to domestic affairs after the war. Empress Joséphine had still not given birth to a child from Napoleon, who became worried about the future of his empire following his death. Desperate for a legitimate heir, Napoleon divorced Joséphine in January 1810 and started looking for a new wife. Hoping to cement the recent alliance with Austria through a family connection, Napoleon married the Archduchess Marie Louise, who was 18 years old at the time. On 20 March 1811, Marie Louise gave birth to a baby boy, whom Napoleon made heir apparent and bestowed the title of King of Rome. His son never actually ruled the empire, but historians still refer to him as Napoleon II.
rewrite: Following the conclusion of the war, Napoleon directed his attention to matters at home. Concerned about the succession of his empire due to the lack of a biological child with Empress Joséphine, he sought a lawful heir. This led him to dissolve their marriage in early 1810 and pursue a new union. To strengthen the freshly formed pact with Austria, he wed the young Archduchess Marie Louise. She later bore a son in March 1811, who was promptly named the successor and given the designation King of Rome. Although this son never exercised power, history records him as Napoleon II.

input: During the First Opium War, the British navy defeated Eight Banners forces at Ningbo and Dinghai. Under the terms of the Treaty of Nanking, signed in 1843, Ningbo became one of the five Chinese treaty ports opened to virtually unrestricted foreign trade. Much of Zhejiang came under the control of the Taiping Heavenly Kingdom during the Taiping Rebellion, which resulted in a considerable loss of life in the province. In 1876, Wenzhou became Zhejiang's second treaty port.
rewrite: In the First Opium War, British naval forces overcame Qing Dynasty troops at Ningbo and Dinghai. The subsequent Treaty of Nanking, finalized in 1843, designated Ningbo among five ports for extensive international commerce. The Taiping Rebellion later placed much of Zhejiang under Taiping Heavenly Kingdom rule, causing severe provincial casualties. Finally, Wenzhou gained status as another treaty port within the province in 1876.

input: The most recognizable icon of Mexico City is the golden Angel of Independence on the wide, elegant avenue Paseo de la Reforma, modeled by the order of the Emperor Maximilian of Mexico after the Champs-Élysées in Paris. This avenue was designed over the Americas' oldest known major roadway in the 19th century to connect the National Palace (seat of government) with the Castle of Chapultepec, the imperial residence. Today, this avenue is an important financial district in which the Mexican Stock Exchange and several corporate headquarters are located. Another important avenue is the Avenida de los Insurgentes, which extends 28.8 km (17.9 mi) and is one of the longest single avenues in the world.
rewrite: The golden Angel of Independence, standing on the grand Paseo de la Reforma, serves as Mexico City's defining symbol. This majestic boulevard, inspired by Paris's Champs-Élysées and commissioned by Emperor Maximilian, was built in the 1800s over an ancient continental route. It originally linked the government's National Palace to the imperial home at Chapultepec Castle. Presently, the area forms a key economic hub, hosting the national stock exchange and numerous corporate offices. A second major thoroughfare is Avenida de los Insurgentes, stretching nearly 29 kilometers and ranking among the world's longest continuous avenues.

input: In December 1978, Gaddafi stepped down as Secretary-General of the GPC, announcing his new focus on revolutionary rather than governmental activities; this was part of his new emphasis on separating the apparatus of the revolution from the government. Although no longer in a formal governmental post, he adopted the title of "Leader of the Revolution" and continued as commander-in-chief of the armed forces. He continued exerting considerable influence over Libya, with many critics insisting that the structure of Libya's direct democracy gave him "the freedom to manipulate outcomes".
rewrite: In late 1978, Gaddafi relinquished his role as GPC Secretary-General. He declared a shift in his efforts toward revolutionary pursuits, distinct from official state duties, aiming to clearly divide the revolution's operations from the government's. Despite holding no formal office, he assumed the designation "Leader of the Revolution" and remained head of the military. He retained significant control in Libya, with detractors arguing the nation's system of direct democracy allowed him to easily steer results.

input: Feathers being critical to the survival of a bird, require maintenance. Apart from physical wear and tear, feathers face the onslaught of fungi, ectoparasitic feather mites and birdlice. The physical condition of feathers are maintained by preening often with the application of secretions from the preen gland. Birds also bathe in water or dust themselves. While some birds dip into shallow water, more aerial species may make aerial dips into water and arboreal species often make use of dew or rain that collect on leaves. Birds of arid regions make use of loose soil to dust-bathe. A behaviour termed as anting in which the bird encourages ants to run through their plumage is also thought to help them reduce the ectoparasite load in feathers. Many species will spread out their wings and expose them to direct sunlight and this too is thought to help in reducing fungal and ectoparasitic activity that may lead to feather damage.
rewrite: Feathers are essential for a bird's existence and must be kept in good condition. They deteriorate not only from everyday use but also from threats like fungi, mites, and lice. To care for them, birds regularly preen, frequently using oil from a specialized gland. They also clean themselves by bathing in water or rolling in dust. Species that live near water may wade in, while birds adept at flight might skim the surface. Tree-dwelling birds sometimes use moisture gathered on foliage. In dry areas, birds often bathe in fine soil. Another curious behavior, known as anting, involves birds letting insects crawl through their feathers, which may lower parasite numbers. Additionally, many birds will sunbathe with wings outstretched, a practice believed to suppress harmful fungi and parasites that can degrade feathers.

input: The world's first institution of technology or technical university with tertiary technical education is the Banská Akadémia in Banská Štiavnica, Slovakia, founded in 1735, Academy since December 13, 1762 established by queen Maria Theresa in order to train specialists of silver and gold mining and metallurgy in neighbourhood. Teaching started in 1764. Later the department of Mathematics, Mechanics and Hydraulics and department of Forestry were settled. University buildings are still at their place today and are used for teaching. University has launched the first book of electrotechnics in the world.
rewrite: The earliest technical university offering higher education was established in Banská Štiavnica, Slovakia. Originally founded in 1735, it was officially chartered as an academy by Empress Maria Theresa in 1762 to educate experts in precious metal mining and processing. Instruction commenced in 1764, later expanding to include mathematics, mechanics, hydraulics, and forestry. Its historic campus remains in use for education today. This institution also published the world's inaugural textbook on electrical engineering.

input: A study published in the Neuropsychopharmacology journal in 2013 revealed the finding that the flavour of beer alone could provoke dopamine activity in the brain of the male participants, who wanted to drink more as a result. The 49 men in the study were subject to positron emission tomography scans, while a computer-controlled device sprayed minute amounts of beer, water and a sports drink onto their tongues. Compared with the taste of the sports drink, the taste of beer significantly increased the participants desire to drink. Test results indicated that the flavour of the beer triggered a dopamine release, even though alcohol content in the spray was insufficient for the purpose of becoming intoxicated.
rewrite: A 2013 study in the journal Neuropsychopharmacology showed that merely tasting beer could increase dopamine release in the brains of men, thereby boosting their urge to consume more. Researchers used PET scans to monitor 49 male subjects as a specialized device administered tiny quantities of beer, water, and a sports beverage onto their tongues. The flavor of beer, as opposed to the sports drink, notably heightened the participants' craving to drink. This dopamine response occurred despite the sprayed beer containing too little alcohol to cause any intoxication.

input: The human brain is not fully developed by the time a person reaches puberty. Between the ages of 10 and 25, the brain undergoes changes that have important implications for behavior (see Cognitive development below). The brain reaches 90% of its adult size by the time a person is six years of age. Thus, the brain does not grow in size much during adolescence. However, the creases in the brain continue to become more complex until the late teens. The biggest changes in the folds of the brain during this time occur in the parts of the cortex that process cognitive and emotional information.
rewrite: The brain remains underdeveloped beyond puberty, continuing to mature significantly between ages 10 and 25, which influences conduct. While it attains nearly its full physical size around age six, showing little growth during teenage years, its internal structure evolves. Complexity within the folds increases until about age 20, with the most substantial development happening in areas responsible for managing thought and feeling.

input: On 17 March 1883, she fell down some stairs at Windsor, which left her lame until July; she never fully recovered and was plagued with rheumatism thereafter. Brown died 10 days after her accident, and to the consternation of her private secretary, Sir Henry Ponsonby, Victoria began work on a eulogistic biography of Brown. Ponsonby and Randall Davidson, Dean of Windsor, who had both seen early drafts, advised Victoria against publication, on the grounds that it would stoke the rumours of a love affair. The manuscript was destroyed. In early 1884, Victoria did publish More Leaves from a Journal of a Life in the Highlands, a sequel to her earlier book, which she dedicated to her "devoted personal attendant and faithful friend John Brown". On the day after the first anniversary of Brown's death, Victoria was informed by telegram that her youngest son, Leopold, had died in Cannes. He was "the dearest of my dear sons", she lamented. The following month, Victoria's youngest child, Beatrice, met and fell in love with Prince Henry of Battenberg at the wedding of Victoria's granddaughter Princess Victoria of Hesse and by Rhine to Henry's brother Prince Louis of Battenberg. Beatrice and Henry planned to marry, but Victoria opposed the match at first, wishing to keep Beatrice at home to act as her companion. After a year, she was won around to the marriage by Henry and Beatrice's promise to remain living with and attending her.
rewrite: On 17 March 1883, a fall down a staircase at Windsor left her with a lameness that persisted until July. She did not completely regain her health, suffering from recurring rheumatism in the years that followed. Her attendant, John Brown, passed away just ten days after her mishap. Shortly after, to the dismay of her private secretary Sir Henry Ponsonby, she commenced writing an admiring biographical account of Brown. Both Ponsonby and Randall Davidson, the Dean of Windsor, who reviewed initial versions, counseled the queen against making it public, warning it would fuel existing gossip about a romantic relationship. Consequently, the manuscript was discarded. However, in early 1884, Victoria did release *More Leaves from a Journal of a Life in the Highlands*, a follow-up to her previous publication, which she inscribed to Brown as her "devoted personal attendant and faithful friend." The day after the first anniversary of Brown's death, she received a telegram announcing the death of her youngest son, Leopold, in Cannes. She mourned him as "the dearest of my dear sons." The next month, at the wedding of her granddaughter Princess Victoria of Hesse to Prince Louis of Battenberg, Victoria's youngest daughter, Beatrice, met and became enamored with the groom's brother, Prince Henry of Battenberg. Though Beatrice and Henry intended to wed, Victoria initially objected, hoping to keep her daughter at her side as a companion. After a year, she relented, persuaded by their pledge to continue residing with and caring for her.

input: Madonna's Italian-Catholic background and her relationship with her parents are reflected in the album Like a Prayer. It was an evocation of the impact religion had on her career. Her video for the title track contains Catholic symbolism, such as the stigmata. During The Virgin Tour, she wore a rosary and prayed with it in the music video for "La Isla Bonita". The "Open Your Heart" video sees her boss scolding her in the Italian language. On the Who's That Girl World Tour, she dedicated the song "Papa Don't Preach" to Pope John Paul II.
rewrite: Madonna's album Like a Prayer draws upon her upbringing in an Italian-Catholic family and her parental connections. The work explores the profound influence of faith on her public life. Catholic imagery, including depictions of stigmata, appears in the title track's video. She also used a rosary in prayer during "La Isla Bonita" on The Virgin Tour. In the "Open Your Heart" video, her employer reprimands her in Italian. Later, on the Who's That Girl tour, she offered "Papa Don't Preach" to the Pope.

input: In the early 20th century, many anthropologists accepted and taught the belief that biologically distinct races were isomorphic with distinct linguistic, cultural, and social groups, while popularly applying that belief to the field of eugenics, in conjunction with a practice that is now called scientific racism. After the Nazi eugenics program, racial essentialism lost widespread popularity. Race anthropologists were pressured to acknowledge findings coming from studies of culture and population genetics, and to revise their conclusions about the sources of phenotypic variation. A significant number of modern anthropologists and biologists in the West came to view race as an invalid genetic or biological designation.
rewrite: During the first decades of the 1900s, it was common for anthropologists to endorse the idea that biological races corresponded directly to separate language, cultural, and societal units. This concept was often publicly used to support eugenics and what is now termed scientific racism. Following the eugenics policies of the Nazi era, this rigid view of race declined in acceptance. Specialists in race studies were compelled to integrate new cultural and genetic research, adjusting their views on the origins of physical differences. Consequently, many contemporary Western anthropologists and biologists now reject race as a legitimate biological or genetic category.

input: However, several de facto standards for tag formats exist. As of 2010, the most widespread are ID3v1 and ID3v2, and the more recently introduced APEv2. These tags are normally embedded at the beginning or end of MP3 files, separate from the actual MP3 frame data. MP3 decoders either extract information from the tags, or just treat them as ignorable, non-MP3 junk data.
rewrite: Numerous informal standards for metadata tags have emerged. Currently, ID3v1, ID3v2, and the newer APEv2 are the most common. These tags are placed at the start or finish of an MP3 file, distinct from the audio frames. Decoders may read this information or simply disregard it as irrelevant non-audio data.

input: UNFPA provided aid to Peru's reproductive health program in the mid-to-late '90s. When it was discovered a Peruvian program had been engaged in carrying out coercive sterilizations, UNFPA called for reforms and protocols to protect the rights of women seeking assistance. UNFPA was not involved in the scandal, but continued work with the country after the abuses had become public to help end the abuses and reform laws and practices.
rewrite: During the late 1990s, UNFPA supported Peru's reproductive health initiatives. Following revelations that a local program had performed forced sterilizations, the agency demanded new safeguards to ensure women's rights. Although not implicated, UNFPA maintained its partnership with Peru after the scandal emerged, aiming to halt the violations and revise relevant legislation and procedures.

input: The Guardian Council comprises twelve jurists including six appointed by the Supreme Leader. The others are elected by the Iranian Parliament from among the jurists nominated by the Head of the Judiciary. The Council interprets the constitution and may veto Parliament. If a law is deemed incompatible with the constitution or Sharia (Islamic law), it is referred back to Parliament for revision. The Expediency Council has the authority to mediate disputes between Parliament and the Guardian Council, and serves as an advisory body to the Supreme Leader, making it one of the most powerful governing bodies in the country. Local city councils are elected by public vote to four-year terms in all cities and villages of Iran.
rewrite: Composed of twelve legal experts, the Guardian Council has half its members selected by the Supreme Leader. The remaining six are chosen by Parliament from a list provided by the Head of the Judiciary. This body holds the power of constitutional review and can reject parliamentary legislation. Laws considered unconstitutional or contrary to Islamic principles are returned to Parliament for amendment. Resolving legislative conflicts between Parliament and the Guardian Council falls to the Expediency Council, which also advises the Supreme Leader, granting it significant influence. Separately, locally elected councils serve four-year terms in every city and village nationwide.

input: iPod batteries are not designed to be removed or replaced by the user, although some users have been able to open the case themselves, usually following instructions from third-party vendors of iPod replacement batteries. Compounding the problem, Apple initially would not replace worn-out batteries. The official policy was that the customer should buy a refurbished replacement iPod, at a cost almost equivalent to a brand new one. All lithium-ion batteries lose capacity during their lifetime even when not in use (guidelines are available for prolonging life-span) and this situation led to a market for third-party battery replacement kits.
rewrite: iPod batteries are not intended for customer removal or exchange. Despite this, certain individuals have managed to open the device, often guided by instructions from external suppliers selling substitute batteries. Initially, Apple did not offer a service for swapping depleted batteries, instead directing customers to purchase a refurbished iPod at a price close to that of a new unit. Since all lithium-ion cells degrade over time, even without use, a sector emerged offering independent battery replacement solutions.

input: France's major upscale department stores are Galeries Lafayette and Le Printemps, which both have flagship stores on Boulevard Haussmann in Paris and branches around the country. The first department store in France, Le Bon Marché in Paris, was founded in 1852 and is now owned by the luxury goods conglomerate LVMH. La Samaritaine, another upscale department store also owned by LVMH, closed in 2005. Mid-range department stores chains also exist in France such as the BHV (Bazar de l'Hotel de Ville), part of the same group as Galeries Lafayette.
rewrite: France's premier luxury department stores include Galeries Lafayette and Le Printemps, each with their main location on Paris's Boulevard Haussmann and additional outlets nationwide. The country's earliest such store, Paris's Le Bon Marché, opened in 1852 and is currently a holding of the LVMH luxury group. Another high-end retailer under LVMH, La Samaritaine, shut its doors in 2005. France also has mid-market chains like the BHV (Bazar de l'Hotel de Ville), which operates under the same corporate umbrella as Galeries Lafayette.

input: Federalism has a long tradition in German history. The Holy Roman Empire comprised many petty states numbering more than 300 around 1796. The number of territories was greatly reduced during the Napoleonic Wars (1796–1814). After the Congress of Vienna (1815), 39 states formed the German Confederation. The Confederation was dissolved after the Austro-Prussian War and replaced by a North German Federation under Prussian hegemony; this war left Prussia dominant in Germany, and German nationalism would compel the remaining independent states to ally with Prussia in the Franco-Prussian War of 1870–71, and then to accede to the crowning of King Wilhelm of Prussia as German Emperor. The new German Empire included 25 states (three of them, Hanseatic cities) and the imperial territory of Alsace-Lorraine. The empire was dominated by Prussia, which controlled 65% of the territory and 62% of the population. After the territorial losses of the Treaty of Versailles, the remaining states continued as republics of a new German federation. These states were gradually de facto abolished and reduced to provinces under the Nazi regime via the Gleichschaltung process, as the states administratively were largely superseded by the Nazi Gau system.
rewrite:
The concept of federalism is deeply rooted in Germany's past. Historically, the region was fragmented into numerous small entities, exemplified by the over three hundred minor states within the Holy Roman Empire near the end of the 18th century. This patchwork was consolidated following the Napoleonic conflicts. Subsequently, the German Confederation emerged from the Congress of Vienna, uniting 39 distinct territories. This structure dissolved after the Austro-Prussian conflict, leading to a Prussian-led North German Federation. Prussian dominance, fueled by nationalist sentiments, prompted other German states to join Prussia against France, culminating in the proclamation of a German Emperor.

The resulting German Empire contained 25 states, including three city-states, plus the annexed region of Alsace-Lorraine. Prussia was the overwhelming power within this union, holding most of the land and people. Following World War I and the Treaty of Versailles, the states persisted within a republican federal system. However, the Nazi regime effectively dismantled this federal structure through its policy of forced coordination, eroding the states' authority and replacing it with its own regional administrative districts.

input: The 1981 film Fort Apache, The Bronx is another film that used the Bronx's gritty image for its storyline. The movie's title is from the nickname for the 41st Police Precinct in the South Bronx which was nicknamed "Fort Apache". Also from 1981 is the horror film Wolfen making use of the rubble of the Bronx as a home for werewolf type creatures. Knights of the South Bronx, a true story of a teacher who worked with disadvantaged children, is another film also set in the Bronx released in 2005. The Bronx was the setting for the 1983 film Fuga dal Bronx, also known as Bronx Warriors 2 and Escape 2000, an Italian B-movie best known for its appearance on the television series Mystery Science Theatre 3000. The plot revolves around a sinister construction corporation's plans to depopulate, destroy and redevelop the Bronx, and a band of rebels who are out to expose the corporation's murderous ways and save their homes. The film is memorable for its almost incessant use of the phrase, "Leave the Bronx!" Many of the movie's scenes were filmed in Queens, substituting as the Bronx. Rumble in the Bronx was a 1995 Jackie Chan kung-fu film, another which popularised the Bronx to international audiences. Last Bronx, a 1996 Sega game played on the bad reputation of the Bronx to lend its name to an alternate version of post-Japanese bubble Tokyo, where crime and gang warfare is rampant.
rewrite: Several movies have drawn upon the Bronx's reputation as a tough urban environment. The 1981 police drama *Fort Apache, The Bronx* takes its name from the colloquial term for a precinct in the South Bronx. That same year, the horror feature *Wolfen* depicted the borough's abandoned lots as the domain of supernatural beasts. A more uplifting 2005 film, *Knights of the South Bronx*, tells the factual account of an educator helping underprivileged youth. Another notable setting is the 1983 Italian cult film *Fuga dal Bronx* (also titled *Bronx Warriors 2*). Its story involves an evil company scheming to evacuate, demolish, and rebuild the area, with heroes fighting to reveal its deadly plot and protect their neighborhood. The movie is famous for characters repeatedly shouting, "Leave the Bronx!" Though set in the Bronx, much of it was actually shot in Queens. Jackie Chan's 1995 action movie *Rumble in the Bronx* further cemented the borough's image for global viewers. Beyond cinema, the 1996 Sega game *Last Bronx* borrowed the locale's notoriety for its title, presenting a fictional, crime-ridden version of Tokyo.

input: After repeated efforts by the Samoan independence movement, the New Zealand Western Samoa Act 1961 of 24 November 1961 granted Samoa independence effective 1 January 1962, upon which the Trusteeship Agreement terminated. Samoa also signed a friendship treaty with New Zealand. Samoa, the first small-island country in the Pacific to become independent, joined the Commonwealth of Nations on 28 August 1970. While independence was achieved at the beginning of January, Samoa annually celebrates 1 June as its independence day.
rewrite: Following persistent advocacy by Samoan nationalists, New Zealand passed the Western Samoa Act in late 1961, establishing independence from the start of 1962 and ending its trusteeship. A subsequent friendship treaty was concluded with New Zealand. As the Pacific's first independent small island state, Samoa entered the Commonwealth in August 1970. Although sovereignty was attained in January, the nation observes Independence Day each year on the first of June.

input: The Buddha's death is seen as an illusion, he is living on in other planes of existence, and monks are therefore permitted to offer "new truths" based on his input. Mahayana also differs from Theravada in its concept of śūnyatā (that ultimately nothing has existence), and in its belief in bodhisattvas (enlightened people who vow to continue being reborn until all beings can be enlightened).
rewrite: The Buddha's passing is considered illusory, as he continues to exist in other realms, allowing monks to introduce fresh teachings inspired by him. Mahayana further diverges from Theravada through its view of śūnyatā—the ultimate emptiness of all things—and its faith in bodhisattvas, enlightened beings committed to rebirth until universal enlightenment is achieved.

input: This meant that nearly one-third of the U.S. lending mechanism was frozen and continued to be frozen into June 2009. According to the Brookings Institution, the traditional banking system does not have the capital to close this gap as of June 2009: "It would take a number of years of strong profits to generate sufficient capital to support that additional lending volume". The authors also indicate that some forms of securitization are "likely to vanish forever, having been an artifact of excessively loose credit conditions". While traditional banks have raised their lending standards, it was the collapse of the shadow banking system that is the primary cause of the reduction in funds available for borrowing.
rewrite: As a result, close to a third of America's credit apparatus remained locked and inactive through June 2009. The Brookings Institution notes that conventional banks lacked the resources to bridge this shortfall at that time, stating that building the necessary capital through earnings would require many years of robust profitability. The analysis further suggests certain securitization practices, born of an era of overly easy credit, may have disappeared for good. Although mainstream banks tightened their loan criteria, the main driver behind the contraction in lendable capital was the failure of the shadow banking sector.

input: Most modern air defence systems are fairly mobile. Even the larger systems tend to be mounted on trailers and are designed to be fairly quickly broken down or set up. In the past, this was not always the case. Early missile systems were cumbersome and required much infrastructure; many could not be moved at all. With the diversification of air defence there has been much more emphasis on mobility. Most modern systems are usually either self-propelled (i.e. guns or missiles are mounted on a truck or tracked chassis) or easily towed. Even systems that consist of many components (transporter/erector/launchers, radars, command posts etc.) benefit from being mounted on a fleet of vehicles. In general, a fixed system can be identified, attacked and destroyed whereas a mobile system can show up in places where it is not expected. Soviet systems especially concentrate on mobility, after the lessons learnt in the Vietnam war between the USA and Vietnam. For more information on this part of the conflict, see SA-2 Guideline.
rewrite: Contemporary air defense units are typically designed for easy relocation. Even larger configurations are often placed on towable platforms, allowing them to be rapidly assembled or disassembled. Historically, such flexibility was uncommon. Initial anti-aircraft missile setups were often unwieldy, dependent on substantial permanent installations, and frequently immobile. The evolution and broadening of aerial threats have since placed a greater priority on the ability to move. Today's defenses are commonly either integrated onto self-driven vehicle platforms or are readily transportable by towing. Complex systems involving multiple units like launchers, detection sensors, and control centers gain a tactical edge by being distributed across several mobile carriers. Essentially, a stationary installation is vulnerable to detection and neutralization, while a movable one can deploy unpredictably. The strategic focus on mobility is particularly pronounced in Soviet and successor-state designs, influenced by experiences from the U.S.-Vietnam War. Additional details regarding this historical context can be found under the entry for the SA-2 Guideline missile system.

input: The Strumica Carnival (Macedonian: Струмички Карневал, translated Strumichki Karneval) has been held since at least 1670, when the Turkish author Evlija Chelebija wrote while staying there, "I came into a town located in the foothills of a high hillock and what I saw that night was masked people running house–to–house, with laughter, scream and song." The Carnival took an organized form in 1991; in 1994, Strumica became a member of FECC and in 1998 hosted the XVIII International Congress of Carnival Cities. The Strumica Carnival opens on a Saturday night at a masked ball where the Prince and Princess are chosen; the main Carnival night is on Tuesday, when masked participants (including groups from abroad) compete in various subjects. As of 2000, the Festival of Caricatures and Aphorisms has been held as part of Strumica's Carnival celebrations.
rewrite: Dating back to at least 1670, the Strumica Carnival is a historic tradition. Early accounts from a Turkish traveler describe a night of masked revelers moving between homes amid merriment and noise. The event became formally structured in 1991. By 1994, Strumica joined the Federation of European Carnival Cities and later held its international congress in 1998. The festivities commence with a Saturday masked ball to select a Prince and Princess. The primary event occurs on Tuesday, featuring costumed competitors, including international groups, in themed contests. Since the year 2000, the Carnival has also included a Festival of Caricatures and Aphorisms.

input: In 1955, with both the United States and the Soviet Union building ballistic missiles that could be utilized to launch objects into space, the "starting line" was drawn for the Space Race. In separate announcements, just four days apart, both nations publicly announced that they would launch artificial Earth satellites by 1957 or 1958. On July 29, 1955, James C. Hagerty, president Dwight D. Eisenhower's press secretary, announced that the United States intended to launch "small Earth circling satellites" between July 1, 1957, and December 31, 1958, as part of their contribution to the International Geophysical Year (IGY). Four days later, at the Sixth Congress of International Astronautical Federation in Copenhagen, scientist Leonid I. Sedov spoke to international reporters at the Soviet embassy, and announced his country's intention to launch a satellite as well, in the "near future". On August 30, 1955, Korolev managed to get the Soviet Academy of Sciences to create a commission whose purpose was to beat the Americans into Earth orbit: this was the de facto start date for the Space Race. The Council of Ministers of the Soviet Union began a policy of treating development of its space program as a classified state secret.
rewrite: The competition to explore space began in earnest in 1955, as the U.S. and the U.S.S.R. each developed ballistic missile technology capable of propelling objects beyond Earth's atmosphere. Within a span of just four days, both countries declared their plans to deploy man-made satellites by the end of the 1950s. The American commitment came first, with a White House statement issued on July 29 detailing intentions to orbit scientific devices during the International Geophysical Year, targeting a launch window from mid-1957 through 1958. Shortly thereafter, a leading Soviet scientist informed the global press in Copenhagen that his nation had similar ambitions for a satellite launch in the coming years. By late August, Soviet authorities, driven by designer Sergei Korolev, had formally established a scientific group with the explicit goal of reaching orbit before the United States. This move effectively marked the true commencement of the rivalry. Subsequently, the Soviet government chose to shroud all advancements in its cosmic endeavors in secrecy, classifying the entire program.

input: In the 16th century, Count Hieronymus Schlick of Bohemia began minting coins known as Joachimstalers (from German thal, or nowadays usually Tal, "valley", cognate with "dale" in English), named for Joachimstal, the valley where the silver was mined (St. Joachim's Valley, now Jáchymov; then part of the Kingdom of Bohemia, now part of the Czech Republic). Joachimstaler was later shortened to the German Taler, a word that eventually found its way into Danish and Swedish as daler, Norwegian as dalar and daler, Dutch as daler or daalder, Ethiopian as ታላሪ (talari), Hungarian as tallér, Italian as tallero, and English as dollar. Alternatively, thaler is said to come from the German coin Guldengroschen ("great guilder", being of silver but equal in value to a gold guilder), minted from the silver from Joachimsthal.
rewrite: During the 1500s, Count Hieronymus Schlick of Bohemia initiated the production of coins called Joachimstalers. This name derived from Joachimstal, meaning "St. Joachim's Valley," the source of the silver. The term "Joachimstaler" was subsequently abbreviated in German to "Taler." This root word spread across languages, evolving into forms like "daler" in Scandinavian tongues, "daalder" in Dutch, "tallér" in Hungarian, "tallero" in Italian, and ultimately "dollar" in English. Another account suggests "thaler" originated from the "Guldengroschen," a silver coin valued equally to a gold guilder, which was also minted using silver from the Joachimsthal mines.

input: Communal shelters never housed more than one seventh of Greater London residents, however. Peak use of the Underground as shelter was 177,000 on 27 September 1940, and a November 1940 census of London found that about 4% of residents used the Tube and other large shelters; 9% in public surface shelters; and 27% in private home shelters, implying that the remaining 60% of the city likely stayed at home. The government distributed Anderson shelters until 1941 and that year began distributing the Morrison shelter, which could be used inside homes.:190
rewrite: At their peak, communal refuges accommodated less than a seventh of London's population. The highest recorded number of people using the Underground for safety was 177,000 in late September 1940. A survey that November indicated only 4% used the Tube or similar large shelters, with 9% in public street shelters and 27% in domestic shelters, suggesting 60% remained in their homes. The government provided Anderson shelters until 1941, then introduced the indoor Morrison shelter.

input: Extending across the north and south side of the Alps in west-central Europe, Switzerland encompasses a great diversity of landscapes and climates on a limited area of 41,285 square kilometres (15,940 sq mi). The population is about 8 million, resulting in an average population density of around 195 people per square kilometre (500/sq mi). The more mountainous southern half of the country is far more sparsely populated than the northern half. In the largest Canton of Graubünden, lying entirely in the Alps, population density falls to 27 /km² (70 /sq mi).
rewrite: Situated on both sides of the Alps in central Europe, Switzerland packs a remarkable variety of terrains and weather into its modest 41,285 square kilometers. With roughly 8 million residents, the average density approaches 195 per square kilometer. The more rugged southern region is significantly less inhabited than the north. For example, in the entirely alpine canton of Graubünden, the largest by area, density drops to just 27 people per square kilometer.

input: At about the same time, Charles Coffin, leading the Thomson-Houston Electric Company, acquired a number of competitors and gained access to their key patents. General Electric was formed through the 1892 merger of Edison General Electric Company of Schenectady, New York, and Thomson-Houston Electric Company of Lynn, Massachusetts, with the support of Drexel, Morgan & Co. Both plants continue to operate under the GE banner to this day. The company was incorporated in New York, with the Schenectady plant used as headquarters for many years thereafter. Around the same time, General Electric's Canadian counterpart, Canadian General Electric, was formed.
rewrite: During a similar period, Charles Coffin, at the helm of the Thomson-Houston Electric Company, purchased several rival firms, securing their essential patents. In 1892, with backing from Drexel, Morgan & Co., Edison General Electric Company and Thomson-Houston Electric Company merged to establish General Electric. The original facilities in Schenectady and Lynn remain active as part of GE. Incorporated in New York, the company long headquartered at the Schenectady site. Concurrently, its Canadian affiliate, Canadian General Electric, was also created.

input: In Alghero, the IEC has adapted its standard to the Alguerese dialect. In this standard one can find, among other features: the definite article lo instead of el, special possessive pronouns and determinants la mia ('mine'), lo sou/la sua ('his/her'), lo tou/la tua ('yours'), and so on, the use of -v- /v/ in the imperfect tense in all conjugations: cantava, creixiva, llegiva; the use of many archaic words, usual words in Alguerese: manco instead of menys ('less'), calqui u instead of algú ('someone'), qual/quala instead of quin/quina ('which'), and so on; and the adaptation of weak pronouns.
rewrite: In Alghero, the IEC has tailored its guidelines to fit the local Alguerese dialect. This version includes distinct elements such as the definite article "lo" replacing "el," along with unique possessive forms like "la mia" for "mine." It also features a consistent -v- sound in imperfect verbs, such as "cantava." Additionally, many traditional terms are used, like "manco" for "less," and adjusted weak pronouns are incorporated.

input: Before the release of iOS 5, the iPod branding was used for the media player included with the iPhone and iPad, a combination of the Music and Videos apps on the iPod Touch. As of iOS 5, separate apps named "Music" and "Videos" are standardized across all iOS-powered products. While the iPhone and iPad have essentially the same media player capabilities as the iPod line, they are generally treated as separate products. During the middle of 2010, iPhone sales overtook those of the iPod.
