It was founded in 1992 from Polytechnic South West (formerly Plymouth Polytechnic) following the Further and Higher Education Act 1992. It has courses in maritime business, marine engineering, marine biology and Earth, ocean and environmental sciences, surf science, shipping and logistics. The university formed a joint venture with the fellow Devonian University of Exeter in 2000, establishing the Peninsula College of Medicine and Dentistry. The college is ranked 8th out of 30 universities in the UK in 2011 for medicine. Its dental school was established in 2006, which also provides free dental care in an attempt to improve access to dental care in the South West.
rewrite: As of the 2014/15 academic year, the University of Plymouth had a student population of 25,895, ranking it 22nd in size among 165 UK institutions. It supports a workforce of 3,000 and generates an annual revenue of approximately £160 million. The university originated in 1992 under the Further and Higher Education Act, evolving from the former Polytechnic South West. Its academic offerings include specialized programs in maritime studies, oceanography, environmental science, and surf science, alongside shipping and logistics. In a 2000 collaboration with the University of Exeter, it founded the Peninsula College of Medicine and Dentistry. This college was rated 8th for medicine among 30 UK universities in 2011. The dental school, opened in 2006, offers complimentary services to enhance regional access to dental treatment.

input: While H2 is not very reactive under standard conditions, it does form compounds with most elements. Hydrogen can form compounds with elements that are more electronegative, such as halogens (e.g., F, Cl, Br, I), or oxygen; in these compounds hydrogen takes on a partial positive charge. When bonded to fluorine, oxygen, or nitrogen, hydrogen can participate in a form of medium-strength noncovalent bonding with other similar molecules between their hydrogens called hydrogen bonding, which is critical to the stability of many biological molecules. Hydrogen also forms compounds with less electronegative elements, such as the metals and metalloids, in which it takes on a partial negative charge. These compounds are often known as hydrides.
rewrite: Under normal circumstances, hydrogen gas exhibits low reactivity, yet it still combines with a wide variety of other elements. It bonds with highly electronegative atoms like oxygen and the halogens, acquiring a slight positive charge in the process. Notably, when linked to fluorine, oxygen, or nitrogen, hydrogen can engage in moderately strong intermolecular attractions known as hydrogen bonds. These forces are essential for the structural integrity of numerous biological compounds. Conversely, hydrogen also joins with less electronegative substances, including metals and metalloids, where it carries a partial negative charge. Substances of this type are commonly referred to as hydrides.

input: In 1877, Thomas Edison invented the phonograph. Unlike the phonautograph, it was capable of both recording and reproducing sound. Despite the similarity of name, there is no documentary evidence that Edison's phonograph was based on Scott's phonautograph. Edison first tried recording sound on a wax-impregnated paper tape, with the idea of creating a "telephone repeater" analogous to the telegraph repeater he had been working on. Although the visible results made him confident that sound could be physically recorded and reproduced, his notes do not indicate that he actually reproduced sound before his first experiment in which he used tinfoil as a recording medium several months later. The tinfoil was wrapped around a grooved metal cylinder and a sound-vibrated stylus indented the tinfoil while the cylinder was rotated. The recording could be played back immediately. The Scientific American article that introduced the tinfoil phonograph to the public mentioned Marey, Rosapelly and Barlow as well as Scott as creators of devices for recording but, importantly, not reproducing sound. Edison also invented variations of the phonograph that used tape and disc formats. Numerous applications for the phonograph were envisioned, but although it enjoyed a brief vogue as a startling novelty at public demonstrations, the tinfoil phonograph proved too crude to be put to any practical use. A decade later, Edison developed a greatly improved phonograph that used a hollow wax cylinder instead of a foil sheet. This proved to be both a better-sounding and far more useful and durable device. The wax phonograph cylinder created the recorded sound market at the end of the 1880s and dominated it through the early years of the 20th century.
rewrite: Thomas Edison created the phonograph in 1877. This device could both capture and replay audio, a capability that distinguished it from earlier inventions like the phonautograph. While their names are similar, no records confirm that Edison derived his design from Édouard-Léon Scott de Martinville's phonautograph. Edison's initial approach involved using a paper tape coated in wax, inspired by his concept for a "telephone repeater" similar to a telegraph repeater. The patterns he observed on this tape convinced him that sound could be physically captured and replayed, though his documentation does not show he successfully reproduced audio until a later experiment. That pivotal test employed a thin sheet of foil wrapped around a grooved metal cylinder. As the cylinder turned, a stylus, vibrating from sound, pressed indentations into the foil. This method allowed for instant playback. When Scientific America first presented the tinfoil phonograph, it acknowledged other innovators like Marey, Rosapelly, Barlow, and Scott for making recording apparatuses, but highlighted that their devices could not reproduce sound. Edison also experimented with alternative tape and disc designs. Many potential uses were imagined for the phonograph, and while it generated brief public fascination as a remarkable novelty, the tinfoil version was too imperfect for practical application. After about ten years, Edison introduced a much-enhanced model that replaced the foil with a solid wax cylinder. This new design offered superior audio quality, greater durability, and real utility. The wax cylinder phonograph effectively launched the commercial recording industry in the late 1880s and remained the dominant format into the early 1900s.

input: San Diego County has one of the highest counts of animal and plant species that appear on the endangered species list among counties in the United States. Because of its diversity of habitat and its position on the Pacific Flyway, San Diego County has recorded the presence of 492 bird species, more than any other region in the country. San Diego always scores very high in the number of bird species observed in the annual Christmas Bird Count, sponsored by the Audubon Society, and it is known as one of the "birdiest" areas in the United States.
rewrite: San Diego County contains a greater number of endangered animal and plant species than nearly all other U.S. counties. Its variety of ecosystems and location along the Pacific Flyway migration route make it a national leader in documented bird diversity, with 492 species recorded. The region consistently ranks at the top for species sightings in the Audubon Society's yearly Christmas Bird Count, earning it a reputation as one of America's premier locations for birdwatching.

input: At the same time, these movements were influenced by, and in some respects continued, philosophical thought within the Vedic tradition as reflected e.g. in the Upanishads. These movements included, besides Buddhism, various skeptics (such as Sanjaya Belatthiputta), atomists (such as Pakudha Kaccayana), materialists (such as Ajita Kesakambali), antinomians (such as Purana Kassapa); the most important ones in the 5th century BCE were the Ajivikas, who emphasized the rule of fate, the Lokayata (materialists), the Ajnanas (agnostics) and the Jains, who stressed that the soul must be freed from matter. Many of these new movements shared the same conceptual vocabulary—atman ("Self"), buddha ("awakened one"), dhamma ("rule" or "law"), karma ("action"), nirvana ("extinguishing"), samsara ("eternal recurrence") and yoga ("spiritual practice").[note 24] The shramanas rejected the Veda, and the authority of the brahmans, who claimed they possessed revealed truths not knowable by any ordinary human means. Moreover, they declared that the entire Brahmanical system was fraudulent: a conspiracy of the brahmans to enrich themselves by charging exorbitant fees to perform bogus rites and give useless advice.
rewrite: During the same period, these emerging schools of thought were shaped by, and in certain ways extended, earlier philosophical ideas found in the Vedic tradition, like those in the Upanishads. Alongside Buddhism, these groups encompassed a range of thinkers: skeptics like Sanjaya Belatthiputta, proponents of atomism such as Pakudha Kaccayana, materialists including Ajita Kesakambali, and antinomian figures like Purana Kassapa. Prominent in the fifth century BCE were the Ajivikas, focusing on predestination; the materialist Lokayata; the agnostic Ajnanas; and the Jains, who taught liberation of the soul from material existence. These diverse movements often employed a common set of terms—atman (the Self), buddha (an awakened one), dhamma (law or truth), karma (action), nirvana (liberation), samsara (cycle of rebirth), and yoga (discipline). The shramana ascetics explicitly rejected the Vedas and the authority of brahmans, who asserted exclusive access to divinely revealed knowledge. They further condemned the Brahmanical structure as a deceitful scheme, accusing priests of exploiting others through costly but meaningless rituals and fraudulent counsel for their own gain.

input: In DC circuits and pulsed circuits, current and voltage reversal are affected by the damping of the system. Voltage reversal is encountered in RLC circuits that are under-damped. The current and voltage reverse direction, forming a harmonic oscillator between the inductance and capacitance. The current and voltage will tend to oscillate and may reverse direction several times, with each peak being lower than the previous, until the system reaches an equilibrium. This is often referred to as ringing. In comparison, critically damped or over-damped systems usually do not experience a voltage reversal. Reversal is also encountered in AC circuits, where the peak current will be equal in each direction.
rewrite: In direct current and pulsed systems, the damping level influences whether current and voltage change direction. Under-damped RLC circuits exhibit this reversal, as energy shifts between inductive and capacitive elements, creating oscillatory behavior. These oscillations, known as ringing, gradually diminish with each cycle until stability is achieved. Conversely, circuits that are critically or over-damped typically prevent such directional changes. Alternating current circuits also see reversals, but here the peak current magnitude remains consistent in both directions.

input: In a June 2008 speech, President and CEO of the New York Federal Reserve Bank Timothy Geithner—who in 2009 became Secretary of the United States Treasury—placed significant blame for the freezing of credit markets on a "run" on the entities in the "parallel" banking system, also called the shadow banking system. These entities became critical to the credit markets underpinning the financial system, but were not subject to the same regulatory controls. Further, these entities were vulnerable because of maturity mismatch, meaning that they borrowed short-term in liquid markets to purchase long-term, illiquid and risky assets. This meant that disruptions in credit markets would make them subject to rapid deleveraging, selling their long-term assets at depressed prices. He described the significance of these entities:
rewrite: During a June 2008 address, Timothy Geithner, then head of the New York Federal Reserve and later U.S. Treasury Secretary, attributed much of the credit market paralysis to a sudden withdrawal from institutions within the shadow banking sector. This parallel financial network had grown essential for providing credit yet operated outside conventional regulatory oversight. Its participants were particularly at risk due to a structural imbalance: they relied on short-term, easily accessible borrowing to invest in long-term, less liquid, and higher-risk holdings. Consequently, any credit market instability forced them to quickly reduce debt by selling off these long-term investments at severely reduced values. Geithner emphasized the crucial role these entities played in the broader financial framework.

input: The AVL, created by the Valencian parliament, is in charge of dictating the official rules governing the use of Valencian, and its standard is based on the Norms of Castelló (Normes de Castelló). Currently, everyone who writes in Valencian uses this standard, except the Royal Academy of Valencian Culture (Acadèmia de Cultura Valenciana, RACV), which uses for Valencian an independent standard.
rewrite: The Valencian parliament established the AVL to set the official regulations for Valencian usage, following the Norms of Castelló. Today, all writers of Valencian adhere to this standard, with the sole exception of the Royal Academy of Valencian Culture, which employs its own separate norm.

input: Many instruments originated during the Renaissance; others were variations of, or improvements upon, instruments that had existed previously. Some have survived to the present day; others have disappeared, only to be recreated in order to perform music of the period on authentic instruments. As in the modern day, instruments may be classified as brass, strings, percussion, and woodwind.
rewrite: Numerous musical devices emerged in the Renaissance, while some evolved from earlier models. A number persist today, whereas others vanished and were later reconstructed for period-accurate performances. Similar to contemporary practice, these instruments are grouped into brass, string, percussion, and woodwind families.

input: Various classes of Vajrayana literature developed as a result of royal courts sponsoring both Buddhism and Saivism. The Mañjusrimulakalpa, which later came to classified under Kriyatantra, states that mantras taught in the Saiva, Garuda and Vaisnava tantras will be effective if applied by Buddhists since they were all taught originally by Manjushri. The Guhyasiddhi of Padmavajra, a work associated with the Guhyasamaja tradition, prescribes acting as a Saiva guru and initiating members into Saiva Siddhanta scriptures and mandalas. The Samvara tantra texts adopted the pitha list from the Saiva text Tantrasadbhava, introducing a copying error where a deity was mistaken for a place.
rewrite: Royal patronage of both Buddhist and Saiva traditions led to diverse Vajrayana texts. The Mañjusrimulakalpa, later categorized as Kriyatantra, asserts that mantras from Saiva, Garuda, and Vaisnava tantras are valid for Buddhists, as Manjushri first taught them all. In the Guhyasamaja lineage, Padmavajra's Guhyasiddhi advises practitioners to pose as Saiva teachers and initiate followers into Saiva Siddhanta rites and diagrams. Additionally, the Samvara tantras borrowed their list of sacred sites from the Saiva Tantrasadbhava, inadvertently misreading a goddess's name as a location.

input: The process was completed in 27 BC when the Roman Emperor Augustus annexed the rest of Greece and constituted it as the senatorial province of Achaea. Despite their military superiority, the Romans admired and became heavily influenced by the achievements of Greek culture, hence Horace's famous statement: Graecia capta ferum victorem cepit ("Greece, although captured, took its wild conqueror captive"). The epics of Homer inspired the Aeneid of Virgil, and authors such as Seneca the younger wrote using Greek styles. Roman heroes such as Scipio Africanus, tended to study philosophy and regarded Greek culture and science as an example to be followed. Similarly, most Roman emperors maintained an admiration for things Greek in nature. The Roman Emperor Nero visited Greece in AD 66, and performed at the Ancient Olympic Games, despite the rules against non-Greek participation. Hadrian was also particularly fond of the Greeks; before he became emperor he served as an eponymous archon of Athens.
rewrite: In 27 BC, Emperor Augustus incorporated the remaining Greek territories into the Roman Empire, organizing them as the province of Achaea under senatorial governance. Though Rome held military dominance, it deeply revered and assimilated many aspects of Greek civilization. This cultural absorption is captured in Horace’s remark that “conquered Greece captivated its rough victor.” Virgil’s Aeneid drew inspiration from Homer’s works, and writers like Seneca adopted Hellenic literary forms. Prominent Romans, including Scipio Africanus, engaged with Greek philosophy and saw its arts and sciences as models to emulate. Many emperors shared this esteem for Greek traditions. Nero, for instance, competed in the Olympic Games in AD 66, flouting regulations that barred non-Greeks. Hadrian, too, demonstrated his affinity; prior to his rule, he held the position of archon in Athens.

input: The managing director of London Weekend Television (LWT), Greg Dyke, met with the representatives of the "big five" football clubs in England in 1990. The meeting was to pave the way for a break away from The Football League. Dyke believed that it would be more lucrative for LWT if only the larger clubs in the country were featured on national television and wanted to establish whether the clubs would be interested in a larger share of television rights money. The five clubs decided it was a good idea and decided to press ahead with it; however, the league would have no credibility without the backing of The Football Association and so David Dein of Arsenal held talks to see whether the FA were receptive to the idea. The FA did not enjoy an amicable relationship with the Football League at the time and considered it as a way to weaken the Football League's position.
rewrite: In 1990, Greg Dyke, who was the managing director at London Weekend Television, held discussions with officials from England's five leading football clubs. The purpose was to explore the possibility of forming a separate league distinct from the existing Football League. Dyke's view was that televising matches involving only the major clubs would generate higher revenue for LWT, and he sought to gauge their interest in securing a greater portion of broadcasting income. The clubs responded favorably and agreed to proceed. Recognizing that the new venture needed legitimacy, Arsenal's David Dein approached The Football Association to assess their support. At that time, the FA had a strained relationship with the Football League and saw this proposal as an opportunity to diminish the League's influence.

input: In abstract algebra, more general structures are defined by relaxing some of the axioms defining a group. For example, if the requirement that every element has an inverse is eliminated, the resulting algebraic structure is called a monoid. The natural numbers N (including 0) under addition form a monoid, as do the nonzero integers under multiplication (Z ∖ {0}, ·), see above. There is a general method to formally add inverses to elements to any (abelian) monoid, much the same way as (Q ∖ {0}, ·) is derived from (Z ∖ {0}, ·), known as the Grothendieck group. Groupoids are similar to groups except that the composition a • b need not be defined for all a and b. They arise in the study of more complicated forms of symmetry, often in topological and analytical structures, such as the fundamental groupoid or stacks. Finally, it is possible to generalize any of these concepts by replacing the binary operation with an arbitrary n-ary one (i.e. an operation taking n arguments). With the proper generalization of the group axioms this gives rise to an n-ary group. The table gives a list of several structures generalizing groups.
rewrite: In abstract algebra, broader mathematical constructs can be created by weakening certain conditions required for a group. For instance, removing the necessity for each element to possess an inverse yields a structure known as a monoid. The set of natural numbers including zero, with addition, constitutes a monoid, as does the set of nonzero integers under multiplication. A standard technique exists for formally introducing inverses to elements within any commutative monoid, analogous to how the nonzero rational numbers under multiplication are constructed from the nonzero integers; this process is referred to as forming the Grothendieck group. Groupoids resemble groups but differ in that the combination of two elements is not necessarily always defined. These emerge when analyzing more intricate symmetry types, frequently within topological or analytical contexts, like the fundamental groupoid or stacks. Furthermore, these ideas can be extended by substituting the standard binary operation with one that accepts any number of arguments. Appropriately adapting the group conditions then leads to the concept of an n-ary group. The accompanying table enumerates various constructs that are extensions of groups.

input: The most notable cricket club in Cork is Cork County Cricket Club, which was formed in 1874. Although located within the Munster jurisdiction, the club plays in the Leinster Senior League. The club plays at the Mardyke, a ground which has hosted three first-class matches in 1947, 1961 and 1973. All three involved Ireland playing Scotland. The Cork Cricket Academy operates within the city, with the stated aim of introducing the sport to schools in the city and county. Cork's other main cricket club, Harlequins Cricket Club, play close to Cork Airport.
rewrite: Cork's premier cricket organization is Cork County Cricket Club, established in 1874. Despite being part of Munster, it competes in the Leinster Senior League. Its home venue is the Mardyke, a site of three first-class fixtures between Ireland and Scotland in 1947, 1961, and 1973. The Cork Cricket Academy also functions locally, seeking to bring cricket to area schools. Another significant club, Harlequins Cricket Club, is situated near Cork Airport.

input: Throughout its prehistory and early history, the region and its vicinity in the Yangtze region was the cradle of unique local civilizations which can be dated back to at least the 15th century BC and coinciding with the later years of the Shang and Zhou dynasties in North China. Sichuan was referred to in ancient Chinese sources as Ba-Shu (巴蜀), an abbreviation of the kingdoms of Ba and Shu which existed within the Sichuan Basin. Ba included Chongqing and the land in eastern Sichuan along the Yangtze and some tributary streams, while Shu included today's Chengdu, its surrounding plain and adjacent territories in western Sichuan.
rewrite: From ancient times, the Yangtze River area fostered distinct local cultures, traceable to the 15th century BC, a period overlapping with the late Shang and Zhou dynasties of northern China. In early Chinese records, this territory was called Ba-Shu, named for the Ba and Shu kingdoms within the Sichuan Basin. The Ba realm encompassed Chongqing and eastern Sichuan along the Yangtze and its branches, whereas the Shu domain covered present-day Chengdu, its plains, and nearby western regions.

input: In addressing the question of who invented the incandescent lamp, historians Robert Friedel and Paul Israel list 22 inventors of incandescent lamps prior to Joseph Swan and Thomas Edison. They conclude that Edison's version was able to outstrip the others because of a combination of three factors: an effective incandescent material, a higher vacuum than others were able to achieve (by use of the Sprengel pump) and a high resistance that made power distribution from a centralized source economically viable.
rewrite: Historians Robert Friedel and Paul Israel note that over twenty individuals created early incandescent bulbs before Swan and Edison. They argue Edison's design surpassed its predecessors due to three key advantages: a superior filament, a better vacuum achieved with a Sprengel pump, and a high-resistance system enabling cost-effective centralized power distribution.

input: Literature consists of written productions, often restricted to those deemed to have artistic or intellectual value. Its Latin root literatura/litteratura (derived itself from littera, letter or handwriting) was used to refer to all written accounts, but intertwined with the roman concept of cultura: learning or cultivation. Literature often uses language differently than ordinary language (see literariness). Literature can be classified according to whether it is fiction or non-fiction and whether it is poetry or prose; it can be further distinguished according to major forms such as the novel, short story or drama; and works are often categorised according to historical periods or their adherence to certain aesthetic features or expectations (genre).
rewrite: Literary works are writings generally considered to possess aesthetic or intellectual merit. The term originates from the Latin "literatura," which initially described any form of written text but was closely linked to ideas of education and refinement. Literary language frequently deviates from everyday speech. Categorizations of literature include divisions between fiction and non-fiction, poetry and prose, and further into specific forms like novels, plays, or short stories. Works are also commonly grouped by historical era or by shared stylistic conventions and themes, known as genres.

input: The court ruled in 2014, after lengthy testimony, that at least two districts had to be redrawn because of gerrymandering. After this was appealed, in July 2015 the Florida Supreme Court ruled that lawmakers had followed an illegal and unconstitutional process overly influenced by party operatives, and ruled that at least eight districts had to be redrawn. On December 2, 2015, a 5-2 majority of the Court accepted a new map of congressional districts, some of which was drawn by challengers. Their ruling affirmed the map previously approved by Leon County Judge Terry Lewis, who had overseen the original trial. It particularly makes changes in South Florida. There are likely to be additional challenges to the map and districts.
rewrite: In 2014, the court decided, following extensive hearings, that a minimum of two electoral areas required redesign due to partisan boundary manipulation. Upon appeal, the state's high court determined in July 2015 that the legislative process was illicit and violated constitutional principles, being unduly shaped by political agents, and ordered no fewer than eight districts to be reconfigured. That December, the Court endorsed a revised congressional plan by a 5-2 vote, incorporating proposals from opposing parties. This decision upheld an earlier validation from Judge Terry Lewis of Leon County, the presiding official at the initial case. The revisions notably affect South Florida. Further legal disputes over the plan are anticipated.

input: All signatories to the CPPCG are required to prevent and punish acts of genocide, both in peace and wartime, though some barriers make this enforcement difficult. In particular, some of the signatories—namely, Bahrain, Bangladesh, India, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore, the United States, Vietnam, Yemen, and former Yugoslavia—signed with the proviso that no claim of genocide could be brought against them at the International Court of Justice without their consent. Despite official protests from other signatories (notably Cyprus and Norway) on the ethics and legal standing of these reservations, the immunity from prosecution they grant has been invoked from time to time, as when the United States refused to allow a charge of genocide brought against it by former Yugoslavia following the 1999 Kosovo War.
rewrite: Every nation that has ratified the Convention on the Prevention and Punishment of the Crime of Genocide (CPPCG) is obligated to stop and penalize genocide during both war and peace. However, fulfilling this duty faces significant obstacles. A key issue involves reservations made by several countries, including Bahrain, Bangladesh, India, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore, the United States, Vietnam, Yemen, and the former Yugoslavia. These nations agreed to the treaty with the specific condition that they cannot face genocide charges at the International Court of Justice without their own approval. Although other parties, such as Cyprus and Norway, have formally objected to these opt-outs on legal and moral grounds, the protections have been utilized. For example, the United States invoked this immunity to dismiss a genocide case filed by the former Yugoslavia after the 1999 Kosovo War.

input: In the high villages people live in homes built according to medieval designs that withstand cold winters. The kitchen is separated from the living area (called the stube, the area of the home heated by a stove), and second-floor bedrooms benefit from rising heat. The typical Swiss chalet originated in the Bernese Oberland. Chalets often face south or downhill, and are built of solid wood, with a steeply gabled roof to allow accumulated snow to slide off easily. Stairs leading to upper levels are sometimes built on the outside, and balconies are sometimes enclosed.
rewrite: Residents of elevated settlements dwell in houses constructed using age-old architectural plans suited for harsh winter conditions. The cooking space is distinct from the main living quarters, known as the stube, which is warmed by a stove. Heat ascends to warm sleeping rooms on the upper floor. These classic chalets, emerging from the Bernese Oberland, are commonly oriented southward or down a slope. Built from sturdy timber, they feature sharply angled roofs that shed snow. External staircases and occasionally enclosed balconies are also characteristic.

input: Like other governmental economic activities, also privatization, such as in the sale of government-owned property, is particularly at the risk of cronyism. Privatizations in Russia, Latin America, and East Germany were accompanied by large-scale corruption during the sale of the state owned companies. Those with political connections unfairly gained large wealth, which has discredited privatization in these regions. While media have reported widely the grand corruption that accompanied the sales, studies have argued that in addition to increased operating efficiency, daily petty corruption is, or would be, larger without privatization, and that corruption is more prevalent in non-privatized sectors. Furthermore, there is evidence to suggest that extralegal and unofficial activities are more prevalent in countries that privatized less.
rewrite: Similar to other state-led economic initiatives, the transfer of public assets to private hands is especially vulnerable to favoritism toward allies. Instances in Russia, Latin America, and East Germany saw significant corrupt practices when state enterprises were sold, allowing politically linked individuals to amass fortunes and tarnishing the concept of privatization there. Although prominent corruption during these sales receives considerable media attention, research indicates that routine, small-scale corruption is actually greater, or would be, in the absence of privatization, and that such practices are more common in sectors remaining under state control. Additionally, data shows nations with less privatization tend to have higher levels of informal and illicit economic activity.

input: Marvel held its own comic book convention, Marvelcon '75, in spring 1975, and promised a Marvelcon '76. At the 1975 event, Stan Lee used a Fantastic Four panel discussion to announce that Jack Kirby, the artist co-creator of most of Marvel's signature characters, was returning to Marvel after having left in 1970 to work for rival DC Comics. In October 1976, Marvel, which already licensed reprints in different countries, including the UK, created a superhero specifically for the British market. Captain Britain debuted exclusively in the UK, and later appeared in American comics.
rewrite: In the spring of 1975, Marvel hosted its own fan convention, Marvelcon '75, and announced plans for a 1976 follow-up. During a Fantastic Four session there, Stan Lee revealed that legendary artist Jack Kirby, co-creator of many iconic Marvel heroes, was coming back to the company after a stint at DC Comics. Later, in October 1976, Marvel introduced a new hero designed for its British audience, Captain Britain, who first appeared in UK publications before crossing over to the U.S. market.

input: Caesar became consul in 59 BC. His colleague, Marcus Calpurnius Bibulus, was an extreme aristocrat. Caesar submitted the laws that he had promised Pompey to the assemblies. Bibulus attempted to obstruct the enactment of these laws, and so Caesar used violent means to ensure their passage. Caesar was then made governor of three provinces. He facilitated the election of the former patrician Publius Clodius Pulcher to the tribunate for 58 BC. Clodius set about depriving Caesar's senatorial enemies of two of their more obstinate leaders in Cato and Cicero. Clodius was a bitter opponent of Cicero because Cicero had testified against him in a sacrilege case. Clodius attempted to try Cicero for executing citizens without a trial during the Catiline conspiracy, resulting in Cicero going into self-imposed exile and his house in Rome being burnt down. Clodius also passed a bill that forced Cato to lead the invasion of Cyprus which would keep him away from Rome for some years. Clodius also passed a law to expand the previous partial grain subsidy to a fully free grain dole for citizens.
rewrite: In 59 BC, Julius Caesar assumed the consulship alongside Marcus Calpurnius Bibulus, a staunch conservative. To fulfill commitments made to Pompey, Caesar presented new legislation to the public assemblies. When Bibulus tried to block these measures, Caesar resorted to force to push them through. Following his term, Caesar secured governance over three provinces. He also engineered the election of Publius Clodius Pulcher as tribune for 58 BC. Clodius targeted Caesar's key adversaries in the Senate, namely Cato and Cicero. His animosity toward Cicero stemmed from Cicero's testimony in a prior sacrilege trial. Clodius prosecuted Cicero for unlawfully executing citizens during the Catiline affair, compelling Cicero to flee Rome and seeing his home destroyed. Additionally, Clodius assigned Cato to oversee the Cyprus campaign, removing him from the city for an extended period. He further enacted legislation that transformed the existing grain subsidy into a completely free distribution for Roman citizens.

input: In the early 1970s (1973, to be particular) when the military junta took over power in Uruguay, art suffered in Montevideo. The art studios went into protest mode, with Rimer Cardillo, one of the country's leading artists, making the National Institute of Fine Arts, Montevideo a "hotbed of resistance". This resulted in the military junta coming down heavily on artists by closing the Fine Art Institute and carting away all the presses and other studio equipment. Consequently, the learning of fine arts was only in private studios run by people who had been let out of jail, in works of printing and on paper and also painting and sculpture. It resumed much later.
rewrite: When Uruguay's military regime seized control in 1973, artistic expression in Montevideo was severely stifled. Prominent creator Rimer Cardillo transformed the National Institute of Fine Arts into a center of defiance, prompting a harsh official response. The authorities shut down the institute, confiscating all printing presses and studio tools. As a result, artistic education was forced underground, continuing only in private workshops. These were often led by former political prisoners and focused on printmaking, works on paper, painting, and sculpture. Formal institutional training would not be restored until many years afterward.

input: Native American music in North America is almost entirely monophonic, but there are notable exceptions. Traditional Native American music often centers around drumming. Rattles, clappersticks, and rasps were also popular percussive instruments. Flutes were made of rivercane, cedar, and other woods. The tuning of these flutes is not precise and depends on the length of the wood used and the hand span of the intended player, but the finger holes are most often around a whole step apart and, at least in Northern California, a flute was not used if it turned out to have an interval close to a half step. The Apache fiddle is a single stringed instrument.
rewrite: Indigenous musical traditions across North America are predominantly single-voiced, though some distinct variations exist. Drumming forms the core of many traditional practices. Other common rhythm instruments include rattles, clappersticks, and rasps. Crafted from materials like rivercane and cedar, wooden flutes have imprecise tunings, relying on the instrument's length and the player's hand size. Their finger holes are generally spaced a whole step apart; historically, in Northern California, flutes producing a near half-step interval were avoided. Another instrument is the single-string Apache fiddle.

input: A revolution in 1332 resulted in a broad-based city government with participation of the guilds, and Strasbourg declared itself a free republic. The deadly bubonic plague of 1348 was followed on 14 February 1349 by one of the first and worst pogroms in pre-modern history: over a thousand Jews were publicly burnt to death, with the remainder of the Jewish population being expelled from the city. Until the end of the 18th century, Jews were forbidden to remain in town after 10 pm. The time to leave the city was signalled by a municipal herald blowing the Grüselhorn (see below, Museums, Musée historique);. A special tax, the Pflastergeld (pavement money), was furthermore to be paid for any horse that a Jew would ride or bring into the city while allowed to.
rewrite: In 1332, an uprising established an inclusive civic administration that incorporated guild representation, leading Strasbourg to proclaim its status as an autonomous republic. The catastrophic Black Death in 1348 preceded the severe massacre of February 14, 1349, among the earliest and most brutal of its kind in medieval Europe, where more than a thousand Jewish individuals were executed by public burning and the rest banished. Subsequently, Jewish people faced a curfew prohibiting their presence in the city past 10 o'clock each evening, enforced by a town crier sounding a horn called the Grüselhorn. Additionally, a unique levy known as Pflastergeld was imposed for each horse ridden or introduced by a Jewish visitor during permitted hours.

input: Valleys and plains are found along the coastline and rivers. The north of the province lies just south of the Yangtze Delta, and consists of plains around the cities of Hangzhou, Jiaxing, and Huzhou, where the Grand Canal of China enters from the northern border to end at Hangzhou. Another relatively flat area is found along the Qu River around the cities of Quzhou and Jinhua. Major rivers include the Qiangtang and Ou Rivers. Most rivers carve out valleys in the highlands, with plenty of rapids and other features associated with such topography. Well-known lakes include the West Lake of Hangzhou and the South Lake of Jiaxing.
rewrite: Flat and low-lying lands are situated near the coast and waterways. The province's northern section, positioned directly below the Yangtze Delta, contains level terrain surrounding Hangzhou, Jiaxing, and Huzhou. Here, the Grand Canal crosses the northern boundary and terminates in Hangzhou. A separate area of gentle topography follows the Qu River near Quzhou and Jinhua. Key waterways like the Qiangtang and Ou Rivers flow through the highlands, creating steep valleys marked by rapids and similar formations. Notable lakes are Hangzhou's West Lake and Jiaxing's South Lake.

input: After almost a year in the area around Peenemünde, Soviet officials moved most of the captured German rocket specialists to Gorodomlya Island on Lake Seliger, about 240 kilometers (150 mi) northwest of Moscow. They were not allowed to participate in Soviet missile design, but were used as problem-solving consultants to the Soviet engineers. They helped in the following areas: the creation of a Soviet version of the A-4; work on "organizational schemes"; research in improving the A-4 main engine; development of a 100-ton engine; assistance in the "layout" of plant production rooms; and preparation of rocket assembly using German components. With their help, particularly Helmut Groettrup's group, Korolev reverse-engineered the A-4 and built his own version of the rocket, the R-1, in 1948. Later, he developed his own distinct designs, though many of these designs were influenced by the Groettrup Group's G4-R10 design from 1949. The Germans were eventually repatriated in 1951–53.
rewrite: Following nearly a year near Peenemünde, the majority of the detained German rocket experts were relocated by Soviet authorities to Gorodomlya Island in Lake Seliger, roughly 150 miles northwest of Moscow. Their role was not to directly shape Soviet missile plans, but rather to serve as advisory resources for troubleshooting. Their contributions included aiding in the development of a Soviet replica of the A-4 rocket, refining organizational processes, enhancing the primary engine of the A-4, progressing toward a 100-ton engine design, advising on factory floor plans for manufacturing, and guiding the assembly of rockets from German parts. Notably, Sergei Korolev, with significant input from Helmut Groettrup's team, replicated the A-4 to produce the R-1 by 1948. Subsequent original designs from Korolev were still shaped by concepts from the Groettrup Group's 1949 G4-R10 project. The German specialists were finally sent back to their homeland between 1951 and 1953.

input: Various evolutionary ideas had already been proposed to explain new findings in biology. There was growing support for such ideas among dissident anatomists and the general public, but during the first half of the 19th century the English scientific establishment was closely tied to the Church of England, while science was part of natural theology. Ideas about the transmutation of species were controversial as they conflicted with the beliefs that species were unchanging parts of a designed hierarchy and that humans were unique, unrelated to other animals. The political and theological implications were intensely debated, but transmutation was not accepted by the scientific mainstream.
rewrite: Numerous theories of evolution emerged to account for recent biological discoveries. Although these concepts gained traction with certain radical anatomists and the broader populace, the English scientific elite in the early 1800s remained aligned with the Church of England, viewing science through the lens of natural theology. Proposals that species could change were contentious, opposing established views of a fixed, designed natural order and human exceptionalism. While their social and religious ramifications were hotly contested, such transformative ideas were rejected by prevailing scientific thought.

input: In May 1967, the Eastern Region declared independence as a state called the Republic of Biafra, under the leadership of Lt. Colonel Emeka Ojukwu. The Nigerian Civil War began as the official Nigerian government side (predominated by soldiers from the North and West) attacked Biafra (Southeastern) on 6 July 1967 at Garkem. The 30 month war, with a long siege of Biafra and its isolation from trade and supplies, ended in January 1970. Estimates of the number of dead in the former Eastern Region are between 1 and 3 million people, from warfare, disease, and starvation, during the 30-month civil war.
rewrite: In May 1967, Lt. Colonel Emeka Ojukwu led the Eastern Region to secede, forming the Republic of Biafra. This prompted the Nigerian government, largely supported by northern and western military forces, to initiate the Nigerian Civil War with an assault on Biafra at Garkem on July 6, 1967. The conflict lasted for thirty months, characterized by a prolonged blockade that cut off Biafra from commerce and aid. It concluded in January 1970. The war resulted in an estimated one to three million fatalities in the former Eastern Region due to combat, illness, and famine.

input: Meleager and the infantry supported the candidacy of Alexander's half-brother, Philip Arrhidaeus, while Perdiccas, the leading cavalry commander, supported waiting until the birth of Alexander's unborn child by Roxana. After the infantry stormed the palace of Babylon, a compromise was arranged – Arrhidaeus (as Philip III) should become king, and should rule jointly with Roxana's child, assuming that it was a boy (as it was, becoming Alexander IV). Perdiccas himself would become regent (epimeletes) of the empire, and Meleager his lieutenant. Soon, however, Perdiccas had Meleager and the other infantry leaders murdered, and assumed full control. The generals who had supported Perdiccas were rewarded in the partition of Babylon by becoming satraps of the various parts of the empire, but Perdiccas' position was shaky, because, as Arrian writes, "everyone was suspicious of him, and he of them".
rewrite: Following Alexander the Great's death, a dispute over succession arose. Meleager, leading the infantry, advocated for Alexander's half-brother, Philip Arrhidaeus. In contrast, Perdiccas, the chief cavalry officer, favored awaiting the birth of Alexander's posthumous son by Roxana. After a forceful entry into the Babylonian palace by the foot soldiers, a settlement was reached. Arrhidaeus, as Philip III, would be king and co-rule with Roxana's child if it were male, which it was, named Alexander IV. Perdiccas was appointed imperial regent, with Meleager as his deputy. Perdiccas quickly consolidated power, however, by eliminating Meleager and other infantry commanders. He granted provincial governorships to his loyal generals in the ensuing territorial division, yet his authority remained tenuous. Mutual distrust prevailed, as noted by the historian Arrian, between the regent and his subordinates.

input: In 1873, one of the first papers in modern medicine on the subject tried to explain the pathophysiology of the disease while one in 1872, concluded that asthma can be cured by rubbing the chest with chloroform liniment. Medical treatment in 1880, included the use of intravenous doses of a drug called pilocarpin. In 1886, F.H. Bosworth theorized a connection between asthma and hay fever. Epinephrine was first referred to in the treatment of asthma in 1905. Oral corticosteroids began to be used for this condition in the 1950s while inhaled corticosteroids and selective short acting beta agonist came into wide use in the 1960s.
rewrite: Early modern medical literature from the 1870s attempted to describe asthma's physiological mechanisms, with one 1872 article suggesting chest rubs with chloroform liniment as a cure. By 1880, treatments involved injecting pilocarpin intravenously. A link between asthma and hay fever was proposed by F.H. Bosworth in 1886. The use of epinephrine for asthma was documented in 1905. Oral corticosteroids were introduced in the 1950s, followed by the widespread adoption of inhaled corticosteroids and specific short-acting beta agonists in the 1960s.

input: In January 2008, Kaz Hirai, CEO of Sony Computer Entertainment, suggested that the console may start making a profit by early 2009, stating that, "the next fiscal year starts in April and if we can try to achieve that in the next fiscal year that would be a great thing" and that "[profitability] is not a definite commitment, but that is what I would like to try to shoot for". However, market analysts Nikko Citigroup have predicted that PlayStation 3 could be profitable by August 2008. In a July 2008 interview, Hirai stated that his objective is for PlayStation 3 to sell 150 million units by its ninth year, surpassing PlayStation 2's sales of 140 million in its nine years on the market. In January 2009 Sony announced that their gaming division was profitable in Q3 2008.
rewrite: In early 2008, Sony Computer Entertainment's chief executive Kaz Hirai expressed hope that the PlayStation 3 console could become profitable in the fiscal year beginning April 2008, though he emphasized this was a goal rather than a guarantee. Meanwhile, analysts from Nikko Citigroup forecasted the system might reach profitability even sooner, by that August. Later in 2008, Hirai outlined a long-term ambition for the PS3 to exceed the lifetime sales of its predecessor, targeting over 150 million units sold within nine years. By early 2009, Sony confirmed that its video game sector had returned to profitability during the third quarter of 2008.

input: Besides emptiness, Mahayana schools often place emphasis on the notions of perfected spiritual insight (prajñāpāramitā) and Buddha-nature (tathāgatagarbha). There are conflicting interpretations of the tathāgatagarbha in Mahāyāna thought. The idea may be traced to Abhidharma, and ultimately to statements of the Buddha in the Nikāyas. In Tibetan Buddhism, according to the Sakya school, tathāgatagarbha is the inseparability of the clarity and emptiness of one's mind. In Nyingma, tathāgatagarbha also generally refers to inseparability of the clarity and emptiness of one's mind. According to the Gelug school, it is the potential for sentient beings to awaken since they are empty (i.e. dependently originated). According to the Jonang school, it refers to the innate qualities of the mind that expresses themselves as omniscience etc. when adventitious obscurations are removed. The "Tathāgatagarbha Sutras" are a collection of Mahayana sutras that present a unique model of Buddha-nature. Even though this collection was generally ignored in India, East Asian Buddhism provides some significance to these texts.
rewrite: In addition to the concept of emptiness, Mahayana traditions also highlight the importance of perfected wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) and the inherent potential for Buddhahood (tathāgatagarbha). Within Mahayana philosophy, the interpretation of tathāgatagarbha is not uniform. This concept finds its roots in earlier Abhidharma thought and, ultimately, in discourses attributed to the Buddha within the Nikāyas. Various Tibetan Buddhist schools offer distinct explanations. The Sakya and Nyingma traditions both describe it as the indivisible union of the mind's luminous awareness and its empty nature. The Gelug perspective views it as the capacity for enlightenment present in all beings, stemming from their dependent and empty existence. Conversely, the Jonang school sees it as the mind's innate qualities, such as all-knowing wisdom, which become fully manifest when temporary obscurations are cleared. A set of scriptures known as the "Tathāgatagarbha Sutras" outlines a particular framework for this Buddha-nature doctrine. While these texts received little attention in India, they hold a notable place in the Buddhist traditions of East Asia.

input: In 1978, Josep Lluís Núñez became the first elected president of FC Barcelona, and, since then, the members of Barcelona have elected the club president. The process of electing a president of FC Barcelona was closely tied to Spain's transition to democracy in 1974 and the end of Franco's dictatorship. The new president's main objective was to develop Barcelona into a world-class club by giving it stability both on and off the pitch. His presidency was to last for 22 years, and it deeply affected the image of Barcelona, as Núñez held to a strict policy regarding wages and discipline, letting go of such players as Maradona, Romário and Ronaldo rather than meeting their demands.
rewrite: In 1978, Josep Lluís Núñez was chosen by the membership as the inaugural democratically selected president of FC Barcelona. This electoral system emerged alongside Spain's democratic reforms following the Franco regime. Núñez aimed to build Barcelona into an elite global institution, seeking comprehensive stability. His 22-year tenure profoundly shaped the club's identity through a firm stance on financial and team discipline. Notably, he allowed star players like Maradona, Romário, and Ronaldo to depart instead of acquiescing to their contractual requests.

input: The United Kingdom's constitution, being uncodified and largely unwritten, makes no mention of a prime minister. Though it had de facto existed for centuries, its first mention in official state documents did not occur until the first decade of the twentieth century. Accordingly, it is often said "not to exist", indeed there are several instances of parliament declaring this to be the case. The prime minister sits in the cabinet solely by virtue of occupying another office, either First Lord of the Treasury (office in commission), or more rarely Chancellor of the Exchequer (the last of whom was Balfour in 1905).
rewrite: The constitution of the United Kingdom, which is not consolidated into a single document and is mostly based on convention, contains no reference to the position of prime minister. While the role had been practically established for hundreds of years, it was only formally acknowledged in government records in the early 1900s. As a result, it is frequently described as having no legal standing, a view parliament itself has affirmed on multiple occasions. The prime minister's place in the cabinet is derived entirely from holding a separate ministerial post, typically that of First Lord of the Treasury, or occasionally Chancellor of the Exchequer, as was the case with Balfour in 1905.

input: The earliest known avialan fossils come from the Tiaojishan Formation of China, which has been dated to the late Jurassic period (Oxfordian stage), about 160 million years ago. The avialan species from this time period include Anchiornis huxleyi, Xiaotingia zhengi, and Aurornis xui. The well-known early avialan, Archaeopteryx, dates from slightly later Jurassic rocks (about 155 million years old) from Germany. Many of these early avialans shared unusual anatomical features that may be ancestral to modern birds, but were later lost during bird evolution. These features include enlarged claws on the second toe which may have been held clear of the ground in life, and long feathers or "hind wings" covering the hind limbs and feet, which may have been used in aerial maneuvering.
rewrite: The oldest fossils recognized as avialans, or early birds, originate from China's Tiaojishan Formation. These deposits are from the Oxfordian stage of the late Jurassic, roughly 160 million years in age. Species such as *Anchiornis huxleyi*, *Xiaotingia zhengi*, and *Aurornis xui* are known from this era. A slightly younger example, the famous *Archaeopteryx*, comes from German rocks dated to approximately 155 million years ago. These primitive avialans possessed several distinctive traits, potentially ancestral to contemporary birds but later abandoned. Among these were oversized second-toe claws, likely raised when walking, and lengthy leg feathers that might have functioned as auxiliary wings for flight control.

input: Also in 2005, Spielberg directed a modern adaptation of War of the Worlds (a co-production of Paramount and DreamWorks), based on the H. G. Wells book of the same name (Spielberg had been a huge fan of the book and the original 1953 film). It starred Tom Cruise and Dakota Fanning, and, as with past Spielberg films, Industrial Light & Magic (ILM) provided the visual effects. Unlike E.T. and Close Encounters of the Third Kind, which depicted friendly alien visitors, War of the Worlds featured violent invaders. The film was another huge box office smash, grossing over $591 million worldwide.
rewrite: In 2005, Steven Spielberg helmed a contemporary version of *War of the Worlds*, a joint venture between Paramount and DreamWorks. An admirer of H.G. Wells' original novel and its 1953 movie adaptation, Spielberg cast Tom Cruise and Dakota Fanning. The visual effects were handled by Industrial Light & Magic, a frequent collaborator. input: Alongside the capital, the most popular tourist destinations are Isfahan, Mashhad and Shiraz. In the early 2000s, the industry faced serious limitations in infrastructure, communications, industry standards and personnel training. The majority of the 300,000 tourist visas granted in 2003 were obtained by Asian Muslims, who presumably intended to visit important pilgrimage sites in Mashhad and Qom. input: During the Reformation, the term was hardly used outside of the German politics. The word evangelical (German: evangelisch), which refers to the gospel, was much more widely used for those involved in the religious movement. Nowadays, this word is still preferred among some of the historical Protestant denominations, above all the ones in the German-speaking area such as the EKD. The German word evangelisch means Protestant, and is different from the German evangelikal, which refers to churches shaped by Evangelicalism. The English word evangelical usually refers to Evangelical Protestant churches, and therefore not to Protestantism as a whole. It traces its roots back to the Puritans in England, where Evangelicalism originated, and then was brought to the United States. The word reformatorisch is used as an alternative for evangelisch in German, and is different from English reformed (German: reformiert), which refers to churches shaped by ideas of John Calvin, Huldrych Zwingli and other Reformed theologians.
rewrite: Throughout the Reformation era, the specific term saw little use beyond the sphere of German political discourse. The descriptor "evangelical" (German: *evangelisch*), denoting a connection to the gospel, was far more common for participants in the movement. In contemporary times, this designation remains favored by certain traditional Protestant groups, particularly within German-speaking regions like the EKD. In German, *evangelisch* equates to Protestant generally, distinct from *evangelikal*, which describes churches influenced by Evangelicalism. The English term "evangelical" typically denotes Evangelical Protestant denominations specifically, rather than encompassing all Protestant faiths. Its origins lie with the English Puritans, from whom Evangelicalism sprang before spreading to America. In German, *reformatorisch* serves as another word for *evangelisch*, and should not be confused with the English "reformed" (German: *reformiert*), which pertains to churches following the doctrines of John Calvin, Huldrych Zwingli, and similar theologians.

input: Roofs are traditionally constructed from Alpine rocks such as pieces of schist, gneiss or slate. Such chalets are typically found in the higher parts of the valleys, as in the Maurienne valley in Savoy, where the amount of snow during the cold months is important. The inclination of the roof cannot exceed 40%, allowing the snow to stay on top, thereby functioning as insulation from the cold. In the lower areas where the forests are widespread, wooden tiles are traditionally used. Commonly made of Norway spruce, they are called "tavaillon". The Alpine regions are multicultural and linguistically diverse. Dialects are common, and vary from valley to valley and region to region. In the Slavic Alps alone 19 dialects have been identified. Some of the French dialects spoken in the French, Swiss and Italian alps of Aosta Valley derive from Arpitan, while the southern part of the western range is related to Old Provençal; the German dialects derive from Germanic tribal languages. Romansh, spoken by two percent of the population in southeast Switzerland, is an ancient Rhaeto-Romanic language derived from Latin, remnants of ancient Celtic languages and perhaps Etruscan.
rewrite:
In Alpine architecture, roofs are often built using local stone, including varieties like schist, gneiss, or slate. These structures are common at higher elevations, such as in Savoy's Maurienne valley, where heavy snowfall occurs in winter. The roof slope is kept at a maximum of 40 percent so that snow accumulates, providing a layer of thermal insulation. At lower altitudes, where trees are abundant, wooden shingles are the classic material. Typically fashioned from Norway spruce, these are known as "tavaillon."

The Alps host a rich tapestry of cultures and languages. Distinct dialects exist, often changing between neighboring valleys and areas. For example, within the Slavic Alps, researchers have cataloged nineteen separate dialects. In the French, Swiss, and Italian Alps of the Aosta Valley, certain French dialects trace their roots to Arpitan, whereas those in the southern western Alps connect to Old Provençal. German dialects in the region evolved from early Germanic tongues. Additionally, Romansh—spoken by a small minority in southeastern Switzerland—is a Rhaeto-Romanic language with Latin origins, also preserving elements of ancient Celtic and possibly Etruscan speech.

input: There was a linguistic predisposition to use such terms. The Romans had used them in near Gaul / far Gaul, near Spain / far Spain and others. Before them the Greeks had the habit, which appears in Linear B, the oldest known script of Europe, referring to the near province and the far province of the kingdom of Pylos. Usually these terms were given with reference to a geographic feature, such as a mountain range or a river.
rewrite: A tendency existed in language to employ these expressions. Romans applied them to regions like Gaul and Spain, distinguishing between nearby and distant areas. Earlier, Greeks displayed this practice in Linear B, Europe's earliest writing, noting proximal and remote provinces of Pylos. Typically, such terms were assigned relative to physical landmarks like rivers or mountains.

input: Winter, and a deteriorating supply situation on both sides of troops and materiel, led to a halt in ground operations. Sevastopol remained invested by the allies, while the allied armies were hemmed in by the Russian army in the interior. On 14 November a storm sank thirty allied transport ships including HMS Prince which was carrying a cargo of winter clothing.:435 The storm and heavy traffic caused the road from the coast to the troops to disintegrate into a quagmire, requiring engineers to devote most of their time to its repair including quarrying stone. A tramroad was ordered. It arrived in January with a civilian engineering crew, however it was March before it was sufficiently advanced to be of any appreciable value.:439 An Electrical telegraph was also ordered, but the frozen ground delayed its installation until March, when communications from the base port of Balaklava to the British HQ was established. The Pipe-and-cable-laying plough failed because of the hard frozen soil, but even so 21 miles of cable were laid.:449
rewrite: As winter set in, worsening shortages of personnel and equipment for all forces brought land campaigns to a standstill. The allied forces maintained their siege of Sevastopol, yet their own positions inland were effectively blockaded by Russian troops. A severe storm on 14 November resulted in the loss of thirty allied supply vessels, among them HMS Prince, laden with essential cold-weather gear. This tempest, combined with constant military traffic, turned the vital coastal road into an impassable bog, forcing engineers to focus relentlessly on repairs and even to quarry stone for the purpose. The construction of a tramway was authorized; it reached the area in January along with a team of civilian engineers, but it did not become operational until March. Similarly, plans for an electrical telegraph were hampered by frozen terrain, delaying its completion until spring, when a line was finally set up between Balaklava and British headquarters. Attempts to use a specialized plough for laying cable and pipe were thwarted by the hardened ground, despite which over twenty miles of line were successfully installed.

input: In November 1790, François-Louis-Thibault de Menonville, a member of the National Assembly of France, wrote to Burke, praising Reflections and requesting more "very refreshing mental food" that he could publish. This Burke did in April 1791 when he published A Letter to a Member of the National Assembly. Burke called for external forces to reverse the revolution and included an attack on the late French philosopher Jean-Jacques Rousseau, as being the subject of a personality cult that had developed in revolutionary France. Although Burke conceded that Rousseau sometimes showed "a considerable insight into human nature" he mostly was critical. Although he did not meet Rousseau on his visit to Britain in 1766–7 Burke was a friend of David Hume, with whom Rousseau had stayed. Burke said Rousseau "entertained no principle either to influence of his heart, or to guide his understanding—but vanity"—which he "was possessed to a degree little short of madness". He also cited Rousseau's Confessions as evidence that Rousseau had a life of "obscure and vulgar vices" that was not "chequered, or spotted here and there, with virtues, or even distinguished by a single good action". Burke contrasted Rousseau's theory of universal benevolence and his having sent his children to a foundling hospital: "a lover of his kind, but a hater of his kindred".
rewrite:
In April 1791, Edmund Burke issued *A Letter to a Member of the National Assembly*. This work was a response to an earlier request from François-Louis-Thibault de Menonville, a French legislator, who had written in November 1790 to commend Burke’s *Reflections on the Revolution in France* and to ask for further intellectual sustenance. Within the letter, Burke urged foreign powers to intervene and overturn the revolutionary changes in France. He also launched a pointed critique of Jean-Jacques Rousseau, who had died more than a decade earlier, accusing him of becoming the object of a cult-like admiration among the revolutionaries.

While Burke acknowledged that Rousseau occasionally demonstrated perceptive views on human behavior, his overall assessment was harsh. Although the two never met during Rousseau’s stay in Britain in the 1760s, Burke was close to the philosopher David Hume, who had hosted Rousseau. Burke asserted that Rousseau was driven almost exclusively by an insane level of pride, lacking any sincere moral or intellectual compass. He pointed to Rousseau’s own *Confessions* as revealing an existence marred by commonplace moral failings, unrelieved by any notable virtuous acts. Burke highlighted the contradiction between Rousseau’s advocacy for general human compassion and his personal decision to place his offspring in a foundling home, sarcastically labeling him a man who professed love for humanity but neglected his own family.

input: In some cases a wrestler may possess admirable physical traits but perceived mediocre public speaking abilities (such as Brock Lesnar), or their gimmick may be that of a "wild savage" needing a handler (such as Kamala). Such performers have historically employed a manager, who speaks on their behalf and adds to the performance. Managers have sometimes become major personalities, including Bobby Heenan, Paul Heyman, Ernie Roth, and Paul Bearer. A manager role may also be filled by a "valet", typically an appealing female who may participate in love triangle storylines, "damsel in distress" situations, and scripted fights with female wrestlers. Some of these have also gone on to become recognized stars, such as Tammy Lynn Sytch, Stacy Keibler, and Miss Elizabeth.
rewrite: Certain wrestlers may exhibit impressive athleticism yet be viewed as lacking in charisma or verbal skills, like Brock Lesnar, or portray an untamed character requiring supervision, such as Kamala. Historically, these individuals have utilized a manager to act as their spokesperson and enhance their act. These managers themselves have often risen to prominence, with figures like Bobby Heenan and Paul Heyman becoming iconic. Alternatively, a "valet"—often an attractive woman—might assume this role, involving herself in romantic plots, perilous scenarios, or staged conflicts with other women. Notable valets like Miss Elizabeth and Stacy Keibler have also achieved significant fame in the industry.

input: The clock does not run during convert attempts in the last three minutes of a half. If the 15 minutes of a quarter expire while the ball is live, the quarter is extended until the ball becomes dead. If a quarter's time expires while the ball is dead, the quarter is extended for one more scrimmage. A quarter cannot end while a penalty is pending: after the penalty yardage is applied, the quarter is extended one scrimmage. Note that the non-penalized team has the option to decline any penalty it considers disadvantageous, so a losing team cannot indefinitely prolong a game by repeatedly committing infractions.
rewrite: During the final three minutes of each half, the game clock is stopped for conversion tries. Should a quarter's fifteen minutes elapse with the ball in play, play continues until the ball is dead. If time runs out while the ball is dead, the quarter gets one additional scrimmage. A period cannot conclude with a penalty pending; following the enforcement, one more play is run. Importantly, the team not penalized may decline any penalty, preventing a trailing team from endlessly extending the game by committing fouls.

input: In the 1840s Nicholas I reduced 64,000 szlachta to commoner status. Despite this, 62.8% of Russia's nobles were szlachta in 1858 and still 46.1% in 1897. Serfdom was abolished in Russian Poland on February 19, 1864. It was deliberately enacted in a way that would ruin the szlachta. It was the only area where peasants paid the market price in redemption for the land (the average for the empire was 34% above the market price). All land taken from Polish peasants since 1846 was to be returned without redemption payments. The ex serfs could only sell land to other peasants, not szlachta. 90% of the ex serfs in the empire who actually gained land after 1861 were in the 8 western provinces. Along with Romania, Polish landless or domestic serfs were the only ones to be given land after serfdom was abolished. All this was to punish the szlachta's role in the uprisings of 1830 and 1863. By 1864 80% of szlachta were déclassé, 1/4 petty nobles were worse off than the average serf, 48.9% of land in Russian Poland was in peasant hands, nobles still held 46%. In Second Polish Republic the privileges of the nobility were lawfully abolished by the March Constitution in 1921 and as such not granted by any future Polish law.
rewrite: During the 1840s, Tsar Nicholas I stripped approximately 64,000 members of the Polish nobility, or szlachta, of their noble rank. Nevertheless, this group continued to constitute a majority of Russia's nobles in 1858 at 62.8%, and still represented 46.1% by 1897. Serfdom was ended in Russian Poland on February 19, 1864, through a decree specifically designed to weaken the szlachta economically. Unlike in other parts of the empire, where peasants paid redemption fees averaging 34% over market value for land, here they paid the market price. Additionally, any land taken from peasants after 1846 was restored without any compensation required. Former serfs were also prohibited from selling their land back to the nobility. Notably, 90% of former serfs in the empire who obtained land after the 1861 reforms resided in eight western provinces. Alongside Romania, Polish landless or domestic serfs were uniquely granted land upon emancipation. These measures collectively served as retribution for the szlachta's involvement in the 1830 and 1863 insurrections. By 1864, 80% of the szlachta had lost their social standing, with a quarter of minor nobles living in conditions worse than the average serf. Land ownership in Russian Poland shifted, with peasants holding 48.9% and nobles retaining 46%. Later, in the Second Polish Republic, the March Constitution of 1921 legally terminated all noble privileges, a status never reinstated by subsequent legislation.

input: In 1976 the future Labour prime minister James Callaghan launched what became known as the 'great debate' on the education system. He went on to list the areas he felt needed closest scrutiny: the case for a core curriculum, the validity and use of informal teaching methods, the role of school inspection and the future of the examination system. Comprehensive school remains the most common type of state secondary school in England, and the only type in Wales. They account for around 90% of pupils, or 64% if one does not count schools with low-level selection. This figure varies by region.
rewrite: In 1976, James Callaghan, who would later become the Labour Prime Minister, initiated a significant national discussion concerning education. He highlighted several key issues for examination, including the potential need for a standardized core curriculum, the effectiveness of relaxed teaching approaches, the function of school inspections, and how assessments should evolve. In England, the comprehensive model continues to dominate the state secondary sector, and it is the exclusive form in Wales. Approximately 90% of students attend such schools, dropping to 64% when excluding those with minimal selective intake, with regional differences affecting these statistics.

input: Kerry's commanding officer, Lieutenant Commander George Elliott, stated to Douglas Brinkley in 2003 that he did not know whether to court-martial Kerry for beaching the boat without orders or give him a medal for saving the crew. Elliott recommended Kerry for the Silver Star, and Zumwalt flew into An Thoi to personally award medals to Kerry and the rest of the sailors involved in the mission. The Navy's account of Kerry's actions is presented in the original medal citation signed by Zumwalt. The engagement was documented in an after-action report, a press release written on March 1, 1969, and a historical summary dated March 17, 1969.
rewrite: In 2003, Lieutenant Commander George Elliott, who oversaw Kerry, told historian Douglas Brinkley he was conflicted: he considered both disciplining Kerry for grounding the vessel without authorization and commending him for safeguarding the men. Ultimately, Elliott put Kerry forward for the Silver Star. Admiral Zumwalt traveled to An Thoi to present the award to Kerry and his fellow crew members. The official Navy record of these events is contained in the original citation endorsed by Zumwalt. Details of the incident were also recorded in a subsequent operational report, a press statement from March 1, 1969, and a historical account dated March 17, 1969.

input: Carrying a Louis Vuitton backpack filled with old disks and demos to the studio and back, West crafted much of his production for his debut album in less than fifteen minutes at a time. He recorded the remainder of the album in Los Angeles while recovering from the car accident. Once he had completed the album, it was leaked months before its release date. However, West decided to use the opportunity to review the album, and The College Dropout was significantly remixed, remastered, and revised before being released. As a result, certain tracks originally destined for the album were subsequently retracted, among them "Keep the Receipt" with Ol' Dirty Bastard and "The Good, the Bad, and the Ugly" with Consequence. West meticulously refined the production, adding string arrangements, gospel choirs, improved drum programming and new verses. West's perfectionism led The College Dropout to have its release postponed three times from its initial date in August 2003.
rewrite: Kanye West often produced tracks for his first album in brief, intense bursts, sometimes taking under fifteen minutes to create a beat while transporting his materials in a Louis Vuitton bag. After a serious car crash, he finished recording the project in Los Angeles during his recuperation. The completed work was unexpectedly leaked well ahead of schedule. Rather than seeing this as a setback, West treated it as a chance to critically re-evaluate his music. He undertook a comprehensive overhaul of *The College Dropout*, which included remixing, remastering, and rewriting much of the content. This process involved incorporating new elements like string sections and gospel vocals, enhancing the drum patterns, and recording additional lyrics. Due to this meticulous revision, several planned songs were ultimately cut from the final tracklist. His relentless drive for perfection also caused the album's launch to be delayed on three separate occasions from its original August 2003 schedule.

input: Instead, he formulated the spearhead model of evolution, a version of genetic pluralism. According to this model, living organisms themselves have goals, and act according to these goals, each guided by a central control. In its most sophisticated form, this is the brain of humans, but controls also exist in much less sophisticated ways for species of lower complexity, such as the amoeba. This control organ plays a special role in evolution—it is the "spearhead of evolution". The goals bring the purpose into the world. Mutations in the genes that determine the structure of the control may then cause drastic changes in behaviour, preferences and goals, without having an impact on the organism's phenotype. Popper postulates that such purely behavioural changes are less likely to be lethal for the organism compared to drastic changes of the phenotype.
rewrite: He proposed an evolutionary framework centered on genetic diversity, where life forms pursue inherent aims under the guidance of a primary regulating mechanism. In advanced creatures like humans, this regulator is the brain, while simpler beings such as amoebas possess more basic versions. This controlling element acts as the driving force or forefront of evolutionary change. Purpose enters nature through these objectives. Alterations in the genes shaping the regulator can lead to significant shifts in behavior, desires, and aims, even if the physical form remains unchanged. It is suggested that such behavioral adjustments are generally less dangerous to survival than sudden transformations of the body's structure.

input: Political color schemes in the United States diverge from international norms. Since 2000, red has become associated with the right-wing Republican Party and blue with the left-wing Democratic Party. However, unlike political color schemes of other countries, the parties did not choose those colors; they were used in news coverage of 2000 election results and ensuing legal battle and caught on in popular usage. Prior to the 2000 election the media typically alternated which color represented which party each presidential election cycle.
