The color scheme happened to get inordinate attention that year, so the cycle was stopped lest it cause confusion the following election.
rewrite: In the United States, the political color system differs from global conventions. The Republican Party, representing the right, is now linked to red, while the left-leaning Democratic Party is tied to blue. These associations were not selected by the parties themselves. Instead, they originated from television news graphics during the protracted 2000 election dispute and then entered common parlance. Before that year, media outlets would routinely swap the colors assigned to each major party with every new presidential race. The particular scheme used in 2000 received exceptional focus, leading to its fixed adoption to prevent public confusion in future elections.

input: Marvel counts among its characters such well-known superheroes as Spider-Man, Iron Man, Captain America, Wolverine, Thor, Hulk, Ant-Man, such teams as the Avengers, the Guardians of the Galaxy, the Fantastic Four, the Inhumans and the X-Men, and antagonists such as Doctor Doom, The Enchantress, Green Goblin, Ultron, Doctor Octopus, Thanos, Magneto and Loki. Most of Marvel's fictional characters operate in a single reality known as the Marvel Universe, with locations that mirror real-life cities. Characters such as Spider-Man, the Fantastic Four, the Avengers, Daredevil and Doctor Strange are based in New York City, whereas the X-Men have historically been based in Salem Center, New York and Hulk's stories often have been set in the American Southwest.
rewrite: Marvel's roster includes iconic heroes like Spider-Man, Iron Man, and Captain America, alongside groups such as the Avengers, X-Men, and Fantastic Four. Notable villains feature Doctor Doom, Magneto, and Thanos. The majority of these characters inhabit a shared reality called the Marvel Universe, which parallels real-world settings. For instance, New York City serves as the backdrop for Spider-Man, the Avengers, and Daredevil, while the X-Men are traditionally associated with Salem Center, New York. The Hulk's adventures frequently unfold across the American Southwest.

input: The Macintosh (/ˈmækᵻntɒʃ/ MAK-in-tosh; branded as Mac since 1997) is a series of personal computers (PCs) designed, developed, and marketed by Apple Inc. Steve Jobs introduced the original Macintosh computer on January 24, 1984. This was the first mass-market personal computer featuring an integral graphical user interface and mouse. This first model was later renamed to "Macintosh 128k" for uniqueness amongst a populous family of subsequently updated models which are also based on Apple's same proprietary architecture. Since 1998, Apple has largely phased out the Macintosh name in favor of "Mac", though the product family has been nicknamed "Mac" or "the Mac" since the development of the first model.
rewrite: Introduced by Steve Jobs in early 1984, the original Macintosh was a landmark personal computer from Apple Inc. It stood out as the first widely sold PC to include a built-in graphical interface and a mouse. This inaugural version was later distinguished as the "Macintosh 128k" within a growing line of successors sharing Apple's unique internal architecture. While officially branded simply as "Mac" since 1997, and colloquially called that since its inception, the product series retains its foundational identity.

input: Even though, both Kashmir Shaivism and Advaita Vedanta are non-dual philosophies which give primacy to Universal Consciousness (Chit or Brahman), in Kashmir Shavisim, as opposed to Advaita, all things are a manifestation of this Consciousness. This implies that from the point of view of Kashmir Shavisim, the phenomenal world (Śakti) is real, and it exists and has its being in Consciousness (Chit). Whereas, Advaita holds that Brahman is inactive (niṣkriya) and the phenomenal world is an illusion (māyā). The objective of human life, according to Kashmir Shaivism, is to merge in Shiva or Universal Consciousness, or to realize one's already existing identity with Shiva, by means of wisdom, yoga and grace.
rewrite: While Kashmir Shaivism and Advaita Vedanta both center on a supreme Universal Consciousness, they diverge significantly. Kashmir Shaivism views all reality as a genuine expression of this Consciousness; the material world is real and inherent within it. Conversely, Advaita Vedanta sees the supreme principle as static and regards the perceived universe as illusory. For followers of Kashmir Shaivism, the ultimate human aim is to unite with this divine Consciousness, recognizing one's fundamental oneness with it through insight, disciplined practice, and divine blessing.

input: The broad field of animal communication encompasses most of the issues in ethology. Animal communication can be defined as any behavior of one animal that affects the current or future behavior of another animal. The study of animal communication, called zoo semiotics (distinguishable from anthroposemiotics, the study of human communication) has played an important part in the development of ethology, sociobiology, and the study of animal cognition. Animal communication, and indeed the understanding of the animal world in general, is a rapidly growing field, and even in the 21st century so far, a great share of prior understanding related to diverse fields such as personal symbolic name use, animal emotions, animal culture and learning, and even sexual conduct, long thought to be well understood, has been revolutionized. A special field of animal communication has been investigated in more detail such as vibrational communication.
rewrite: The discipline of ethology largely involves the extensive study of how animals communicate. This communication occurs when one creature's actions influence the behavior of another, either immediately or later. Research in this area, known as zoo semiotics—separate from the study of human signals—has significantly contributed to advances in ethology, sociobiology, and understanding animal minds. Knowledge of animal interaction and the natural world is expanding quickly. Even in recent decades, many long-held assumptions across various domains, including the use of individual names, emotional experiences, cultural practices, learning, and mating behaviors, have been fundamentally transformed. More focused research continues to explore specific channels, such as communication through vibrations.

input: Barcelona is one of the most supported teams in the world, and has the largest social media following in the world among sports teams. Barcelona's players have won a record number of Ballon d'Or awards (11), as well as a record number of FIFA World Player of the Year awards (7). In 2010, the club made history when three players who came through its youth academy (Messi, Iniesta and Xavi) were chosen as the three best players in the world in the FIFA Ballon d'Or awards, an unprecedented feat for players from the same football school.
rewrite: With a massive global fanbase, Barcelona leads all sports franchises in social media followers. Its athletes have earned a record eleven Ballon d’Or honors and seven FIFA World Player of the Year titles. The club achieved a unique milestone in 2010 when the top three spots for the FIFA Ballon d’Or were all taken by graduates of its youth system—Messi, Iniesta, and Xavi—marking the first time a single academy produced the world’s top trio.

input: Craig Venter and Francis Collins of the National Institute of Health jointly made the announcement of the mapping of the human genome in 2000. Upon examining the data from the genome mapping, Venter realized that although the genetic variation within the human species is on the order of 1–3% (instead of the previously assumed 1%), the types of variations do not support notion of genetically defined races. Venter said, "Race is a social concept. It's not a scientific one. There are no bright lines (that would stand out), if we could compare all the sequenced genomes of everyone on the planet." "When we try to apply science to try to sort out these social differences, it all falls apart."
rewrite: In 2000, Craig Venter and Francis Collins from the National Institutes of Health together revealed the completed human genome. After studying this genetic map, Venter noted that human genetic diversity is about 1–3%, slightly higher than earlier estimates. However, he found that the patterns of this variation do not align with the idea of biologically distinct races. Venter emphasized that race is a societal construct, not a scientific classification. He explained that if we analyzed every person's genome, no clear genetic boundaries would emerge to separate racial groups. Applying scientific scrutiny to these social categories, he argued, reveals their lack of a biological foundation.

input: There are several sources of the seedlessness trait, and essentially all commercial cultivators get it from one of three sources: Thompson Seedless, Russian Seedless, and Black Monukka, all being cultivars of Vitis vinifera. There are currently more than a dozen varieties of seedless grapes. Several, such as Einset Seedless, Benjamin Gunnels's Prime seedless grapes, Reliance, and Venus, have been specifically cultivated for hardiness and quality in the relatively cold climates of northeastern United States and southern Ontario.
rewrite: The trait of lacking seeds originates from multiple sources, yet nearly all commercial growers obtain it from three specific Vitis vinifera types: Thompson Seedless, Russian Seedless, and Black Monukka. Over a dozen seedless grape varieties exist today. Some, like Einset Seedless, Benjamin Gunnels's Prime, Reliance, and Venus, were bred for resilience and superior fruit in colder regions such as the northeastern U.S. and southern Ontario.

input: Philosophical empiricists hold no knowledge to be properly inferred or deduced unless it is derived from one's sense-based experience. This view is commonly contrasted with rationalism, which states that knowledge may be derived from reason independently of the senses. For example, John Locke held that some knowledge (e.g. knowledge of God's existence) could be arrived at through intuition and reasoning alone. Similarly Robert Boyle, a prominent advocate of the experimental method, held that we have innate ideas. The main continental rationalists (Descartes, Spinoza, and Leibniz) were also advocates of the empirical "scientific method".
rewrite: Empiricists in philosophy assert that genuine knowledge must originate from sensory experiences, rather than being concluded through inference alone. This stands in opposition to rationalism, which maintains that reason alone can be a source of knowledge, separate from the senses. Figures like John Locke believed certain truths, such as the existence of God, could be grasped through intuition and reason. Even early scientists like Robert Boyle, while championing experimentation, accepted innate ideas. Notably, key rationalist thinkers, including Descartes, also endorsed empirical scientific approaches.

input: There has, however, been interest among railroad operators in returning to DC use at higher voltages than previously used. At the same voltage, DC often has less loss than AC, and for this reason high-voltage direct current is already used on some bulk power transmission lines. DC avoids the electromagnetic radiation inherent with AC, and on a railway this also reduces interference with signalling and communications and mitigates hypothetical EMF risks. DC also avoids the power factor problems of AC. Of particular interest to railroading is that DC can supply constant power with a single ungrounded wire. Constant power with AC requires three-phase transmission with at least two ungrounded wires. Another important consideration is that mains-frequency 3-phase AC must be carefully planned to avoid unbalanced phase loads. Parts of the system are supplied from different phases on the assumption that the total loads of the 3 phases will even out. At the phase break points between regions supplied from different phases, long insulated supply breaks are required to avoid them being shorted by rolling stock using more than one pantograph at a time. A few railroads have tried 3-phase but its substantial complexity has made single-phase standard practice despite the interruption in power flow that occurs twice every cycle. An experimental 6 kV DC railway was built in the Soviet Union.
rewrite:
Rail companies are now exploring the potential of using direct current at increased voltage levels. Direct current systems typically experience lower energy loss compared to alternating current when operating at the same voltage, a principle already applied in certain long-distance electrical grids. DC power does not produce the same electromagnetic emissions as AC, which on railways means less disruption to signals and communication systems, along with reduced concerns about electromagnetic field exposure. Additionally, DC sidesteps the power factor issues associated with AC.

For rail operations, a significant advantage of DC is its ability to deliver steady power through just one ungrounded wire. Achieving consistent power with AC necessitates a three-phase system with a minimum of two such wires. Another key factor is that standard three-phase AC requires meticulous design to prevent uneven loading across phases. Different sections of track are fed from separate phases, relying on the overall system load to balance them. At the boundaries where these phases meet, extensive insulated gaps are essential to prevent short circuits, especially if a train uses multiple overhead collectors simultaneously. While a handful of railways have tested three-phase AC, its considerable complexity has led to the widespread adoption of single-phase AC, despite its periodic power interruptions. Historically, an experimental railway in the Soviet Union operated using a 6,000-volt DC system.

input: At times a character may "turn", altering their face/heel alignment. This may be an abrupt, surprising event, or it may slowly build up over time. It almost always is accomplished with a markable change in behavior on the part of the character. Some turns become defining points in a wrestler's career, as was the case when Hulk Hogan turned heel after being a top face for over a decade. Others may have no noticeable effect on the character's status. If a character repeatedly switches between being a face and heel, this lessens the effect of such turns, and may result in apathy from the audience. Vince McMahon is a good example of having more heel and face turns than anyone in WWE history.
rewrite: Occasionally, a performer in wrestling will undergo a significant shift in their moral alignment, switching from hero to villain or vice versa. This transformation can occur suddenly or develop gradually through a series of events. It is typically signaled by a distinct and observable change in the wrestler's conduct and demeanor. Certain realignments become iconic, career-defining moments, such as Hulk Hogan's infamous shift to villainy following years as a celebrated hero. Others may pass with little lasting impact. When a character frequently alternates between these roles, the dramatic weight of each change diminishes, potentially leading to viewer indifference. Vince McMahon exemplifies this, having reversed his persona more often than any other figure in the promotion's history.

input: Chengdu Hi-tech Development Zone covers an area of 82.5 km2 (31.9 sq mi), consisting of the South Park and the West Park. By relying on the city sub-center, which is under construction, the South Park is focusing on creating a modernized industrial park of science and technology with scientific and technological innovation, incubation R&D, modern service industry and Headquarters economy playing leading roles. Priority has been given to the development of software industry. Located on both sides of the "Chengdu-Dujiangyan-Jiuzhaigou" golden tourism channel, the West Park aims at building a comprehensive industrial park targeting at industrial clustering with complete supportive functions. The West Park gives priority to three major industries i.e. electronic information, biomedicine and precision machinery.
rewrite: The Chengdu Hi-tech Development Zone spans 82.5 square kilometers and is divided into two primary sections: the South Park and the West Park. The South Park leverages the emerging city sub-center to establish a contemporary science and technology hub. This area emphasizes technological innovation, research incubation, modern services, and corporate headquarters, with a particular focus on advancing the software sector. Situated along the key "Chengdu-Dujiangyan-Jiuzhaigou" tourism route, the West Park is designed as an integrated industrial cluster with full supporting infrastructure. It prioritizes three core industries: electronic information, biomedicine, and precision machinery.

input: In 1960, Columbia/CBS began negotiations with its main international distributor Philips Records with the goal of CBS starting its own global record company. Philips' acquisition of Mercury Records in the US in 1961 paved the way for this. CBS only had the rights to the Columbia name in North America; therefore the international arm founded in 1961 and launched in 1962 utilized the "CBS Records" name only, with Philips Records distributing the label in Europe. CBS's Mexican record company, Discos Columbia, was renamed Discos CBS by 1963.
rewrite: In 1960, Columbia/CBS entered talks with its primary overseas partner, Philips Records, aiming to establish a worldwide record division under CBS. The 1961 purchase of Mercury Records by Philips in the U.S. facilitated this move. Since CBS held the Columbia trademark solely in North America, the new international branch, created in 1961 and introduced in 1962, operated exclusively as "CBS Records," distributed in Europe by Philips. By 1963, the Mexican affiliate Discos Columbia had also been rebranded as Discos CBS.

input: According to the tradition, Virgil traveled to Greece in about 19 BC to revise the Aeneid. After meeting Augustus in Athens and deciding to return home, Virgil caught a fever while visiting a town near Megara. After crossing to Italy by ship, weakened with disease, Virgil died in Brundisium harbor on September 21, 19 BC. Augustus ordered Virgil's literary executors, Lucius Varius Rufus and Plotius Tucca, to disregard Virgil's own wish that the poem be burned, instead ordering it published with as few editorial changes as possible. As a result, the text of the Aeneid that exists may contain faults which Virgil was planning to correct before publication. However, the only obvious imperfections are a few lines of verse that are metrically unfinished (i.e. not a complete line of dactylic hexameter). Some scholars have argued that Virgil deliberately left these metrically incomplete lines for dramatic effect. Other alleged imperfections are subject to scholarly debate.
rewrite: As recorded, the poet Virgil journeyed to Greece around 19 BCE to make final improvements to his epic, the Aeneid. While returning to Italy after encountering Emperor Augustus in Athens, he fell ill with a fever near Megara. Though he reached Italy by sea, his health had deteriorated, and he passed away upon arrival at Brundisium on September 21 of that year. Contrary to Virgil's directive to destroy the manuscript, Augustus commanded his literary heirs, Varius Rufus and Plotius Tucca, to publish the work with minimal alterations. Consequently, the surviving version likely includes errors the author intended to fix. The most noticeable flaws are a handful of metrically incomplete verses. While some interpreters suggest these half-lines were intentional artistic choices, other potential defects remain topics of academic discussion.

input: The team placed fifth in the Premier League automatically qualifies for the UEFA Europa League, and the sixth and seventh-placed teams can also qualify, depending on the winners of the two domestic cup competitions i.e. the FA Cup and the Capital One Cup (League Cup). Two Europa League places are reserved for the winners of each tournament; if the winner of either the FA Cup or League Cup qualifies for the Champions League, then that place will go to the next-best placed finisher in the Premier League. A further place in the UEFA Europa League is also available via the Fair Play initiative. If the Premier League has one of the three highest Fair Play rankings in Europe, the highest ranked team in the Premier League Fair Play standings which has not already qualified for Europe will automatically qualify for the UEFA Europa League first qualifying round.
rewrite: Securing fifth position in the Premier League grants an automatic entry into the UEFA Europa League. Additionally, the clubs finishing sixth and seventh have opportunities to qualify, contingent on the outcomes of the FA Cup and the League Cup. Each of these domestic cup victories provides a Europa League berth. Should a cup champion already earn a spot in the Champions League, their Europa League place is then transferred to the highest-ranking Premier League side not yet qualified for Europe. Another potential route is through the Fair Play system. If the Premier League ranks among the top three in Europe for Fair Play, the highest-rated team in its Fair Play table that hasn't secured European competition entry will earn a place in the Europa League's initial qualifying stage.

input: Hokkien /hɒˈkiɛn/ (traditional Chinese: 福建話; simplified Chinese: 福建话; pinyin: Fújiànhuà; Pe̍h-ōe-jī: Hok-kiàn oē) or Quanzhang (Quanzhou–Zhangzhou / Chinchew–Changchew; BP: Zuánziū–Ziāngziū) is a group of mutually intelligible Min Nan Chinese dialects spoken throughout Southeast Asia, Taiwan, and by many other overseas Chinese. Hokkien originated from a dialect in southern Fujian. It is closely related to the Teochew, though mutual comprehension is difficult, and is somewhat more distantly related to Hainanese. Besides Hokkien, there are also other Min and Hakka dialects in Fujian province, most of which are not mutually intelligible with Hokkien.
rewrite: Hokkien, also known as Quanzhang, refers to a collection of similar Min Nan language varieties. These dialects are spoken widely in Southeast Asia, Taiwan, and among overseas Chinese communities. The language traces its roots to southern Fujian province. While it shares connections with Teochew, understanding between speakers is limited, and its relation to Hainanese is more distant. Within Fujian, numerous other Min and Hakka dialects exist, most of which cannot be easily understood by Hokkien speakers.

input: Santa Monica is a beachfront city in western Los Angeles County, California, United States. The city is named after the Christian saint, Monica. Situated on Santa Monica Bay, it is bordered on three sides by the city of Los Angeles – Pacific Palisades to the north, Brentwood on the northeast, Sawtelle on the east, Mar Vista on the southeast, and Venice on the south. Santa Monica is well known for its affluent single-family neighborhoods but also has many neighborhoods consisting primarily of condominiums and apartments. Over two-thirds of Santa Monica's residents are renters. The Census Bureau population for Santa Monica in 2010 was 89,736.
rewrite: Located in California's Los Angeles County, Santa Monica is a coastal community facing the Pacific Ocean. Its name honors Saint Monica, a Christian figure. The city is nearly encircled by Los Angeles, with boundaries touching areas like Pacific Palisades, Brentwood, and Venice. While famous for its wealthy neighborhoods of standalone homes, a significant portion of its housing includes condos and apartment buildings. Most people living here lease their homes. The 2010 census recorded the population as nearly 90,000.

input: In 1862, paper money was issued without the backing of precious metals, due to the Civil War. Silver and gold coins continued to be issued and in 1878 the link between paper money and coins was reinstated. This disconnection from gold and silver backing also occurred during the War of 1812. The use of paper money not backed by precious metals had also occurred under the Articles of Confederation from 1777 to 1788. With no solid backing and being easily counterfeited, the continentals quickly lost their value, giving rise to the phrase "not worth a continental". This was a primary reason for the "No state shall... make any thing but gold and silver coin a tender in payment of debts" clause in article 1, section 10 of the United States Constitution.
rewrite: During the Civil War in 1862, currency was printed without being convertible into gold or silver, though minting of those coins persisted. The convertibility of paper to specie was restored in 1878. A similar suspension of metal backing had happened earlier, in the War of 1812. Even prior to that, from 1777 to 1788 under the Articles of Confederation, unbacked paper bills were circulated. These "continentals," lacking intrinsic value and being simple to forge, rapidly became nearly worthless, leading to the famous expression "not worth a continental." This severe devaluation was a key factor in the constitutional prohibition, found in Article I, Section 10, against states legally recognizing any form of money other than gold or silver coin for settling debts.

input: Somali society is traditionally ethnically endogamous. So to extend ties of alliance, marriage is often to another ethnic Somali from a different clan. Thus, for example, a recent study observed that in 89 marriages contracted by men of the Dhulbahante clan, 55 (62%) were with women of Dhulbahante sub-clans other than those of their husbands; 30 (33.7%) were with women of surrounding clans of other clan families (Isaaq, 28; Hawiye, 3); and 3 (4.3%) were with women of other clans of the Darod clan family (Majerteen 2, Ogaden 1).
rewrite: In Somali culture, marriage typically occurs within the same ethnic group. To build broader alliances, however, individuals often marry ethnic Somalis from separate clans. A study of Dhulbahante clan marriages illustrates this: out of 89 unions, most were with women from different Dhulbahante sub-clans. A significant portion were with women from distinct clan families like Isaaq or Hawiye, and a few were with women from other clans within the larger Darod family.

input: The monastic communities of the Judean Desert also decorated their monasteries with mosaic floors. The Monastery of Martyrius was founded in the end of the 5th century and it was re-discovered in 1982–85. The most important work of art here is the intact geometric mosaic floor of the refectory although the severely damaged church floor was similarly rich. The mosaics in the church of the nearby Monastery of Euthymius are of later date (discovered in 1930). They were laid down in the Umayyad era, after a devastating earthquake in 659. Two six pointed stars and a red chalice are the most important surviving features.
rewrite: Monasteries in the Judean Desert featured mosaic flooring. The Monastery of Martyrius, established in the late fifth century and uncovered in the early 1980s, contains a key piece: a fully preserved geometric mosaic in the dining hall. While the church floor there is heavily ruined, it was once equally elaborate. At the adjacent Monastery of Euthymius, mosaics from a later period were found in 1930. These were installed during the Umayyad period following a major earthquake in 659, with two six-pointed stars and a red chalice remaining as their most notable elements.

input: Many arrangements of electrical contacts are used. Large lamps may have a screw base (one or more contacts at the tip, one at the shell) or a bayonet base (one or more contacts on the base, shell used as a contact or used only as a mechanical support). Some tubular lamps have an electrical contact at either end. Miniature lamps may have a wedge base and wire contacts, and some automotive and special purpose lamps have screw terminals for connection to wires. Contacts in the lamp socket allow the electric current to pass through the base to the filament. Power ratings for incandescent light bulbs range from about 0.1 watt to about 10,000 watts.
rewrite: A variety of electrical contact configurations exist for light bulbs. For larger models, bases often include screw types—featuring contacts at both the tip and shell—or bayonet styles, where contacts are on the base and the shell may serve as a contact or just for support. Tubular designs frequently have a contact on each end. Smaller lamps might use a wedge base with wire leads, while certain automotive and specialty bulbs employ screw terminals for wire attachment. Within the socket, these contacts enable current to reach the filament. Incandescent bulbs are available with power capacities spanning from roughly 0.1 watts up to 10,000 watts.

input: During the revival, in 1809 linguist and historian Josef Dobrovský released a German-language grammar of Old Czech entitled Ausführliches Lehrgebäude der böhmischen Sprache (Comprehensive Doctrine of the Bohemian Language). Dobrovský had intended his book to be descriptive, and did not think Czech had a realistic chance of returning as a major language. However, Josef Jungmann and other revivalists used Dobrovský's book to advocate for a Czech linguistic revival. Changes during this time included spelling reform (notably, í in place of the former j and j in place of g), the use of t (rather than ti) to end infinitive verbs and the non-capitalization of nouns (which had been a late borrowing from German). These changes differentiated Czech from Slovak. Modern scholars disagree about whether the conservative revivalists were motivated by nationalism or considered contemporary spoken Czech unsuitable for formal, widespread use.
rewrite: In 1809, scholar Josef Dobrovský published a detailed German grammar on Old Czech, called "Comprehensive Doctrine of the Bohemian Language." His work was meant as a historical record, and he doubted Czech could regain prominence. Yet, figures like Josef Jungmann later used this text to fuel a movement to revive the language. This period introduced several reforms: spelling was altered, such as replacing *j* with *í* and *g* with *j*; infinitives ended with *t* instead of *ti*; and nouns were no longer capitalized, a practice borrowed from German. These adjustments helped distinguish Czech from Slovak. Today, experts debate whether the revivalists were driven by national pride or a belief that everyday Czech was inadequate for formal and broad communication.

input: In 1997, the mammals were comprehensively revised by Malcolm C. McKenna and Susan K. Bell, which has resulted in the McKenna/Bell classification. Their 1997 book, Classification of Mammals above the Species Level, is the most comprehensive work to date on the systematics, relationships, and occurrences of all mammal taxa, living and extinct, down through the rank of genus, though recent molecular genetic data challenge several of the higher level groupings. The authors worked together as paleontologists at the American Museum of Natural History, New York. McKenna inherited the project from Simpson and, with Bell, constructed a completely updated hierarchical system, covering living and extinct taxa that reflects the historical genealogy of Mammalia.
rewrite: In 1997, paleontologists Malcolm C. McKenna and Susan K. Bell, both affiliated with the American Museum of Natural History in New York, completed an extensive overhaul of mammalian taxonomy. Their collaborative work, presented in the publication *Classification of Mammals above the Species Level*, established the now-standard McKenna/Bell system. This volume remains the most thorough reference on the systematics and evolutionary connections of all mammal genera, both extant and fossil. While modern genetic evidence has contested some of its broader categories, the classification provides a fully revised hierarchy intended to mirror the true ancestral lineage of mammals, a project McKenna originally took over from George Gaylord Simpson.

input: The structure of the Swiss militia system stipulates that the soldiers keep their Army issued equipment, including all personal weapons, at home. Some organizations and political parties find this practice controversial but mainstream Swiss opinion is in favour of the system. Compulsory military service concerns all male Swiss citizens; women can serve voluntarily. Men usually receive military conscription orders for training at the age of 18. About two thirds of the young Swiss are found suited for service; for those found unsuited, various forms of alternative service exist. Annually, approximately 20,000 persons are trained in recruit centres for a duration from 18 to 21 weeks. The reform "Army XXI" was adopted by popular vote in 2003, it replaced the previous model "Army 95", reducing the effectives from 400,000 to about 200,000. Of those, 120,000 are active in periodic Army training and 80,000 are non-training reserves.
rewrite: Under Switzerland's militia framework, personnel are required to store their assigned military gear, such as individual firearms, in their own residences. While certain groups and political factions view this policy as contentious, it retains broad public support within the country. Mandatory service applies to all male citizens, whereas female participation is optional. Typically, men are summoned for initial training upon turning eighteen. Roughly two-thirds of Swiss youth are deemed fit for duty; alternatives are provided for those who are not. Each year, close to 20,000 recruits undergo instruction over an 18- to 21-week period in training facilities. The "Army XXI" overhaul, approved by referendum in 2003, succeeded the earlier "Army 95" structure, cutting total personnel from 400,000 to around 200,000. From this number, 120,000 engage in recurrent training, with the remaining 80,000 serving as reserve personnel without active training obligations.

input: More than 200 newspapers and 350 consumer magazines have an office in the city, and the publishing industry employs about 25,000 people. Two of the three national daily newspapers in the United States are New York papers: The Wall Street Journal and The New York Times, which has won the most Pulitzer Prizes for journalism. Major tabloid newspapers in the city include: The New York Daily News, which was founded in 1919 by Joseph Medill Patterson and The New York Post, founded in 1801 by Alexander Hamilton. The city also has a comprehensive ethnic press, with 270 newspapers and magazines published in more than 40 languages. El Diario La Prensa is New York's largest Spanish-language daily and the oldest in the nation. The New York Amsterdam News, published in Harlem, is a prominent African American newspaper. The Village Voice is the largest alternative newspaper.
rewrite: New York City serves as a central hub for the publishing sector, hosting over 200 newspaper offices and more than 350 consumer magazine offices. This industry provides jobs for approximately 25,000 individuals. Among the three major national daily newspapers in the U.S., two are based in New York: The Wall Street Journal and The New York Times, the latter holding the record for the greatest number of Pulitzer Prizes in journalism. Prominent local tabloids are The New York Daily News, established in 1919 by Joseph Medill Patterson, and The New York Post, started in 1801 by Alexander Hamilton. The city also boasts a vast ethnic media landscape, with 270 periodicals printed in over 40 languages. Key publications include El Diario La Prensa, the country's oldest and New York's biggest Spanish-language daily; the notable African American paper The New York Amsterdam News from Harlem; and the leading alternative newspaper, The Village Voice.

input: The main crops grown are barley, wheat, buckwheat, rye, potatoes, and assorted fruits and vegetables. Tibet is ranked the lowest among China’s 31 provinces on the Human Development Index according to UN Development Programme data. In recent years, due to increased interest in Tibetan Buddhism, tourism has become an increasingly important sector, and is actively promoted by the authorities. Tourism brings in the most income from the sale of handicrafts. These include Tibetan hats, jewelry (silver and gold), wooden items, clothing, quilts, fabrics, Tibetan rugs and carpets. The Central People's Government exempts Tibet from all taxation and provides 90% of Tibet's government expenditures. However most of this investment goes to pay migrant workers who do not settle in Tibet and send much of their income home to other provinces.
rewrite: The primary agricultural products consist of barley, wheat, buckwheat, rye, potatoes, and various fruits and vegetables. According to UN metrics, Tibet holds the lowest position on the Human Development Index among China's 31 provincial regions. Growing fascination with Tibetan Buddhism has recently made tourism a key economic area, encouraged by local officials. This industry generates significant revenue through handicraft sales, such as traditional hats, silver and gold jewelry, wooden goods, apparel, quilts, textiles, and rugs. While the national government funds 90% of Tibet's budget and imposes no taxes, a large portion of this spending pays migrant laborers who typically remit earnings to their home provinces rather than settling locally.

input: Providing 25% of Namibia's revenue, mining is the single most important contributor to the economy. Namibia is the fourth largest exporter of non-fuel minerals in Africa and the world's fourth largest producer of uranium. There has been significant investment in uranium mining and Namibia is set to become the largest exporter of uranium by 2015. Rich alluvial diamond deposits make Namibia a primary source for gem-quality diamonds. While Namibia is known predominantly for its gem diamond and uranium deposits, a number of other minerals are extracted industrially such as lead, tungsten, gold, tin, fluorspar, manganese, marble, copper and zinc. There are offshore gas deposits in the Atlantic Ocean that are planned to be extracted in the future. According to "The Diamond Investigation", a book about the global diamond market, from 1978, De Beers, the largest diamond company, bought most of the Namibian diamonds, and would continue to do so, because "whatever government eventually comes to power they will need this revenue to survive".
rewrite: Mining generates a quarter of Namibia's income, making it the nation's foremost economic sector. The country ranks as Africa's fourth biggest exporter of non-fuel minerals and holds the same global position for uranium output. Substantial capital has flowed into uranium operations, positioning Namibia to become the leading global exporter of this resource. Its substantial alluvial diamond reserves establish it as a key origin for high-quality gem diamonds. Beyond these prominent resources, industrial mining extracts various other minerals including lead, tungsten, gold, tin, fluorspar, manganese, marble, copper, and zinc. Future plans include tapping offshore natural gas reserves located in the Atlantic Ocean. As noted in the 1978 publication "The Diamond Investigation," which examines the worldwide diamond trade, the major firm De Beers historically purchased the bulk of Namibia's diamonds. The text suggests this practice was expected to persist, as any governing administration would depend on this vital income stream.

input: French members of Parliament and other French politicians also organised a protest. All political parties in Parliament—UMP, Socialists, New Centre, Communists, Democratic Movement (centre) and Greens—jointly requested a pause in the National Assembly's session, which was granted, so that MPs could step outside and unfurl a banner which read "Respect for Human Rights in China". The coach containing the torch drove past the National Assembly and the assembled protesting MPs, who shouted "Freedom for Tibet!" several times as it passed.
rewrite: French legislators and political figures coordinated a demonstration. Every parliamentary group—spanning the UMP, Socialists, New Centre, Communists, the centrist Democratic Movement, and the Greens—collectively asked for and received an interruption to the Assembly's proceedings. This allowed deputies to gather outside and display a banner advocating for human rights in China. As the torch relay vehicle went by the Assembly, the gathered politicians repeatedly chanted "Freedom for Tibet!"

input: Plymouth lies between the River Plym to the east and the River Tamar to the west; both rivers flow into the natural harbour of Plymouth Sound. Since 1967, the unitary authority of Plymouth has included the, once independent, towns of Plympton and Plymstock which lie along the east of the River Plym. The River Tamar forms the county boundary between Devon and Cornwall and its estuary forms the Hamoaze on which is sited Devonport Dockyard.
rewrite: The city of Plymouth is bordered by the Plym River on its eastern side and the Tamar River to the west, both emptying into Plymouth Sound's harbor. Since 1967, the city's administrative area has incorporated the formerly separate towns of Plympton and Plymstock, located east of the Plym. The Tamar serves as the border between Devon and Cornwall, with its estuary creating the Hamoaze, home to the Devonport Dockyard.

input: Meanwhile, in Renaissance Italy, a new period in the history of translation had opened in Florence with the arrival, at the court of Cosimo de' Medici, of the Byzantine scholar Georgius Gemistus Pletho shortly before the fall of Constantinople to the Turks (1453). A Latin translation of Plato's works was undertaken by Marsilio Ficino. This and Erasmus' Latin edition of the New Testament led to a new attitude to translation. For the first time, readers demanded rigor of rendering, as philosophical and religious beliefs depended on the exact words of Plato, Aristotle and Jesus.
rewrite: In Florence during the Italian Renaissance, a fresh chapter in translation began when the Byzantine thinker Georgius Gemistus Pletho reached Cosimo de' Medici's court, not long before Constantinople fell in 1453. Marsilio Ficino produced a Latin version of Plato's writings. Alongside Erasmus’ Latin New Testament, this fostered a novel approach. Readers now insisted on strict accuracy, since the precise texts of figures like Plato, Aristotle, and Jesus were foundational to doctrine and philosophy.

input: After the English Civil War the Royal Citadel was built in 1666 on the east end of Plymouth Hoe, to defend the port from naval attacks, suppress Plymothian Parliamentary leanings and to train the armed forces. Guided tours are available in the summer months. Further west is Smeaton's Tower, which was built in 1759 as a lighthouse on rocks 14 miles (23 km) off shore, but dismantled and the top two thirds rebuilt on the Hoe in 1877. It is open to the public and has views over the Plymouth Sound and the city from the lantern room. Plymouth has 20 war memorials of which nine are on The Hoe including: Plymouth Naval Memorial, to remember those killed in World Wars I and II, and the Armada Memorial, to commemorate the defeat of the Spanish Armada.
rewrite: Following the English Civil War, the Royal Citadel was constructed in 1666 at the eastern edge of Plymouth Hoe. Its purposes were to protect the harbor from sea-based assaults, to curb local support for Parliament, and to serve as a military training ground. Summer visitors can join guided tours of the site. Located farther west is Smeaton's Tower. Originally erected in 1759 as a lighthouse on distant offshore rocks, it was taken apart and its upper sections were reassembled on the Hoe in 1877. Now open for visits, its lantern room provides panoramic vistas of Plymouth Sound and the urban area. The Hoe features nine of the city's twenty war memorials, such as the Plymouth Naval Memorial, honoring the fallen of both world wars, and the Armada Memorial, which marks the repulsion of the Spanish fleet.

input: Plymouth was granted the dignity of Lord Mayor by King George V in 1935. The position is elected each year by a group of six councillors. It is traditional that the position of the Lord Mayor alternates between the Conservative Party and the Labour Party annually and that the Lord Mayor chooses the Deputy Lord Mayor. Conservative councillor Dr John Mahony is the incumbent for 2015–16.
rewrite: In 1935, King George V bestowed the title of Lord Mayor upon Plymouth. Annually, six councillors elect the individual to fill this role. By custom, the appointment alternates yearly between the Conservative and Labour parties, and the chosen Lord Mayor then selects a Deputy. For the 2015–16 term, Conservative councillor Dr John Mahony holds the office.

input: The Consortium first published The Unicode Standard (ISBN 0-321-18578-1) in 1991 and continues to develop standards based on that original work. The latest version of the standard, Unicode 8.0, was released in June 2015 and is available from the consortium's website. The last of the major versions (versions x.0) to be published in book form was Unicode 5.0 (ISBN 0-321-48091-0), but since Unicode 6.0 the full text of the standard is no longer being published in book form. In 2012, however, it was announced that only the core specification for Unicode version 6.1 would be made available as a 692-page print-on-demand paperback. Unlike the previous major version printings of the Standard, the print-on-demand core specification does not include any code charts or standard annexes, but the entire standard, including the core specification, will still remain freely available on the Unicode website.
rewrite: The Unicode Consortium initially released The Unicode Standard (ISBN 0-321-18578-1) in 1991, and it has built upon that foundation ever since. Unicode 8.0, the most recent edition, became available in June 2015 on the organization's site. The final major release issued as a physical book was version 5.0 (ISBN 0-321-48091-0). Starting with Unicode 6.0, the complete standard ceased to be printed in book format. An exception occurred in 2012, when the core specification for version 6.1 was offered as a 692-page paperback via print-on-demand. This paperback version omits the code charts and annexes found in earlier printed editions. Nevertheless, the full standard, along with all its components, continues to be accessible at no cost on the official Unicode website.

input: The American observer Ingersoll reported at this time that "as to the accuracy of the bombing of military objectives, here I make no qualifications. The aim is surprisingly, astonishingly, amazingly inaccurate ... The physical damage to civilian London, to sum up, was more general and more extensive than I had imagined. The damage to military targets much less", and stated that he had seen numerous examples of untouched targets surrounded by buildings destroyed by errant bombs. For example, in two months of bombing, Battersea Power Station, perhaps the largest single target in London, had only received one minor hit ("a nick"). No bridge over the Thames had been hit, and the docks were still functioning despite great damage. An airfield was hit 56 times but the runways were never damaged and the field was never out of operation, despite German pilots' familiarity with it from prewar commercial flights. Ingersoll wrote that the difference between the failure of the German campaign against military targets versus its success in continental Europe was the RAF retaining control of the air.:79–80,174
rewrite: During this period, the American correspondent Ingersoll noted that the precision of bombing raids on strategic sites was remarkably poor. He described it as unexpectedly, even shockingly, off-target. He summarized that the widespread destruction across civilian areas of London exceeded his expectations, while damage to actual military objectives was far less than anticipated. Ingersoll mentioned observing many instances where intended targets remained completely unscathed, encircled by homes and other structures leveled by stray bombs. To illustrate, over two months of attacks, Battersea Power Station—likely London's most prominent single target—sustained merely a slight hit. Every Thames bridge remained intact, and the docks, though heavily damaged, continued operations. An airfield was struck dozens of times, yet its runways were never impaired and it stayed operational, despite German pilots knowing its layout from prewar civilian flights. Ingersoll attributed the German campaign's failure against military targets in Britain, in contrast to its successes in Europe, to the Royal Air Force maintaining air superiority.

input: As in much of Europe, the prosperity of Alsace came to an end in the 14th century by a series of harsh winters, bad harvests, and the Black Death. These hardships were blamed on Jews, leading to the pogroms of 1336 and 1339. In 1349, Jews of Alsace were accused of poisoning the wells with plague, leading to the massacre of thousands of Jews during the Strasbourg pogrom. Jews were subsequently forbidden to settle in the town. An additional natural disaster was the Rhine rift earthquake of 1356, one of Europe's worst which made ruins of Basel. Prosperity returned to Alsace under Habsburg administration during the Renaissance.
rewrite: Similar to other European regions, Alsace's thriving period ceased during the 1300s due to severe winters, crop failures, and the plague. Jewish communities were scapegoated for these troubles, resulting in violent persecutions in 1336 and 1339. In 1349, accusations that Jews had poisoned wells to spread disease led to the Strasbourg massacre, where thousands were killed, followed by a ban on Jewish settlement there. Further devastation came with the major 1356 Rhine earthquake, which destroyed Basel. The area later recovered its wealth under Habsburg rule in the Renaissance era.

input: Industrialized societies generally follow a clock-based schedule for daily activities that do not change throughout the course of the year. The time of day that individuals begin and end work or school, and the coordination of mass transit, for example, usually remain constant year-round. In contrast, an agrarian society's daily routines for work and personal conduct are more likely governed by the length of daylight hours and by solar time, which change seasonally because of the Earth's axial tilt. North and south of the tropics daylight lasts longer in summer and shorter in winter, the effect becoming greater as one moves away from the tropics.
rewrite: In modern industrial cultures, daily life typically adheres to a fixed, clock-driven timetable that remains the same across all seasons. Start and end times for employment or education, as well as public transportation schedules, are consistent throughout the year. Conversely, agricultural communities often base their work and daily routines on the sun's position and the amount of daylight, which shift with the seasons due to the tilt of the Earth's axis. Moving farther from the tropics, the variation in day length between summer and winter becomes more pronounced.

input: Much of the early paper made from wood pulp contained significant amounts of alum, a variety of aluminium sulfate salts that is significantly acidic. Alum was added to paper to assist in sizing, making it somewhat water resistant so that inks did not "run" or spread uncontrollably. Early papermakers did not realize that the alum they added liberally to cure almost every problem encountered in making their product would eventually be detrimental. The cellulose fibres that make up paper are hydrolyzed by acid, and the presence of alum would eventually degrade the fibres until the paper disintegrated in a process that has come to be known as "slow fire". Documents written on rag paper were significantly more stable. The use of non-acidic additives to make paper is becoming more prevalent, and the stability of these papers is less of an issue.
rewrite: Early wood pulp paper often included high concentrations of alum, an acidic compound derived from aluminum sulfate. This additive was commonly used during sizing to help paper repel water, preventing ink from bleeding. However, manufacturers of the time were unaware that their frequent application of alum to solve production issues would later cause severe damage. Acidic substances like alum break down cellulose fibers through hydrolysis, gradually weakening the paper in a destructive process often called "slow fire." In contrast, paper produced from rag-based materials demonstrated far greater durability. Today, the increasing adoption of acid-free alternatives in papermaking has substantially reduced concerns over long-term preservation.

input: In October 2014, it was announced that Beyoncé with her management company Parkwood Entertainment would be partnering with London-based fashion retailer Topshop, in a new 50/50 split subsidiary business named Parkwood Topshop Athletic Ltd. The new division was created for Topshop to break into the activewear market, with an athletic, street wear brand being produced. "Creating a partnership with Beyoncé, one of the most hard-working and talented people in the world, who spends many hours of her life dancing, rehearsing and training is a unique opportunity to develop this category" stated Sir Philip Green on the partnership. The company and collection is set to launch and hit stores in the fall of 2015.
rewrite: In the autumn of 2014, a joint venture was revealed between Beyoncé’s firm, Parkwood Entertainment, and the UK fashion chain Topshop. The equal partnership, called Parkwood Topshop Athletic Ltd., aimed to launch an activewear line for the retailer, blending athletic and street-style designs. Sir Philip Green remarked that collaborating with Beyoncé—an exceptionally dedicated artist whose career involves constant dance and training—presented a singular chance to enter this market. The new brand and its offerings are scheduled for release and to arrive in retail outlets by fall 2015.

input: In grading lumber and structural timber, knots are classified according to their form, size, soundness, and the firmness with which they are held in place. This firmness is affected by, among other factors, the length of time for which the branch was dead while the attaching stem continued to grow.
rewrite: When evaluating lumber and structural timber, knots are categorized based on their shape, dimensions, condition, and how securely they are embedded. This security is influenced by factors like how long the branch was dead before the surrounding wood grew around it.

input: The Nabatean Kingdom was an Arab state located between the Sinai Peninsula and the Arabian Peninsula. Its capital was the city of Petra, an important trading city on the incense route. The Nabateans resisted the attacks of Antigonous and were allies of the Hasmoneans in their struggle against the Seleucids, but later fought against Herod the great. The hellenization of the Nabateans accured relatively late in comparison to the surrounding regions. Nabatean material culture does not show any Greek influence until the reign of Aretas III Philhellene in the 1st century BCE. Aretas captured Damascus and built the Petra pool complex and gardens in the Hellenistic style. Though the Nabateans originally worshipped their traditional gods in symbolic form such as stone blocks or pillars, during the Hellenistic period they began to identify their gods with Greek gods and depict them in figurative forms influenced by Greek sculpture. Nabatean art shows Greek influences and paintings have been found depicting Dionysian scenes. They also slowly adopted Greek as a language of commerce along with Aramaic and Arabic.
rewrite: Situated between the Sinai and Arabian Peninsulas, the ancient Nabatean state established its capital at Petra, a vital hub along the incense trade network. This Arab kingdom successfully repelled invasions by Antigonous and initially supported the Hasmoneans against the Seleucid Empire, though it later entered into conflict with Herod the Great. Hellenistic cultural influence reached the Nabateans later than their neighbors. Evidence from their artifacts reveals no Greek impact until the rule of Aretas III Philhellene during the first century BCE. This king seized Damascus and commissioned Hellenistic-style gardens and a pool complex at Petra. Originally, their deities were represented aniconically as pillars or stone blocks. However, in the Hellenistic era, they started equating these gods with Greek counterparts, portraying them in statuary inspired by Greek art. Their own artistic works began to display Greek motifs, including frescoes with themes related to Dionysus. Gradually, Greek also came into use alongside Aramaic and Arabic for trade.

input: In the mid 1970s, various American groups (some with ties to Downtown Manhattan's punk scene, including Television and Suicide) had begun expanding on the vocabulary of punk music. Midwestern groups such as Pere Ubu and Devo drew inspiration from the region's derelict industrial environments, employing conceptual art techniques, musique concrète and unconventional verbal styles that would presage the post-punk movement by several years. A variety of subsequent groups, including New York-based Talking Heads and Boston-based Mission of Burma, combined elements of punk with art school sensibilities. In 1978, the former band began a series of collaborations with British ambient pioneer and ex-Roxy Music member Brian Eno, experimenting with Dada-influenced lyrical techniques, dance music, and African polyrhythms. San Francisco's vibrant post-punk scene was centered around such groups as Chrome, the Residents and Tuxedomoon, who incorporated multimedia experimentation, film and ideas from Antonin Artaud's Theater of Cruelty.
rewrite: During the 1970s, several U.S. bands started to broaden the scope of punk rock. Artists connected to New York's punk community, like Television and Suicide, were among these innovators. In the Midwest, acts such as Pere Ubu and Devo found creative stimulus in decaying factory settings, using avant-garde art methods, experimental sound collages, and odd lyrical approaches. Their work foreshadowed the post-punk era well before it emerged. Later bands, including Talking Heads from New York and Mission of Burma from Boston, merged punk's energy with artistic concepts from art colleges. In 1978, Talking Heads started working with Brian Eno, a leading figure in ambient music and former Roxy Music participant. Together, they explored lyrical styles inspired by Dada, dance rhythms, and complex African drum patterns. Meanwhile, San Francisco's active scene featured groups like Chrome, the Residents, and Tuxedomoon. These artists blended performance art, cinema, and principles from Antonin Artaud's radical theater into their music.

input: According to Martin Heidegger we do not exist inside time, we are time. Hence, the relationship to the past is a present awareness of having been, which allows the past to exist in the present. The relationship to the future is the state of anticipating a potential possibility, task, or engagement. It is related to the human propensity for caring and being concerned, which causes "being ahead of oneself" when thinking of a pending occurrence. Therefore, this concern for a potential occurrence also allows the future to exist in the present. The present becomes an experience, which is qualitative instead of quantitative. Heidegger seems to think this is the way that a linear relationship with time, or temporal existence, is broken or transcended. We are not stuck in sequential time. We are able to remember the past and project into the future—we have a kind of random access to our representation of temporal existence; we can, in our thoughts, step out of (ecstasis) sequential time.
rewrite: Martin Heidegger proposes that human existence is not merely contained within time but is fundamentally temporal in nature. Our connection to the past is not a distant memory but a current recognition of what has been, thereby making the past a living part of the now. Similarly, our orientation toward the future is defined by an active anticipation of what may come, rooted in our inherent capacity for care and concern. This forward-looking engagement brings the future into our immediate awareness. Consequently, the present moment transforms into a qualitative experience rather than a mere point on a quantitative timeline. Heidegger suggests this understanding allows us to overcome a strictly linear perception of time. We are not confined to a sequential order; instead, we possess the ability to recall the past and envision the future freely. This grants us a form of direct access to our temporal reality, enabling the mind to momentarily transcend the ordinary flow of time.

input: The events of the summer of 1974 dominate the politics on the island, as well as Greco-Turkish relations. Around 150,000 settlers from Turkey are believed to be living in the north—many of whom were forced from Turkey by the Turkish government—in violation of the Geneva Convention and various UN resolutions. Following the invasion and the capture of its northern territory by Turkish troops, the Republic of Cyprus announced that all of its ports of entry in the north were closed, as they were effectively not under its control.[citation needed]
rewrite: The political landscape of Cyprus and relations between Greece and Turkey remain heavily influenced by the 1974 conflict. An estimated 150,000 Turkish nationals, many relocated by their government, now reside in the northern area, an act considered contrary to international law. After Turkish forces took control of this region, the Cypriot government declared its northern ports shut, as it could no longer administer them.

input: International influences help to encourage legal actions to be taken in India, such as the Geneva Declaration of the Right of Children Act was passed in 1924. This act was followed by The Universal Declaration of Human Rights in 1948 to which incorporated the basic human rights and needs of children for proper progression and growth in their younger years. These international acts encouraged major changes to the workforce in India which occurred in 1986 when the Child Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act was put into place. This act prohibited hiring children younger than the age of 14, and from working in hazardous conditions.
rewrite: Global advocacy has spurred legislative reforms in India. For instance, the 1924 Geneva Declaration on children's rights prompted national action. Subsequently, the 1948 Universal Declaration of Human Rights explicitly included the essential rights and developmental necessities for young people. These international standards drove significant labor policy shifts, culminating in the 1986 Child Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act. This law bans the employment of those under 14 and prevents children from working in dangerous environments.

input: The Government of Punjab is a provincial government in the federal structure of Pakistan, is based in Lahore, the capital of the Punjab Province. The Chief Minister of Punjab (CM) is elected by the Provincial Assembly of the Punjab to serve as the head of the provincial government in Punjab, Pakistan. The current Chief Minister is Shahbaz Sharif, who became the Chief Minister of Punjab as being restored after Governor's rule starting from 25 February 2009 to 30 March 2009. Thereafter got re-elected as a result of 11 May 2013 elections. The Provincial Assembly of the Punjab is a unicameral legislature of elected representatives of the province of Punjab, which is located in Lahore in eastern Pakistan. The Assembly was established under Article 106 of the Constitution of Pakistan as having a total of 371 seats, with 66 seats reserved for women and eight reserved for non-Muslims.
rewrite: The provincial administration of Punjab operates within Pakistan's federal system, with its headquarters situated in Lahore, the provincial capital. The head of this regional government, known as the Chief Minister, is chosen by the members of the Punjab Provincial Assembly. Shahbaz Sharif currently holds this position; he initially resumed the office following a brief period of governor's rule in early 2009 and was later returned to power through the general elections held in May 2013. The law-making body for the province is the unicameral Punjab Provincial Assembly, also located in Lahore in eastern Pakistan. Formed according to Article 106 of the nation's constitution, this legislature comprises 371 seats in total. Among these, 66 are allocated for female representatives and a further eight are set aside for members belonging to religious minorities.

input: Differences in feasts may also originate from doctrinal issues—the Feast of the Assumption is such an example. Given that there is no agreement among all Christians on the circumstances of the death, Dormition or Assumption of Mary, the feast of assumption is celebrated among some denominations and not others.  While the Catholic Church celebrates the Feast of the Assumption on August 15, some Eastern Catholics celebrate it as Dormition of the Theotokos, and may do so on August 28, if they follow the Julian calendar. The Eastern Orthodox also celebrate it as the Dormition of the Theotokos, one of their 12 Great Feasts. Protestants do not celebrate this, or any other Marian feasts.
rewrite: Variations in religious observances can stem from theological disagreements, as seen with the Feast of the Assumption. Since Christians hold differing beliefs regarding the end of Mary's life, this occasion is not universally kept. For instance, the Catholic Church observes it on August 15. Many Eastern Catholics and Eastern Orthodox churches, however, commemorate it as the Dormition of the Theotokos, a principal feast, sometimes on August 28 per the Julian calendar. Protestant traditions generally do not observe this or any other feast days dedicated to Mary.

input: The Greek economy is classified as advanced and high-income. Greece was a founding member of the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) and the Organization of the Black Sea Economic Cooperation (BSEC). In 1979 the accession of the country in the European Communities and the single market was signed, and the process was completed in 1982. Greece was accepted into the Economic and Monetary Union of the European Union on 19 June 2000, and in January 2001 adopted the Euro as its currency, replacing the Greek drachma at an exchange rate of 340.75 drachma to the Euro. Greece is also a member of the International Monetary Fund and the World Trade Organization, and is ranked 24th on the KOF Globalization Index for 2013.
rewrite: Greece possesses a developed, high-income economy. It was among the original members of both the OECD and the Black Sea Economic Cooperation organization. The nation's entry into the European Communities and its unified market was formalized in 1979, concluding in 1982. On June 19, 2000, Greece joined the EU's Economic and Monetary Union, adopting the euro in January 2001 to replace the drachma at a fixed rate of 340.75 drachma per euro. Additionally, the country holds membership in the International Monetary Fund and the World Trade Organization. In 2013, it occupied the 24th position on the KOF Globalization Index.

input: Due to the lack of success lately on the international level, in recent years, Armenia has rebuilt 16 Soviet-era sports schools and furnished them with new equipment for a total cost of $1.9 million. The rebuilding of the regional schools was financed by the Armenian government. $9.3 million has been invested in the resort town of Tsaghkadzor to improve the winter sports infrastructure because of dismal performances at recent winter sports events. In 2005, a cycling center was opened in Yerevan with the aim of helping produce world class Armenian cyclists. The government has also promised a cash reward of $700,000 to Armenians who win a gold medal at the Olympics.
rewrite: In response to disappointing results in global competitions, Armenia has renovated 16 former Soviet sports academies and supplied them with modern gear, a project totaling $1.9 million funded by the state. Additionally, $9.3 million was allocated to upgrade winter sports facilities in Tsaghkadzor following poor showings in recent events. A cycling center opened in Yerevan in 2005 to develop elite athletes in that discipline. The government further incentivizes success by offering a $700,000 prize to any Armenian athlete who secures an Olympic gold medal.

input: All of the highways into Wenchuan, and others throughout the province, were damaged, resulting in delayed arrival of the rescue troops. In Beichuan County, 80% of the buildings collapsed according to Xinhua News. In the city of Shifang, the collapse of two chemical plants led to leakage of some 80 tons of liquid ammonia, with hundreds of people reported buried. In the city of Dujiangyan, south-east of the epicenter, a whole school collapsed with 900 students buried and fewer than 60 survived. The Juyuan Middle School, where many teenagers were buried, was excavated by civilians and cranes. Dujiangyan is home of the Dujiangyan Irrigation System, an ancient water diversion project which is still in use and is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. The project's famous Fish Mouth was cracked but not severely damaged otherwise.
rewrite: Roads leading into Wenchuan and across the region were compromised, hindering emergency response efforts. Xinhua reported that in Beichuan County, the vast majority of structures were destroyed. Two chemical facilities in Shifang failed, releasing approximately 80 tons of liquid ammonia and trapping hundreds. Southeast of the quake's origin in Dujiangyan, a school fell, entombing 900 pupils; under 60 were rescued. At Juyuan Middle School, numerous adolescents were recovered by locals using construction machinery. Dujiangyan contains the ancient, operational Dujiangyan Irrigation System, a UNESCO site. Its notable Fish Mouth feature sustained a fracture but remained largely intact.

input: At the beginning of the 13th century, there were reasonably accurate Latin translations of the main works of almost all the intellectually crucial ancient authors, allowing a sound transfer of scientific ideas via both the universities and the monasteries. By then, the natural philosophy contained in these texts began to be extended by notable scholastics such as Robert Grosseteste, Roger Bacon, Albertus Magnus and Duns Scotus. Precursors of the modern scientific method, influenced by earlier contributions of the Islamic world, can be seen already in Grosseteste's emphasis on mathematics as a way to understand nature, and in the empirical approach admired by Bacon, particularly in his Opus Majus. Pierre Duhem's provocative thesis of the Catholic Church's Condemnation of 1277 led to the study of medieval science as a serious discipline, "but no one in the field any longer endorses his view that modern science started in 1277". However, many scholars agree with Duhem's view that the Middle Ages were a period of important scientific developments.
rewrite: By the early 1200s, the core writings of most significant thinkers from antiquity had been rendered into Latin with considerable precision. This enabled a reliable dissemination of scholarly concepts through monastic and university channels. Around this period, the natural philosophy within these works was being expanded by eminent medieval thinkers, including Robert Grosseteste, Roger Bacon, Albertus Magnus, and Duns Scotus. Early elements of what would become the modern scientific approach, which owed some debt to prior Islamic scholarship, are evident. Grosseteste stressed using mathematics to comprehend the natural world, while Bacon championed an observational method, notably in his *Opus Majus*. The historian Pierre Duhem proposed a contentious idea linking the 1277 condemnations by the Catholic Church to the origins of modern science, prompting serious academic study of medieval science. Although specialists now reject the claim that science began precisely in 1277, numerous academics concur with Duhem's broader assertion that the Middle Ages were a time of substantial scientific progress.

input: Japan conscripted many soldiers from its colonies of Korea and Formosa (Taiwan). To a small extent, some Vichy French, Indian National Army, and Burmese National Army forces were active in the area of the Pacific War. Collaborationist units from Hong Kong (reformed ex-colonial police), Philippines, Dutch East Indies (the PETA) and Dutch Guinea, British Malaya and British Borneo, Inner Mongolia and former French Indochina (after the overthrow of Vichy French regime) as well as Timorese militia also assisted Japanese war efforts.
rewrite: Japan recruited numerous troops from its colonial holdings in Korea and Taiwan. A limited number of soldiers from the Vichy French, Indian National Army, and Burmese National Army also operated in the Pacific theater. Furthermore, collaborative forces from Hong Kong, the Philippines, the Dutch East Indies, Dutch Guinea, British Malaya, British Borneo, Inner Mongolia, former French Indochina, and Timor supported Japan's military operations.

input: By the mid-18th century, the Qing had successfully put outer regions such as Inner and Outer Mongolia, Tibet and Xinjiang under its control. Imperial commissioners and garrisons were sent to Mongolia and Tibet to oversee their affairs. These territories were also under supervision of a central government institution called Lifan Yuan. Qinghai was also put under direct control of the Qing court. Xinjiang, also known as Chinese Turkestan, was subdivided into the regions north and south of the Tian Shan mountains, also known today as Dzungaria and Tarim Basin respectively, but the post of Ili General was established in 1762 to exercise unified military and administrative jurisdiction over both regions. Dzungaria was fully opened to Han migration by the Qianlong Emperor from the beginning. Han migrants were at first forbidden from permanently settling in the Tarim Basin but were the ban was lifted after the invasion by Jahangir Khoja in the 1820s. Likewise, Manchuria was also governed by military generals until its division into provinces, though some areas of Xinjiang and Northeast China were lost to the Russian Empire in the mid-19th century. Manchuria was originally separated from China proper by the Inner Willow Palisade, a ditch and embankment planted with willows intended to restrict the movement of the Han Chinese, as the area was off-limits to civilian Han Chinese until the government started colonizing the area, especially since the 1860s.
rewrite: By the middle of the 1700s, the Qing Dynasty had extended its dominion over several frontier areas, including Inner and Outer Mongolia, Tibet, and Xinjiang. To manage these regions, the court dispatched imperial officials and stationed troops in Mongolia and Tibet. A specialized central agency, the Lifan Yuan, was tasked with supervising these territories. Qinghai similarly came under the direct administration of the Qing government. Xinjiang, sometimes referred to as Chinese Turkestan, was historically divided into the zones north and south of the Tian Shan range, corresponding to Dzungaria and the Tarim Basin. However, in 1762, the creation of the Ili General provided a single military and administrative authority over the entire area. The Qianlong Emperor permitted Han Chinese settlement in Dzungaria from the outset. While Han migrants were initially barred from establishing permanent homes in the Tarim Basin, this restriction was removed following an incursion by Jahangir Khoja in the 1820s. Manchuria, meanwhile, was administered by military commanders until it was later organized into provinces. It is notable that during the 1800s, portions of Xinjiang and Northeast China were ceded to Russia. Originally, the Inner Willow Palisade—a barrier of ditches, embankments, and trees—was erected to separate Manchuria from China proper and to limit Han Chinese movement into this restricted zone. This policy changed when the government began actively encouraging Han settlement there, particularly from the 1860s onward.

input: The first known smelting of iron began in Anatolia, around 1800 BC. Called the bloomery process, it produced very soft but ductile wrought iron. By 800 BC, iron-making technology had spread to Europe, arriving in Japan around 700 AD. Pig iron, a very hard but brittle alloy of iron and carbon, was being produced in China as early as 1200 BC, but did not arrive in Europe until the Middle Ages. Pig iron has a lower melting point than iron, and was used for making cast-iron. However, these metals found little practical use until the introduction of crucible steel around 300 BC. These steels were of poor quality, and the introduction of pattern welding, around the 1st century AD, sought to balance the extreme properties of the alloys by laminating them, to create a tougher metal. Around 700 AD, the Japanese began folding bloomery-steel and cast-iron in alternating layers to increase the strength of their swords, using clay fluxes to remove slag and impurities. This method of Japanese swordsmithing produced one of the purest steel-alloys of the early Middle Ages.
rewrite: The earliest known production of iron through smelting occurred in Anatolia approximately 3,800 years ago. This method, known as the bloomery process, created wrought iron, a malleable yet soft metal. The knowledge of iron production reached Europe by about 800 BC and Japan around 700 AD. In China, a hard but fragile iron-carbon alloy called pig iron was made as early as 1200 BC, though it only appeared in Europe centuries later during the medieval period. With a relatively low melting temperature, it was suitable for casting. These early iron variants saw limited application until roughly 300 BC with the advent of crucible steel, which was initially of low grade. By the first century AD, pattern welding emerged, layering different alloys to combine their properties and achieve a more resilient material. Near 700 AD, Japanese swordsmiths developed a technique of repeatedly folding and forge-welding layers of bloomery steel and cast iron. They employed clay fluxes to purge impurities, resulting in exceptionally refined steel alloys for that era.

input: On 16 March 1934, President Franklin D. Roosevelt signed the Migratory Bird Hunting Stamp Act, which requires an annual stamp purchase by all hunters over the age of sixteen. The stamps are created on behalf of the program by the US Postal Service and depict wildlife artwork chosen through an annual contest.
