They play an important role in habitat conservation because ninety-eight percent of all funds generated by their sale go directly toward the purchase or lease of wetland habitat for protection in the National Wildlife Refuge System.[citation needed] In addition to waterfowl, it is estimated that one third of the nation's endangered species seek food and shelter in areas protected using Duck Stamp funds.[citation needed]
rewrite: On March 16, 1934, a law enacted by President Franklin D. Roosevelt mandated that hunters aged sixteen and older buy a yearly stamp. The U.S. Postal Service issues these stamps featuring winning designs from a yearly art competition. Nearly all revenue from sales—98 percent—is allocated to acquiring or leasing wetlands for safeguarding within the National Wildlife Refuge System, making the stamps vital for conserving habitats. Beyond aiding waterfowl, roughly a third of America's threatened species depend on the sanctuaries funded by these Duck Stamp proceeds for sustenance and refuge.

input: Before World War II, Oklahoma City developed major stockyards, attracting jobs and revenue formerly in Chicago and Omaha, Nebraska. With the 1928 discovery of oil within the city limits (including under the State Capitol), Oklahoma City became a major center of oil production. Post-war growth accompanied the construction of the Interstate Highway System, which made Oklahoma City a major interchange as the convergence of I-35, I-40 and I-44. It was also aided by federal development of Tinker Air Force Base.
rewrite: Prior to WWII, Oklahoma City established significant livestock markets, drawing employment and income that had previously been concentrated in Chicago and Omaha. The 1928 finding of oil inside the city, even beneath the State Capitol, established it as a key petroleum hub. After the war, expansion continued with the Interstate Highway System, positioning the city as a crucial junction for I-35, I-40, and I-44, and further supported by the federal establishment of Tinker Air Force Base.

input: Very small lamps may have the filament support wires extended through the base of the lamp, and can be directly soldered to a printed circuit board for connections. Some reflector-type lamps include screw terminals for connection of wires. Most lamps have metal bases that fit in a socket to support the lamp and conduct current to the filament wires. In the late 19th century, manufacturers introduced a multitude of incompatible lamp bases. General Electric introduced standard base sizes for tungsten incandescent lamps under the Mazda trademark in 1909. This standard was soon adopted across the US, and the Mazda name was used by many manufacturers under license through 1945. Today most incandescent lamps for general lighting service use an Edison screw in candelabra, intermediate, or standard or mogul sizes, or double contact bayonet base. Technical standards for lamp bases include ANSI standard C81.67 and IEC standard 60061-1 for common commercial lamp sizes, to ensure interchangeablitity between different manufacturer's products. Bayonet base lamps are frequently used in automotive lamps to resist loosening due to vibration. A bipin base is often used for halogen or reflector lamps.
rewrite: Miniature lamps can have their internal support wires pass through the bottom, allowing them to be soldered directly onto circuit boards. Certain lamps with built-in reflectors feature screw terminals for attaching electrical wires. Typically, lamps possess metal bases that insert into a socket, providing both physical support and an electrical pathway to the filament. The late 1800s saw a proliferation of non-interchangeable base designs. In 1909, General Electric established uniform base dimensions for tungsten filament lamps under the Mazda brand, a standard quickly embraced nationwide. Licensed use of the Mazda name continued until 1945. Modern general-service incandescent bulbs commonly employ an Edison screw base in various sizes or a double-contact bayonet style. Interchangeability is guaranteed by technical specifications like ANSI C81.67 and IEC 60061-1. Bayonet bases, which resist vibration-induced loosening, are standard in many automotive lights. Halogen and specialized reflector lamps often utilize a bipin base design.

input: An antenna transmits and receives radio waves with a particular polarization which can be reoriented by tilting the axis of the antenna in many (but not all) cases. The physical size of an antenna is often a practical issue, particularly at lower frequencies (longer wavelengths). Highly directional antennas need to be significantly larger than the wavelength. Resonant antennas usually use a linear conductor (or element), or pair of such elements, each of which is about a quarter of the wavelength in length (an odd multiple of quarter wavelengths will also be resonant). Antennas that are required to be small compared to the wavelength sacrifice efficiency and cannot be very directional. Fortunately at higher frequencies (UHF, microwaves) trading off performance to obtain a smaller physical size is usually not required.
rewrite: Antennas send and receive radio signals with a specific wave orientation, which can frequently be adjusted by changing the antenna's angle, though this is not universally possible. Their actual dimensions are a common design concern, especially for lower-frequency applications with longer wavelengths. To achieve a narrow, focused signal beam, antennas must be considerably bigger than the wavelength they operate with. For resonant designs, a straight conductive element—or a pair—is typically employed, with each segment measuring roughly one-quarter of the wavelength; odd multiples of this length also produce resonance. When antennas are made much smaller than the wavelength, they lose effectiveness and gain, becoming less able to focus energy. At higher frequencies like UHF and microwaves, however, reducing size generally does not demand a major compromise in capability.

input: In flood lamps used for photographic lighting, the tradeoff is made in the other direction. Compared to general-service bulbs, for the same power, these bulbs produce far more light, and (more importantly) light at a higher color temperature, at the expense of greatly reduced life (which may be as short as two hours for a type P1 lamp). The upper temperature limit for the filament is the melting point of the metal. Tungsten is the metal with the highest melting point, 3,695 K (6,191 °F). A 50-hour-life projection bulb, for instance, is designed to operate only 50 °C (122 °F) below that melting point. Such a lamp may achieve up to 22 lumens per watt, compared with 17.5 for a 750-hour general service lamp.
rewrite: Photographic flood lamps prioritize performance over longevity, unlike standard bulbs. For equivalent energy input, they generate significantly greater luminous output and, crucially, light with a higher color temperature. This comes at the cost of a dramatically shortened operational life—sometimes merely two hours, as with P1 lamps. The filament's maximum heat is constrained by its material's melting point. Tungsten, with a melting point of 3,695 K, is used for this purpose. A projection bulb rated for 50 hours, for example, runs just 50 °C below that critical threshold. This design allows efficiency of about 22 lumens per watt, whereas a typical 750-hour bulb produces roughly 17.5.

input: The noise-based speed is defined as the exposure that will lead to a given signal-to-noise ratio on individual pixels. Two ratios are used, the 40:1 ("excellent image quality") and the 10:1 ("acceptable image quality") ratio. These ratios have been subjectively determined based on a resolution of 70 pixels per cm (178 DPI) when viewed at 25 cm (9.8 inch) distance. The signal-to-noise ratio is defined as the standard deviation of a weighted average of the luminance and color of individual pixels. The noise-based speed is mostly determined by the properties of the sensor and somewhat affected by the noise in the electronic gain and AD converter.
rewrite: Noise-based speed refers to the exposure level needed to achieve a specific signal-to-noise ratio per pixel. Two benchmarks are applied: a 40:1 ratio for high-quality images and a 10:1 ratio for adequate results. These thresholds were established through visual assessment at a resolution of 70 pixels per centimeter, observed from a distance of 25 centimeters. The ratio itself measures the variation in a computed blend of each pixel's brightness and color. This speed metric is primarily influenced by sensor characteristics and, to a lesser extent, by electronic amplification and analog-to-digital conversion noise.

input: Islamic art frequently adopts the use of geometrical floral or vegetal designs in a repetition known as arabesque. Such designs are highly nonrepresentational, as Islam forbids representational depictions as found in pre-Islamic pagan religions. Despite this, there is a presence of depictional art in some Muslim societies, notably the miniature style made famous in Persia and under the Ottoman Empire which featured paintings of people and animals, and also depictions of Quranic stories and Islamic traditional narratives. Another reason why Islamic art is usually abstract is to symbolize the transcendence, indivisible and infinite nature of God, an objective achieved by arabesque. Islamic calligraphy is an omnipresent decoration in Islamic art, and is usually expressed in the form of Quranic verses. Two of the main scripts involved are the symbolic kufic and naskh scripts, which can be found adorning the walls and domes of mosques, the sides of minbars, and so on.
rewrite: Islamic art often employs intricate, repeating patterns of geometric shapes and plant-like forms, known as arabesque. This style is largely non-figurative, reflecting religious guidelines that discourage representational imagery common in earlier pagan traditions. However, some Muslim cultures have developed depictional arts, such as the Persian and Ottoman miniature paintings that illustrate people, animals, and scenes from religious texts. The prevalent abstraction also serves a spiritual purpose: to evoke the boundless, eternal, and unified essence of the divine, a concept effectively conveyed through endless arabesque designs. Additionally, calligraphy is a fundamental decorative element, most often showcasing verses from the Quran. Prominent scripts like the angular kufic and cursive naskh are widely used to ornament mosque architecture, including domes, walls, and pulpits.

input: Since 2001, Miami has been undergoing a large building boom with more than 50 skyscrapers rising over 400 feet (122 m) built or currently under construction in the city. Miami's skyline is ranked third-most impressive in the U.S., behind New York City and Chicago, and 19th in the world according to the Almanac of Architecture and Design. The city currently has the eight tallest (as well as thirteen of the fourteen tallest) skyscrapers in the state of Florida, with the tallest being the 789-foot (240 m) Four Seasons Hotel & Tower.
rewrite: Beginning in 2001, Miami has experienced a major construction surge, with over 50 towers exceeding 400 feet either completed or being built. Its cityscape is considered the third most notable in the United States, after New York and Chicago, and ranks 19th globally per the Almanac of Architecture and Design. Florida's eight highest structures, led by the 789-foot Four Seasons Hotel & Tower, are all located in the city, which also claims thirteen of the state's fourteen tallest buildings.

input: In Darwin's time there was no agreed-upon model of heredity; in Chapter I Darwin admitted, "The laws governing inheritance are quite unknown." He accepted a version of the inheritance of acquired characteristics (which after Darwin's death came to be called Lamarckism), and Chapter V discusses what he called the effects of use and disuse; he wrote that he thought "there can be little doubt that use in our domestic animals strengthens and enlarges certain parts, and disuse diminishes them; and that such modifications are inherited", and that this also applied in nature. Darwin stated that some changes that were commonly attributed to use and disuse, such as the loss of functional wings in some island dwelling insects, might be produced by natural selection. In later editions of Origin, Darwin expanded the role attributed to the inheritance of acquired characteristics. Darwin also admitted ignorance of the source of inheritable variations, but speculated they might be produced by environmental factors. However, one thing was clear: whatever the exact nature and causes of new variations, Darwin knew from observation and experiment that breeders were able to select such variations and produce huge differences in many generations of selection. The observation that selection works in domestic animals is not destroyed by lack of understanding of the underlying hereditary mechanism.
rewrite: During Darwin's era, a consistent theory of heredity had not yet been established. In the opening chapter of his work, Darwin himself acknowledged that the principles dictating inheritance were still largely a mystery. He supported a concept—later termed Lamarckism—wherein traits acquired during an organism's lifetime could be passed on. This idea is explored in Chapter V, where he examines the impacts of use and disuse, contending that in domesticated species, active use enhances certain structures while neglect reduces them, and these alterations are heritable, a process he believed also occurred in wild populations. Darwin noted, however, that some apparent cases of disuse, like flightless insects on islands, might actually result from natural selection. In subsequent versions of *On the Origin of Species*, he gave greater emphasis to this inheritance of acquired traits. While uncertain about the origins of heritable variation—suggesting environmental influences might play a role—Darwin was certain of one key fact: through careful observation and breeding experiments, it was evident that selecting for these variations could, over many generations, produce dramatic changes. The success of selective breeding in domestic animals remained a robust observation, undiminished by the limited knowledge of the genetic mechanisms at work.

input: Many ancient works, such as the Bible and the Greek tragedies,[citation needed] survive in hundreds of copies, and the relationship of each copy to the original may be unclear. Textual scholars have debated for centuries which sources are most closely derived from the original, hence which readings in those sources are correct.[citation needed] Although biblical books that are letters, like Greek plays, presumably had one original, the question of whether some biblical books, like the Gospels, ever had just one original has been discussed. Interest in applying textual criticism to the Qur'an has also developed after the discovery of the Sana'a manuscripts in 1972, which possibly date back to the 7–8th centuries.
rewrite: Numerous classical texts, including the Bible and Greek dramas, exist today through numerous copies, making it difficult to trace their lineage back to a single source. For ages, textual experts have contested which manuscripts are most faithful to the originals and which versions contain the most accurate content. While epistolary biblical texts and classical plays likely began as singular documents, scholars question if books like the Gospels ever had one definitive original. The 1972 finding of the Sana'a manuscripts, potentially originating in the 7th or 8th century, has further spurred scholarly examination into the textual history of the Qur'an.

input: The Bovington signal course's director reported that Gaddafi successfully overcame problems learning English, displaying a firm command of voice procedure. Noting that Gaddafi's favourite hobbies were reading and playing football, he thought him an "amusing officer, always cheerful, hard-working, and conscientious." Gaddafi disliked England, claiming British Army officers racially insulted him and finding it difficult adjusting to the country's culture; asserting his Arab identity in London, he walked around Piccadilly wearing traditional Libyan robes. He later related that while he travelled to England believing it more advanced than Libya, he returned home "more confident and proud of our values, ideals and social character."
rewrite: According to the head of the Bovington signal program, Gaddafi initially struggled with but ultimately mastered English and military communications. Described as a diligent and good-humored officer, he enjoyed reading and soccer. However, he felt alienated in England, alleging racial prejudice from officers and cultural dissonance; in London, he publicly wore Libyan attire to affirm his heritage. Although he originally viewed England as more developed, he stated that returning to Libya strengthened his confidence and pride in his own nation's principles and society.

input: In addition to Somali, Arabic, which is also an Afro-Asiatic tongue, is an official national language in both Somalia and Djibouti. Many Somalis speak it due to centuries-old ties with the Arab world, the far-reaching influence of the Arabic media, and religious education. Somalia and Djibouti are also both members of the Arab League.
rewrite: Arabic is an official language in Somalia and Djibouti, alongside Somali. Its use among Somalis stems from historical Arab connections, widespread Arabic media, and Islamic teaching. Both nations are additionally part of the Arab League.

input: Because of a low literacy rate among the public (about 2–3% until the early 19th century and just about 15% at the end of 19th century),[citation needed] ordinary people had to hire scribes as "special request-writers" (arzuhâlcis) to be able to communicate with the government. The ethnic groups continued to speak within their families and neighborhoods (mahalles) with their own languages (e.g., Jews, Greeks, Armenians, etc.). In villages where two or more populations lived together, the inhabitants would often speak each other's language. In cosmopolitan cities, people often spoke their family languages; many of those who were not ethnic Turks spoke Turkish as a second language.
rewrite: Due to widespread illiteracy, which remained as low as 2–3% until the 1800s and rose only to roughly 15% by 1900, common citizens frequently employed professional scribes, known as "arzuhâlcis," to draft petitions and official correspondence. Within their own households and local communities, various ethnicities—such as Jewish, Greek, and Armenian residents—continued using their native tongues. In mixed villages, it was common for neighbors to learn and converse in each other's languages. In diverse urban centers, while many spoke their heritage language at home, Turkish was often adopted as a secondary language by non-Turkish groups.

input: New Haven Harbor is home to the Port of New Haven, a deep-water seaport with three berths capable of hosting vessels and barges as well as the facilities required to handle break bulk cargo. The port has the capacity to load 200 trucks a day from the ground or via loading docks. Rail transportation access is available, with a private switch engine for yard movements and private siding for loading and unloading. Approximately 400,000 square feet (40,000 m2) of inside storage and 50 acres (200,000 m2) of outside storage are available at the site. Five shore cranes with a 250-ton capacity and 26 forklifts, each with a 26-ton capacity, are also available.
rewrite: The Port of New Haven is a deep-water facility located within New Haven Harbor. It features three berths for ships and barges, along with the necessary infrastructure for managing break bulk goods. Daily, the port can accommodate up to 200 trucks, serviced either at ground level or from loading docks. Rail service is supported by a private switching locomotive and dedicated sidings for transferring cargo. The site provides roughly 400,000 square feet of indoor warehouse space and 50 acres of open storage area. Equipment includes five dockside cranes, each able to lift 250 tons, and 26 forklifts with a 26-ton capacity apiece.

input: Scientists do not know the exact cause of sexual orientation, but they believe that it is caused by a complex interplay of genetic, hormonal, and environmental influences. They favor biologically-based theories, which point to genetic factors, the early uterine environment, both, or the inclusion of genetic and social factors. There is no substantive evidence which suggests parenting or early childhood experiences play a role when it comes to sexual orientation. Research over several decades has demonstrated that sexual orientation ranges along a continuum, from exclusive attraction to the opposite sex to exclusive attraction to the same sex.
rewrite: The precise origins of sexual orientation remain unclear to researchers, who attribute it to a multifaceted combination of genetic, hormonal, and environmental factors. Scientific consensus leans toward biological explanations, involving genetics, conditions in the womb, or a blend of hereditary and social elements. Studies indicate that upbringing or early life events do not substantially influence it. Decades of investigation show that orientation exists on a spectrum, varying from exclusive attraction to the opposite gender to exclusive attraction to the same gender.

input: When military conflicts broke out between the Ottoman Empire and other states, Greeks usually took arms against the Empire, with few exceptions. Prior to the Greek revolution, there had been a number of wars which saw Greeks fight against the Ottomans, such as the Greek participation in the Battle of Lepanto in 1571, the Epirus peasants' revolts of 1600–1601, the Morean War of 1684–1699, and the Russian-instigated Orlov Revolt in 1770, which aimed at breaking up the Ottoman Empire in favor of Russian interests.[page needed] These uprisings were put down by the Ottomans with great bloodshed.
rewrite: During hostilities involving the Ottoman Empire, Greek forces typically opposed it, with only rare instances of alignment. Before the national uprising, several earlier conflicts featured Greek opposition. Examples include their role in the 1571 Lepanto engagement, the peasant rebellions in Epirus around 1600, the Morean War in the late 17th century, and the 1770 Orlov Revolt, a Russian-backed effort to dismantle Ottoman power. The Ottoman authorities suppressed all these movements with severe violence.

input: Many of London's pubs are known to have been used by famous people, but in some cases, such as the association between Samuel Johnson and Ye Olde Cheshire Cheese, this is speculative, based on little more than the fact that the person is known to have lived nearby. However, Charles Dickens is known to have visited the Cheshire Cheese, the Prospect of Whitby, Ye Olde Cock Tavern and many others. Samuel Pepys is also associated with the Prospect of Whitby and the Cock Tavern.
rewrite: Numerous London pubs claim ties to notable figures, though some links, like Samuel Johnson's to Ye Olde Cheshire Cheese, rely mainly on proximity. In contrast, Charles Dickens' patronage of establishments such as the Cheshire Cheese, Prospect of Whitby, and Ye Olde Cock Tavern is well-documented. Similarly, Samuel Pepys is historically connected to the Prospect of Whitby and the Cock Tavern.

input: Myanmar (myan-MAR i/miɑːnˈmɑːr/ mee-ahn-MAR, /miˈɛnmɑːr/ mee-EN-mar or /maɪˈænmɑːr/ my-AN-mar (also with the stress on first syllable); Burmese pronunciation: [mjəmà]),[nb 1] officially the Republic of the Union of Myanmar and also known as Burma, is a sovereign state in Southeast Asia bordered by Bangladesh, India, China, Laos and Thailand. One-third of Myanmar's total perimeter of 1,930 km (1,200 miles) forms an uninterrupted coastline along the Bay of Bengal and the Andaman Sea. The country's 2014 census revealed a much lower population than expected, with 51 million people recorded. Myanmar is 676,578 square kilometres (261,227 sq mi) in size. Its capital city is Naypyidaw and its largest city is Yangon (Rangoon).
rewrite: Myanmar, formally called the Republic of the Union of Myanmar and historically referred to as Burma, is a Southeast Asian nation. It shares land borders with Bangladesh, India, China, Laos, and Thailand. Approximately a third of its 1,930-kilometer frontier is a continuous coast on the Bay of Bengal and the Andaman Sea. The country spans about 676,578 square kilometers. Its capital is Naypyidaw, while Yangon (formerly Rangoon) is its most populous city. A 2014 national count showed a population of 51 million, which was significantly less than earlier estimates.

input: Widespread rumors of Napoleon's return from St. Helena and Napoleon as an inspiration for patriotism, individual and collective liberties, and political mobilization manifested themselves in seditious materials, displaying the tricolor and rosettes. There were also subversive activities celebrating anniversaries of Napoleon's life and reign and disrupting royal celebrations—they demonstrated the prevailing and successful goal of the varied supporters of Napoleon to constantly destabilize the Bourbon regime.
rewrite: Persistent reports of Napoleon's comeback from exile, alongside his symbolic role in fueling national pride, personal freedoms, and political activism, appeared in rebellious items featuring revolutionary colors. Commemorations of his rule and interference with royal events further revealed the core, effective aim of his diverse followers: to relentlessly undermine the Bourbon monarchy.

input: Anthropologists have most frequently employed the term 'identity' to refer to this idea of selfhood in a loosely Eriksonian way (Erikson 1972) properties based on the uniqueness and individuality which makes a person distinct from others. Identity became of more interest to anthropologists with the emergence of modern concerns with ethnicity and social movements in the 1970s. This was reinforced by an appreciation, following the trend in sociological thought, of the manner in which the individual is affected by and contributes to the overall social context. At the same time, the Eriksonian approach to identity remained in force, with the result that identity has continued until recently to be used in a largely socio-historical way to refer to qualities of sameness in relation to a person's connection to others and to a particular group of people.
rewrite: Within anthropology, the concept of 'identity' has commonly been understood as the self, drawing generally on Erik Erikson's framework. This perspective emphasizes the distinctive traits that differentiate one individual from another. Anthropological focus on identity grew during the 1970s, spurred by rising academic attention to ethnicity and various societal movements. This interest was further shaped by sociological influences, which highlighted the reciprocal relationship between an individual and their broader social environment. Despite these evolving perspectives, the foundational Eriksonian view persisted. Consequently, the term has predominantly retained a socio-historical meaning, denoting shared characteristics that link a person to a wider community or collective.

input: Epic poetry, notably the "acritic songs", flourished during Middle Ages. Two chronicles, one written by Leontios Machairas and the other by Georgios Voustronios, cover the entire Middle Ages until the end of Frankish rule (4th century–1489). Poèmes d'amour written in medieval Greek Cypriot date back from the 16th century. Some of them are actual translations of poems written by Petrarch, Bembo, Ariosto and G. Sannazzaro. Many Cypriot scholars fled Cyprus at troubled times such as Ioannis Kigalas (c. 1622–1687) who migrated from Cyprus to Italy in the 17th century, several of his works have survived in books of other scholars.
rewrite: The "acritic songs" represent a significant form of epic poetry from the medieval period. The era is fully documented in two key chronicles by Leontios Machairas and Georgios Voustronios, spanning from the 4th century to 1489, when Frankish dominion concluded. Love poems in the medieval Cypriot Greek dialect emerged in the 1500s, with several being direct renditions of works by Petrarch, Bembo, Ariosto, and Sannazzaro. During periods of instability, numerous Cypriot intellectuals left the island; for instance, Ioannis Kigalas (c. 1622–1687) relocated to Italy in the 1600s, and fragments of his writing persist within other authors' publications.

input: Sevastopol fell after eleven months, and formerly neutral countries began to join the allied cause. Isolated and facing a bleak prospect of invasion from the west if the war continued, Russia sued for peace in March 1856. This was welcomed by France and the UK, where the citizens began to turn against their governments as the war dragged on. The war was officially ended by the Treaty of Paris, signed on 30 March 1856. Russia lost the war, and was forbidden from hosting warships in the Black Sea. The Ottoman vassal states of Wallachia and Moldavia became largely independent. Christians were granted a degree of official equality, and the Orthodox church regained control of the Christian churches in dispute.:415
rewrite: Following an eleven-month siege, Sevastopol was captured, prompting previously unaligned nations to align with the allies. With its isolation complete and the grim threat of a western invasion looming should the conflict persist, Russia sought peace in March 1856. France and Britain, where public support for the war was waning, accepted this overture. The formal conclusion came with the Treaty of Paris on March 30, 1856. Defeated Russia was prohibited from stationing naval forces in the Black Sea. The Ottoman territories of Wallachia and Moldavia gained significant autonomy. The settlement also established a measure of legal equality for Christians and restored control of the contested churches to the Orthodox authority.

input: According to the latest International Monetary Fund estimates, its per capita GDP (adjusted for purchasing power) at $30,769 is just above the average of the European Union.[citation needed] Cyprus has been sought as a base for several offshore businesses for its low tax rates. Tourism, financial services and shipping are significant parts of the economy. Economic policy of the Cyprus government has focused on meeting the criteria for admission to the European Union. The Cypriot government adopted the euro as the national currency on 1 January 2008.
rewrite: Based on recent IMF data, Cyprus has a purchasing power-adjusted GDP per capita of $30,769, slightly exceeding the EU average. The nation attracts numerous offshore companies due to favorable tax policies. Key economic sectors include tourism, finance, and maritime services. Historically, government policy prioritized qualifying for EU membership, which led to the adoption of the euro as the official currency at the start of 2008.

input: Four separate and distinct state universities are located in Houston. The University of Houston is a nationally recognized Tier One research university, and is the flagship institution of the University of Houston System. The third-largest university in Texas, the University of Houston has nearly 40,000 students on its 667-acre campus in southeast Houston. The University of Houston–Clear Lake and the University of Houston–Downtown are stand-alone universities; they are not branch campuses of the University of Houston. Located in the historic community of Third Ward is Texas Southern University, one of the largest historically black colleges and universities in the United States.
rewrite: Houston is home to four independent public universities. The most prominent is the University of Houston, a top-tier research institution and the primary campus within its system. With close to 40,000 students, it is Texas's third largest university, situated on a large southeast campus. Two other autonomous universities in the system are the University of Houston–Clear Lake and the University of Houston–Downtown, which are not satellite branches. Additionally, Texas Southern University, a major historically Black university, resides in the city's Third Ward.

input: 1,500 V DC is used in the Netherlands, Japan, Republic Of Indonesia, Hong Kong (parts), Republic of Ireland, Australia (parts), India (around the Mumbai area alone, has been converted to 25 kV AC like the rest of India), France (also using 25 kV 50 Hz AC), New Zealand (Wellington) and the United States (Chicago area on the Metra Electric district and the South Shore Line interurban line). In Slovakia, there are two narrow-gauge lines in the High Tatras (one a cog railway). In Portugal, it is used in the Cascais Line and in Denmark on the suburban S-train system.
rewrite: A 1,500-volt direct current system powers railways in several regions globally. These include areas of the Netherlands, Japan, Indonesia, Hong Kong, Ireland, Australia, and New Zealand's Wellington. In the United States, it serves Chicago's Metra Electric and South Shore Line. While India's Mumbai area and France have largely transitioned to 25 kV AC, this DC standard remains in use on specific lines in Slovakia's High Tatras, Portugal's Cascais Line, and Denmark's S-train network.

input: The fate of Willett's 1907 proposal illustrates several political issues involved. The proposal attracted many supporters, including Balfour, Churchill, Lloyd George, MacDonald, Edward VII (who used half-hour DST at Sandringham), the managing director of Harrods, and the manager of the National Bank. However, the opposition was stronger: it included Prime Minister H. H. Asquith, Christie (the Astronomer Royal), George Darwin, Napier Shaw (director of the Meteorological Office), many agricultural organizations, and theatre owners. After many hearings the proposal was narrowly defeated in a Parliament committee vote in 1909. Willett's allies introduced similar bills every year from 1911 through 1914, to no avail. The US was even more skeptical: Andrew Peters introduced a DST bill to the US House of Representatives in May 1909, but it soon died in committee.
rewrite: The political challenges surrounding daylight saving time are well demonstrated by the outcome of Willett's 1907 plan. It gained notable backing from figures such as Balfour, Churchill, Lloyd George, MacDonald, King Edward VII—who had already adopted a similar schedule at his estate—along with the heads of Harrods and the National Bank. Yet, resistance proved more formidable, led by Prime Minister Asquith, Astronomer Royal Christie, scientist George Darwin, meteorologist Napier Shaw, numerous farming groups, and theater proprietors. Following extensive debate, a parliamentary committee narrowly rejected the measure in 1909. Despite annual legislative efforts by its supporters from 1911 to 1914, the idea failed to advance. In the United States, skepticism was greater still; a 1909 bill submitted to Congress by Andrew Peters saw no progress and was quickly shelved.

input: The term "Moors" has been used in Europe in a broader, somewhat derogatory sense to refer to Muslims, especially those of Arab or Berber descent, whether living in North Africa or Iberia. Moors were not a distinct or self-defined people. Medieval and early modern Europeans applied the name to Muslim Arabs, Berbers, Black Africans and Europeans alike.
rewrite: Historically, Europeans broadly and often pejoratively used "Moors" to describe Muslims, particularly those from Arab or Berber backgrounds in North Africa and Iberia. It was not a term for a unified group, but a label applied indiscriminately to Muslims of various ethnic origins.

input: Thousands of Soviet troops were sent to the Fergana Valley, southeast of the Uzbek capital Tashkent, to re-establish order after clashes in which local Uzbeks hunted down members of the Meskhetian minority in several days of rioting between June 4–11, 1989; about 100 people were killed. On June 23, 1989, Gorbachev removed Rafiq Nishonov as First Secretary of the Communist Party of the Uzbek SSR and replaced him with Karimov, who went on to lead Uzbekistan as a Soviet Republic and subsequently as an independent state.
rewrite: In June 1989, violent riots erupted in Uzbekistan's Fergana Valley. Over several days, ethnic Uzbeks targeted the Meskhetian community, resulting in approximately one hundred deaths. To quell the unrest, the USSR dispatched thousands of soldiers to the region. Later that month, Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev replaced the Uzbek Communist Party's First Secretary, Rafiq Nishonov, with Islam Karimov. Karimov would later govern Uzbekistan both as a Soviet republic and, eventually, as a sovereign nation.

input: Broadcasters were faced with having to adapt daily to the varied recording characteristics of many sources: various makers of "home recordings" readily available to the public, European recordings, lateral-cut transcriptions, and vertical-cut transcriptions. Efforts were started in 1942 to standardize within the National Association of Broadcasters (NAB), later known as the National Association of Radio and Television Broadcasters (NARTB). The NAB, among other items, issued recording standards in 1949 for laterally and vertically cut records, principally transcriptions. A number of 78 rpm record producers as well as early LP makers also cut their records to the NAB/NARTB lateral standard.
rewrite: Broadcasters constantly adjusted to the differing audio qualities from numerous sources, including consumer home recordings, European imports, and both lateral and vertical transcriptions. Starting in 1942, the National Association of Broadcasters (later renamed NARTB) began working to establish industry-wide uniformity. This initiative led to the 1949 release of official standards for transcription records, covering both lateral and vertical cuts. Consequently, many producers of 78 rpm discs and early LPs adopted the NAB/NARTB lateral specification.

input: A satellite ground station with a 7.6-metre (25 ft) satellite dish installed in 1989 at The Briars is the only international connection providing satellite links through Intelsat 707 to Ascension island and the United Kingdom. Since all international telephone and internet communications are relying on this single satellite link both internet and telephone service are subject to sun outages.
rewrite: A 7.6-meter dish was set up at The Briars in 1989. This station is the sole international satellite link, connecting via Intelsat 707 to Ascension Island and the UK. All phone and internet traffic depends on this single connection, making both services vulnerable to sun outages.

input: The 1950s and early 1960s are considered by many to be a golden age of Greek cinema. Directors and actors of this era were recognized as important historical figures in Greece and some gained international acclaim: Irene Papas, Melina Mercouri, Mihalis Kakogiannis, Alekos Sakellarios, Nikos Tsiforos, Iakovos Kambanelis, Katina Paxinou, Nikos Koundouros, Ellie Lambeti, and others. More than sixty films per year were made, with the majority having film noir elements. Notable films were Η κάλπικη λίρα (1955 directed by Giorgos Tzavellas), Πικρό Ψωμί (1951, directed by Grigoris Grigoriou), O Drakos (1956 directed by Nikos Koundouros), Stella (1955 directed by Cacoyannis and written by Kampanellis).
rewrite: Many regard the period from the 1950s to early 1960s as a peak era for film in Greece. The leading creators and performers from this time are celebrated as significant cultural icons domestically, with several achieving fame abroad. This prolific period saw annual production exceed sixty movies, most incorporating stylistic traits of film noir. Among the standout works are *Η κάλπικη λίρα* (1955), *Πικρό Ψωμί* (1951), *O Drakos* (1956), and *Stella* (1955).

input: Alpine glaciers can be straight rivers of ice, long sweeping rivers, spread in a fan-like shape (Piedmont glaciers), and curtains of ice that hang from vertical slopes of the mountain peaks. The stress of the movement causes the ice to break and crack loudly, perhaps explaining why the mountains were believed to be home to dragons in the medieval period. The cracking creates unpredictable and dangerous crevasses, often invisible under new snowfall, which cause the greatest danger to mountaineers.
rewrite: Alpine glaciers take various forms, from linear ice streams and broad, fan-shaped flows to frozen sheets draping steep cliffs. Their shifting weight fractures the ice with loud reports, which may have inspired medieval tales of mountain-dwelling dragons. These fractures produce hidden crevasses, frequently concealed by fresh snow, posing the most severe risks to climbers.

input: Drinks especially high in simple sugars, such as soft drinks and fruit juices, are not recommended in children under 5 years of age as they may increase dehydration. A too rich solution in the gut draws water from the rest of the body, just as if the person were to drink sea water. Plain water may be used if more specific and effective ORT preparations are unavailable or are not palatable. Additionally, a mix of both plain water and drinks perhaps too rich in sugar and salt can alternatively be given to the same person, with the goal of providing a medium amount of sodium overall. A nasogastric tube can be used in young children to administer fluids if warranted.
rewrite: Beverages with excessive simple sugars, like sodas and fruit juices, should be avoided for children under five, as they can worsen dehydration. A highly concentrated solution in the intestines pulls fluids from bodily tissues, similar to the effect of consuming seawater. If more targeted oral rehydration therapy options are inaccessible or unappealing, ordinary water is a suitable substitute. Another approach is to offer a combination of plain water and beverages that might be overly high in sugar and salt, aiming to achieve a moderate total sodium intake. For young children requiring medical intervention, fluids can be delivered via a nasogastric tube.

input: According to the U.S. Census Bureau, in 2004, Miami had the third highest incidence of family incomes below the federal poverty line in the United States, making it the third poorest city in the USA, behind only Detroit, Michigan (ranked #1) and El Paso, Texas (ranked #2). Miami is also one of the very few cities where its local government went bankrupt, in 2001. However, since that time, Miami has experienced a revival: in 2008, Miami was ranked as "America's Cleanest City" according to Forbes for its year-round good air quality, vast green spaces, clean drinking water, clean streets and city-wide recycling programs. In a 2009 UBS study of 73 world cities, Miami was ranked as the richest city in the United States (of four U.S. cities included in the survey) and the world's fifth-richest city, in terms of purchasing power.
rewrite: In 2004, U.S. Census data placed Miami as the nation's third most impoverished city, with only Detroit and El Paso having a greater share of families living under the poverty line. The city had also faced a municipal bankruptcy in 2001. A significant transformation followed. By 2008, Forbes magazine named Miami "America's Cleanest City," citing its excellent air, abundant parks, pure water, tidy public areas, and extensive recycling efforts. Furthermore, a 2009 UBS survey of 73 global urban centers positioned Miami as the wealthiest city in the United States and the fifth wealthiest worldwide when measured by the purchasing power of its residents.

input: Napoleon ended lawlessness and disorder in post-Revolutionary France. He was, however, considered a tyrant and usurper by his opponents. His critics charge that he was not significantly troubled when faced with the prospect of war and death for thousands, turned his search for undisputed rule into a series of conflicts throughout Europe and ignored treaties and conventions alike. His role in the Haitian Revolution and decision to reinstate slavery in France's oversea colonies are controversial and have an impact on his reputation.
rewrite: Napoleon brought stability to France after the Revolution, though adversaries viewed him as an oppressive usurper. Critics accuse him of pursuing absolute power through relentless European wars, showing little concern for the resulting widespread casualties and disregarding international agreements. His actions during the Haitian Revolution and his reinstatement of slavery in the colonies remain contentious, negatively affecting his historical standing.

input: In Prussia, some officials considered a war against France both inevitable and necessary to arouse German nationalism in those states that would allow the unification of a great German empire. This aim was epitomized by Prussian Chancellor Otto von Bismarck's later statement: "I did not doubt that a Franco-German war must take place before the construction of a United Germany could be realised." Bismarck also knew that France should be the aggressor in the conflict to bring the southern German states to side with Prussia, hence giving Germans numerical superiority. Many Germans also viewed the French as the traditional destabilizer of Europe, and sought to weaken France to prevent further breaches of the peace.
rewrite: Prussian leaders believed conflict with France was unavoidable and essential to inspire nationalist sentiment across German territories, paving the way for a unified empire. Otto von Bismarck, the Prussian chancellor, later reflected that such a war was a prerequisite for achieving German unity. He calculated that if France initiated hostilities, the southern German states would ally with Prussia, ensuring a demographic advantage. Additionally, widespread German opinion saw France as a persistent source of European instability, and aimed to diminish its power to foster lasting peace.

input: Feathers require maintenance and birds preen or groom them daily, spending an average of around 9% of their daily time on this. The bill is used to brush away foreign particles and to apply waxy secretions from the uropygial gland; these secretions protect the feathers' flexibility and act as an antimicrobial agent, inhibiting the growth of feather-degrading bacteria. This may be supplemented with the secretions of formic acid from ants, which birds receive through a behaviour known as anting, to remove feather parasites.
rewrite: Birds devote roughly nine percent of each day to grooming their feathers. They use their beaks to clean off debris and spread protective oils from a gland near the tail. This wax preserves feather condition and prevents harmful microbes. Some species also employ ants, utilizing the insects' formic acid secretions during a practice called anting to eliminate parasites.

input: Maintaining the household was the main duty of samurai women. This was especially crucial during early feudal Japan, when warrior husbands were often traveling abroad or engaged in clan battles. The wife, or okugatasama (meaning: one who remains in the home), was left to manage all household affairs, care for the children, and perhaps even defend the home forcibly. For this reason, many women of the samurai class were trained in wielding a polearm called a naginata or a special knife called the kaiken in an art called tantojutsu (lit. the skill of the knife), which they could use to protect their household, family, and honor if the need arose.
rewrite: The primary responsibility of women in samurai families was managing the home. This role became particularly vital in Japan's early feudal era, as their husbands were frequently away fighting in wars or on other military campaigns. Left behind, the wife, known as the okugatasama, oversaw domestic operations, raised children, and stood ready to guard the residence. Consequently, numerous women from this warrior class learned martial skills, such as handling the naginata polearm or mastering tantojutsu—the art of using a kaiken dagger. This training enabled them to safeguard their household, relatives, and personal honor if threatened.

input: Early house music was generally dance-based music characterized by repetitive 4/4 beats, rhythms mainly provided by drum machines, off-beat hi-hat cymbals, and synthesized basslines. While house displayed several characteristics similar to disco music, it was more electronic and minimalistic, and the repetitive rhythm of house was more important than the song itself. House music in the 2010s, while keeping several of these core elements, notably the prominent kick drum on every beat, varies widely in style and influence, ranging from the soulful and atmospheric deep house to the more minimalistic microhouse. House music has also fused with several other genres creating fusion subgenres, such as euro house, tech house, electro house and jump house.
rewrite: Originating as a rhythm-focused genre for dance floors, early house music was built on steady four-beat patterns. Its foundational sounds came from drum machines, featuring prominent synthesized bass and hi-hats accenting the off-beat. Though it shared some traits with disco, house was more minimalist and electronically driven, prioritizing its persistent groove over vocal or melodic content. Modern house, particularly in the 2010s, retains core elements like the consistent kick drum but spans a broad spectrum. Styles now range from atmospheric deep house to stark microhouse. The genre has further diversified by blending with others, giving rise to hybrids like tech house, electro house, and euro house.

input: The Umayyad Caliphate (Arabic: الخلافة الأموية‎, trans. Al-Khilāfat al-ʾumawiyya) was the second of the four major Islamic caliphates established after the death of Muhammad. This caliphate was centered on the Umayyad dynasty (Arabic: الأمويون‎, al-ʾUmawiyyūn, or بنو أمية, Banū ʾUmayya, "Sons of Umayya"), hailing from Mecca. The Umayyad family had first come to power under the third caliph, Uthman ibn Affan (r. 644–656), but the Umayyad regime was founded by Muawiya ibn Abi Sufyan, long-time governor of Syria, after the end of the First Muslim Civil War in 661 CE/41 AH. Syria remained the Umayyads' main power base thereafter, and Damascus was their capital. The Umayyads continued the Muslim conquests, incorporating the Caucasus, Transoxiana, Sindh, the Maghreb and the Iberian Peninsula (Al-Andalus) into the Muslim world. At its greatest extent, the Umayyad Caliphate covered 15 million km2 (5.79 million square miles), making it the largest empire (in terms of area - not in terms of population) the world had yet seen, and the fifth largest ever to exist.
rewrite: Following the passing of the Prophet Muhammad, the Umayyad Caliphate emerged as the second great Islamic state. It was ruled by the Umayyad dynasty, whose origins trace back to Mecca. While the family initially gained influence during the caliphate of Uthman ibn Affan, the regime was formally established by Muawiya ibn Abi Sufyan. He was the former governor of Syria, and after the conclusion of the First Muslim Civil War in 661 CE, he consolidated power. Syria, with its capital at Damascus, served as the enduring center of Umayyad authority. The caliphate aggressively expanded the frontiers of Islam, conquering vast territories including North Africa, the Iberian Peninsula, Central Asia, and parts of the Indian subcontinent. At its peak, it spanned approximately 15 million square kilometers, ranking it as history's most extensive empire by land area at that time and the fifth-largest of all time.

input: The scope of the term "post-punk" has been subject to controversy. While some critics, such as AllMusic's Stephen Thomas Erlewine, have employed the term "post-punk" to denote "a more adventurous and arty form of punk", others have suggested it pertains to a set of artistic sensibilities and approaches rather than any unifying style. Music journalist and post-punk scholar Simon Reynolds has advocated that post-punk be conceived as "less a genre of music than a space of possibility", suggesting that "what unites all this activity is a set of open-ended imperatives: innovation; willful oddness; the willful jettisoning of all things precedented or 'rock'n'roll'". Nicholas Lezard, problematizing the categorization of post-punk as a genre, described the movement as "so multifarious that only the broadest use of the term is possible".
rewrite: The definition of "post-punk" is debated. Certain reviewers, like Stephen Thomas Erlewine of AllMusic, use the label to describe a more experimental and artistic branch of punk rock. Conversely, many argue it represents a particular creative mindset and methodology, not a coherent musical style. Scholar Simon Reynolds proposes viewing post-punk not as a genre, but as an arena of potential, united by drives toward novelty, deliberate eccentricity, and a rejection of established rock conventions. Echoing this complexity, critic Nicholas Lezard contends the movement is too diverse for any narrow classification, making only a very general application of the term feasible.

input: The centre of Paris contains the most visited monuments in the city, including the Notre Dame Cathedral and the Louvre as well as the Sainte-Chapelle; Les Invalides, where the tomb of Napoleon is located, and the Eiffel Tower are located on the Left Bank south-west of the centre. The banks of the Seine from the Pont de Sully to the Pont d'Iéna have been listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1991. Other landmarks are laid out east to west along the historic axis of Paris, which runs from the Louvre through the Tuileries Garden, the Luxor Column in the Place de la Concorde, the Arc de Triomphe, to the Grande Arche of La Défense.
rewrite: At the heart of Paris lie its most frequented sites, such as Notre Dame, the Louvre, and the Sainte-Chapelle. To the southwest, on the Left Bank, one finds Les Invalides—home to Napoleon's tomb—and the Eiffel Tower. Since 1991, the Seine's embankments between the Pont de Sully and the Pont d'Iéna have held UNESCO World Heritage status. Additional major monuments align along the city's historic east-west axis, extending from the Louvre and the Tuileries Garden, past the Luxor Column at Place de la Concorde and the Arc de Triomphe, all the way to La Défense's Grande Arche.

input: His family was long associated with the teaching of elocution: his grandfather, Alexander Bell, in London, his uncle in Dublin, and his father, in Edinburgh, were all elocutionists. His father published a variety of works on the subject, several of which are still well known, especially his The Standard Elocutionist (1860), which appeared in Edinburgh in 1868. The Standard Elocutionist appeared in 168 British editions and sold over a quarter of a million copies in the United States alone. In this treatise, his father explains his methods of how to instruct deaf-mutes (as they were then known) to articulate words and read other people's lip movements to decipher meaning. Bell's father taught him and his brothers not only to write Visible Speech but to identify any symbol and its accompanying sound. Bell became so proficient that he became a part of his father's public demonstrations and astounded audiences with his abilities. He could decipher Visible Speech representing virtually every language, including Latin, Scottish Gaelic, and even Sanskrit, accurately reciting written tracts without any prior knowledge of their pronunciation.
rewrite: For generations, his family was deeply involved in elocution instruction. His grandfather, Alexander Bell, practiced in London, an uncle in Dublin, and his father, Melville Bell, in Edinburgh. His father authored numerous texts on the subject, many remaining notable. Among these, *The Standard Elocutionist*, first published in Edinburgh in 1868 (though dated 1860), achieved remarkable success. It went through 168 editions in Britain and sold more than 250,000 copies just in the U.S. Within this work, his father detailed techniques for teaching articulation and lip-reading to deaf individuals, then termed deaf-mutes. Bell and his brothers received thorough training from their father in Visible Speech, learning both to write it and to recognize every symbol and its corresponding sound. Bell excelled, eventually participating in public exhibitions where he would amaze onlookers. He demonstrated the skill of reading aloud from Visible Speech transcriptions of diverse languages—including Latin, Scottish Gaelic, and Sanskrit—accurately pronouncing them despite having no previous familiarity.

input: Melbourne has a temperate oceanic climate (Köppen climate classification Cfb) and is well known for its changeable weather conditions. This is mainly due to Melbourne's location situated on the boundary of the very hot inland areas and the cool southern ocean. This temperature differential is most pronounced in the spring and summer months and can cause very strong cold fronts to form. These cold fronts can be responsible for all sorts of severe weather from gales to severe thunderstorms and hail, large temperature drops, and heavy rain.
rewrite: Melbourne experiences a temperate maritime climate, characterized by unpredictable weather patterns. This variability stems from the city's position between warm continental interiors and the colder Southern Ocean. During spring and summer, the significant contrast in temperature often generates intense cold fronts. These fronts may lead to extreme conditions, including powerful winds, serious thunderstorms with hail, sharp declines in temperature, and substantial rainfall.

input: John XXIII died of peritonitis caused by a perforated stomach at 19:49 local time on 3 June 1963 at the age of 81, ending a historic pontificate of four years and seven months. He died just as a Mass for him finished in Saint Peter's Square below, celebrated by Luigi Traglia. After he died, his brow was ritually tapped to see if he was dead, and those with him in the room said prayers. Then the room was illuminated, thus informing the people of what had happened. He was buried on 6 June in the Vatican grottos. Two wreaths, placed on the two sides of his tomb, were donated by the prisoners of the Regina Coeli prison and the Mantova jail in Verona. On 22 June 1963, one day after his friend and successor Pope Paul VI was elected, the latter prayed at his tomb.
rewrite: Pope John XXIII passed away at 7:49 p.m. on June 3, 1963, due to peritonitis from a stomach perforation. He was 81 years old. His impactful time as pope, lasting four years and seven months, concluded at that moment. A Mass held in Saint Peter's Square, led by Luigi Traglia, had just ended. Following his death, a customary check was performed by lightly touching his forehead, and prayers were offered by those present. The lighting of his room then signaled the news to those awaiting outside. His interment occurred on June 6 within the Vatican grottos. Two floral tributes flanking his grave came from inmates at Regina Coeli and Verona's Mantova prison. The next pope, Paul VI, who was also his friend, visited the tomb to pray on June 22, the day after his own election.

input: The capital city, Washington, District of Columbia, is a federal district located on land donated by the state of Maryland. (Virginia had also donated land, but it was returned in 1849.) The United States also has overseas territories with varying levels of independence and organization: in the Caribbean the territories of Puerto Rico and the U.S. Virgin Islands, and in the Pacific the inhabited territories of Guam, American Samoa, and the Northern Mariana Islands, along with a number of uninhabited island territories.
rewrite: Washington, D.C., the nation's capital, is a federal district established on land ceded by Maryland. (Virginia also provided territory, but it was given back in 1849.) Beyond the mainland, the U.S. administers several overseas possessions. These include Puerto Rico and the U.S. Virgin Islands in the Caribbean, as well as Guam, American Samoa, and the Northern Mariana Islands in the Pacific, in addition to various unpopulated islands.

input: New York's non-white population was 36,620 in 1890. New York City was a prime destination in the early twentieth century for African Americans during the Great Migration from the American South, and by 1916, New York City was home to the largest urban African diaspora in North America. The Harlem Renaissance of literary and cultural life flourished during the era of Prohibition. The larger economic boom generated construction of skyscrapers competing in height and creating an identifiable skyline.
rewrite: In 1890, New York had 36,620 non-white residents. The city became a key destination for African Americans moving north in the early 1900s Great Migration, hosting North America's biggest urban Black community by 1916. During Prohibition, the Harlem Renaissance thrived culturally. Concurrently, a major economic upswing spurred a race to build ever-taller skyscrapers, forging the city's iconic skyline.

input: In eastern Pennsylvania the Great Appalachian Valley, or Great Valley, was accessible by reason of a broad gateway between the end of South Mountain and the Highlands, and many Germans and Moravians settled here between the Susquehanna and Delaware Rivers forming the Pennsylvania Dutch community, some of whom even now speak a unique American dialect of German known as the "Pennsylvania German language" or "Pennsylvania Dutch." These latecomers to the New World were forced to the frontier to find cheap land. With their followers of both German, English and Scots-Irish origin, they worked their way southward and soon occupied all of the Shenandoah Valley, ceded by the Iroquois, and the upper reaches of the Great Valley tributaries of the Tennessee River, ceded by the Cherokee.
rewrite: In eastern Pennsylvania, the expansive Great Appalachian Valley offered an inviting entry point through a wide gap flanked by South Mountain and the Highlands. This drew numerous German and Moravian settlers to the region between the Susquehanna and Delaware Rivers, establishing the Pennsylvania Dutch community. Many in this group still use a distinctive American German dialect, often called Pennsylvania German or Pennsylvania Dutch. Arriving later to the Americas, these settlers sought affordable land on the frontier. Alongside followers of German, English, and Scots-Irish descent, they moved southward, eventually populating the entire Shenandoah Valley—land relinquished by the Iroquois—as well as the upper sections of the Tennessee River's tributaries within the Great Valley, which had been ceded by the Cherokee.

input: Temperatures below 0 °C (32 °F) or above 25 °C (77 °F) are rare. Cork Airport records an average of 1,227.9 millimetres (4.029 ft) of precipitation annually, most of which is rain. The airport records an average of 7 days of hail and 11 days of snow or sleet a year; though it only records lying snow for 2 days of the year. The low altitude of the city, and moderating influences of the harbour, mean that lying snow very rarely occurs in the city itself. There are on average 204 "rainy" days a year (over 0.2 millimetres (0.0079 in) of rainfall), of which there are 73 days with "heavy rain" (over 5 millimetres (0.20 in)). Cork is also a generally foggy city, with an average of 97 days of fog a year, most common during mornings and during winter. Despite this, however, Cork is also one of Ireland's sunniest cities, with an average of 3.9 hours of sunshine every day and only having 67 days where there is no "recordable sunshine", mostly during and around winter.
rewrite:
Extreme cold or heat is uncommon, with temperatures seldom dropping below freezing or rising above 25 °C (77 °F). Annual rainfall at Cork Airport averages approximately 1,228 millimetres, predominantly as rain. The area experiences limited wintry precipitation, averaging about 7 days of hail and 11 days with snow or sleet annually, yet snow accumulates on the ground for only around 2 days. Cork's low elevation and the tempering effect of its harbour make settled snow exceedingly rare within the city proper.

On average, 204 days each year see measurable rainfall exceeding 0.2 millimetres, including 73 days classified with heavy rain of over 5 millimetres. Fog is frequent, occurring on roughly 97 days annually, primarily in winter mornings. Despite this prevalent fog, Cork enjoys considerable sunshine for Ireland, averaging nearly 4 hours per day. Days with no measurable sunshine are relatively infrequent, numbering about 67 per year and largely concentrated in the winter months.

input: After the scandal, actress Brigitte Nielsen came forward and stated that she too had an affair with Schwarzenegger while he was in a relationship with Shriver, saying, "Maybe I wouldn't have got into it if he said 'I'm going to marry Maria' and this is dead serious, but he didn't, and our affair carried on." When asked in 2014 "Of all the things you are famous for … which are you least proud of?", Schwarzenegger replied "I'm least proud of the mistakes I made that caused my family pain and split us up".
rewrite: Actress Brigitte Nielsen later revealed she was also involved with Arnold Schwarzenegger during his time with Maria Shriver. Nielsen suggested that if he had expressed serious marital intentions, she might have ended the relationship, but he did not, so it continued. Years later, when questioned about his biggest regret, Schwarzenegger cited the errors that hurt his family and led to their separation.

input: A more sophisticated MP3 encoder can produce variable bitrate audio. MPEG audio may use bitrate switching on a per-frame basis, but only layer III decoders must support it. VBR is used when the goal is to achieve a fixed level of quality. The final file size of a VBR encoding is less predictable than with constant bitrate. Average bitrate is VBR implemented as a compromise between the two: the bitrate is allowed to vary for more consistent quality, but is controlled to remain near an average value chosen by the user, for predictable file sizes. Although an MP3 decoder must support VBR to be standards compliant, historically some decoders have bugs with VBR decoding, particularly before VBR encoders became widespread.
rewrite: Advanced MP3 encoding methods allow for variable bitrate output. While MPEG audio standards permit adjusting bitrates between individual frames, this capability is mandatory only for layer III playback devices. Variable bitrate encoding aims to maintain consistent audio quality, though it results in less certain final file sizes compared to constant bitrate methods. A middle approach is average bitrate encoding, which permits fluctuation for quality purposes but is regulated to hover close to a user-defined average, offering more predictable storage requirements. Despite MP3 standards requiring decoder support for variable bitrate, some early players contained errors in processing such files, especially prior to the common adoption of VBR encoders.

input: During the early 20th century it became increasingly common to bury cremated remains rather than coffins in the abbey. In 1905 the actor Sir Henry Irving was cremated and his ashes buried in Westminster Abbey, thereby becoming the first person ever to be cremated prior to interment at the abbey. The majority of interments at the Abbey are of cremated remains, but some burials still take place - Frances Challen, wife of the Rev Sebastian Charles, Canon of Westminster, was buried alongside her husband in the south choir aisle in 2014. Members of the Percy Family have a family vault, The Northumberland Vault, in St Nicholas's chapel within the abbey.
rewrite: In the early 1900s, interring cremated ashes instead of caskets grew more frequent at the abbey. Sir Henry Irving, the actor, was cremated in 1905, and his ashes were placed there, marking the first instance of cremation before burial in the abbey. Today, most increments there involve ashes, though full-body burials occasionally occur, such as Frances Challen's in 2014. Additionally, certain families, like the Percys, maintain dedicated burial spaces, such as the Northumberland Vault in St. Nicholas's chapel.

input: Subsequently, it became one of Britain's most significant honours to be buried or commemorated in the abbey. The practice of burying national figures in the abbey began under Oliver Cromwell with the burial of Admiral Robert Blake in 1657. The practice spread to include generals, admirals, politicians, doctors and scientists such as Isaac Newton, buried on 4 April 1727, and Charles Darwin, buried 26 April 1882. Another was William Wilberforce who led the movement to abolish slavery in the United Kingdom and the Plantations, buried on 3 August 1833. Wilberforce was buried in the north transept, close to his friend, the former Prime Minister, William Pitt.[citation needed]
rewrite: Over time, interment or commemoration within the abbey grew into one of the nation's highest distinctions. This tradition of laying notable citizens to rest there originated in 1657 with Admiral Robert Blake during Cromwell's era. It later expanded to encompass military leaders, statesmen, physicians, and eminent scientists like Isaac Newton and Charles Darwin. Also included was William Wilberforce, a key figure in ending slavery across Britain and its colonies. He was interred in the north transept near his ally, ex-Prime Minister William Pitt.

input: The geographical regions in which Iranian languages were spoken were pushed back in several areas by newly neighbouring languages. Arabic spread into some parts of Western Iran (Khuzestan), and Turkic languages spread through much of Central Asia, displacing various Iranian languages such as Sogdian and Bactrian in parts of what is today Turkmenistan, Uzbekistan and Tajikistan. In Eastern Europe, mostly comprising the territory of modern-day Ukraine, southern European Russia, and parts of the Balkans, the core region of the native Scythians, Sarmatians, and Alans had been decisively been taken over as a result of absorption and assimilation (e.g. Slavicisation) by the various Proto-Slavic population of the region, by the 6th century AD. This resulted in the displacement and extinction of the once predominant Scythian languages of the region. Sogdian's close relative Yaghnobi barely survives in a small area of the Zarafshan valley east of Samarkand, and Saka as Ossetic in the Caucasus, which is the sole remnant of the once predominant Scythian languages in Eastern Europe proper and large parts of the North Caucasus. Various small Iranian languages in the Pamirs survive that are derived from Eastern Iranian.
rewrite: The territories where Iranian languages were historically spoken have been reduced over time due to encroachment by other language groups. In Western Iran, specifically Khuzestan, Arabic made significant inroads. Across Central Asia, Turkic languages expanded widely, replacing Iranian tongues like Sogdian and Bactrian in areas now within Turkmenistan, Uzbekistan, and Tajikistan. In Eastern Europe—covering modern Ukraine, southern European Russia, and sections of the Balkans—the indigenous Scythian, Sarmatian, and Alanic peoples were largely absorbed by Proto-Slavic communities through processes like Slavicization by around the 6th century AD. Consequently, the once-dominant Scythian languages in that region were displaced and ultimately vanished. Today, only a few remnants persist: Yaghnobi, related to Sogdian, endures in a limited zone of the Zarafshan valley near Samarkand, while Saka survives as Ossetic in the Caucasus. Ossetic is the last vestige of the Scythian languages that were once prevalent across Eastern Europe and much of the North Caucasus. Additionally, several minor Eastern Iranian languages continue in the Pamir Mountains.

input: All iPods except for the iPod Touch can function in "disk mode" as mass storage devices to store data files but this may not be the default behavior, and in the case of the iPod Touch, requires special software.[citation needed] If an iPod is formatted on a Mac OS computer, it uses the HFS+ file system format, which allows it to serve as a boot disk for a Mac computer. If it is formatted on Windows, the FAT32 format is used. With the release of the Windows-compatible iPod, the default file system used on the iPod line switched from HFS+ to FAT32, although it can be reformatted to either file system (excluding the iPod Shuffle which is strictly FAT32). Generally, if a new iPod (excluding the iPod Shuffle) is initially plugged into a computer running Windows, it will be formatted with FAT32, and if initially plugged into a Mac running Mac OS it will be formatted with HFS+.
rewrite: Most iPod models, aside from the iPod Touch, can be set to operate as external storage drives for general file data, though this often requires adjusting the settings. The iPod Touch specifically needs additional applications to achieve this functionality. When an iPod is initially set up with a Mac, it adopts the HFS+ file structure, enabling it to start up a Mac system. Conversely, connection to a Windows PC results in formatting with FAT32. Following the introduction of Windows-compatible iPods, FAT32 became the standard across the lineup, moving away from the earlier HFS+ default. Users can typically reformat most iPods to either system, with the exception of the iPod Shuffle, which is restricted to FAT32. In practice, a new iPod (excluding the Shuffle) will be formatted as FAT32 if first connected to a Windows machine, or as HFS+ if first linked to a Mac.

input: Cardigan formed up his unit and charged the length of the Valley of the Balaclava, under fire from Russian batteries in the hills. The charge of the Light Brigade caused 278 casualties of the 700-man unit. The Light Brigade was memorialized in the famous poem by Alfred Lord Tennyson, "The Charge of the Light Brigade." Although traditionally the charge of the Light Brigade was looked upon as a glorious but wasted sacrifice of good men and horses, recent historians say that the charge of the Light Brigade did succeed in at least some of its objectives. The aim of any cavalry charge is to scatter the enemy lines and frighten the enemy off the battlefield. The charge of the Light Brigade had so unnerved the Russian cavalry, which had previously been routed by the Heavy Brigade, that the Russian Cavalry was set to full-scale flight by the subsequent charge of the Light Brigade.:252
rewrite: Lord Cardigan organized his troops and led an assault across the Balaclava Valley, enduring artillery attacks from Russian positions on the surrounding high ground. This action, known as the Charge of the Light Brigade, resulted in 278 casualties from the roughly 700 soldiers involved. Alfred Lord Tennyson later immortalized the event in his renowned poem of the same name. While long viewed as a tragically futile yet heroic loss of soldiers and mounts, modern historical analysis suggests the charge partially achieved its goals. The primary purpose of a cavalry attack is to break enemy formations and instill panic. In this case, the Light Brigade’s advance profoundly demoralized the Russian cavalry, which was already shaken from an earlier engagement with the Heavy Brigade, ultimately causing them to retreat in full disarray.

input: Larry Christenson, a Lutheran theologian based in San Pedro, California, did much in the 1960s and 1970s to interpret the charismatic movement for Lutherans. A very large annual conference regarding that matter was held in Minneapolis. Charismatic Lutheran congregations in Minnesota became especially large and influential; especially "Hosanna!" in Lakeville, and North Heights in St. Paul. The next generation of Lutheran charismatics cluster around the Alliance of Renewal Churches. There is considerable charismatic activity among young Lutheran leaders in California centered around an annual gathering at Robinwood Church in Huntington Beach. Richard A. Jensen's Touched by the Spirit published in 1974, played a major role of the Lutheran understanding to the charismatic movement.
rewrite: During the 1960s and 1970s, Lutheran theologian Larry Christenson, from San Pedro, California, worked extensively to explain the charismatic movement to his denomination. A major yearly conference on this topic took place in Minneapolis. In Minnesota, charismatic Lutheran churches, such as Lakeville's "Hosanna!" and North Heights in St. Paul, grew notably large and impactful. Today, newer Lutheran charismatics are primarily connected through the Alliance of Renewal Churches. Significant charismatic engagement also exists among younger Lutheran pastors in California, focusing on a yearly event at Huntington Beach's Robinwood Church. Richard A. Jensen's 1974 book, *Touched by the Spirit*, was highly influential in shaping Lutheran perspectives on the movement.

input: The other directly attested Old Iranian dialects are the two forms of Avestan, which take their name from their use in the Avesta, the liturgical texts of indigenous Iranian religion that now goes by the name of Zoroastrianism but in the Avesta itself is simply known as vohu daena (later: behdin). The language of the Avesta is subdivided into two dialects, conventionally known as "Old (or 'Gathic') Avestan", and "Younger Avestan". These terms, which date to the 19th century, are slightly misleading since 'Younger Avestan' is not only much younger than 'Old Avestan', but also from a different geographic region. The Old Avestan dialect is very archaic, and at roughly the same stage of development as Rigvedic Sanskrit. On the other hand, Younger Avestan is at about the same linguistic stage as Old Persian, but by virtue of its use as a sacred language retained its "old" characteristics long after the Old Iranian languages had yielded to their Middle Iranian stage. Unlike Old Persian, which has Middle Persian as its known successor, Avestan has no clearly identifiable Middle Iranian stage (the effect of Middle Iranian is indistinguishable from effects due to other causes).
rewrite: The remaining Old Iranian languages that are directly documented include two variants of Avestan. This name derives from their appearance in the Avesta, which comprises the ritual scriptures of the native Iranian faith. That religion is presently called Zoroastrianism, though within the Avesta it is referred to simply as vohu daena (later termed behdin). Scholars typically divide the language of these texts into two forms: "Old Avestan" (also called Gathic) and "Younger Avestan." These labels originated in the 1800s and are somewhat imprecise, because Younger Avestan is not only considerably more recent than Old Avestan but also stems from a distinct geographical area. Old Avestan is linguistically very ancient, showing a developmental stage comparable to that of Rigvedic Sanskrit. In contrast, Younger Avestan is roughly contemporaneous with Old Persian in terms of linguistic evolution. However, because it served as a liturgical language, it preserved archaic features well after other Old Iranian tongues had transitioned into their Middle Iranian phases.
