As Western Europe developed ocean routes circumventing the Middle East and Mediterranean, the importance of overland eastern trade corridors diminished—a decline that coincided with the empire's own waning power. Within this progression, agreements like the Anglo-Ottoman Treaty (the Treaty of Balta Liman), which exposed Ottoman markets directly to British and French commercial rivalry, are viewed as key milestones.

input: Traditionally, subspecies are seen as geographically isolated and genetically differentiated populations. That is, "the designation 'subspecies' is used to indicate an objective degree of microevolutionary divergence" One objection to this idea is that it does not specify what degree of differentiation is required. Therefore, any population that is somewhat biologically different could be considered a subspecies, even to the level of a local population. As a result, Templeton has argued that it is necessary to impose a threshold on the level of difference that is required for a population to be designated a subspecies.
rewrite: Subspecies are typically defined as genetically distinct groups separated by geography, representing measurable evolutionary divergence. However, a key criticism is that this concept lacks clear criteria for how much differentiation is necessary. Consequently, even slightly distinct local groups might qualify, making the designation overly broad. In response, researchers like Templeton advocate for establishing a minimum threshold of genetic or biological difference to justify the subspecies classification.

input: At the Salon d'Automne of the same year, in addition to the Indépendants group of Salle 41, were exhibited works by André Lhote, Marcel Duchamp, Jacques Villon, Roger de La Fresnaye, André Dunoyer de Segonzac and František Kupka. The exhibition was reviewed in the October 8, 1911 issue of The New York Times. This article was published a year after Gelett Burgess' The Wild Men of Paris, and two years prior to the Armory Show, which introduced astonished Americans, accustomed to realistic art, to the experimental styles of the European avant garde, including Fauvism, Cubism, and Futurism. The 1911 New York Times article portrayed works by Picasso, Matisse, Derain, Metzinger and others dated before 1909; not exhibited at the 1911 Salon. The article was titled The "Cubists" Dominate Paris' Fall Salon and subtitled Eccentric School of Painting Increases Its Vogue in the Current Art Exhibition - What Its Followers Attempt to Do.
rewrite: At the 1911 Salon d'Automne, pieces by artists such as André Lhote, Marcel Duchamp, and František Kupka were shown alongside those from the Indépendants collective. A critique of this event appeared in The New York Times on October 8, 1911. This review came one year following Gelett Burgess' piece, "The Wild Men of Paris," and preceded the 1913 Armory Show by two years. That later exhibition would first expose American audiences, then familiar only with representational art, to radical European movements like Fauvism, Cubism, and Futurism. The 1911 article, named The "Cubists" Dominate Paris' Fall Salon, with a secondary heading noting the growing popularity of this unconventional painting style, discussed pre-1909 works by Picasso, Matisse, and others—pieces not actually on display at that year's Salon.

input: For example, 1920×1080p25 identifies progressive scanning format with 25 frames per second, each frame being 1,920 pixels wide and 1,080 pixels high. The 1080i25 or 1080i50 notation identifies interlaced scanning format with 25 frames (50 fields) per second, each frame being 1,920 pixels wide and 1,080 pixels high. The 1080i30 or 1080i60 notation identifies interlaced scanning format with 30 frames (60 fields) per second, each frame being 1,920 pixels wide and 1,080 pixels high. The 720p60 notation identifies progressive scanning format with 60 frames per second, each frame being 720 pixels high; 1,280 pixels horizontally are implied.
rewrite: The notation 1920×1080p25 indicates a progressive scan video with 25 frames each second, where every image measures 1,920 pixels in width by 1,080 in height. Formats like 1080i25 or 1080i50 denote interlaced scanning, offering 25 complete frames (or 50 fields) per second at the same 1920x1080 resolution. Similarly, 1080i30 or 1080i60 specifies 30 frames (60 fields) per second. Meanwhile, 720p60 represents a progressive format with 60 frames per second, each having a height of 720 pixels and an understood width of 1,280 pixels.

input: No further attempts to establish English colonies in the Americas were made until well into the reign of Queen Elizabeth I, during the last decades of the 16th century. In the meantime the Protestant Reformation had turned England and Catholic Spain into implacable enemies . In 1562, the English Crown encouraged the privateers John Hawkins and Francis Drake to engage in slave-raiding attacks against Spanish and Portuguese ships off the coast of West Africa with the aim of breaking into the Atlantic trade system. This effort was rebuffed and later, as the Anglo-Spanish Wars intensified, Elizabeth I gave her blessing to further privateering raids against Spanish ports in the Americas and shipping that was returning across the Atlantic, laden with treasure from the New World. At the same time, influential writers such as Richard Hakluyt and John Dee (who was the first to use the term "British Empire") were beginning to press for the establishment of England's own empire. By this time, Spain had become the dominant power in the Americas and was exploring the Pacific ocean, Portugal had established trading posts and forts from the coasts of Africa and Brazil to China, and France had begun to settle the Saint Lawrence River area, later to become New France.
rewrite: Following the initial ventures, there was a prolonged pause in England's efforts to found settlements in the Americas. This hiatus lasted until the latter part of the sixteenth century, under Queen Elizabeth I. This period also saw the deepening divide of the Protestant Reformation, which set England against Catholic Spain in a fierce rivalry. In 1562, with royal support, privateers like John Hawkins and Francis Drake assaulted Spanish and Portuguese vessels near West Africa to seize slaves, aiming to infiltrate the Atlantic commerce. These attempts were ultimately unsuccessful. As hostilities between England and Spain escalated, Queen Elizabeth sanctioned additional raids by privateers on Spanish colonial ports and on treasure fleets sailing from the New World. Concurrently, prominent thinkers, including Richard Hakluyt and John Dee—who coined the phrase "British Empire"—argued for England to pursue its own imperial ambitions. During this era, Spain had achieved preeminence in the Americas and was venturing into the Pacific, Portugal had built a network of commercial and military outposts from Africa and Brazil to China, and France was initiating colonization along the Saint Lawrence River, the region that would become New France.

input: In a movie theater, steps in the aisles are usually marked with a row of small lights for convenience and safety, when the film has started and the other lights are off. Traditionally made up of small low wattage, low voltage lamps in a track or translucent tube, these are rapidly being replaced with LED based versions.
rewrite: Aisles in cinemas often feature small lights along the steps for safety and ease of movement after the main lights dim. While these were traditionally low-power bulbs set in a track or tube, they are now quickly being substituted by LED alternatives.

input: Chopin's polonaises show a marked advance on those of his Polish predecessors in the form (who included his teachers Zywny and Elsner). As with the traditional polonaise, Chopin's works are in triple time and typically display a martial rhythm in their melodies, accompaniments and cadences. Unlike most of their precursors, they also require a formidable playing technique.
rewrite: Chopin's polonaises significantly surpass those of earlier Polish composers, including his own instructors. While maintaining the classic triple meter and martial cadence throughout, his versions demand a far more advanced level of technical skill from the performer.

input: Erich Koch headed the East Prussian Nazi party from 1928. He led the district from 1932. This period was characterized by efforts to collectivize the local agriculture and ruthlessness in dealing with his critics inside and outside the Party. He also had long-term plans for mass-scale industrialization of the largely agricultural province. These actions made him unpopular among the local peasants. In 1932 the local paramilitary SA had already started to terrorise their political opponents. On the night of 31 July 1932 there was a bomb attack on the headquarters of the Social Democrats in Königsberg, the Otto-Braun-House. The Communist politician Gustav Sauf was killed; the executive editor of the Social Democrat "Königsberger Volkszeitung", Otto Wyrgatsch, and the German People's Party politician Max von Bahrfeldt were severely injured. Members of the Reichsbanner were attacked and the local Reichsbanner Chairman of Lötzen, Kurt Kotzan, was murdered on 6 August 1932.
rewrite: Erich Koch assumed leadership of the Nazi organization in East Prussia in 1928, taking full control of the district by 1932. His tenure involved aggressive policies to collectivize farming and harsh suppression of dissent, alongside ambitious schemes to industrialize the primarily rural region. These measures fostered significant resentment among the agrarian population. Concurrently, the regional SA paramilitary intensified a campaign of intimidation against political adversaries. This violence culminated in late July 1932 with the bombing of the Social Democratic headquarters in Königsberg, killing Communist figure Gustav Sauf and severely injuring Otto Wyrgatsch, a newspaper editor, and politician Max von Bahrfeldt. Further attacks followed, including the murder of Kurt Kotzan, a local Reichsbanner leader, in early August.

input:
Spanish Supreme Court is the highest court for all cases in Spain (both private and public). Only those cases related to human rights can be appealed at the Constitutional Court (which also decides about acts accordance with Spanish Constitution).
In Spain, high courts cannot create binding precedents; however, lower rank courts usually observe Supreme Court interpretations. In most private law cases, two Supreme Court judgements supporting a claim are needed to appeal at the Supreme Court.
Five sections form the Spanish Supreme court:
rewrite: The Supreme Court in Spain serves as the ultimate judicial authority for all legal matters, encompassing both civil and public issues. Appeals concerning human rights are directed to the Constitutional Court, which also rules on constitutional compliance. While high courts do not set binding precedents, lower courts typically follow Supreme Court rulings. For many civil cases, appealing to the Supreme Court requires two prior favorable judgments. This court is organized into five distinct chambers.

input: The High Middle Ages was a period of tremendous expansion of population. The estimated population of Europe grew from 35 to 80 million between 1000 and 1347, although the exact causes remain unclear: improved agricultural techniques, the decline of slaveholding, a more clement climate and the lack of invasion have all been suggested. As much as 90 per cent of the European population remained rural peasants. Many were no longer settled in isolated farms but had gathered into small communities, usually known as manors or villages. These peasants were often subject to noble overlords and owed them rents and other services, in a system known as manorialism. There remained a few free peasants throughout this period and beyond, with more of them in the regions of Southern Europe than in the north. The practice of assarting, or bringing new lands into production by offering incentives to the peasants who settled them, also contributed to the expansion of population.
rewrite: During the High Middle Ages, Europe experienced significant demographic growth. From the year 1000 until 1347, the number of inhabitants is thought to have risen from approximately 35 million to around 80 million. The precise reasons for this surge are debated, but proposed factors include advancements in farming, a reduction in slavery, favorable weather patterns, and a period free from major invasions. Approximately ninety percent of Europeans lived in the countryside as peasants. Increasingly, these individuals clustered into small settlements—manors or villages—rather than living on separate farmsteads. Under the manorial system, most peasants were tied to a lord, owing various rents and labor duties. However, a minority remained free, particularly in southern regions. Population expansion was further aided by assarting, the process of clearing new lands for cultivation by attracting settlers with special privileges.

input: Small-scale artisanal mining of gold is another source of dangerous child labour in poor rural areas in certain parts of the world. This form of mining uses labour-intensive and low-tech methods. It is informal sector of the economy. Human Rights Watch group estimates that about 12 percent of global gold production comes from artisanal mines. In west Africa, in countries such as Mali - the third largest exporter of gold in Africa - between 20,000 and 40,000 children work in artisanal mining. Locally known as orpaillage, children as young as 6 years old work with their families. These children and families suffer chronic exposure to toxic chemicals including mercury, and do hazardous work such as digging shafts and working underground, pulling up, carrying and crushing the ore. The poor work practices harm the long term health of children, as well as release hundreds of tons of mercury every year into local rivers, ground water and lakes. Gold is important to the economy of Mali and Ghana. For Mali, it is the second largest earner of its export revenue. For many poor families with children, it is the primary and sometimes the only source of income.
rewrite: In some impoverished rural regions globally, the informal practice of small-scale, manual gold mining subjects children to hazardous labor. This low-technology, labor-driven sector operates outside formal economic structures. According to Human Rights Watch, artisanal mines contribute roughly twelve percent of the world's gold supply. In West African nations like Mali—Africa's third-largest gold exporter—an estimated 20,000 to 40,000 minors are engaged in this work. Referred to locally as orpaillage, the practice involves children from as young as six laboring alongside their families. These miners face ongoing contact with poisonous substances like mercury and perform dangerous tasks, including excavating deep pits, working below ground, and hauling, lifting, and breaking apart raw ore. Such unsafe conditions severely damage children's long-term well-being and also result in the annual discharge of hundreds of tons of mercury into nearby waterways, aquifers, and lakes. Gold plays a crucial economic role for countries such as Mali and Ghana; in Mali, it ranks as the second-largest export revenue source. For numerous impoverished households with children, this mining activity represents their main, and often sole, means of earning a livelihood.

input: In past times, mending was an art. A meticulous tailor or seamstress could mend rips with thread raveled from hems and seam edges so skillfully that the tear was practically invisible. When the raw material – cloth – was worth more than labor, it made sense to expend labor in saving it. Today clothing is considered a consumable item. Mass-manufactured clothing is less expensive than the labor required to repair it. Many people buy a new piece of clothing rather than spend time mending. The thrifty still replace zippers and buttons and sew up ripped hems.
rewrite: Historically, repairing garments was a valued craft. Skilled artisans could seamlessly fix tears using threads carefully drawn from the fabric's own edges, rendering the damage undetectable. This practice was economical when materials were costly relative to the work of saving them. Now, most apparel is seen as disposable; it is often cheaper to replace mass-produced items than to pay for repairs. Consequently, many opt for new purchases over mending, though frugal individuals still undertake basic fixes like replacing fasteners or stitching seams.

input: In early 1757, Frederick II again took the initiative by marching into the Kingdom of Bohemia, hoping to inflict a decisive defeat on Austrian forces. After winning the bloody Battle of Prague on 6 May 1757, in which both forces suffered major casualties, the Prussians forced the Austrians back into the fortifications of Prague. The Prussian army then laid siege to the city. Following the battle at Prague, Frederick took 5,000 troops from the siege at Prague and sent them to reinforce the 19,000-man army under the Duke of Brunswick-Bevern at Kolin in Bohemia. Austrian Marshal Daun arrived too late to participate in the battle of Prague, but picked up 16,000 men who had escaped from the battle. With this army he slowly moved to relieve Prague. The Prussian army was too weak to simultaneously besiege Prague and keep Daun away, and Frederick was forced to attack prepared positions. The resulting Battle of Kolin was a sharp defeat for Frederick, his first military defeat. His losses further forced him to lift the siege and withdraw from Bohemia altogether.
rewrite: At the outset of 1757, Frederick II resumed offensive operations by advancing his forces into Bohemia, aiming to deliver a crippling blow to the Habsburg armies. A fierce engagement at Prague on May 6th resulted in severe losses on both sides, compelling the Austrians to retreat behind the city's defenses, where Prussian troops subsequently confined them. After this clash, Frederick diverted 5,000 soldiers from the ongoing blockade to strengthen the Duke of Brunswick-Bevern's command of 19,000 men positioned near Kolin. Austrian commander Marshal Daun, having missed the Prague conflict, gathered 16,000 survivors from that fight. He cautiously advanced with this force to break the siege. Frederick's stretched resources could not maintain the investment of Prague while also countering Daun's approach, leaving him no choice but to assault entrenched Austrian lines. The encounter at Kolin ended in a clear Prussian reversal, marking Frederick's initial defeat in the field. These casualties necessitated abandoning the siege and a full Prussian retreat from Bohemian territory.

input: A new generation of clubs such as Liverpool's Cream and the Ministry of Sound were opened to provide a venue for more commercial sounds. Major record companies began to open "superclubs" promoting their own acts. These superclubs entered into sponsorship deals initially with fast food, soft drinks, and clothing companies. Flyers in clubs in Ibiza often sported many corporate logos. A new subgenre, Chicago hard house, was developed by DJs such as Bad Boy Bill, DJ Lynnwood, DJ Irene, Richard "Humpty" Vission and DJ Enrie, mixing elements of Chicago house, funky house and hard house together. Additionally, Producers such as George Centeno, Darren Ramirez, and Martin O. Cairo would develop the Los Angeles Hard House sound. Similar to gabber or hardcore techno from the Netherlands, this sound was often associated with the "rebel" culture of the time. These 3 producers are often considered "ahead of their time" since many of the sounds they engineered during the late 20th century became more prominent during the 21st century.
rewrite: Emerging venues like Liverpool's Cream and the Ministry of Sound catered to a more mainstream audience with accessible music. Major labels launched their own "superclubs" to feature artists from their rosters, securing early sponsorships from brands in fast food, beverage, and apparel industries. Club advertisements in Ibiza became crowded with corporate branding. Meanwhile, a fresh style called Chicago hard house was crafted by DJs including Bad Boy Bill, DJ Lynnwood, DJ Irene, Richard "Humpty" Vission, and DJ Enrie, blending components of Chicago house, funky house, and hard house. In parallel, figures like George Centeno, Darren Ramirez, and Martin O. Cairo pioneered a distinct Los Angeles Hard House scene. This aggressive style, reminiscent of Dutch gabber or hardcore techno, resonated with the era's countercultural movements. These three innovators are frequently viewed as precursors, as the sonic elements they crafted in the late 1900s gained much wider recognition in the 2000s.

input: In August 1836, two real estate entrepreneurs—Augustus Chapman Allen and John Kirby Allen—from New York, purchased 6,642 acres (26.88 km2) of land along Buffalo Bayou with the intent of founding a city. The Allen brothers decided to name the city after Sam Houston, the popular general at the Battle of San Jacinto, who was elected President of Texas in September 1836. The great majority of slaves in Texas came with their owners from the older slave states. Sizable numbers, however, came through the domestic slave trade. New Orleans was the center of this trade in the Deep South, but there were slave dealers in Houston. Thousands of enslaved African-Americans lived near the city before the Civil War. Many of them near the city worked on sugar and cotton plantations, while most of those in the city limits had domestic and artisan jobs. In 1860 forty-nine percent of the city's population was enslaved. A few slaves, perhaps as many as 2,000 between 1835 and 1865, came through the illegal African trade. Post-war Texas grew rapidly as migrants poured into the cotton lands of the state. They also brought or purchased enslaved African Americans, whose numbers nearly tripled in the state from 1850 to 1860, from 58,000 to 182,566.
rewrite: In August of 1836, Augustus Chapman Allen and John Kirby Allen, brothers and land speculators originally from New York, acquired over 6,600 acres bordering Buffalo Bayou to establish a new settlement. They chose to honor Sam Houston, a revered military leader from the Battle of San Jacinto who would become Texas president that September, by naming the city after him. Most enslaved people in Texas arrived with migrating owners from established slaveholding states, though a significant portion was also trafficked via the domestic slave market. While New Orleans served as the primary hub for this trade in the region, Houston itself housed slave dealers. Prior to the Civil War, thousands of enslaved African Americans resided in the area. Those on outlying plantations typically labored in sugar and cotton cultivation, whereas those within the urban center often held domestic or skilled trade positions. By 1860, enslaved individuals comprised forty-nine percent of Houston’s inhabitants. A small number, estimated up to 2,000 from 1835 to 1865, were illegally imported from Africa. After the war, Texas expanded quickly as settlers flooded into its cotton regions. These migrants either brought with them or subsequently acquired enslaved African Americans, leading the state's enslaved population to surge from approximately 58,000 in 1850 to over 182,500 by 1860.

input: Early Muslim armies stayed in encampments away from cities because Umar feared that they might get attracted to wealth and luxury. In the process, they might turn away from the worship of God and start accumulating wealth and establishing dynasties. When Uthman ibn al-Affan became very old, Marwan I, a relative of Muawiyah I, slipped into the vacuum, became his secretary, slowly assumed more control and relaxed some of these restrictions. Marwan I had previously been excluded from positions of responsibility. In 656, Muhammad ibn Abi Bakr, the son of Abu Bakr, the adopted son of Ali ibn Abi Talib, and the great grandfather of Ja'far al-Sadiq, showed some Egyptians the house of Uthman ibn al-Affan. Later the Egyptians ended up killing Uthman ibn al-Affan.
rewrite: To prevent early Muslim forces from being drawn to affluence and opulence, Caliph Umar stationed them in separate camps outside urban areas. He worried that proximity to city life would lead them to abandon devout practices, hoard riches, and found hereditary rules. As Caliph Uthman aged, his influence waned, allowing Marwan I—a kinsman of Muawiyah I and formerly barred from authority—to become his aide. Marwan gradually seized greater power and loosened Umar's stringent rules. Subsequently, in 656, Muhammad ibn Abi Bakr, who was Abu Bakr's son, Ali's adopted child, and an ancestor of Ja'far al-Sadiq, guided a group of Egyptians to Uthman's residence. This event culminated in Uthman's assassination by those Egyptians.

input: In the lead up to the Iraq War, Kerry said on October 9, 2002; "I will be voting to give the President of the United States the authority to use force, if necessary, to disarm Saddam Hussein because I believe that a deadly arsenal of weapons of mass destruction in his hands is a real and grave threat to our security." Bush relied on that resolution in ordering the 2003 invasion of Iraq. Kerry also gave a January 23, 2003 speech to Georgetown University saying "Without question, we need to disarm Saddam Hussein. He is a brutal, murderous dictator; leading an oppressive regime he presents a particularly grievous threat because he is so consistently prone to miscalculation. So the threat of Saddam Hussein with weapons of mass destruction is real." Kerry did, however, warn that the administration should exhaust its diplomatic avenues before launching war: "Mr. President, do not rush to war, take the time to build the coalition, because it's not winning the war that's hard, it's winning the peace that's hard."
rewrite: Prior to the onset of the Iraq War, Senator John Kerry expressed his position on October 9, 2002. He stated his intention to support a measure granting the President the power to employ military action to disarm Saddam Hussein, should it become unavoidable. Kerry justified this by citing his conviction that Hussein's possession of a lethal stockpile of weapons of mass destruction constituted a serious and genuine danger to American safety. President Bush later invoked this congressional authorization when initiating the invasion in 2003. In a subsequent address at Georgetown University on January 23, 2003, Kerry reiterated that disarming the Iraqi leader was unquestionably necessary, describing him as a cruel and calculating despot whose history of misjudgment made his potential ownership of such armaments a tangible peril. Nevertheless, Kerry concurrently urged caution, advising the administration to fully pursue all diplomatic options before committing to conflict. He emphasized that constructing a strong international alliance was crucial, as the greater challenge lay not in military victory but in securing a stable peace afterward.

input: The same considerations about barriers and detours that apply to long-distance land-bird migration apply to water birds, but in reverse: a large area of land without bodies of water that offer feeding sites may also be a barrier to a bird that feeds in coastal waters. Detours avoiding such barriers are observed: for example, brent geese Branta bernicla migrating from the Taymyr Peninsula to the Wadden Sea travel via the White Sea coast and the Baltic Sea rather than directly across the Arctic Ocean and northern Scandinavia.
rewrite: Similar obstacles and alternate routes that affect land birds during their migrations also influence water birds, but in an opposite manner. For species that rely on coastal feeding, extensive dry regions lacking aquatic food sources can act as significant barriers. Consequently, birds often take longer paths to avoid these areas. Brent geese, for instance, journey from the Taymyr Peninsula to the Wadden Sea by following the White Sea and Baltic coastlines instead of flying straight over the Arctic Ocean and northern Scandinavia.

input: Domestication of sheep and goats reached Egypt from the Near East possibly as early as 6,000 BC. Graeme Barker states "The first indisputable evidence for domestic plants and animals in the Nile valley is not until the early fifth millennium bc in northern Egypt and a thousand years later further south, in both cases as part of strategies that still relied heavily on fishing, hunting, and the gathering of wild plants" and suggests that these subsistence changes were not due to farmers migrating from the Near East but was an indigenous development, with cereals either indigenous or obtained through exchange. Other scholars argue that the primary stimulus for agriculture and domesticated animals (as well as mud-brick architecture and other Neolithic cultural features) in Egypt was from the Middle East.
rewrite: Sheep and goats were likely introduced to Egypt from the Near East around 6000 BC. According to Graeme Barker, definitive proof of farming in the Nile region appears only by the early fifth millennium BC in the north, and around a thousand years after that in the south. These early communities continued to depend significantly on fishing, hunting, and foraging. Barker proposes this shift was a local evolution, not caused by an influx of Near Eastern farmers, with grains being either native or acquired via trade. Conversely, some experts maintain that key Neolithic elements in Egypt, including farming, livestock, and mud-brick structures, originated primarily from the Middle East.

input: The story sees Bond pitted against the global criminal organisation Spectre, marking the group's first appearance in an Eon Productions film since 1971's Diamonds Are Forever,[N 2] and tying Craig's series of films together with an overarching storyline. Several recurring James Bond characters, including M, Q and Eve Moneypenny return, with the new additions of Léa Seydoux as Dr. Madeleine Swann, Dave Bautista as Mr. Hinx, Andrew Scott as Max Denbigh and Monica Bellucci as Lucia Sciarra.
rewrite: In this film, Bond confronts the criminal network Spectre, which has not been featured in an Eon Productions movie since Diamonds Are Forever in 1971. This installment connects Daniel Craig's Bond movies through a continuous narrative. Familiar faces like M, Q, and Moneypenny reappear, joined by new characters portrayed by Léa Seydoux, Dave Bautista, Andrew Scott, and Monica Bellucci.

input: Trading companies became active in Tuvalu in the mid-19th century; the trading companies engaged palagi traders who lived on the islands. John (also known as Jack) O'Brien was the first European to settle in Tuvalu, he became a trader on Funafuti in the 1850s. He married Salai, the daughter of the paramount chief of Funafuti. Louis Becke, who later found success as a writer, was a trader on Nanumanga from April 1880 until the trading-station was destroyed later that year in a cyclone. He then became a trader on Nukufetau.
rewrite: During the 1800s, commercial enterprises began operating in Tuvalu, employing foreign traders who resided locally. The initial European to establish permanent residence was John (or Jack) O'Brien, who started his commerce on Funafuti in the 1850s and wed Salai, the daughter of the island's highest-ranking chief. Later, author Louis Becke worked as a merchant on Nanumanga starting in April 1880, until a cyclone ruined his post; he subsequently moved his operations to Nukufetau.

input: Following their wedding, the couple leased Windlesham Moor, near Windsor Castle, until 4 July 1949, when they took up residence at Clarence House in London. At various times between 1949 and 1951, the Duke of Edinburgh was stationed in the British Crown Colony of Malta as a serving Royal Navy officer. He and Elizabeth lived intermittently, for several months at a time, in the hamlet of Gwardamanġa, at Villa Guardamangia, the rented home of Philip's uncle, Lord Mountbatten. The children remained in Britain.
rewrite: After marrying, the couple initially rented Windlesham Moor near Windsor Castle. They moved to London's Clarence House in July 1949. From 1949 to 1951, the Duke served in the Royal Navy in Malta. During his postings, he and Elizabeth stayed for months at Villa Guardamangia in Gwardamanġa, a property leased by his uncle, Lord Mountbatten. Their children stayed behind in Britain during these periods.

input: Ann Arbor is part of Michigan's 12th congressional district, represented in Congress by Representative Debbie Dingell, a Democrat. On the state level, the city is part of the 18th district in the Michigan Senate, represented by Democrat Rebekah Warren. In the Michigan House of Representatives, representation is split between the 55th district (northern Ann Arbor, part of Ann Arbor Township, and other surrounding areas, represented by Democrat Adam Zemke), the 53rd district (most of downtown and the southern half of the city, represented by Democrat Jeff Irwin) and the 52nd district (southwestern areas outside Ann Arbor proper and western Washtenaw County, represented by Democrat Gretchen Driskell).
rewrite: Ann Arbor lies within Michigan's 12th U.S. congressional district, which sends Democrat Debbie Dingell to the House of Representatives. At the state senate level, the city falls into the 18th district, represented by Democrat Rebekah Warren. In the state House, three Democratic legislators share the duty: Adam Zemke for the 55th district covering the north, Jeff Irwin for the 53rd district encompassing the central and southern sections, and Gretchen Driskell for the 52nd district, which includes southwestern outskirts and parts of western Washtenaw County.

input: On 5 July 2004, the BBC celebrated the fiftieth anniversary of its television news bulletins (although it had produced the Television Newsreel for several years before 1954). This event was marked by the release of a DVD, which showed highlights of the BBC's television coverage of significant events over the half-century, as well as changes in the format of the BBC television news; from the newsreel format of the first BBC Television News bulletins, to the 24-hour, worldwide news coverage available in 2004. A special edition of Radio Times was also produced, as well as a special section of the BBC News Online website. In 2005 the pioneering BBC television series Little Angels won a BAFTA award. Little Angels was the first reality parenting show and its most famous episode saw Welsh actress Jynine James try to cope with the tantrums of her six-year-old son.
rewrite: On July 5, 2004, the BBC commemorated five decades of its televised news programs, having launched these regular broadcasts in 1954 after earlier newsreel offerings. To honor this milestone, a compilation DVD was issued, featuring key moments from the BBC's television reporting across those fifty years. It also illustrated the evolution of the news presentation, tracing the journey from initial newsreel styles to the continuous global reporting accessible by 2004. Accompanying this release were a dedicated issue of Radio Times magazine and a commemorative segment on the BBC News website. The following year, the groundbreaking BBC program Little Angels received a BAFTA award. As the inaugural reality series about parenting, its notable episodes included one where Welsh performer Jynine James managed the outbursts of her young son.

input: Though the true dimensions of species diversity remain uncertain, estimates range from 2.6–7.8 million species with a mean of 5.5 million. This probably represents less than 20% of all species on Earth[citation needed], and with only about 20,000 new species of all organisms being described each year, most species likely will remain undescribed for many years unless species descriptions increase in rate. About 850,000–1,000,000 of all described species are insects. Of the 24 orders of insects, four dominate in terms of numbers of described species, with at least 3 million species included in Coleoptera, Diptera, Hymenoptera and Lepidoptera. A recent study estimated the number of beetles at 0.9–2.1 million with a mean of 1.5 million.
rewrite: The full scope of species variety is still unknown, with approximations suggesting between 2.6 and 7.8 million distinct forms, averaging around 5.5 million. This likely constitutes under one-fifth of Earth's total biodiversity. Given that annual descriptions of new organisms only reach roughly 20,000, the majority of species may stay unidentified for the foreseeable future unless the pace of discovery accelerates significantly. Insects account for approximately 850,000 to one million of all cataloged species. Among insect groups, four orders are exceptionally populous, collectively encompassing at least three million species: beetles, flies, wasps and ants, and butterflies and moths. Beetles alone are recently estimated to number between 0.9 and 2.1 million, with a central figure of 1.5 million.

input: Since before 2000 BC, humans have utilized pesticides to protect their crops. The first known pesticide was elemental sulfur dusting used in ancient Sumer about 4,500 years ago in ancient Mesopotamia. The Rig Veda, which is about 4,000 years old, mentions the use of poisonous plants for pest control. By the 15th century, toxic chemicals such as arsenic, mercury, and lead were being applied to crops to kill pests. In the 17th century, nicotine sulfate was extracted from tobacco leaves for use as an insecticide. The 19th century saw the introduction of two more natural pesticides, pyrethrum, which is derived from chrysanthemums, and rotenone, which is derived from the roots of tropical vegetables. Until the 1950s, arsenic-based pesticides were dominant. Paul Müller discovered that DDT was a very effective insecticide. Organochlorines such as DDT were dominant, but they were replaced in the U.S. by organophosphates and carbamates by 1975. Since then, pyrethrin compounds have become the dominant insecticide. Herbicides became common in the 1960s, led by "triazine and other nitrogen-based compounds, carboxylic acids such as 2,4-dichlorophenoxyacetic acid, and glyphosate".
rewrite: For millennia, agricultural practices have included the use of substances to deter crop pests. Historical records indicate that elemental sulfur was employed as a dust in Sumer, around 2500 BC. Approximately 500 years later, ancient Indian texts refer to utilizing toxic botanicals for this purpose. By the 1400s, farmers were applying heavy metals like arsenic, mercury, and lead to their fields. The 1600s brought the extraction of nicotine sulfate from tobacco to combat insects. In the 1800s, two plant-derived agents entered use: pyrethrum, from chrysanthemum flowers, and rotenone, from the roots of certain tropical plants. Arsenical solutions remained the primary choice until the mid-20th century. The discovery of DDT's insecticidal power by Paul Müller then ushered in an era of organochlorine chemicals. These were largely supplanted in the United States by organophosphates and carbamates around 1975, with synthetic pyrethroids later rising to prominence. The 1960s also saw the widespread adoption of herbicides, including triazine derivatives, nitrogen-based formulas, carboxylic acids like 2,4-D, and glyphosate.

input: Precipitation is moderate and somewhat evenly distributed throughout the year, although the warmer months such as May and June average more, averaging 33.5 inches (850 mm) annually, but historically ranging from 20.49 in (520 mm) in 1963 to 47.70 in (1,212 mm) in 2011. Snowfall, which typically falls in measurable amounts between November 15 through April 4 (occasionally in October and very rarely in May), averages 42.5 inches (108 cm) per season, although historically ranging from 11.5 in (29 cm) in 1881−82 to 94.9 in (241 cm) in 2013−14. A thick snowpack is not often seen, with an average of only 27.5 days with 3 in (7.6 cm) or more of snow cover. Thunderstorms are frequent in the Detroit area. These usually occur during spring and summer.
rewrite: Rainfall in the region is fairly consistent year-round, with slightly higher amounts from May to June. The yearly average is about 33.5 inches (850 mm), though records show a wide variation from 20.49 inches (520 mm) in 1963 to 47.70 inches (1,212 mm) in 2011. Snow is common from mid-November to early April, sometimes beginning in October and seldom extending into May. Seasonal accumulation averages 42.5 inches (108 cm), but has historically fluctuated between 11.5 inches (29 cm) and 94.9 inches (241 cm). Deep snow accumulation is uncommon, with only about 27.5 days per season having at least 3 inches (7.6 cm) on the ground. Additionally, thunderstorms are a regular occurrence, particularly in the spring and summer months around Detroit.

input: Ben Goldacre has argued that regulators – such as the Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency (MHRA) in the UK, or the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) in the United States – advance the interests of the drug companies rather than the interests of the public due to revolving door exchange of employees between the regulator and the companies and friendships develop between regulator and company employees. He argues that regulators do not require that new drugs offer an improvement over what is already available, or even that they be particularly effective.
rewrite: Ben Goldacre contends that regulatory bodies like the UK's MHRA and the US FDA prioritize pharmaceutical industry interests over public welfare. This bias stems from a "revolving door" of personnel moving between these agencies and drug firms, alongside close professional relationships. He further asserts that these regulators often approve new medications without demanding they demonstrate superior efficacy or significant improvement compared to existing treatments.

input: New Haven has a variety of museums, many of them associated with Yale. The Beinecke Rare Book and Manuscript Library features an original copy of the Gutenberg Bible. There is also the Connecticut Children's Museum; the Knights of Columbus museum near that organization's world headquarters; the Peabody Museum of Natural History; the Yale University Collection of Musical Instruments; the Eli Whitney Museum (across the town line in Hamden, Connecticut, on Whitney Avenue); the Yale Center for British Art, which houses the largest collection of British art outside the U.K., and the Yale University Art Gallery, the nation's oldest college art museum.[citation needed] New Haven is also home to the New Haven Museum and Historical Society on Whitney Avenue, which has a library of many primary source treasures dating from Colonial times to the present.
rewrite: New Haven offers numerous museums, several connected to Yale University. Among these is the Beinecke Rare Book and Manuscript Library, which holds a Gutenberg Bible. Other institutions include the Connecticut Children's Museum, the Knights of Columbus museum close to its international headquarters, and the Peabody Museum of Natural History. The city also features the Yale University Collection of Musical Instruments, the Eli Whitney Museum located just over the border in Hamden, and the Yale Center for British Art, containing the most extensive British art collection outside the United Kingdom. Additionally, visitors can explore the Yale University Art Gallery, the oldest university art museum in the United States, and the New Haven Museum and Historical Society on Whitney Avenue, which maintains an archive of valuable historical documents from the Colonial era to modern times.

input: From around 750, during the Abbasid Caliphate, women “became renowned for their brains as well as their beauty”. In particular, many well known women of the time were trained from childhood in music, dancing and poetry. Mahbuba was one of these. Another feminine figure to be remembered for her achievements was Tawaddud, "a slave girl who was said to have been bought at great cost by Hārūn al-Rashīd because she had passed her examinations by the most eminent scholars in astronomy, medicine, law, philosophy, music, history, Arabic grammar, literature, theology and chess". Moreover, among the most prominent feminine figures was Shuhda who was known as "the Scholar" or "the Pride of Women" during the 12th century in Baghdad. Despite the recognition of women's aptitudes during the Abbasid dynasty, all these came to an end in Iraq with the sack of Baghdad in 1258.
rewrite: Beginning in the mid-eighth century under Abbasid rule, women gained distinction for their intellect alongside their appearance. Numerous prominent women received rigorous early education in artistic and literary arts such as poetry, music, and dance, exemplified by figures like Mahbuba. The accomplished Tawaddud also stands out; historical accounts note the Caliph Hārūn al-Rashīd paid a high price for this enslaved woman after she demonstrated exceptional knowledge before leading experts in diverse fields including law, philosophy, science, and chess. Another leading intellectual was the twelfth-century Baghdadi scholar Shuhda, celebrated as "the Pride of Women." However, this era of acknowledged female achievement in Iraq ceased following the devastating Mongol invasion of Baghdad in 1258.

input: The classification of speech varieties as dialects or languages and their relationship to other varieties of speech can be controversial and the verdicts inconsistent. English and Serbo-Croatian illustrate the point. English and Serbo-Croatian each have two major variants (British and American English, and Serbian and Croatian, respectively), along with numerous other varieties. For political reasons, analyzing these varieties as "languages" or "dialects" yields inconsistent results: British and American English, spoken by close political and military allies, are almost universally regarded as dialects of a single language, whereas the standard languages of Serbia and Croatia, which differ from each other to a similar extent as the dialects of English, are being treated by some linguists from the region as distinct languages, largely because the two countries oscillate from being brotherly to being bitter enemies. (The Serbo-Croatian language article deals with this topic much more fully.)
rewrite: Determining whether different forms of speech are separate languages or dialects of the same language is often a contentious and inconsistent process. The cases of English and Serbo-Croatian demonstrate this. Each possesses two primary standardized forms—British and American for English, and Serbian and Croatian for Serbo-Croatian—plus many other local versions. Political dynamics heavily influence this classification, leading to contradictory outcomes. The British and American variants, used by nations with strong political and military ties, are almost always considered dialects of one language. In contrast, the standard forms of Serbian and Croatian, which exhibit a comparable degree of difference to the English dialects, are classified by some local linguists as separate languages. This distinction stems largely from the volatile political relationship between Serbia and Croatia, which has ranged from fraternal to hostile. A more detailed examination is available in the article on Serbo-Croatian.

input: Although the numbered streets begin just north of East Houston Street in the East Village, they generally do not extend west into Greenwich Village, which already had streets when the grid plan was laid out by the Commissioners' Plan of 1811. Streets that do continue farther west change direction before reaching the Hudson River. The grid covers the length of the island from 14th Street north.
rewrite: The numbered streets start north of East Houston Street in the East Village but typically do not reach Greenwich Village to the west, as its streets predated the 1811 grid plan. Those that extend further shift direction before arriving at the Hudson River. This grid system spans Manhattan from 14th Street upward.

input: Gaddafi was later infuriated when Egypt and Syria planned the Yom Kippur War against Israel without consulting him, and was angered when Egypt conceded to peace talks rather than continuing the war. Gaddafi become openly hostile to Egypt's leader, calling for Sadat's overthrow, and when Sudanese President Gaafar Nimeiry took Sadat's side, Gaddafi by 1975 sponsored the Sudan People's Liberation Army to overthrow Nimeiry. Focusing his attention elsewhere in Africa, in late 1972 and early 1973, Libya invaded Chad to annex the uranium-rich Aouzou Strip. Offering financial incentives, he successfully convinced 8 African states to break off diplomatic relations with Israel in 1973. Intent on propagating Islam, in 1973 Gaddafi founded the Islamic Call Society, which had opened 132 centres across Africa within a decade. In 1973 he converted Gabonese President Omar Bongo, an action which he repeated three years later with Jean-Bédel Bokassa, president of the Central African Republic.
rewrite: Gaddafi grew furious after Egypt and Syria excluded him from planning the Yom Kippur War against Israel, and his anger deepened when Egypt pursued peace negotiations instead of prolonged conflict. This led him to openly oppose Egyptian leadership, demanding Sadat's removal. When Sudan's President Nimeiry supported Sadat, Gaddafi responded by backing the Sudan People's Liberation Army in an effort to topple Nimeiry by 1975. Shifting focus, Libya moved into Chad in late 1972 and early 1973 to seize the mineral-rich Aouzou Strip. That same year, Gaddafi used financial offers to persuade eight African nations to cut ties with Israel. Dedicated to spreading Islam, he established the Islamic Call Society in 1973, which expanded to 132 African centers within ten years. His efforts included converting Gabon's President Omar Bongo in 1973 and, three years later, the Central African Republic's leader Jean-Bédel Bokassa.

input: Another occasionally used criterion for discriminating dialects from languages is that of linguistic authority, a more sociolinguistic notion. According to this definition, two varieties are considered dialects of the same language if (under at least some circumstances) they would defer to the same authority regarding some questions about their language. For instance, to learn the name of a new invention, or an obscure foreign species of plant, speakers of Bavarian German and East Franconian German might each consult a German dictionary or ask a German-speaking expert in the subject. By way of contrast, although Yiddish is classified by linguists as a language in the "Middle High German" group of languages, a Yiddish speaker would not consult a German dictionary to determine the word to use in such a case.
rewrite: A further, though less common, standard for distinguishing between dialects and languages involves the concept of linguistic authority, which is rooted in sociolinguistics. This perspective holds that two speech forms are dialects of a single language if they recognize a common reference point for resolving certain linguistic questions. For example, if needing a term for a novel object or an unfamiliar foreign plant, both Bavarian and East Franconian speakers would likely turn to a standard German reference or specialist. In comparison, Yiddish, while linguistically grouped with Middle High German languages, would not use a German dictionary for such a purpose.

input: The northern side of the borough includes the largest park in New York City—Pelham Bay Park, which includes Orchard Beach—and the fourth largest, Van Cortlandt Park, which is west of Woodlawn Cemetery and borders Yonkers. Also in the northern Bronx, Wave Hill, the former estate of George W. Perkins—known for a historic house, gardens, changing site-specific art installations and concerts—overlooks the New Jersey Palisades from a promontory on the Hudson in Riverdale. Nearer the borough's center, and along the Bronx River, is Bronx Park; its northern end houses the New York Botanical Gardens, which preserve the last patch of the original hemlock forest that once covered the entire county, and its southern end the Bronx Zoo, the largest urban zoological gardens in the United States. Just south of Van Cortlandt Park is the Jerome Park Reservoir, surrounded by 2 miles (3 km) of stone walls and bordering several small parks in the Bedford Park neighborhood; the reservoir was built in the 1890s on the site of the former Jerome Park Racetrack. Further south is Crotona Park, home to a 3.3-acre (1.3 ha) lake, 28 species of trees, and a large swimming pool. The land for these parks, and many others, was bought by New York City in 1888, while land was still open and inexpensive, in anticipation of future needs and future pressures for development.
rewrite:
The borough's northern area contains two of New York City's biggest parks. Pelham Bay Park, the city's largest, features Orchard Beach. To the west, near Yonkers and adjacent to Woodlawn Cemetery, lies Van Cortlandt Park, the fourth most expansive. Riverdale's northern section offers Wave Hill, the old George W. Perkins property. This site presents a historic mansion, landscaped grounds, rotating art displays, and musical events, all positioned on a Hudson River bluff with views toward the Palisades in New Jersey.

Closer to the Bronx's middle section, following the Bronx River, is Bronx Park. The New York Botanical Garden occupies its northern portion, safeguarding the last remnant of the native hemlock woods that formerly blanketed the region. The park's southern area contains the Bronx Zoo, the biggest metropolitan zoo in the nation. Just below Van Cortlandt Park sits the Jerome Park Reservoir, encircled by stone walls stretching two miles and next to minor parks in Bedford Park. This reservoir was constructed during the 1890s where the Jerome Park Racetrack once operated.

Farther south is Crotona Park, which boasts a lake spanning over three acres, twenty-eight varieties of trees, and a sizable public pool. The property for these and numerous other parks was acquired by the city in 1888. At that time, parcels remained readily available and affordable, securing the land ahead of coming demands and the expected push for urban expansion.

input: The public water supply network was completed in 1850, and in 1858 the architects Sebastián Monleón Estellés, Antonino Sancho, and Timoteo Calvo drafted a general expansion project for the city that included demolishing its ancient walls (a second version was printed in 1868). Neither proposed project received final approval, but they did serve as a guide, though not closely followed, for future growth. By 1860 the municipality had 140,416 inhabitants, and beginning in 1866 the ancient city walls were almost entirely demolished to facilitate urban expansion. Electricity was introduced to Valencia in 1882.
rewrite: Valencia's municipal water system was finished in 1850. A few years later, in 1858, architects Sebastián Monleón Estellés, Antonino Sancho, and Timoteo Calvo designed a comprehensive city expansion plan, which involved removing the old walls; a revised edition was published a decade later. While neither proposal was officially adopted, they provided a loose framework for subsequent development. The population reached 140,416 by 1860, and the historic walls were largely torn down starting in 1866 to enable the city's growth. Electrical power arrived in 1882.

input: Fossilized spores suggest that higher plants (embryophytes) have lived on land for at least 475 million years. Early land plants reproduced sexually with flagellated, swimming sperm, like the green algae from which they evolved. An adaptation to terrestrialization was the development of upright meiosporangia for dispersal by spores to new habitats. This feature is lacking in the descendants of their nearest algal relatives, the Charophycean green algae. A later terrestrial adaptation took place with retention of the delicate, avascular sexual stage, the gametophyte, within the tissues of the vascular sporophyte. This occurred by spore germination within sporangia rather than spore release, as in non-seed plants. A current example of how this might have happened can be seen in the precocious spore germination in Selaginella, the spike-moss. The result for the ancestors of angiosperms was enclosing them in a case, the seed. The first seed bearing plants, like the ginkgo, and conifers (such as pines and firs), did not produce flowers. The pollen grains (males) of Ginkgo and cycads produce a pair of flagellated, mobile sperm cells that "swim" down the developing pollen tube to the female and her eggs.
rewrite: Evidence from ancient spores indicates that complex plants, known as embryophytes, have existed on land for approximately 475 million years. These early terrestrial plants reproduced sexually using sperm that moved with flagella, similar to their aquatic ancestors, the green algae. A key evolutionary step for life on land was the formation of upright spore-producing structures, which allowed spores to spread to new areas—a trait not found in their closest algal relatives, the Charophyceans. Another major adaptation involved protecting the fragile reproductive phase, the gametophyte, inside the more robust vascular sporophyte. This was achieved by spores sprouting inside their protective capsules instead of being released, a process still observable today in plants like the spike-moss Selaginella. For the predecessors of flowering plants, this ultimately led to the development of the seed as a protective enclosure. The earliest seed-producing plants, such as ginkgoes and conifers, did not bear flowers. In ginkgoes and cycads, pollen grains generate motile, flagellated sperm cells that navigate through the pollen tube to reach and fertilize the egg cells.

input: In July 2012, Ancestry.com reported on historic and DNA research by its staff that discovered that Obama is likely a descendant through his mother of John Punch, considered by some historians to be the first African slave in the Virginia colony. An indentured servant, he was "bound for life" in 1640 after trying to escape. The story of him and his descendants is that of multi-racial America since it appeared he and his sons married or had unions with white women, likely indentured servants and working-class like them. Their multi-racial children were free because they were born to free English women. Over time, Obama's line of the Bunch family (as they became known) were property owners and continued to "marry white"; they became part of white society, likely by the early to mid-18th century.
rewrite: In July 2012, Ancestry.com released findings from genealogical and genetic studies indicating President Barack Obama’s maternal line may extend to John Punch. Historians often regard Punch as one of the earliest enslaved Africans in colonial Virginia; originally an indentured servant, he received a lifetime sentence after an attempted escape in 1640. His lineage reflects America's multi-racial history, as he and his sons are believed to have partnered with white women, often indentured servants of similar social standing. Since these women were free, their children were born free. This branch of the family, later named Bunch, acquired property and continued intermarrying with white communities, gradually integrating into white society by the mid-1700s.

input: Most French rulers since the Middle Ages made a point of leaving their mark on a city that, contrary to many other of the world's capitals, has never been destroyed by catastrophe or war. In modernising its infrastructure through the centuries, Paris has preserved even its earliest history in its street map.[citation needed] At its origin, before the Middle Ages, the city was composed around several islands and sandbanks in a bend of the Seine; of those, two remain today: the île Saint-Louis, the île de la Cité; a third one is the 1827 artificially created île aux Cygnes. Modern Paris owes much to its late 19th century Second Empire remodelling by the Baron Haussmann: many of modern Paris' busiest streets, avenues and boulevards today are a result of that city renovation. Paris also owes its style to its aligned street-fronts, distinctive cream-grey "Paris stone" building ornamentation, aligned top-floor balconies, and tree-lined boulevards. The high residential population of its city centre makes it much different from most other western global cities.
rewrite: For centuries, French monarchs have consistently aimed to imprint their legacy upon Paris. Unlike numerous other global capitals, the city has avoided catastrophic destruction from war or disaster. Through ongoing updates to its urban framework over the ages, Paris has maintained a street layout that echoes its most ancient past. Originally, before the medieval period, the settlement formed on several islands and sandbanks within a curve of the River Seine. Only two natural islands persist from that era: Île Saint-Louis and Île de la Cité, joined by the man-made Île aux Cygnes, created in 1827. The Paris of today is largely shaped by the extensive renovations overseen by Baron Haussmann during the Second Empire in the 1800s, which produced many of its now-bustling thoroughfares. The city's distinctive aesthetic arises from uniform building fronts, ornamentation made from a characteristic cream-grey limestone, consistent balcony designs on upper levels, and avenues flanked by trees. Furthermore, its densely populated central district distinguishes it from most other major cities in the Western world.

input: A local industry manufacturing fibre from New Zealand flax was successfully reestablished in 1907 and generated considerable income during the First World War. Ascension Island was made a dependency of Saint Helena in 1922, and Tristan da Cunha followed in 1938. During the Second World War, the United States built Wideawake airport on Ascension in 1942, but no military use was made of Saint Helena.
rewrite: In 1907, a regional business began producing fiber from New Zealand flax again, becoming profitable in World War I. Ascension Island became a territory of Saint Helena in 1922, with Tristan da Cunha added in 1938. The U.S. constructed Wideawake airfield on Ascension during World War II, though Saint Helena saw no military activity.

input: Scientists are still debating when people started wearing clothes. Ralf Kittler, Manfred Kayser and Mark Stoneking, anthropologists at the Max Planck Institute for Evolutionary Anthropology, have conducted a genetic analysis of human body lice that suggests clothing originated quite recently, around 170,000 years ago. Body lice is an indicator of clothes-wearing, since most humans have sparse body hair, and lice thus require human clothing to survive. Their research suggests the invention of clothing may have coincided with the northward migration of modern Homo sapiens away from the warm climate of Africa, thought to have begun between 50,000 and 100,000 years ago. However, a second group of researchers using similar genetic methods estimate that clothing originated around 540,000 years ago (Reed et al. 2004. PLoS Biology 2(11): e340). For now, the date of the origin of clothing remains unresolved.[citation needed]
rewrite: The precise era when humans first began using garments continues to be a topic of scientific discussion. Research by anthropologists from the Max Planck Institute involved studying the DNA of body lice, which rely on apparel to live due to humans' minimal body hair. Their findings propose that clothing emerged approximately 170,000 years in the past. This timing might align with early modern humans migrating from Africa into cooler northern regions. Conversely, another team applying comparable genetic techniques has estimated a much older origin for clothing, dating it to roughly 540,000 years ago. As these differing conclusions show, pinpointing when people started to dress themselves is still an unanswered question in anthropological study.

input: As soon as Schwarzenegger was elected governor, Willie Brown said he would start a drive to recall the governor. Schwarzenegger was equally entrenched in what he considered to be his mandate in cleaning up gridlock. Building on a catchphrase from the sketch "Hans and Franz" from Saturday Night Live (which partly parodied his bodybuilding career), Schwarzenegger called the Democratic State politicians "girlie men".
rewrite: Upon taking office, Governor Schwarzenegger faced a recall effort announced by Willie Brown. The governor was firmly committed to his perceived duty of resolving political standstills. Adopting a term from a "Saturday Night Live" skit that mocked his past, he labeled Democratic state legislators "girlie men."

input: Also founded in 1935 and based in Detroit the Michigan Chronicle is one of the oldest and most respected African-American weekly newspapers in America. Covering politics, entertainment, sports and community events. The Detroit television market is the 11th largest in the United States; according to estimates that do not include audiences located in large areas of Ontario, Canada (Windsor and its surrounding area on broadcast and cable TV, as well as several other cable markets in Ontario, such as the city of Ottawa) which receive and watch Detroit television stations.
rewrite: Established in 1935 and headquartered in Detroit, the Michigan Chronicle is a venerable and highly regarded weekly publication serving the African-American community. It reports on civic affairs, culture, athletics, and local happenings. The Detroit TV market ranks as the nation's 11th biggest. This standing does not account for many viewers in Ontario, Canada—including Windsor and Ottawa—who regularly tune in to Detroit broadcasts via cable or over-the-air signals.

input: Besides their traditional areas of inhabitation in Greater Somalia, a Somali community mainly consisting of entrepreneurs, academics, and students also exists in Egypt. In addition, there is an historical Somali community in the general Sudan area. Primarily concentrated in the north and Khartoum, the expatriate community mainly consists of students as well as some businesspeople. More recently, Somali entrepreneurs have established themselves in Kenya, investing over $1.5 billion in the Somali enclave of Eastleigh alone. In South Africa, Somali businesspeople also provide most of the retail trade in informal settlements around the Western Cape province.
rewrite: Somali populations extend beyond their native territories in Greater Somalia. Egypt hosts a community of entrepreneurs, scholars, and students. Historically, Somalis have also resided in the Sudan region, with current groups largely in the north and Khartoum comprising students and merchants. Recently, significant Somali investment, exceeding $1.5 billion, has flowed into Kenya's Eastleigh district. Furthermore, in South Africa's Western Cape, Somali merchants dominate the retail sector within many informal settlements.

input: Gaddafi organized demonstrations and distributed posters criticizing the monarchy. In October 1961, he led a demonstration protesting Syria's secession from the United Arab Republic. During this they broke windows of a local hotel accused of serving alcohol. Catching the authorities' attention, they expelled his family from Sabha. Gaddafi moved to Misrata, there attending Misrata Secondary School. Maintaining his interest in Arab nationalist activism, he refused to join any of the banned political parties active in the city – including the Arab Nationalist Movement, the Arab Socialist Ba'ath Party, and the Muslim Brotherhood – claiming he rejected factionalism. He read voraciously on the subjects of Nasser and the French Revolution of 1789, as well as the works of Syrian political theorist Michel Aflaq and biographies of Abraham Lincoln, Sun Yat-sen, and Mustafa Kemal Atatürk.
rewrite: Gaddafi mobilized protests and circulated materials denouncing the royal government. In late 1961, he headed a rally against Syria's withdrawal from the United Arab Republic, which involved damaging a hotel believed to sell alcohol. This drew official scrutiny, resulting in his family's forced removal from Sabha. Relocating to Misrata, he enrolled in its secondary school. He continued his Arab nationalist efforts but declined membership in all prohibited local groups, such as the Arab Nationalist Movement, the Ba'ath Party, and the Muslim Brotherhood, stating he opposed sectarian divisions. His extensive reading included studies of Nasser, the 1789 French Revolution, the writings of Michel Aflaq, and life stories of figures like Lincoln, Sun Yat-sen, and Atatürk.

input: Although provision is made in Title 10 of the United States Code for the Secretary of the Air Force to appoint warrant officers, the Air Force does not currently use warrant officer grades, and is the only one of the U.S. Armed Services not to do so. The Air Force inherited warrant officer ranks from the Army at its inception in 1947, but their place in the Air Force structure was never made clear.[citation needed] When the Congress authorized the creation of two new senior enlisted ranks in 1958, Air Force officials privately concluded that these two new "super grades" could fill all Air Force needs then performed at the warrant officer level, although this was not publicly acknowledged until years later.[citation needed] The Air Force stopped appointing warrant officers in 1959, the same year the first promotions were made to the new top enlisted grade, Chief Master Sergeant. Most of the existing Air Force warrant officers entered the commissioned officer ranks during the 1960s, but small numbers continued to exist in the warrant officer grades for the next 21 years.
rewrite: While U.S. law under Title 10 permits the Air Force Secretary to designate warrant officers, the branch presently does not utilize these ranks, distinguishing it as the sole U.S. military service without them. The Air Force originally adopted warrant officer positions from the Army upon its establishment in 1947, yet their specific role within the organization remained ambiguous. Following congressional approval in 1958 to introduce two new senior enlisted tiers, Air Force leadership internally determined that these advanced "super grades" could address all functions previously handled by warrant officers, a stance not publicly confirmed until much later. The service halted new warrant officer appointments in 1959, coinciding with the inaugural promotions to the senior enlisted rank of Chief Master Sergeant. Throughout the subsequent decade, the majority of remaining warrant officers transitioned to commissioned officer status, though a limited number persisted in their existing roles for an additional two decades.

input: As a schoolboy, Gaddafi adopted the ideologies of Arab nationalism and Arab socialism, influenced in particular by Nasserism, the thought of Egyptian revolutionary and president Gamal Abdel Nasser, whom Gaddafi adopted as his hero. During the early 1970s, Gaddafi formulated his own particular approach to Arab nationalism and socialism, known as Third International Theory, which has been described as a combination of "utopian socialism, Arab nationalism, and the Third World revolutionary theory that was in vogue at the time". He laid out the principles of this Theory in the three volumes of The Green Book, in which he sought to "explain the structure of the ideal society." His Arab nationalist views led him to believe that there needed to be unity across the Arab world, combining the Arab nation under a single nation-state. He described his approach to economics as "Islamic socialism", although biographers Blundy and Lycett noted that Gaddafi's socialism had a "curiously Marxist undertone", with political scientist Sami Hajjar arguing that Gaddafi's model of socialism offered a simplification of Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels' theories. Gaddafi saw his socialist Jamahiriyah as a model for the Arab, Islamic, and non-aligned worlds to follow.
rewrite:
From a young age, Gaddafi was drawn to the principles of Arab nationalism and socialism, finding a primary inspiration in the Nasserist ideals of Egypt's Gamal Abdel Nasser, who became his personal idol. By the early 1970s, he had developed his own distinct framework, termed the Third International Theory. This ideology blended utopian socialism, pan-Arab nationalism, and contemporary revolutionary thought from the developing world. He detailed its tenets in his three-part work, *The Green Book*, presenting it as a blueprint for a perfected society. A core component of his belief was the necessity for a unified Arab state, merging all Arab peoples into a single political entity.

Economically, he referred to his system as "Islamic socialism." However, observers like biographers Blundy and Lycett pointed out a discernible, if unexpected, Marxist leaning in his socialist concepts. Scholar Sami Hajjar suggested Gaddafi's model essentially streamlined the theories of Marx and Engels. Gaddafi envisioned his socialist state, the Jamahiriyah, as a guiding example not only for the Arab world but also for Islamic nations and the broader non-aligned movement.

input: Bird eggs are usually laid in a nest. Most species create somewhat elaborate nests, which can be cups, domes, plates, beds scrapes, mounds, or burrows. Some bird nests, however, are extremely primitive; albatross nests are no more than a scrape on the ground. Most birds build nests in sheltered, hidden areas to avoid predation, but large or colonial birds—which are more capable of defence—may build more open nests. During nest construction, some species seek out plant matter from plants with parasite-reducing toxins to improve chick survival, and feathers are often used for nest insulation. Some bird species have no nests; the cliff-nesting common guillemot lays its eggs on bare rock, and male emperor penguins keep eggs between their body and feet. The absence of nests is especially prevalent in ground-nesting species where the newly hatched young are precocial.
rewrite: Bird eggs are typically deposited in a nest. Many birds craft relatively intricate structures, which may take forms such as cups, domes, simple scrapes, mounds, or burrows. In contrast, certain species like albatrosses use only a basic depression in the earth. To protect against predators, most birds position their nests in concealed locations, though larger or colonial birds, better able to defend themselves, sometimes opt for exposed sites. When building, some birds select specific plant materials containing natural toxins to reduce parasites and boost offspring health, while feathers are commonly incorporated for warmth. Not all birds use nests; for instance, the common guillemot lays directly on rocky cliffs, and emperor penguin males balance eggs on their feet, covered by a brood pouch. This lack of a nest is common among ground-nesting birds whose chicks are mobile soon after hatching.

input: The game features nine dungeons—large, contained areas where Link battles enemies, collects items, and solves puzzles. Link navigates these dungeons and fights a boss at the end in order to obtain an item or otherwise advance the plot. The dungeons are connected by a large overworld, across which Link can travel on foot; on his horse, Epona; or by teleporting.
rewrite: In this game, players explore nine distinct dungeons, each a sizable, self-contained zone. Within them, they combat foes, gather objects, and work through puzzles. Conquering a dungeon's final boss yields a key item or progresses the story. A vast overworld links these areas, traversable by walking, riding the horse Epona, or using teleportation.

input: Cork was originally a monastic settlement, reputedly founded by Saint Finbarr in the 6th century. Cork achieved an urban character at some point between 915 and 922 when Norseman (Viking) settlers founded a trading port. It has been proposed that, like Dublin, Cork was an important trading centre in the global Scandinavian trade network. The ecclesiastical settlement continued alongside the Viking longphort, with the two developing a type of symbiotic relationship; the Norsemen providing otherwise unobtainable trade goods for the monastery, and perhaps also military aid.
rewrite: The city of Cork began as a religious community, traditionally established by Saint Finbarr during the sixth century. It took on a more town-like identity after Norse Vikings created a commercial harbor there in the early 900s. Scholars suggest Cork, similar to Dublin, was a significant hub in the widespread Scandinavian trading system. The original monastery and the Viking outpost coexisted, forming a mutually beneficial partnership where the Norse supplied scarce imported items and possibly protection to the religious settlement.

input: The abbey became the coronation site of Norman kings. None were buried there until Henry III, intensely devoted to the cult of the Confessor, rebuilt the abbey in Anglo-French Gothic style as a shrine to venerate King Edward the Confessor and as a suitably regal setting for Henry's own tomb, under the highest Gothic nave in England. The Confessor's shrine subsequently played a great part in his canonisation. The work continued between 1245 and 1517 and was largely finished by the architect Henry Yevele in the reign of Richard II. Henry III also commissioned unique Cosmati pavement in front of the High Altar (the pavement has recently undergone a major cleaning and conservation programme and was re-dedicated by the Dean at a service on 21 May 2010).
rewrite: Norman monarchs chose the abbey for their coronations, but it was not used as a royal burial ground until the time of Henry III. Deeply dedicated to the cult of Edward the Confessor, Henry rebuilt the church in the Anglo-French Gothic manner. His aims were to create a shrine for the venerated king and a majestic location for his own future tomb, beneath what would become England's tallest Gothic nave. This shrine later significantly aided Edward's canonization. Construction, spanning from 1245 to 1517, was mostly completed by the architect Henry Yevele under Richard II. Henry III also ordered the distinctive Cosmati pavement before the High Altar, which was recently cleaned, conserved, and re-consecrated in a 2010 ceremony.

input: The use of traditional Chinese characters versus simplified Chinese characters varies greatly, and can depend on both the local customs and the medium. Before the official reform, character simplifications were not officially sanctioned and generally adopted vulgar variants and idiosyncratic substitutions. Orthodox variants were mandatory in printed works, while the (unofficial) simplified characters would be used in everyday writing or quick notes. Since the 1950s, and especially with the publication of the 1964 list, the People's Republic of China has officially adopted simplified Chinese characters for use in mainland China, while Hong Kong, Macau, and the Republic of China (Taiwan) were not affected by the reform. There is no absolute rule for using either system, and often it is determined by what the target audience understands, as well as the upbringing of the writer.
