rewrite: The choice between traditional and simplified Chinese characters differs widely, influenced by regional practices and context. Prior to formal standardization, simplifications were informal, typically drawing from common shorthand and personal adaptations. Official publications required classical forms, with simplified versions reserved for casual writing or quick jottings. Beginning in the 1950s, and notably after the 1964 official list, mainland China formally instituted simplified characters. This change did not extend to Hong Kong, Macau, or Taiwan. Usage today is not strictly governed; it often hinges on the reader's familiarity and the writer's own background.

input: In May 1778, Burke supported a parliamentary motion revising restrictions on Irish trade. His constituents, citizens of the great trading city of Bristol, however urged Burke to oppose free trade with Ireland. Burke resisted their protestations and said: "If, from this conduct, I shall forfeit their suffrages at an ensuing election, it will stand on record an example to future representatives of the Commons of England, that one man at least had dared to resist the desires of his constituents when his judgment assured him they were wrong".
rewrite: In May 1778, Burke voted in Parliament to ease trade limits affecting Ireland. His electorate, the people of Bristol—a major commercial center—pressured him to reject such economic liberalization. Defying their demands, Burke declared that should this stance cost him future votes, it would serve as a lasting model: a solitary member of the Commons had the courage to defy his voters when his conscience deemed them mistaken.

input: Her mature artistic statement was visible in True Blue (1986) and Like a Prayer (1989). In True Blue, she incorporated classical music in order to engage an older audience who had been skeptical of her music. Like a Prayer introduced live recorded songs and incorporated different genres of music, including dance, funk, R&B and gospel music. Her versatility was further shown on I'm Breathless, which consists predominantly of the 1940s Broadway showtune-flavoured jazz, swing and big band tracks. Madonna continued to compose ballads and uptempo dance songs for Erotica (1992) and Bedtime Stories (1994). Both albums explored element of new jack swing, with Jim Farber from Entertainment Weekly saying that "she could actually be viewed as new jack swing's godmother." She tried to remain contemporary by incorporating samples, drum loops and hip hop into her music. With Ray of Light, Madonna brought electronic music from its underground status into massive popularity in mainstream music scene.
rewrite: Madonna’s artistic evolution became fully evident with her albums *True Blue* (1986) and *Like a Prayer* (1989). The former used classical influences to appeal to older listeners who had previously doubted her work. The latter featured songs recorded with live instrumentation and blended styles such as dance, funk, R&B, and gospel. Her adaptability was also apparent on *I’m Breathless*, an album largely filled with jazz, swing, and big band pieces reminiscent of 1940s Broadway. For *Erotica* (1992) and *Bedtime Stories* (1994), she maintained a mix of ballads and energetic dance tracks, both records delving into new jack swing—a connection noted by critic Jim Farber, who suggested she could be considered that genre’s foundational figure. She stayed current by weaving in samples, drum loops, and hip-hop elements. Later, with *Ray of Light*, she propelled electronic music from niche audiences into widespread mainstream acceptance.

input: Perhaps the most prominent, controversial and far-reaching theory in all of science has been the theory of evolution by natural selection put forward by the British naturalist Charles Darwin in his book On the Origin of Species in 1859. Darwin proposed that the features of all living things, including humans, were shaped by natural processes over long periods of time. The theory of evolution in its current form affects almost all areas of biology. Implications of evolution on fields outside of pure science have led to both opposition and support from different parts of society, and profoundly influenced the popular understanding of "man's place in the universe". In the early 20th century, the study of heredity became a major investigation after the rediscovery in 1900 of the laws of inheritance developed by the Moravian monk Gregor Mendel in 1866. Mendel's laws provided the beginnings of the study of genetics, which became a major field of research for both scientific and industrial research. By 1953, James D. Watson, Francis Crick and Maurice Wilkins clarified the basic structure of DNA, the genetic material for expressing life in all its forms. In the late 20th century, the possibilities of genetic engineering became practical for the first time, and a massive international effort began in 1990 to map out an entire human genome (the Human Genome Project).
rewrite:
One of science's most significant, debated, and impactful ideas is Charles Darwin's theory of natural selection, introduced in his 1859 work *On the Origin of Species*. The British naturalist suggested that all organisms, humanity included, acquired their traits through gradual, natural mechanisms across vast timescales. Today, evolutionary theory underpins nearly every biological discipline. Its reach beyond pure science has sparked societal debate, reshaping common views on humanity's role in nature.

In the 1900s, heredity emerged as a key focus following the renewed attention to Gregor Mendel's 1866 principles of inheritance. These rules launched the field of genetics, which grew into a vital domain for both academic and applied study. The fundamental architecture of DNA, the molecule responsible for transmitting life's instructions, was determined by James Watson, Francis Crick, and Maurice Wilkins in 1953. Decades later, genetic manipulation turned feasible, leading to the 1990 launch of the Human Genome Project—a global initiative to sequence all human genetic information.

input: It has been pointed out that Khmer and Indonesian classical arts were concerned with depicting the life of the gods, but to the Southeast Asian mind the life of the gods was the life of the peoples themselves—joyous, earthy, yet divine. The Tai, coming late into Southeast Asia, brought with them some Chinese artistic traditions, but they soon shed them in favour of the Khmer and Mon traditions, and the only indications of their earlier contact with Chinese arts were in the style of their temples, especially the tapering roof, and in their lacquerware.
rewrite: Classical arts in Khmer and Indonesian cultures focused on representing divine life, which Southeast Asians viewed as a reflection of their own—full of joy, earthly essence, and sacredness. Although the Tai people arrived later with Chinese artistic influences, they quickly adopted local Khmer and Mon styles. Traces of their earlier Chinese connection remained only in certain architectural features, like the sloping temple roofs, and in their lacquerware designs.

input: Popular opinion remained firmly behind the celebration of Mary's conception. In 1439, the Council of Basel, which is not reckoned an ecumenical council, stated that belief in the immaculate conception of Mary is in accord with the Catholic faith. By the end of the 15th century the belief was widely professed and taught in many theological faculties, but such was the influence of the Dominicans, and the weight of the arguments of Thomas Aquinas (who had been canonised in 1323 and declared "Doctor Angelicus" of the Church in 1567) that the Council of Trent (1545–63)—which might have been expected to affirm the doctrine—instead declined to take a position.
rewrite: Public support for honoring Mary's conception stayed strong. The Council of Basel in 1439, though not considered fully ecumenical, declared this belief aligned with Catholic teaching. By the 1400s' close, it was commonly held and instructed in numerous schools of theology. However, Dominican influence and the powerful reasoning of Thomas Aquinas—canonized in 1323 and later named the "Angelic Doctor"—carried such weight that the Council of Trent, while a likely venue for endorsement, chose not to formally settle the matter.

input: In May 2014, the Government of China banned the internal purchase of Windows 8-based products under government contracts requiring "energy-efficient" devices. The Xinhua News Agency claimed that Windows 8 was being banned in protest of Microsoft's support lifecycle policy and the end of support for Windows XP (which, as of January 2014, had a market share of 49% in China), as the government "obviously cannot ignore the risks of running OS [sic] without guaranteed technical support." However, Ni Guangnan of the Chinese Academy of Sciences had also previously warned that Windows 8 could allegedly expose users to surveillance by the United States government due to its heavy use of internet-based services.
rewrite: In May 2014, Chinese authorities prohibited government agencies from buying computers with Windows 8 for official use, mandating energy-efficient alternatives instead. Official reports stated the move was a response to Microsoft's support policies, particularly the discontinued assistance for Windows XP. At that time, XP still powered nearly half of the country's computers, and officials cited the security dangers of using an unsupported operating system. Additionally, a prominent Chinese academic had earlier cautioned that the system's reliance on online services might allow U.S. government espionage.

input: Filming temporarily returned to England to shoot scenes at Blenheim Palace in Oxfordshire, which stood in for a location in Rome, before moving on to the city itself for a five-week shoot across the city, with locations including the Ponte Sisto bridge and the Roman Forum. The production faced opposition from a variety of special interest groups and city authorities, who were concerned about the potential for damage to historical sites around the city, and problems with graffiti and rubbish appearing in the film. A car chase scene set along the banks of the Tiber River and through the streets of Rome featured an Aston Martin DB10 and a Jaguar C-X75. The C-X75 was originally developed as a hybrid electric vehicle with four independent electric engines powered by two jet turbines, before the project was cancelled. The version used for filming was converted to use a conventional internal combustion engine, to minimise the potential for disruption from mechanical problems with the complex hybrid system. The C-X75s used for filming were developed by the engineering division of Formula One racing team Williams, who built the original C-X75 prototype for Jaguar.
rewrite: After completing work at England's Blenheim Palace, a stand-in for a Roman setting, the production relocated to Rome for approximately five weeks. Key sites there included the Ponte Sisto bridge and the Roman Forum. This phase encountered resistance from local officials and advocacy organizations worried about harm to ancient landmarks, as well as the portrayal of litter and graffiti. A major sequence filmed was a car pursuit along the Tiber River and through Roman streets, featuring an Aston Martin DB10 and a Jaguar C-X75. The Jaguar model had initially been conceived as a hybrid with four electric motors driven by twin turbines, but that design was abandoned. For the film, the cars were modified with standard petrol engines to reduce the risk of breakdowns inherent in the intricate hybrid technology. The filming versions were adapted by Williams Advanced Engineering, the Formula One team's technical arm, which had also constructed the original C-X75 concept for Jaguar.

input: The Scottish philosopher David Hume (1711–1776) responded to Berkeley's criticisms of Locke, as well as other differences between early modern philosophers, and moved empiricism to a new level of skepticism. Hume argued in keeping with the empiricist view that all knowledge derives from sense experience, but he accepted that this has implications not normally acceptable to philosophers. He wrote for example, "Locke divides all arguments into demonstrative and probable. On this view, we must say that it is only probable that all men must die or that the sun will rise to-morrow, because neither of these can be demonstrated. But to conform our language more to common use, we ought to divide arguments into demonstrations, proofs, and probabilities—by ‘proofs’ meaning arguments from experience that leave no room for doubt or opposition." And,
rewrite: David Hume (1711–1776), a Scottish thinker, addressed Berkeley's objections to Locke and further developed the disputes among early modern philosophers, advancing empiricism toward a more skeptical position. While maintaining that all understanding originates from sensory impressions, Hume acknowledged that this principle leads to conclusions many philosophers would reject. For instance, he noted that Locke categorized arguments as either demonstrative or probable. Under that framework, one could only claim it is probable that all humans will die or that the sun will rise tomorrow, since neither event can be logically proven. However, Hume suggested adjusting terminology to align with everyday speech by classifying arguments into three types: demonstrations, proofs, and probabilities. Here, "proofs" refer to inferences from experience that are so certain they exclude doubt or contradiction.

input: Modern Nationalism, as developed especially since the French Revolution, has made the distinction between "language" and "dialect" an issue of great political importance. A group speaking a separate "language" is often seen as having a greater claim to being a separate "people", and thus to be more deserving of its own independent state, while a group speaking a "dialect" tends to be seen not as "a people" in its own right, but as a sub-group, part of a bigger people, which must content itself with regional autonomy.[citation needed] The distinction between language and dialect is thus inevitably made at least as much on a political basis as on a linguistic one, and can lead to great political controversy, or even armed conflict.
rewrite: Since the era of the French Revolution, the ideology of Modern Nationalism has elevated the differentiation between what is termed a "language" and what is considered a "dialect" into a matter of significant political consequence. Communities identified with a distinct "language" are frequently granted stronger legitimacy as a unique national group, thereby bolstering arguments for sovereign statehood. Conversely, those speaking a "dialect" are often perceived not as an independent nation, but merely as a component of a larger national body, whose political aspirations might be limited to regional self-governance. Consequently, this classification is unavoidably influenced by political motives alongside linguistic criteria, a reality that can generate substantial political dispute and, in extreme cases, escalate into violent confrontation.

input: In 2014 the Notre Dame student body consisted of 12,179 students, with 8,448 undergraduates, 2,138 graduate and professional and 1,593 professional (Law, M.Div., Business, M.Ed.) students. Around 21–24% of students are children of alumni, and although 37% of students come from the Midwestern United States, the student body represents all 50 states and 100 countries. As of March 2007[update] The Princeton Review ranked the school as the fifth highest 'dream school' for parents to send their children. As of March 2015[update] The Princeton Review ranked Notre Dame as the ninth highest. The school has been previously criticized for its lack of diversity, and The Princeton Review ranks the university highly among schools at which "Alternative Lifestyles [are] Not an Alternative." It has also been commended by some diversity oriented publications; Hispanic Magazine in 2004 ranked the university ninth on its list of the top–25 colleges for Latinos, and The Journal of Blacks in Higher Education recognized the university in 2006 for raising enrollment of African-American students. With 6,000 participants, the university's intramural sports program was named in 2004 by Sports Illustrated as the best program in the country, while in 2007 The Princeton Review named it as the top school where "Everyone Plays Intramural Sports." The annual Bookstore Basketball tournament is the largest outdoor five-on-five tournament in the world with over 700 teams participating each year, while the Notre Dame Men's Boxing Club hosts the annual Bengal Bouts tournament that raises money for the Holy Cross Missions in Bangladesh.
rewrite:
In 2014, the University of Notre Dame enrolled a total of 12,179 students. This figure included 8,448 pursuing bachelor’s degrees, 2,138 in graduate and professional programs, and an additional 1,593 in specific professional fields such as Law, Divinity, Business, and Education. Approximately one-fifth to one-quarter of undergraduates are legacies, with children of alumni comprising a notable portion. While over a third of students hail from the Midwest, the campus community draws from every U.S. state and about one hundred nations globally.

The Princeton Review has consistently recognized Notre Dame as a top choice for families. In 2007, it was listed as the fifth most desired institution for parents; by 2015, it held the ninth position. The university has faced some scrutiny over historical diversity levels, and The Princeton Review has noted a campus environment where non-traditional lifestyles are less visible. However, it has also earned praise for inclusivity efforts: Hispanic Magazine placed it ninth among top colleges for Latino students in 2004, and The Journal of Blacks in Higher Education acknowledged its progress in enrolling African-American students in 2006.

Notre Dame’s intramural athletics are highly regarded, involving around 6,000 participants. Sports Illustrated celebrated the program as the nation’s best in 2004, and The Princeton Review later called it the top school for widespread intramural participation. Campus traditions include the massive Bookstore Basketball tournament, the world’s largest outdoor five-on-five event, with more than 700 teams competing annually. Additionally, the Men’s Boxing Club organizes the Bengal Bouts fundraiser each year, generating support for Holy Cross Missions in Bangladesh.

input: The Constitution does not explicitly indicate the pre-eminence of any particular branch of government. However, James Madison wrote in Federalist 51, regarding the ability of each branch to defend itself from actions by the others, that "it is not possible to give to each department an equal power of self-defense. In republican government, the legislative authority necessarily predominates."
rewrite: The Constitution does not directly state which governmental branch holds supreme authority. Yet, in Federalist 51, James Madison observed that while each division must protect itself from the others, equal defensive power is unattainable. In a republic, he noted, the legislative branch inherently holds the greatest influence.

input: To put it another way, a thing or person is often seen as having a "defining essence" or a "core identity" that is unchanging, and describes what the thing or person really is. In this way of thinking, things and people are seen as fundamentally the same through time, with any changes being qualitative and secondary to their core identity (e.g. "Mark's hair has turned gray as he has gotten older, but he is still the same person"). But in Whitehead's cosmology, the only fundamentally existent things are discrete "occasions of experience" that overlap one another in time and space, and jointly make up the enduring person or thing. On the other hand, what ordinary thinking often regards as "the essence of a thing" or "the identity/core of a person" is an abstract generalization of what is regarded as that person or thing's most important or salient features across time. Identities do not define people, people define identities. Everything changes from moment to moment, and to think of anything as having an "enduring essence" misses the fact that "all things flow", though it is often a useful way of speaking.
rewrite: In contrast to conventional perspectives, entities and individuals are typically considered to possess an inherent and fixed "essential nature" or "fundamental self," which captures their true being. This viewpoint treats objects and persons as fundamentally consistent over time, where alterations are seen as surface-level modifications that do not affect the core (for instance, graying hair does not alter who Mark is). However, according to Whitehead’s framework, the basic units of reality are individual "experiential events," which interweave across temporal and spatial dimensions to collectively form what we perceive as a continuous entity or individual. Conversely, what is commonly thought of as an object's "essence" or a person's "true identity" is actually a distilled abstraction, highlighting the traits deemed most significant or noticeable throughout their existence. Identities are not predetermined templates for people; rather, people shape their own identities. Reality is in constant flux, with every element transforming continuously. To attribute a permanent, unchanging core to anything overlooks the principle that "everything is in motion," even though such language can be practically convenient.

input: According to statistics published by the American Pet Products Manufacturers Association in the National Pet Owner Survey in 2009–2010, it is estimated there are 77.5 million people with pet dogs in the United States. The same survey shows nearly 40% of American households own at least one dog, of which 67% own just one dog, 25% two dogs and nearly 9% more than two dogs. There does not seem to be any gender preference among dogs as pets, as the statistical data reveal an equal number of female and male dog pets. Yet, although several programs are undergoing to promote pet adoption, less than a fifth of the owned dogs come from a shelter.
rewrite: The 2009–2010 National Pet Owner Survey indicates that approximately 77.5 million Americans have pet dogs. This represents close to 40% of all U.S. households. Among these dog-owning homes, about 67% have a single dog, a quarter have two, and roughly 9% care for more than two. Statistics show no gender bias in pet dogs, with equal numbers of females and males. Despite active campaigns encouraging the adoption of shelter animals, fewer than 20% of owned dogs are obtained from these facilities.

input: The second main principle, sola fide (by faith alone), states that faith in Christ is sufficient alone for eternal salvation. Though argued from scripture, and hence logically consequent to sola scriptura, this is the guiding principle of the work of Luther and the later reformers. Because sola scriptura placed the Bible as the only source of teaching, sola fide epitomises the main thrust of the teaching the reformers wanted to get back to, namely the direct, close, personal connection between Christ and the believer, hence the reformers' contention that their work was Christocentric.
rewrite: Sola fide, meaning "by faith alone," asserts that belief in Christ is all that is required to attain salvation. This tenet, derived from biblical interpretation and following from sola scriptura, became the central focus for Luther and subsequent reformers. By establishing scripture as the sole authority, sola fide captures the core objective of the Reformation: to restore an immediate and personal relationship between the believer and Christ, which is why the reformers viewed their mission as fundamentally centered on Christ.

input: A common misperception is that the Supreme Court is the only court that may determine constitutionality; the power is exercised even by the inferior courts. But only Supreme Court decisions are binding across the nation. Decisions of a Court of Appeals, for instance, are binding only in the circuit over which the court has jurisdiction.
rewrite: Many mistakenly believe only the Supreme Court can rule on constitutionality, but lower courts also hold this power. However, only Supreme Court rulings apply nationally. For example, a Court of Appeals decision is binding solely within its own judicial circuit.

input: Unicode has become the dominant scheme for internal processing and storage of text. Although a great deal of text is still stored in legacy encodings, Unicode is used almost exclusively for building new information processing systems. Early adopters tended to use UCS-2 (the fixed-width two-byte precursor to UTF-16) and later moved to UTF-16 (the variable-width current standard), as this was the least disruptive way to add support for non-BMP characters. The best known such system is Windows NT (and its descendants, Windows 2000, Windows XP, Windows Vista and Windows 7), which uses UTF-16 as the sole internal character encoding. The Java and .NET bytecode environments, Mac OS X, and KDE also use it for internal representation. Unicode is available on Windows 95 through Microsoft Layer for Unicode, as well as on its descendants, Windows 98 and Windows ME.
rewrite: Unicode now serves as the primary method for handling and saving text data in computing. While many older systems continue to rely on previous encoding formats, nearly all newly developed software and platforms are built using Unicode. Initially, many chose UCS-2, a fixed two-byte format that later evolved into the variable-length UTF-16 standard. This shift allowed for the inclusion of additional characters beyond the Basic Multilingual Plane with minimal system changes. Operating systems like Windows NT and its successors, including Windows XP and Windows 7, employ UTF-16 as their core encoding. Similarly, technologies such as Java, .NET, Mac OS X, and KDE utilize it for internal operations. Even earlier Windows versions, like Windows 95 and 98, can support Unicode through additional compatibility layers.

input: In 1238, King James I of Aragon, with an army composed of Aragonese, Catalans, Navarrese and crusaders from the Order of Calatrava, laid siege to Valencia and on 28 September obtained a surrender. Fifty thousand Moors were forced to leave. Poets such as Ibn al-Abbar and Ibn Amira mourned this exile from their beloved Valencia. After the Christian victory and the expulsion of the Muslim population the city was divided between those who had participated in the conquest, according to the testimony in the Llibre del Repartiment (Book of Distribution). James I granted the city new charters of law, the Furs of Valencia, which later were extended to the whole kingdom of Valencia. Thenceforth the city entered a new historical stage in which a new society and a new language developed, forming the basis of the character of the Valencian people as they are known today.
rewrite: In September of 1238, forces led by King James I of Aragon secured the surrender of Valencia following a siege. His troops included men from Aragon, Catalonia, Navarre, and knights from the Calatrava order. Approximately fifty thousand Muslims were subsequently compelled to depart. Contemporary poets, including Ibn al-Abbar and Ibn Amira, lamented this profound loss of their home. Following this Christian triumph and the removal of the Muslim inhabitants, the conquered lands were apportioned among the victors, a process documented in the *Llibre del Repartiment*. The king also instituted new legal codes, the Furs of Valencia, which would eventually govern the entire kingdom. This pivotal moment launched a distinct historical era, marked by the evolution of a novel social structure and the emergence of a unique language, foundational elements of Valencian identity that endure.

input: The executive branch consists of the Governor, their staff, and other elected officials. The principal head of government, the Governor is the chief executive of the Oklahoma executive branch, serving as the ex officio Commander-in-Chief of the Oklahoma National Guard when not called into Federal use and reserving the power to veto bills passed through the Legislature. The responsibilities of the Executive branch include submitting the budget, ensuring that state laws are enforced, and ensuring peace within the state is preserved.
rewrite: The executive branch includes the Governor, their team, and various elected officers. As the primary leader, the Governor oversees this branch, acts as the automatic head of the state's National Guard unless federalized, and can reject legislation. This branch's duties involve proposing the budget, upholding state laws, and maintaining public order.

input: Some of the best-known traditions, including carnal parades and masquerade balls, were first recorded in medieval Italy. The carnival of Venice was, for a long time, the most famous carnival (although Napoleon abolished it in 1797 and only in 1979 was the tradition restored). From Italy, Carnival traditions spread to Spain, Portugal and France and from France to New France in North America. From Spain and Portugal it spread with colonization to the Caribbean and Latin America. In the early 19th century in the German Rhineland and Southern Netherlands, the weakened medieval tradition also revive. Continuously in the 18th and 19th centuries CE, as part of the annual Saturnalia abuse of the carnival in Rome, rabbis of the ghetto were forced to march through the city streets wearing foolish guise, jeered upon and pelted by a variety of missiles from the crowd. A petition of the Jewish community of Rome sent in 1836 to Pope Gregory XVI to stop the annual anti-semitic Saturnalia abuse got a negation: “It is not opportune to make any innovation.”
rewrite: Many iconic customs, such as festive street processions and elaborate costume parties, trace their documented origins to Italy in the Middle Ages. Venice's celebration was long considered the preeminent carnival, despite being suppressed by Napoleon in 1797 and not formally revived until 1979. These practices extended from Italy to the Iberian Peninsula and France, and French influence carried them to colonial North America. Spanish and Portuguese colonization further disseminated the traditions throughout the Caribbean and Latin America. A fading medieval practice also saw a resurgence in the early 1800s within the German Rhineland and the Southern Netherlands. Elsewhere, during the 18th and 19th centuries, the Roman carnival's Saturnalia included a deeply anti-Semitic ritual: rabbis from the ghetto were compelled to parade in ridiculous costumes, subjected to public ridicule and hurled objects. An 1836 appeal from Rome's Jewish community to Pope Gregory XVI, requesting an end to this annual abuse, was dismissed with the statement that it was "not opportune to make any innovation."

input: The first issue was ammunition. Before the war it was recognised that ammunition needed to explode in the air. Both high explosive (HE) and shrapnel were used, mostly the former. Airburst fuses were either igniferious (based on a burning fuse) or mechanical (clockwork). Igniferious fuses were not well suited for anti-aircraft use. The fuse length was determined by time of flight, but the burning rate of the gunpowder was affected by altitude. The British pom-poms had only contact-fused ammunition. Zeppelins, being hydrogen filled balloons, were targets for incendiary shells and the British introduced these with airburst fuses, both shrapnel type-forward projection of incendiary 'pot' and base ejection of an incendiary stream. The British also fitted tracers to their shells for use at night. Smoke shells were also available for some AA guns, these bursts were used as targets during training.
rewrite: A primary challenge involved munitions. Prior to the conflict, it was understood that shells required mid-air detonation. Both high explosive and shrapnel rounds saw use, with high explosive being more common. Fuses to achieve this were either time-based, relying on a burning train, or mechanical timers. The burning fuses proved inadequate for anti-aircraft purposes because, while set for a flight duration, the powder's burn speed changed with altitude. British pom-pom guns initially used only impact-detonated shells. Against hydrogen-filled Zeppelins, incendiary ammunition became vital. The British developed such shells with airburst fuses, designed to either hurl incendiary canisters forward or eject a fiery trail from the base. Tracers were added to rounds for nocturnal engagements. Additionally, smoke shells existed for certain guns, their plumes serving as practice targets.

input: Eventually, the Licchavi ruler Gunakamadeva merged Koligram and Dakshin Koligram, founding the city of Kathmandu. The city was designed in the shape of Chandrahrasa, the sword of Manjushri. The city was surrounded by eight barracks guarded by Ajimas. One of these barracks is still in use at Bhadrakali (in front of Singha Durbar). The city served as an important transit point in the trade between India and Tibet, leading to tremendous growth in architecture. Descriptions of buildings such as Managriha, Kailaskut Bhawan, and Bhadradiwas Bhawan have been found in the surviving journals of travelers and monks who lived during this era. For example, the famous 7th-century Chinese traveller Xuanzang described Kailaskut Bhawan, the palace of the Licchavi king Amshuverma. The trade route also led to cultural exchange as well. The artistry of the Newar people—the indigenous inhabitants of the Kathmandu Valley—became highly sought after during this era, both within the Valley and throughout the greater Himalayas. Newar artists travelled extensively throughout Asia, creating religious art for their neighbors. For example, Araniko led a group of his compatriot artists through Tibet and China. Bhrikuti, the princess of Nepal who married Tibetan monarch Songtsän Gampo, was instrumental in introducing Buddhism to Tibet.
rewrite: Under the reign of Licchavi king Gunakamadeva, the settlements of Koligram and Dakshin Koligram were combined to establish Kathmandu. Its layout was planned to mirror the form of Manjushri's blade, known as Chandrahrasa. Eight military posts, protected by Ajima deities, encircled the settlement; one such post remains operational near Bhadrakali, facing Singha Durbar. Positioned on a crucial commercial corridor linking India and Tibet, the city experienced a major surge in architectural development. Accounts of structures like Managriha, Kailaskut Bhawan, and Bhadradiwas Bhawan are recorded in the diaries of visiting monks and travelers from that period. The seventh-century Chinese pilgrim Xuanzang, for instance, documented the palace of King Amshuverma, Kailaskut Bhawan. This trading network also facilitated a significant interchange of culture. The Newars, the original residents of the Kathmandu Valley, saw their craftsmanship become widely prized across the Valley and the broader Himalayan region. Newar artisans journeyed far across Asia to produce sacred artworks for other societies. A notable example is Araniko, who guided a team of fellow artists into Tibet and China. Furthermore, the Nepali princess Bhrikuti, upon marrying Tibetan ruler Songtsän Gampo, played a key role in bringing Buddhist teachings to Tibet.

input: In addition to concerns over subsidies, the cotton industries of some countries are criticized for employing child labor and damaging workers' health by exposure to pesticides used in production. The Environmental Justice Foundation has campaigned against the prevalent use of forced child and adult labor in cotton production in Uzbekistan, the world's third largest cotton exporter. The international production and trade situation has led to "fair trade" cotton clothing and footwear, joining a rapidly growing market for organic clothing, fair fashion or "ethical fashion". The fair trade system was initiated in 2005 with producers from Cameroon, Mali and Senegal.
rewrite: Beyond subsidy issues, certain nations' cotton sectors face condemnation for utilizing underage workers and endangering laborer health through pesticide exposure. In Uzbekistan, a top global cotton exporter, the Environmental Justice Foundation has actively opposed widespread forced labor involving both children and adults. This global landscape has spurred "fair trade" cotton apparel and shoes, entering the expanding market for organic and ethically conscious fashion. Starting in 2005, the fair trade framework initially involved producers from Cameroon, Mali, and Senegal.

input: The capital is Nashville, though Knoxville, Kingston, and Murfreesboro have all served as state capitals in the past. Memphis has the largest population of any city in the state. Nashville's 13-county metropolitan area has been the state's largest since c. 1990. Chattanooga and Knoxville, both in the eastern part of the state near the Great Smoky Mountains, each has approximately one-third of the population of Memphis or Nashville. The city of Clarksville is a fifth significant population center, some 45 miles (72 km) northwest of Nashville. Murfreesboro is the sixth-largest city in Tennessee, consisting of some 108,755 residents.
rewrite: Nashville is the present capital, yet several other cities including Knoxville, Kingston, and Murfreesboro previously held that role. Memphis is Tennessee's most populous city. The Nashville metropolitan region, encompassing thirteen counties, became the state's biggest around 1990. Located near the Great Smoky Mountains in eastern Tennessee, Chattanooga and Knoxville each have populations roughly a third the size of Memphis or Nashville. Another major hub is Clarksville, situated about 45 miles northwest of Nashville. With around 108,755 people, Murfreesboro ranks as the sixth largest city.

input: The first half of the 14th century saw much important scientific work being done, largely within the framework of scholastic commentaries on Aristotle's scientific writings. William of Ockham introduced the principle of parsimony: natural philosophers should not postulate unnecessary entities, so that motion is not a distinct thing but is only the moving object and an intermediary "sensible species" is not needed to transmit an image of an object to the eye. Scholars such as Jean Buridan and Nicole Oresme started to reinterpret elements of Aristotle's mechanics. In particular, Buridan developed the theory that impetus was the cause of the motion of projectiles, which was a first step towards the modern concept of inertia. The Oxford Calculators began to mathematically analyze the kinematics of motion, making this analysis without considering the causes of motion.
rewrite: During the initial decades of the 1300s, significant advances in science occurred, primarily through academic discussions centered on Aristotle's works. William of Ockham proposed a key idea of simplicity, arguing that thinkers should avoid inventing needless components. He asserted that movement isn't a separate entity but rather the object itself in motion, and visual perception does not require an intermediate "sensible species" to convey images. Other thinkers, including Jean Buridan and Nicole Oresme, began to reassess aspects of Aristotelian physics. Buridan, for instance, advanced the notion of impetus to explain projectile movement, foreshadowing the later principle of inertia. Meanwhile, the Oxford Calculators applied mathematical methods to study motion itself, deliberately setting aside questions about its origins.

input: The modern Conservative Party was created out of the 'Pittite' Tories of the early 19th century. In the late 1820s disputes over political reform broke up this grouping. A government led by the Duke of Wellington collapsed amidst dire election results. Following this disaster Robert Peel set about assembling a new coalition of forces. Peel issued the Tamworth Manifesto in 1834 which set out the basic principles of Conservatism; – the necessity in specific cases of reform in order to survive, but an opposition to unnecessary change, that could lead to "a perpetual vortex of agitation". Meanwhile, the Whigs, along with free trade Tory followers of Robert Peel, and independent Radicals, formed the Liberal Party under Lord Palmerston in 1859, and transformed into a party of the growing urban middle-class, under the long leadership of William Ewart Gladstone.
rewrite: The contemporary Conservative Party originated from the Pittite Tory faction in the early 1800s. This alliance fragmented in the late 1820s due to conflicts regarding political reform. The Duke of Wellington's administration fell following particularly poor electoral performance. In the aftermath, Robert Peel began constructing a fresh political alliance. His 1834 Tamworth Manifesto established core Conservative tenets, advocating for measured reform when essential for preservation, while rejecting needless transformations that might create endless turmoil. Concurrently, the Whigs, Peelite Tories who supported free trade, and unaffiliated Radicals united in 1859 to establish the Liberal Party, led by Lord Palmerston. This party later evolved, particularly under William Gladstone's lengthy leadership, to represent the expanding urban middle class.

input: Several versions of a semi-official, structured pantheon were developed during the political, social and religious instability of the Late Republican era. Jupiter, the most powerful of all gods and "the fount of the auspices upon which the relationship of the city with the gods rested", consistently personified the divine authority of Rome's highest offices, internal organization and external relations. During the archaic and early Republican eras, he shared his temple, some aspects of cult and several divine characteristics with Mars and Quirinus, who were later replaced by Juno and Minerva. A conceptual tendency toward triads may be indicated by the later agricultural or plebeian triad of Ceres, Liber and Libera, and by some of the complementary threefold deity-groupings of Imperial cult. Other major and minor deities could be single, coupled, or linked retrospectively through myths of divine marriage and sexual adventure. These later Roman pantheistic hierarchies are part literary and mythographic, part philosophical creations, and often Greek in origin. The Hellenization of Latin literature and culture supplied literary and artistic models for reinterpreting Roman deities in light of the Greek Olympians, and promoted a sense that the two cultures had a shared heritage.
rewrite: During the turbulent Late Republican period, marked by political and religious upheaval, various formalized versions of a state pantheon emerged. Jupiter, as the supreme deity and the source of the auspices fundamental to Rome’s sacred covenant, continually embodied the divine sanction for its leading magistracies, civic order, and foreign affairs. In earlier, archaic times, his worship, temple, and certain attributes were closely associated with Mars and Quirinus, deities later supplanted by Juno and Minerva. This inclination toward groupings of three is also suggested by subsequent triads like the plebeian one of Ceres, Liber, and Libera, and by various triple divine associations in the Imperial cult. Numerous other gods and goddesses, whether venerated singly, in pairs, or connected later through tales of marriage and liaisons, populated the system. These structured hierarchies from later Roman times are products blending mythology, literature, and philosophy, frequently influenced by Greek thought. The Hellenistic influence on Roman literature and art provided templates for reimagining native gods in terms of Greek counterparts, fostering a perception of a common mythological legacy between the two civilizations.

input: From the second half of the 20th century on parties which continued to rely on donations or membership subscriptions ran into mounting problems. Along with the increased scrutiny of donations there has been a long-term decline in party memberships in most western democracies which itself places more strains on funding. For example, in the United Kingdom and Australia membership of the two main parties in 2006 is less than an 1/8 of what it was in 1950, despite significant increases in population over that period.
rewrite: Beginning in the latter part of the 1900s, political organizations depending on contributions or member dues faced growing difficulties. Enhanced oversight of financial gifts coincided with a persistent drop in enrolled supporters across many Western nations, further tightening monetary pressures. To illustrate, by 2006 the combined membership for the primary parties in both the UK and Australia had fallen to under one-eighth of their 1950 figures, even as the overall population rose substantially.

input: A route through Beringia is seen as more likely than the Solutrean hypothesis. Kashani et al. 2012 state that "The similarities in ages and geographical distributions for C4c and the previously analyzed X2a lineage provide support to the scenario of a dual origin for Paleo-Indians. Taking into account that C4c is deeply rooted in the Asian portion of the mtDNA phylogeny and is indubitably of Asian origin, the finding that C4c and X2a are characterized by parallel genetic histories definitively dismisses the controversial hypothesis of an Atlantic glacial entry route into North America."
rewrite: Current research favors the Beringia migration route over the Solutrean theory. According to Kashani et al. (2012), the parallel genetic histories of mitochondrial lineages C4c and X2a indicate a dual ancestry for Paleo-Indians. Since C4c is unequivocally of Asian origin, this evidence strongly refutes the idea of an ancient Atlantic crossing into North America during the glacial period.

input: Fetuvalu offers the Cambridge syllabus. Motufoua offers the Fiji Junior Certificate (FJC) at year 10, Tuvaluan Certificate at Year 11 and the Pacific Senior Secondary Certificate (PSSC) at Year 12, set by the Fiji-based exam board SPBEA. Sixth form students who pass their PSSC go on to the Augmented Foundation Programme, funded by the government of Tuvalu. This program is required for tertiary education programmes outside of Tuvalu and is available at the University of the South Pacific (USP) Extension Centre in Funafuti.
rewrite: Fetuvalu follows the Cambridge curriculum. At Motufoua, students take the Fiji Junior Certificate in Year 10, the Tuvaluan Certificate in Year 11, and the SPBEA-administered Pacific Senior Secondary Certificate in Year 12. Successful Year 12 graduates enter the government-funded Augmented Foundation Programme. This course, essential for university studies abroad, is provided at the USP Extension Centre in Funafuti.

input: The largest ethnic groups are Newar (29.6%), Matwali (25.1% Sunuwar, Gurung, Magars, Tamang etc.), Khas Brahmins (20.51%) and Chettris (18.5%) . Tamangs originating from surrounding hill districts can be seen in Kathmandu. More recently, other hill ethnic groups and Caste groups from Terai have come to represent a substantial proportion of the city's population. The major languages are Nepali and Nepal Bhasa, while English is understood by many, particularly in the service industry. The major religions are Hinduism and Buddhism.
rewrite: The predominant communities include Newar, Matwali (encompassing Sunuwar, Gurung, Magar, and Tamang peoples), Khas Brahmins, and Chettris. Many Tamang people have moved to Kathmandu from nearby hill areas. Additionally, numerous groups from the hills and the Terai region now form a significant part of the city's inhabitants. Commonly spoken languages are Nepali and Nepal Bhasa, with English also widely used, especially in services. Hinduism and Buddhism are the primary faiths.

input: Galileo Galilei was brought before the Inquisition for heresy, but abjured his views and was sentenced to house arrest, under which he spent the rest of his life. Galileo was found "vehemently suspect of heresy", namely of having held the opinions that the Sun lies motionless at the centre of the universe, that the Earth is not at its centre and moves, and that one may hold and defend an opinion as probable after it has been declared contrary to Holy Scripture. He was required to "abjure, curse and detest" those opinions.
rewrite: Galileo Galilei faced trial for heresy by the Inquisition. Forced to renounce his beliefs, he was convicted of being strongly suspected of heresy. His condemned views included that the Sun is stationary and central, while the Earth moves and is not the center of the cosmos, and that such ideas could be considered plausible even if scripture opposed them. He was compelled to publicly reject and condemn these ideas, spending his remaining years confined to his home.

input: According to reciprocity, the efficiency of an antenna used as a receiving antenna is identical to the efficiency as defined above. The power that an antenna will deliver to a receiver (with a proper impedance match) is reduced by the same amount. In some receiving applications, the very inefficient antennas may have little impact on performance. At low frequencies, for example, atmospheric or man-made noise can mask antenna inefficiency. For example, CCIR Rep. 258-3 indicates man-made noise in a residential setting at 40 MHz is about 28 dB above the thermal noise floor. Consequently, an antenna with a 20 dB loss (due to inefficiency) would have little impact on system noise performance. The loss within the antenna will affect the intended signal and the noise/interference identically, leading to no reduction in signal to noise ratio (SNR).
rewrite: The principle of reciprocity states that an antenna's efficiency remains the same whether it is transmitting or receiving. Therefore, the power delivered to a receiver with correct impedance matching is equally diminished. In certain reception scenarios, highly inefficient antennas may not significantly degrade overall operation. This is because, particularly at lower frequencies, external noise from the environment or human activity often overwhelms the inherent losses of a poor antenna. To illustrate, a documented report shows that in a typical neighborhood at 40 MHz, artificial noise is roughly 28 dB higher than basic thermal noise. Thus, an antenna suffering 20 dB of efficiency loss would barely influence the system's noise characteristics. Since the antenna's internal loss attenuates both the desired signal and the background noise equally, the signal-to-noise ratio remains unchanged.

input: In 2011, Bandai posted a countdown on a teaser site. Once the countdown was finished, it revealed a reboot of the Digimon World series titled Digimon World Re:Digitize. An enhanced version of the game released on Nintendo 3DS as Digimon World Re:Digitize Decode in 2013. Another role-playing game by the name Digimon Story: Cyber Sleuth is set for release in 2015 for PlayStation Vita. It is part of the Digimon Story sub-series, originally on Nintendo DS and has also been released with English subtitles in North America.
rewrite: In 2011, Bandai launched a teaser website featuring a timer. At its conclusion, the site unveiled a revival of the Digimon World franchise called Digimon World Re:Digitize. An upgraded edition, named Digimon World Re:Digitize Decode, arrived on the Nintendo 3DS in 2013. Additionally, a separate role-playing game titled Digimon Story: Cyber Sleuth is scheduled for a 2015 PlayStation Vita release. This title belongs to the Digimon Story line, which began on the Nintendo DS and has seen English-subtitled versions in North America.

input: On 25 February 1991, the Warsaw Pact was declared disbanded at a meeting of defense and foreign ministers from remaining Pact countries meeting in Hungary. On 1 July 1991, in Prague, the Czechoslovak President Václav Havel formally ended the 1955 Warsaw Treaty Organization of Friendship, Cooperation, and Mutual Assistance and so disestablished the Warsaw Treaty after 36 years of military alliance with the USSR. In fact, the treaty was de facto disbanded in December 1989 during the violent revolution in Romania, which toppled the communist government, without military intervention form other member states. The USSR disestablished itself in December 1991.
rewrite: During a gathering in Hungary on February 25, 1991, defense and foreign ministers from the nations still in the Warsaw Pact announced its termination. That July, in Prague, Czechoslovak leader Václav Havel officially dissolved the 1955 Treaty of Friendship, Cooperation, and Mutual Assistance, concluding 36 years of a Soviet-led military pact. However, the alliance had effectively collapsed in December 1989 amid Romania's violent revolution, which overthrew its communist regime without interference from fellow members. The Soviet Union itself ceased to exist in December 1991.

input: Public funding and private investment have also been made with promises to rehabilitate neighborhoods. In April 2008, the city announced a $300-million stimulus plan to create jobs and revitalize neighborhoods, financed by city bonds and paid for by earmarking about 15% of the wagering tax. The city's working plans for neighborhood revitalizations include 7-Mile/Livernois, Brightmoor, East English Village, Grand River/Greenfield, North End, and Osborn. Private organizations have pledged substantial funding to the efforts. Additionally, the city has cleared a 1,200-acre (490 ha) section of land for large-scale neighborhood construction, which the city is calling the Far Eastside Plan. In 2011, Mayor Bing announced a plan to categorize neighborhoods by their needs and prioritize the most needed services for those neighborhoods.
rewrite: Both public and private resources have been committed to renewing urban areas. In 2008, a municipal job creation and community renewal initiative valued at $300 million was launched, funded by city bonds and supported by allocating roughly 15% of the wagering tax revenue. Key areas identified for these improvements are 7-Mile/Livernois, Brightmoor, East English Village, Grand River/Greenfield, North End, and Osborn. Private groups have also contributed significant financial support. The city has also prepared a 1,200-acre parcel for extensive development, known as the Far Eastside Plan. Furthermore, in 2011, a strategy was introduced to classify communities based on their specific requirements and to focus essential services where they are most urgently needed.

input: In Epperson v. Arkansas, 393 U.S. 97 (1968), the Supreme Court considered an Arkansas law that made it a crime "to teach the theory or doctrine that mankind ascended or descended from a lower order of animals," or "to adopt or use in any such institution a textbook that teaches" this theory in any school or university that received public funds. The court's opinion, written by Justice Abe Fortas, ruled that the Arkansas law violated "the constitutional prohibition of state laws respecting an establishment of religion or prohibiting the free exercise thereof. The overriding fact is that Arkansas' law selects from the body of knowledge a particular segment which it proscribes for the sole reason that it is deemed to conflict with a particular religious doctrine; that is, with a particular interpretation of the Book of Genesis by a particular religious group." The court held that the Establishment Clause prohibits the state from advancing any religion, and that "[T]he state has no legitimate interest in protecting any or all religions from views distasteful to them."
rewrite: In the 1968 case Epperson v. Arkansas, the U.S. Supreme Court reviewed a statute from Arkansas. This statute criminalized instructing students in publicly funded schools about evolutionary theory, specifically the idea that humans evolved from other species. It also banned using textbooks containing such material. Justice Abe Fortas authored the decision, which found the law unconstitutional. The ruling stated it breached the First Amendment's Establishment Clause, which forbids government from endorsing or supporting any religion. The Court determined that the statute singled out a specific scientific concept for prohibition solely because it contradicted certain religious beliefs, namely a literal reading of Genesis by some groups. The opinion emphasized that government has no valid role in shielding religious doctrines from opposing scientific perspectives they may find offensive.

input: Although unpleasantness is an essential part of the IASP definition of pain, it is possible to induce a state described as intense pain devoid of unpleasantness in some patients, with morphine injection or psychosurgery. Such patients report that they have pain but are not bothered by it; they recognize the sensation of pain but suffer little, or not at all. Indifference to pain can also rarely be present from birth; these people have normal nerves on medical investigations, and find pain unpleasant, but do not avoid repetition of the pain stimulus.
rewrite: While the standard medical definition of pain includes distress, certain treatments like morphine or specific brain surgeries can create a state of severe pain without the associated suffering. Individuals in this condition acknowledge the painful sensation but experience minimal or no distress from it. Separately, a rare congenital absence of pain response also exists. These individuals possess normal neurological function and perceive pain as unpleasant, yet they do not attempt to avoid the painful stimulus.

input: The Qur'an relates detailed narrative accounts of Maryam (Mary) in two places, Qur'an 3:35–47 and 19:16–34. These state beliefs in both the Immaculate Conception of Mary and the Virgin birth of Jesus. The account given in Sura 19 is nearly identical with that in the Gospel according to Luke, and both of these (Luke, Sura 19) begin with an account of the visitation of an angel upon Zakariya (Zecharias) and Good News of the birth of Yahya (John), followed by the account of the annunciation. It mentions how Mary was informed by an angel that she would become the mother of Jesus through the actions of God alone.
rewrite: The Qur'an presents the story of Mary in two detailed sections, specifically chapters 3 and 19. These passages affirm the virgin birth of Jesus and Mary's own purity. The narrative in chapter 19 closely parallels the one found in the Gospel of Luke. Both accounts start by describing an angel's visit to Zechariah, announcing the coming birth of John. This is followed by the angel Gabriel informing Mary that she will miraculously conceive and give birth to Jesus through divine will alone.

input: As a relatively small and isolated oceanic island, Norfolk has few land birds but a high degree of endemicity among them. Many of the endemic species and subspecies have become extinct as a result of massive clearance of the island's native vegetation of subtropical rainforest for agriculture, hunting and persecution as agricultural pests. The birds have also suffered from the introduction of mammals such as rats, cats, pigs and goats, as well as from introduced competitors such as common blackbirds and crimson rosellas.
rewrite: Norfolk Island's limited size and remote location have resulted in a sparse but unique population of native land birds. Numerous endemic varieties have vanished, primarily due to the extensive removal of the original subtropical rainforest for farming. Additional pressures include hunting, being viewed as pests, and the arrival of invasive mammals like rats and cats, along with competing bird species such as blackbirds and rosellas.

input: Physical pain is an important political topic in relation to various issues, including pain management policy, drug control, animal rights or animal welfare, torture, and pain compliance. In various contexts, the deliberate infliction of pain in the form of corporal punishment is used as retribution for an offence, or for the purpose of disciplining or reforming a wrongdoer, or to deter attitudes or behaviour deemed unacceptable. In some cultures, extreme practices such as mortification of the flesh or painful rites of passage are highly regarded.
rewrite: The experience of bodily suffering holds significant political relevance across numerous domains, such as regulations for pain relief, narcotics legislation, the ethical treatment of animals, the use of torture, and enforcing obedience through discomfort. Corporal punishment is often administered intentionally as a penalty for crimes, a method for correction, or a deterrent against unwanted actions. Certain societies also value severe physical trials, including self-denial rituals or arduous initiation ceremonies.

input: This trend for the king to rely on his own men at the expense of the barons was exacerbated by the tradition of Angevin royal ira et malevolentia – "anger and ill-will" – and John's own personality. From Henry II onwards, ira et malevolentia had come to describe the right of the king to express his anger and displeasure at particular barons or clergy, building on the Norman concept of malevoncia – royal ill-will. In the Norman period, suffering the king's ill-will meant difficulties in obtaining grants, honours or petitions; Henry II had infamously expressed his fury and ill-will towards Thomas Becket; this ultimately resulted in Becket's death. John now had the additional ability to "cripple his vassals" on a significant scale using his new economic and judicial measures, which made the threat of royal anger all the more serious.
rewrite: The king's growing dependence on his personal followers, rather than the nobility, was intensified by the Angevin practice of royal "ira et malevolentia," meaning "anger and ill-will," combined with King John's character. Beginning with Henry II, this idea formalized the monarch's prerogative to show displeasure toward specific barons or church officials, extending the older Norman notion of royal displeasure. Under Norman rule, falling from favor created obstacles in securing lands, titles, or requests; Henry II notoriously directed his wrath and ill-will at Thomas Becket, leading to Becket's murder. John further amplified the danger of royal disfavor by employing fresh fiscal and legal policies that enabled him to financially devastate his nobles on an unprecedented scale.

input: During the 1960s and 1970s, the city gained a reputation as an important center for liberal politics. Ann Arbor also became a locus for left-wing activism and served as a hub for the civil-rights movement and anti-Vietnam War movement, as well as the student movement. The first major meetings of the national left-wing campus group Students for a Democratic Society took place in Ann Arbor in 1960; in 1965, the city was home to the first U.S. teach-in against the Vietnam War. During the ensuing 15 years, many countercultural and New Left enterprises sprang up and developed large constituencies within the city. These influences washed into municipal politics during the early and mid-1970s when three members of the Human Rights Party (HRP) won city council seats on the strength of the student vote. During their time on the council, HRP representatives fought for measures including pioneering antidiscrimination ordinances, measures decriminalizing marijuana possession, and a rent-control ordinance; many of these remain in effect in modified form. Alongside these liberal and left-wing efforts, a small group of conservative institutions were born in Ann Arbor. These include Word of God (established in 1967), a charismatic inter-denominational movement; and the Thomas More Law Center (established in 1999), a religious-conservative advocacy group.
rewrite:
In the 1960s and 1970s, Ann Arbor emerged as a significant focal point for progressive thought and action. It was known as a bastion for liberal political activity and a central gathering place for various activist causes, including the struggle for civil rights and opposition to the Vietnam War, alongside broader student-led initiatives. The national organization Students for a Democratic Society, a prominent left-wing student group, held its foundational assemblies there in 1960. By 1965, the city hosted the inaugural American teach-in to protest the Vietnam conflict. Over the next decade and a half, numerous alternative and New Left organizations arose, attracting substantial local followings.

This activist energy translated directly into local governance in the early to mid-1970s, when three candidates from the Human Rights Party secured positions on the city council, propelled largely by student support. While in office, these council members championed progressive policies such as early anti-discrimination laws, initiatives to reduce penalties for cannabis possession, and rent stabilization rules; versions of these measures are still active today. Concurrently with these liberal and leftist movements, a few conservative organizations also found their roots in the city. Among them are the Word of God, a charismatic Christian fellowship founded in 1967, and the Thomas More Law Center, established in 1999 as a legal advocacy group promoting religious conservative principles.

input: The USA PATRIOT Act of October 2001 dramatically reduces restrictions on law enforcement agencies' ability to search telephone, e-mail communications, medical, financial, and other records; eases restrictions on foreign intelligence gathering within the United States; expands the Secretary of the Treasury's authority to regulate financial transactions, particularly those involving foreign individuals and entities; and broadens the discretion of law enforcement and immigration authorities in detaining and deporting immigrants suspected of terrorism-related acts. The act also expanded the definition of terrorism to include domestic terrorism, thus enlarging the number of activities to which the USA PATRIOT Act's expanded law enforcement powers could be applied. A new Terrorist Finance Tracking Program monitored the movements of terrorists' financial resources (discontinued after being revealed by The New York Times). Global telecommunication usage, including those with no links to terrorism, is being collected and monitored through the NSA electronic surveillance program. The Patriot Act is still in effect.
rewrite: Enacted in October 2001, the USA PATRIOT Act significantly loosened limits on how investigative bodies can access personal records, such as those from phones, emails, medical files, and banks. It also relaxed constraints on collecting foreign intelligence inside the U.S. and gave the Treasury Secretary greater power to oversee monetary dealings, especially with non-domestic parties. The law increased the leeway for officials in law enforcement and immigration to hold and remove non-citizens believed to be connected to terrorist activities. Furthermore, it redefined terrorism to cover acts within the country's borders, thereby extending the reach of its enhanced authorities. Initiatives like a Terrorist Finance Tracking Program watched monetary flows until its exposure led to termination. Broader surveillance, like the NSA's program, gathers global communications data, even from those not suspected of terrorism. The legislation remains active today.

input: On February 8, 1847, Doniphan continued his march with 924 men mostly from Missouri; he accompanied a train of 315 wagons of a large commercial caravan heading to the state capital. Meanwhile, the Mexican forces in the state had time to prepare a defense against the Americans. About 20 miles (32 km) north of the capital where two mountain ranges join from east to west is the only pass into the capital; known as Sacramento Pass, this point is now part of present-day Chihuahua City. The Battle of Sacramento was the most important battle fought in the state of Chihuahua because it was the sole defense for the state capital. The battle ended quickly because of some devastating defensive errors from the Mexican forces and the ingenious strategic moves by the American forces. After their loss at the Battle of Sacramento, the remaining Mexican soldiers retreated south, leaving the city to American occupation. Almost 300 Mexicans were killed in the battle, as well as almost 300 wounded. The Americans also confiscated large amounts of Mexican supplies and took 400 Mexican soldiers prisoners of war. American forces maintained an occupation of the state capital for the rest of the Mexican–American War.
rewrite: On February 8, 1847, Colonel Doniphan advanced with a force of 924 soldiers, predominantly Missourians. His unit traveled alongside a substantial merchant convoy of 315 wagons bound for the capital of Chihuahua. This delay provided Mexican troops in the region an opportunity to organize their resistance. Approximately 20 miles north of the city, the sole accessible route through the adjoining eastern and western mountain chains was Sacramento Pass, a location now within modern Chihuahua City. The clash that occurred there, the Battle of Sacramento, proved decisive for the entire state, as it represented the final protective barrier for its capital. The engagement concluded rapidly due to critical tactical mistakes by the defending Mexican army and clever maneuvers by the U.S. troops. Following this defeat, the remaining Mexican forces withdrew southward, abandoning the city to American control. The battle resulted in nearly 300 Mexican fatalities and a similar number of injuries. U.S. forces also captured significant Mexican provisions and took 400 soldiers as prisoners. American occupation of the state capital persisted for the duration of the Mexican-American War.

input: Lester Brown has argued that "a world facing the prospect of economically disruptive climate change can no longer justify subsidies to expand the burning of coal and oil. Shifting these subsidies to the development of climate-benign energy sources such as wind, solar, biomass, and geothermal power is the key to stabilizing the earth's climate." The International Solar Energy Society advocates "leveling the playing field" by redressing the continuing inequities in public subsidies of energy technologies and R&D, in which the fossil fuel and nuclear power receive the largest share of financial support.
rewrite: Lester Brown contends that with the threat of climate disruption, subsidizing coal and oil is indefensible. Redirecting this funding toward sustainable sources like wind, solar, biomass, and geothermal energy is essential for climate stability. Similarly, the International Solar Energy Society calls for correcting imbalances in public funding and research support, which currently heavily favor fossil fuels and nuclear power, to create fair conditions for all energy technologies.

input: Several hundred pro-Tibet protesters gathered at the Trocadéro with banners and Tibetan flags, and remained there for a peaceful protest, never approaching the torch relay itself. Among them was Jane Birkin, who spoke to the media about the "lack of freedom of speech" in China. Also present was Thupten Gyatso, President of the French Tibetan community, who called upon pro-Tibet demonstrators to "remain calm, non-violent, peaceful".
rewrite: Hundreds of Tibet supporters assembled peacefully at the Trocadéro, displaying signs and flags while keeping their distance from the torch relay. Actress Jane Birkin addressed reporters, criticizing China's restrictions on expression. Thupten Gyatso, leader of France's Tibetan community, urged those gathered to maintain a calm and non-violent demonstration.

input: The Dutch written grammar has simplified over the past 100 years: cases are now mainly used for the pronouns, such as ik (I), mij, me (me), mijn (my), wie (who), wiens (whose: masculine or neuter singular), wier (whose: feminine singular; masculine, feminine or neuter plural). Nouns and adjectives are not case inflected (except for the genitive of proper nouns (names): -s, -'s or -'). In the spoken language cases and case inflections had already gradually disappeared from a much earlier date on (probably the 15th century) as in many continental West Germanic dialects.
rewrite: Over the last century, written Dutch has become less complex grammatically. Cases now primarily apply to pronouns like "ik" (I) or "mijn" (my). For nouns and adjectives, case endings are no longer used, aside from the possessive form of names. In everyday speech, these case distinctions began fading much earlier, likely around the 1400s, mirroring changes in other related Germanic languages.

input: The World Health Organization and the UN Environment Programme estimate that each year, 3 million workers in agriculture in the developing world experience severe poisoning from pesticides, about 18,000 of whom die. Owing to inadequate regulation and safety precautions, 99% of pesticide related deaths occur in developing countries that account for only 25% of pesticide usage. According to one study, as many as 25 million workers in developing countries may suffer mild pesticide poisoning yearly. There are several careers aside from agriculture that may also put individuals at risk of health effects from pesticide exposure including pet groomers, groundskeepers, and fumigators.
rewrite: According to estimates from the World Health Organization and the UN Environment Programme, roughly three million agricultural workers in developing nations suffer acute pesticide poisoning annually, resulting in approximately 18,000 fatalities. A striking 99% of these deaths happen in developing countries, which use just a quarter of the world's pesticides, highlighting major gaps in regulation and protective measures. Research further indicates up to 25 million such workers may endure mild poisoning each year. Beyond farming, other professions like pet grooming, landscaping, and fumigation also pose significant risks of exposure to these harmful chemicals.

input: Peel, widely regarded as the father of modern policing, was heavily influenced by the social and legal philosophy of Jeremy Bentham, who called for a strong and centralized, but politically neutral, police force for the maintenance of social order, for the protection of people from crime and to act as a visible deterrent to urban crime and disorder. Peel decided to standardise the police force as an official paid profession, to organise it in a civilian fashion, and to make it answerable to the public.
rewrite: Sir Robert Peel, considered the founder of contemporary law enforcement, drew significant inspiration from Jeremy Bentham's ideas on society and law. Bentham advocated for a robust, centralized police service that remained apolitical, aiming to preserve public order, safeguard citizens, and visibly discourage crime in cities. In response, Peel formalized policing into a salaried public occupation, structured it along non-military lines, and established its accountability to the community.

input: The western section of the state is part of the Appalachian Mountain range. Among the subranges of the Appalachians located in the state are the Great Smoky Mountains, Blue Ridge Mountains, Great Balsam Mountains, and Black Mountains. The Black Mountains are the highest in the eastern United States, and culminate in Mount Mitchell at 6,684 feet (2,037 m) the highest point east of the Mississippi River. Although agriculture still remains important, tourism has become a dominant industry in the mountains. Growing Christmas trees has recently become an important industry as well. Because of the higher altitude, the climate in the mountains often differs markedly from that of the rest of the state. Winter in western North Carolina typically features high snowfall and subfreezing temperatures more akin to those of a midwestern state than of a southern state.
rewrite: The state's western region lies within the Appalachian Mountains. This area includes such subranges as the Great Smoky, Blue Ridge, Great Balsam, and Black Mountains. The Black Mountains, home to Mount Mitchell's 6,684-foot summit, represent the tallest peaks in the eastern U.S., marking the highest elevation east of the Mississippi. While farming continues here, tourism now drives the local economy, joined more recently by significant Christmas tree cultivation. The elevated terrain creates a distinct climate, setting it apart from the rest of the state. Winters in this part of North Carolina bring substantial snow and freezing temperatures, resembling conditions more common in the Midwest than the South.

input: Within six years of the official criminalization of heresy by the Emperor, the first Christian heretic to be executed, Priscillian, was condemned in 386 by Roman secular officials for sorcery, and put to death with four or five followers. However, his accusers were excommunicated both by Ambrose of Milan and Pope Siricius, who opposed Priscillian's heresy, but "believed capital punishment to be inappropriate at best and usually unequivocally evil". For some years after the Reformation, Protestant churches were also known to execute those they considered heretics, including Catholics. The last known heretic executed by sentence of the Roman Catholic Church was Spanish schoolmaster Cayetano Ripoll in 1826. The number of people executed as heretics under the authority of the various "ecclesiastical authorities"[note 1] is not known.[note 2] One of the first examples of the word as translated from the Nag Hammadi's Apocalypse of Peter was" they will cleave to the name of a dead man thinking that they will become pure. But they will become greatly defiled and they will fall into the name of error and into the hands of an evil cunning man and a manifold dogma, and they will be ruled heretically".
rewrite: Six years after heresy was formally outlawed by imperial decree, Priscillian became the first Christian heretic to be put to death. In 386, Roman civil authorities convicted him of witchcraft, and he was executed alongside a small group of his adherents. Notably, the figures who accused him, Ambrose of Milan and Pope Siricius, were themselves excommunicated. While they rejected Priscillian’s beliefs, they also held that the death penalty was, at the very least, unsuitable and often profoundly immoral. Following the Reformation, Protestant denominations similarly carried out executions against those deemed heretical, including Catholics. The final such execution ordered by the Roman Catholic Church occurred in 1826, when Spanish teacher Cayetano Ripoll was killed. The total number of individuals executed as heretics under different religious authorities remains unknown. An early instance of the term "heretic" appears in the Nag Hammadi library’s Apocalypse of Peter, which describes individuals clinging to a deceased figure’s name in the belief it will purify them. Instead, they are corrupted, led into doctrinal error, and fall under the sway of a deceitful leader and complex false teachings, thus coming to be governed by heretical principles.

input: Greece is today relatively homogeneous in linguistic terms, with a large majority of the native population using Greek as their first or only language.
