Among the Greek-speaking population, speakers of the distinctive Pontic dialect came to Greece from Asia Minor after the Greek genocide and constitute a sizable group. The Cappadocian dialect came to Greece due to the genocide as well, but is endangered and is barely spoken now. Indigenous Greek dialects include the archaic Greek spoken by the Sarakatsani, traditionally transhument mountain shepherds of Greek Macedonia and other parts of Northern Greece. The Tsakonian language, a distinct Greek language deriving from Doric Greek instead of Ionic Greek, is still spoken in some villages in the southeastern Peloponnese.
rewrite: Contemporary Greece exhibits considerable linguistic uniformity, with most of its native inhabitants speaking Greek as their primary or sole language. Within this group, a significant number speak the Pontic dialect, originating from communities in Asia Minor that resettled in Greece following the genocide. Similarly displaced, speakers of the Cappadocian dialect are now very few, placing that variety at risk of extinction. Among the indigenous linguistic varieties are the archaic form used by the Sarakatsani, a historically nomadic pastoral people of Greek Macedonia and northern regions. Additionally, the unique Tsakonian language, which evolved from ancient Doric rather than Ionic Greek, persists in several villages in the southeastern Peloponnese.

input: The Bologna process has been adopted, since 2006, by Portuguese universities and poly-technical institutes. Higher education in state-run educational establishments is provided on a competitive basis, a system of numerus clausus is enforced through a national database on student admissions. However, every higher education institution offers also a number of additional vacant places through other extraordinary admission processes for sportsmen, mature applicants (over 23 years old), international students, foreign students from the Lusosphere, degree owners from other institutions, students from other institutions (academic transfer), former students (readmission), and course change, which are subject to specific standards and regulations set by each institution or course department. Most student costs are supported with public money. However, with the increasing tuition fees a student has to pay to attend a Portuguese state-run higher education institution and the attraction of new types of students (many as part-time students or in evening classes) like employees, businessmen, parents, and pensioners, many departments make a substantial profit from every additional student enrolled in courses, with benefits for the college or university's gross tuition revenue and without loss of educational quality (teacher per student, computer per student, classroom size per student, etc.).
rewrite:
Since 2006, Portuguese universities and polytechnics have followed the Bologna framework. Admission to public higher education is competitive, managed via a national database that limits placements. Beyond this primary system, institutions also allocate extra spots through special admissions channels. These cater to athletes, older candidates above age 23, international students, individuals from Portuguese-speaking nations, graduates from other schools, transferring students, returning former students, and those switching programs. Each institution or department defines its own rules for these cases.

While public funds cover the majority of educational expenses, rising tuition fees have altered the financial landscape. The enrollment of new student profiles—such as working professionals, entrepreneurs, parents, and retirees, often studying part-time or in evening sessions—has allowed many departments to gain significant surplus revenue from each additional enrollee. This boosts the institution’s overall tuition income without compromising educational standards, as key metrics like instructor-student ratios, access to technology, and class sizes are maintained.

input: The loss of industrial and working-class jobs in the city has resulted in high rates of poverty and associated problems. From 2000 to 2009, the city's estimated median household income fell from $29,526 to $26,098. As of 2010[update] the mean income of Detroit is below the overall U.S. average by several thousand dollars. Of every three Detroit residents, one lives in poverty. Luke Bergmann, author of Getting Ghost: Two Young Lives and the Struggle for the Soul of an American City, said in 2010, "Detroit is now one of the poorest big cities in the country."
rewrite: The decline of manufacturing and blue-collar employment in Detroit has led to widespread poverty and related issues. Between 2000 and 2009, the city's median household income dropped from $29,526 to $26,098. By 2010, Detroit's average income was thousands of dollars less than the national figure. Approximately one in three residents lives below the poverty line. In 2010, author Luke Bergmann noted that Detroit had become among the nation's most impoverished major cities.

input: The Bithynians were a Thracian people living in northwest Anatolia. After Alexander's conquests the region of Bithynia came under the rule of the native king Bas, who defeated Calas, a general of Alexander the Great, and maintained the independence of Bithynia. His son, Zipoetes I of Bithynia maintained this autonomy against Lysimachus and Seleucus I, and assumed the title of king (basileus) in 297 BCE. His son and successor, Nicomedes I, founded Nicomedia, which soon rose to great prosperity, and during his long reign (c. 278 – c. 255 BCE), as well as those of his successors, the kingdom of Bithynia held a considerable place among the minor monarchies of Anatolia. Nicomedes also invited the Celtic Galatians into Anatolia as mercenaries, and they later turned on his son Prusias I, who defeated them in battle. Their last king, Nicomedes IV, was unable to maintain himself against Mithridates VI of Pontus, and, after being restored to his throne by the Roman Senate, he bequeathed his kingdom by will to the Roman republic (74 BCE).
rewrite: The Bithynians, an ancient Thracian group, inhabited northwestern Anatolia. Following Alexander the Great's campaigns, this area emerged under the control of a local ruler named Bas. He achieved a military victory over Alexander's commander Calas, thereby securing Bithynia's freedom from external domination. His heir, Zipoetes I, successfully preserved this self-rule against challenges from successors of Alexander, Lysimachus and Seleucus I, and formally declared himself king in 297 BCE. Nicomedes I, the next ruler, established the city of Nicomedia, which rapidly became affluent. Throughout his extended rule and those of the kings that followed, Bithynia remained a significant power among the smaller Anatolian states. Nicomedes I recruited Galatian Celts as paid soldiers, though they eventually rebelled against his son, Prusias I, who overcame them in combat. The final monarch, Nicomedes IV, struggled to resist Pontus's King Mithridates VI. Though the Roman Senate reinstated him, he ultimately chose to leave his entire kingdom to the Roman Republic upon his death in 74 BCE.

input: The Space Race was a 20th-century competition between two Cold War rivals, the Soviet Union (USSR) and the United States (US), for supremacy in spaceflight capability. It had its origins in the missile-based nuclear arms race between the two nations that occurred following World War II, enabled by captured German rocket technology and personnel. The technological superiority required for such supremacy was seen as necessary for national security, and symbolic of ideological superiority. The Space Race spawned pioneering efforts to launch artificial satellites, unmanned space probes of the Moon, Venus, and Mars, and human spaceflight in low Earth orbit and to the Moon. The competition began on August 2, 1955, when the Soviet Union responded to the US announcement four days earlier of intent to launch artificial satellites for the International Geophysical Year, by declaring they would also launch a satellite "in the near future". The Soviet Union beat the US to this, with the October 4, 1957 orbiting of Sputnik 1, and later beat the US to the first human in space, Yuri Gagarin, on April 12, 1961. The Space Race peaked with the July 20, 1969 US landing of the first humans on the Moon with Apollo 11. The USSR tried but failed manned lunar missions, and eventually cancelled them and concentrated on Earth orbital space stations. A period of détente followed with the April 1972 agreement on a co-operative Apollo–Soyuz Test Project, resulting in the July 1975 rendezvous in Earth orbit of a US astronaut crew with a Soviet cosmonaut crew.
rewrite:
During the Cold War, the United States and the Soviet Union engaged in a prolonged struggle for dominance in space exploration, known as the Space Race. This contest grew out of the post-World War II nuclear arms race, which relied on missile technology developed from captured German research and scientists. Both nations viewed technological leadership in space as crucial for their security and as a testament to the superiority of their political ideologies. This rivalry drove early achievements, including deploying the first artificial satellites, sending robotic probes to the Moon and planets, and conducting crewed missions both in Earth's orbit and to the lunar surface.

The competition formally started in early August 1955, when the USSR, reacting to an American plan, announced its own intention to launch a satellite. The Soviets took an early lead by successfully orbiting Sputnik 1 in October 1957 and later by sending the first human, Yuri Gagarin, into space in April 1961. The Race reached its climax when the United States landed astronauts on the Moon with Apollo 11 in July 1969. After unsuccessful attempts at manned lunar missions, the Soviet Union shifted its focus to constructing space stations in Earth orbit. Tensions eased in the early 1970s, leading to a cooperative mission, the Apollo-Soyuz Test Project. This partnership culminated in a historic joint orbital meeting between American and Soviet crews in July 1975.

input: The last major building work took place during the reign of King George V when, in 1913, Sir Aston Webb redesigned Blore's 1850 East Front to resemble in part Giacomo Leoni's Lyme Park in Cheshire. This new, refaced principal façade (of Portland stone) was designed to be the backdrop to the Victoria Memorial, a large memorial statue of Queen Victoria, placed outside the main gates. George V, who had succeeded Edward VII in 1910, had a more serious personality than his father; greater emphasis was now placed on official entertaining and royal duties than on lavish parties. He arranged a series of command performances featuring jazz musicians such as the Original Dixieland Jazz Band (1919) – the first jazz performance for a head of state, Sidney Bechet, and Louis Armstrong (1932), which earned the palace a nomination in 2009 for a (Kind of) Blue Plaque by the Brecon Jazz Festival as one of the venues making the greatest contribution to jazz music in the United Kingdom. George V's wife Queen Mary was a connoisseur of the arts, and took a keen interest in the Royal Collection of furniture and art, both restoring and adding to it. Queen Mary also had many new fixtures and fittings installed, such as the pair of marble Empire-style chimneypieces by Benjamin Vulliamy, dating from 1810, which the Queen had installed in the ground floor Bow Room, the huge low room at the centre of the garden façade. Queen Mary was also responsible for the decoration of the Blue Drawing Room. This room, 69 feet (21 metres) long, previously known as the South Drawing Room, has a ceiling designed specially by Nash, coffered with huge gilt console brackets.
rewrite:
The final significant architectural changes to the structure occurred under King George V. In 1913, Sir Aston Webb undertook a redesign of the East Front, originally created by Blore in 1850, incorporating stylistic elements reminiscent of Giacomo Leoni’s work at Lyme Park in Cheshire. This redesigned primary facade, clad in Portland stone, was intended to serve as a grand setting for the Victoria Memorial statue of Queen Victoria situated before the gates. Having ascended to the throne in 1910, George V possessed a more solemn disposition than his predecessor, Edward VII. His reign saw a shift in focus toward formal state functions and official responsibilities, moving away from the extravagant social gatherings of the prior era. He pioneered royal support for jazz, organizing command performances by pioneering artists like the Original Dixieland Jazz Band in 1919—marking the first jazz performance for a monarch—followed by Sidney Bechet and Louis Armstrong in 1932. This legacy led the palace to be nominated in 2009 by the Brecon Jazz Festival for a special recognition, acknowledging its role in the history of British jazz.

Queen Mary, George V’s consort, was a knowledgeable patron of the arts. She took an active role in managing the Royal Collection, both restoring existing pieces and acquiring new works of art and furniture. She oversaw numerous interior updates, including the installation of a pair of Benjamin Vulliamy’s marble Empire-style chimneypieces from 1810 in the ground-floor Bow Room, a spacious, low-ceilinged area at the center of the garden-facing side of the building. Additionally, Queen Mary directed the redecoration of the Blue Drawing Room. Previously called the South Drawing Room, this 69-foot-long space features an elaborate ceiling designed by Nash, adorned with substantial gilded console brackets and a coffered design.

input: In 2011, the Aragonese government passed a decree for the establishment of a new language regulator of Catalan in La Franja (the so-called Catalan-speaking areas of Aragon). The new entity, designated as Acadèmia Aragonesa del Català, shall allow a facultative education in Catalan and a standardization of the Catalan language in La Franja.
rewrite: In 2011, Aragon's government created a new regulatory body for the Catalan language in its eastern region, La Franja. Named the Acadèmia Aragonesa del Català, it will enable optional Catalan schooling and promote linguistic standardization in the area.

input: An influx of interstate and overseas migrants, particularly Irish, German and Chinese, saw the development of slums including a temporary "tent city" established on the southern banks of the Yarra. Chinese migrants founded the Melbourne Chinatown in 1851, which remains the longest continuous Chinese settlement in the Western World. In the aftermath of the Eureka Stockade, mass public support for the plight of the miners resulted in major political changes to the colony, including changes to working conditions across local industries including mining, agriculture and manufacturing. The nationalities involved in the Eureka revolt and Burke and Wills expedition gave an indication of immigration flows in the second half of the nineteenth century.
rewrite: A surge of newcomers from other states and abroad, especially those of Irish, German, and Chinese origin, led to the growth of impoverished areas. This included a makeshift encampment along the Yarra River's south shore. The Chinese community established Melbourne's Chinatown in 1851, which continues to be the oldest enduring Chinese enclave outside Asia. Following the Eureka Stockade, widespread sympathy for the miners' cause brought significant political reforms to the colony, improving labor conditions in sectors like mining, farming, and production. The diverse origins of participants in both the Eureka rebellion and the Burke and Wills journey reflected broader immigration trends during the latter 1800s.

input: In December 1994, after being tipped off by his former FBI handler about a pending indictment under the Racketeer Influenced and Corrupt Organizations Act, Bulger fled Boston and went into hiding. For 16 years, he remained at large. For 12 of those years, Bulger was prominently listed on the FBI Ten Most Wanted Fugitives list. Beginning in 1997, the New England media exposed criminal actions by federal, state, and local law enforcement officials tied to Bulger. The revelation caused great embarrassment to the FBI. In 2002, Special Agent John J Connolly was convicted of federal racketeering charges for helping Bulger avoid arrest. In 2008, Special Agent Connolly completed his term on the federal charges and was transferred to Florida where he was convicted of helping plan the murder of John B Callahan, a Bulger rival. In 2014, that conviction was overturned on a technicality. Connolly was the agent leading the investigation of Bulger.
rewrite: In December 1994, upon learning from his former FBI contact of an imminent RICO indictment, James Bulger escaped Boston and disappeared. He evaded capture for sixteen years. For over a decade of that period, he was a mainstay on the FBI’s Ten Most Wanted list. Starting in 1997, New England news outlets began uncovering crimes committed by various law enforcement officers connected to Bulger, disclosures that severely humiliated the FBI. John J. Connolly, the FBI agent who had headed the Bulger probe, was found guilty in 2002 of federal racketeering for aiding Bulger’s flight. After finishing that federal sentence in 2008, he was moved to Florida and convicted for his role in plotting the killing of a rival, John B. Callahan. That 2008 murder conviction was later reversed in 2014 due to a legal technicality.

input: Ecuador was the site of many indigenous cultures, and civilizations of different proportions. An early sedentary culture, known as the Valdivia culture, developed in the coastal region, while the Caras and the Quitus unified to form an elaborate civilization that ended at the birth of the Capital Quito. The Cañaris near Cuenca were the most advanced, and most feared by the Inca, due to their fierce resistance to the Incan expansion. Their architecture remains were later destroyed by Spaniards and the Incas.
rewrite: Ecuador hosted numerous indigenous groups and varied civilizations. Among the earliest settled communities was the Valdivia culture along the coast. Later, the Caras and Quitus merged, creating a sophisticated society centered on Quito. The most formidable group was the Cañaris near Cuenca, who fiercely opposed Inca conquest, earning deep respect from their adversaries. Unfortunately, the architectural remnants of these cultures were ultimately demolished by both Inca and Spanish forces.

input: Only the Theravada school does not include the Mahayana scriptures in its canon. As the modern Theravada school is descended from a branch of Buddhism that diverged and established itself in Sri Lanka prior to the emergence of the Mahayana texts, debate exists as to whether the Theravada were historically included in the hinayana designation; in the modern era, this label is seen as derogatory, and is generally avoided.
rewrite: The Theravada tradition excludes Mahayana texts from its accepted scriptures. This branch of Buddhism separated and took root in Sri Lanka before those texts appeared. Consequently, scholars discuss if Theravada was originally classified as hinayana, a term now considered pejorative and seldom used today.

input: In 2006, Jian Li, a Chinese undergraduate at Yale University, filed a civil rights complaint with the Office for Civil Rights against Princeton University, claiming that his race played a role in their decision to reject his application for admission and seeking the suspension of federal financial assistance to the university until it "discontinues discrimination against Asian Americans in all forms" by eliminating race and legacy preferences. Princeton Dean of Admissions Janet Rapelye responded to the claims in the November 30, 2006, issue of the Daily Princetonian by stating that "the numbers don't indicate [discrimination]." She said that Li was not admitted because "many others had far better qualifications." Li's extracurricular activities were described as "not all that outstanding". Li countered in an email, saying that his placement on the waitlist undermines Rapelye's claim. "Princeton had initially waitlisted my application," Li said. "So if it were not for a yield which was higher than expected, the admissions office very well may have admitted a candidate whose "outside activities were not all that outstanding".
rewrite: In 2006, Yale University student Jian Li, who is of Chinese descent, submitted a formal complaint to the Office for Civil Rights. He alleged that Princeton University denied his admission application due to his racial background. Li requested that federal funding for Princeton be halted until the institution ended what he described as discriminatory practices against Asian Americans by removing considerations of race and legacy status from its admissions process. Janet Rapelye, Princeton's Dean of Admissions, addressed the allegations in a late November 2006 article in the Daily Princetonian. She asserted that statistical evidence did not support the discrimination charge, explaining that Li was rejected because numerous other applicants possessed significantly stronger credentials, and his extracurricular involvement was deemed unexceptional. Li responded via email, arguing that his placement on the waitlist contradicted Rapelye's statement. He noted that Princeton had initially waitlisted him, suggesting that had the acceptance yield been lower, the admissions office might have offered him a spot despite the perceived ordinariness of his activities outside academics.

input: The Monreale mosaics constitute the largest decoration of this kind in Italy, covering 0,75 hectares with at least 100 million glass and stone tesserae. This huge work was executed between 1176 and 1186 by the order of King William II of Sicily. The iconography of the mosaics in the presbytery is similar to Cefalu while the pictures in the nave are almost the same as the narrative scenes in the Cappella Palatina. The Martorana mosaic of Roger II blessed by Christ was repeated with the figure of King William II instead of his predecessor. Another panel shows the king offering the model of the cathedral to the Theotokos.
rewrite: The mosaics at Monreale form Italy's most extensive collection of this art form, spanning approximately 0.75 hectares and incorporating over one hundred million individual glass and stone pieces. Created from 1176 to 1186 under the directive of Sicily's King William II, their imagery varies by location. The presbytery scenes resemble those in Cefalù, whereas the nave illustrations closely mirror the story sequences found in the Palatine Chapel. One artwork substitutes William II for Roger II in a depiction of a ruler receiving Christ's blessing, while another presents the king giving a model of the church to the Virgin Mary.

input: Following the 2013 emergencies, the Minister of Foreign Affairs Tony de Brum was encouraged by the Obama administration in the United States to turn the crises into an opportunity to promote action against climate change. De Brum demanded new commitment and international leadership to stave off further climate disasters from battering his country and other similarly vulnerable countries. In September 2013, the Marshall Islands hosted the 44th Pacific Islands Forum summit. De Brum proposed a Majuro Declaration for Climate Leadership to galvanize concrete action on climate change.
rewrite: After facing multiple crises in 2013, Marshall Islands Foreign Minister Tony de Brum was urged by U.S. President Obama's administration to leverage these events to advance global climate initiatives. De Brum called for renewed dedication and worldwide guidance to protect his nation and other at-risk states from future environmental catastrophes. During the Pacific Islands Forum that September, he introduced the Majuro Declaration for Climate Leadership, aiming to spur definitive measures against climate change.

input: Composers of classical music have often made use of folk music (music created by musicians who are commonly not classically trained, often from a purely oral tradition). Some composers, like Dvořák and Smetana, have used folk themes to impart a nationalist flavor to their work, while others like Bartók have used specific themes lifted whole from their folk-music origins.
rewrite: Classical composers frequently incorporate folk music, which is typically passed down orally by non-classically trained musicians. Figures such as Dvořák and Smetana employed folk themes to evoke national identity, whereas composers like Bartók directly borrowed authentic folk melodies in their original form.

input: Ronald Inden writes that by the 8th century CE symbols of Hindu gods "replaced the Buddha at the imperial centre and pinnacle of the cosmo-political system, the image or symbol of the Hindu god comes to be housed in a monumental temple and given increasingly elaborate imperial-style puja worship". Although Buddhism did not disappear from India for several centuries after the eighth, royal proclivities for the cults of Vishnu and Shiva weakened Buddhism's position within the sociopolitical context and helped make possible its decline.
rewrite: According to Ronald Inden, around the 8th century, representations of Hindu deities supplanted the Buddha at the heart of the empire and its cosmic order. These icons were enshrined in grand temples and honored with elaborate, royal ceremonies. While Buddhism persisted in India for many more centuries, the growing royal preference for Vishnu and Shiva worship eroded its sociopolitical standing, contributing to its eventual downturn.

input: In fledgling democracies funding can also be provided by foreign aid. International donors provide financing to political parties in developing countries as a means to promote democracy and good governance. Support can be purely financial or otherwise. Frequently it is provided as capacity development activities including the development of party manifestos, party constitutions and campaigning skills. Developing links between ideologically linked parties is another common feature of international support for a party. Sometimes this can be perceived as directly supporting the political aims of a political party, such as the support of the US government to the Georgian party behind the Rose Revolution. Other donors work on a more neutral basis, where multiple donors provide grants in countries accessible by all parties for various aims defined by the recipients. There have been calls by leading development think-tanks, such as the Overseas Development Institute, to increase support to political parties as part of developing the capacity to deal with the demands of interest-driven donors to improve governance.
rewrite: In emerging democratic nations, financial assistance from abroad can serve as a vital resource. International contributors often allocate funds to political groups within developing states, aiming to foster democratic principles and sound administration. This aid may take monetary forms or involve other types of backing. Often, it includes initiatives to build capabilities, such as helping craft party platforms, establish internal governing documents, and enhance electioneering techniques. Another typical aspect is fostering connections between parties that share similar ideologies. At times, such assistance may be viewed as overtly endorsing a party’s political objectives, exemplified by U.S. backing for the Georgian party instrumental in the Rose Revolution. Alternatively, many donors operate impartially, offering grants in certain nations that are available to all parties for purposes set by the recipients themselves. Prominent policy research organizations, like the Overseas Development Institute, have advocated for greater support to political parties. They argue that strengthening parties is essential to building resilience against the pressures of donors with specific interests, thereby advancing better governance.

input: Swayambhu is a Buddhist stupa atop a hillock at the northwestern part of the city. This is among the oldest religious sites in Nepal. Although the site is considered Buddhist, it is revered by both Buddhists and Hindus. The stupa consists of a dome at the base; above the dome, there is a cubic structure with the eyes of Buddha looking in all four directions.[clarification needed] There are pentagonal Toran above each of the four sides, with statues engraved on them. Behind and above the torana there are thirteen tiers. Above all the tiers, there is a small space above which lies a gajur.
rewrite: Perched on a hill in the city's northwest, Swayambhu is an ancient Buddhist stupa and one of Nepal's most venerable shrines. It holds deep significance for both Buddhists and Hindus. The structure features a foundational dome, topped by a cube adorned with Buddha's all-seeing eyes on each side. Above every side, carved statues decorate pentagonal toranas. Rising behind these are thirteen stepped tiers, culminating in a pinnacle known as a gajur.

input: In 1887, the British Empire celebrated Victoria's Golden Jubilee. Victoria marked the fiftieth anniversary of her accession on 20 June with a banquet to which 50 kings and princes were invited. The following day, she participated in a procession and attended a thanksgiving service in Westminster Abbey. By this time, Victoria was once again extremely popular. Two days later on 23 June, she engaged two Indian Muslims as waiters, one of whom was Abdul Karim. He was soon promoted to "Munshi": teaching her Hindustani, and acting as a clerk. Her family and retainers were appalled, and accused Abdul Karim of spying for the Muslim Patriotic League, and biasing the Queen against the Hindus. Equerry Frederick Ponsonby (the son of Sir Henry) discovered that the Munshi had lied about his parentage, and reported to Lord Elgin, Viceroy of India, "the Munshi occupies very much the same position as John Brown used to do." Victoria dismissed their complaints as racial prejudice. Abdul Karim remained in her service until he returned to India with a pension on her death.
rewrite: In 1887, the British Empire commemorated Queen Victoria's fifty-year reign with Golden Jubilee festivities. On June 20th, she hosted a grand dinner for fifty royal figures from across Europe. The next day, she rode in a public parade and then attended a special religious ceremony at Westminster Abbey. Victoria had by then regained widespread public affection. Shortly after, on June 23rd, she hired two Indian Muslim attendants. One, Abdul Karim, was quickly elevated to the role of "Munshi." His duties involved instructing the Queen in Hindustani and performing secretarial tasks. This appointment caused dismay among her household and relatives, who suspected Karim of being a spy for a Muslim political group and of turning Victoria against her Hindu subjects. After an investigation, a courtier found the Munshi had been dishonest about his family background and warned the Viceroy of India that his influence mirrored that of a previous favorite. The Queen attributed these objections to bigotry. Abdul Karim continued in her employ until Victoria's passing, when he received a pension and went back to India.

input: Some new immigrants arrived as refugees with no possessions and were housed in temporary camps known as ma'abarot; by 1952, over 200,000 immigrants were living in these tent cities. During this period, food, clothes and furniture had to be rationed in what became known as the Austerity Period. The need to solve the crisis led Ben-Gurion to sign a reparations agreement with West Germany that triggered mass protests by Jews angered at the idea that Israel could accept monetary compensation for the Holocaust.
rewrite: New arrivals often came as refugees with nothing, staying in provisional camps called ma'abarot; these tent settlements held more than 200,000 people by 1952. Essentials like food, clothing, and furnishings were subject to strict rationing, a time called the Austerity Period. To address the emergency, Ben-Gurion agreed to a reparations deal with West Germany. This sparked large-scale protests from Jews who were outraged at accepting financial payments for Holocaust atrocities.

input: Asthma is thought to be caused by a combination of genetic and environmental factors. Environmental factors include exposure to air pollution and allergens. Other potential triggers include medications such as aspirin and beta blockers. Diagnosis is usually based on the pattern of symptoms, response to therapy over time, and spirometry. Asthma is classified according to the frequency of symptoms, forced expiratory volume in one second (FEV1), and peak expiratory flow rate. It may also be classified as atopic or non-atopic where atopy refers to a predisposition toward developing a type 1 hypersensitivity reaction.
rewrite: Asthma arises from an interplay of inherited traits and external influences like pollutants or allergens. Certain drugs, including aspirin and beta blockers, can also induce symptoms. Diagnosis typically relies on observing symptom patterns, gauging response to treatment, and conducting spirometry tests. The condition is categorized based on how often symptoms occur, along with measurements of FEV1 and peak expiratory flow. Additionally, it can be designated as atopic or non-atopic, with atopy indicating a tendency for allergic hypersensitivity reactions.

input: There are 17 universities of technology in Germany with about 290,000 students enrolled. The four states of Bremen, Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, Saxony-Anhalt and Schleswig-Holstein are not operating a Technische Universität. Saxony and Lower Saxony have the highest counts of TUs, while in Saxony three out of four universities are universities of technology.
rewrite: Germany hosts 17 technical universities, enrolling approximately 290,000 students. The states of Bremen, Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, Saxony-Anhalt, and Schleswig-Holstein lack such institutions. Saxony and Lower Saxony contain the most, with three of Saxony's four universities being technical.

input: At the end of 2004, May and Taylor announced that they would reunite and return to touring in 2005 with Paul Rodgers (founder and former lead singer of Free and Bad Company). Brian May's website also stated that Rodgers would be "featured with" Queen as "Queen + Paul Rodgers", not replacing Mercury. The retired John Deacon would not be participating. In November 2004, Queen were among the inaugural inductees into the UK Music Hall of Fame, and the award ceremony was the first event at which Rodgers joined May and Taylor as vocalist.
rewrite: In late 2004, Brian May and Roger Taylor declared plans to revive Queen for concerts in 2005, joined by vocalist Paul Rodgers. Officially billed as "Queen + Paul Rodgers," the collaboration explicitly noted Rodgers was appearing alongside the band, not as a substitute for Freddie Mercury. Bassist John Deacon, having retired, chose not to be involved. That November, Queen was inducted into the new UK Music Hall of Fame, with Rodgers performing live with May and Taylor for the first time at the ceremony.

input: South West Africa became known as Namibia by the UN when the General Assembly changed the territory's name by Resolution 2372 (XXII) of 12 June 1968. In 1978 the UN Security Council passed UN Resolution 435 which planned a transition toward independence for Namibia. Attempts to persuade South Africa to agree to the plan's implementation were not successful until 1988 when the transition to independence finally started under a diplomatic agreement between South Africa, Angola and Cuba, with the USSR and the USA as observers, under which South Africa agreed to withdraw and demobilise its forces in Namibia. As a result, Cuba agreed to pull back its troops in southern Angola sent to support the MPLA in its war for control of Angola with UNITA.
rewrite: The United Nations General Assembly officially designated South West Africa as Namibia in June 1968. A decade later, the UN Security Council established a framework for Namibian independence through Resolution 435. However, South Africa resisted enacting this plan for years. A breakthrough occurred in 1988, when a tripartite accord involving South Africa, Angola, and Cuba—monitored by the United States and the Soviet Union—initiated the independence process. This agreement mandated South Africa's military withdrawal from Namibia. In a corresponding move, Cuba consented to redeploy its forces, which had been stationed in southern Angola to aid the MPLA government in its conflict with UNITA rebels.

input: Von Neumann worked on lattice theory between 1937 and 1939. Von Neumann provided an abstract exploration of dimension in completed complemented modular topological lattices: "Dimension is determined, up to a positive linear transformation, by the following two properties. It is conserved by perspective mappings ("perspectivities") and ordered by inclusion. The deepest part of the proof concerns the equivalence of perspectivity with "projectivity by decomposition"—of which a corollary is the transitivity of perspectivity." Garrett Birkhoff writes: "John von Neumann's brilliant mind blazed over lattice theory like a meteor".
rewrite: Between 1937 and 1939, John von Neumann conducted research in lattice theory. He offered an abstract analysis of dimension within a specific class of complete modular topological lattices, showing it is defined, except for a linear scaling factor, by being preserved under perspectivities and ordered by set inclusion. A key proof establishes that perspectivity equals projectivity through decomposition, implying perspectivity is transitive. Garrett Birkhoff likened von Neumann's impactful, brief work in the field to a meteor streaking across the sky.

input: From early in its development, ASCII was intended to be just one of several national variants of an international character code standard, ultimately published as ISO/IEC 646 (1972), which would share most characters in common but assign other locally useful characters to several code points reserved for "national use." However, the four years that elapsed between the publication of ASCII-1963 and ISO's first acceptance of an international recommendation during 1967 caused ASCII's choices for the national use characters to seem to be de facto standards for the world, causing confusion and incompatibility once other countries did begin to make their own assignments to these code points.
rewrite: Originally designed as a national version of a broader international standard (later ISO/IEC 646), ASCII was meant to use common core characters while allowing local adaptations in specific reserved slots. Yet, the significant delay between ASCII's 1963 release and the international standard's adoption around 1967 led ASCII's specific national character assignments to become widely entrenched. This unintended global adoption created significant confusion and technical conflicts when other nations later began implementing their own unique characters in those same reserved code positions.

input: A striking technical innovation of the Komnenian period was the production of very precious, miniature mosaic icons. In these icons the small tesserae (with sides of 1 mm or less) were set on wax or resin on a wooden panel. These products of extraordinary craftmanship were intended for private devotion. The Louvre Transfiguration is a very fine example from the late 12th century. The miniature mosaic of Christ in the Museo Nazionale at Florence illustrates the more gentle, humanistic conception of Christ which appeared in the 12th century.
rewrite: During the Komnenian era, a notable artistic advancement involved crafting highly valuable, small-scale mosaic icons. These works featured minute tesserae, often measuring one millimeter or smaller, embedded in wax or resin on wooden boards. Such exceptional artifacts were created for personal worship. An excellent late-12th century specimen is the Transfiguration at the Louvre. Meanwhile, a miniature mosaic of Christ in Florence's Museo Nazionale reflects the softer, more human-focused depiction that emerged during this period.

input: Modern Orthodoxy, as a stream of Orthodox Judaism represented by institutions such as the U.S. National Council for Young Israel, is pro-Zionist and thus places a high national, as well as religious, significance on the State of Israel, and its affiliates are, typically, Zionist in orientation. It also practices involvement with non-Orthodox Jews that extends beyond "outreach (Kiruv)" to continued institutional relations and cooperation; see further under Torah Umadda. Other "core beliefs" are a recognition of the value and importance of secular studies, a commitment to equality of education for both men and women, and a full acceptance of the importance of being able to financially support oneself and one's family.
rewrite: Modern Orthodoxy, a branch of Orthodox Judaism exemplified by groups like the National Council for Young Israel in the United States, strongly supports Zionism. It attributes profound national and religious meaning to Israel, with its members generally embracing Zionist ideals. This movement also maintains ongoing engagement and collaborative ties with Jews outside its own Orthodox community, moving beyond mere outreach efforts. Additional fundamental principles include appreciating secular knowledge, advocating for equal educational opportunities for males and females, and affirming the necessity of achieving economic self-sufficiency for individuals and their households.

input: Strasbourg is situated on the eastern border of France with Germany. This border is formed by the River Rhine, which also forms the eastern border of the modern city, facing across the river to the German town Kehl. The historic core of Strasbourg however lies on the Grande Île in the River Ill, which here flows parallel to, and roughly 4 kilometres (2.5 mi) from, the Rhine. The natural courses of the two rivers eventually join some distance downstream of Strasbourg, although several artificial waterways now connect them within the city.
rewrite: Strasbourg lies at France's eastern frontier with Germany, demarcated by the Rhine River. This waterway also serves as the city's modern eastern boundary, directly opposite the German municipality of Kehl. The old town is centered on the Grande Île, an island within the Ill River. The Ill runs parallel to the Rhine, approximately four kilometers away, before their natural channels merge farther downstream. Today, they are also linked by constructed canals inside the city.

input: As Universal's main product had always been low-budget film, it was one of the last major studios to have a contract with Technicolor. The studio did not make use of the three-strip Technicolor process until Arabian Nights (1942), starring Jon Hall and Maria Montez. The following year, Technicolor was also used in Universal's remake of their 1925 horror melodrama, Phantom of the Opera with Claude Rains and Nelson Eddy. With the success of their first two pictures, a regular schedule of high-budget, Technicolor films followed.
rewrite: Universal primarily produced inexpensive films, making it among the final large studios to adopt Technicolor. The studio first employed the three-strip method for 1942's *Arabian Nights*, featuring Jon Hall and Maria Montez. In 1943, their *Phantom of the Opera* remake, starring Claude Rains and Nelson Eddy, also used the process. Encouraged by these two films' positive results, Universal began consistently releasing costly, color features.

input: Digimon started out as digital pets called "Digital Monsters", similar in style and concept to the Tamagotchi. It was planned by WiZ and released by Bandai on June 26, 1997. The toy began as the simple concept of a Tamagotchi mainly for boys. The V-Pet is similar to its predecessors, with the exceptions of being more difficult and being able to fight other Digimon v-pets. Every owner would start with a Baby Digimon, train it, evolve it, take care of it, and then have battles with other Digimon owners to see who was stronger. The Digimon pet had several evolution capabilities and abilities too, so many owners had different Digimon. In December, the second generation of Digital Monster was released, followed by a third edition in 1998.
rewrite: Originally conceived as a digital companion toy aimed primarily at boys, the Digital Monster line launched on June 26, 1997. Developed by WiZ and brought to market by Bandai, these virtual pets expanded on the Tamagotchi model by introducing greater complexity and combat features. Users would raise a creature from its infant stage, nurturing and training it to evolve. A key innovation was the ability to link devices for battles against other owners' creatures. With multiple possible evolutionary paths, each pet could develop uniquely. The product line saw rapid iteration, with a second version released that same December and a third following in 1998.

input: The element was probably named by the alchemist Paracelsus after the German word Zinke (prong, tooth). German chemist Andreas Sigismund Marggraf is credited with discovering pure metallic zinc in 1746. Work by Luigi Galvani and Alessandro Volta uncovered the electrochemical properties of zinc by 1800. Corrosion-resistant zinc plating of iron (hot-dip galvanizing) is the major application for zinc. Other applications are in batteries, small non-structural castings, and alloys, such as brass. A variety of zinc compounds are commonly used, such as zinc carbonate and zinc gluconate (as dietary supplements), zinc chloride (in deodorants), zinc pyrithione (anti-dandruff shampoos), zinc sulfide (in luminescent paints), and zinc methyl or zinc diethyl in the organic laboratory.
rewrite: The name likely originates from the alchemist Paracelsus, who derived it from the German term "Zinke," meaning prong or tooth. Pure zinc metal was first isolated in 1746 by the German chemist Andreas Sigismund Marggraf. By 1800, researchers Luigi Galvani and Alessandro Volta had revealed its electrochemical nature. The primary use of zinc is in galvanizing iron to prevent rust. It also appears in batteries, minor castings, and alloys like brass. Common zinc compounds serve various purposes: dietary supplements (e.g., zinc carbonate), deodorants (zinc chloride), anti-dandruff shampoos (zinc pyrithione), luminescent paints (zinc sulfide), and organic chemistry reagents (zinc methyl or diethyl).

input: During the 1920s and 1930s, British civil servants and politicians, looking back at the performance of the state during World War I, concluded that there was a need for greater co-ordination between the three Services that made up the armed forces of the United Kingdom—the British Army, the Royal Navy, and the Royal Air Force. The formation of a united ministry of defence was rejected by David Lloyd George's coalition government in 1921; but the Chiefs of Staff Committee was formed in 1923, for the purposes of inter-Service co-ordination. As rearmament became a concern during the 1930s, Stanley Baldwin created the position of Minister for Coordination of Defence. Lord Chatfield held the post until the fall of Neville Chamberlain's government in 1940; his success was limited by his lack of control over the existing Service departments and his limited political influence.
rewrite: In the interwar period, reflecting on the state's role in the First World War, British officials and statesmen determined that improved collaboration was essential among the UK's military branches: the Army, Navy, and Air Force. Although a single defence ministry was dismissed by the coalition government under David Lloyd George in 1921, the Chiefs of Staff Committee was established two years later to foster joint planning. With the growing urgency of rearmament in the 1930s, Prime Minister Stanley Baldwin instituted the role of Minister for Coordination of Defence. Occupied by Lord Chatfield until 1940, this office achieved little, hampered by its minimal authority over the separate service ministries and its weak standing in political circles.

input: Under contract from the U.S. Military, Matrox produced a combination computer/LaserDisc player for instructional purposes. The computer was a 286, the LaserDisc player only capable of reading the analog audio tracks. Together they weighed 43 lb (20 kg) and sturdy handles were provided in case two people were required to lift the unit. The computer controlled the player via a 25-pin serial port at the back of the player and a ribbon cable connected to a proprietary port on the motherboard. Many of these were sold as surplus by the military during the 1990s, often without the controller software. Nevertheless, it is possible to control the unit by removing the ribbon cable and connecting a serial cable directly from the computer's serial port to the port on the LaserDisc player.
rewrite: Commissioned by the U.S. Military, Matrox developed an integrated computer and LaserDisc system for training. The device housed a 286 processor and a disc player that could only access analog audio. The entire assembly was quite heavy at 43 pounds (20 kilograms), and it included robust handles to facilitate lifting by two individuals. A 25-pin serial interface on the rear of the player linked to the computer, using a ribbon cable attached to a special motherboard connector. In the 1990s, the military frequently sold these units as surplus, typically missing the original control program. However, operation is still achievable by disconnecting the ribbon cable and linking a standard serial cable from a computer directly to the player's serial port.

input: In the United Kingdom, a bill is presented for royal assent after it has passed all the required stages in both the House of Commons and the House of Lords. Under the Parliament Acts 1911 and 1949, the House of Commons may, under certain circumstances, direct that a bill be presented for assent despite lack of passage by the House of Lords. Officially, assent is granted by the sovereign or by Lords Commissioners authorised to act by letters patent. It may be granted in parliament or outside parliament; in the latter case, each house must be separately notified before the bill takes effect.
rewrite: In the UK, proposed legislation is submitted for royal approval following its successful progression through the House of Commons and the House of Lords. According to the Parliament Acts of 1911 and 1949, the Commons can sometimes bypass the Lords' approval and send a bill directly for assent. The monarch, or appointed Lords Commissioners acting on their behalf, formally provides this consent. Approval can be given within or outside of Parliament; if done externally, both legislative chambers must be informed individually before the law is enacted.

input: In the late eighteenth- and early nineteenth-century Germany, three pioneer physical educators – Johann Friedrich GutsMuths (1759–1839) and Friedrich Ludwig Jahn (1778–1852) – created exercises for boys and young men on apparatus they had designed that ultimately led to what is considered modern gymnastics. Don Francisco Amorós y Ondeano, was born on February 19, 1770 in Valence and died on August 8, 1848 in Paris. He was a Spanish colonel, and the first person to introduce educative gymnastic in France. Jahn promoted the use of parallel bars, rings and high bar in international competition.
rewrite: During the late 1700s and early 1800s in Germany, two early innovators in physical training, Johann Friedrich GutsMuths and Friedrich Ludwig Jahn, developed apparatus-based workouts for youth. Their apparatus designs formed the foundation for contemporary gymnastics. Separately, the Spanish colonel Don Francisco Amorós y Ondeano (1770–1848) pioneered instructional gymnastics in France. Jahn was particularly instrumental in establishing parallel bars, rings, and the high bar as standard fixtures in global competitions.

input: As the President, Tito had access to extensive (state-owned) property associated with the office, and maintained a lavish lifestyle. In Belgrade he resided in the official residence, the Beli dvor, and maintained a separate private home. The Brijuni islands were the site of the State Summer Residence from 1949 on. The pavilion was designed by Jože Plečnik, and included a zoo. Close to 100 foreign heads of state were to visit Tito at the island residence, along with film stars such as Elizabeth Taylor, Richard Burton, Sophia Loren, Carlo Ponti, and Gina Lollobrigida.
rewrite: During his presidency, Tito enjoyed the use of considerable government assets linked to his position, enabling an opulent way of life. His official Belgrade home was the Beli dvor, and he also possessed a personal residence. The official summer retreat, established on the Brijuni islands in 1949, featured a pavilion by architect Jože Plečnik and even a small zoo. This island compound hosted nearly a hundred visiting national leaders, as well as celebrities from the film industry including Elizabeth Taylor and Sophia Loren.

input: The tradition holds that Virgil was born in the village of Andes, near Mantua in Cisalpine Gaul. Analysis of his name has led to beliefs that he descended from earlier Roman colonists. Modern speculation ultimately is not supported by narrative evidence either from his own writings or his later biographers. Macrobius says that Virgil's father was of a humble background; however, scholars generally believe that Virgil was from an equestrian landowning family which could afford to give him an education. He attended schools in Cremona, Mediolanum, Rome and Naples. After considering briefly a career in rhetoric and law, the young Virgil turned his talents to poetry.
rewrite: According to custom, the poet Virgil first saw the world in Andes, a small settlement close to Mantua within Cisalpine Gaul. Interpretations of his family name suggest ancestry tied to early Roman settlers. Contemporary theories about his origins, however, lack direct confirmation from his poetry or ancient biographies. While Macrobius describes Virgil's father as a man of modest means, most experts conclude the poet belonged to a prosperous landowning class that provided him with formal schooling. He studied in Cremona, Mediolanum, Rome, and Naples. Initially drawn to oratory and legal studies, Virgil soon devoted himself entirely to verse.

input: Longstanding political tensions from the 27 year rule of William Tubman resulted in a military coup in 1980 that overthrew the leadership soon after his death, marking the beginning of political instability. Five years of military rule by the People's Redemption Council and five years of civilian rule by the National Democratic Party of Liberia were followed by the First and Second Liberian Civil Wars. These resulted in the deaths and displacement of more than half a million people and devastated Liberia's economy. A peace agreement in 2003 led to democratic elections in 2005. Recovery proceeds but about 85% of the population live below the international poverty line.
rewrite: Following William Tubman's 27-year presidency, unresolved conflicts led to a 1980 military takeover shortly after his passing, initiating a period of unrest. This included five years under a military council and another five under a civilian government, preceding two devastating civil wars. The conflicts killed and displaced over 500,000 individuals, crippling the nation's economy. A 2003 peace deal enabled elections two years later. While rebuilding continues, approximately 85% of Liberians remain in extreme poverty.

input: The production for sulfidic zinc ores produces large amounts of sulfur dioxide and cadmium vapor. Smelter slag and other residues of process also contain significant amounts of heavy metals. About 1.1 million tonnes of metallic zinc and 130 thousand tonnes of lead were mined and smelted in the Belgian towns of La Calamine and Plombières between 1806 and 1882. The dumps of the past mining operations leach significant amounts of zinc and cadmium, and, as a result, the sediments of the Geul River contain significant amounts of heavy metals. About two thousand years ago emissions of zinc from mining and smelting totaled 10 thousand tonnes a year. After increasing 10-fold from 1850, zinc emissions peaked at 3.4 million tonnes per year in the 1980s and declined to 2.7 million tonnes in the 1990s, although a 2005 study of the Arctic troposphere found that the concentrations there did not reflect the decline. Anthropogenic and natural emissions occur at a ratio of 20 to 1.
rewrite: Processing zinc sulfide ores releases substantial quantities of sulfur dioxide and cadmium vapors. Smelting waste, including slag, retains high concentrations of toxic heavy metals. From 1806 to 1882, mining and smelting operations in the Belgian localities of La Calamine and Plombières yielded roughly 1.1 million tons of zinc and 130,000 tons of lead. Historical mining waste piles continue to release zinc and cadmium through leaching, leading to elevated levels of these metals in the sediments of the Geul River. Two millennia ago, annual zinc releases from these activities reached approximately 10,000 tons. Following a tenfold rise after 1850, emissions crested at 3.4 million tons per year in the 1980s before falling to 2.7 million tons in the 1990s. However, a 2005 analysis of the Arctic atmosphere showed that pollutant levels there did not match this decrease. Human-caused emissions now exceed natural sources by a factor of twenty to one.

input: The first written account of a game played was on October 15, 1862, on the Montreal Cricket Grounds. It was between the First Battalion Grenadier Guards and the Second Battalion Scots Fusilier Guards resulting in a win by the Grenadier Guards 3 goals, 2 rouges to nothing.[citation needed] In 1864, at Trinity College, Toronto, F. Barlow Cumberland, Frederick A. Bethune, and Christopher Gwynn, one of the founders of Milton, Massachusetts, devised rules based on rugby football. The game gradually gained a following, with the Hamilton Football Club formed on November 3, 1869, (the oldest football club in Canada). Montreal formed a team April 8, 1872, Toronto was formed on October 4, 1873, and the Ottawa FBC on September 20, 1876.
rewrite: The earliest recorded match occurred on October 15, 1862, at the Montreal Cricket Grounds. The First Battalion Grenadier Guards defeated the Second Battalion Scots Fusilier Guards with a score of three goals and two rouges to zero. Subsequently, in 1864, F. Barlow Cumberland, Frederick A. Bethune, and Christopher Gwynn, a co-founder of Milton, Massachusetts, established a formal set of regulations at Trinity College in Toronto, drawing from rugby. The sport's popularity slowly grew, leading to the creation of the Hamilton Football Club on November 3, 1869, which is recognized as Canada's oldest such club. Teams in Montreal, Toronto, and Ottawa were established in April 1872, October 1873, and September 1876, respectively.

input: In 1982, Regis McKenna was brought in to shape the marketing and launch of the Macintosh. Later the Regis McKenna team grew to include Jane Anderson, Katie Cadigan and Andy Cunningham, who eventually led the Apple account for the agency. Cunningham and Anderson were the primary authors of the Macintosh launch plan. The launch of the Macintosh pioneered many different tactics that are used today in launching technology products, including the "multiple exclusive," event marketing (credited to John Sculley, who brought the concept over from Pepsi), creating a mystique around a product and giving an inside look into a product's creation.
rewrite: In 1982, Regis McKenna was enlisted to oversee the Macintosh's marketing and introduction. His team later expanded to incorporate Jane Anderson, Katie Cadigan, and Andy Cunningham, with Cunningham ultimately managing the Apple business for the firm. Anderson and Cunningham played the lead roles in drafting the launch strategy. The Macintosh introduction innovated numerous approaches now standard in tech product releases, such as the "multiple exclusive," event-based promotions (an idea attributed to John Sculley, who adapted it from Pepsi), fostering an aura of intrigue around an item, and offering a behind-the-scenes view of its development.

input: As of 2012, renewable energy plays a major role in the energy mix of many countries globally. Renewables are becoming increasingly economic in both developing and developed countries. Prices for renewable energy technologies, primarily wind power and solar power, continued to drop, making renewables competitive with conventional energy sources. Without a level playing field, however, high market penetration of renewables is still dependent on a robust promotional policies. Fossil fuel subsidies, which are far higher than those for renewable energy, remain in place and quickly need to be phased out.
rewrite: By 2012, clean energy sources had become a significant component of national power supplies worldwide. These alternatives are growing more cost-effective across all economies. The costs for key technologies, especially wind and solar, have consistently fallen, allowing them to rival traditional power generation. Yet, achieving widespread adoption still requires strong supportive regulations, as the market is not yet balanced. Current subsidies heavily favor fossil fuels over renewables and must be rapidly eliminated.

input: The region, as part of Lorraine, was part of the Holy Roman Empire, and then was gradually annexed by France in the 17th century, and formalized as one of the provinces of France. The Calvinist manufacturing republic of Mulhouse, known as Stadtrepublik Mülhausen, became a part of Alsace after a vote by its citizens on 4 January 1798. Alsace is frequently mentioned with and as part of Lorraine and the former duchy of Lorraine, since it was a vital part of the duchy, and later because German possession as the imperial province (Alsace-Lorraine, 1871–1918) was contested in the 19th and 20th centuries; France and Germany exchanged control of parts of Lorraine (including Alsace) four times in 75 years.
rewrite: Historically within Lorraine, this area belonged to the Holy Roman Empire before being progressively incorporated into France during the 1600s, eventually becoming a formal French province. Mulhouse, a Calvinist industrial city-state called Stadtrepublik Mülhausen, joined Alsace following a public referendum in early 1798. The name Alsace is often linked to Lorraine, both due to its central role in the old Duchy of Lorraine and because of the later, disputed German administration of the combined imperial territory from 1871 to 1918. This conflict led France and Germany to swap sovereignty over these lands, including Alsace, on four occasions within a 75-year period during the 19th and 20th centuries.

input: Armenians have had a presence in the Armenian Highland for over four thousand years, since the time when Hayk, the legendary patriarch and founder of the first Armenian nation, led them to victory over Bel of Babylon. Today, with a population of 3.5 million, they not only constitute an overwhelming majority in Armenia, but also in the disputed region of Nagorno-Karabakh. Armenians in the diaspora informally refer to them as Hayastantsis (Հայաստանցի), meaning those that are from Armenia (that is, those born and raised in Armenia). They, as well as the Armenians of Iran and Russia speak the Eastern dialect of the Armenian language. The country itself is secular as a result of Soviet domination, but most of its citizens identify themselves as Apostolic Armenian Christian.
rewrite: For more than four millennia, Armenians have inhabited the Armenian Highland, tracing their origins to the mythical figure Hayk, who established the initial Armenian state by defeating the Babylonian ruler Bel. Presently, numbering around 3.5 million, they form the vast majority not just within Armenia, but also in the contested area of Nagorno-Karabakh. Those residing outside the homeland often call Armenians from the republic Hayastantsis, indicating they originate from Armenia proper. These individuals, along with Armenian communities in Iran and Russia, primarily use the Eastern Armenian dialect. While the nation is officially secular due to its Soviet history, the predominant religious identity among its people remains Apostolic Armenian Christianity.

input: According to a National Geographic article, the novel is so revered in Monroeville that people quote lines from it like Scripture; yet Harper Lee herself refused to attend any performances, because "she abhors anything that trades on the book's fame". To underscore this sentiment, Lee demanded that a book of recipes named Calpurnia's Cookbook not be published and sold out of the Monroe County Heritage Museum. David Lister in The Independent states that Lee's refusal to speak to reporters made them desire to interview her all the more, and her silence "makes Bob Dylan look like a media tart". Despite her discouragement, a rising number of tourists made to Monroeville a destination, hoping to see Lee's inspiration for the book, or Lee herself. Local residents call them "Mockingbird groupies", and although Lee was not reclusive, she refused publicity and interviews with an emphatic "Hell, no!"
rewrite: A piece from National Geographic notes that in Monroeville, the book is held in such high regard that passages are recited almost as if from a sacred text. However, the author consistently avoided all adaptations, disliking any exploitation of the novel's reputation. This stance was clear when she blocked the release of a cookbook titled after the character Calpurnia from the local museum. As reported by David Lister in The Independent, her persistent avoidance of the press only intensified their eagerness to secure a conversation, with her quiet demeanor highlighting a level of media shyness that surpasses even famously reticent figures. This allure, despite her clear disinterest, draws increasing visitors to the town seeking connections to the story or a glimpse of the writer. Locals refer to these enthusiasts with a playful label, and while Lee engaged with her community, she met any request for public attention with an absolute and famously blunt refusal.

input: The Hanoverian king George II of Great Britain was passionately devoted to his family’s continental holdings, but his commitments in Germany were counterbalanced by the demands of the British colonies overseas. If war against France for colonial expansion was to be resumed, then Hanover had to be secured against Franco-Prussian attack. France was very much interested in colonial expansion and was willing to exploit the vulnerability of Hanover in war against Great Britain, but it had no desire to divert forces to central Europe for Prussia's interest.
rewrite: King George II of Great Britain, a Hanoverian, deeply prioritized his German territories. However, these European concerns were offset by the needs of the growing British empire abroad. To restart colonial conflicts with France, protecting Hanover from a joint French and Prussian assault was essential. France, equally eager for overseas empire, aimed to leverage Hanover's exposure against Britain. Yet, it refused to deploy troops into central Europe merely to aid Prussian ambitions.

input: Meanwhile, with the advent and popularity of Internet-based distribution of files in lossily-compressed audio formats such as MP3, sales of CDs began to decline in the 2000s. For example, between 2000 - 2008, despite overall growth in music sales and one anomalous year of increase, major-label CD sales declined overall by 20%, although independent and DIY music sales may be tracking better according to figures released 30 March 2009, and CDs still continue to sell greatly. As of 2012, CDs and DVDs made up only 34 percent of music sales in the United States. In Japan, however, over 80 percent of music was bought on CDs and other physical formats as of 2015.
rewrite: The rise of online file sharing and lossy audio formats like MP3 led to a downturn in CD sales starting in the 2000s. For instance, from 2000 to 2008, major-label compact disc revenues fell by 20 percent, even as total music sales grew and independent sectors showed more resilience, according to a 2009 report. Despite this decline, physical discs remained a significant market segment. By 2012, they accounted for just 34% of U.S. music purchases. In contrast, as of 2015, over 80 percent of music sales in Japan were still through CDs and similar tangible media.

input: Following the Norman Conquest in 1066, Southampton became the major port of transit between the then capital of England, Winchester, and Normandy. Southampton Castle was built in the 12th century and by the 13th century Southampton had become a leading port, particularly involved in the import of French wine in exchange for English cloth and wool.
rewrite: After the Normans took control in 1066, Southampton served as the primary harbor connecting Winchester, England's capital at the time, to Normandy. The town's castle was constructed in the 1100s, and within the next century it grew into a key trading hub, notably exchanging English textiles and wool for French wines.

input: Air defence in naval tactics, especially within a carrier group, is often built around a system of concentric layers with the aircraft carrier at the centre. The outer layer will usually be provided by the carrier's aircraft, specifically its AEW&C aircraft combined with the CAP. If an attacker is able to penetrate this layer, then the next layers would come from the surface-to-air missiles carried by the carrier's escorts; the area-defence missiles, such as the RIM-67 Standard, with a range of up to 100 nmi, and the point-defence missiles, like the RIM-162 ESSM, with a range of up to 30 nmi. Finally, virtually every modern warship will be fitted with small-calibre guns, including a CIWS, which is usually a radar-controlled Gatling gun of between 20mm and 30mm calibre capable of firing several thousand rounds per minute.
rewrite: Naval air defense, particularly for an aircraft carrier and its accompanying vessels, is structured in multiple protective rings centered on the carrier itself. The outermost ring typically relies on the carrier's own planes, especially airborne early warning and control aircraft working alongside combat air patrols. Should a threat breach this zone, the next line of defense involves missiles launched from surrounding escort ships. These include long-range area defense missiles, which can engage targets nearly 100 nautical miles away, and shorter-range point defense missiles effective out to about 30 nautical miles. As a final protective measure, nearly all contemporary warships are equipped with rapid-firing, small-caliber automatic guns. These close-in weapon systems often use radar-guided Gatling-style mechanisms to unleash thousands of rounds per minute against incoming threats.

input: Throughout history there have been a series of lingua francas in the area to allow for better communication. The dialects spoken in Hangzhou, Shaoxing, and Ningbo have taken on this role historically. Since the founding of the People's Republic of China in 1949, Mandarin, which is not mutually intelligible with any of the local dialects, has been promoted as the standard language of communication throughout China. As a result, most of the population now can, to some degree, speak and comprehend Mandarin and can code-switch when necessary. A majority of the population educated since 1978 can speak Mandarin. Urban residents tend to be more fluent in Mandarin than rural people. Nevertheless, a Zhejiang accent is detectable in almost everyone from the area communicating in Mandarin, and the home dialect remains an important part of the everyday lives and cultural identities of most Zhejiang residents.
rewrite: The region has historically relied on a succession of common languages to facilitate understanding. Local variants from cities like Hangzhou, Shaoxing, and Ningbo have each served this purpose in the past. Following the establishment of the People's Republic in 1949, the national government actively encouraged the use of Mandarin, a language distinct from the native tongues of the area, as the country's uniform mode of speech. Consequently, a large portion of the populace has acquired at least a basic proficiency in Mandarin and can alternate between it and their local speech as needed. Most people schooled after the late 1970s are able to use Mandarin. Proficiency is generally higher in cities than in the countryside. However, nearly all local speakers retain a recognizable Zhejiang inflection when using Mandarin, and the native dialect continues to play a vital role in daily life and cultural belonging for the majority of the province's inhabitants.

input: The major opponent of Freemasonry was the Roman Catholic Church, so that in countries with a large Catholic element, such as France, Italy, Spain, and Mexico, much of the ferocity of the political battles involve the confrontation between what Davies calls the reactionary Church and enlightened Freemasonry. Even in France, Masons did not act as a group. American historians, while noting that Benjamin Franklin and George Washington were indeed active Masons, have downplayed the importance of Freemasonry in causing the American Revolution because the Masonic order was non-political and included both Patriots and their enemy the Loyalists.
rewrite: The Roman Catholic Church stood as the primary adversary of Freemasonry. Consequently, in nations with substantial Catholic populations, including France, Italy, Spain, and Mexico, political strife was often intensely shaped by this clash between a conservative Church and a progressive Masonic movement. Even in France, Masons did not operate collectively. In the American context, historians acknowledge the Masonic participation of figures like Franklin and Washington but minimize the order's role in the Revolution, citing its apolitical nature and membership among both Patriots and Loyalists.

input: A German ethnicity emerged in the course of the Middle Ages, ultimately as a result of the formation of the kingdom of Germany within East Francia and later the Holy Roman Empire, beginning in the 9th century. The process was gradual and lacked any clear definition, and the use of exonyms designating "the Germans" develops only during the High Middle Ages. The title of rex teutonicum "King of the Germans" is first used in the late 11th century, by the chancery of Pope Gregory VII, to describe the future Holy Roman Emperor of the German Nation Henry IV. Natively, the term ein diutscher ("a German") is used for the people of Germany from the 12th century.
rewrite: The German people gradually formed during the medieval period, a process originating in the 9th century with the establishment of the German kingdom inside East Francia, which evolved into the Holy Roman Empire. This development was slow and without precise boundaries. Names for "the Germans" created by outsiders only became common in the High Middle Ages. The designation "King of the Germans" (rex teutonicum) was first applied in the late 11th century by Pope Gregory VII's office, referring to Henry IV, who would become Holy Roman Emperor. From the 12th century onward, the native phrase "a German" was used for the population.

input: The rise of port cities saw the clustering of populations caused by the development of steamships and railroads. Urbanization increased from 1700 to 1922, with towns and cities growing. Improvements in health and sanitation made them more attractive to live and work in. Port cities like Salonica, in Greece, saw its population rise from 55,000 in 1800 to 160,000 in 1912 and İzmir which had a population of 150,000 in 1800 grew to 300,000 by 1914. Some regions conversely had population falls – Belgrade saw its population drop from 25,000 to 8,000 mainly due to political strife.
rewrite: The growth of ports, facilitated by steamships and railways, led to population concentration in urban areas. Between 1700 and 1922, cities expanded as better health and sanitation conditions made them more desirable. For example, Salonica, Greece, grew from 55,000 residents in 1800 to 160,000 by 1912, while İzmir doubled from 150,000 to 300,000 between 1800 and 1914. In contrast, some areas declined, such as Belgrade, whose population fell from 25,000 to 8,000 largely because of political conflict.

input: The state is well known for its handicrafts. The carpets, leather works, shawls, metalware, woodwork and paintings are worth appreciating. Pashmina shawls are a product that is highly in demand in Himachal and all over the country. Himachali caps are famous art work of the people. Extreme cold winters of Himachal necessitated wool weaving. Nearly every household in Himachal owns a pit-loom. Wool is considered as pure and is used as a ritual cloth. The well-known woven object is the shawl, ranging from fine pashmina to the coarse desar. Kullu is famous for its shawls with striking patterns and vibrant colours. Kangra and Dharamshala are famous for Kangra miniature paintings.
rewrite: This region is celebrated for its traditional crafts, including carpets, leather goods, metal and wood items, and paintings. Pashmina shawls from here are sought after both locally and nationally. Distinctive Himachali caps are a notable local art form. The harsh winter climate fostered a strong tradition of wool weaving, with nearly every home containing a pit-loom. Wool is regarded as sacred and used in ceremonies. Woven shawls are particularly prominent, varying from delicate pashmina to rougher desar fabric. Kullu is renowned for its brightly patterned shawls, while Kangra and Dharamshala are noted for miniature paintings.

input: On 16 June 2006, it was announced that Everton had entered into talks with Knowsley Council and Tesco over the possibility of building a new 55,000 seat stadium, expandable to over 60,000, in Kirkby. The club took the unusual move of giving its supporters a say in the club's future by holding a ballot on the proposal, finding a split of 59% to 41% in favour. Opponents to the plan included other local councils concerned by the effect of a large Tesco store being built as part of the development, and a group of fans demanding that Everton should remain within the city boundaries of Liverpool.
rewrite: On June 16, 2006, Everton Football Club revealed it was negotiating with Knowsley Council and Tesco regarding a potential new arena in Kirkby. This venue would initially hold 55,000 spectators, with a design allowing growth beyond 60,000. In a rare step, the club allowed its fans to vote on the plan. The result showed 59% approval against 41% opposition. Critics included neighboring councils worried about the impact of a major Tesco within the project, as well as a contingent of supporters insisting the club stay inside Liverpool's city limits.

input: On 25 May 2011 the Swiss government announced that it plans to end its use of nuclear energy in the next 2 or 3 decades.
