This trick thoroughly alarmed his coworker, Frederic de Hoffmann, who at first feared a foreign agent had compromised vital atomic secrets. Feynman also frequently borrowed a car from Klaus Fuchs to visit his sick wife in Albuquerque; it was later revealed that Fuchs was an actual Soviet spy, using his vehicle to smuggle nuclear information to Santa Fe.

input: The resultant South Korean government promulgated a national political constitution on 17 July 1948, and elected Syngman Rhee as President on 20 July 1948. The Republic of Korea (South Korea) was established on 15 August 1948. In the Russian Korean Zone of Occupation, the Soviet Union established a Communist North Korean government led by Kim Il-sung. President Rhee's régime excluded communists and leftists from southern politics. Disenfranchised, they headed for the hills, to prepare for guerrilla war against the US-sponsored ROK Government.
rewrite: On July 17, 1948, South Korea's new leadership enacted its foundational constitution, appointing Syngman Rhee as president three days later. The Republic of Korea was formally founded on August 15 that year. Meanwhile, the Soviet Union fostered a communist administration under Kim Il-sung in its northern occupation zone. Rhee's government banned communist and leftist participation in the south, driving many of the excluded to retreat into remote areas and organize armed resistance against the American-backed state.

input: In addition, the city has about 160 museums—the world's greatest single metropolitan concentration —over 100 art galleries, and some 30 concert halls, all of which maintain a constant cultural activity during the whole year. It has either the third or fourth-highest number of theatres in the world after New York, London and perhaps Toronto. Many areas (e.g. Palacio Nacional and the National Institute of Cardiology) have murals painted by Diego Rivera. He and his wife Frida Kahlo lived in Coyoacán, where several of their homes, studios, and art collections are open to the public. The house where Leon Trotsky was initially granted asylum and finally murdered in 1940 is also in Coyoacán.
rewrite: The city also boasts roughly 160 museums, forming the largest such cluster found in any urban area globally, alongside more than 100 art galleries and approximately 30 concert halls. These venues ensure a continuous schedule of cultural events throughout the year. Its quantity of theaters ranks among the top globally, following cities like New York, London, and possibly Toronto. Numerous sites, including the Palacio Nacional and the National Institute of Cardiology, feature murals by Diego Rivera. He and his spouse, Frida Kahlo, resided in Coyoacán, where several of their former residences and studios, now displaying their art, are publicly accessible. The Coyoacán district also contains the house where Leon Trotsky was first given refuge and later assassinated in 1940.

input: Stressful life experiences may be a cause of memory loss as a person ages. Glucocorticoids that are released during stress damage neurons that are located in the hippocampal region of the brain. Therefore, the more stressful situations that someone encounters, the more susceptible they are to memory loss later on. The CA1 neurons found in the hippocampus are destroyed due to glucocorticoids decreasing the release of glucose and the reuptake of glutamate. This high level of extracellular glutamate allow calcium to enter NMDA receptors which in return kills neurons. Stressful life experiences can also cause repression of memories where a person moves an unbearable memory to the unconscious mind. This directly relates to traumatic events in one's past such as kidnappings, being prisoners of war or sexual abuse as a child.
rewrite: Exposure to significant stress over a lifetime can contribute to memory decline in older adults. When the body responds to stress, it releases hormones called glucocorticoids, which harm nerve cells in the hippocampus, a brain area vital for memory. Consequently, greater cumulative stress increases vulnerability to memory impairment. Specifically, these hormones impair the supply of energy and the regulation of a neurotransmitter called glutamate in hippocampal CA1 neurons. The resulting excess glutamate outside the cells triggers a harmful influx of calcium through NMDA receptors, leading to neuronal death. Additionally, extreme stress can push distressing memories, like those from trauma or abuse, into the unconscious mind, a process known as repression.

input: The battle in the Marshall Islands caused irreparable damage, especially on Japanese bases. During the American bombing, the islands' population suffered from lack of food and various injuries. U.S. attacks started in mid-1943, and caused half the Japanese garrison of 5,100 people in the atoll Mili to die from hunger by August 1945.
rewrite: The conflict in the Marshall Islands inflicted lasting destruction, particularly on Japan's military sites. American air raids beginning in 1943 led to widespread starvation and wounds among the inhabitants. On Mili Atoll, this resulted in half of the 5,100 Japanese troops starving to death by 1945.

input: For at least a century before the establishment of the Augustan principate, Jews and Judaism were tolerated in Rome by diplomatic treaty with Judaea's Hellenised elite. Diaspora Jews had much in common with the overwhelmingly Hellenic or Hellenised communities that surrounded them. Early Italian synagogues have left few traces; but one was dedicated in Ostia around the mid-1st century BC and several more are attested during the Imperial period. Judaea's enrollment as a client kingdom in 63 BC increased the Jewish diaspora; in Rome, this led to closer official scrutiny of their religion. Their synagogues were recognised as legitimate collegia by Julius Caesar. By the Augustan era, the city of Rome was home to several thousand Jews. In some periods under Roman rule, Jews were legally exempt from official sacrifice, under certain conditions. Judaism was a superstitio to Cicero, but the Church Father Tertullian described it as religio licita (an officially permitted religion) in contrast to Christianity.
rewrite: For over a hundred years prior to the rise of Augustus’s rule, Jewish people and their faith were accepted in Rome through formal agreements with the Hellenized ruling class of Judaea. Jews living outside their homeland shared many cultural attributes with the predominantly Greek or Greek-influenced societies around them. While little remains of early synagogues in Italy, one was founded in Ostia near the middle of the first century BCE, with others documented later under the Empire. After Judaea became a client state in 63 BCE, the dispersed Jewish population grew, prompting Roman authorities to observe their religious practices more closely. Julius Caesar formally acknowledged their synagogues as lawful associations. By the time of Augustus, thousands of Jews resided in Rome itself. At various times, Roman law granted Jews specific exemptions from mandatory public sacrifices. Cicero viewed Judaism as a superstition, but later, Tertullian labeled it a *religio licita*—a legally sanctioned religion—unlike Christianity.

input: The existence of a "global carrying capacity", limiting the amount of life that can live at once, is debated, as is the question of whether such a limit would also cap the number of species. While records of life in the sea shows a logistic pattern of growth, life on land (insects, plants and tetrapods)shows an exponential rise in diversity. As one author states, "Tetrapods have not yet invaded 64 per cent of potentially habitable modes, and it could be that without human influence the ecological and taxonomic diversity of tetrapods would continue to increase in an exponential fashion until most or all of the available ecospace is filled."
rewrite: The concept of a worldwide limit on total biomass and species count is contested. Marine life appears to follow a constrained growth pattern, whereas terrestrial groups like insects, plants, and four-limbed animals exhibit a rapid, unchecked increase in variety. One analysis suggests that tetrapods have occupied only about a third of their viable niches. Without human intervention, their biological and categorical variety might keep rising exponentially until the majority of suitable ecological space is occupied.

input: In manufacturing the glass bulb, a type of "ribbon machine" is used. A continuous ribbon of glass is passed along a conveyor belt, heated in a furnace, and then blown by precisely aligned air nozzles through holes in the conveyor belt into molds. Thus the glass bulbs are created. After the bulbs are blown, and cooled, they are cut off the ribbon machine; a typical machine of this sort produces 50,000 bulbs per hour. The filament and its supports are assembled on a glass stem, which is fused to the bulb. The air is pumped out of the bulb, and the evacuation tube in the stem press is sealed by a flame. The bulb is then inserted into the lamp base, and the whole assembly tested.
rewrite: A "ribbon machine" is employed to fabricate glass bulbs in manufacturing. This process involves moving an unbroken glass strip on a conveyor through a heating furnace. Precisely arranged air jets then force the softened glass upward through openings in the belt and into shaping molds, forming the bulbs. Once shaped and cooled, they are detached from the continuous ribbon; such equipment can make roughly 50,000 bulbs each hour. Next, the filament and its mounting structure are attached to a glass stem, which is sealed to the bulb. Air is removed from the interior, and the exhaust tube on the stem is closed with a flame. Finally, the bulb is attached to its base, and the complete unit undergoes quality testing.

input: Jews originated as a national and religious group in the Middle East during the second millennium BCE, in the part of the Levant known as the Land of Israel. The Merneptah Stele appears to confirm the existence of a people of Israel, associated with the god El, somewhere in Canaan as far back as the 13th century BCE. The Israelites, as an outgrowth of the Canaanite population, consolidated their hold with the emergence of the Kingdom of Israel, and the Kingdom of Judah. Some consider that these Canaanite sedentary Israelites melded with incoming nomadic groups known as 'Hebrews'. Though few sources in the Bible mention the exilic periods in detail, the experience of diaspora life, from the Ancient Egyptian rule over the Levant, to Assyrian Captivity and Exile, to Babylonian Captivity and Exile, to Seleucid Imperial rule, to the Roman occupation, and the historical relations between Israelites and the homeland, became a major feature of Jewish history, identity and memory.
rewrite: The Jewish people trace their beginnings to the ancient Middle East, emerging as a distinct nation and faith in the region of the Levant called the Land of Israel around 2000 BCE. Archaeological evidence, like the Merneptah Stele, suggests a community identifying with Israel and the deity El was present in Canaan by the 1200s BCE. Evolving from local Canaanite societies, these Israelites established their political presence through the Kingdoms of Israel and Judah. This core population is thought to have integrated with nomadic 'Hebrew' tribes. A defining element of Jewish heritage is the recurring experience of displacement and life outside the homeland. This pattern, from subjugation under ancient Egypt and exile by Assyrian and Babylonian empires to later rule by Seleucid and Roman powers, profoundly shaped Jewish historical consciousness, culture, and sense of identity.

input: In 1948, Eisenhower became President of Columbia University, an Ivy League university in New York City. The assignment was described as not being a good fit in either direction. During that year Eisenhower's memoir, Crusade in Europe, was published. Critics regarded it as one of the finest U.S. military memoirs, and it was a major financial success as well. Eisenhower's profit on the book was substantially aided by an unprecedented ruling by the U.S. Department of the Treasury that Eisenhower was not a professional writer, but rather, marketing the lifetime asset of his experiences, and thus he only had to pay capital gains tax on his $635,000 advance instead of the much higher personal tax rate. This ruling saved Eisenhower about $400,000.
rewrite: In 1948, Dwight Eisenhower assumed the role of President at Columbia University, a prestigious Ivy League institution located in New York. This appointment was widely viewed as an awkward match for both parties involved. That same year also saw the release of Eisenhower's wartime memoir, *Crusade in Europe*. The work was praised by reviewers as among the best accounts of military service from an American author and proved highly lucrative. A key factor in its financial success was a unique decision by the U.S. Treasury Department, which determined that Eisenhower was not a professional author but was instead selling the accumulated value of his personal experiences. Consequently, he was taxed at the lower capital gains rate on his $635,000 advance rather than facing standard income taxes, a ruling that spared him approximately $400,000.

input: After the defeat of the Confederacy, federal forces remained in Charleston during the city's reconstruction. The war had shattered the prosperity of the antebellum city. Freed slaves were faced with poverty and discrimination, but a large community of free people of color had been well-established in the city before the war and became the leaders of the postwar Republican Party and its legislators. Men who had been free people of color before the war comprised 26% of those elected to state and federal office in South Carolina from 1868 to 1876.
rewrite: Following the Civil War, Union troops stayed in Charleston to oversee its rebuilding. The conflict had destroyed the city's former wealth. While newly emancipated individuals encountered hardship and bias, a significant pre-existing community of free Black citizens provided leadership within the postwar Republican Party. These men, free before the war, made up over a quarter of South Carolina's elected officials to state and national positions between 1868 and 1876.

input: In 1880, the newspapers News and Observer combined to form The News & Observer. It remains Raleigh's primary daily newspaper. The North Carolina College of Agriculture and Mechanic Arts, now known as North Carolina State University, was founded as a land-grant college in 1887. The city's Rex Hospital opened in 1889 and included the state's first nursing school. The Baptist Women's College, now known as Meredith College, opened in 1891, and in 1898, The Academy of Music, a private music conservatory, was established.
rewrite: In 1880, two papers, the News and the Observer, merged to create The News & Observer, which continues as Raleigh's main daily. North Carolina State University began in 1887 as a land-grant agricultural and mechanical college. Rex Hospital, founded in 1889, housed the state's inaugural nursing school. Meredith College opened in 1891 as the Baptist Women's College, and a private conservatory, The Academy of Music, was founded in 1898.

input: The free trade spirit of the time received a strong augmentation through the development of a modern, effective stock market in the Low Countries. The Netherlands has the oldest stock exchange in the world, founded in 1602 by the Dutch East India Company. While Rotterdam has the oldest bourse in the Netherlands, the world's first stock exchange – that of the Dutch East-India Company – went public in six different cities. Later, a court ruled that the company had to reside legally in a single city, so Amsterdam is recognized as the oldest such institution based on modern trading principles. While the banking system evolved in the Low Countries, it was quickly incorporated by the well-connected English, stimulating English economic output.
rewrite: The era's commitment to open commerce was significantly bolstered by the establishment of an advanced and efficient securities market in the Low Countries. Home to the world's most ancient exchange, created in 1602 by the Dutch East India Company, the region saw this pioneering institution publicly listed across six urban centers. Rotterdam contains the Netherlands' oldest bourse, but Amsterdam ultimately gained recognition as the primary historic seat, following a legal mandate for the company to have a singular headquarters, aligning it with contemporary market practices. Concurrently, the evolving financial structures from this area were adeptly adopted by the English, who leveraged these innovations to enhance their own economic productivity.

input: In 2000, Apple released the Power Mac G4 Cube, their first desktop since the discontinued Power Macintosh G3, to slot between the iMac G3 and the Power Mac G4. Even with its innovative design, it was initially priced US$200 higher than the comparably-equipped and more-expandable base Power Mac G4, while also not including a monitor, making it too expensive and resulting in slow sales. Apple sold just 29,000 Cubes in Q4 of 2000 which was one third of expectations, compared to 308,000 Macs during that same quarter, and Cube sales dropped to 12,000 units in Q1 of 2001. A price drop and hardware upgrades could not offset the earlier perception of the Cube's reduced value compared to the iMac and Power Mac G4 lineup, and it was discontinued in July 2001.
rewrite: Apple introduced the Power Mac G4 Cube in 2000 as a new desktop model, filling a gap between the iMac G3 and the more powerful Power Mac G4. Despite its unique and compact design, its launch price was $200 above the standard Power Mac G4, which offered greater expansion options and included a display. This high cost, without a monitor, led to poor market reception. Only 29,000 units were sold in the last quarter of 2000—far below projections—while overall Mac sales exceeded 308,000. By early 2001, Cube sales fell to 12,000. Subsequent price reductions and component improvements failed to change the prevailing view that it offered less value than other Apple desktops, leading to its discontinuation in July 2001.

input: It is commonly believed that the earlier a defect is found, the cheaper it is to fix it. The following table shows the cost of fixing the defect depending on the stage it was found. For example, if a problem in the requirements is found only post-release, then it would cost 10–100 times more to fix than if it had already been found by the requirements review. With the advent of modern continuous deployment practices and cloud-based services, the cost of re-deployment and maintenance may lessen over time.
rewrite: The expense of correcting a flaw typically increases the later it is discovered. As illustrated, a requirements issue detected after release can cost 10 to 100 times more to resolve than if identified during the initial review. However, contemporary methods like continuous deployment and cloud services might gradually reduce the expenses associated with updates and ongoing maintenance.

input: The owner, tenant or manager (licensee) of a pub is properly known as the "pub landlord". The term publican (in historical Roman usage a public contractor or tax farmer) has come into use since Victorian times to designate the pub landlord. Known as "locals" to regulars, pubs are typically chosen for their proximity to home or work, the availability of a particular beer, as a place to smoke (or avoid it), hosting a darts team, having a pool or snooker table, or appealing to friends.
rewrite: The individual who runs a pub, whether as proprietor, renter, or manager, is correctly called the "pub landlord." Since the Victorian era, the title "publican" has also been used. Patrons often refer to their favored establishments as "locals," selecting them for convenience, preferred drinks, smoking policies, social circles, or amenities like dartboards and pool tables.

input: On 7 June 1981, the Israeli air force destroyed Iraq's sole nuclear reactor, in order to impede Iraq's nuclear weapons program. The reactor was under construction just outside Baghdad. Following a series of PLO attacks in 1982, Israel invaded Lebanon that year to destroy the bases from which the PLO launched attacks and missiles into northern Israel. In the first six days of fighting, the Israelis destroyed the military forces of the PLO in Lebanon and decisively defeated the Syrians. An Israeli government inquiry – the Kahan Commission – would later hold Begin, Sharon and several Israeli generals as indirectly responsible for the Sabra and Shatila massacre. In 1985, Israel responded to a Palestinian terrorist attack in Cyprus by bombing the PLO headquarters in Tunis. Israel withdrew from most of Lebanon in 1986, but maintained a borderland buffer zone in southern Lebanon until 2000, from where Israeli forces engaged in conflict with Hezbollah.
rewrite: On June 7, 1981, Israeli warplanes eliminated Iraq's only nuclear reactor to halt its atomic arms development. The facility was being built near Baghdad. In 1982, after multiple assaults by the Palestine Liberation Organization, Israel entered Lebanon to eradicate the PLO's operational sites used to strike northern Israel. Within the initial week of combat, Israeli troops dismantled the PLO's military presence in Lebanon and overpowered Syrian forces. A subsequent Israeli investigation, the Kahan Commission, later attributed indirect accountability for the Sabra and Shatila killings to Prime Minister Begin, Defense Minister Sharon, and senior military officials. In 1985, following a Palestinian terrorist incident in Cyprus, Israel launched an air strike on the PLO's command center in Tunis. While Israeli troops pulled back from the majority of Lebanese territory in 1986, they continued to occupy a security zone in the south until the year 2000, clashing there with Hezbollah fighters.

input: Mīmāṃsā gave rise to the study of philology and the philosophy of language. While their deep analysis of language and linguistics influenced other schools, their views were not shared by others. Mīmāṃsākas considered the purpose and power of language was to clearly prescribe the proper, correct and right. In contrast, Vedantins extended the scope and value of language as a tool to also describe, develop and derive. Mīmāṃsākas considered orderly, law-driven, procedural life as central purpose and noblest necessity of dharma and society, and divine (theistic) sustenance means to that end. The Mimamsa school was influential and foundational to the Vedanta school, with the difference that Mīmāṃsā school developed and emphasized karmakāṇḍa (that part of the śruti which relates to ceremonial acts and sacrificial rites, the early parts of the Vedas), while the Vedanta school developed and emphasized jñānakāṇḍa (that portion of the Vedas which relates to knowledge of monism, the latter parts of the Vedas).
rewrite: The Mīmāṃsā tradition originated the disciplines of philology and linguistic philosophy. Its profound examination of language impacted other systems of thought, though its specific perspectives were not universally adopted. Followers of Mīmāṃsā held that the essential function of language was to issue precise, authoritative commands for proper conduct. Vedantins, however, broadened language’s role to include describing reality and facilitating philosophical inquiry. For Mīmāṃsākas, the highest aim of dharma and social order was a life governed by strict ritual procedures, viewing divine principles as supportive of this goal. Although Mīmāṃsā provided a crucial foundation for Vedanta, the two schools diverged in focus: Mīmāṃsā concentrated on the *karmakāṇḍa*, the Vedic sections detailing rituals and sacrifices, whereas Vedanta emphasized the *jñānakāṇḍa*, the later portions concerning metaphysical knowledge and unity.

input: Nothing in the principle of any of the motors described above requires that the iron (steel) portions of the rotor actually rotate. If the soft magnetic material of the rotor is made in the form of a cylinder, then (except for the effect of hysteresis) torque is exerted only on the windings of the electromagnets. Taking advantage of this fact is the coreless or ironless DC motor, a specialized form of a PM DC motor. Optimized for rapid acceleration, these motors have a rotor that is constructed without any iron core. The rotor can take the form of a winding-filled cylinder, or a self-supporting structure comprising only the magnet wire and the bonding material. The rotor can fit inside the stator magnets; a magnetically soft stationary cylinder inside the rotor provides a return path for the stator magnetic flux. A second arrangement has the rotor winding basket surrounding the stator magnets. In that design, the rotor fits inside a magnetically soft cylinder that can serve as the housing for the motor, and likewise provides a return path for the flux.
rewrite: The fundamental design of the previously mentioned motors does not depend on the rotation of their iron-based rotor components. When the rotor's soft magnetic material is shaped into a cylinder, the resulting torque—excluding hysteresis effects—acts solely upon the electromagnetic coils. This principle is utilized in the coreless DC motor, a specialized type of permanent magnet DC motor. Designed for quick acceleration, its rotor lacks an iron core entirely. Instead, it may be a cylinder packed with windings or a self-sufficient structure made only of coated wire and adhesive. In one configuration, the rotor is positioned within the stator magnets, with a fixed, magnetically permeable cylinder inside it to channel the stator's magnetic flux. An alternative layout places the rotor's winding assembly around the stator magnets. Here, the rotor sits inside a permeable cylinder that can also act as the motor casing, similarly guiding the flux return.

input: Unlike in multicellular organisms, increases in cell size (cell growth) and reproduction by cell division are tightly linked in unicellular organisms. Bacteria grow to a fixed size and then reproduce through binary fission, a form of asexual reproduction. Under optimal conditions, bacteria can grow and divide extremely rapidly, and bacterial populations can double as quickly as every 9.8 minutes. In cell division, two identical clone daughter cells are produced. Some bacteria, while still reproducing asexually, form more complex reproductive structures that help disperse the newly formed daughter cells. Examples include fruiting body formation by Myxobacteria and aerial hyphae formation by Streptomyces, or budding. Budding involves a cell forming a protrusion that breaks away and produces a daughter cell.
rewrite: In single-celled life forms, cell enlargement and division are interconnected processes essential for reproduction. For instance, bacterial cells expand to a predetermined limit before splitting via binary fission, an asexual method. Given ideal circumstances, this cycle occurs at a remarkable pace, allowing a colony to double in under ten minutes. Division typically yields two genetically identical offspring. Certain bacteria develop specialized structures to aid in spreading these new cells, despite remaining asexual. Myxobacteria generate fruiting bodies, Streptomyces create aerial filaments, and some species employ budding, where an outgrowth separates to become a new individual.

input: The elimination of wolves from Yellowstone National Park had profound impacts on the trophic pyramid. Without predation, herbivores began to over-graze many woody browse species, affecting the area's plant populations. In addition, wolves often kept animals from grazing in riparian areas, which protected beavers from having their food sources encroached upon. The removal of wolves had a direct effect on beaver populations, as their habitat became territory for grazing. Furthermore, predation keeps hydrological features such as creeks and streams in normal working order. Increased browsing on willows and conifers along Blacktail Creek due to a lack of predation caused channel incision because they helped slow the water down and hold the soil in place.
rewrite: The absence of wolves in Yellowstone significantly disrupted the ecosystem's food web. Freed from predatory pressure, grazing animals consumed excessive amounts of trees and shrubs, depleting key vegetation. Wolves had also previously prevented overgrazing in streamside zones, which safeguarded the food supply for beavers. Their disappearance directly harmed beavers by transforming this habitat. Predation also plays a crucial role in maintaining healthy waterways. For example, without wolves, heavy grazing on plants along Blacktail Creek removed vegetation that stabilized banks and moderated flow, leading to severe erosion of the stream channel.

input: Symbiosis (from Greek σύν "together" and βίωσις "living") is close and often long-term interaction between two different biological species. In 1877 Albert Bernhard Frank used the word symbiosis (which previously had been used to depict people living together in community) to describe the mutualistic relationship in lichens. In 1879, the German mycologist Heinrich Anton de Bary defined it as "the living together of unlike organisms."
rewrite: Symbiosis describes enduring close associations between distinct species. The term originates from Greek words for "together" and "living." Albert Bernhard Frank first applied it biologically in 1877 to lichens' mutualism, broadening its prior social meaning. Later, Heinrich Anton de Bary characterized it in 1879 as the cohabitation of dissimilar life forms.

input: Of the territories of Poland annexed by the Soviet Union between 1939 and 1940, the region around Białystok and a minor part of Galicia east of the San river around Przemyśl were returned to the Polish state at the end of World War II. Of all other territories annexed by the USSR in 1939–40, the ones detached from Finland (Karelia, Petsamo), Estonia (Ingrian area and Petseri County) and Latvia (Abrene) remained part of the Russian Federation, the successor state of the Soviet Union, after 1991. Northern Bukovina, Southern Bessarabia and Hertza remain part of Ukraine.
rewrite: Following World War II, Poland regained the area near Białystok and a small section of Galicia east of the San River from the Soviet-annexed lands of 1939–1940. All other territories seized by the USSR during that period were retained after its dissolution. Those taken from Finland, Estonia, and Latvia are now part of the Russian Federation. The regions of Northern Bukovina, Southern Bessarabia, and Hertza continue to belong to Ukraine.

input: The city is home to 261,546 (mid-2014 est.) people, making it the 30th most populous built-up area in the United Kingdom. It is governed locally by Plymouth City Council and is represented nationally by three MPs. Plymouth's economy remains strongly influenced by shipbuilding and seafaring including ferry links to Brittany (Roscoff and St Malo) and Spain (Santander), but has tended toward a service-based economy since the 1990s. It has the largest operational naval base in Western Europe – HMNB Devonport and is home to Plymouth University.
rewrite: With an estimated population of 261,546 as of mid-2014, Plymouth ranks as the UK's 30th largest urban center. Local governance falls under Plymouth City Council, and three Members of Parliament represent it nationally. Historically centered on maritime industries like shipbuilding and ferry services to France and Spain, the city's economic focus has shifted primarily to services since the 1990s. It hosts the biggest working naval base in Western Europe, HMNB Devonport, and Plymouth University.

input: The northern section of the Divide, where the mountains give way rapidly to prairie, is part of the Rocky Mountain Front. The front is most pronounced in the Lewis Range, located primarily in Glacier National Park. Due to the configuration of mountain ranges in Glacier National Park, the Northern Divide (which begins in Alaska's Seward Peninsula) crosses this region and turns east in Montana at Triple Divide Peak. It causes the Waterton River, Belly, and Saint Mary rivers to flow north into Alberta, Canada. There they join the Saskatchewan River, which ultimately empties into Hudson Bay.
rewrite: The Rocky Mountain Front includes the northern area of the Continental Divide, where the terrain quickly transitions from peaks to plains. This feature is especially distinct within Glacier National Park's Lewis Range. Here, the Northern Divide—originating in Alaska—shifts eastward at Montana's Triple Divide Peak. This divergence directs the Waterton, Belly, and Saint Mary rivers northward into Alberta. These waters merge with the Saskatchewan River, eventually draining into Hudson Bay.

input: In The Open Society and Its Enemies and The Poverty of Historicism, Popper developed a critique of historicism and a defence of the "Open Society". Popper considered historicism to be the theory that history develops inexorably and necessarily according to knowable general laws towards a determinate end. He argued that this view is the principal theoretical presupposition underpinning most forms of authoritarianism and totalitarianism. He argued that historicism is founded upon mistaken assumptions regarding the nature of scientific law and prediction. Since the growth of human knowledge is a causal factor in the evolution of human history, and since "no society can predict, scientifically, its own future states of knowledge", it follows, he argued, that there can be no predictive science of human history. For Popper, metaphysical and historical indeterminism go hand in hand.
rewrite: In his works *The Open Society and Its Enemies* and *The Poverty of Historicism*, Karl Popper formulated a criticism of historicism and advocated for an "Open Society." He defined historicism as the belief that history follows inevitable, discoverable laws toward a specific destiny. Popper maintained that this idea is a key foundation for authoritarian and totalitarian systems. He contended that historicism relies on flawed views about scientific laws and forecasting. Because human knowledge expands over time and influences historical change, and since no community can scientifically foresee its own future knowledge, Popper concluded that a predictive science of history is impossible. In his view, metaphysical and historical indeterminism are closely linked.

input: IBM's employee management practices can be traced back to its roots. In 1914, CEO Thomas J. Watson boosted company spirit by creating employee sports teams, hosting family outings, and furnishing a company band. IBM sports teams still continue in the present day; the IBM Big Blue continue to exist as semi-professional company rugby and American football teams. In 1924 the Quarter Century Club, which recognizes employees with 25 years of service, was organized and the first issue of Business Machines, IBM's internal publication, was published. In 1925, the first meeting of the Hundred Percent Club, composed of IBM salesmen who meet their quotas, convened in Atlantic City, New Jersey.
rewrite: IBM's approach to managing its workforce has deep historical origins. In 1914, under CEO Thomas J. Watson, morale was raised through organized sports teams, family events, and a corporate band. The tradition of company athletics persists, with the semi-professional IBM Big Blue rugby and football teams still active. The Quarter Century Club, honoring a quarter-century of service, began in 1924, the same year the internal newsletter *Business Machines* launched. A year later, the Hundred Percent Club, for salespeople achieving their targets, held its inaugural gathering in Atlantic City.

input: Appointments to the Order of the British Empire were at first made on the nomination of the self-governing Dominions of the Empire, the Viceroy of India, and the colonial governors, as well as on nominations from within the United Kingdom. As the Empire evolved into the Commonwealth, nominations continued to come from the Commonwealth realms, in which the monarch remained head of state. These overseas nominations have been discontinued in realms that have established their own Orders—such as the Order of Australia, the Order of Canada, and the New Zealand Order of Merit—but members of the Order are still appointed in the British Overseas Territories.
rewrite: Initially, appointments to the Order of the British Empire were based on recommendations from the self-governing Dominions, the Viceroy of India, colonial governors, and the United Kingdom itself. As the Empire transitioned to the Commonwealth, nominations persisted from Commonwealth nations that retained the monarch. However, such nominations from abroad ceased in realms that created their own national honors, like Australia, Canada, and New Zealand. Appointments continue within the British Overseas Territories.

input: After several failed attempts, in 1930 the first aeroplane reached Bermuda. A Stinson Detroiter seaplane flying from New York, it had to land twice in the ocean: once because of darkness and again to refuel. Navigation and weather forecasting improved in 1933 when the Royal Air Force (then responsible for providing equipment and personnel for the Royal Navy's Fleet Air Arm) established a station at the Royal Naval Dockyard to repair (and supply replacement) float planes for the fleet. In 1936 Luft Hansa began to experiment with seaplane flights from Berlin via the Azores with continuation to New York City.
rewrite: Following multiple unsuccessful efforts, the inaugural aircraft arrived in Bermuda in 1930. This Stinson Detroiter, a seaplane traveling from New York, was forced to touch down on the water twice—first due to nightfall and later for more fuel. Advancements in guiding aircraft and predicting conditions came in 1933. That year, the Royal Air Force set up a base at the Royal Naval Dockyard to maintain and provide spare seaplanes for the Fleet Air Arm. By 1936, Luft Hansa started testing seaplane routes from Berlin to New York, stopping at the Azores.

input: There are four hundred securities listed on the stock exchange, of which almost three hundred are offshore funds and alternative investment structures attracted by Bermuda's regulatory environment. The Exchange specialises in listing and trading of capital market instruments such as equities, debt issues, funds (including hedge fund structures) and depository receipt programmes. The BSX is a full member of the World Federation of Exchanges and is located in an OECD member nation. It also has Approved Stock Exchange status under Australia's Foreign Investment Fund (FIF) taxation rules and Designated Investment Exchange status by the UK's Financial Services Authority.
rewrite: The stock exchange features four hundred listed securities, with close to three hundred being offshore funds and alternative investment vehicles drawn to Bermuda's regulatory framework. It focuses on listing and trading instruments like equities, debt offerings, various funds, and depository receipt programs. As a full member of the World Federation of Exchanges and based in an OECD country, the BSX holds recognized status under both Australia's Foreign Investment Fund tax regulations and the UK Financial Services Authority's designation for investment exchanges.

input: During the Protestant Reformation, the Church of England (Anglicans) separated from the Roman Catholic Church. There were some Christians who were not content with the achievements of the mainstream Protestant Reformation. There also were Christians who were disappointed that the Church of England had not made corrections of what some considered to be errors and abuses. Of those most critical of the Church's direction, some chose to stay and try to make constructive changes from within the Anglican Church. They became known as "Puritans" and are described by Gourley as cousins of the English Separatists. Others decided they must leave the Church because of their dissatisfaction and became known as the Separatists.
rewrite: Amidst the Protestant Reformation, England's national church broke away from Roman Catholicism. However, certain believers felt the broader Reformation had not gone far enough. Others were dismayed that the newly formed Church of England retained, in their view, persistent flaws and corrupt practices. From this critical faction, one group remained within Anglicanism to advocate for internal reform; these were the Puritans, whom historian Gourley likens to relatives of the Separatists. A second group, concluding the church was beyond correction, chose to depart entirely, forming the Separatist movement.

input: Important Justinian era mosaics decorated the Saint Catherine's Monastery on Mount Sinai in Egypt. Generally wall mosaics have not survived in the region because of the destruction of buildings but the St. Catherine's Monastery is exceptional. On the upper wall Moses is shown in two panels on a landscape background. In the apse we can see the Transfiguration of Jesus on a golden background. The apse is surrounded with bands containing medallions of apostles and prophets, and two contemporary figure, "Abbot Longinos" and "John the Deacon". The mosaic was probably created in 565/6.
rewrite: The Saint Catherine's Monastery at Mount Sinai in Egypt features significant mosaics from the time of Justinian. While most wall mosaics in the area have been lost to building destruction, this site remains uniquely preserved. Two scenes depict Moses against a landscape on an upper wall. The apse presents the Transfiguration of Jesus set against gold, encircled by decorative bands. These bands hold medallions portraying apostles, prophets, and two contemporary individuals: Abbot Longinos and John the Deacon. This artwork likely dates to 565 or 566 AD.

input: The rivalry between Nintendo and Sega resulted in what has been described as one of the most notable console wars in video game history, in which Sega positioned the Genesis as the "cool" console, with more mature titles aimed at older gamers, and edgy advertisements that occasionally attacked the competition. Nintendo however, scored an early public relations advantage by securing the first console conversion of Capcom's arcade classic Street Fighter II for SNES, which took over a year to make the transition to Genesis. Despite the Genesis's head start, much larger library of games, and lower price point, the Genesis only represented an estimated 60% of the American 16-bit console market in June 1992, and neither console could maintain a definitive lead for several years. Donkey Kong Country is said to have helped establish the SNES's market prominence in the latter years of the 16-bit generation, and for a time, maintain against the PlayStation and Saturn. According to Nintendo, the company had sold more than 20 million SNES units in the U.S. According to a 2014 Wedbush Securities report based on NPD sales data, the SNES ultimately outsold the Genesis in the U.S. market.
rewrite:
The competition between Nintendo and Sega created one of the most famous battles in gaming, often called the console wars. Sega marketed its Genesis system as the edgier choice, targeting an older audience with mature games and bold marketing that sometimes directly criticized Nintendo. In response, Nintendo gained an early publicity win by exclusively releasing the first home version of Capcom's hugely popular arcade game, Street Fighter II, for its Super Nintendo. This version remained exclusive for over a year before arriving on Genesis.

Even with the Genesis launching earlier, offering a more extensive game catalog, and having a cheaper price, it only captured about 60% of the U.S. 16-bit market by mid-1992. For years, neither console could secure a lasting advantage. The release of Donkey Kong Country later helped solidify the Super Nintendo's lead in the final years of the 16-bit era, even providing some competition against the next generation of consoles, like the PlayStation and Saturn. Nintendo claims U.S. sales of over 20 million Super Nintendo units. Ultimately, sales data indicates the Super Nintendo surpassed the Genesis in total U.S. sales.

input: Economic sanctions against Iran, such as the embargo against Iranian crude oil, have affected the economy. Sanctions have led to a steep fall in the value of the rial, and as of April 2013 one US dollar is worth 36,000 rial, compared with 16,000 in early 2012. Following a successful implementation of the 2015 nuclear and sanctions relief deal, the resulting benefits might not be distributed evenly across the Iranian economy as political elites such as the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps have garnered more resources and economic interests.
rewrite: International economic penalties, including restrictions on Iran's oil exports, have significantly impacted its financial system. These measures caused the national currency to plummet, with the exchange rate falling from 16,000 rials to the U.S. dollar in 2012 to 36,000 by April 2013. Even after the 2015 nuclear agreement brought some relief, the economic gains have been unevenly shared, as groups like the Revolutionary Guard have secured a disproportionate share of resources and commercial advantages.

input: Norfolk Island was originally a colony acquired by settlement but was never within the British Settlements Act. It was accepted as a territory of Australia, separate from any state, by the Norfolk Island Act 1913 (Cth), passed under the territories power (Constitution section 122) and made effective in 1914. In 1976 the High Court of Australia held unanimously that Norfolk Island is a part of the Commonwealth. Again, in 2007 the High Court of Australia affirmed the validity of legislation that made Australian citizenship a necessary qualification for voting for, and standing for election to, the Legislative Assembly of Norfolk Island.
rewrite: Norfolk Island initially became a British colony through settlement, though it was not covered by the British Settlements Act. The Norfolk Island Act of 1913, enacted under the constitutional territories power, formally recognized it as an Australian external territory, effective in 1914. In 1976, the High Court of Australia unanimously ruled the island was part of the Commonwealth. Later, in 2007, the High Court upheld laws requiring Australian citizenship to vote or run for office in the Norfolk Island Legislative Assembly.

input: In some cases and in some places the edicts were strictly enforced: some Christians resisted and were imprisoned or martyred. Others complied. Some local communities were not only pre-dominantly Christian, but powerful and influential; and some provincial authorities were lenient, notably the Caesar in Gaul, Constantius Chlorus, the father of Constantine I. Diocletian's successor Galerius maintained anti-Christian policy until his deathbed revocation in 311, when he asked Christians to pray for him. "This meant an ofﬁcial recognition of their importance in the religious world of the Roman empire, although one of the tetrarchs, Maximinus Daia, still oppressed Christians in his part of the empire up to 313."
rewrite: In certain regions, the decrees were applied rigorously, leading to the imprisonment or martyrdom of Christians who defied them, while some adherents chose to comply. Several local populations were not only largely Christian but also held considerable sway. Provincial officials varied in their approach, with figures like Constantius Chlorus in Gaul showing notable leniency. Following Diocletian, Galerius upheld anti-Christian measures until recanting on his deathbed in 311, requesting prayers from Christians. This act acknowledged their growing significance within the empire’s religious landscape, despite ongoing persecution under Maximinus Daia until 313.

input: These areas contain some spectacular scenery as well, as evidenced by such national parks as Yosemite and Mount Rainier. West of the Cascades and Sierra Nevada is a series of valleys, such as the Central Valley in California and the Willamette Valley in Oregon. Along the coast is a series of low mountain ranges known as the Pacific Coast Ranges. Much of the Pacific Northwest coast is inhabited by some of the densest vegetation outside of the Tropics, and also the tallest trees in the world (the Redwoods).
rewrite: This region also boasts remarkable landscapes, highlighted by national parks like Yosemite and Mount Rainier. To the west of the major mountain ranges lie fertile valleys, including California's Central Valley and Oregon's Willamette Valley. Coastal areas feature the low Pacific Coast Ranges. The northwestern coastline supports exceptionally thick forests, rivaling tropical density, and is home to the planet's tallest trees, the Redwoods.

input: In the field of music, Germany claims some of the most renowned classical composers of the world including Bach, Mozart and Beethoven, who marked the transition between the Classical and Romantic eras in Western classical music. Other composers of the Austro-German tradition who achieved international fame include Brahms, Wagner, Haydn, Schubert, Händel, Schumann, Liszt, Mendelssohn Bartholdy, Johann Strauss II, Bruckner, Mahler, Telemann, Richard Strauss, Schoenberg, Orff, and most recently, Henze, Lachenmann, and Stockhausen.
rewrite: Germany is celebrated for its many influential classical composers, such as Bach, Mozart, and Beethoven, who bridged the Classical and Romantic periods. The broader Austro-German tradition also produced globally famous figures like Brahms, Wagner, Haydn, and Schubert, extending to modern innovators including Henze, Lachenmann, and Stockhausen.

input: iPods have been criticized for alleged short life-span and fragile hard drives. A 2005 survey conducted on the MacInTouch website found that the iPod line had an average failure rate of 13.7% (although they note that comments from respondents indicate that "the true iPod failure rate may be lower than it appears"). It concluded that some models were more durable than others. In particular, failure rates for iPods employing hard drives was usually above 20% while those with flash memory had a failure rate below 10%. In late 2005, many users complained that the surface of the first generation iPod Nano can become scratched easily, rendering the screen unusable. A class action lawsuit was also filed. Apple initially considered the issue a minor defect, but later began shipping these iPods with protective sleeves.[citation needed]
rewrite: iPods have faced scrutiny over concerns regarding their limited durability and delicate internal components. According to a 2005 poll on MacInTouch, the overall malfunction rate for these devices was approximately 13.7%. The survey's authors suggested the actual figure might be even lower based on user feedback. Findings indicated that models varied in reliability; those using traditional hard drives showed failure rates exceeding 20%, whereas versions with flash memory fell below 10%. Later that year, numerous customers reported that the screens on first-generation iPod Nanos were prone to scratching, often making them difficult to read. This led to legal action against Apple. The company first downplayed the problem as insignificant but eventually addressed it by including protective cases with new units.

input: Numerous recordings of Chopin's works are available. On the occasion of the composer's bicentenary, the critics of The New York Times recommended performances by the following contemporary pianists (among many others): Martha Argerich, Vladimir Ashkenazy, Emanuel Ax, Evgeny Kissin, Murray Perahia, Maurizio Pollini and Krystian Zimerman. The Warsaw Chopin Society organizes the Grand prix du disque de F. Chopin for notable Chopin recordings, held every five years.
rewrite: Many recordings of Chopin's compositions exist. For his 200th birthday, The New York Times reviewers suggested interpretations by modern pianists like Martha Argerich and Evgeny Kissin, alongside several other noted artists. Every five years, the Warsaw Chopin Society awards the Grand prix du disque de F. Chopin to honor exceptional recorded works of the composer.

input: In 1978, Jim Shooter became Marvel's editor-in-chief. Although a controversial personality, Shooter cured many of the procedural ills at Marvel, including repeatedly missed deadlines. During Shooter's nine-year tenure as editor-in-chief, Chris Claremont and John Byrne's run on the Uncanny X-Men and Frank Miller's run on Daredevil became critical and commercial successes. Shooter brought Marvel into the rapidly evolving direct market, institutionalized creator royalties, starting with the Epic Comics imprint for creator-owned material in 1982; introduced company-wide crossover story arcs with Contest of Champions and Secret Wars; and in 1986 launched the ultimately unsuccessful New Universe line to commemorate the 25th anniversary of the Marvel Comics imprint. Star Comics, a children-oriented line differing from the regular Marvel titles, was briefly successful during this period.
rewrite: Jim Shooter assumed the role of editor-in-chief at Marvel in 1978. Despite his divisive nature, he effectively resolved numerous operational issues, most notably chronic lateness in publication. His nine-year leadership saw acclaimed and popular runs on titles like Uncanny X-Men by Chris Claremont and John Byrne, and Daredevil by Frank Miller. Shooter strategically moved Marvel into the growing direct sales market and established royalty systems for creators, initiating the Epic Comics imprint for creator-owned work in 1982. He pioneered expansive crossover events with Contest of Champions and Secret Wars. In 1986, he introduced the New Universe line for Marvel's 25th anniversary, though it did not succeed. The era also included a short-lived but popular children's line called Star Comics.

input: While the cardinalate has long been expanded beyond the Roman pastoral clergy and Roman Curia, every cardinal priest has a titular church in Rome, though they may be bishops or archbishops elsewhere, just as cardinal bishops are given one of the suburbicarian dioceses around Rome. Pope Paul VI abolished all administrative rights cardinals had with regard to their titular churches, though the cardinal's name and coat of arms are still posted in the church, and they are expected to celebrate mass and preach there if convenient when they are in Rome.
rewrite: Although the College of Cardinals now includes members from outside Rome, each cardinal priest is still assigned a titular church in the city. Similarly, cardinal bishops receive a suburbicarian diocese near Rome. Administrative control over these churches was removed by Pope Paul VI. However, a cardinal's name and heraldry remain displayed, and he is to lead Mass and give sermons there when visiting Rome.

input: Retail versions of Windows 8 are only able to install these apps through Windows Store—a namesake distribution platform which offers both apps, and listings for desktop programs certified for comparability with Windows 8. A method to sideload apps from outside Windows Store is available to devices running Windows 8 Enterprise and joined to a domain; Windows 8 Pro and Windows RT devices that are not part of a domain can also sideload apps, but only after special product keys are obtained through volume licensing.
rewrite: Windows 8 retail editions restrict app installation to the official Windows Store, which provides both apps and verified desktop software listings. However, sideloading from external sources is permitted for enterprise domain-joined devices. Non-domain Pro and RT versions can also enable this feature, but only after acquiring specific volume licensing keys.

input: Raleigh is home to numerous cultural, educational, and historic sites. The Duke Energy Center for the Performing Arts in Downtown Raleigh features three theater venues and serves as the home for the North Carolina Symphony and the Carolina Ballet. Walnut Creek Amphitheatre is a large music amphitheater located in Southeast Raleigh. Museums in Raleigh include the North Carolina Museum of Art in West Raleigh, as well as the North Carolina Museum of History and North Carolina Museum of Natural Sciences located next to each other near the State Capitol in Downtown Raleigh. Several major universities and colleges call Raleigh home, including North Carolina State University, the largest public university in the state, and Shaw University, the first historically black university in the American South and site of the foundation of the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee, an important civil rights organization of the 1960s. One U.S. president, Andrew Johnson, was born in Raleigh.
rewrite: Raleigh boasts a wealth of cultural, educational, and historical landmarks. In its downtown core, the Duke Energy Center for the Performing Arts houses three distinct theaters and is the principal venue for both the North Carolina Symphony and the Carolina Ballet. Southeast Raleigh contains the sizable Walnut Creek Amphitheatre, a premier spot for live music. The city's museum offerings are significant, featuring the North Carolina Museum of Art in its western section, while the Museum of History and the Museum of Natural Sciences sit adjacent to one another near the Capitol downtown. Academically, Raleigh hosts several major institutions, most notably North Carolina State University, the state's biggest public university, and Shaw University, the South's first historically black college, where the pivotal Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee was formed. Additionally, Raleigh is the birthplace of President Andrew Johnson.

input: Federal law and treaties, so long as they are in accordance with the Constitution, preempt conflicting state and territorial laws in the 50 U.S. states and in the territories. However, the scope of federal preemption is limited because the scope of federal power is not universal. In the dual-sovereign system of American federalism (actually tripartite because of the presence of Indian reservations), states are the plenary sovereigns, each with their own constitution, while the federal sovereign possesses only the limited supreme authority enumerated in the Constitution. Indeed, states may grant their citizens broader rights than the federal Constitution as long as they do not infringe on any federal constitutional rights. Thus, most U.S. law (especially the actual "living law" of contract, tort, property, criminal, and family law experienced by the majority of citizens on a day-to-day basis) consists primarily of state law, which can and does vary greatly from one state to the next.
rewrite: When federal statutes and treaties align with the Constitution, they override any contradictory laws enacted by states or territories. This federal supremacy is not all-encompassing, however, as the authority of the national government is itself constrained. The United States employs a system of dual sovereignty—more accurately tripartite when considering tribal lands—where individual states hold full governing power under their own constitutions. The federal government's supreme power is restricted to those specific areas listed in the Constitution. Consequently, states are free to provide their residents with more extensive protections than those in the federal charter, provided no national constitutional rights are violated. As a result, the bulk of everyday legal matters for Americans—including contracts, personal injury, property, crime, and family issues—are governed by state statutes, which differ significantly across the country.

input: In four months, Aonuma's team managed to present realistic horseback riding,[l] which Nintendo later revealed to the public with a trailer at Electronic Entertainment Expo 2004. The game was scheduled to be released the next year, and was no longer a follow-up to The Wind Waker; a true sequel to it was released for the Nintendo DS in 2007, in the form of Phantom Hourglass. Miyamoto explained in interviews that the graphical style was chosen to satisfy demand, and that it better fit the theme of an older incarnation of Link. The game runs on a modified The Wind Waker engine.
rewrite: Within a span of four months, the group led by Aonuma successfully developed authentic equestrian mechanics for a new game. Nintendo first showcased this feature in a 2004 E3 preview. Initially planned for launch the following year, this project diverged from being a direct successor to *The Wind Waker*; that true sequel, *Phantom Hourglass*, arrived on the Nintendo DS in 2007. According to Miyamoto, the visual approach was selected in response to player requests and because it more appropriately matched the concept of a more mature Link. The title operates using an altered version of *The Wind Waker*'s core software.

input: Freedom of the press is ostensibly officially guaranteed by the government, but independent press outlets remain restricted, as does a substantial amount of web content. According to the Institute for War & Peace Reporting, access is blocked to local and foreign websites including avesta.tj, Tjknews.com, ferghana.ru, centrasia.ru and journalists are often obstructed from reporting on controversial events. In practice, no public criticism of the regime is tolerated and all direct protest is severely suppressed and does not receive coverage in the local media.
rewrite: While the government claims to protect press freedom, independent media and much online material face limitations. The Institute for War & Peace Reporting notes that numerous local and international sites are inaccessible, and journalists are frequently hindered from covering sensitive issues. Effectively, any open disapproval of the authorities is forbidden, with all overt dissent being harshly quashed and absent from domestic news reports.

input: The most commonly used forms of medium distance transport in Hyderabad include government owned services such as light railways and buses, as well as privately operated taxis and auto rickshaws. Bus services operate from the Mahatma Gandhi Bus Station in the city centre and carry over 130 million passengers daily across the entire network.:76 Hyderabad's light rail transportation system, the Multi-Modal Transport System (MMTS), is a three line suburban rail service used by over 160,000 passengers daily. Complementing these government services are minibus routes operated by Setwin (Society for Employment Promotion & Training in Twin Cities). Intercity rail services also operate from Hyderabad; the main, and largest, station is Secunderabad Railway Station, which serves as Indian Railways' South Central Railway zone headquarters and a hub for both buses and MMTS light rail services connecting Secunderabad and Hyderabad. Other major railway stations in Hyderabad are Hyderabad Deccan Station, Kachiguda Railway Station, Begumpet Railway Station, Malkajgiri Railway Station and Lingampally Railway Station. The Hyderabad Metro, a new rapid transit system, is to be added to the existing public transport infrastructure and is scheduled to operate three lines by 2015.
rewrite:
In Hyderabad, the primary modes of transport for intermediate distances encompass both public and private options. Public offerings consist of suburban light rail and extensive bus networks, while taxis and auto rickshaws fill the private role. Buses, originating from the central Mahatma Gandhi Bus Station, facilitate more than 130 million passenger journeys each day across their system. The suburban rail, known as the Multi-Modal Transport System (MMTS), runs on three lines and serves upwards of 160,000 commuters daily. This public framework is supplemented by Setwin, an organization providing minibus routes.

For travel beyond the city, Hyderabad functions as a significant rail hub. The central Secunderabad Railway Station acts as the headquarters for a major regional division of Indian Railways and integrates connections for buses and the MMTS. Additional key stations include Hyderabad Deccan, Kachiguda, Begumpet, Malkajgiri, and Lingampally. Furthermore, the forthcoming Hyderabad Metro, a rapid transit network, is planned to launch with three lines, enhancing the city's transit framework.

input: Philadelphia is home to many national historical sites that relate to the founding of the United States. Independence National Historical Park is the center of these historical landmarks being one of the country's 22 UNESCO World Heritage Sites. Independence Hall, where the Declaration of Independence was signed, and the Liberty Bell are the city's most famous attractions. Other historic sites include homes for Edgar Allan Poe, Betsy Ross, and Thaddeus Kosciuszko, early government buildings like the First and Second Banks of the United States, Fort Mifflin, and the Gloria Dei (Old Swedes') Church. Philadelphia alone has 67 National Historic Landmarks, the third most of any city in the country.
rewrite: Philadelphia contains numerous sites significant to America's founding. The heart of this heritage is Independence National Historical Park, a UNESCO World Heritage site. Key attractions there are Independence Hall, where the nation's founding document was adopted, and the Liberty Bell. The city also preserves residences of figures like Edgar Allan Poe and Betsy Ross, early federal banks, Fort Mifflin, and the historic Gloria Dei Church. With sixty-seven designated landmarks, Philadelphia holds the third-highest total of National Historic Landmarks in the United States.

input: New York is a prominent location for the American entertainment industry, with many films, television series, books, and other media being set there. As of 2012, New York City was the second largest center for filmmaking and television production in the United States, producing about 200 feature films annually, employing 130,000 individuals, and generating an estimated $7.1 billion in direct expenditures, and by volume, New York is the world leader in independent film production; one-third of all American independent films are produced in New York City. The Association of Independent Commercial Producers is also based in New York. In the first five months of 2014 alone, location filming for television pilots in New York City exceeded the record production levels for all of 2013, with New York surpassing Los Angeles as the top North American city for the same distinction during the 2013/2014 cycle.
rewrite: New York holds a central position in the nation's entertainment sector, serving as a frequent backdrop for countless movies, TV shows, and literary works. By 2012, it ranked as the country's second biggest hub for film and television creation, responsible for roughly 200 theatrical releases each year. This activity provided jobs for 130,000 people and contributed an estimated $7.1 billion in direct spending. The city is also the global capital for independent filmmaking, accounting for one-third of all such U.S. productions. Furthermore, the Association of Independent Commercial Producers calls New York home. Notably, in just the initial five months of 2014, the number of TV pilots shot on location there broke the previous full-year record set in 2013. During the 2013/2014 period, New York also overtook Los Angeles to become the leading city for this activity in North America.

input: Control of labour and inter-group conflict is characteristic of corporate-level or 'tribal' groups, headed by a charismatic individual; whether a 'big man' or a proto-chief, functioning as a lineage-group head. Whether a non-hierarchical system of organization existed is debatable, and there is no evidence that explicitly suggests that Neolithic societies functioned under any dominating class or individual, as was the case in the chiefdoms of the European Early Bronze Age. Theories to explain the apparent implied egalitarianism of Neolithic (and Paleolithic) societies have arisen, notably the Marxist concept of primitive communism.
rewrite: Managing workforces and resolving conflicts between groups are typical features of larger, clan-like communities led by a compelling figure, such as a prominent leader or an early chief, who acts as the head of a kinship network. The possibility of entirely non-hierarchical structures remains uncertain, with no clear proof that Neolithic cultures were ruled by a dominant class or person, unlike later European Bronze Age chiefdoms. Ideas like the Marxist notion of primitive communism have emerged to account for the seeming equality observed in Neolithic and Paleolithic groups.

input: Following the success of season one, the second season was moved up to air in January 2003. The number of episodes increased, as did the show's budget and the charge for commercial spots. Dunkleman left the show, leaving Seacrest as the lone host. Kristin Adams was a correspondent for this season.

input: The Times Literary Supplement (TLS) first appeared in 1902 as a supplement to The Times, becoming a separately paid-for weekly literature and society magazine in 1914. The Times and the TLS have continued to be co-owned, and as of 2012 the TLS is also published by News International and cooperates closely with The Times, with its online version hosted on The Times website, and its editorial offices based in Times House, Pennington Street, London.
rewrite: Launched in 1902 as an addition to The Times, the Times Literary Supplement began operating as an independent weekly publication focusing on literary and social matters in 1914. It remains under the same ownership as the newspaper. Since 2012, News International has also published the TLS, which maintains strong ties to The Times. Its digital edition is located on the newspaper's site, and its main offices are at Times House in London.

input: Congo is located in the central-western part of sub-Saharan Africa, along the Equator, lying between latitudes 4°N and 5°S, and longitudes 11° and 19°E. To the south and east of it is the Democratic Republic of Congo. It is also bounded by Gabon to the west, Cameroon and the Central African Republic to the north, and Cabinda (Angola) to the southwest. It has a short coast on the Atlantic Ocean.
rewrite: Situated in west-central Africa astride the Equator, the Congo spans from roughly 4° north to 5° south in latitude and between 11° and 19° east in longitude. Its borders include Gabon to the west, Cameroon and the Central African Republic to the north, and the Angolan exclave of Cabinda to the southwest. The country shares its southern and eastern frontiers with the Democratic Republic of the Congo and possesses a limited Atlantic coastline.

input: In 1219 Pope Honorius III invited Saint Dominic and his companions to take up residence at the ancient Roman basilica of Santa Sabina, which they did by early 1220. Before that time the friars had only a temporary residence in Rome at the convent of San Sisto Vecchio which Honorius III had given to Dominic circa 1218 intending it to become a convent for a reformation of nuns at Rome under Dominic's guidance. In May 1220 at Bologna the order's first General Chapter mandated that each new priory of the order maintain its own studium conventuale thus laying the foundation of the Dominican tradition of sponsoring widespread institutions of learning. The official foundation of the Dominican convent at Santa Sabina with its studium conventuale occurred with the legal transfer of property from Honorius III to the Order of Preachers on June 5, 1222. This studium was transformed into the order's first studium provinciale by Saint Thomas Aquinas in 1265. Part of the curriculum of this studium was relocated in 1288 at the studium of Santa Maria sopra Minerva which in the 16th century world be transformed into the College of Saint Thomas (Latin: Collegium Divi Thomæ). In the 20th century the college would be relocated to the convent of Saints Dominic and Sixtus and would be transformed into the Pontifical University of Saint Thomas Aquinas, Angelicum.
rewrite:
In 1219, Pope Honorius III offered Saint Dominic and his followers the use of the historic Santa Sabina basilica in Rome, a move completed in early 1220. Previously, the friars had been temporarily housed at San Sisto Vecchio, a convent granted to Dominic around 1218. The Pope’s initial plan for that site was to establish a reformed community of nuns there under Dominic’s direction. During the order’s inaugural General Chapter in Bologna in May 1220, a significant decision was made: every new Dominican priory was required to found its own house of study, or *studium conventuale*. This decree initiated the Dominicans' enduring commitment to creating educational centers.

The formal establishment of the Dominican community at Santa Sabina, complete with its *studium*, was finalized on June 5, 1222, through a legal property transfer from Honorius III to the Order of Preachers. In 1265, Saint Thomas Aquinas elevated this school into the order’s first *studium provinciale*, a higher-level institution. A portion of its academic program was transferred in 1288 to the *studium* at Santa Maria sopra Minerva. That school was later converted in the sixteenth century into the College of Saint Thomas. During the twentieth century, this college was moved to the convent of Saints Dominic and Sixtus and ultimately became the Pontifical University of Saint Thomas Aquinas, known as the Angelicum.

input: Because of Oklahoma's position between zones of differing prevailing temperature and winds, weather patterns within the state can vary widely over relatively short distances and can change drastically in a short time. As an example, on November 11, 1911, the temperature at Oklahoma City reached 83 °F (28 °C) in the afternoon (the record high for that date), then an Arctic cold front of unprecedented intensity slammed across the state, causing the temperature to crash 66 degrees, down to 17 °F (−8 °C) at midnight (the record low for that date); thus, both the record high and record low for November 11 were set on the same date. This type of phenomenon is also responsible for many of the tornadoes in the area, such as the 1912 Oklahoma tornado outbreak, when a warm front traveled along a stalled cold front, resulting in an average of about one tornado per hour over the course of a day.
rewrite: Oklahoma's location at the convergence of distinct air masses and wind patterns leads to highly localized and rapidly shifting weather conditions. A striking instance occurred on November 11, 1911, in Oklahoma City. That afternoon, the mercury hit 83°F, setting a daily high record. Shortly after, an exceptionally powerful Arctic front swept through, plunging temperatures by 66 degrees to a record low of 17°F by midnight. Consequently, both the highest and lowest temperatures for that calendar date were established in a single day. Similar atmospheric clashes, where warm fronts override stationary cold fronts, generate the severe storms that frequent the region. This mechanism triggered events like the 1912 tornado outbreak, during which tornadoes formed at a rate of roughly one every hour for an entire day.

input: On September 21, 1529, Álvaro de Saavedra Cerón commanded the Spanish ship Florida, on his second attempt to recross the Pacific from the Maluku Islands. He stood off a group of islands from which local inhabitants hurled stones at his ship. These islands, which he named "Los Pintados", may have been Ujelang. On October 1, he found another group of islands where he went ashore for eight days, exchanged gifts with the local inhabitants and took on water. These islands, which he named "Los Jardines", may have been Enewetak or Bikini Atoll.
rewrite: On September 21, 1529, Spanish commander Álvaro de Saavedra Cerón, aboard the Florida, made a renewed effort to sail back across the Pacific from the Maluku region. His vessel faced stone-throwing residents near an island chain he called "Los Pintados," potentially Ujelang. By October 1, he reached another archipelago, possibly Enewetak or Bikini Atoll. There, he spent over a week ashore, engaged in friendly gift exchanges with locals, and replenished his water supplies, naming these islands "Los Jardines."

input: Modern navies that operate such aircraft carriers treat them as the capital ship of the fleet, a role previously held by the battleship. This change took place during World War II in response to air power becoming a significant factor in warfare, driven by the superior range, flexibility and effectiveness of carrier-launched aircraft. Following the war, carrier operations continued to increase in size and importance. Supercarriers, displacing 75,000 tonnes or greater, have become the pinnacle of carrier development. Some are powered by nuclear reactors and form the core of a fleet designed to operate far from home. Amphibious assault ships, such as USS Tarawa and HMS Ocean, serve the purpose of carrying and landing Marines, and operate a large contingent of helicopters for that purpose. Also known as "commando carriers" or "helicopter carriers", many have the capability to operate VSTOL aircraft.
rewrite: In contemporary naval forces, aircraft carriers are regarded as the principal vessels within a fleet, a status once occupied by battleships. This shift occurred throughout the Second World War as air power emerged as a decisive element in combat, largely due to the greater reach, adaptability, and potency of aircraft deployed from carriers. After the war, the scale and strategic value of carrier operations grew further. The apex of this evolution is the supercarrier, with displacements exceeding 75,000 tons. Many utilize nuclear propulsion and act as the central component of expeditionary fleets intended for distant operations. Ships like the USS Tarawa and HMS Ocean are amphibious assault vessels, designed to transport and deploy marine forces using a substantial complement of helicopters. Often called "commando" or "helicopter carriers," such ships frequently can also support vertical or short take-off and landing fixed-wing aircraft.

input: The earliest known human activity on the island dates to around the 10th millennium BC. Archaeological remains from this period include the well-preserved Neolithic village of Khirokitia, and Cyprus is home to some of the oldest water wells in the world. Cyprus was settled by Mycenaean Greeks in two waves in the 2nd millennium BC. As a strategic location in the Middle East, it was subsequently occupied by several major powers, including the empires of the Assyrians, Egyptians and Persians, from whom the island was seized in 333 BC by Alexander the Great. Subsequent rule by Ptolemaic Egypt, the Classical and Eastern Roman Empire, Arab caliphates for a short period, the French Lusignan dynasty and the Venetians, was followed by over three centuries of Ottoman rule between 1571 and 1878 (de jure until 1914).
rewrite: Human presence on the island can be traced as far back as approximately 10,000 BC. Evidence from this era features the remarkably intact Neolithic settlement of Khirokitia, alongside some of the planet's most ancient water wells. During the second millennium BC, Mycenaean Greeks established communities there in two distinct phases.
