Feynman alone agreed to testify. He argued the bar served an essential community function, listing its diverse clientele of tradespeople, engineers, laborers, and even an academic like himself. Although the establishment did not win its legal battle, it stayed in operation awaiting the result of a related appeal.

input: The period between 1815 and 1871 saw a large number of revolutionary attempts and independence wars. Balkan nations began to regain independence from the Ottoman Empire. Italy unified into a nation state. The capture of Rome in 1870 ended the Papal temporal power. Rivalry in a scramble for empires spread in what is known as The Age of Empire.
rewrite: From 1815 to 1871, numerous revolutions and wars for independence occurred. Balkan countries started winning freedom from Ottoman rule, while Italy became a unified state. The 1870 seizure of Rome concluded the Pope's worldly authority. Competition to build colonial empires intensified during this so-called Age of Empire.

input: The simplest way to gain information about brain anatomy is by visual inspection, but many more sophisticated techniques have been developed. Brain tissue in its natural state is too soft to work with, but it can be hardened by immersion in alcohol or other fixatives, and then sliced apart for examination of the interior. Visually, the interior of the brain consists of areas of so-called grey matter, with a dark color, separated by areas of white matter, with a lighter color. Further information can be gained by staining slices of brain tissue with a variety of chemicals that bring out areas where specific types of molecules are present in high concentrations. It is also possible to examine the microstructure of brain tissue using a microscope, and to trace the pattern of connections from one brain area to another.
rewrite: The most basic method for studying the brain's structure is through direct observation, though numerous advanced approaches now exist. Natural brain matter is overly soft for handling, but it can be solidified using preservatives like alcohol, then cut into thin sections to reveal its internal features. Inside, the brain displays regions of darker grey matter, interspersed with lighter white matter. Additional details emerge when applying chemical stains to tissue slices, which highlight zones rich in particular molecules. Microscopic analysis allows for the inspection of fine tissue details, and mapping techniques can reveal the connective pathways linking different brain regions.

input: Marvel earned a great deal of money and recognition during the comic book boom of the early 1990s, launching the successful 2099 line of comics set in the future (Spider-Man 2099, etc.) and the creatively daring though commercially unsuccessful Razorline imprint of superhero comics created by novelist and filmmaker Clive Barker. In 1990, Marvel began selling Marvel Universe Cards with trading card maker SkyBox International. These were collectible trading cards that featured the characters and events of the Marvel Universe. The 1990s saw the rise of variant covers, cover enhancements, swimsuit issues, and company-wide crossovers that affected the overall continuity of the fictional Marvel Universe
rewrite: During the comic industry's peak in the early 1990s, Marvel achieved significant financial success and acclaim. It introduced its futuristic 2099 series, including titles like Spider-Man 2099, and the Razorline imprint, a bold but less profitable superhero venture developed by Clive Barker. In 1990, Marvel partnered with SkyBox International to release collectible trading cards depicting its characters and stories. That decade also witnessed popular trends such as special edition covers, annual swimsuit editions, and expansive crossover events that shaped the broader Marvel narrative.

input: Von Neumann was the first to establish a rigorous mathematical framework for quantum mechanics, known as the Dirac–von Neumann axioms, with his 1932 work Mathematical Foundations of Quantum Mechanics. After having completed the axiomatization of set theory, he began to confront the axiomatization of quantum mechanics. He realized, in 1926, that a state of a quantum system could be represented by a point in a (complex) Hilbert space that, in general, could be infinite-dimensional even for a single particle. In this formalism of quantum mechanics, observable quantities such as position or momentum are represented as linear operators acting on the Hilbert space associated with the quantum system.
rewrite: John von Neumann pioneered a precise mathematical structure for quantum theory, referred to as the Dirac–von Neumann postulates, in his 1932 book. Following his earlier work in formalizing set theory, he turned to establishing quantum mechanics on an axiomatic basis. As early as 1926, he recognized that a quantum state could be described by a vector within a potentially infinite-dimensional complex Hilbert space, even for simple systems. Within this framework, measurable properties like position and momentum are characterized by linear operators working upon that system's Hilbert space.

input: Modern computers based on integrated circuits are millions to billions of times more capable than the early machines, and occupy a fraction of the space. Computers are small enough to fit into mobile devices, and mobile computers can be powered by small batteries. Personal computers in their various forms are icons of the Information Age and are generally considered as "computers". However, the embedded computers found in many devices from MP3 players to fighter aircraft and from electronic toys to industrial robots are the most numerous.
rewrite: Today's integrated circuit-based computers possess millions or billions of times the capacity of their predecessors, while taking up far less room. They are now compact enough for mobile devices, running on small batteries. While personal computers in diverse shapes symbolize the Information Age and are commonly seen as the standard, the most abundant type is actually the embedded computer, present in everything from MP3 players and toys to military jets and factory robots.

input: Countrywide, sued by California Attorney General Jerry Brown for "unfair business practices" and "false advertising" was making high cost mortgages "to homeowners with weak credit, adjustable rate mortgages (ARMs) that allowed homeowners to make interest-only payments". When housing prices decreased, homeowners in ARMs then had little incentive to pay their monthly payments, since their home equity had disappeared. This caused Countrywide's financial condition to deteriorate, ultimately resulting in a decision by the Office of Thrift Supervision to seize the lender.
rewrite: California's Attorney General Jerry Brown accused Countrywide of deceptive marketing and unethical operations, citing how the company issued expensive loans to borrowers with poor credit. These adjustable-rate mortgages permitted payments covering only interest. As property values fell, homeowners lost equity and motivation to continue payments, severely weakening Countrywide's finances. This decline led the Office of Thrift Supervision to take control of the lender.

input: According to the Hebrew Bible narrative, Jewish ancestry is traced back to the Biblical patriarchs such as Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, and the Biblical matriarchs Sarah, Rebecca, Leah, and Rachel, who lived in Canaan around the 18th century BCE. Jacob and his family migrated to Ancient Egypt after being invited to live with Jacob's son Joseph by the Pharaoh himself. The patriarchs' descendants were later enslaved until the Exodus led by Moses, traditionally dated to the 13th century BCE, after which the Israelites conquered Canaan.[citation needed]
rewrite: As depicted in the Hebrew Bible, Jewish lineage originates with the early forefathers and foremothers, including Abraham and Sarah, who resided in Canaan during the 1700s BCE. Their descendant Jacob's family later relocated to Egypt upon Joseph's invitation. Following a period of enslavement, their descendants, the Israelites, escaped under Moses's leadership in the 1200s BCE and subsequently settled in Canaan.

input: In May 2015, a coalition of more than 60 Asian-American organizations filed federal complaints with the Education and Justice Departments against Harvard University. The coalition asked for a civil rights investigation into what they described as Harvard's discriminatory admission practices against Asian-American applicants. The complaint asserts that recent studies indicate that Harvard has engaged in systematic and continuous discrimination against Asian Americans in its "holistic" admissions process. Asian-American applicants with near-perfect test scores, top-one-percent grade point averages, academic awards, and leadership positions are allegedly rejected by Harvard because the university uses racial stereotypes, racially differentiated standards, and de facto racial quotas. This federal complaint was dismissed in July 2015 because the Students for Fair Admissions lawsuit makes similar allegations.
rewrite: In May 2015, over sixty groups representing Asian-Americans submitted formal grievances to the U.S. Departments of Education and Justice targeting Harvard University. They requested an inquiry into alleged civil rights violations, charging the institution with biased treatment of Asian-American candidates during admissions. According to the filing, research shows Harvard has consistently discriminated within its comprehensive review system. Even candidates possessing exceptional grades, nearly flawless exam results, leadership roles, and scholastic honors reportedly face rejection. The complaint claims the university employs prejudiced assumptions, varying standards by race, and unofficial quotas. This federal action was closed in July 2015, as comparable claims were being pursued in an existing suit by Students for Fair Admissions.

input: The Georgics' tone wavers between optimism and pessimism, sparking critical debate on the poet's intentions, but the work lays the foundations for later didactic poetry. Virgil and Maecenas are said to have taken turns reading the Georgics to Octavian upon his return from defeating Antony and Cleopatra at the Battle of Actium in 31 BC.
rewrite: The Georgics' mood shifts from hopeful to bleak, fueling scholarly discussion over Virgil's aims, yet it established key conventions for future instructional verse. Reportedly, Virgil and Maecenas alternately recited the work to Octavian after his victory at Actium in 31 BC.

input: IBM has been a leading proponent of the Open Source Initiative, and began supporting Linux in 1998. The company invests billions of dollars in services and software based on Linux through the IBM Linux Technology Center, which includes over 300 Linux kernel developers. IBM has also released code under different open source licenses, such as the platform-independent software framework Eclipse (worth approximately US$40 million at the time of the donation), the three-sentence International Components for Unicode (ICU) license, and the Java-based relational database management system (RDBMS) Apache Derby. IBM's open source involvement has not been trouble-free, however (see SCO v. IBM).
rewrite: IBM has long championed open source efforts, adopting Linux as early as 1998. Through its Linux Technology Center, which employs hundreds of kernel developers, the corporation channels significant investment into Linux-related services and software. It has contributed substantial projects to the open source community, including the Eclipse framework, the International Components for Unicode, and the Apache Derby database system. Despite this strong commitment, IBM's open source journey has encountered legal challenges, such as the notable lawsuit with SCO.

input: Plans for arena football were put on hold in 1982 as the United States Football League was launched. Foster left the NFL to accept a position in the USFL. He eventually became executive vice-president with the Chicago Blitz, where he returned to his concept of arena football. In 1983, he began organizing the test game in his spare time from his job with the Blitz. By 1985, the USFL had ceased football operations and he began devoting all his time to arena football, and on April 27, 1986, his concept was realized when the test game was played.
rewrite: The introduction of the United States Football League in 1982 delayed arena football's development. Foster departed the NFL to join the USFL, later rising to executive vice-president for the Chicago Blitz. There, he revisited his indoor football idea. Starting in 1983, he used his spare moments while with the Blitz to plan a trial match. After the USFL ended operations in 1985, he focused entirely on this project. His vision came to life on April 27, 1986, when the experimental game was finally held.

input: When auto-changing turntables were commonplace, records were typically pressed with a raised (or ridged) outer edge and a raised label area, allowing records to be stacked onto each other without the delicate grooves coming into contact, reducing the risk of damage. Auto-changers included a mechanism to support a stack of several records above the turntable itself, dropping them one at a time onto the active turntable to be played in order. Many longer sound recordings, such as complete operas, were interleaved across several 10-inch or 12-inch discs for use with auto-changing mechanisms, so that the first disk of a three-disk recording would carry sides 1 and 6 of the program, while the second disk would carry sides 2 and 5, and the third, sides 3 and 4, allowing sides 1, 2, and 3 to be played automatically; then the whole stack reversed to play sides 4, 5, and 6.
rewrite: During the era when automatic record players were widely used, vinyl discs were manufactured with elevated rims and central label sections. This design enabled them to be safely stacked, preventing the sensitive grooves from touching and thus minimizing potential wear. These auto-changing systems featured a specialized apparatus that held multiple records above the platter, releasing them sequentially to be played in a set order. Extended audio works, like full operas, were often distributed across multiple 10- or 12-inch records, arranged specifically for such devices. For a three-disc set, the sides would be sequenced so that disc one contained parts 1 and 6, disc two held parts 2 and 5, and disc three included parts 3 and 4. This arrangement allowed the first three sides to play automatically; the entire stack would then be flipped to play the remaining three sides in correct order.

input: Tehran is the country's capital and largest city, as well as its leading cultural and economic center. Iran is a major regional and middle power, exerting considerable influence in international energy security and the world economy through its large reserves of fossil fuels, which include the largest natural gas supply in the world and the fourth-largest proven oil reserves. Iran's rich cultural legacy is reflected in part by its 19 UNESCO World Heritage Sites, the fourth-largest number in Asia and 12th-largest in the world.
rewrite: As Iran's primary city, Tehran serves as the national capital and its foremost hub for culture and commerce. The nation holds significant regional and global influence, largely due to its extensive fossil fuel resources; it possesses the biggest natural gas reserves and the fourth-largest proven oil deposits globally. This impact extends to world energy security and the economy. Iran's deep cultural history is evidenced by its 19 UNESCO World Heritage locations, ranking fourth in Asia and twelfth worldwide.

input: Model plants such as Arabidopsis thaliana are used for studying the molecular biology of plant cells and the chloroplast. Ideally, these organisms have small genomes that are well known or completely sequenced, small stature and short generation times. Corn has been used to study mechanisms of photosynthesis and phloem loading of sugar in C4 plants. The single celled green alga Chlamydomonas reinhardtii, while not an embryophyte itself, contains a green-pigmented chloroplast related to that of land plants, making it useful for study. A red alga Cyanidioschyzon merolae has also been used to study some basic chloroplast functions. Spinach, peas, soybeans and a moss Physcomitrella patens are commonly used to study plant cell biology.
rewrite: Research in plant molecular biology and chloroplast function often employs specific model organisms. Arabidopsis thaliana is widely chosen due to its compact, fully sequenced genome, small size, and rapid life cycle. For exploring photosynthesis and sugar transport in C4 plants, corn serves as a key subject. The green alga Chlamydomonas reinhardtii, though not a land plant, possesses a similar chloroplast and is valuable for analysis. Studies of fundamental chloroplast operations sometimes utilize the red alga Cyanidioschyzon merolae. Additionally, common systems for cellular research include spinach, peas, soybeans, and the moss Physcomitrella patens.

input: Following the German unconditional surrender, Eisenhower was appointed Military Governor of the U.S. Occupation Zone, based at the IG Farben Building in Frankfurt am Main. He had no responsibility for the other three zones, controlled by Britain, France and the Soviet Union, except for the city of Berlin, which was managed by the Four-Power Authorities through the Allied Kommandatura as the governing body. Upon discovery of the Nazi concentration camps, he ordered camera crews to document evidence of the atrocities in them for use in the Nuremberg Trials. He reclassified German prisoners of war (POWs) in U.S. custody as Disarmed Enemy Forces (DEFs), who were no longer subject to the Geneva Convention. Eisenhower followed the orders laid down by the Joint Chiefs of Staff (JCS) in directive JCS 1067, but softened them by bringing in 400,000 tons of food for civilians and allowing more fraternization. In response to the devastation in Germany, including food shortages and an influx of refugees, he arranged distribution of American food and medical equipment. His actions reflected the new American attitudes of the German people as Nazi victims not villains, while aggressively purging the ex-Nazis.
rewrite:
After Germany's complete capitulation, Eisenhower assumed the role of Military Governor for the American sector of occupation, operating from Frankfurt am Main's IG Farben Building. His authority was confined to this zone, with the British, French, and Soviet administrations controlling the others. A shared responsibility existed only for Berlin, governed collectively by the four Allied powers via the Allied Kommandatura. When Nazi death camps were uncovered, he directed film teams to record the horrors to provide evidence for the upcoming war crimes tribunals at Nuremberg. He also changed the status of captured German soldiers under American watch to Disarmed Enemy Forces, thereby removing their protections under international prisoner of war treaties.

While implementing the strict occupation policies mandated by the Joint Chiefs of Staff, Eisenhower introduced mitigating measures. These included importing substantial food supplies for the populace and permitting more interaction between troops and civilians. Confronted with widespread ruin, famine, and a flood of displaced persons, he organized the provision of U.S. food and medicine. His conduct demonstrated a shifting U.S. perspective that viewed the German public more as casualties of the Nazi regime than as accomplices, even as he pursued a vigorous campaign to remove former party members from influence.

input: These critics of the modern separation of church and state also note the official establishment of religion in several of the states at the time of ratification, to suggest that the modern incorporation of the Establishment Clause as to state governments goes against the original constitutional intent.[citation needed] The issue is complex, however, as the incorporation ultimately bases on the passage of the 14th Amendment in 1868, at which point the first amendment's application to the state government was recognized. Many of these constitutional debates relate to the competing interpretive theories of originalism versus modern, progressivist theories such as the doctrine of the Living Constitution. Other debates center on the principle of the law of the land in America being defined not just by the Constitution's Supremacy Clause, but also by legal precedence, making an accurate reading of the Constitution subject to the mores and values of a given era, and rendering the concept of historical revisionism irrelevant when discussing the Constitution.
rewrite: Some commentators who question the contemporary division between religious institutions and government point to the fact that several states had officially sanctioned religions when the Constitution was ratified. They argue this indicates that applying the Establishment Clause to state governments today contradicts the framers' initial purpose. The situation is nuanced, however, because this application stems from the Fourteenth Amendment, adopted in 1868, which later led to the First Amendment being extended to the states. These discussions often stem from broader conflicts between originalist interpretation and evolving doctrines like the Living Constitution. Further debates highlight that American jurisprudence is shaped not only by the Constitution's supreme authority but also by judicial precedent. This means constitutional understanding is inevitably influenced by the prevailing norms of the time, which makes the idea of historical revisionism largely moot in constitutional analysis.

input: The official language of the Republic is Modern Standard Arabic. Arabic was adopted by the Egyptians after the Arab invasion of Egypt. The spoken languages are: Egyptian Arabic (68%), Sa'idi Arabic (29%), Eastern Egyptian Bedawi Arabic (1.6%), Sudanese Arabic (0.6%), Domari (0.3%), Nobiin (0.3%), Beja (0.1%), Siwi and others. Additionally, Greek, Armenian and Italian are the main languages of immigrants. In Alexandria in the 19th century there was a large community of Italian Egyptians and Italian was the "lingua franca" of the city.
rewrite: Modern Standard Arabic serves as the official language of the Republic, introduced historically following the Arab conquest. Common spoken dialects include Egyptian and Sa'idi Arabic, alongside smaller communities using Bedawi, Sudanese, Domari, Nobiin, Beja, and Siwi. Immigrant populations primarily speak Greek, Armenian, and Italian. Notably, during the 1800s, Italian functioned as the common tongue in Alexandria due to a significant Italian-Egyptian community.

input: Catalan is split in two major dialectal blocks: Eastern Catalan, and Western Catalan. The main difference lies in the treatment of unstressed a and e; which have merged to /ə/ in Eastern dialects, but which remain distinct as /a/ and /e/ in Western dialects. There are a few other differences in pronunciation, verbal morphology, and vocabulary.
rewrite: Catalan divides into two principal dialect groups: Eastern and Western. Their key distinction involves unstressed vowels a and e; these blend into /ə/ in the east but stay separate as /a/ and /e/ in the west. Additional variations occur in sound, verb forms, and words.

input: On basic Church teachings, the pope was unwavering. On the tenth anniversary of Humanae vitae, he reconfirmed this teaching. In his style and methodology, he was a disciple of Pius XII, whom he deeply revered. He suffered for the attacks on Pius XII for his alleged silences during the Holocaust. Pope Paul VI was less outstanding than his predecessors: he was not credited with an encyclopedic memory, nor a gift for languages, nor the brilliant writing style of Pius XII, nor did he have the charisma and outpouring love, sense of humor and human warmth of John XXIII. He took on himself the unfinished reform work of these two popes, bringing them diligently with great humility and common sense and without much fanfare to conclusion. In doing so, Paul VI saw himself following in the footsteps of the Apostle Paul, torn to several directions as Saint Paul, who said, "I am attracted to two sides at once, because the Cross always divides."
rewrite: Regarding fundamental Church doctrine, the pope remained resolute. Marking a decade since Humanae vitae, he reaffirmed its principles. In his approach and execution, he followed the example of Pius XII, for whom he held profound respect, and he felt pain over criticisms directed at Pius concerning his purported quiet during the Holocaust. Pope Paul VI did not possess the exceptional qualities of those before him: he lacked the vast memory, linguistic talent, or eloquent prose of Pius XII, and he did not exhibit the charismatic affection, wit, or approachability of John XXIII. He assumed the incomplete reforms initiated by both pontiffs, carrying them forward with quiet dedication, marked by humility and practicality, to their fulfillment. In this endeavor, Paul VI perceived himself as emulating the Apostle Paul, feeling similarly pulled in conflicting directions, much as Saint Paul expressed being drawn to opposing forces, since the Cross inherently creates division.

input: The earliest known document in Galician-Portuguese dates from 1228. The Foro do bo burgo do Castro Caldelas was granted by Alfonso IX of León to the town of Burgo, in Castro Caldelas, after the model of the constitutions of the town of Allariz. A distinct Galician Literature emerged during the Middle Ages: In the 13th century important contributions were made to the romance canon in Galician-Portuguese, the most notable those by the troubadour Martín Codax, the priest Airas Nunes, King Denis of Portugal and King Alfonso X of Castile, Alfonso O Sabio ("Alfonso the Wise"), the same monarch who began the process of establishing the hegemony of Castilian. During this period, Galician-Portuguese was considered the language of love poetry in the Iberian Romance linguistic culture. The names and memories of Codax and other popular cultural figures are well preserved in modern Galicia and, despite the long period of Castilian linguistic domination, these names are again household words.
rewrite: The oldest surviving text written in Galician-Portuguese originates from 1228. This document, the Foro do bo burgo do Castro Caldelas, was a charter given by King Alfonso IX of León to the town of Burgo. It was modeled on the legal framework established for Allariz. A unique literary tradition in Galician began to flourish in the medieval era. The 13th century, in particular, saw major works added to the romance genre in Galician-Portuguese. Prominent authors from this time include the troubadour Martín Codax, the cleric Airas Nunes, Portuguese King Denis, and Alfonso X of Castile, known as "the Wise," whose reign also initiated the rise of Castilian Spanish. At that time, Galician-Portuguese was regarded as the principal language for lyric poetry across the Iberian Peninsula. The legacies of Codax and similar iconic figures remain strongly alive in Galicia today. Even after centuries of Castilian linguistic influence, these names are once again commonly recognized.

input: The city is home to New Haven Promise, a scholarship funded by Yale University for students who meet the requirements. Students must be enrolled in a public high school (charters included) for four years, be a resident of the city during that time, carry a 3.0 cumulative grade-point average, have a 90-percent attendance rate and perform 40 hours of service to the city. The initiative was launched in 2010 and there are currently more than 500 Scholars enrolled in qualifying Connecticut colleges and universities. There are more than 60 cities in the country that have a Promise-type program for their students.
rewrite: New Haven Promise is a Yale University-funded scholarship available to local students. To qualify, applicants must complete all four years at a public or charter high school within the city, maintain a 3.0 GPA, achieve 90% attendance, and contribute 40 hours of community service. Established in 2010, the program now supports over 500 Scholars attending eligible colleges across Connecticut. Similar initiatives, known as Promise programs, exist in more than 60 other cities nationwide.

input: Red was the color of the banner of the Byzantine emperors. In Western Europe, Emperor Charlemagne painted his palace red as a very visible symbol of his authority, and wore red shoes at his coronation. Kings, princes and, beginning in 1295, Roman Catholic cardinals began to wear red costumes. When Abbe Suger rebuilt Saint Denis Basilica outside Paris in the early 12th century, he added stained glass windows colored blue cobalt glass and red glass tinted with copper. Together they flooded the basilica with a mystical light. Soon stained glass windows were being added to cathedrals all across France, England and Germany. In Medieval painting red was used to attract attention to the most important figures; both Christ and the Virgin Mary were commonly painted wearing red mantles.
rewrite: The Byzantine imperial standard prominently featured the color red. In the West, Charlemagne chose red for his palace walls to clearly convey his power, and he donned red footwear during his coronation ceremony. Royalty and high nobility adopted red garments, as did Catholic cardinals from 1295 onward. During the reconstruction of Saint Denis Basilica near Paris in the 1100s, Abbe Suger installed stained glass using cobalt for blue and copper for red, filling the church with an ethereal glow. This style of stained glass rapidly spread to cathedrals throughout France, England, and Germany. In medieval art, red hues were strategically employed to highlight central subjects, such as the red robes often worn by figures of Christ and the Virgin Mary.

input: Democratic Party candidates were consistently elected to local office, increasing the city's ties to the South and its dominant party. In 1861, Mayor Fernando Wood called on the aldermen to declare independence from Albany and the United States after the South seceded, but his proposal was not acted on. Anger at new military conscription laws during the American Civil War (1861–1865), which spared wealthier men who could afford to pay a $300 (equivalent to $5,766 in 2016) commutation fee to hire a substitute, led to the Draft Riots of 1863, whose most visible participants were ethnic Irish working class. The situation deteriorated into attacks on New York's elite, followed by attacks on black New Yorkers and their property after fierce competition for a decade between Irish immigrants and blacks for work. Rioters burned the Colored Orphan Asylum to the ground, but more than 200 children escaped harm due to efforts of the New York City Police Department, which was mainly made up of Irish immigrants. According to historian James M. McPherson (2001), at least 120 people were killed. In all, eleven black men were lynched over five days, and the riots forced hundreds of blacks to flee the city for Williamsburg, Brooklyn, as well as New Jersey; the black population in Manhattan fell below 10,000 by 1865, which it had last been in 1820. The white working class had established dominance. Violence by longshoremen against black men was especially fierce in the docks area. It was one of the worst incidents of civil unrest in American history.
rewrite: Local elections repeatedly saw Democratic Party candidates win, strengthening the city's connections to the South and its leading political faction. Following Southern secession in 1861, Mayor Fernando Wood urged the city council to proclaim independence from both the state and federal governments, though this suggestion was ultimately ignored. Widespread resentment erupted during the Civil War over conscription policies that allowed affluent individuals to avoid service by paying a $300 fee to provide a substitute. This anger fueled the 1863 Draft Riots, where Irish immigrant laborers formed a conspicuous segment of the mob. Protests rapidly devolved into assaults against the city's wealthy, and then turned brutally toward African American residents and their homes, fueled by years of intense job rivalry between Irish newcomers and black workers. Rioters destroyed the Colored Orphan Asylum by fire, but police—many of whom were Irish immigrants—ensured the safe escape of over two hundred children. Historical accounts, including those by scholar James M. McPherson, report a minimum of 120 fatalities. Over the five-day upheaval, eleven black men were lynched, and hundreds fled to places like Williamsburg, Brooklyn, and New Jersey. Manhattan's African American population plummeted, dropping under 10,000 by 1865—a level not seen since 1820. This cemented control by the white laboring class, with particularly brutal violence against black men occurring along the waterfront. The episode stands among the most severe cases of domestic strife in the nation's past.

input: 90th Street is split into two segments. The first segment, West 90th Street begins at Riverside Drive and ends at Central Park West or West Drive, when it is open, in Central Park on the Upper West Side. The second segment of East 90th Street begins at East Drive, at Engineers Gate of Central Park. When East Drive is closed, East 90th Street begins at Fifth Avenue on the Upper East Side and curves to the right at the FDR Drive becoming East End Avenue. Our Lady of Good Counsel Church, is located on East 90th Street between Third Avenue and Second Avenue, across the street from Ruppert Towers (1601 and 1619 Third Avenue) and Ruppert Park. Asphalt Green, which is located on East 90th Street between York Avenue and East End Avenue.
rewrite: Nineteeth Street consists of two separate parts. On the Upper West Side, West 90th Street runs from Riverside Drive to the edge of Central Park, terminating at Central Park West or, when accessible, West Drive. Conversely, East 90th Street starts at Engineers Gate on East Drive within the park. If that route is blocked, it commences at Fifth Avenue on the Upper East Side, bending right near the FDR Drive to become East End Avenue. Key landmarks include Our Lady of Good Counsel Church, situated between Third and Second Avenues opposite Ruppert Towers and its adjacent park, and Asphalt Green, found between York Avenue and East End Avenue.

input: Tuvalu participates in the Alliance of Small Island States (AOSIS), which is a coalition of small island and low-lying coastal countries that have concerns about their vulnerability to the adverse effects of global climate change. Under the Majuro Declaration, which was signed on 5 September 2013, Tuvalu has commitment to implement power generation of 100% renewable energy (between 2013 and 2020), which is proposed to be implemented using Solar PV (95% of demand) and biodiesel (5% of demand). The feasibility of wind power generation will be considered. Tuvalu participates in the operations of the Pacific Islands Applied Geoscience Commission (SOPAC) and the Secretariat of the Pacific Regional Environment Programme (SPREP).
rewrite: Tuvalu is a member of the Alliance of Small Island States (AOSIS), a group of island and coastal nations particularly threatened by climate change impacts. Through the Majuro Declaration of September 2013, the nation pledged to achieve total renewable power generation by 2020. This plan primarily involves using solar photovoltaics to meet 95% of energy needs, supplemented by biodiesel for the remaining 5%. The potential for wind energy is also under assessment. Additionally, Tuvalu takes part in the activities of the Pacific Islands Applied Geoscience Commission and the Secretariat of the Pacific Regional Environment Programme.

input: In higher organisms (like people), these two modes of perception combine into what Whitehead terms "symbolic reference", which links appearance with causation in a process that is so automatic that both people and animals have difficulty refraining from it. By way of illustration, Whitehead uses the example of a person's encounter with a chair. An ordinary person looks up, sees a colored shape, and immediately infers that it is a chair. However, an artist, Whitehead supposes, "might not have jumped to the notion of a chair", but instead "might have stopped at the mere contemplation of a beautiful color and a beautiful shape." This is not the normal human reaction; most people place objects in categories by habit and instinct, without even thinking about it. Moreover, animals do the same thing. Using the same example, Whitehead points out that a dog "would have acted immediately on the hypothesis of a chair and would have jumped onto it by way of using it as such." In this way symbolic reference is a fusion of pure sense perceptions on the one hand and causal relations on the other, and that it is in fact the causal relationships that dominate the more basic mentality (as the dog illustrates), while it is the sense perceptions which indicate a higher grade mentality (as the artist illustrates).
rewrite: In complex life forms such as humans, these two perceptual methods merge into what Whitehead calls "symbolic reference." This process connects sensory impressions with cause-and-effect understanding so seamlessly that both people and animals find it hard to avoid. To demonstrate, Whitehead describes someone noticing a chair. A typical individual glances at a colored form and instantly concludes it is a chair. In contrast, an artist, Whitehead suggests, may pause at simply admiring the pleasing hue and contour, without rushing to label it. This reflective response is uncommon; usually, humans and animals alike classify things automatically through ingrained habit. A dog, for instance, would promptly accept the object as a chair and leap onto it for use. Thus, symbolic reference blends raw sensory data with interpretations of causality. The more primitive mental tendency, shown by the dog, is governed by immediate practical relations. Meanwhile, a more advanced mentality, exemplified by the artist, gives greater emphasis to the sensory qualities themselves.

input: Above the forestry, there is often a band of short pine trees (Pinus mugo), which is in turn superseded by Alpenrosen, dwarf shrubs, typically Rhododendron ferrugineum (on acid soils) or Rhododendron hirsutum (on alkaline soils). Although the Alpenrose prefers acidic soil, the plants are found throughout the region. Above the tree line is the area defined as "alpine" where in the alpine meadow plants are found that have adapted well to harsh conditions of cold temperatures, aridity, and high altitudes. The alpine area fluctuates greatly because of regional fluctuations in tree lines.
rewrite: Above the forested areas, a zone of low-growing mountain pines (Pinus mugo) commonly appears, followed by Alpenrosen—small shrubs, usually Rhododendron ferrugineum in acidic earth or Rhododendron hirsutum in alkaline conditions. While these shrubs favor acidic soil, they grow across the entire region. Beyond the tree line lies the alpine zone, characterized by meadows where vegetation has adjusted to severe cold, dryness, and elevation. This alpine region varies significantly due to local differences in where trees can grow.

input: Carpet-weaving is historically a major traditional profession for the majority of Armenian women, including many Armenian families. Prominent Karabakh carpet weavers there were men too. The oldest extant Armenian carpet from the region, referred to as Artsakh (see also Karabakh carpet) during the medieval era, is from the village of Banants (near Gandzak) and dates to the early 13th century. The first time that the Armenian word for carpet, gorg, was used in historical sources was in a 1242–1243 Armenian inscription on the wall of the Kaptavan Church in Artsakh.
rewrite: Historically, carpet-weaving has been a primary vocation for most Armenian women and their households. Notably, in Karabakh, skilled male weavers also practiced the craft. The region's earliest surviving Armenian carpet originates from Banants village near Gandzak and was made in the 13th century. Additionally, the term "gorg," meaning carpet in Armenian, first appears in historical records from a 1242–1243 inscription on the Kaptavan Church in Artsakh.

input: "Azure, three ships with three masts, rigged and under full sail, the sails, pennants and ensigns Argent, each charged with a cross Gules; on a chief of the second a pale quarterly Azure and Gules, on the 1st and 4th a fleur-de-lis or, on the 2nd and 3rd a leopard or, between two roses Gules seeded Or barbed Vert." The shield had as a crest: "A sphere without a frame, bounded with the Zodiac in bend Or, between two pennants flottant Argent, each charged with a cross Gules, over the sphere the words DEUS INDICAT" (Latin: God Indicates). The supporters were two sea lions (lions with fishes' tails) and the motto was DEO DUCENTE NIL NOCET (Latin: Where God Leads, Nothing Hurts).
rewrite: On an azure field, three silver sailing ships with three masts display red crosses on their sails, flags, and pennants. Above this, a silver band features a central vertical stripe divided into blue and red quarters. The blue quarters each bear a gold fleur-de-lis, while the red quarters show a gold leopard, all positioned between two red roses with gold seeds and green leaves. The crest above the shield is a golden celestial sphere encircled by a zodiac band, flanked by two floating silver pennants marked with red crosses, and inscribed with "DEUS INDICAT." The shield is supported by two sea lions and bears the motto "DEO DUCENTE NIL NOCET."

input: Immunology is a branch of biomedical science that covers the study of immune systems in all organisms. It charts, measures, and contextualizes the: physiological functioning of the immune system in states of both health and diseases; malfunctions of the immune system in immunological disorders (such as autoimmune diseases, hypersensitivities, immune deficiency, and transplant rejection); the physical, chemical and physiological characteristics of the components of the immune system in vitro, in situ, and in vivo. Immunology has applications in numerous disciplines of medicine, particularly in the fields of organ transplantation, oncology, virology, bacteriology, parasitology, psychiatry, and dermatology.
rewrite: Immunology is a field of biomedical research focused on understanding immune systems across various life forms. It examines and interprets the normal and diseased operations of these defenses, including failures like autoimmune conditions, allergies, immunodeficiency, and transplant rejection. The discipline also analyzes the properties and behaviors of immune components in laboratory, natural, and living settings. Its insights are crucial to many medical areas, including transplant medicine, cancer treatment, infectious disease studies, and specialties like psychiatry and dermatology.

input: In 1911 arsphenamine, the first synthetic anti-infective drug, was developed by Paul Ehrlich and chemist Alfred Bertheim of the Institute of Experimental Therapy in Berlin. The drug was given the commercial name Salvarsan. Ehrlich, noting both the general toxicity of arsenic and the selective absorption of certain dyes by bacteria, hypothesized that an arsenic-containing dye with similar selective absorption properties could be used to treat bacterial infections. Arsphenamine was prepared as part of a campaign to synthesize a series of such compounds, and found to exhibit partially selective toxicity. Arsphenamine proved to be the first effective treatment for syphilis, a disease which prior to that time was incurable and led inexorably to severe skin ulceration, neurological damage, and death.[citation needed]
rewrite: In 1911, Paul Ehrlich and Alfred Bertheim, working at Berlin's Institute of Experimental Therapy, created arsphenamine. Marketed as Salvarsan, this was the initial man-made medication designed to fight infections. Ehrlich's idea stemmed from observing that while arsenic is poisonous, some dyes are absorbed specifically by bacteria. He theorized that a dye containing arsenic could exploit this to target infections without excessive harm to the patient. This drug resulted from a systematic effort to produce such targeted compounds and demonstrated a degree of this selective toxicity. It became the pioneering cure for syphilis, a previously untreatable illness that always progressed to devastating skin sores, nerve destruction, and fatality.

input: This constitution was created when the U.S. Congress directed local government to organize a constitutional convention to write the Puerto Rico Constitution in 1951. The acceptance of that constitution by Puerto Rico's electorate, the U.S. Congress, and the U.S. president occurred in 1952. In addition, the rights, privileges and immunities attendant to United States citizens are "respected in Puerto Rico to the same extent as though Puerto Rico were a state of the union" through the express extension of the Privileges and Immunities Clause of the U.S. Constitution by the U.S. Congress in 1948.
rewrite: In 1951, the U.S. Congress instructed Puerto Rico's government to convene a body for drafting its own constitution. This document was subsequently ratified in 1952 by the island's voters, Congress, and the President. Furthermore, since 1948, Congress has explicitly applied the U.S. Constitution's Privileges and Immunities Clause to the territory. This ensures that the rights and protections for U.S. citizens are upheld in Puerto Rico as fully as they would be in any state.

input: Today, this term also refers to the doctrines and practices of the Reformed churches of which Calvin was an early leader. Less commonly, it can refer to the individual teaching of Calvin himself. The particulars of Calvinist theology may be stated in a number of ways. Perhaps the best known summary is contained in the five points of Calvinism, though these points identify the Calvinist view on soteriology rather than summarizing the system as a whole. Broadly speaking, Calvinism stresses the sovereignty or rule of God in all things — in salvation but also in all of life. This concept is seen clearly in the doctrines of predestination and total depravity.
rewrite: In contemporary usage, this designation encompasses the beliefs and customs of the Reformed Christian tradition, a movement John Calvin helped pioneer. On occasion, it may denote Calvin's personal theological positions. The tenets of this theology can be articulated through various frameworks. Its most famous outline is the five points of Calvinism, which specifically detail its perspective on salvation rather than providing a complete overview. Generally, Calvinism emphasizes God's supreme authority over everything—not only in redemption but across all existence. This foundational principle is particularly evident in the teachings of predestination and total human depravity.

input: The Pagode de Vincennes Buddhist temple, near Lake Daumesnil in the Bois de Vincennes, is the former Cameroon pavilion from the 1931 Paris Colonial Exposition. It hosts several different schools of Buddhism, and does not have a single leader. It shelters the biggest Buddha statue in Europe, more than nine metres high. There are two other small temples located in the Asian community in the 13th arrondissement. A Hindu temple, dedicated to Ganesh, on Rue Pajol in the 18th arrondissement, opened in 1985.
rewrite: Originally built as the Cameroon pavilion for the 1931 Colonial Exposition in Paris, the Pagode de Vincennes now serves as a Buddhist temple near Bois de Vincennes' Lake Daumesnil. It accommodates multiple Buddhist traditions without a central authority and houses Europe's tallest Buddha statue, standing over nine meters. Additionally, two smaller temples exist in the 13th arrondissement's Asian district, and a Hindu temple devoted to Ganesh has operated on Rue Pajol in the 18th arrondissement since 1985.

input: There have been cases of a variety of speech being deliberately reclassified to serve political purposes. One example is Moldovan. In 1996, the Moldovan parliament, citing fears of "Romanian expansionism", rejected a proposal from President Mircea Snegur to change the name of the language to Romanian, and in 2003 a Moldovan–Romanian dictionary was published, purporting to show that the two countries speak different languages. Linguists of the Romanian Academy reacted by declaring that all the Moldovan words were also Romanian words; while in Moldova, the head of the Academy of Sciences of Moldova, Ion Bărbuţă, described the dictionary as a politically motivated "absurdity".
rewrite: Political objectives have sometimes driven the reclassification of language varieties. For instance, in Moldova, the state language remains officially designated as Moldovan. In 1996, the parliament, expressing concerns over potential "Romanian expansionism," declined a presidential initiative to rename it Romanian. Later, a 2003 dictionary aimed to demonstrate a distinction between Moldovan and Romanian. Romanian linguists countered that its entries were entirely encompassed within Romanian, and a leading Moldovan academic dismissed the work as a politically fueled absurdity.

input: The Neapolitan style has an almond-shaped body resembling a bowl, constructed from curved strips of wood. It usually has a bent sound table, canted in two planes with the design to take the tension of the 8 metal strings arranged in four courses. A hardwood fingerboard sits on top of or is flush with the sound table. Very old instruments may use wooden tuning pegs, while newer instruments tend to use geared metal tuners. The bridge is a movable length of hardwood. A pickguard is glued below the sound hole under the strings. European roundbacks commonly use a 13-inch scale instead of the 13.876 common on archtop Mandolins.
rewrite: Neapolitan mandolins feature an almond-like body formed into a bowl shape using bent wooden segments. Their soundboard is intentionally arched in two directions to withstand the pull of eight metal strings, which are grouped in four pairs. The fingerboard, made of hardwood, is positioned level with or atop this soundboard. While antique versions often have simple wooden pegs for tuning, modern ones typically employ geared metal machines. The hardwood bridge can be adjusted, and a protective pickguard is fixed beneath the sound hole. These European roundbacks usually have a string scale of 13 inches, shorter than the 13.876 inches typical of archtop mandolins.

input: Midtown Raleigh is a residential and commercial area just North of the I-440 Beltline and is part of North Raleigh. It is roughly framed by Glenwood/Creedmoor Road to the West, Wake Forest Road to the East, and Millbrook Road to the North. It includes shopping centers such as North Hills and Crabtree Valley Mall. It also includes North Hills Park and part of the Raleigh Greenway System. The term was coined by the Greater Raleigh Chamber of Commerce, developer John Kane and planning director Mitchell Silver. The News & Observer newspaper started using the term for marketing purposes only. The Midtown Raleigh Alliance was founded on July 25, 2011 as a way for community leaders to promote the area.
rewrite: Located north of the I-440 Beltline within North Raleigh, Midtown Raleigh is a mixed-use neighborhood. Its approximate boundaries are Glenwood/Creedmoor Road on the west, Wake Forest Road on the east, and Millbrook Road to the north. The district features retail hubs like North Hills and Crabtree Valley Mall, along with North Hills Park and a section of the Raleigh Greenway trails. The name originated from a collaboration between the Greater Raleigh Chamber of Commerce, developer John Kane, and planning director Mitchell Silver. Initially adopted for promotional use by The News & Observer, the area gained a formal advocacy group when the Midtown Raleigh Alliance was established on July 25, 2011.

input: During the fighting, the Communards killed c. 500 people, including the Archbishop of Paris, and burned down many government buildings, including the Tuileries Palace and the Hotel de Ville. Communards captured with weapons were routinely shot by the army and Government troops killed from 7,000–30,000 Communards in the fighting and in massacres of men, women, and children during and after the Commune. More recent histories, based on studies of the number buried in Paris cemeteries and in mass graves after the fall of the Commune, put the number killed at between 6,000 and 10,000. Twenty-six courts were established to try more than 40,000 people who had been arrested, which took until 1875 and imposed 95 death sentences, of which 23 were inflicted. Forced labour for life was imposed on 251 people, 1,160 people were transported to "a fortified place" and 3,417 people were transported. About 20,000 Communards were held in prison hulks until released in 1872 and a great many Communards fled abroad to England, Switzerland, Belgium or the United States. The survivors were amnestied by a bill introduced by Gambetta in 1880 and allowed to return.
rewrite: Amidst the conflict, the Communards were responsible for approximately 500 fatalities, among them the Archbishop of Paris, and the destruction of numerous official structures, such as the Tuileries Palace and the Hotel de Ville. In turn, army forces summarily executed any captured Communard found armed, and governmental troops slaughtered thousands—estimates range from 7,000 to 30,000—of the Commune's supporters, encompassing men, women, and children both during and after the uprising. Contemporary analysis, examining burial records from Paris cemeteries and mass graves following the Commune's defeat, suggests the actual death toll likely fell between 6,000 and 10,000. Subsequent legal proceedings involved 26 tribunals adjudicating over 40,000 detainees, a process lasting until 1875. These trials resulted in 95 death penalties, with 23 carried out, 251 individuals receiving life sentences of hard labor, and 1,160 being exiled to fortified locations, while 3,417 others were transported. Roughly 20,000 were confined to prison ships until their 1872 release, and many more sought exile in nations like England, Switzerland, Belgium, or the United States. Ultimately, the remaining exiles were granted amnesty through legislation championed by Gambetta in 1880, permitting their repatriation.

input: In the Roman Catholic Church, obstinate and willful manifest heresy is considered to spiritually cut one off from the Church, even before excommunication is incurred. The Codex Justinianus (1:5:12) defines "everyone who is not devoted to the Catholic Church and to our Orthodox holy Faith" a heretic. The Church had always dealt harshly with strands of Christianity that it considered heretical, but before the 11th century these tended to centre around individual preachers or small localised sects, like Arianism, Pelagianism, Donatism, Marcionism and Montanism. The diffusion of the almost Manichaean sect of Paulicians westwards gave birth to the famous 11th and 12th century heresies of Western Europe. The first one was that of Bogomils in modern day Bosnia, a sort of sanctuary between Eastern and Western Christianity. By the 11th century, more organised groups such as the Patarini, the Dulcinians, the Waldensians and the Cathars were beginning to appear in the towns and cities of northern Italy, southern France and Flanders.
rewrite: Within Roman Catholic doctrine, persistent and deliberate public heresy is seen as severing a person's spiritual connection to the Church, an automatic separation that occurs prior to any formal excommunication. The Codex Justinianus similarly labels anyone not adhering to the Catholic and Orthodox faith as heretical. Historically, the Church responded with severity to Christian movements it deemed heretical. Prior to the 1000s, however, such challenges typically arose from lone preachers or confined communities, such as the followers of Arius, Pelagius, Donatus, Marcion, or Montanus. The westward spread of the Paulicians, a sect with near-Manichaean beliefs, later fueled the major heretical movements of the eleventh and twelfth centuries in Western Europe. This began with the Bogomils in present-day Bosnia, a region serving as an intermediary zone between Eastern and Western Christian traditions. Subsequently, more structured sects like the Patarini, Dulcinians, Waldensians, and Cathars emerged within the urban centers of northern Italy, southern France, and Flanders.

input: Relying exclusively on unedited machine translation, however, ignores the fact that communication in human language is context-embedded and that it takes a person to comprehend the context of the original text with a reasonable degree of probability. It is certainly true that even purely human-generated translations are prone to error; therefore, to ensure that a machine-generated translation will be useful to a human being and that publishable-quality translation is achieved, such translations must be reviewed and edited by a human.
rewrite: Depending solely on raw machine translation overlooks how human communication depends on context, which only a person can reliably interpret. While even human translators make mistakes, a machine's output must be checked and refined by a person to be genuinely helpful and to meet standards suitable for publication.

input: During the same court battle, Viacom won a court ruling requiring YouTube to hand over 12 terabytes of data detailing the viewing habits of every user who has watched videos on the site. The decision was criticized by the Electronic Frontier Foundation, which called the court ruling "a setback to privacy rights". In June 2010, Viacom's lawsuit against Google was rejected in a summary judgment, with U.S. federal Judge Louis L. Stanton stating that Google was protected by provisions of the Digital Millennium Copyright Act. Viacom announced its intention to appeal the ruling.
rewrite: Amid ongoing litigation, Viacom secured a court order compelling YouTube to provide 12 terabytes of information, documenting the viewing history of all its users. The Electronic Frontier Foundation denounced this as a violation of personal privacy rights. However, in June 2010, a U.S. federal judge dismissed Viacom's copyright case against Google, citing protections under the Digital Millennium Copyright Act. Viacom stated it would challenge this decision.

input: The largest and bloodiest American battle came at Okinawa, as the U.S. sought airbases for 3,000 B-29 bombers and 240 squadrons of B-17 bombers for the intense bombardment of Japan's home islands in preparation for a full-scale invasion in late 1945. The Japanese, with 115,000 troops augmented by thousands of civilians on the heavily populated island, did not resist on the beaches—their strategy was to maximize the number of soldier and Marine casualties, and naval losses from Kamikaze attacks. After an intense bombardment the Americans landed on 1 April 1945 and declared victory on 21 June. The supporting naval forces were the targets for 4,000 sorties, many by Kamikaze suicide planes. U.S. losses totaled 38 ships of all types sunk and 368 damaged with 4,900 sailors killed. The Americans suffered 75,000 casualties on the ground; 94% of the Japanese soldiers died along with many civilians.
rewrite: The Battle of Okinawa was the most significant and costly conflict for American forces in the Pacific. The United States aimed to secure airfields to station thousands of bombers, which were crucial for the planned massive aerial assault on Japan ahead of an anticipated invasion. Defending the island were over 100,000 Japanese soldiers, joined by many local residents. Rather than confronting the initial landings, their tactic was to inflict severe losses on American infantry and naval vessels, the latter through devastating suicide aircraft assaults. Following a heavy preliminary barrage, U.S. forces came ashore in April 1945 and secured the island by late June. The fleet endured thousands of aerial attacks. American naval losses included dozens of vessels sunk and hundreds damaged, with thousands of sailors killed. Ground forces sustained tens of thousands of casualties, while nearly the entire Japanese garrison perished, alongside a great number of Okinawan civilians.

input: Plymouth is home to the Marine Biological Association of the United Kingdom (MBA) which conducts research in all areas of the marine sciences. The Plymouth Marine Laboratory is an offshoot of the MBA. Together with the National Marine Aquarium, the Sir Alister Hardy Foundation for Ocean Sciences, Plymouth University's Marine Institute and the Diving Diseases Research Centre, these marine-related organisations form the Plymouth Marine Sciences Partnership. The Plymouth Marine Laboratory, which focuses on global issues of climate change and sustainability. It monitors the effects of ocean acidity on corals and shellfish and reports the results to the UK government. It also cultivates algae that could be used to make biofuels or in the treatment of waste water by using technology such as photo-bioreactors. It works alongside the Boots Group to investigate the use of algae in skin care protects, taking advantage of the chemicals they contain that adapt to protect themselves from the sun.
rewrite: The city of Plymouth hosts the Marine Biological Association of the United Kingdom (MBA), an institution dedicated to broad scientific study of the sea. An independent entity originating from the MBA is the Plymouth Marine Laboratory. This laboratory, along with other local institutions including the National Marine Aquarium, the Sir Alister Hardy Foundation for Ocean Sciences, the Marine Institute at Plymouth University, and the Diving Diseases Research Centre, constitutes the Plymouth Marine Sciences Partnership. The Plymouth Marine Laboratory addresses worldwide environmental challenges, particularly climate change and sustainable practices. Its research tracks how increasing ocean acidity impacts marine life like corals and shellfish, findings which are communicated to government authorities. Additionally, the lab grows algae using specialized systems like photo-bioreactors; this algae has potential applications in creating biofuels or purifying wastewater. In a collaboration with the Boots Group, it also explores incorporating algae into skincare products, utilizing the organisms' natural sun-protective compounds.

input: Hellenistic poets now sought patronage from kings, and wrote works in their honor. The scholars at the libraries in Alexandria and Pergamon focused on the collection, cataloging, and literary criticism of classical Athenian works and ancient Greek myths. The poet-critic Callimachus, a staunch elitist, wrote hymns equating Ptolemy II to Zeus and Apollo. He promoted short poetic forms such as the epigram, epyllion and the iambic and attacked epic as base and common ("big book, big evil" was his doctrine). He also wrote a massive catalog of the holdings of the library of Alexandria, the famous Pinakes. Callimachus was extremely influential in his time and also for the development of Augustan poetry. Another poet, Apollonius of Rhodes, attempted to revive the epic for the Hellenistic world with his Argonautica. He had been a student of Callimachus and later became chief librarian (prostates) of the library of Alexandria, Apollonius and Callimachus spent much of their careers feuding with each other. Pastoral poetry also thrived during the Hellenistic era, Theocritus was a major poet who popularized the genre.
rewrite: During the Hellenistic period, poets turned to royal courts for support, composing pieces dedicated to their sovereigns. Academic efforts in Alexandria and Pergamon centered on gathering, organizing, and analyzing the texts and mythological traditions of classical Greece. The influential poet and critic Callimachus, who held elitist views, produced hymns that glorified Ptolemy II by comparing him to deities like Zeus and Apollo. He championed concise poetic styles, including epigrams and short narrative poems, while dismissing lengthy epics as vulgar—summarized by his belief that "a large book is a great nuisance." Additionally, he compiled the extensive Pinakes, a detailed inventory of the Alexandria Library's collection. Callimachus left a lasting impact on his contemporaries and later influenced Roman poetry under Augustus. His one-time pupil, Apollonius of Rhodes, countered this by striving to rejuvenate epic poetry through his work, the Argonautica. After studying under Callimachus, Apollonius eventually rose to lead the Alexandria Library, and the two engaged in a prolonged professional rivalry. This era also saw the flourishing of pastoral verse, largely due to the innovations of Theocritus, who helped establish the genre.

input: Chopin was educated in the tradition of Beethoven, Haydn, Mozart and Clementi; he used Clementi's piano method with his own students. He was also influenced by Hummel's development of virtuoso, yet Mozartian, piano technique. He cited Bach and Mozart as the two most important composers in shaping his musical outlook. Chopin's early works are in the style of the "brilliant" keyboard pieces of his era as exemplified by the works of Ignaz Moscheles, Friedrich Kalkbrenner, and others. Less direct in the earlier period are the influences of Polish folk music and of Italian opera. Much of what became his typical style of ornamentation (for example, his fioriture) is taken from singing. His melodic lines were increasingly reminiscent of the modes and features of the music of his native country, such as drones.
rewrite: Chopin's training was grounded in the classical approaches of composers like Beethoven, Haydn, Mozart, and Clementi, whose instructional techniques he employed in teaching. He further absorbed Hummel's method of blending virtuosic skill with a Mozartian elegance. For Chopin, Bach and Mozart were foundational to his artistic development. His initial compositions mirrored the popular "brilliant" style of piano works by contemporaries such as Moscheles and Kalkbrenner. During this time, elements of Polish folk music and Italian opera were more subtle, though his distinctive ornamental style, including fioriture, drew inspiration from vocal music. Over time, his melodies began to more clearly echo the tonal qualities and structures, like drones, found in the music of Poland.

input: Work is undertaken from an early age by vast numbers of children in the world and may have a natural place in growing up. Work can contribute to the well-being of children in a variety of ways; children often choose to work to improve their lives, both in the short- and long-term. At the material level, children’s work often contributes to producing food or earning income that benefits themselves and their families; and such income is especially important when the families are poor. Work can provide an escape from debilitating poverty, sometimes by allowing a young person to move away from an impoverished environment. Young people often enjoy their work, especially paid work, or when work involves the company of peers. Even when work is intensive and enforced, children often find ways to combine their work with play.
rewrite: Across the globe, many children begin labor at a young age, which can be a normal aspect of development. Engaging in work supports child welfare in numerous respects; frequently, youths opt to labor as a means to enhance their immediate and future circumstances. On a practical level, this labor often aids in generating food or wages that support both the children and their households, with this financial contribution being crucial for families in poverty. Labor can offer a route out of severe deprivation, at times enabling a youth to leave a destitute setting. Adolescents commonly take pleasure in their labor, particularly when it is remunerated or occurs alongside friends. Even under demanding or compulsory conditions, children typically manage to integrate elements of play into their tasks.

input: The 18th century saw a huge growth in the number of drinking establishments, primarily due to the introduction of gin. Gin was brought to England by the Dutch after the Glorious Revolution of 1688 and became very popular after the government created a market for "cuckoo grain" or "cuckoo malt" that was unfit to be used in brewing and distilling by allowing unlicensed gin and beer production, while imposing a heavy duty on all imported spirits. As thousands of gin-shops sprang up all over England, brewers fought back by increasing the number of alehouses. By 1740 the production of gin had increased to six times that of beer and because of its cheapness it became popular with the poor, leading to the so-called Gin Craze. Over half of the 15,000 drinking establishments in London were gin shops.
rewrite: The eighteenth century witnessed a significant expansion in drinking venues, largely fueled by the rise of gin. Introduced to England from the Netherlands following the 1688 revolution, gin's popularity surged when authorities permitted unregulated production of beer and gin. This policy was coupled with high taxes on imported liquor and the creation of a market for low-quality grain unsuitable for standard brewing. In response to the proliferation of gin shops, beer producers expanded their own network of alehouses. By the 1740s, gin output was sixfold that of beer, and its low cost made it the drink of choice for impoverished citizens, sparking the period known as the Gin Craze. In London, gin shops constituted more than half of the city's 15,000 public houses.

input: The east coast Appalachian system, originally forest covered, is relatively low and narrow and is bordered on the southeast and south by an important coastal plain. The Cordilleran system on the western side of the continent is lofty, broad and complicated having two branches, the Rocky Mountain System and the Pacific Mountain System. In between these mountain systems lie the Intermontaine Plateaus. Both the Columbia River and Colorado River rise far inland near the easternmost members of the Cordilleran system, and flow through plateaus and intermontaine basins to the ocean. Heavy forests cover the northwest coast, but elsewhere trees are found only on the higher ranges below the Alpine region. The intermontane valleys, plateaus and basins range from treeless to desert with the most arid region being in the southwest.
rewrite: The forested Appalachian range along the eastern seaboard is modest in height and width, giving way to a significant coastal plain to its southeast and south. On the opposite side of the continent, the extensive and rugged Cordilleran system divides into two primary chains: the Rockies and the Pacific ranges. Between these lies the area known as the Intermontane Plateaus. Both the Columbia and Colorado Rivers begin deep inland close to the Cordilleran system's eastern edges, carving paths across these plateaus and interior basins to reach the sea. While dense woodlands characterize the northwestern coastline, trees elsewhere are confined to lower mountain slopes. The interior valleys and plateaus vary from having no trees to being fully desert, with the driest conditions located in the southwest.

input: Philip V, who came to power when Doson died in 221 BC, was the last Macedonian ruler with both the talent and the opportunity to unite Greece and preserve its independence against the "cloud rising in the west": the ever-increasing power of Rome. He was known as "the darling of Hellas". Under his auspices the Peace of Naupactus (217 BC) brought the latest war between Macedon and the Greek leagues (the social war 220-217) to an end, and at this time he controlled all of Greece except Athens, Rhodes and Pergamum.
rewrite: Philip V assumed the Macedonian throne following the death of Doson in 221 BC. He is often regarded as the final king capable of uniting Greece and defending its autonomy against the growing threat of Rome. Called "the beloved of Hellas," he oversaw the Peace of Naupactus in 217 BC, concluding a recent conflict. At that juncture, his dominion extended over most of Greece, with only Athens, Rhodes, and Pergamum remaining outside his control.

input: Many were surprised by these changes to the CBC schedule, which were apparently intended to attract a younger audience to the network; some suggested they might alienate the core CBC viewership. Another note of criticism was made when the network decided to move The National in some time zones to simulcast the American version of The One over the summer. This later became a moot point, as The One was taken off the air after two weeks after extremely low American and Canadian ratings, and the newscast resumed its regular schedule.
rewrite: The CBC's schedule adjustments, aimed at drawing in younger viewers, caught many off guard and raised concerns about potentially losing their established audience. Further disapproval arose when the network temporarily replaced The National in certain regions with the American program The One for summer simulcasting. However, this issue became irrelevant when The One was canceled within two weeks due to poor ratings in both countries, allowing the newscast to return to its normal timeslot.

input: Natural theology was not a unified doctrine, and while some such as Louis Agassiz were strongly opposed to the ideas in the book, others sought a reconciliation in which evolution was seen as purposeful. In the Church of England, some liberal clergymen interpreted natural selection as an instrument of God's design, with the cleric Charles Kingsley seeing it as "just as noble a conception of Deity". In the second edition of January 1860, Darwin quoted Kingsley as "a celebrated cleric", and added the phrase "by the Creator" to the closing sentence, which from then on read "life, with its several powers, having been originally breathed by the Creator into a few forms or into one". While some commentators have taken this as a concession to religion that Darwin later regretted, Darwin's view at the time was of God creating life through the laws of nature, and even in the first edition there are several references to "creation".
rewrite: Natural theology did not represent a single, cohesive belief system. Figures like Louis Agassiz vehemently disagreed with the work's concepts, while other thinkers attempted to find a middle ground, viewing evolutionary change as a directed process. Within the Anglican Church, certain progressive clergy members interpreted natural selection as a mechanism through which divine purpose operated. The clergyman Charles Kingsley, for instance, regarded it as an equally majestic view of God. Darwin included a quotation from this "eminent cleric" in his book's second edition early in 1860. He also modified the final line to state that life, with all its capacities, was initially "breathed by the Creator" into one or a few primordial forms. Although some observers have interpreted this as a religious compromise he later came to dislike, Darwin's contemporary perspective was of a deity working through natural laws. References to "creation" were, in fact, present even in the original text.

input: The concept of a group arose from the study of polynomial equations, starting with Évariste Galois in the 1830s. After contributions from other fields such as number theory and geometry, the group notion was generalized and firmly established around 1870. Modern group theory—an active mathematical discipline—studies groups in their own right.a[›] To explore groups, mathematicians have devised various notions to break groups into smaller, better-understandable pieces, such as subgroups, quotient groups and simple groups. In addition to their abstract properties, group theorists also study the different ways in which a group can be expressed concretely (its group representations), both from a theoretical and a computational point of view. A theory has been developed for finite groups, which culminated with the classification of finite simple groups announced in 1983.aa[›] Since the mid-1980s, geometric group theory, which studies finitely generated groups as geometric objects, has become a particularly active area in group theory.
rewrite: The idea of groups originated in the 1830s with Évariste Galois's work on solving polynomial equations. Over subsequent decades, insights from geometry and number theory helped broaden and solidify the concept, leading to its formal establishment around 1870. Today, group theory is a vibrant field of mathematics concerned with investigating groups as abstract entities in themselves. Researchers have developed concepts like subgroups, quotient groups, and simple groups to decompose groups into more manageable components. Beyond abstract analysis, the discipline examines concrete expressions of groups, known as group representations, from both theoretical and computational perspectives. A major achievement was the classification of finite simple groups, completed in the 1980s. More recently, starting around the mid-1980s, geometric group theory—which views finitely generated groups through a geometric lens—has emerged as a highly dynamic research area.

input: Many visitors to BYU, and Utah Valley as a whole, report being surprised by the culturally conservative environment. Brigham Young University's Honor Code, which all BYU students agree to follow as a condition of studying at BYU, prohibits the consumption of alcoholic beverages, tobacco, etc. As mentioned earlier, The Princeton Review has rated BYU the "#1 stone cold sober school" in the nation for several years running, an honor which the late LDS Church president Gordon B. Hinckley had commented on with pride. BYU's 2014 "#1 stone cold" sober rating marked the 17th year in a row that the school had earned that rating. BYU has used this and other honors awarded to the school to advertise itself to prospective students, showing that BYU is proud of the rating. According to the Uniform Crime Reports, incidents of crime in Provo are lower than the national average. Murder is rare, and robberies are about 1/10 the national average. Business Insider rated BYU as the #1 safest college campus in the nation.
rewrite: Those traveling to Brigham Young University and the wider Utah Valley area often express astonishment at the region's traditional cultural atmosphere. Enrolled students must adhere to the university's Honor Code, a commitment that forbids the use of alcohol and tobacco. This policy has consistently led The Princeton Review to rank BYU as the country's most sober school for numerous consecutive years, an achievement the late LDS Church leader Gordon B. Hinckley once praised. The 2014 designation represented the seventeenth annual recognition, a distinction the institution highlights in its outreach to potential applicants. Concurrently, crime statistics for Provo fall well below national figures, with homicides being uncommon and thefts occurring at roughly one-tenth the U.S. rate.
