This safety record contributed to Business Insider naming BYU the nation's safest college campus.

input: Grazing organisms may also kill their prey species, but this is seldom the case. While some herbivores like zooplankton live on unicellular phytoplankton and therefore, by the individualized nature of the organism, kill their prey, many only eat a small part of the plant. Grazing livestock may pull some grass out at the roots, but most is simply grazed upon, allowing the plant to regrow once again. Kelp is frequently grazed in subtidal kelp forests, but regrows at the base of the blade continuously to cope with browsing pressure. Animals may also be 'grazed' upon; female mosquitos land on hosts briefly to gain sufficient proteins for the development of their offspring. Starfish may be grazed on, being capable of regenerating lost arms.
rewrite: Although grazing creatures can sometimes cause the death of their food sources, this outcome is not common. Many plant-eaters consume only portions of a plant, such as livestock that mostly trim grass blades, permitting regrowth. Similarly, kelp in underwater forests endures continual grazing but persists by growing anew from its base. This dynamic also applies to certain animals. For instance, mosquitoes briefly feed on hosts to acquire necessary nutrients, while starfish can regenerate limbs that have been eaten.

input: On April 26, 1496 King John I Albert granted the Privilege of Piotrków (Polish: "Przywilej piotrkowski", "konstytucja piotrkowska" or "statuty piotrkowskie"), increasing the nobility's feudal power over serfs. It bound the peasant to the land, as only one son (not the eldest) was permitted to leave the village; townsfolk (Polish: "mieszczaństwo") were prohibited from owning land; and positions in the Church hierarchy could be given only to nobles.
rewrite: On April 26, 1496, King John I Albert issued the Piotrków Privilege. This decree greatly strengthened the aristocracy's control over the peasantry by tying serfs to the land, allowing just one non-firstborn son to depart. It also barred townspeople from holding land and reserved high Church offices exclusively for the nobility.

input: Christoph Waltz was cast in the role of Franz Oberhauser, though he refused to comment on the nature of the part. It was later revealed with the film's release that he is Ernst Stavro Blofeld. Dave Bautista was cast as Mr. Hinx after producers sought an actor with a background in contact sports. After casting Bérénice Lim Marlohe, a relative newcomer, as Sévérine in Skyfall, Mendes consciously sought out a more experienced actor for the role of Madeleine Swann, ultimately casting Léa Seydoux in the role. Monica Bellucci joined the cast as Lucia Sciarra, becoming, at the age of fifty, the oldest actress to be cast as a Bond girl. In a separate interview with Danish website Euroman, Jesper Christensen revealed he would be reprising his role as Mr. White from Casino Royale and Quantum of Solace. Christensen's character was reportedly killed off in a scene intended to be used as an epilogue to Quantum of Solace, before it was removed from the final cut of the film, enabling his return in Spectre.
rewrite: Christoph Waltz took on the part of Franz Oberhauser, initially withholding any details about the character. Upon the movie's debut, it became clear he portrayed Ernst Stavro Blofeld. The producers selected Dave Bautista for Mr. Hinx, specifically wanting someone skilled in physical sports. Following the choice of the less-established Bérénice Lim Marlohe for Sévérine in the prior film, director Sam Mendes deliberately looked for a seasoned performer to play Madeleine Swann, which led to Léa Seydoux securing the part. Monica Bellucci was added as Lucia Sciarra, making her, at fifty, the most senior actress ever to be designated a Bond girl. In another discussion with the Danish outlet Euroman, Jesper Christensen confirmed he would again play Mr. White, a role he originated in two earlier Bond films. His character was originally written to die in a deleted epilogue, a decision that allowed for his reappearance in this installment.

input: Although John was the Count of Poitou and therefore the rightful feudal lord over the Lusignans, they could legitimately appeal John's actions in France to his own feudal lord, Philip. Hugh did exactly this in 1201 and Philip summoned John to attend court in Paris in 1202, citing the Le Goulet treaty to strengthen his case. John was unwilling to weaken his authority in western France in this way. He argued that he need not attend Philip's court because of his special status as the Duke of Normandy, who was exempt by feudal tradition from being called to the French court. Philip argued that he was summoning John not as the Duke of Normandy, but as the Count of Poitou, which carried no such special status. When John still refused to come, Philip declared John in breach of his feudal responsibilities, reassigned all of John's lands that fell under the French crown to Arthur – with the exception of Normandy, which he took back for himself – and began a fresh war against John.
rewrite: Despite being the Count of Poitou and thus the feudal superior of the Lusignan family, John's decisions in France were subject to appeal before his own overlord, King Philip. Hugh of Lusignan pursued this option in 1201, leading Philip to call John to the Paris court in 1202, invoking the Treaty of Le Goulet for support. John resisted, fearing the erosion of his power in western French territories. He claimed immunity from such a summons due to his role as Duke of Normandy, a position traditionally granting that privilege. Philip countered that the summons was for John specifically in his capacity as Count of Poitou, a title affording no special protection. John's continued refusal prompted Philip to declare him a feudal delinquent. Consequently, Philip redistributed John's French holdings, granting them to Arthur, while he personally reclaimed Normandy. This triggered a renewed military conflict.

input: The Jordan River runs along the Jordan Rift Valley, from Mount Hermon through the Hulah Valley and the Sea of Galilee to the Dead Sea, the lowest point on the surface of the Earth. Further south is the Arabah, ending with the Gulf of Eilat, part of the Red Sea. Unique to Israel and the Sinai Peninsula are makhteshim, or erosion cirques. The largest makhtesh in the world is Ramon Crater in the Negev, which measures 40 by 8 kilometers (25 by 5 mi). A report on the environmental status of the Mediterranean basin states that Israel has the largest number of plant species per square meter of all the countries in the basin.
rewrite: Flowing through the Jordan Rift Valley, the Jordan River travels from Mount Hermon, passing the Hulah Valley and the Sea of Galilee, until it reaches the Dead Sea at Earth's lowest elevation. South of this lies the Arabah region, which extends to the Gulf of Eilat on the Red Sea. The area encompassing Israel and the Sinai Peninsula features distinctive erosion cirques called makhteshim. The biggest of these globally is the Negev's Ramon Crater, spanning 40 by 8 kilometers. According to a Mediterranean environmental study, Israel possesses the greatest density of plant species per unit area within the basin.

input: Manhattan Island is linked to New York City's outer boroughs and New Jersey by several tunnels as well. The Lincoln Tunnel, which carries 120,000 vehicles a day under the Hudson River between New Jersey and Midtown Manhattan, is the busiest vehicular tunnel in the world. The tunnel was built instead of a bridge to allow unfettered passage of large passenger and cargo ships that sailed through New York Harbor and up the Hudson River to Manhattan's piers. The Holland Tunnel, connecting Lower Manhattan to Jersey City, New Jersey, was the world's first mechanically ventilated vehicular tunnel when it opened in 1927. The Queens-Midtown Tunnel, built to relieve congestion on the bridges connecting Manhattan with Queens and Brooklyn, was the largest non-federal project in its time when it was completed in 1940. President Franklin D. Roosevelt was the first person to drive through it. The Hugh L. Carey Tunnel runs underneath Battery Park and connects the Financial District at the southern tip of Manhattan to Red Hook in Brooklyn.
rewrite: Manhattan is connected to the surrounding boroughs and New Jersey via multiple underwater passages. The Lincoln Tunnel, facilitating about 120,000 daily trips beneath the Hudson River between New Jersey and central Manhattan, holds the title as the globe's most heavily used road tunnel. Opting for a tunnel over a bridge ensured that large commercial and passenger vessels could move freely through the harbor and along the Hudson to Manhattan's docks. Another key link, the Holland Tunnel, joining lower Manhattan with Jersey City, pioneered the use of mechanical ventilation for car tunnels upon its 1927 debut. To ease traffic on the bridges to Queens and Brooklyn, the Queens-Midtown Tunnel was constructed, becoming the biggest publicly funded endeavor of its era when finished in 1940, with President Franklin D. Roosevelt as its first motorist. Further south, the Hugh L. Carey Tunnel passes below Battery Park, linking Manhattan's Financial District to the Red Hook area of Brooklyn.

input: However, civil war flared again when the Second Triumvirate of Octavian, Lepidus and Mark Antony failed. The ambitious Octavian built a power base of patronage and then launched a campaign against Mark Antony. At the naval Battle of Actium off the coast of Greece, Octavian decisively defeated Antony and Cleopatra. Octavian was granted a series of special powers including sole "imperium" within the city of Rome, permanent consular powers and credit for every Roman military victory, since all future generals were assumed to be acting under his command. In 27 BC Octavian was granted the use of the names "Augustus" and "Princeps", indicating his primary status above all other Romans, and he adopted the title "Imperator Caesar" making him the first Roman Emperor.
rewrite: Nevertheless, internal conflict reignited following the collapse of the Second Triumvirate, an alliance between Octavian, Lepidus, and Mark Antony. Octavian, driven by ambition, first consolidated influence through a network of loyal supporters before turning his forces against Antony. The decisive confrontation occurred at the naval Battle of Actium near Greece, where Octavian triumphed over the combined forces of Antony and Cleopatra. Subsequently, he was awarded unique authorities: exclusive command in Rome, lifelong consular status, and recognition for all military successes, as future commanders were considered his subordinates. In 27 BC, he received the honorific titles "Augustus" and "Princeps," signifying his supreme rank, and embraced the designation "Imperator Caesar," thereby becoming Rome's inaugural emperor.

input: On June 14, 1987, about 5,000 people gathered again at Freedom Monument in Riga, and laid flowers to commemorate the anniversary of Stalin's mass deportation of Latvians in 1941. This was the first large demonstration in the Baltic republics to commemorate the anniversary of an event contrary to official Soviet history. The authorities did not crack down on demonstrators, which encouraged more and larger demonstrations throughout the Baltic States. The next major anniversary after the August 23 Molotov Pact demonstration was on November 18, the date of Latvia’s independence in 1918. On November 18, 1987, hundreds of police and civilian militiamen cordoned off the central square to prevent any demonstration at Freedom Monument, but thousands lined the streets of Riga in silent protest regardless.
rewrite: On June 14, 1987, approximately five thousand individuals reconvened at Riga’s Freedom Monument, placing floral tributes to mark the 1941 deportations of Latvians under Stalin. This gathering represented the initial sizable public observance in the Baltic region for a historical event that contradicted the Soviet narrative. Officials chose not to intervene, a decision that spurred increasingly larger protests across the area. Following a key demonstration on August 23 for the Molotov Pact anniversary, the next significant date was November 18, Latvia’s Independence Day from 1918. That day in 1987, despite hundreds of police and militia blocking the central square around the monument to stop a rally, thousands of people still stood silently along nearby streets in a powerful, wordless demonstration.

input: In 1989, Gaddafi was overjoyed by the foundation of the Arab Maghreb Union, uniting Libya in an economic pact with Mauritania, Morocco, Tunisia and Algeria, viewing it as beginnings of a new Pan-Arab union. Meanwhile, Libya stepped up its support for anti-western militants such as the Provisional IRA, and in 1988, Pan Am Flight 103 was blown up over Lockerbie in Scotland, killing 243 passengers and 16 crew members, plus 11 people on the ground. British police investigations identified two Libyans – Abdelbaset al-Megrahi and Lamin Khalifah Fhimah – as the chief suspects, and in November 1991 issued a declaration demanding that Libya hand them over. When Gaddafi refused, citing the Montreal Convention, the United Nations (UN) imposed Resolution 748 in March 1992, initiating economic sanctions against Libya which had deep repercussions for the country's economy. The country suffered an estimated $900 million financial loss as a result. Further problems arose with the west when in January 1989, two Libyan warplanes were shot down by the U.S. off the Libyan coast. Many African states opposed the UN sanctions, with Mandela criticising them on a visit to Gaddafi in October 1997, when he praised Libya for its work in fighting apartheid and awarded Gaddafi the Order of Good Hope. They would only be suspended in 1998 when Libya agreed to allow the extradition of the suspects to the Scottish Court in the Netherlands, in a process overseen by Mandela.
rewrite:
The year 1989 brought Gaddafi significant satisfaction with the establishment of the Arab Maghreb Union. This economic bloc joined Libya with Mauritania, Morocco, Tunisia, and Algeria, a development he interpreted as the initial phase of a broader Arab federation. Concurrently, the regime intensified its backing for various militant groups hostile to Western interests, including the Provisional IRA. A tragic event linked to this period was the destruction of Pan Am Flight 103 over Lockerbie, Scotland, in December 1988, which resulted in 270 fatalities. Subsequent inquiries by British authorities pointed to two Libyan nationals, Abdelbaset al-Megrahi and Lamin Khalifah Fhimah, as the primary accused. By late 1991, an official request was made for their surrender.

Gaddafi declined, invoking the Montreal Convention. In response, the United Nations enacted sanctions in March 1992 through Resolution 748, imposing severe economic penalties that cost Libya roughly $900 million. Tensions with Western nations were further exacerbated by a January 1989 incident where U.S. forces downed two Libyan jets near the coast. However, the UN measures faced criticism from numerous African countries. Nelson Mandela notably voiced opposition during an October 1997 trip to Libya, commending the nation's anti-apartheid efforts and bestowing an honor upon Gaddafi. The sanctions were temporarily lifted in 1998 after Libya consented to transfer the suspects for trial before a Scottish court convened in the Netherlands, a negotiation facilitated by Mandela.

input: Each code point has a single General Category property. The major categories are: Letter, Mark, Number, Punctuation, Symbol, Separator and Other. Within these categories, there are subdivisions. The General Category is not useful for every use, since legacy encodings have used multiple characteristics per single code point. E.g., U+000A <control-000A> Line feed (LF) in ASCII is both a control and a formatting separator; in Unicode the General Category is "Other, Control". Often, other properties must be used to specify the characteristics and behaviour of a code point. The possible General Categories are:
rewrite: Every character in Unicode is assigned a General Category, which groups it into broad types like Letter, Number, or Punctuation. These main groups are further divided into subcategories. However, this classification alone is sometimes insufficient because older systems often assigned multiple roles to a single character. For instance, the line feed control code is categorized simply as "Other, Control" in Unicode, requiring additional properties to fully define its function and traits. The complete list of possible categories includes Letter, Mark, Number, Punctuation, Symbol, Separator, and Other.

input: French political scientist Maurice Duverger drew a distinction between cadre parties and mass parties. Cadre parties were political elites that were concerned with contesting elections and restricted the influence of outsiders, who were only required to assist in election campaigns. Mass parties tried to recruit new members who were a source of party income and were often expected to spread party ideology as well as assist in elections.Socialist parties are examples of mass parties, while the British Conservative Party and the German Christian Democratic Union are examples of hybrid parties. In the United States, where both major parties were cadre parties, the introduction of primaries and other reforms has transformed them so that power is held by activists who compete over influence and nomination of candidates.
rewrite: Maurice Duverger, a French political scholar, identified two primary party models: cadre and mass. The cadre type consists of an elite group focused on winning elections, limiting broader participation largely to campaign support roles. In contrast, mass parties actively seek a large membership. These members provide financial resources and are typically tasked with promoting the party's beliefs in addition to helping during electoral contests. Socialist parties exemplify the mass model. Some parties, like the British Conservatives and Germany's Christian Democratic Union, blend both forms. Meanwhile, the United States historically featured cadre-style major parties. However, the adoption of primary elections and similar changes has shifted power toward engaged activists, who now vie for control over candidate selection and internal sway.

input: The NTFS file system used by recent versions of Windows stores the file with a UTC time stamp, but displays it corrected to local—or seasonal—time. However, the FAT filesystem commonly used on removable devices stores only the local time. Consequently, when a file is copied from the hard disk onto separate media, its time will be set to the current local time. If the time adjustment is changed, the timestamps of the original file and the copy will be different. The same effect can be observed when compressing and uncompressing files with some file archivers. It is the NTFS file that changes seen time. This effect should be kept in mind when trying to determine if a file is a duplicate of another, although there are other methods of comparing files for equality (such as using a checksum algorithm).
rewrite: Modern Windows operating systems utilize the NTFS file system, which records file timestamps in Coordinated Universal Time (UTC) but shows them adjusted to the user's local time zone, including daylight saving. In contrast, the FAT system, often found on portable drives, saves timestamps solely in local time. Therefore, transferring a file from an internal NTFS drive to external FAT media updates its timestamp to the present local time. Altering the system's time zone or clock settings afterward will cause the original and copied files to show different times. Certain compression tools can produce a similar discrepancy during archive operations, as the displayed time for the NTFS file shifts. This timing variation is important to consider when checking for duplicate files, even though more reliable comparison techniques, like generating checksums, are available.

input: The tourism industry began in the early 19th century when foreigners visited the Alps, traveled to the bases of the mountains to enjoy the scenery, and stayed at the spa-resorts. Large hotels were built during the Belle Époque; cog-railways, built early in the 20th century, brought tourists to ever higher elevations, with the Jungfraubahn terminating at the Jungfraujoch, well above the eternal snow-line, after going through a tunnel in Eiger. During this period winter sports were slowly introduced: in 1882 the first figure skating championship was held in St. Moritz, and downhill skiing became a popular sport with English visitors early in the 20th century, as the first ski-lift was installed in 1908 above Grindelwald.
rewrite: Tourism first emerged in the 1800s as international travelers journeyed to the Alpine region. They admired the mountain vistas from the valleys and frequented nearby health resorts. The Belle Époque era saw the construction of grand hotels. In the early 1900s, cogwheel trains allowed access to higher altitudes, exemplified by the Jungfrau railway, which tunnels through the Eiger to reach the perpetual snows of the Jungfraujoch. Winter activities gradually gained prominence; the inaugural figure skating competition took place in St. Moritz in 1882. Downhill skiing grew fashionable among British tourists in the early twentieth century, especially after the inaugural ski tow commenced operation above Grindelwald in 1908.

input: The last king of the Roman Kingdom, Lucius Tarquinius Superbus, was overthrown in 509 BC by a group of noblemen led by Lucius Junius Brutus. Tarquin made a number of attempts to retake the throne, including the Tarquinian conspiracy, the war with Veii and Tarquinii and finally the war between Rome and Clusium, all of which failed to achieve Tarquin's objectives. The most important constitutional change during the transition from kingdom to republic concerned the chief magistrate. Before the revolution, a king would be elected by the senators for a life term. Now, two consuls were elected by the citizens for an annual term. Each consul would check his colleague, and their limited term in office would open them up to prosecution if they abused the powers of their office. Consular political powers, when exercised conjointly with a consular colleague, were no different from those of the old king.
rewrite: In 509 BC, Lucius Tarquinius Superbus, the final monarch of Rome, was deposed in a revolt spearheaded by the aristocrat Lucius Junius Brutus. Following his exile, Tarquin launched several unsuccessful campaigns to reclaim power, such as an internal conspiracy, conflicts with the cities of Veii and Tarquinii, and a subsequent war against Clusium. The fundamental shift from a monarchy to a republic centered on the executive authority. Previously, kings were chosen by the senate to rule for life. This was replaced by a system where two consuls were elected annually by the people. These consuls held mutual veto power, and their short tenure made them accountable to the law, facing potential charges for misconduct. While their combined authority mirrored that of a king, it was now constrained by collegiality and term limits.

input: Antibiotics are screened for any negative effects on humans or other mammals before approval for clinical use, and are usually considered safe and most are well tolerated. However, some antibiotics have been associated with a range of adverse side effects. Side-effects range from mild to very serious depending on the antibiotics used, the microbial organisms targeted, and the individual patient. Side effects may reflect the pharmacological or toxicological properties of the antibiotic or may involve hypersensitivity reactions or anaphylaxis. Safety profiles of newer drugs are often not as well established as for those that have a long history of use. Adverse effects range from fever and nausea to major allergic reactions, including photodermatitis and anaphylaxis. Common side-effects include diarrhea, resulting from disruption of the species composition in the intestinal flora, resulting, for example, in overgrowth of pathogenic bacteria, such as Clostridium difficile. Antibacterials can also affect the vaginal flora, and may lead to overgrowth of yeast species of the genus Candida in the vulvo-vaginal area. Additional side-effects can result from interaction with other drugs, such as elevated risk of tendon damage from administration of a quinolone antibiotic with a systemic corticosteroid. Some scientists have hypothesized that the indiscriminate use of antibiotics alter the host microbiota and this has been associated with chronic disease.
rewrite: Before being authorized for medical applications, antibiotics undergo testing to ensure they do not harm humans or other mammals, and they are generally regarded as secure with good patient tolerance. Nonetheless, certain antibiotics can produce various undesirable reactions. These effects vary from minor to severe, influenced by the specific drug, the microbes it aims to combat, and the patient's unique physiology. Reactions might stem from the drug's inherent pharmacological or toxic traits, or they could include allergic responses, including extreme hypersensitivity. Newer medications frequently have less documented safety records compared to older, long-established ones. Possible issues span from mild fever and upset stomach to significant allergies, such as skin reactions to sunlight or life-threatening anaphylaxis. A frequent issue is diarrhea, often caused by an imbalance in gut bacteria that can allow harmful pathogens like Clostridium difficile to proliferate. Antibacterial treatments may also disturb vaginal bacterial balance, potentially causing yeast overgrowth from Candida species. Drug interactions can introduce further risks; for example, combining quinolone antibiotics with corticosteroids may increase chances of tendon injury. Additionally, some researchers suggest that excessive antibiotic use changes the body's microbial communities, which might be linked to long-term health conditions.

input: Beginning in August, the competition proceeds as a knockout tournament throughout, consisting of twelve rounds, a semi-final and then a final, in May. A system of byes ensures clubs above Level 9 and 10 enter the competition at later stages. There is no seeding, the fixtures in each round being determined by a random draw. Prior to the semi-finals, fixtures ending in a tie are replayed once only. The first six rounds are qualifiers, with the draws organised on a regional basis. The next six rounds are the "proper" rounds where all clubs are in one draw.
rewrite: Starting in August, the tournament follows a knockout format across twelve initial rounds, leading to semifinals and a final held in May. Higher-tier clubs join in later rounds through allocated byes. Matchups are randomly drawn without any seeding. Games before the semifinals that finish as draws are replayed just once. The initial six rounds serve as regional qualifiers, while the subsequent six rounds constitute the main competition, combining all clubs into a single draw.

input: Gaddafi's earliest education was of a religious nature, imparted by a local Islamic teacher. Subsequently moving to nearby Sirte to attend elementary school, he progressed through six grades in four years. Education in Libya was not free, but his father thought it would greatly benefit his son despite the financial strain. During the week Gaddafi slept in a mosque, and at weekends walked 20 miles to visit his parents. Bullied for being a Bedouin, he was proud of his identity and encouraged pride in other Bedouin children. From Sirte, he and his family moved to the market town of Sabha in Fezzan, south-central Libya, where his father worked as a caretaker for a tribal leader while Muammar attended secondary school, something neither parent had done. Gaddafi was popular at school; some friends made there received significant jobs in his later administration, most notably his best friend Abdul Salam Jalloud.
rewrite: Gaddafi's initial schooling focused on religious instruction under a local Islamic scholar. He then went to elementary school in the neighboring town of Sirte, completing the six-year program in only four years. Although Libyan families had to pay for schooling, his father prioritized this opportunity despite the cost. Gaddafi stayed at a mosque during the school week, traveling the considerable distance home to his family on foot each weekend. He faced bullying for his Bedouin heritage but remained defiantly proud of it, inspiring similar pride in other Bedouin pupils. Later, his family relocated to Sabha in central Libya, where his father took a caretaker position for a tribal elder. There, Gaddafi became the first in his family to pursue a secondary education. He was well-liked in school, and several friendships formed during this period, most importantly with Abdul Salam Jalloud, led to key roles in his future government.

input: At the end of the Rigvedic period, the Aryan society began to expand from the northwestern region of the Indian subcontinent, into the western Ganges plain. It became increasingly agricultural and was socially organised around the hierarchy of the four varnas, or social classes. This social structure was characterized both by syncretising with the native cultures of northern India, but also eventually by the excluding of indigenous peoples by labelling their occupations impure. During this period, many of the previous small tribal units and chiefdoms began to coalesce into monarchical, state-level polities.
rewrite: Toward the close of the Rigvedic era, Aryan communities extended their reach from the subcontinent's northwest into the western Gangetic plains. Their society grew more focused on farming and adopted a stratified system based on the four primary social divisions. This framework involved integrating with local northern Indian cultures while also marginalizing native groups by deeming their work unclean. Many former minor tribes and chiefdoms gradually merged during this time, forming larger kingdoms and states.

input: After being rendered obsolete by the redesign, the 1895 replica was presented in 1910 to the FA's long-serving president Lord Kinnaird. Kinnaird died in 1923, and his family kept it in their possession, out of view, until putting it up for auction in 2005. It was duly sold at Christie's auction house on 19 May 2005 for £420,000 (£478,400 including auction fees and taxes). The sale price set a new world record for a piece of football memorabilia, surpassing the £254,000 paid for the Jules Rimet World Cup Trophy in 1997. The successful bidder was David Gold, the then joint chairman of Birmingham City; claiming the FA and government were doing nothing proactive to ensure the trophy remained in the country, Gold stated his purchase was motivated by wanting to save it for the nation. Accordingly, Gold presented the trophy to the National Football Museum in Preston on 20 April 2006, where it went on immediate public display. It later moved with the museum to its new location in Manchester. In November 2012, it was ceremonially presented to Royal Engineers, after they beat Wanderers 7–1 in a charity replay of the first FA Cup final.
rewrite: Following its replacement due to a new design, the 1895 duplicate was gifted in 1910 to Lord Kinnaird, the Football Association's veteran president. After his death in 1923, the artifact remained with his heirs, stored away from public sight, until its 2005 auction. On May 19, 2005, Christie's successfully auctioned it for £420,000 (or £478,400 with fees and taxes). This figure established a global high for football collectibles, exceeding the 1997 sale of the Jules Rimet Trophy for £254,000. The winning bid came from David Gold, then co-chairman of Birmingham City, who argued that neither the FA nor authorities were acting to keep the trophy domestically. He declared his intent was to preserve it for the nation. True to his word, Gold donated the cup to the National Football Museum in Preston on April 20, 2006, where it was instantly exhibited. The trophy later relocated with the museum to Manchester. In a November 2012 ceremony, it was handed to the Royal Engineers after they won a charity rematch of the inaugural FA Cup final, defeating Wanderers 7–1.

input: In 1971, Akira Endo, a Japanese biochemist working for the pharmaceutical company Sankyo, identified mevastatin (ML-236B), a molecule produced by the fungus Penicillium citrinum, as an inhibitor of HMG-CoA reductase, a critical enzyme used by the body to produce cholesterol. Animal trials showed very good inhibitory effect as in clinical trials, however a long term study in dogs found toxic effects at higher doses and as a result mevastatin was believed to be too toxic for human use. Mevastatin was never marketed, because of its adverse effects of tumors, muscle deterioration, and sometimes death in laboratory dogs.
rewrite: In 1971, Japanese scientist Akira Endo, employed by Sankyo, discovered mevastatin. This compound, derived from the Penicillium citrinum mold, blocks the HMG-CoA reductase enzyme, which is essential for cholesterol synthesis. Initial animal and clinical tests indicated strong effectiveness. However, extended dog studies revealed toxicity at elevated doses, including tumors, muscle degradation, and fatalities. Consequently, mevastatin was deemed unsafe for people and was never commercialized as a drug.

input: In his Science of Logic (1812–1814) Hegel argues that finite qualities are not fully "real" because they depend on other finite qualities to determine them. Qualitative infinity, on the other hand, would be more self-determining and hence more fully real. Similarly finite natural things are less "real"—because they are less self-determining—than spiritual things like morally responsible people, ethical communities and God. So any doctrine, such as materialism, that asserts that finite qualities or natural objects are fully real is mistaken.
rewrite: Hegel contends in his Science of Logic that limited qualities lack complete reality, as their definition relies on other finite attributes. True infinity, by contrast, is more self-sufficient and thus more genuinely real. In the same way, physical entities are less real than spiritual ones—such as moral individuals, ethical societies, or God—due to their lesser self-determination. Therefore, materialist philosophies that claim full reality for finite qualities or natural objects are incorrect.

input: Technology magazine T3 gave the Super Slim model a positive review, stating the console is almost "nostalgic" in the design similarities to the original "fat" model, "While we don’t know whether it will play PS3 games or Blu-ray discs any differently yet, the look and feel of the new PS3 Slim is an obvious homage to the original PS3, minus the considerable excess weight. Immediately we would be concerned about the durability of the top loading tray that feels like it could be yanked straight out off the console, but ultimately it all feels like Sony's nostalgic way of signing off the current generation console in anticipation for the PS4."
rewrite: T3 magazine reviewed the Super Slim PS3 favorably, noting its design evokes nostalgia by closely resembling the first, bulkier version. The publication remarked that, although performance with PS3 games and Blu-rays remains to be seen, the new Slim’s appearance is a clear tribute to its predecessor, just much lighter. They expressed some worry over the sturdiness of the top-loading disc tray, which seems potentially fragile. Overall, the review concluded this design feels like Sony’s sentimental farewell to this console generation as the PS4 approaches.

input: The British, for their part, lacked both a unified command and a clear strategy for winning. With the use of the Royal Navy, the British were able to capture coastal cities, but control of the countryside eluded them. A British sortie from Canada in 1777 ended with the disastrous surrender of a British army at Saratoga. With the coming in 1777 of General von Steuben, the training and discipline along Prussian lines began, and the Continental Army began to evolve into a modern force. France and Spain then entered the war against Great Britain as Allies of the US, ending its naval advantage and escalating the conflict into a world war. The Netherlands later joined France, and the British were outnumbered on land and sea in a world war, as they had no major allies apart from Indian tribes.
rewrite: British leadership suffered from fragmented command and an unclear vision for achieving victory. While the Royal Navy secured several port cities, they failed to dominate the inland regions. An offensive launched from Canada in 1777 culminated in the catastrophic defeat and surrender of British forces at Saratoga. That same year, the arrival of General von Steuben introduced Prussian-style drills and discipline, transforming the Continental Army into a more professional military. The subsequent entry of France and Spain as American allies stripped Britain of its maritime supremacy and expanded the war globally. The later involvement of the Netherlands further isolated Britain, which, lacking significant European partners and relying primarily on indigenous alliances, found itself outmatched on multiple fronts across the world.

input: The word genocide was later included as a descriptive term to the process of indictment, but not yet as a formal legal term According to Lemming, genocide was defined as "a coordinated strategy to destroy a group of people, a process that could be accomplished through total annihilation as well as strategies that eliminate key elements of the group's basic existence, including language, culture, and economic infrastructure.” He created a concept of mobilizing much of the international relations and community, to working together and preventing the occurrence of such events happening within history and the international society. Australian anthropologist Peg LeVine coined the term "ritualcide" to describe the destruction of a group's cultural identity without necessarily destroying its members.
rewrite: The term genocide was subsequently adopted to describe the charges in the indictment process, though it was not yet an official legal category. Lemming characterized genocide as an organized plan to eradicate a population, which might involve outright physical extermination or methods that target fundamental aspects of the group’s life, such as its language, culture, and economic foundations. His framework aimed to galvanize international relations and the global community toward cooperation in preventing these atrocities throughout history and across societies. Separately, anthropologist Peg LeVine from Australia introduced "ritualcide" to refer to the elimination of a group's cultural identity, even if its individual members are not physically destroyed.

input: Production capacity in Britain and the United States was improved by the invention of the cotton gin by the American Eli Whitney in 1793. Before the development of cotton gins, the cotton fibers had to be pulled from the seeds tediously by hand. By the late 1700s a number of crude ginning machines had been developed. However, to produce a bale of cotton required over 600 hours of human labor, making large-scale production uneconomical in the United States, even with the use of humans as slave labor. The gin that Whitney manufactured (the Holmes design) reduced the hours down to just a dozen or so per bale. Although Whitney patented his own design for a cotton gin, he manufactured a prior design from Henry Odgen Holmes, for which Holmes filed a patent in 1796. Improving technology and increasing control of world markets allowed British traders to develop a commercial chain in which raw cotton fibers were (at first) purchased from colonial plantations, processed into cotton cloth in the mills of Lancashire, and then exported on British ships to captive colonial markets in West Africa, India, and China (via Shanghai and Hong Kong).
rewrite: The cotton gin, invented by American Eli Whitney in 1793, significantly enhanced manufacturing capabilities in both Britain and the United States. Prior to this innovation, separating cotton fibers from seeds was a slow, manual task. By the end of the eighteenth century, several basic ginning devices existed, yet producing a single bale demanded more than 600 hours of work. This extensive labor requirement rendered large-scale operations financially unviable in the U.S., despite the widespread use of enslaved people. Whitney’s version of the gin, based on a model by Henry Odgen Holmes, slashed this time to roughly twelve hours per bale. While Whitney secured a patent for his own model, he actually produced Holmes’s earlier design, which Holmes patented in 1796. Advances in technology and growing dominance in international trade enabled British merchants to establish a commercial network. This system involved buying raw cotton from colonial estates, weaving it into fabric in Lancashire mills, and then shipping the finished goods via British vessels to controlled colonial outlets in regions like West Africa, India, and China.

input: The inclusiveness of Weinreich's definition (above) directs attention to the totality of one's identity at a given phase in time, and assists in elucidating component aspects of one's total identity, such as one's gender identity, ethnic identity, occupational identity and so on. The definition readily applies to the young child, to the adolescent, to the young adult, and to the older adult in various phases of the life cycle. Depending on whether one is a young child or an adult at the height of one's powers, how one construes oneself as one was in the past will refer to very different salient experiential markers. Likewise, how one construes oneself as one aspires to be in the future will differ considerably according to one's age and accumulated experiences. (Weinreich & Saunderson, (eds) 2003, pp 26–34).
rewrite: Weinreich's broad conceptualization encourages a holistic view of an individual's sense of self at any specific moment. This perspective helps clarify distinct parts of a person's overall identity, including elements tied to gender, ethnicity, or profession. The framework is relevant across all stages of life, from early childhood and adolescence through to adulthood and later years. A person's current life stage—whether a young child or a capable adult—strongly influences which past experiences they see as most significant when reflecting on who they were. Similarly, one's future aspirations and self-concept are deeply shaped by age and the sum of life experiences gathered over time.

input: The Crimean War marked the ascendancy of France to the position of pre-eminent power on the Continent,:411 the continued decline of the Ottoman Empire, and the beginning of a decline for Tsarist Russia. As Fuller notes, "Russia had been beaten on the Crimean peninsula, and the military feared that it would inevitably be beaten again unless steps were taken to surmount its military weakness." The Crimean War marks the demise of the Concert of Europe, the balance of power that had dominated Europe since the Congress of Vienna in 1815, and which had included France, Russia, Austria and the United Kingdom.
rewrite: The Crimean War established France as the dominant force in Europe, while further weakening the Ottoman Empire and initiating a downturn for imperial Russia. Historians observe that Russia's defeat exposed critical military deficiencies, prompting fears of future losses without reform. Additionally, the conflict led to the collapse of the Concert of Europe. This system, created by the 1815 Congress of Vienna, had maintained a fragile equilibrium among major powers like France, Russia, Austria, and Britain for decades.

input: On the field at the beginning of a play are two teams of 12 (unlike 11 in American football). The team in possession of the ball is the offence and the team defending is referred to as the defence. Play begins with a backwards pass through the legs (the snap) by a member of the offensive team, to another member of the offensive team. This is usually the quarterback or punter, but a "direct snap" to a running back is also not uncommon. If the quarterback or punter receives the ball, he may then do any of the following:
rewrite: At the start of a play, each side fields 12 players, one more than in American football. The offensive team holds the ball, while the opposing side acts as the defense. Action commences with a backward handoff between the legs, known as the snap, from one offensive player to another. Typically, the quarterback or punter receives this snap, though it can go directly to a running back. Upon catching the ball, the quarterback or punter then has several options available.

input: New York City's commuter rail network is the largest in North America. The rail network, connecting New York City to its suburbs, consists of the Long Island Rail Road, Metro-North Railroad, and New Jersey Transit. The combined systems converge at Grand Central Terminal and Pennsylvania Station and contain more than 250 stations and 20 rail lines. In Queens, the elevated AirTrain people mover system connects JFK International Airport to the New York City Subway and the Long Island Rail Road; a separate AirTrain system is planned alongside the Grand Central Parkway to connect LaGuardia Airport to these transit systems. For intercity rail, New York City is served by Amtrak, whose busiest station by a significant margin is Pennsylvania Station on the West Side of Manhattan, from which Amtrak provides connections to Boston, Philadelphia, and Washington, D.C. along the Northeast Corridor, as well as long-distance train service to other North American cities.
rewrite: With the most extensive commuter rail infrastructure on the continent, New York City links to its surrounding regions through three primary systems: the Long Island Rail Road, Metro-North Railroad, and New Jersey Transit. These networks meet at two major hubs, Grand Central Terminal and Pennsylvania Station, encompassing over 250 stops across more than twenty lines. In Queens, an elevated AirTrain shuttle joins John F. Kennedy International Airport to both the subway and the Long Island Rail Road; a future AirTrain is also proposed to link LaGuardia Airport to these networks along the Grand Central Parkway. Regarding longer-distance travel, Amtrak operates from the city, primarily using the heavily trafficked Pennsylvania Station in Manhattan. This station offers frequent routes to Boston, Philadelphia, and Washington, D.C. via the Northeast Corridor, in addition to cross-country journeys to various destinations.

input: LaserDiscs potentially had a much longer lifespan than videocassettes. Because the discs were read optically instead of magnetically, no physical contact needs to be made between the player and the disc, except for the player's clamp that holds the disc at its center as it is spun and read. As a result, playback would not wear the information-bearing part of the discs, and properly manufactured LDs would theoretically last beyond one's lifetime. By contrast, a VHS tape held all of its picture and sound information on the tape in a magnetic coating which is in contact with the spinning heads on the head drum, causing progressive wear with each use (though later in VHS's lifespan, engineering improvements allowed tapes to be made and played back without contact). Also, the tape was thin and delicate, and it was easy for a player mechanism, especially on a low quality or malfunctioning model, to mishandle the tape and damage it by creasing it, frilling (stretching) its edges, or even breaking it.
rewrite: LaserDiscs offered greater durability compared to VHS tapes due to their optical playback mechanism. Since a laser reads the data without touching the disc's surface, the encoded areas experience no degradation during use. Only a central clamp makes physical contact to spin the disc. Consequently, a well-made LaserDisc could remain functional for decades without signal loss from playback wear. In contrast, VHS tapes stored information magnetically on a strip that physically rubbed against spinning heads inside the player. This contact gradually eroded the tape's coating each time it was played, although later technical advances reduced this abrasion. Furthermore, the tape itself was a fragile medium, prone to damage like creasing, edge stretching, or snapping if handled improperly by a faulty or low-end VCR mechanism.

input: In the longer run, however, with the NES near its end of its life many third-party publishers such as Electronic Arts supported upstart competing consoles with less strict licensing terms such as the Sega Genesis and then the PlayStation, which eroded and then took over Nintendo's dominance in the home console market, respectively. Consoles from Nintendo's rivals in the post-SNES era had always enjoyed much stronger third-party support than Nintendo, which relied more heavily on first-party games.
rewrite: As the NES approached its final years, several third-party companies, including Electronic Arts, began backing newer competing systems like the Sega Genesis and later the PlayStation. These consoles offered more flexible licensing agreements, which gradually undermined and eventually supplanted Nintendo's control over the home console market. Following the SNES era, Nintendo's competitors consistently received greater support from external developers, while Nintendo depended more on its own internally produced games.

input: Adolescents can conceptualize multiple "possible selves" that they could become and long-term possibilities and consequences of their choices. Exploring these possibilities may result in abrupt changes in self-presentation as the adolescent chooses or rejects qualities and behaviors, trying to guide the actual self toward the ideal self (who the adolescent wishes to be) and away from the feared self (who the adolescent does not want to be). For many, these distinctions are uncomfortable, but they also appear to motivate achievement through behavior consistent with the ideal and distinct from the feared possible selves.
rewrite: Teenagers often envision various future identities they might adopt, considering both the potential outcomes and lasting impacts of their decisions. This exploration can lead to sudden shifts in how they present themselves, as they accept or dismiss certain traits and actions. The goal is to steer their real identity closer to an idealized version and further from a dreaded one. While such contrasts can be unsettling, they also seem to drive success by encouraging conduct that aligns with positive aspirations and avoids negative ones.

input: In the private sector, corruption increases the cost of business through the price of illicit payments themselves, the management cost of negotiating with officials and the risk of breached agreements or detection. Although some claim corruption reduces costs by cutting bureaucracy, the availability of bribes can also induce officials to contrive new rules and delays. Openly removing costly and lengthy regulations are better than covertly allowing them to be bypassed by using bribes. Where corruption inflates the cost of business, it also distorts the playing field, shielding firms with connections from competition and thereby sustaining inefficient firms.
rewrite: Corruption in business raises expenses not only through bribe payments, but also via the resources spent on arranging them and the potential fallout from exposure. While some argue it streamlines cumbersome processes, the possibility of extortion can actually motivate officials to create additional red tape. Eliminating burdensome regulations transparently is superior to secretly circumventing them through illicit means. Such practices skew market fairness by protecting well-connected companies from rivals, which in turn allows unproductive enterprises to endure.

input: After Germany invaded the Soviet Union on 22 June 1941, the Wehrmacht crossed the Estonian southern border on 7 July. The Red Army retreated behind the Pärnu River – Emajõgi line on 12 July. At the end of July the Germans resumed their advance in Estonia working in tandem with the Estonian Forest Brothers. Both German troops and Estonian partisans took Narva on 17 August and the Estonian capital Tallinn on 28 August. After the Soviets were driven out from Estonia, German troops disarmed all the partisan groups.
rewrite: Germany's invasion of the Soviet Union in June 1941 led its forces into Estonia by early July. The Soviet Red Army fell back to a defensive position by mid-month. In late July, the German advance continued with support from Estonian resistance fighters, known as the Forest Brothers. Together, they captured the city of Narva in mid-August and the capital, Tallinn, by the month's end. Once Soviet forces were expelled, the German military proceeded to disarm all the local partisan units.

input: In 1957, she made a state visit to the United States, where she addressed the United Nations General Assembly on behalf of the Commonwealth. On the same tour, she opened the 23rd Canadian Parliament, becoming the first monarch of Canada to open a parliamentary session. Two years later, solely in her capacity as Queen of Canada, she revisited the United States and toured Canada. In 1961, she toured Cyprus, India, Pakistan, Nepal, and Iran. On a visit to Ghana the same year, she dismissed fears for her safety, even though her host, President Kwame Nkrumah, who had replaced her as head of state, was a target for assassins. Harold Macmillan wrote, "The Queen has been absolutely determined all through ... She is impatient of the attitude towards her to treat her as ... a film star ... She has indeed 'the heart and stomach of a man' ... She loves her duty and means to be a Queen." Before her tour through parts of Quebec in 1964, the press reported that extremists within the Quebec separatist movement were plotting Elizabeth's assassination. No attempt was made, but a riot did break out while she was in Montreal; the Queen's "calmness and courage in the face of the violence" was noted.
rewrite: In 1957, during an official trip to the United States, she spoke before the United Nations General Assembly representing the Commonwealth. During that journey, she also presided over the opening of Canada’s 23rd Parliament, marking the first time a reigning sovereign had performed that duty in Canada. Two years later, acting specifically as Canada’s Queen, she returned to the U.S. and traveled across Canada. By 1961, her travels extended to Cyprus, India, Pakistan, Nepal, and Iran. That same year, during a trip to Ghana, she showed no concern for her personal security, despite the fact that President Kwame Nkrumah—who had assumed the role of head of state in place of the monarchy—was under threat from would-be assassins. Prime Minister Harold Macmillan observed, “She has been utterly resolute throughout … She dislikes being handled as though she were … a celebrity … She truly possesses ‘the spirit and bravery of a man’ … She is devoted to her role and intends to reign as a true sovereign.” Prior to her 1964 visit to certain areas of Quebec, media outlets suggested that radical factions in the separatist movement were planning to kill her. Although no attack occurred, a violent disturbance erupted during her time in Montreal; observers remarked on her “composure and bravery amid the unrest.”

input: Unlike all other British Government records, the records from the East India Company (and its successor the India Office) are not in The National Archives at Kew, London, but are held by the British Library in London as part of the Asia, Pacific and Africa Collections. The catalogue is searchable online in the Access to Archives catalogues. Many of the East India Company records are freely available online under an agreement that the Families in British India Society has with the British Library. Published catalogues exist of East India Company ships' journals and logs, 1600–1834; and of some of the Company's daughter institutions, including the East India Company College, Haileybury, and Addiscombe Military Seminary.
rewrite: The records of the East India Company and the later India Office form a distinct collection. Unlike other official UK government documents, which are kept at The National Archives in Kew, these materials are housed within the British Library's Asia, Pacific and Africa Collections in London. Their inventory can be explored online via the Access to Archives system. A significant portion of these records has been digitized and made available online through a partnership between the British Library and the Families in British India Society. Additionally, printed guides exist for the Company's ships' logs from 1600 to 1834, as well as for affiliated establishments like Haileybury College and the Addiscombe Military Seminary.

input: Virgil is traditionally ranked as one of Rome's greatest poets. His Aeneid has been considered the national epic of ancient Rome from the time of its composition to the present day. Modeled after Homer's Iliad and Odyssey, the Aeneid follows the Trojan refugee Aeneas as he struggles to fulfill his destiny and arrive on the shores of Italy—in Roman mythology the founding act of Rome. Virgil's work has had wide and deep influence on Western literature, most notably Dante's Divine Comedy, in which Virgil appears as Dante's guide through hell and purgatory.
rewrite: Virgil is widely regarded as among the most important poets of ancient Rome. His epic poem, the Aeneid, has served as the nation's foundational literary work since its creation. Inspired by Homer's epics, it narrates the journey of the Trojan hero Aeneas, whose arrival in Italy is mythologically seen as the origin of Rome. This masterpiece profoundly shaped later Western writing, most directly influencing Dante, who features Virgil as his mentor in the Divine Comedy.

input: During the Permian all the Earth's major land masses, except portions of East Asia, were collected into a single supercontinent known as Pangaea. Pangaea straddled the equator and extended toward the poles, with a corresponding effect on ocean currents in the single great ocean (Panthalassa, the universal sea), and the Paleo-Tethys Ocean, a large ocean that was between Asia and Gondwana. The Cimmeria continent rifted away from Gondwana and drifted north to Laurasia, causing the Paleo-Tethys to shrink. A new ocean was growing on its southern end, the Tethys Ocean, an ocean that would dominate much of the Mesozoic Era. Large continental landmasses create climates with extreme variations of heat and cold ("continental climate") and monsoon conditions with highly seasonal rainfall patterns. Deserts seem to have been widespread on Pangaea.
rewrite: In the Permian period, nearly all major land areas combined to form the supercontinent Pangaea, excluding parts of East Asia. This vast landmass was positioned across the equator and reached toward the poles, significantly influencing currents in the surrounding global ocean, Panthalassa, and the older Paleo-Tethys Ocean that lay between Asia and Gondwana. As the Cimmeria land fragment broke from Gondwana and moved northward toward Laurasia, the Paleo-Tethys began to close. Meanwhile, the younger Tethys Ocean started expanding to the south, later becoming a major feature throughout the Mesozoic. Such enormous continents typically produce severe climates with sharp temperature swings and pronounced seasonal monsoons. Extensive desert regions likely covered much of Pangaea.

Palmisano (IBM, 2000), Joan Spero (Doris Duke Charitable Foundation, 2004), Sidney Taurel (Eli Lilly, 2001), and Lorenzo Zambrano (Cemex, 2003).

input: Though Houston is the largest city in the United States without formal zoning regulations, it has developed similarly to other Sun Belt cities because the city's land use regulations and legal covenants have played a similar role. Regulations include mandatory lot size for single-family houses and requirements that parking be available to tenants and customers. Such restrictions have had mixed results. Though some have blamed the city's low density, urban sprawl, and lack of pedestrian-friendliness on these policies, the city's land use has also been credited with having significant affordable housing, sparing Houston the worst effects of the 2008 real estate crisis. The city issued 42,697 building permits in 2008 and was ranked first in the list of healthiest housing markets for 2009.
rewrite: Despite being the biggest U.S. city lacking official zoning laws, Houston's growth patterns mirror those of other Sun Belt metropolitan areas. This is due to its alternative land use rules and private deed restrictions, which function in a comparable manner. These measures dictate minimum property dimensions for detached homes and ensure parking provisions for residents and businesses. The outcomes of these policies are varied. Critics link them to Houston's expansive layout, limited population concentration, and unwalkable environment. However, proponents argue these same regulations have fostered a substantial amount of reasonably priced homes, which helped shield the city from the severe impacts of the 2008 property downturn. Supporting this, Houston led the nation in building permits issued that year and was named the top performing housing market in 2009.

input: Swaziland is a developing country with a small economy. Its GDP per capita of $9,714 means it is classified as a country with a lower-middle income. As a member of the Southern African Customs Union (SACU) and Common Market for Eastern and Southern Africa (COMESA), its main local trading partner is South Africa. Swaziland's currency, the lilangeni, is pegged to the South African rand. Swaziland's major overseas trading partners are the United States and the European Union. The majority of the country's employment is provided by its agricultural and manufacturing sectors. Swaziland is a member of the Southern African Development Community (SADC), the African Union, the Commonwealth of Nations and the United Nations.
rewrite: Swaziland is a lower-middle income nation, as reflected by its per capita GDP of approximately $9,714. Its modest economy is deeply integrated with regional bodies, including the Southern African Customs Union and the Common Market for Eastern and Southern Africa. South Africa serves as its primary trading partner, a relationship underscored by the fixed exchange rate between the Swazi lilangeni and the South African rand. Beyond the region, key export markets are the United States and the European Union. Domestically, most jobs are found in agriculture and manufacturing. The country also holds membership in several international organizations, such as the Southern African Development Community, the African Union, the Commonwealth, and the United Nations.

input: In Miranda the court created safeguards against self-incriminating statements made after an arrest. The court held that "The prosecution may not use statements, whether exculpatory or inculpatory, stemming from questioning initiated by law enforcement officers after a person has been taken into custody or otherwise deprived of his freedom of action in any significant way, unless it demonstrates the use of procedural safeguards effective to secure the Fifth Amendment's privilege against self-incrimination"
rewrite: The Miranda ruling established protections to prevent self-incrimination following an arrest. It determined that any statements obtained through police interrogation while an individual is in custody cannot be used by prosecutors, unless clear measures are implemented to uphold the constitutional right against compelled self-incrimination.

input: Although the Drive moved to Massachusetts for the 1994 season, the AFL had a number of other teams which it considered "dynasties", including the Tampa Bay Storm (the only team that has existed in some form for all twenty-eight contested seasons), their arch-rival the Orlando Predators, the now-defunct San Jose SaberCats of the present decade, and their rivals the Arizona Rattlers.
rewrite: While the Drive relocated to Massachusetts in 1994, the AFL featured several other dominant franchises. These included the enduring Tampa Bay Storm, present in all 28 seasons, their fierce rivals the Orlando Predators, the now-inactive San Jose SaberCats from the current decade, and the SaberCats' adversaries, the Arizona Rattlers.

input: Dell previously had its headquarters in the Arboretum complex in northern Austin, Texas. In 1989 Dell occupied 127,000 square feet (11,800 m2) in the Arboretum complex. In 1990, Dell had 1,200 employees in its headquarters. In 1993, Dell submitted a document to Round Rock officials, titled "Dell Computer Corporate Headquarters, Round Rock, Texas, May 1993 Schematic Design." Despite the filing, during that year the company said that it was not going to move its headquarters. In 1994, Dell announced that it was moving most of its employees out of the Arboretum, but that it was going to continue to occupy the top floor of the Arboretum and that the company's official headquarters address would continue to be the Arboretum. The top floor continued to hold Dell's board room, demonstration center, and visitor meeting room. Less than one month prior to August 29, 1994, Dell moved 1,100 customer support and telephone sales employees to Round Rock. Dell's lease in the Arboretum had been scheduled to expire in 1994.
rewrite: Originally based in the Arboretum complex located in north Austin, Texas, Dell's corporate home once spanned 127,000 square feet there as of 1989. By 1990, the head office employed 1,200 people. In 1993, the company provided schematic plans to Round Rock authorities for a potential headquarters, yet publicly denied any relocation plans at that time. The following year, Dell declared it would shift the majority of its workforce from the Arboretum while retaining the building's top floor. This space housed essential facilities like the boardroom, demonstration area, and guest meeting rooms, and the complex remained the official corporate address. Shortly before August 29, 1994, approximately 1,100 staff members in customer service and phone sales were transferred to Round Rock. This move coincided with the impending expiration of Dell's Arboretum lease that same year.

input: The New York metropolitan area is home to a self-identifying gay and bisexual community estimated at 568,903 individuals, the largest in the United States and one of the world's largest. Same-sex marriages in New York were legalized on June 24, 2011 and were authorized to take place beginning 30 days thereafter.
rewrite: With an estimated 568,903 gay and bisexual residents, the New York metro area has the nation's biggest such community and ranks among the largest globally. Same-sex marriage became legal there on June 24, 2011, with ceremonies permitted after a 30-day wait.

input: English is the official language in the state of Montana, as it is in many U.S. states. English is also the language of the majority. According to the 2000 U.S. Census, 94.8 percent of the population aged 5 and older speak English at home. Spanish is the language most commonly spoken at home other than English. There were about 13,040 Spanish-language speakers in the state (1.4 percent of the population) in 2011. There were also 15,438 (1.7 percent of the state population) speakers of Indo-European languages other than English or Spanish, 10,154 (1.1 percent) speakers of a Native American language, and 4,052 (0.4 percent) speakers of an Asian or Pacific Islander language. Other languages spoken in Montana (as of 2013) include Assiniboine (about 150 speakers in the Montana and Canada), Blackfoot (about 100 speakers), Cheyenne (about 1,700 speakers), Plains Cree (about 100 speakers), Crow (about 3,000 speakers), Dakota (about 18,800 speakers in Minnesota, Montana, Nebraska, North Dakota, and South Dakota), German Hutterite (about 5,600 speakers), Gros Ventre (about 10 speakers), Kalispel-Pend d'Oreille (about 64 speakers), Kutenai (about 6 speakers), and Lakota (about 6,000 speakers in Minnesota, Montana, Nebraska, North Dakota, South Dakota). The United States Department of Education estimated in 2009 that 5,274 students in Montana spoke a language at home other than English. These included a Native American language (64 percent), German (4 percent), Spanish (3 percent), Russian (1 percent), and Chinese (less than 0.5 percent).
rewrite:
In Montana, English holds official status and is the predominant language, mirroring the situation in most American states. Data from the 2000 census indicates that 94.8% of residents aged five and above use English in their households. The most common non-English language spoken at home is Spanish, with approximately 13,040 individuals, or 1.4% of the population, reported in 2011. Other linguistic groups include speakers of other Indo-European languages (1.7%), Native American languages (1.1%), and Asian or Pacific Islander languages (0.4%).

The state is also home to a variety of indigenous languages. As of 2013, these included Assiniboine, Blackfoot, Cheyenne, Plains Cree, Crow, Gros Ventre, Kalispel-Pend d'Oreille, and Kutenai, with speaker numbers ranging from a handful to several thousand. Additionally, languages like Dakota, German Hutterite, and Lakota have speakers distributed across Montana and neighboring states.

According to a 2009 estimate by the U.S. Department of Education, about 5,274 students in Montana came from homes where a language other than English was spoken. Among these, Native American languages were the most prevalent, accounting for 64%, followed by German, Spanish, Russian, and Chinese.

input: A series of low-lying annexes (largely hidden) flank both ends. Also in the square are the glass-faced Planalto Palace housing the presidential offices, and the Palace of the Supreme Court. Farther east, on a triangle of land jutting into the lake, is the Palace of the Dawn (Palácio da Alvorada; the presidential residence). Between the federal and civic buildings on the Monumental Axis is the city's cathedral, considered by many to be Niemeyer's finest achievement (see photographs of the interior). The parabolically shaped structure is characterized by its 16 gracefully curving supports, which join in a circle 115 feet (35 meters) above the floor of the nave; stretched between the supports are translucent walls of tinted glass. The nave is entered via a subterranean passage rather than conventional doorways. Other notable buildings are Buriti Palace, Itamaraty Palace, the National Theater, and several foreign embassies that creatively embody features of their national architecture. The Brazilian landscape architect Roberto Burle Marx designed landmark modernist gardens for some of the principal buildings.
rewrite: Flanking both sides of the main area are several discreet, single-story extensions. The square itself contains the presidential workplace, the Planalto Palace with its glass exterior, and the Supreme Court's palace. To the east, situated on a peninsula extending into the lake, stands the Palácio da Alvorada, which serves as the president's home. Positioned among the government complexes along the central boulevard is the metropolitan cathedral, often regarded as architect Oscar Niemeyer's most exceptional work. This structure takes a parabolic form, defined by sixteen sweeping concrete ribs that converge high above the main floor. Between these ribs are expansive windows of colored glass. Entry to the main chamber is gained through an underground walkway, not traditional doors. Additional significant structures include the Buriti and Itamaraty palaces, the National Theater, and a number of embassies that incorporate distinctive elements from their home countries' designs. Renowned landscape designer Roberto Burle Marx created celebrated modernist gardens for many key sites.

input: The European Central Bank had stepped up the buying of member nations debt. In response to the crisis of 2010, some proposals have surfaced for a collective European bond issue that would allow the central bank to purchase a European version of US Treasury bills. To make European sovereign debt assets more similar to a US Treasury, a collective guarantee of the member states' solvency would be necessary.[b] But the German government has resisted this proposal, and other analyses indicate that "the sickness of the euro" is due to the linkage between sovereign debt and failing national banking systems. If the European central bank were to deal directly with failing banking systems sovereign debt would not look as leveraged relative to national income in the financially weaker member states.
rewrite: In 2010, the European Central Bank increased its acquisitions of government bonds from countries using the euro. During that period, ideas emerged for a joint debt instrument, akin to U.S. Treasury securities, which the ECB could buy. Creating such a comparable asset would require all member states to mutually assure each other's creditworthiness. However, Germany has opposed this concept. Additional assessments suggest the euro's troubles stem from the connection between government liabilities and struggling domestic banks. Experts argue that if the central bank intervened directly with these faltering banks, public debt in economically vulnerable nations would appear less disproportionate compared to their national earnings.

input: The Zhengde Emperor (r. 1505–1521), who enjoyed the company of lamas at court despite protests from the censorate, had heard tales of a "living Buddha" which he desired to host at the Ming capital; this was none other than the Rinpung-supported Mikyö Dorje, 8th Karmapa Lama then occupying Lhasa. Zhengde's top advisors made every attempt to dissuade him from inviting this lama to court, arguing that Tibetan Buddhism was wildly heterodox and unorthodox. Despite protests by the Grand Secretary Liang Chu, in 1515 the Zhengde Emperor sent his eunuch official Liu Yun of the Palace Chancellery on a mission to invite this Karmapa to Beijing. Liu commanded a fleet of hundreds of ships requisitioned along the Yangtze, consuming 2,835 g (100 oz) of silver a day in food expenses while stationed for a year in Chengdu of Sichuan. After procurring necessary gifts for the mission, he departed with a cavalry force of about 1,000 troops. When the request was delivered, the Karmapa lama refused to leave Tibet despite the Ming force brought to coerce him. The Karmapa launched a surprise ambush on Liu Yun's camp, seizing all the goods and valuables while killing or wounding half of Liu Yun's entire escort. After this fiasco, Liu fled for his life, but only returned to Chengdu several years later to find that the Zhengde Emperor had died.
rewrite:
During his reign from 1505 to 1521, the Zhengde Emperor frequently surrounded himself with Tibetan Buddhist monks, ignoring objections from his censors. He became fascinated by stories of a revered "living Buddha," who was in fact Mikyö Dorje, the Eighth Karmapa Lama. This lama, backed by the Rinpung faction, was residing in Lhasa. The emperor's senior ministers strongly opposed the idea of summoning him to the capital, Beijing, condemning Tibetan Buddhist practices as heretical and incompatible with orthodox teachings. Nevertheless, overriding the strenuous objections of Grand Secretary Liang Chu, the emperor in 1515 dispatched a trusted eunuch, Liu Yun, to extend the invitation.

Liu Yun marshaled immense resources for the journey, requisitioning a flotilla of hundreds of vessels along the Yangtze River. While his expedition was based in Chengdu for a year, the daily cost for provisions alone reached 2,835 grams of silver. After gathering lavish presents intended for the lama, Liu finally set out with a military escort of roughly one thousand cavalrymen. Upon receiving the imperial summons, the Karmapa firmly declined to travel to Beijing, resisting the implied pressure of the Ming detachment. Instead, he orchestrated a sudden attack on Liu Yun's encampment, capturing all the tribute and treasures and slaughtering or injuring around half of the escort force. In the wake of this disastrous encounter, Liu Yun barely escaped. He did not make it back to Chengdu until several years later, only to discover that the Zhengde Emperor had already passed away.

input: Oklahoma City Community College in south Oklahoma City is the second-largest community college in the state. Rose State College is located east of Oklahoma City in suburban Midwest City. On the Westside's Furniture District lies Oklahoma State University–Oklahoma City. Northeast of the city, Langston University serves as Oklahoma's historically black institution, with an additional urban campus on the east side.
