input: The critic Joseph Bédier (1864–1938) launched a particularly withering attack on stemmatics in 1928. He surveyed editions of medieval French texts that were produced with the stemmatic method, and found that textual critics tended overwhelmingly to produce trees divided into just two branches. He concluded that this outcome was unlikely to have occurred by chance, and that therefore, the method was tending to produce bipartite stemmas regardless of the actual history of the witnesses. He suspected that editors tended to favor trees with two branches, as this would maximize the opportunities for editorial judgment (as there would be no third branch to "break the tie" whenever the witnesses disagreed). He also noted that, for many works, more than one reasonable stemma could be postulated, suggesting that the method was not as rigorous or as scientific as its proponents had claimed.
rewrite: In 1928, scholar Joseph Bédier (1864–1938) delivered a severe critique of the stemmatic approach to editing texts. Examining published editions of medieval French works that employed this technique, he observed a striking pattern: editors consistently produced manuscript trees with only two primary branches. Bédier argued this regularity could not be coincidental, implying the method inherently generated two-part stemmas irrespective of the true historical relationships among manuscript copies. He proposed that editors might unconsciously prefer this simplified structure, as a dichotomy offers greater scope for personal interpretation when resolving textual discrepancies—with no third branch to provide decisive evidence. Furthermore, Bédier pointed out that multiple plausible stemmas could often be constructed for the same work, indicating the methodology lacked the objective rigor and scientific certainty its advocates asserted.

input: Some scholars[note 44] use other schemes. Buddhists themselves have a variety of other schemes. Hinayana (literally "lesser vehicle") is used by Mahayana followers to name the family of early philosophical schools and traditions from which contemporary Theravada emerged, but as this term is rooted in the Mahayana viewpoint and can be considered derogatory, a variety of other terms are increasingly used instead, including Śrāvakayāna, Nikaya Buddhism, early Buddhist schools, sectarian Buddhism, conservative Buddhism, mainstream Buddhism and non-Mahayana Buddhism.
rewrite: Certain academics[note 44] employ different frameworks. Buddhists also hold diverse classifications. The term Hinayana ("lesser vehicle"), applied by Mahayana adherents to early philosophical schools ancestral to modern Theravada, is seen as pejorative due to its Mahayana origins. Consequently, numerous alternative designations are now preferred, such as Śrāvakayāna, Nikaya Buddhism, early Buddhist schools, sectarian Buddhism, conservative Buddhism, mainstream Buddhism, and non-Mahayana Buddhism.

input: Following al-Farabi's lead, Avicenna initiated a full-fledged inquiry into the question of being, in which he distinguished between essence (Mahiat) and existence (Wujud). He argued that the fact of existence can not be inferred from or accounted for by the essence of existing things, and that form and matter by themselves cannot interact and originate the movement of the universe or the progressive actualization of existing things. Existence must, therefore, be due to an agent-cause that necessitates, imparts, gives, or adds existence to an essence. To do so, the cause must be an existing thing and coexist with its effect.
rewrite: Inspired by al-Farabi, Avicenna launched a comprehensive investigation into the nature of being. He made a critical separation between an entity's essence and its state of existing. Avicenna maintained that existence itself cannot be logically derived from the concept of a thing, nor can mere form and matter generate cosmic motion or the gradual realization of entities. Consequently, existence must be bestowed by an external, efficient cause. This necessary agent must itself exist and be present simultaneously with whatever it brings into being.

input: The wider New York City metropolitan area, with over 20 million people, about 50% greater than the second-place Los Angeles metropolitan area in the United States, is also ethnically diverse. The New York region continues to be by far the leading metropolitan gateway for legal immigrants admitted into the United States, substantially exceeding the combined totals of Los Angeles and Miami, the next most popular gateway regions. It is home to the largest Jewish as well as Israeli communities outside Israel, with the Jewish population in the region numbering over 1.5 million in 2012 and including many diverse Jewish sects from around the Middle East and Eastern Europe. The metropolitan area is also home to 20% of the nation's Indian Americans and at least 20 Little India enclaves, as well as 15% of all Korean Americans and four Koreatowns; the largest Asian Indian population in the Western Hemisphere; the largest Russian American, Italian American, and African American populations; the largest Dominican American, Puerto Rican American, and South American and second-largest overall Hispanic population in the United States, numbering 4.8 million; and includes at least 6 established Chinatowns within New York City alone, with the urban agglomeration comprising a population of 779,269 overseas Chinese as of 2013 Census estimates, the largest outside of Asia.
rewrite: The New York City metropolitan region, home to more than 20 million residents, significantly outnumbers the Los Angeles metro area, the nation's second most populous, by roughly half. This vast area is marked by profound ethnic variety. It remains the predominant entry point for lawful immigration to the United States, admitting far more individuals than Los Angeles and Miami, the next two leading destinations, combined. The region hosts the world's biggest Jewish and Israeli communities outside Israel itself; its Jewish population surpassed 1.5 million in 2012 and encompasses numerous distinct sects originating from the Middle East and Eastern Europe. Additionally, the metro area contains 20% of all Indian Americans and at least twenty distinct Little India neighborhoods, alongside 15% of Korean Americans and four Koreatowns. It boasts the Western Hemisphere's largest population of Asian Indians, the biggest communities of Russian, Italian, and African Americans, and the largest Dominican, Puerto Rican, and South American populations. This also constitutes the country's second-largest Hispanic community overall, at 4.8 million people. Within New York City proper, there are at least six historic Chinatowns, and the broader urban area was home to nearly 780,000 ethnic Chinese residents as of 2013—the biggest such concentration outside Asia.

input: His organisational skills led him to a career in the Roman Curia, the papal civil service. In 1931, Pacelli appointed him to teach history at the Papal Academy for Diplomats In 1937, after his mentor Giuseppe Pizzardo was named a cardinal and was succeeded by Domenico Tardini, Montini was named Substitute for Ordinary Affairs under Cardinal Pacelli, the Secretary of State under Pope Pius XI. From Pius XI, whom he viewed with awe, he adopted the view, that learning is a life long process, and that history was the magister vitae teacher of life His immediate supervisor in the Vatican was Domenico Tardini, with whom he got along well. The election of Pacelli to the papacy in 1939, anticipated by everybody and openly promoted by Pope Pius XI in his last years, was a good omen for Montini, whose position was confirmed in the position under the new Cardinal Secretary of State Luigi Maglione. He met the pope every morning until 1954 and thus developed a rather close relationship:
rewrite: His administrative abilities guided him into service within the Roman Curia, the administrative body of the Vatican. In 1931, Pacelli assigned him a teaching role in history at the institution training papal diplomats. By 1937, following the elevation of his mentor Giuseppe Pizzardo to cardinal and his replacement by Domenico Tardini, Montini was appointed to the role of Substitute for Ordinary Affairs, serving under Cardinal Pacelli, who was then Secretary of State for Pope Pius XI. From Pius XI, whom he deeply revered, he embraced the conviction that education never truly ends and that historical study serves as life's ultimate instructor. Within the Vatican, his direct superior was Domenico Tardini, with whom he maintained a positive working relationship. The expected election of Pacelli as Pope in 1939, a transition long foreseen and encouraged by the aging Pius XI, proved favorable for Montini. His appointment was reaffirmed under the incoming Cardinal Secretary of State, Luigi Maglione. He held daily meetings with the pope until 1954, fostering a notably close personal connection.

input: During the war, the Paris National Guard, particularly in the working-class neighbourhoods of Paris, had become highly politicised and units elected officers; many refused to wear uniforms or obey commands from the national government. National guard units tried to seize power in Paris on 31 October 1870 and 22 January 1871. On 18 March 1871, when the regular army tried to remove cannons from an artillery park on Montmartre, National Guard units resisted and killed two army generals. The national government and regular army forces retreated to Versailles and a revolutionary government was proclaimed in Paris. A Commune was elected, which was dominated by socialists, anarchists and revolutionaries. The red flag replaced the French tricolour and a civil war began between the Commune and the regular army, which attacked and recaptured Paris from 21–28 May in La Semaine Sanglante (Bloody week).
rewrite: Amidst the conflict, the Paris National Guard grew intensely political, especially in the city's labor districts. Its members elected their own leaders, with numerous guardsmen rejecting official uniforms and defying orders from the national authorities. Attempts to overthrow the government in Paris occurred on October 31, 1870, and again on January 22, 1871. The crisis escalated on March 18, 1871, when regular troops attempted to confiscate cannons from Montmartre. National Guardsmen opposed them, resulting in the deaths of two generals. This prompted the national government and its army to withdraw to Versailles, while a revolutionary administration was declared in Paris. A governing Commune, led largely by socialists, anarchists, and radicals, was elected. They adopted the red flag in place of the national tricolour, sparking a civil war. The regular army assaulted and retook the city from May 21 to 28 during the brutal episode known as the Bloody Week.

input: New Zealand polytechnics are established under the Education Act 1989 as amended, and are considered state-owned tertiary institutions along with universities, colleges of education, and wānanga; there is today often much crossover in courses and qualifications offered between all these types of Tertiary Education Institutions. Some have officially taken the title 'institute of technology' which is a term recognized in government strategies equal to that of the term 'polytechnic'. One has opted for the name 'Universal College of Learning' (UCOL), and another 'Unitec New Zealand'. These are legal names but not recognized terms like 'polytechnic' or 'institute of technology'. Many if not all now grant at least bachelor-level degrees.
rewrite: In New Zealand, polytechnics are public higher education bodies created by the Education Act 1989. They operate alongside universities, teacher training colleges, and wānanga, with significant overlap now existing in their academic programs and credentials. Several of these institutions formally use the designation "institute of technology," a phrase given equal standing in official policy. Others have adopted distinct legal names, such as Universal College of Learning or Unitec New Zealand, though these are not standard classifications. Most, if not all, currently confer qualifications up to the bachelor's degree level.

input: Details of the overall United States intelligence budget are classified. Under the Central Intelligence Agency Act of 1949, the Director of Central Intelligence is the only federal government employee who can spend "un-vouchered" government money. The government has disclosed a total figure for all non-military intelligence spending since 2007; the fiscal 2013 figure is $52.6 billion. According to the 2013 mass surveillance disclosures, the CIA's fiscal 2013 budget is $14.7 billion, 28% of the total and almost 50% more than the budget of the National Security Agency. CIA's HUMINT budget is $2.3 billion, the SIGINT budget is $1.7 billion, and spending for security and logistics of CIA missions is $2.5 billion. "Covert action programs", including a variety of activities such as the CIA's drone fleet and anti-Iranian nuclear program activities, accounts for $2.6 billion.
rewrite: The complete budget for U.S. intelligence operations is not publicly available. Established by 1949 legislation, the Director of Central Intelligence holds the unique authority to expend government funds without the standard accountability procedures. An aggregate amount for non-military intelligence expenditures has been released annually since 2007, reaching $52.6 billion in fiscal year 2013. Disclosures from that year indicate the Central Intelligence Agency received $14.7 billion, representing 28 percent of the total and roughly fifty percent more than the National Security Agency's allocation. Within the CIA, human intelligence operations are funded at $2.3 billion, signals intelligence at $1.7 billion, and mission support for security and logistics at $2.5 billion. An additional $2.6 billion is designated for covert actions, encompassing initiatives like drone operations and efforts to counter Iran's nuclear program.

input: University Hospital Southampton NHS Foundation Trust is one of the city's largest employers. It provides local hospital services to 500,000 people in the Southampton area and specialist regional services to more than 3 million people across the South of England. The Trust owns and manages Southampton General Hospital, the Princess Anne Hospital and a palliative care service at Countess Mountbatten House, part of the Moorgreen Hospital site in the village of West End, just outside the city.
rewrite: As a major employer in Southampton, this NHS Trust delivers standard hospital care to approximately half a million local residents. It also offers specialized treatments to over three million individuals throughout Southern England. The institution operates Southampton General Hospital, the Princess Anne Hospital, and a palliative care facility at Countess Mountbatten House, located at the Moorgreen Hospital site in nearby West End.

input: With the exception of seasons one and two, the contestants in the semifinals onwards perform in front of a studio audience. They perform with a full band in the finals. In the first nine seasons, performances were usually aired live on Tuesday nights, followed by the results shows on Wednesdays in the United States and Canada, but moved to Wednesdays and Thursdays in season ten.

Between the fourth and ninth seasons, the band was directed by Rickey Minor, with Ray Chew assuming the role from the tenth season onward. input: The Early Jurassic spans from 200 million years to 175 million years ago. The climate was much more humid than the Triassic, and as a result, the world was very tropical. In the oceans, Plesiosaurs, Ichthyosaurs and Ammonites fill waters as the dominant races of the seas. On land, dinosaurs and other reptiles stake their claim as the dominant race of the land, with species such as Dilophosaurus at the top. The first true crocodiles evolved, pushing out the large amphibians to near extinction. All-in-all, reptiles rise to rule the world. Meanwhile, the first true mammals evolve, but remained relatively small sized.
rewrite: The Early Jurassic period lasted from approximately 200 to 175 million years before the present. Conditions grew significantly wetter compared to the preceding Triassic, creating widespread tropical environments. Marine life was dominated by creatures like Plesiosaurs, Ichthyosaurs, and Ammonites. On land, dinosaurs and other reptiles became the foremost animals, with predators like Dilophosaurus among the most prominent. Early crocodiles appeared, displacing large amphibians almost entirely. This era marked the ascendancy of reptiles globally. Concurrently, the earliest mammals emerged, yet they stayed quite small in stature.

input: This led Popper to conclude that what were regarded[by whom?] as the remarkable strengths of psychoanalytical theories were actually their weaknesses. Psychoanalytical theories were crafted in a way that made them able to refute any criticism and to give an explanation for every possible form of human behaviour. The nature of such theories made it impossible for any criticism or experiment - even in principle - to show them to be false. This realisation had an important consequence when Popper later tackled the problem of demarcation in the philosophy of science, as it led him to posit that the strength of a scientific theory lies in its both being susceptible to falsification, and not actually being falsified by criticism made of it. He considered that if a theory cannot, in principle, be falsified by criticism, it is not a scientific theory.
rewrite: Popper determined that the apparent advantages of psychoanalytic theories were in fact significant flaws. These theories were constructed so that they could counter any objection and account for all conceivable human actions. Their very structure meant no critique or test could ever disprove them, even theoretically. This insight proved crucial when Popper later addressed the issue of distinguishing science from non-science. It prompted him to propose that a scientific theory's robustness depends on its capacity to be falsified, combined with its ability to withstand attempts to do so. He argued that any theory which is inherently immune to falsification cannot be considered scientific.

input: The best-known medieval Chinese name for Tibet is Tubo (Chinese: 吐蕃 also written as 土蕃 or 土番; pinyin: Tǔbō or Tǔfān). This name first appears in Chinese characters as 土番 in the 7th century (Li Tai) and as 吐蕃 in the 10th-century (Old Book of Tang describing 608–609 emissaries from Tibetan King Namri Songtsen to Emperor Yang of Sui). In the Middle Chinese spoken during that period, as reconstructed by William H. Baxter, 土番 was pronounced thux-phjon and 吐蕃 was pronounced thux-pjon (with the x representing tone).
rewrite: During the medieval era, the most common Chinese term for Tibet was Tubo. This designation, found in historical records with variant characters, initially emerged in the 7th century. By the 10th century, it was documented in official Tang dynasty texts concerning diplomatic exchanges. Linguistic reconstructions of Middle Chinese indicate how these characters were phonetically articulated at the time.

input: Starting in the mid-1990s, Valencia, formerly an industrial centre, saw rapid development that expanded its cultural and touristic possibilities, and transformed it into a newly vibrant city. Many local landmarks were restored, including the ancient Towers of the medieval city (Serrano Towers and Quart Towers), and the San Miguel de los Reyes monastery, which now holds a conservation library. Whole sections of the old city, for example the Carmen Quarter, have been extensively renovated. The Paseo Marítimo, a 4 km (2 mi) long palm tree-lined promenade was constructed along the beaches of the north side of the port (Playa Las Arenas, Playa Cabañal and Playa de la Malvarrosa).
rewrite: Beginning in the mid-1990s, Valencia underwent swift growth, shifting from its industrial past to a dynamic urban destination with enriched cultural and tourist appeal. Key historic sites were revitalized, such as the medieval Serrano and Quart Towers, and the San Miguel de los Reyes monastery, repurposed as a library for preserved works. Large areas of the historic center, like the Carmen Quarter, received comprehensive renewal. Additionally, a four-kilometer waterfront walkway bordered by palms was built beside the northern port beaches, including Las Arenas, Cabañal, and Malvarrosa.

input: Modern historiography on the period has reached a consensus between the two extremes of innovation and crisis. It is now (generally) acknowledged that conditions were vastly different north and south of the Alps, and "Late Middle Ages" is often avoided entirely within Italian historiography. The term "Renaissance" is still considered useful for describing certain intellectual, cultural, or artistic developments, but not as the defining feature of an entire European historical epoch. The period from the early 14th century up until – and sometimes including – the 16th century, is rather seen as characterised by other trends: demographic and economic decline followed by recovery, the end of western religious unity and the subsequent emergence of the nation state, and the expansion of European influence onto the rest of the world.
rewrite: Contemporary historical scholarship regarding this era has found a middle ground, moving past the polarized views of radical change versus total collapse. There is broad agreement that circumstances diverged greatly between regions north and south of the Alps. In Italian historical writing, the label "Late Middle Ages" is frequently rejected altogether. While the concept of a "Renaissance" retains value for analyzing specific intellectual or artistic shifts, it is no longer accepted as the single marker for a pan-European age. Instead, the centuries from roughly the early 1300s through the 1500s are understood through other major currents: a cycle of population and economic downturn and subsequent revival, the fracturing of Western Christendom and the rise of sovereign states, and the beginning of global European expansion.

input: The value of the U.S. dollar declined significantly during wartime, especially during the American Civil War, World War I, and World War II. The Federal Reserve, which was established in 1913, was designed to furnish an "elastic" currency subject to "substantial changes of quantity over short periods", which differed significantly from previous forms of high-powered money such as gold, national bank notes, and silver coins. Over the very long run, the prior gold standard kept prices stable—for instance, the price level and the value of the U.S. dollar in 1914 was not very different from the price level in the 1880s. The Federal Reserve initially succeeded in maintaining the value of the U.S. dollar and price stability, reversing the inflation caused by the First World War and stabilizing the value of the dollar during the 1920s, before presiding over a 30% deflation in U.S. prices in the 1930s.
rewrite: The U.S. dollar's worth often fell sharply in periods of major conflict, including the Civil War and the two World Wars. Created in 1913, the Federal Reserve aimed to provide a flexible money supply capable of rapid expansion or contraction, a departure from earlier, less adaptable monetary bases like gold, silver coinage, and national bank notes. Across extended periods, the earlier gold standard had ensured long-term price stability; for example, the general price level in 1914 was quite similar to that of the 1880s. Initially, the Federal Reserve was effective in upholding the dollar's value and stable prices. It managed to counteract the inflationary surge from World War I and stabilized the currency through the 1920s, though it later oversaw a severe deflation where U.S. prices dropped by roughly 30% in the following decade.

input: On 2 March 1882, Roderick Maclean, a disgruntled poet apparently offended by Victoria's refusal to accept one of his poems, shot at the Queen as her carriage left Windsor railway station. Two schoolboys from Eton College struck him with their umbrellas, until he was hustled away by a policeman. Victoria was outraged when he was found not guilty by reason of insanity, but was so pleased by the many expressions of loyalty after the attack that she said it was "worth being shot at—to see how much one is loved".
rewrite: On March 2, 1882, a dissatisfied poet named Roderick Maclean fired at Queen Victoria's carriage as it departed Windsor station. He was aggrieved because she had declined a poem he wrote. Two Eton students hit the assailant with their umbrellas before an officer arrested him. Although furious over his insanity acquittal, the Queen was deeply moved by the public support following the incident. She remarked that the experience of being shot at was valuable, as it revealed the depth of affection people held for her.

input: In 1816 Byron, Percy Bysshe Shelley and his wife Mary Shelley visited Geneva and all three were inspired by the scenery in their writings. During these visits Shelley wrote the poem "Mont Blanc", Byron wrote "The Prisoner of Chillon" and the dramatic poem Manfred, and Mary Shelley, who found the scenery overwhelming, conceived the idea for the novel Frankenstein in her villa on the shores of Lake Geneva in the midst of a thunderstorm. When Coleridge travelled to Chamonix, he declaimed, in defiance of Shelley, who had signed himself "Atheos" in the guestbook of the Hotel de Londres near Montenvers, "Who would be, who could be an atheist in this valley of wonders". By the mid-19th century scientists began to arrive en masse to study the geology and ecology of the region.
rewrite: During a stay in Geneva in 1816, Lord Byron, Percy Bysshe Shelley, and Mary Shelley each drew creative inspiration from the landscape. Shelley composed "Mont Blanc," Byron produced "The Prisoner of Chillon" and "Manfred," and Mary Shelley, profoundly affected by the environment, formulated the concept for *Frankenstein* during a storm at her Lake Geneva villa. Later, when Samuel Taylor Coleridge journeyed to Chamonix, he publicly challenged Shelley's earlier expressed atheism, exclaiming that no one could deny the divine amidst such natural splendor. By the middle of the 1800s, the area also attracted numerous scientists, who came to conduct research on its geological and ecological features.

input: Although the Palaeologi emperors recaptured Constantinople from the Western Europeans in 1261, they were never able to regain control of much of the former imperial lands. They usually controlled only a small section of the Balkan Peninsula near Constantinople, the city itself, and some coastal lands on the Black Sea and around the Aegean Sea. The former Byzantine lands in the Balkans were divided between the new Kingdom of Serbia, the Second Bulgarian Empire and the city-state of Venice. The power of the Byzantine emperors was threatened by a new Turkish tribe, the Ottomans, who established themselves in Anatolia in the 13th century and steadily expanded throughout the 14th century. The Ottomans expanded into Europe, reducing Bulgaria to a vassal state by 1366 and taking over Serbia after its defeat at the Battle of Kosovo in 1389. Western Europeans rallied to the plight of the Christians in the Balkans and declared a new crusade in 1396; a great army was sent to the Balkans, where it was defeated at the Battle of Nicopolis. Constantinople was finally captured by the Ottomans in 1453.
rewrite: Despite reclaiming Constantinople from Western European forces in 1261, the Palaeologan dynasty failed to restore the Byzantine Empire to its former territorial extent. Their effective dominion was largely confined to Constantinople, its adjacent region in the Balkans, and certain coastal territories bordering the Aegean and Black Seas. The bulk of the erstwhile Byzantine holdings in the Balkans had been partitioned among emerging powers: the Serbian Kingdom, the Second Bulgarian Empire, and the Venetian republic. A growing menace to imperial authority arose from the Ottoman Turks, who, after settling in Anatolia during the thirteenth century, pursued relentless expansion through the 1300s. Their advance into Europe rendered Bulgaria a subordinate state by 1366 and, following the Serbian loss at Kosovo in 1389, absorbed Serbia. Alarmed by the Ottoman encroachment on Balkan Christians, Western European powers launched a crusade in 1396, dispatching a substantial force that was decisively beaten at Nicopolis. The Ottoman conquest culminated in the fall of Constantinople in 1453.

They agreed to maintain homes near each other as to facilitate the shared custody and parenting of their son.:403 Their divorce was recorded as the third most costly celebrity divorce in history.
rewrite: Consequently, they ended their relationship in 1979, yet stayed amicable. They rekindled their partnership in 1984 and wed in November 1985, having already welcomed a son named Max Samuel. Nonetheless, after roughly three and a half years, persistent professional conflicts led to their separation in 1989. To best co-parent their child, they chose to live in proximity. input: Canada's Armed forces operate out of 27 Canadian Forces bases (CFB) across the country, including NDHQ. This number has been gradually reduced since the 1970s with bases either being closed or merged. Both officers and non-commissioned members receive their basic training at the Canadian Forces Leadership and Recruit School in Saint-Jean-sur-Richelieu. Officers will generally either directly enter the Canadian Armed Forces with a degree from a civilian university, or receive their commission upon graduation from the Royal Military College of Canada. Specific element and trade training is conducted at a variety of institutions throughout Canada, and to a lesser extent, the world.
rewrite: The Canadian military maintains 27 bases nationwide, a count that has slowly declined since the 1970s due to closures and consolidations. All recruits complete basic instruction at the Leadership and Recruit School in Saint-Jean-sur-Richelieu. Officers typically join directly with a university degree or are commissioned after finishing studies at the Royal Military College of Canada. Specialized training for different roles and branches occurs at various facilities across Canada and, to a smaller degree, internationally.

input: The Taragaon Museum presents the modern history of the Kathmandu Valley. It seeks to document 50 years of research and cultural heritage conservation of the Kathmandu Valley, documenting what artists photographers architects anthropologists from abroad had contributed in the second half of the 20th century. The actual structure of the Museum showcases restoration and rehabilitation efforts to preserve the built heritage of Kathmandu. It was designed by Carl Pruscha (master-planner of the Kathmandy Valley ) in 1970 and constructed in 1971. Restoration works began in 2010 to rehabilitate the Taragaon hostel into the Taragaon Museum. The design uses local brick along with modern architectural design elements, as well as the use of circle, triangles and squares. The Museum is within a short walk from the Boudhnath stupa, which itself can be seen from the Museum tower.
rewrite: The Taragaon Museum chronicles the contemporary story of the Kathmandu Valley. Its mission is to preserve a record of five decades of study and heritage preservation in the valley, highlighting the work contributed by foreign artists, photographers, architects, and anthropologists after 1950. Housed in a structure that itself exemplifies conservation, the building represents the rescue and renewal of Kathmandu's architectural legacy. Originally designed by Carl Pruscha, the valley's master planner, in 1970 and built the following year, the site was transformed from a hostel into the present museum through a restoration project starting in 2010. Its architecture blends regional brick with modernist features, incorporating geometric shapes like circles, triangles, and squares. Located just minutes from the Boudhanath Stupa, the museum's tower offers a direct view of this iconic monument.

input: If any boy produces an outstanding piece of work, it may be "Sent Up For Good", storing the effort in the College Archives for posterity. This award has been around since the 18th century. As Sending Up For Good is fairly infrequent, the process is rather mysterious to many of Eton's boys. First, the master wishing to Send Up For Good must gain the permission of the relevant Head of Department. Upon receiving his or her approval, the piece of work will be marked with Sent Up For Good and the student will receive a card to be signed by House Master, tutor and division master.
rewrite: When a student creates exceptional academic work, it may be honored as "Sent Up For Good," ensuring its preservation in the school's historical records. This longstanding recognition dates back to the 1700s. Because it is rarely bestowed, the procedure remains unclear to most students. A teacher must initially secure agreement from the department head. Following this approval, the work is officially designated, and the pupil is given a certificate to be signed by their housemaster, tutor, and subject teacher.

input: Shorter, black-and-white daily strips began to appear early in the 20th century, and became established in newspapers after the success in 1907 of Bud Fisher's Mutt and Jeff. Humour strips predominated at first, and in the 1920s and 1930s strips with continuing stories in genres such as adventure and drama also became popular. Thin periodicals called comic books appeared in the 1930s, at first reprinting newspaper comic strips; by the end of the decade, original content began to dominate. The success in 1938 of Action Comics and its lead hero Superman marked the beginning of the Golden Age of Comic Books, in which the superhero genre was prominent.
rewrite: At the start of the 1900s, concise black-and-white comic strips emerged daily. Their place in newspapers was secured following the popularity of Bud Fisher's *Mutt and Jeff* in 1907. Initially, most strips were comedic. However, by the 1920s and 30s, serialized adventure and drama narratives gained significant favor. The 1930s also introduced slim comic books, which initially collected newspaper strips but soon featured primarily new material. *Action Comics* and the debut of Superman in 1938 achieved major success, heralding the superhero-dominated Golden Age of Comic Books.

input: Umar is honored for his attempt to resolve the fiscal problems attendant upon conversion to Islam. During the Umayyad period, the majority of people living within the caliphate were not Muslim, but Christian, Jewish, Zoroastrian, or members of other small groups. These religious communities were not forced to convert to Islam, but were subject to a tax (jizyah) which was not imposed upon Muslims. This situation may actually have made widespread conversion to Islam undesirable from the point of view of state revenue, and there are reports that provincial governors actively discouraged such conversions. It is not clear how Umar attempted to resolve this situation, but the sources portray him as having insisted on like treatment of Arab and non-Arab (mawali) Muslims, and on the removal of obstacles to the conversion of non-Arabs to Islam.
rewrite: Umar is recognized for his efforts to address the financial challenges that arose when individuals embraced Islam. In the Umayyad era, most inhabitants of the caliphate adhered to faiths like Christianity, Judaism, or Zoroastrianism, rather than Islam. Followers of these religions were typically exempt from forced conversion but required to pay a special levy, the jizyah, from which Muslims were free. Consequently, mass conversion could threaten government income, leading some regional officials to oppose it. Although the specifics of Umar's approach are uncertain, historical accounts emphasize his commitment to equal rights for Arab and non-Arab Muslims alike, and his work to eliminate barriers preventing non-Arabs from joining the Islamic faith.

input: In the following decades there was a constant battle between the company lobby and the Parliament. The company sought a permanent establishment, while the Parliament would not willingly allow it greater autonomy and so relinquish the opportunity to exploit the company's profits. In 1712, another act renewed the status of the company, though the debts were repaid. By 1720, 15% of British imports were from India, almost all passing through the company, which reasserted the influence of the company lobby. The licence was prolonged until 1766 by yet another act in 1730.
rewrite: Over the subsequent years, a persistent conflict unfolded between corporate advocates and the legislative body. The business pushed for a lasting charter, but lawmakers resisted granting more independence, unwilling to forfeit access to its revenues. An act in 1712 extended the firm's operations despite settled debts. By 1720, India supplied 15% of Britain's imports, nearly all handled by the enterprise, reinforcing its lobby's power. A further statute in 1730 then continued its license through 1766.

input: In 1899, the university opened a national design contest for the new campus. The renowned Philadelphia firm Cope & Stewardson won unanimously with its plan for a row of Collegiate Gothic quadrangles inspired by Oxford and Cambridge Universities. The cornerstone of the first building, Busch Hall, was laid on October 20, 1900. The construction of Brookings Hall, Ridgley, and Cupples began shortly thereafter. The school delayed occupying these buildings until 1905 to accommodate the 1904 World's Fair and Olympics. The delay allowed the university to construct ten buildings instead of the seven originally planned. This original cluster of buildings set a precedent for the development of the Danforth Campus; Cope & Stewardson’s original plan and its choice of building materials have, with few exceptions, guided the construction and expansion of the Danforth Campus to the present day.
rewrite: In 1899, the university launched a nationwide competition to design its new campus. The Philadelphia architecture firm Cope & Stewardson received the unanimous winning vote for their proposal, which featured a series of Collegiate Gothic courtyards modeled after Oxford and Cambridge. The first structure, Busch Hall, had its cornerstone placed on October 20, 1900. Work soon started on Brookings Hall, Ridgley, and Cupples. However, to make way for the 1904 World's Fair and Olympic Games, the institution postponed moving into these buildings until 1905. This wait enabled the construction of ten buildings rather than the initial seven. This early group established a lasting standard for the Danforth Campus; the firm's initial architectural vision and selected materials have directed nearly all subsequent growth and building on the site ever since.

input: Each team consists of a maximum of eleven players (excluding substitutes), one of whom must be the goalkeeper. Competition rules may state a minimum number of players required to constitute a team, which is usually seven. Goalkeepers are the only players allowed to play the ball with their hands or arms, provided they do so within the penalty area in front of their own goal. Though there are a variety of positions in which the outfield (non-goalkeeper) players are strategically placed by a coach, these positions are not defined or required by the Laws.
rewrite: A soccer team can have up to eleven players on the field at once, including one designated goalkeeper. Regulations often set a lower limit, typically seven players, for a match to proceed. Only the goalkeeper is permitted to handle the ball, and this is restricted to their own penalty area. While coaches assign various tactical roles to the other players, these specific field positions are not officially mandated by the sport's governing rules.

input: The clergy was divided into two types: the secular clergy, who lived out in the world, and the regular clergy, who lived under a religious rule and were usually monks. Throughout the period monks remained a very small proportion of the population, usually less than one per cent. Most of the regular clergy were drawn from the nobility, the same social class that served as the recruiting ground for the upper levels of the secular clergy. The local parish priests were often drawn from the peasant class. Townsmen were in a somewhat unusual position, as they did not fit into the traditional three-fold division of society into nobles, clergy, and peasants. During the 12th and 13th centuries, the ranks of the townsmen expanded greatly as existing towns grew and new population centres were founded. But throughout the Middle Ages the population of the towns probably never exceeded 10 per cent of the total population.
rewrite: The religious ministers of the era fell into two categories: secular clerics, who operated within everyday society, and regular clerics, who resided in monastic communities under a specific rule. Monastic individuals consistently represented a tiny fraction, typically under one percent, of the overall populace. The regular clergy were predominantly recruited from the noble classes, mirroring the social origins of the higher echelons within the secular clergy. In contrast, local parish priests frequently came from peasant stock. Townspeople occupied a more ambiguous social standing, as they did not align neatly with the conventional model of nobles, clergy, and peasants. Between the 1100s and 1200s, the number of urban dwellers increased significantly due to the expansion of established towns and the creation of new settlements. However, even at their peak during the medieval period, urban residents likely constituted no more than ten percent of the total population.

input: It is in this time that the notation of music on a staff and other elements of musical notation began to take shape. This invention made possible the separation of the composition of a piece of music from its transmission; without written music, transmission was oral, and subject to change every time it was transmitted. With a musical score, a work of music could be performed without the composer's presence. The invention of the movable-type printing press in the 15th century had far-reaching consequences on the preservation and transmission of music.
rewrite: During this period, musical notation started to develop, including the use of the staff. This allowed compositions to be recorded independently from their performance, moving beyond an oral tradition that often altered pieces with each retelling. Consequently, music could be reproduced accurately without the composer being present. Later, the emergence of movable-type printing in the 1400s profoundly influenced how music was both preserved and shared.

input: Formal schooling did not start in Hungary until the age of ten. Instead, governesses taught von Neumann, his brothers and his cousins. Max believed that knowledge of languages other than Hungarian was essential, so the children were tutored in English, French, German and Italian. By the age of 8, von Neumann was familiar with differential and integral calculus, but he was particularly interested in history, reading his way through Wilhelm Oncken's Allgemeine Geschichte in Einzeldarstellungen. A copy was contained in a private library Max purchased. One of the rooms in the apartment was converted into a library and reading room, with bookshelves from ceiling to floor.
rewrite: In Hungary, formal education began at ten years old. Prior to that, von Neumann and his siblings and cousins were instructed by governesses. Their father, Max, considered fluency in foreign languages vital, so they received lessons in English, French, German, and Italian. By eight, von Neumann understood advanced calculus, yet his passion was history. He diligently read Wilhelm Oncken's multi-volume historical series, *Allgemeine Geschichte in Einzeldarstellungen*, from a set in his father's personal collection. Max had bought the books and transformed a room into a full library, with tall shelves lining the walls.

input: Despite competition from other materials, copper remains the preferred electrical conductor in nearly all categories of electrical wiring with the major exception being overhead electric power transmission where aluminium is often preferred. Copper wire is used in power generation, power transmission, power distribution, telecommunications, electronics circuitry, and countless types of electrical equipment. Electrical wiring is the most important market for the copper industry. This includes building wire, communications cable, power distribution cable, appliance wire, automotive wire and cable, and magnet wire. Roughly half of all copper mined is used to manufacture electrical wire and cable conductors. Many electrical devices rely on copper wiring because of its multitude of inherent beneficial properties, such as its high electrical conductivity, tensile strength, ductility, creep (deformation) resistance, corrosion resistance, low thermal expansion, high thermal conductivity, solderability, and ease of installation.
rewrite: Copper continues to be the dominant material for electrical conductors across most applications, even as alternatives exist. Its primary competitor is aluminum, which is frequently chosen for overhead power lines. Otherwise, copper is integral to generating, transmitting, and distributing electricity, as well as to telecommunications, electronic circuits, and many kinds of electrical devices. The production of electrical wiring represents the largest segment of the copper market, encompassing building wire, various cables, and magnet wire. Approximately 50% of all mined copper goes toward creating these conductive wires and cables. This reliance stems from copper's superior and numerous natural qualities, including excellent conductivity, strength, flexibility, resistance to corrosion and deformation, favorable thermal properties, and overall ease of use.

input: Canada allows nonprofits to be incorporated or unincorporated. Nonprofits may incorporate either federally, under Part II of the Canada Business Corporations Act or under provincial legislation. Many of the governing Acts for Canadian nonprofits date to the early 1900s, meaning that nonprofit legislation has not kept pace with legislation that governs for-profit corporations; particularly with regards to corporate governance. Federal, and in some provinces (such as Ontario), incorporation is by way of Letters Patent, and any change to the Letters Patent (even a simple name change) requires formal approval by the appropriate government, as do by-law changes. Other provinces (such as Alberta) permit incorporation as of right, by the filing of Articles of Incorporation or Articles of Association.
rewrite: In Canada, nonprofit organizations have the option to exist with or without formal incorporation. They can choose to incorporate at the federal level, guided by specific sections of the Canada Business Corporations Act, or under various provincial laws. Much of the regulatory framework for these entities originates from laws established over a century ago. Consequently, rules for nonprofits have not evolved as dynamically as those for commercial businesses, especially in areas concerning organizational oversight and management. Federally and in provinces like Ontario, incorporation occurs through a Letters Patent system, where even minor amendments demand official governmental consent. Conversely, jurisdictions such as Alberta allow automatic incorporation upon submitting the required foundational documents.

input: In addition to the above, Greece is also to start oil and gas exploration in other locations in the Ionian Sea, as well as the Libyan Sea, within the Greek exclusive economic zone, south of Crete. The Ministry of the Environment, Energy and Climate Change announced that there was interest from various countries (including Norway and the United States) in exploration, and the first results regarding the amount of oil and gas in these locations were expected in the summer of 2012. In November 2012, a report published by Deutsche Bank estimated the value of natural gas reserves south of Crete at €427 billion.
rewrite: Greece has further plans to search for oil and gas in new areas of its own economic waters, specifically in the Ionian and Libyan Seas, including zones south of Crete. According to the nation's environmental and energy ministry, several foreign nations, such as Norway and the U.S., have shown interest in these exploration projects. Initial findings on the resources were anticipated by mid-2012. Later that year, in November, an analysis from Deutsche Bank appraised the natural gas deposits near Crete at approximately €427 billion.

input: In Canada, there are Affiliate Schools, Colleges, Institutes of Technology/Polytechnic Institutes, and Universities that offer instruction in a variety of programs that can lead to: engineering and applied science degrees, apprenticeship and trade programs, certificates, and diplomas. Affiliate Schools are polytechnic divisions belonging to a national university and offer select technical and engineering programs. Colleges, Institutes of Technology/Polytechnic Institutes, and Universities tend to be independent institutions.
rewrite: Canada's educational institutions include Affiliate Schools, Colleges, Institutes of Technology, Polytechnics, and Universities. They provide diverse programs resulting in degrees in engineering and applied science, apprenticeships, trade certifications, and diplomas. Affiliate Schools are specialized technical divisions within a national university. In contrast, Colleges, Institutes of Technology, Polytechnics, and Universities generally operate as separate, independent entities.

input: The Richmond metro area is served by many local television and radio stations. As of 2010[update], the Richmond-Petersburg designated market area (DMA) is the 58th largest in the U.S. with 553,950 homes according to Nielsen Market Research. The major network television affiliates are WTVR-TV 6 (CBS), WRIC-TV 8 (ABC), WWBT 12 (NBC), WRLH-TV 35 (Fox), and WUPV 65 (CW). Public Broadcasting Service stations include WCVE-TV 23 and WCVW 57. There are also a wide variety of radio stations in the Richmond area, catering to many different interests, including news, talk radio, and sports, as well as an eclectic mix of musical interests.
rewrite: The Richmond metropolitan region features numerous television and radio broadcasters. Nielsen Market Research data from 2010 ranks the Richmond-Petersburg market as the nation's 58th largest, reaching approximately 553,950 households. Key commercial TV stations are WTVR-TV (CBS, channel 6), WRIC-TV (ABC, 8), WWBT (NBC, 12), WRLH-TV (Fox, 35), and WUPV (CW, 65). Public television is provided by WCVE-TV and WCVW. Additionally, a diverse array of radio stations serve the area, offering programming such as news, talk, sports, and a broad spectrum of music genres.

input: Another Alaskan transportation method is the dogsled. In modern times (that is, any time after the mid-late 1920s), dog mushing is more of a sport than a true means of transportation. Various races are held around the state, but the best known is the Iditarod Trail Sled Dog Race, a 1,150-mile (1,850 km) trail from Anchorage to Nome (although the distance varies from year to year, the official distance is set at 1,049 miles or 1,688 km). The race commemorates the famous 1925 serum run to Nome in which mushers and dogs like Togo and Balto took much-needed medicine to the diphtheria-stricken community of Nome when all other means of transportation had failed. Mushers from all over the world come to Anchorage each March to compete for cash, prizes, and prestige. The "Serum Run" is another sled dog race that more accurately follows the route of the famous 1925 relay, leaving from the community of Nenana (southwest of Fairbanks) to Nome.
rewrite: In Alaska, dog sledding represents another mode of travel. Today, particularly from the late 1920s onward, it has evolved primarily into a sporting activity rather than a practical transportation system. Across the state, numerous competitions take place, with the most renowned being the Iditarod Trail Sled Dog Race. This event covers a lengthy path from Anchorage to Nome, officially recognized as 1,049 miles. It honors the historic 1925 emergency mission to deliver serum to Nome during a diphtheria outbreak, a feat accomplished by teams including those led by dogs like Togo and Balto after conventional transport methods proved impossible. Each March, mushers globally gather in Anchorage to vie for monetary rewards, awards, and recognition. Additionally, the "Serum Run" race traces a course closer to the original 1925 relay route, starting in Nenana and finishing in Nome.

input: Digimon was first conceived as a virtual pet toy in the vein of Tamagotchis and, as such, took influence from Tamagotchis' cute and round designs. The small areas of the screens (16 by 16 pixels) meant that character designers had to create monsters whose forms would be easily recognizable. As such, many of the early Digimon—including Tyrannomon, the first one ever created—were based on dinosaurs. Many further designs were created by Kenji Watanabe, who was brought in to help with the "X-Antibody" creatures and art for the Digimon collectible card game. Watanabe was one influenced by American comics, which were beginning to gain popularity in Japan, and as such began to make his characters look stronger and "cool." The character creation process, however, has for most of the franchise's history been collaborative and reliant on conversation and brainstorming.
rewrite: Originally inspired by virtual pets like Tamagotchi, Digimon adopted a similarly charming and rounded aesthetic. The limited resolution of early screens required monsters with simple, identifiable shapes, leading to initial designs rooted in dinosaurs, such as the inaugural Tyrannomon. Later, artist Kenji Watanabe contributed significantly, developing designs for the "X-Antibody" line and the card game. Influenced by the growing popularity of American comics in Japan, Watanabe infused the creatures with a more powerful and stylish appearance. Throughout the series, the development of these characters has largely been a group effort, built on discussion and shared ideas.

input: China's network security and information technology leadership team was established February 27, 2014. The leadership team is tasked with national security and long-term development and co-ordination of major issues related to network security and information technology. Economic, political, cultural, social and military fields as related to network security and information technology strategy, planning and major macroeconomic policy are being researched. The promotion of national network security and information technology law are constantly under study for enhanced national security capabilities.
rewrite: China's leading group for cybersecurity and information technology was formed on February 27, 2014. Its role is to oversee national security and forward-looking growth, coordinating significant matters in this domain. The team examines strategy, planning, and key policies linked to economic, political, cultural, social, and defense sectors. It also continually reviews legal advancements to strengthen the country's protective capacities in this area.

input: In 1996, Marvel had some of its titles participate in "Heroes Reborn", a crossover that allowed Marvel to relaunch some of its flagship characters such as the Avengers and the Fantastic Four, and outsource them to the studios of two of the former Marvel artists turned Image Comics founders, Jim Lee and Rob Liefeld. The relaunched titles, which saw the characters transported to a parallel universe with a history distinct from the mainstream Marvel Universe, were a solid success amidst a generally struggling industry, but Marvel discontinued the experiment after a one-year run and returned the characters to the Marvel Universe proper. In 1998, the company launched the imprint Marvel Knights, taking place within Marvel continuity; helmed by soon-to-become editor-in-chief Joe Quesada, it featured tough, gritty stories showcasing such characters as the Inhumans, Black Panther and Daredevil.
rewrite: In 1996, Marvel initiated the "Heroes Reborn" event, a crossover which rebooted key franchises like the Avengers and Fantastic Four. These series were produced externally by studios led by ex-Marvel illustrators and Image Comics co-founders Jim Lee and Rob Liefeld. The stories placed these heroes in an alternate reality with a new history, separate from the core Marvel Universe. Despite a difficult period for comics, the revamped titles performed well commercially. However, after twelve months, Marvel concluded the project and reintegrated the characters into their original setting. Two years later, the company introduced the Marvel Knights imprint, set within the main continuity. Under the direction of future editor-in-chief Joe Quesada, it presented darker, more mature narratives focused on characters including Daredevil, Black Panther, and the Inhumans.

input: In Han government, the emperor was the supreme judge and lawgiver, the commander-in-chief of the armed forces and sole designator of official nominees appointed to the top posts in central and local administrations; those who earned a 600-dan salary-rank or higher. Theoretically, there were no limits to his power. However, state organs with competing interests and institutions such as the court conference (tingyi 廷議)—where ministers were convened to reach majority consensus on an issue—pressured the emperor to accept the advice of his ministers on policy decisions. If the emperor rejected a court conference decision, he risked alienating his high ministers. Nevertheless, emperors sometimes did reject the majority opinion reached at court conferences.
rewrite: Within the Han dynasty's administration, the emperor held ultimate authority as the highest judicial and legislative figure, leader of the military, and the exclusive appointer of all senior officials in the government, specifically those at the 600-dan rank and above. In principle, his authority was absolute. Yet in practice, competing bureaucratic interests and established forums like the court conference—a council of ministers seeking collective agreement—obliged the ruler to seriously consider ministerial counsel. Disregarding such a consensus carried the potential cost of estranging top advisors, though some emperors still chose to override these majority decisions.

input: Bush focused his campaign on national security, presenting himself as a decisive leader and contrasted Kerry as a "flip-flopper." This strategy was designed to convey to American voters the idea that Bush could be trusted to be tough on terrorism while Kerry would be "uncertain in the face of danger." Bush (just as his father did with Dukakis in the 1988 election) also sought to portray Kerry as a "Massachusetts liberal" who was out of touch with mainstream Americans. One of Kerry's slogans was "Stronger at home, respected in the world." This advanced the suggestion that Kerry would pay more attention to domestic concerns; it also encapsulated Kerry's contention that Bush had alienated American allies by his foreign policy.
rewrite: During his campaign, Bush emphasized national security, positioning himself as a resolute commander and framing Kerry as indecisive. This approach aimed to persuade voters that Bush offered steadfastness against threats, whereas Kerry might waver. Mirroring tactics from the 1988 election, Bush also labeled Kerry a detached "Massachusetts liberal," suggesting he was disconnected from ordinary citizens. Kerry’s platform countered with the slogan “Stronger at home, respected in the world,” highlighting his focus on internal issues and criticizing Bush’s foreign policy for straining international alliances. This message argued that Kerry would prioritize domestic affairs and restore global regard.

input: Unlike many religions, Buddhism has no single central text that is universally referred to by all traditions. However, some scholars have referred to the Vinaya Pitaka and the first four Nikayas of the Sutta Pitaka as the common core of all Buddhist traditions.[page needed] This could be considered misleading, as Mahāyāna considers these merely a preliminary, and not a core, teaching. The Tibetan Buddhists have not even translated most of the āgamas (though theoretically they recognize them) and they play no part in the religious life of either clergy or laity in China and Japan. Other scholars say there is no universally accepted common core. The size and complexity of the Buddhist canons have been seen by some (including Buddhist social reformer Babasaheb Ambedkar) as presenting barriers to the wider understanding of Buddhist philosophy.
rewrite: Buddhism lacks a singular scripture embraced by every school of thought. While certain academics point to the Vinaya Pitaka and the initial four Nikayas of the Sutta Pitaka as a foundational element across traditions, this view is contested. Mahāyāna Buddhism, for instance, regards these texts as introductory rather than central. In Tibetan Buddhism, most āgamas remain untranslated and hold no practical role in East Asian religious practice. Some experts argue no such universal foundation exists. The extensive and intricate nature of the Buddhist scriptures has also been noted, with figures like B.R. Ambedkar observing that their sheer volume can obstruct broader engagement with the tradition's philosophical insights.

input: Another format, rhythmic AC, in addition to playing all the popular hot and soft AC music, past and present, places a heavy emphasis on disco as well as 1980s and 1990s dance hits, such as those by Amber, C&C Music Factory and Black Box, and includes dance remixes of pop songs, such as the Soul Solution mix of Toni Braxton's "Unbreak My Heart".
rewrite: Rhythmic AC stations feature a mix of current and classic adult contemporary music, with a particular focus on dance genres. Their playlists highlight disco and dance tracks from the 80s and 90s, including artists like Amber, and often incorporate remixed pop songs, such as a dance version of Toni Braxton's hit.

input: All of the executions which have taken place since the 1936 hanging of Bethea in Owensboro have been conducted within a wall or enclosure. For example, Fred Adams was legally hanged in Kennett, Missouri, on April 2, 1937, within a 10-foot (3 m) wooden stockade. Roscoe "Red" Jackson was hanged within a stockade in Galena, Missouri, on May 26, 1937. Two Kentucky hangings were conducted after Galena in which numerous persons were present within a wooden stockade, that of John "Peter" Montjoy in Covington, Kentucky on December 17, 1937, and that of Harold Van Venison in Covington on June 3, 1938. An estimated 400 witnesses were present for the hanging of Lee Simpson in Ryegate, Montana, on December 30, 1939. The execution of Timothy McVeigh on June 11, 2001 was witnessed by some 300 people, some by closed-circuit television.
rewrite: Since the 1936 public hanging of Bethea in Owensboro, all subsequent executions have occurred behind barriers. For instance, Fred Adams was lawfully hanged inside a ten-foot wooden stockade in Kennett, Missouri, on April 2, 1937. Similarly, Roscoe "Red" Jackson faced execution within a stockade in Galena, Missouri, on May 26 of that year. Later in Kentucky, two hangings—those of John "Peter" Montjoy on December 17, 1937, and Harold Van Venison on June 3, 1938—also took place inside wooden enclosures with many observers present. A crowd of about 400 witnessed Lee Simpson's hanging in Ryegate, Montana, on December 30, 1939. More recently, around 300 people, including some via closed-circuit broadcast, observed Timothy McVeigh's execution on June 11, 2001.

input: Smaller private schools include Babson College, Bentley University, Boston Architectural College, Emmanuel College, Fisher College, MGH Institute of Health Professions, Massachusetts College of Pharmacy and Health Sciences, Simmons College, Wellesley College, Wheelock College, Wentworth Institute of Technology, New England School of Law (originally established as America's first all female law school), and Emerson College.
rewrite: Private institutions such as Babson, Bentley, and Emerson are among the area's smaller colleges. Others include Simmons, Wellesley, Wentworth, and several specialized schools in health, law, and design.

input: Of the remaining land area, the state of Alaska owns 101 million acres (41 million hectares), its entitlement under the Alaska Statehood Act. A portion of that acreage is occasionally ceded to organized boroughs, under the statutory provisions pertaining to newly formed boroughs. Smaller portions are set aside for rural subdivisions and other homesteading-related opportunities. These are not very popular due to the often remote and roadless locations. The University of Alaska, as a land grant university, also owns substantial acreage which it manages independently.
rewrite: Alaska holds 101 million acres of the leftover territory, a right granted by its statehood legislation. Some of this land is periodically transferred to established boroughs as per laws governing their creation. Additional tracts are reserved for rural developments and homesteading, though these see limited interest because of their isolated, inaccessible settings. Furthermore, the University of Alaska possesses significant land holdings, which it oversees autonomously as a land grant institution.

input: By 1640, the town's theocratic government and nine-square grid plan were in place, and the town was renamed Newhaven from Quinnipiac. However, the area north of New Haven remained Quinnipiac until 1678, when it was renamed Hamden. The settlement became the headquarters of the New Haven Colony. At the time, the New Haven Colony was separate from the Connecticut Colony, which had been established to the north centering on Hartford. One of the principal differences between the two colonies was that the New Haven colony was an intolerant theocracy that did not permit other churches to be established, while the Connecticut colony permitted the establishment of other churches.
rewrite: By 1640, the community had established its religiously governed leadership and a layout of nine square blocks, also adopting the name Newhaven in place of Quinnipiac. The northern region kept the original name until 1678, when it became Hamden. This settlement served as the capital of the New Haven Colony. This colony was distinct from the neighboring Connecticut Colony, which was based around Hartford. A key distinction was that New Haven enforced a strict, exclusive state religion, whereas Connecticut allowed multiple churches to exist.

input: The institutions and practices of canon law paralleled the legal development of much of Europe, and consequently both modern civil law and common law (legal system) bear the influences of canon law. Edson Luiz Sampel, a Brazilian expert in canon law, says that canon law is contained in the genesis of various institutes of civil law, such as the law in continental Europe and Latin American countries. Sampel explains that canon law has significant influence in contemporary society.
rewrite: The structures and customs of canon law evolved alongside Europe's broader legal growth, leaving a mark on today's civil and common law systems. According to Brazilian scholar Edson Luiz Sampel, the foundations of canon law are woven into the origins of many civil law institutions, especially across continental Europe and Latin America. He further asserts that its impact remains considerable in modern times.

input: Broadly speaking, Enlightenment science greatly valued empiricism and rational thought, and was embedded with the Enlightenment ideal of advancement and progress. The study of science, under the heading of natural philosophy, was divided into physics and a conglomerate grouping of chemistry and natural history, which included anatomy, biology, geology, mineralogy, and zoology. As with most Enlightenment views, the benefits of science were not seen universally; Rousseau criticized the sciences for distancing man from nature and not operating to make people happier. Science during the Enlightenment was dominated by scientific societies and academies, which had largely replaced universities as centres of scientific research and development. Societies and academies were also the backbone of the maturation of the scientific profession. Another important development was the popularization of science among an increasingly literate population. Philosophes introduced the public to many scientific theories, most notably through the Encyclopédie and the popularization of Newtonianism by Voltaire and Émilie du Châtelet. Some historians have marked the 18th century as a drab period in the history of science; however, the century saw significant advancements in the practice of medicine, mathematics, and physics; the development of biological taxonomy; a new understanding of magnetism and electricity; and the maturation of chemistry as a discipline, which established the foundations of modern chemistry.
rewrite:
During the Enlightenment era, scientific inquiry placed a high priority on observation and logical reasoning, reflecting the period's broader emphasis on human improvement and forward momentum. This pursuit, often termed natural philosophy, was categorized into physics alongside a combined field encompassing chemistry and natural history—the latter covering areas such as anatomy, biology, geology, mineralogy, and zoology. However, Enlightenment thought was not monolithic; figures like Rousseau argued that scientific pursuits alienated humanity from the natural world and failed to enhance genuine happiness.

Scientific activity was primarily centered in specialized societies and academies, which overtook universities as the principal hubs for research and innovation. These institutions played a crucial role in shaping science into a recognized profession. Concurrently, there was a concerted effort to make science accessible to a growing educated public. Philosophers disseminated scientific ideas widely, particularly through works like the Encyclopédie and by promoting Newtonian physics, as done by Voltaire and Émilie du Châtelet.

While some historians view the 18th century as less dynamic in scientific history, it nonetheless witnessed substantial progress. Key achievements included advances in medical practice, mathematics, and physics; the establishment of systematic biological classification; groundbreaking insights into magnetism and electricity; and the evolution of chemistry into a structured discipline, laying the groundwork for its modern form.

input: Hospitals in Liberia include the John F. Kennedy Medical Center in Monrovia and several others. Life expectancy in Liberia is estimated to be 57.4 years in 2012. With a fertility rate of 5.9 births per woman, the maternal mortality rate stood at 990 per 100,000 births in 2010. A number of highly communicable diseases are widespread, including tuberculosis, diarrheal diseases and malaria. In 2007, the HIV infection rates stood at 2% of the population aged 15–49  whereas the incidence of tuberculosis was 420 per 100,000 people in 2008. Approximately 58.2% – 66% of women are estimated to have undergone female genital mutilation.
rewrite: Liberia's healthcare landscape features facilities such as the John F. Kennedy Medical Center in its capital. As of 2012, the average lifespan was roughly 57.4 years. The nation contends with significant health challenges: a maternal death rate of 990 per 100,000 live births in 2010, alongside a fertility rate of 5.9 children per woman. Infectious illnesses like malaria, tuberculosis, and diarrheal conditions are common. In 2008, TB incidence reached 420 cases per 100,000 individuals, and HIV prevalence among adults was 2% in 2007. Additionally, an estimated 58.2% to 66% of women have experienced genital mutilation.

input: On July 8, 2007 The Washington Post published excerpts from UCLA Professor Amy Zegart's book Spying Blind: The CIA, the FBI, and the Origins of 9/11. The Post reported from Zegart's book that government documents show the CIA and FBI missed 23 potential chances to disrupt the terrorist attacks of September 11, 2001. The primary reasons for the failures included: agency cultures resistant to change and new ideas; inappropriate incentives for promotion; and a lack of cooperation between the FBI, CIA and the rest of the United States Intelligence Community. The book blamed the FBI's decentralized structure, which prevented effective communication and cooperation among different FBI offices. The book suggested that the FBI has not evolved into an effective counter-terrorism or counter-intelligence agency, due in large part to deeply ingrained agency cultural resistance to change. For example, FBI personnel practices continue to treat all staff other than special agents as support staff, classifying intelligence analysts alongside the FBI's auto mechanics and janitors.
rewrite: On July 8, 2007, *The Washington Post* featured material from Amy Zegart’s publication *Spying Blind: The CIA, the FBI, and the Origins of 9/11*. According to the professor’s research, official records indicate the CIA and FBI overlooked as many as 23 opportunities to potentially prevent the September 11 attacks. Key factors behind these lapses were institutional mindsets opposed to innovation, reward systems that did not prioritize counterterrorism, and poor coordination across U.S. intelligence agencies. Zegart’s work criticizes the FBI’s fragmented organization, which hindered information sharing among its own field offices. It argues the bureau has failed to transform into a competent counterterrorism body, primarily because of a cultural aversion to reform. This is illustrated by personnel policies that group intelligence analysts with clerical and maintenance roles, rather than treating them as core professionals.

input: Zhu Yousong, however, fared a lot worse than his ancestor Zhu Yuanzhang three centuries earlier. Beset by factional conflicts, his regime could not offer effective resistance to Qing forces, when the Qing army, led by the Manchu prince Dodo approached Jiangnan the next spring. Days after Yangzhou fell to the Manchus in late May 1645, the Hongguang Emperor fled Nanjing, and the imperial Ming Palace was looted by local residents. On June 6, Dodo's troops approached Nanjing, and the commander of the city's garrison, Zhao the Earl of Xincheng, promptly surrendered the city to them. The Manchus soon ordered all male residents of the city to shave their heads in the Manchu queue way. They requisitioned a large section of the city for the bannermen's cantonment, and destroyed the former imperial Ming Palace, but otherwise the city was spared the mass murders and destruction that befell Yangzhou.
rewrite: In contrast to his forebear Zhu Yuanzhang from three hundred years before, Zhu Yousong met a far more unfortunate fate. His rule, weakened by internal divisions, proved incapable of mounting a strong defense against the advancing Qing military. When the Manchu leader Dodo moved toward Jiangnan in the spring of the following year, resistance crumbled. Shortly after Yangzhou was captured by the Manchus in May 1645, the Hongguang Emperor abandoned Nanjing, leading locals to plunder the Ming palace. By June 6, Dodo’s forces neared Nanjing, and the defending commander, Zhao the Earl of Xincheng, quickly capitulated. The Manchus then mandated that all men in the city adopt the Manchu hairstyle, reserved a significant urban area for bannermen, and razed the former imperial palace. However, unlike Yangzhou, Nanjing avoided widespread slaughter and devastation.

input: The Princess Margaret Hospital on Funafuti is the only hospital in Tuvalu. The Tuvaluan medical staff at PMH in 2011 comprised the Director of Health & Surgeon, the Chief Medical Officer Public Health, an anaesthetist, a paediatric medical officer and an obstetrics and gynaecology medical officer. Allied health staff include two radiographers, two pharmacists, three laboratory technicians, two dieticians and 13 nurses with specialised training in fields including surgical nursing, anaesthesia nursing/ICU, paediatric nursing and midwifery. PMH also employs a dentist. The Department of Health also employs nine or ten nurses on the outer islands to provide general nursing and midwifery services.
rewrite: Princess Margaret Hospital, located on Funafuti, serves as Tuvalu's sole medical facility. In 2011, its Tuvaluan clinical team included the Health Director and Surgeon, the Chief Public Health Medical Officer, along with specialists in anaesthesia, paediatrics, and obstetrics and gynaecology. Supporting personnel consisted of two radiographers, two pharmacists, three lab technicians, two dieticians, and 13 nurses with advanced training in areas like surgery, anaesthesia or ICU care, paediatrics, and midwifery. A dentist is also on staff. Additionally, the Health Department stations roughly nine to ten nurses on outer islands to deliver basic nursing and midwifery care.

input: By the late 2000s, Dell's "configure to order" approach of manufacturing—delivering individual PCs configured to customer specifications from its US facilities was no longer as efficient or competitive with high-volume Asian contract manufacturers as PCs became powerful low-cost commodities. Dell closed plants that produced desktop computers for the North American market, including the Mort Topfer Manufacturing Center in Austin, Texas (original location) and Lebanon, Tennessee (opened in 1999) in 2008 and early 2009, respectively. The desktop production plant in Winston-Salem, North Carolina, received US$280 million in incentives from the state and opened in 2005, but ceased operations in November 2010. Dell's contract with the state required them to repay the incentives for failing to meet the conditions, and they sold the North Carolina plant to Herbalife. Most of the work that used to take place in Dell's U.S. plants was transferred to contract manufacturers in Asia and Mexico, or some of Dell's own factories overseas. The Miami, Florida, facility of its Alienware subsidiary remains in operation, while Dell continues to produce its servers (its most profitable products) in Austin, Texas. On January 8, 2009, Dell announced the closure of its manufacturing plant in Limerick, Ireland, with the loss of 1,900 jobs and the transfer of production to its plant in Łodź in Poland.
rewrite:
Toward the end of the first decade of the 2000s, Dell’s business model of building personal computers to match each buyer’s specific requests—shipping them from American factories—grew less viable. As PCs turned into inexpensive, high-volume goods, competing with large-scale Asian producers became difficult.
