input: The next year Madonna and Maverick sued Warner Music Group and its former parent company Time Warner, claiming that mismanagement of resources and poor bookkeeping had cost the company millions of dollars. In return, Warner filed a countersuit alleging that Maverick had lost tens of millions of dollars on its own. The dispute was resolved when the Maverick shares, owned by Madonna and Ronnie Dashev, were purchased by Warner. Madonna and Dashev's company became a wholly owned subsidiary of Warner Music, but Madonna was still signed to Warner under a separate recording contract.
rewrite: In the following year, Madonna and Maverick initiated legal action against Warner Music Group and its prior owner, Time Warner. They asserted that financial mismanagement and inadequate accounting had resulted in multi-million dollar losses for their company. Warner responded with a countersuit, contending Maverick itself was responsible for tens of millions in deficits. The conflict concluded with Warner buying out the shares held by Madonna and Ronnie Dashev. Their enterprise then became a fully owned division of Warner Music, though Madonna remained individually contracted to Warner for her recordings.

input: One of the more prominent contestants this year was Chris Medina, whose story of caring for his brain-damaged fiancée received widespread coverage. Medina was cut in the Top 40 round. Casey Abrams, who suffers from ulcerative colitis, was hospitalized twice and missed the Top 13 result show. The judges used their one save on Abrams on the Top 11, and as a result this was the first season that 11 finalists went on tour instead of 10. In the following week, Naima Adedapo and Thia Megia were both eliminated the following week.
rewrite: This season featured notable participant Chris Medina, whose devotion to his injured partner drew significant attention, though he was eliminated early. Fellow competitor Casey Abrams faced health issues requiring hospitalization, causing him to miss a key episode. The judges intervened to save Abrams later on, leading to an unprecedented eleven contestants joining the tour. Subsequently, both Naima Adedapo and Thia Megia were voted off the following week.

input: Until the 1990s further replays would be played until one team was victorious. Some ties took as many as six matches to settle; in their 1975 campaign, Fulham played a total of 12 games over six rounds, which remains the most games played by a team to reach a final. Replays were traditionally played three or four days after the original game, but from 1991–92 they were staged at least 10 days later on police advice. This led to penalty shoot-outs being introduced, the first of which came on 26 November 1991 when Rotherham United eliminated Scunthorpe United.
rewrite: Before the 1990s, tied matches were decided by repeated games until a winner emerged. Certain draws required up to six rematches; Fulham's 1975 run involved 12 matches across six rounds, still a record for reaching the final. These replays were initially held within days, but starting in the 1991-92 season, they were postponed by at least ten days following police recommendations. This change prompted the adoption of penalty shoot-outs, with the first occurring on November 26, 1991, when Rotherham United defeated Scunthorpe United.

input: "By May 1539, Conquistador Hernando de Soto skirted the coast of Florida, searching for a deep harbor to land. He described seeing a thick wall of red mangroves spread mile after mile, some reaching as high as 70 feet (21 m), with intertwined and elevated roots making landing difficult. Very soon, 'many smokes' appeared 'along the whole coast', billowing against the sky, when the Native ancestors of the Seminole spotted the newcomers and spread the alarm by signal fires". The Spanish introduced Christianity, cattle, horses, sheep, the Spanish language, and more to Florida.[full citation needed] Both the Spanish and French established settlements in Florida, with varying degrees of success. In 1559, Don Tristán de Luna y Arellano established a colony at present-day Pensacola, one of the first European settlements in the continental United States, but it was abandoned by 1561.
rewrite: In May 1539, the explorer Hernando de Soto sailed near Florida's shoreline, seeking a suitable port for disembarkation. He observed extensive forests of tall red mangroves, some towering 70 feet, their dense, raised root systems creating a barrier to the shore. Shortly thereafter, signal fires—described as 'many smokes'—appeared across the coastline as the indigenous predecessors of the Seminole people sighted the foreign ships and raised the alarm. The Spanish brought with them new cultural elements, including Christian teachings, livestock like cattle and horses, and their language. Spanish and French colonists later attempted to found communities in the region with mixed results. Among these, Tristán de Luna y Arellano founded a settlement in 1559 at what is now Pensacola, an early but short-lived European colony in the future United States, abandoned by 1561.

input: The Navy was modernized in the 1880s, and by the 1890s had adopted the naval power strategy of Captain Alfred Thayer Mahan—as indeed did every major navy. The old sailing ships were replaced by modern steel battleships, bringing them in line with the navies of Britain and Germany. In 1907, most of the Navy's battleships, with several support vessels, dubbed the Great White Fleet, were featured in a 14-month circumnavigation of the world. Ordered by President Theodore Roosevelt, it was a mission designed to demonstrate the Navy's capability to extend to the global theater.
rewrite: During the 1880s, the U.S. Navy underwent significant upgrades, shifting from older sailing vessels to contemporary steel warships comparable to those of British and German forces. By the following decade, it, along with other leading naval powers, embraced the strategic doctrines of Captain Alfred Thayer Mahan. In 1907, President Theodore Roosevelt directed a substantial portion of its battleships and auxiliary craft, collectively known as the Great White Fleet, on a worldwide voyage lasting over a year. This journey aimed to showcase the nation's emerging capacity for global naval operations.

input: Jobs expanded so rapidly that 400,000 people were attracted to the city from 1941 to 1943, including 50,000 blacks in the second wave of the Great Migration, and 350,000 whites, many of them from the South. Some European immigrants and their descendants feared black competition for jobs and housing. The federal government prohibited discrimination in defense work but when in June 1943, Packard promoted three blacks to work next to whites on its assembly lines, 25,000 whites walked off the job. The Detroit race riot of 1943 took place three weeks after the Packard plant protest. Over the course of three days, 34 people were killed, of whom 25 were African American, and approximately 600 were injured, 75% black people.
rewrite: Between 1941 and 1943, a surge in employment opportunities drew 400,000 new residents to the city. This influx consisted of 350,000 white individuals, often from southern states, alongside 50,000 African Americans participating in the Great Migration's second phase. Tensions arose as some white residents of European origin worried about economic and residential competition. Although federal rules banned bias in defense industries, the promotion of three Black workers at Packard in June 1943—placing them alongside white assembly line workers—sparked a walkout of 25,000 white employees. Three weeks later, the Detroit race riot erupted. Lasting three days, the violence resulted in 34 deaths, including 25 Black victims, and about 600 injuries, three-quarters of whom were African American.

input: Convinced that he needed a wasta, or an influential intermediary to promote his application above the others, Nasser managed to secure a meeting with Under-Secretary of War Ibrahim Khairy Pasha, the person responsible for the academy's selection board, and requested his help. Khairy Pasha agreed and sponsored Nasser's second application, which was accepted in late 1937. Nasser focused on his military career from then on, and had little contact with his family. At the academy, he met Abdel Hakim Amer and Anwar Sadat, both of whom became important aides during his presidency. After graduating from the academy in July 1938, he was commissioned a second lieutenant in the infantry, and posted to Mankabad. It was here that Nasser and his closest comrades, including Sadat and Amer, first discussed their dissatisfaction at widespread corruption in the country and their desire to topple the monarchy. Sadat would later write that because of his "energy, clear-thinking, and balanced judgement", Nasser emerged as the group's natural leader.
rewrite: Believing that personal connections were essential to advance his candidacy, Nasser arranged an appointment with Under-Secretary of War Ibrahim Khairy Pasha, who oversaw the military academy's admissions. He successfully sought Khairy Pasha's patronage, and with this endorsement, his subsequent application was approved near the end of 1937. From that point forward, Nasser dedicated himself entirely to the army, largely distancing himself from his relatives. While training, he formed friendships with future key presidential associates, Abdel Hakim Amer and Anwar Sadat. Upon receiving his commission as an infantry second lieutenant in July 1938, he was assigned to Mankabad. In this posting, Nasser and his most trusted peers, among them Sadat and Amer, first voiced their shared disillusionment with the pervasive graft in Egypt and their aspiration to overthrow the royal government. Sadat later reflected that Nasser's evident dynamism, intellectual clarity, and sound reasoning naturally established him as the undisputed head of their circle.

input: Once inside the Rotunda for the Charters of Freedom, there are no lines to see the individual documents and visitors are allowed to walk from document to document as they wish. For over 30 years the National Archives have forbidden flash photography but the advent of cameras with automatic flashes have made the rules increasingly difficult to enforce. As a result, all filming, photographing, and videotaping by the public in the exhibition areas has been prohibited since February 25, 2010.
rewrite: Upon entering the Rotunda housing the Charters of Freedom, guests may freely move between the displayed documents without queuing. While flash photography has long been banned, the prevalence of cameras with auto-flash features has complicated enforcement. Consequently, since February 25, 2010, the National Archives has disallowed all public photography, filming, and video recording within these exhibition spaces.

input: The FAA has been cited as an example of regulatory capture, "in which the airline industry openly dictates to its regulators its governing rules, arranging for not only beneficial regulation, but placing key people to head these regulators." Retired NASA Office of Inspector General Senior Special Agent Joseph Gutheinz, who used to be a Special Agent with the Office of Inspector General for the Department of Transportation and with FAA Security, is one of the most outspoken critics of FAA. Rather than commend the agency for proposing a $10.2 million fine against Southwest Airlines for its failure to conduct mandatory inspections in 2008, he was quoted as saying the following in an Associated Press story: "Penalties against airlines that violate FAA directives should be stiffer. At $25,000 per violation, Gutheinz said, airlines can justify rolling the dice and taking the chance on getting caught. He also said the FAA is often too quick to bend to pressure from airlines and pilots." Other experts have been critical of the constraints and expectations under which the FAA is expected to operate. The dual role of encouraging aerospace travel and regulating aerospace travel are contradictory. For example, to levy a heavy penalty upon an airline for violating an FAA regulation which would impact their ability to continue operating would not be considered encouraging aerospace travel.
rewrite: The Federal Aviation Administration is often viewed as a case of regulatory capture, where the commercial aviation sector effectively controls the rules meant to govern it. This influence extends beyond securing favorable policies to include the appointment of industry-aligned individuals to lead the regulatory bodies. Joseph Gutheinz, a former Special Agent for the Department of Transportation’s Inspector General and FAA Security, now a retired NASA investigator, is a prominent FAA critic. Reacting to a proposed $10.2 million fine against Southwest Airlines in 2008 for skipped inspections, he did not praise the action. Instead, in an Associated Press interview, he argued that penalties must be more severe. With fines set around $25,000 per infraction, he stated, carriers may calculate the risk as worth taking. Gutheinz further contended that the FAA frequently yields too easily to lobbying from airlines and pilot groups. Additional analysts have highlighted the conflicting mandates imposed on the agency. It is tasked with both promoting and overseeing air travel, goals that can directly clash. For instance, imposing a crippling financial sanction on an airline for a safety violation—a move that could threaten its viability—would contradict its mission to foster the industry's growth.

input: Plymouth has the first known reference to Jews in the South West from Sir Francis Drake's voyages in 1577 to 1580, as his log mentioned "Moses the Jew" – a man from Plymouth. The Plymouth Synagogue is a Listed Grade II* building, built in 1762 and is the oldest Ashkenazi Synagogue in the English speaking world. There are also places of worship for Islam, Bahá'í, Buddhism, Unitarianism, Chinese beliefs and Humanism.
rewrite: The earliest recorded mention of Jewish people in England's South West appears in logs from Sir Francis Drake's 1577-1580 expeditions, noting a Plymouth resident named "Moses the Jew." The city's synagogue, constructed in 1762, is a Grade II* listed structure and the oldest Ashkenazi synagogue in the English-speaking world. Additional faiths represented include Islam, Bahá'í, Buddhism, Unitarianism, Chinese beliefs, and Humanism.

input: In several countries, like Germany, the Netherlands, Switzerland and Turkey, institutes of technology and polytechnics are institutions of higher education, and have been accredited to award academic degrees and doctorates. Famous examples are the Istanbul Technical University, ETH Zurich, İYTE, Delft University of Technology and RWTH Aachen, all considered universities.[citation needed]
rewrite: In nations such as Germany and Turkey, technical and polytechnic institutes are recognized as degree-granting higher education establishments, including doctoral degrees. Notable universities in this category encompass ETH Zurich, Istanbul Technical University, and RWTH Aachen.

input: The Licchavi era was followed by the Malla era. Rulers from Tirhut, upon being attacked by Muslims, fled north to the Kathmandu valley. They intermarried with Nepali royalty, and this led to the Malla era. The early years of the Malla era were turbulent, with raids and attacks from Khas and Turk Muslims. There was also a devastating earthquake which claimed the lives of a third of Kathmandu's population, including the king Abhaya Malla. These disasters led to the destruction of most of the architecture of the Licchavi era (such as Mangriha and Kailashkut Bhawan), and the loss of literature collected in various monasteries within the city. Despite the initial hardships, Kathmandu rose to prominence again and, during most of the Malla era, dominated the trade between India and Tibet. Nepali currency became the standard currency in trans-Himalayan trade.
rewrite: Following the Licchavi period, the Malla dynasty emerged. This transition occurred when nobles from Tirhut, retreating from Muslim incursions, moved north into the Kathmandu valley. Through marriages with local ruling families, they established Malla rule. The dynasty's beginnings were unstable, marked by assaults from Khas groups and Turkic Muslims. A catastrophic earthquake further devastated the valley, killing a third of Kathmandu's inhabitants, among them King Abhaya Malla. These events ruined much Licchavi architecture, like Mangriha and Kailashkut Bhawan, and destroyed numerous literary works housed in city monasteries. However, after these early struggles, Kathmandu regained its stature. For the bulk of the Malla period, it served as the central hub for commerce linking India and Tibet, with Nepali coinage becoming the accepted currency across the Himalayan trade routes.

input: In February 2010 Shell and Cosan formed a 50:50 joint-venture, Raízen, comprising all of Cosan's Brazilian ethanol, energy generation, fuel distribution and sugar activities, and all of Shell's Brazilian retail fuel and aviation distribution businesses. In March 2010, Shell announced the sale of some of its assets, including its liquid petroleum gas (LPG) business, to meet the cost of a planned $28bn capital spending programme. Shell invited buyers to submit indicative bids, due by 22 March, with a plan to raise $2–3bn from the sale. In June 2010, Royal Dutch Shell agreed to acquire all the business of East Resources for a cash consideration of $4.7 billion. The transaction included East Resources' tight gas fields.
rewrite: In early 2010, Shell and Cosan established Raízen, an equally owned partnership. This new entity absorbed Cosan's operations in Brazil related to ethanol, power production, fuel distribution, and sugar, alongside Shell's local retail fuel and aviation distribution divisions. That same March, Shell revealed plans to divest certain holdings, such as its liquefied petroleum gas unit, to fund a $28 billion investment initiative. The company sought preliminary offers by late March, aiming to generate $2 to $3 billion from these disposals. Subsequently, in June, Shell committed to purchasing East Resources outright for $4.7 billion in cash, gaining control of its extensive tight gas reserves.

input: Near the end of the NES's lifespan, upon the release of the AV Famicom and the top-loading NES 2, the design of the game controllers was modified slightly. Though the original button layout was retained, the redesigned device abandoned the brick shell in favor of a dog bone shape. In addition, the AV Famicom joined its international counterpart and dropped the hardwired controllers in favor of detachable controller ports. However, the controllers included with the Famicom AV had cables which were 90 cm (3 feet) long, as opposed to the standard 180 cm(6 feet) of NES controllers.
rewrite: As the original Nintendo Entertainment System was being phased out, its final hardware revisions introduced updated gamepads. The new top-loading NES 2 and the AV Famicom featured controllers that kept the same button arrangement but swapped the earlier rectangular form for a more rounded, "dog bone" silhouette. Both models also adopted removable controllers instead of fixed ones. Notably, the cords for the AV Famicom's controllers were shorter, measuring about three feet compared to the six-foot cables standard for the NES.

input: Centered on Post Oak Boulevard and Westheimer Road, the Uptown District boomed during the 1970s and early 1980s when a collection of mid-rise office buildings, hotels, and retail developments appeared along Interstate 610 west. Uptown became one of the most prominent instances of an edge city. The tallest building in Uptown is the 64-floor, 901-foot (275 m)-tall, Philip Johnson and John Burgee designed landmark Williams Tower (known as the Transco Tower until 1999). At the time of construction, it was believed to be the world's tallest skyscraper outside of a central business district. The new 20-story Skanska building and BBVA Compass Plaza are the newest office buildings built in Uptown after 30 years. The Uptown District is also home to buildings designed by noted architects I. M. Pei, César Pelli, and Philip Johnson. In the late 1990s and early 2000s decade, there was a mini-boom of mid-rise and high-rise residential tower construction, with several over 30 stories tall. Since 2000 more than 30 high-rise buildings have gone up in Houston; all told, 72 high-rises tower over the city, which adds up to about 8,300 units. In 2002, Uptown had more than 23 million square feet (2,100,000 m²) of office space with 16 million square feet (1,500,000 m²) of Class A office space.
rewrite: Focused around the crossroads of Post Oak Boulevard and Westheimer Road, Houston's Uptown District experienced significant growth in the 1970s and early 1980s. This period saw the rise of numerous medium-height offices, hotels, and shopping centers near the western segment of Interstate 610, establishing the area as a classic example of an edge city. Its most recognizable structure is the Williams Tower, a 64-story, 901-foot skyscraper conceived by architects Philip Johnson and John Burgee. Originally named the Transco Tower, this landmark was once considered the tallest building globally not situated within a traditional downtown core. Following a three-decade lull in major office development, recent additions include the 20-story Skanska building and BBVA Compass Plaza. The district features architectural works from famous designers like I. M. Pei, César Pelli, and Philip Johnson. A surge in residential construction occurred from the late 1990s into the 2000s, producing numerous mid-rise and high-rise apartment towers, many exceeding thirty floors. Houston has witnessed the completion of over thirty new high-rises since the year 2000, contributing to a citywide total of 72 such structures containing approximately 8,300 residential units. By 2002, Uptown provided more than 23 million square feet of office inventory, with 16 million square feet classified as premier Class A space.

input: The Communist Party of China, founded in 1920, adopted the red flag and hammer and sickle emblem of the Soviet Union, which became the national symbols when the Party took power in China in 1949. Under Party leader Mao Zedong, the Party anthem became "The East Is Red", and Mao Zedong himself was sometimes referred to as a "red sun". During the Cultural Revolution in China, Party ideology was enforced by the Red Guards, and the sayings of Mao Zedong were published as a small red book in hundreds of millions of copies. Today the Communist Party of China claims to be the largest political party in the world, with eighty million members.
rewrite: Founded in 1920, the Communist Party of China initially embraced the crimson banner and the hammer and sickle insignia from the Soviet Union. These were later established as official national emblems following the Party's rise to governance in 1949. Under the leadership of Mao Zedong, the song "The East Is Red" served as the Party's hymn, and Mao was occasionally likened to a "red sun." The Cultural Revolution saw the Red Guards rigorously impose Party doctrine, while Mao's quotations were disseminated globally in a compact red volume, printed in vast quantities. Presently, the Party asserts it is the globe's biggest political organization, boasting a membership exceeding eighty million.

input: Manifold vacuum can be used to drive accessories on automobiles. The best-known application is the vacuum servo, used to provide power assistance for the brakes. Obsolete applications include vacuum-driven windscreen wipers and Autovac fuel pumps. Some aircraft instruments (Attitude Indicator (AI) and the Heading Indicator (HI)) are typically vacuum-powered, as protection against loss of all (electrically powered) instruments, since early aircraft often did not have electrical systems, and since there are two readily available sources of vacuum on a moving aircraft—the engine and an external venturi. Vacuum induction melting uses electromagnetic induction within a vacuum.
rewrite: Vacuum from engine intake manifolds can power various vehicle components. A common example is the brake booster, which assists braking. Older uses, now outdated, involved operating windshield wipers and fuel pumps. In aviation, instruments like the attitude and heading indicators often rely on vacuum systems. This provides a backup if electrical power fails, especially since early planes lacked such systems, and vacuum is easily sourced from the engine or a venturi during flight. Additionally, electromagnetic induction in a vacuum enables vacuum induction melting.

input: Sanskrit, as defined by Pāṇini, evolved out of the earlier Vedic form. The present form of Vedic Sanskrit can be traced back to as early as the second millennium BCE (for Rig-vedic). Scholars often distinguish Vedic Sanskrit and Classical or "Pāṇinian" Sanskrit as separate dialects. Though they are quite similar, they differ in a number of essential points of phonology, vocabulary, grammar and syntax. Vedic Sanskrit is the language of the Vedas, a large collection of hymns, incantations (Samhitas) and theological and religio-philosophical discussions in the Brahmanas and Upanishads. Modern linguists consider the metrical hymns of the Rigveda Samhita to be the earliest, composed by many authors over several centuries of oral tradition. The end of the Vedic period is marked by the composition of the Upanishads, which form the concluding part of the traditional Vedic corpus; however, the early Sutras are Vedic, too, both in language and content.
rewrite: According to Pāṇini's description, Sanskrit developed from an older version known as Vedic. The earliest examples of Vedic Sanskrit date back to around 2000 BCE, particularly in the Rigveda. Experts typically classify Vedic Sanskrit and the later Classical, or Pāṇinian, Sanskrit as distinct variations of the language. While closely related, they show significant differences in sounds, word choice, and sentence structure. Vedic Sanskrit is used in the Vedas, which include hymns, ritual chants, and philosophical texts like the Brahmanas and Upanishads. Linguists believe the poetic hymns of the Rigveda are the most ancient, created by numerous authors across generations through oral transmission. The Vedic era concludes with the writing of the Upanishads, which complete the traditional Vedic texts, though early Sutras also share the language and themes of this period.

input: Another 44 million acres (18 million hectares) are owned by 12 regional, and scores of local, Native corporations created under the Alaska Native Claims Settlement Act (ANCSA) of 1971. Regional Native corporation Doyon, Limited often promotes itself as the largest private landowner in Alaska in advertisements and other communications. Provisions of ANCSA allowing the corporations' land holdings to be sold on the open market starting in 1991 were repealed before they could take effect. Effectively, the corporations hold title (including subsurface title in many cases, a privilege denied to individual Alaskans) but cannot sell the land. Individual Native allotments can be and are sold on the open market, however.
rewrite: An additional 44 million acres belong to numerous local and 12 regional Native corporations established through the 1971 Alaska Native Claims Settlement Act. Among these, Doyon, Limited frequently advertises itself as Alaska's biggest private landholder. Although initial ANCSA terms would have permitted these corporations to sell their lands openly after 1991, those provisions were canceled beforehand. Consequently, while the corporations retain ownership—often including underground rights not available to individuals—they cannot sell the property. In contrast, individual Native allotments may be sold freely.

input: Following the defeat in World War I, influence of German-speaking elites over Central and Eastern Europe was greatly limited. At the treaty of Versailles Germany was substantially reduced in size. Austria-Hungary was split up. Rump-Austria, which to a certain extent corresponded to the German-speaking areas of Austria-Hungary (a complete split into language groups was impossible due to multi-lingual areas and language-exclaves) adopted the name "German-Austria" (German: Deutschösterreich). The name German-Austria was forbidden by the victorious powers of World War I. Volga Germans living in the Soviet Union were interned in gulags or forcibly relocated during the Second World War.
rewrite: After World War I, the authority of German-speaking leadership across Central and Eastern Europe sharply declined. The Versailles treaty significantly shrank Germany's borders and dismantled the Austro-Hungarian Empire. The remaining Austrian state, largely comprising German-speaking regions from the former empire, chose the title "German-Austria." However, the Allied victors prohibited this name. Later, during World War II, ethnic Germans residing in the Soviet Union's Volga region were placed in labor camps or expelled from their homes.

input: By the verse Quran, 2:124, Shias believe that Imamah is a divine position always Imamah is accompanied by the word guidance, of course a guidance by God's Command.A kind of guidance which brings humanity to the goal. Regarding 17:71, no age can be without an Imam. So, according to the upper verse 1.Imamah is a position which is appointed by God and must be specified by Him 2.Imam is protected by a divine protection and no one exceles him in nobility 3. No age can be without an Imam and finally Imam knows everything which is needed for human being to get to the truth and goal.
rewrite: According to Shia interpretation of Quranic verse 2:124, the institution of Imamah is a spiritual office established by God, inherently linked with divine direction. This form of guidance, ordained by God, leads people toward their ultimate purpose. Citing 17:71, they hold that every era must have an Imam. Thus, based on these scriptures: the Imam is selected and designated by God; he enjoys divine safeguard and unsurpassed virtue; his presence is essential in all times; and he possesses complete knowledge necessary to guide humanity to truth and fulfillment.

input: Ibn Sīnā wrote extensively on early Islamic philosophy, especially the subjects logic, ethics, and metaphysics, including treatises named Logic and Metaphysics. Most of his works were written in Arabic – then the language of science in the Middle East – and some in Persian. Of linguistic significance even to this day are a few books that he wrote in nearly pure Persian language (particularly the Danishnamah-yi 'Ala', Philosophy for Ala' ad-Dawla'). Ibn Sīnā's commentaries on Aristotle often criticized the philosopher,[citation needed] encouraging a lively debate in the spirit of ijtihad.
rewrite: Ibn Sīnā authored many works on foundational Islamic philosophy, covering areas such as logic, ethics, and metaphysics, with specific texts dedicated to these fields. He primarily used Arabic, the scientific lingua franca of his era, but also composed some writings in Persian. Notably, a few of his books, like the *Danishnamah-yi 'Ala'*, are valued for their use of classical Persian. His critiques of Aristotle's writings stimulated vigorous intellectual discussion, promoting an environment of independent scholarly interpretation.

input: From the German point of view, March 1941 saw an improvement. The Luftwaffe flew 4,000 sorties that month, including 12 major and three heavy attacks. The electronic war intensified but the Luftwaffe flew major inland missions only on moonlit nights. Ports were easier to find and made better targets. To confuse the British, radio silence was observed until the bombs fell. X- and Y-Gerät beams were placed over false targets and switched only at the last minute. Rapid frequency changes were introduced for X-Gerät, whose wider band of frequencies and greater tactical flexibility ensured it remained effective at a time when British selective jamming was degrading the effectiveness of Y-Gerät.
rewrite: In March 1941, the German perspective noted a positive shift. That month, the Luftwaffe conducted 4,000 missions, featuring twelve large and three particularly intense raids. While the electronic conflict escalated, significant operations over inland areas were restricted to nights with a bright moon. Ports, being more identifiable, became preferred objectives. To mislead British defenses, radio communications were halted until the moment of bombardment. Navigational beams were directed at decoy locations and shifted to real targets at the final instant. The X-Gerät system adopted quick frequency shifts; its broader frequency range and adaptability allowed it to stay reliable just as British jamming began reducing the potency of the Y-Gerät system.

input: President Benito Juárez was re-elected in the general election of 1867 in which he received strong liberal support, especially in Chihuahua. Luis Terrazas was confirmed by the people of Chihuahua to be governor of the state. But soon after the election, President Juárez had another crisis on his hands; the Juárez administration was suspected to be involved in the assassination of the military chief José María Patoni executed by General Canto in August 1868. General Canto turned himself over to Donato Guerra. Canto was sentenced to death, but later his sentence changed to 10 years imprisonment. The sense of injustice gave rise to a new rebellion in 1869 that threatened the federal government. In response, the Juárez administration took drastic measures by temporarily suspending constitutional rights, but the governor of Chihuahua did not support this action. Hostilities continued to increase especially after the election of 1871 which was perceived to be fraudulent. A new popular leader arose among the rebels, Porfirio Díaz. The federal government was successful in quelling rebellions in Durango an Chihuahua. On July 18, 1872, President Juárez died from a heart attack; soon after, many of his supporters ceased the fighting. Peace returned to Chihuahua and the new government was led by Governor Antonio Ochoa (formerly a co-owner of the Batopilas silver mines) in 1873 after Luis Terrazas finished his term in 1872.
rewrite:
Following his victory in the 1867 general election, Benito Juárez returned to the presidency with considerable backing from liberal factions, particularly in Chihuahua. In that state, Luis Terrazas was popularly affirmed as governor. However, the administration soon faced a major scandal, accused of complicity in the killing of military leader José María Patoni, carried out by General Canto in August 1868. After surrendering to Donato Guerra, Canto initially received a death penalty, later commuted to a decade in prison. This perceived miscarriage of justice fueled a fresh uprising in 1869, endangering federal authority.

To counter the threat, Juárez’s government imposed severe controls, including a provisional suspension of constitutional guarantees—a move opposed by Chihuahua’s governor. Tensions escalated further following the widely disputed 1871 presidential election, during which the rebel figure Porfirio Díaz gained prominence. Although federal forces suppressed revolts in Durango and Chihuahua, the conflict persisted until Juárez’s death from a heart attack on July 18, 1872. This event prompted numerous loyalists to lay down their arms.

Calm was restored in Chihuahua after Luis Terrazas concluded his term in 1872. The subsequent state administration, established in 1873, was headed by Governor Antonio Ochoa, previously a part-owner of the Batopilas silver mines.

input: After the war, Nasser returned to his role as an instructor at the Royal Military Academy. He sent emissaries to forge an alliance with the Muslim Brotherhood in October 1948, but soon concluded that the religious agenda of the Brotherhood was not compatible with his nationalism. From then on, Nasser prevented the Brotherhood's influence over his cadres' activities without severing ties with the organization. Nasser was sent as a member of the Egyptian delegation to Rhodes in February 1949 to negotiate a formal armistice with Israel, and reportedly considered the terms to be humiliating, particularly because the Israelis were able to easily occupy the Eilat region while negotiating with the Arabs in March.
rewrite: Following the conflict, Nasser resumed teaching at the Royal Military Academy. In October 1948, he dispatched representatives to establish a partnership with the Muslim Brotherhood. However, he quickly determined that the group's religious objectives conflicted with his own nationalist views. Consequently, Nasser worked to limit the Brotherhood's impact on his officers' endeavors, though he maintained a connection with them. In February 1949, he participated in Egypt's delegation to Rhodes to discuss an official ceasefire with Israel. He later expressed that he found the agreed conditions deeply demeaning, especially due to Israel's unopposed capture of the Eilat area during the talks in March.

input: Monopole antennas consist of a single radiating element such as a metal rod, often mounted over a conducting surface, a ground plane. One side of the feedline from the receiver or transmitter is connected to the rod, and the other side to the ground plane, which may be the Earth. The most common form is the quarter-wave monopole which is one-quarter of a wavelength long and has a gain of 5.12 dBi when mounted over a ground plane. Monopoles have an omnidirectional radiation pattern, so they are used for broad coverage of an area, and have vertical polarization. The ground waves used for broadcasting at low frequencies must be vertically polarized, so large vertical monopole antennas are used for broadcasting in the MF, LF, and VLF bands. Small monopoles are used as nondirectional antennas on portable radios in the HF, VHF, and UHF bands.
rewrite: A monopole antenna is built from a solitary conductive component like a metallic pole, typically positioned above a ground plane, which is a conductive base. The feed cable linking to either a transmitter or receiver attaches one lead to this pole and the other to the ground surface, possibly the Earth itself. A frequent design is the quarter-wave version, measuring a fourth of the signal's wavelength; it achieves about 5.12 dBi gain over a ground plane. These antennas emit signals uniformly in all horizontal directions, offering wide-area coverage with vertical polarization. Since ground wave propagation at lower frequencies requires vertical polarization, sizable vertical monopoles are employed for MF, LF, and VLF band broadcasting. Compact monopoles serve as omnidirectional antennas in portable devices operating across HF, VHF, and UHF ranges.

input: The official English name of the system is BeiDou Navigation Satellite System. It is named after the Big Dipper constellation, which is known in Chinese as Běidǒu. The name literally means "Northern Dipper", the name given by ancient Chinese astronomers to the seven brightest stars of the Ursa Major constellation. Historically, this set of stars was used in navigation to locate the North Star Polaris. As such, the name BeiDou also serves as a metaphor for the purpose of the satellite navigation system.
rewrite: The BeiDou Navigation Satellite System derives its official English title from the Big Dipper, or Běidǒu in Chinese. This term translates to "Northern Dipper," referencing the seven prominent stars in Ursa Major. Ancient Chinese astronomers utilized this constellation for navigation by finding Polaris, the North Star. Consequently, the name BeiDou symbolically reflects the system's own function of providing directional guidance.

input: Luís Cabral, brother of Amílcar and co-founder of PAIGC, was appointed the first President of Guinea-Bissau. Following independence, the PAIGC killed thousands of local Guinean soldiers who had fought along with the Portuguese Army against guerrillas. Some escaped to settle in Portugal or other African nations. One of the massacres occurred in the town of Bissorã. In 1980 the PAIGC acknowledged in its newspaper Nó Pintcha (dated 29 November 1980) that many Gueinean soldiers had been executed and buried in unmarked collective graves in the woods of Cumerá, Portogole, and Mansabá.
rewrite: Luís Cabral, sibling of Amílcar and a PAIGC founder, became the inaugural President of Guinea-Bissau. After independence, the ruling party executed numerous Guinean troops who had served alongside the Portuguese military. Certain soldiers fled to Portugal or elsewhere in Africa. A notable killing took place in Bissorã. In 1980, the PAIGC admitted in its official newspaper that many such soldiers had been killed and interred in unmarked mass graves within forests at Cumerá, Portogole, and Mansabá.

input: In the Battle of Cowan's Ford, Cornwallis met resistance along the banks of the Catawba River at Cowan's Ford on February 1, 1781, in an attempt to engage General Morgan's forces during a tactical withdrawal. Morgan had moved to the northern part of the state to combine with General Greene's newly recruited forces. Generals Greene and Cornwallis finally met at the Battle of Guilford Courthouse in present-day Greensboro on March 15, 1781. Although the British troops held the field at the end of the battle, their casualties at the hands of the numerically superior Continental Army were crippling. Following this "Pyrrhic victory", Cornwallis chose to move to the Virginia coastline to get reinforcements, and to allow the Royal Navy to protect his battered army. This decision would result in Cornwallis' eventual defeat at Yorktown, Virginia, later in 1781. The Patriots' victory there guaranteed American independence.
rewrite: On February 1, 1781, British General Cornwallis confronted opposition at Cowan’s Ford on the Catawba River, seeking to intercept General Morgan’s retreating troops. Morgan had withdrawn northward to merge his forces with fresh soldiers assembled by General Greene. The two opposing commanders ultimately clashed at Guilford Courthouse in modern-day Greensboro on March 15. While the British technically won the engagement, they suffered devastating losses against a larger American force. After this costly triumph, Cornwallis decided to relocate toward the Virginia coast to obtain additional support and secure protection from the Royal Navy for his weakened army. This strategic shift ultimately led to his surrender at Yorktown later that same year, a decisive Patriot success that ensured the independence of the United States.

input: Having been capital of a vast pre-Hispanic empire, and also the capital of richest viceroyalty within the Spanish Empire (ruling over a vast territory in the Americas and Spanish West Indies), and, finally, the capital of the United Mexican States, Mexico City has a rich history of artistic expression. Since the mesoamerican pre-Classical period the inhabitants of the settlements around Lake Texcoco produced many works of art and complex craftsmanship, some of which are today displayed at the world-renowned National Museum of Anthropology and the Templo Mayor museum. While many pieces of pottery and stone-engraving have survived, the great majority of the Amerindian iconography was destroyed during the Conquest of Mexico.
rewrite: Mexico City has served as the center of a major pre-Columbian empire, the most prosperous Spanish viceroyalty in the Americas, and the modern nation of Mexico, fostering a deep artistic legacy. From ancient times, people living near Lake Texcoco created sophisticated art and crafts, examples of which are now held in famous institutions like the National Museum of Anthropology. However, most indigenous imagery was lost following the Spanish conquest, though some pottery and carved stone works endure.

input: In 1853, Victoria gave birth to her eighth child, Leopold, with the aid of the new anaesthetic, chloroform. Victoria was so impressed by the relief it gave from the pain of childbirth that she used it again in 1857 at the birth of her ninth and final child, Beatrice, despite opposition from members of the clergy, who considered it against biblical teaching, and members of the medical profession, who thought it dangerous. Victoria may have suffered from post-natal depression after many of her pregnancies. Letters from Albert to Victoria intermittently complain of her loss of self-control. For example, about a month after Leopold's birth Albert complained in a letter to Victoria about her "continuance of hysterics" over a "miserable trifle".
rewrite: In 1853, Queen Victoria delivered her eighth child, Prince Leopold, using chloroform as an anesthetic. She found the pain relief so significant that she chose it once more for the birth of her final child, Beatrice, in 1857. This decision was made despite resistance from some clergy, who viewed it as contrary to scripture, and certain doctors, who deemed it unsafe. Historical evidence suggests Victoria likely experienced postpartum depression following several of her pregnancies. Correspondence from her husband, Prince Albert, occasionally references her diminished composure. For instance, roughly a month after Leopold's birth, Albert wrote to Victoria, expressing concern over her persistent "hysterics" regarding a minor issue.

input: In 1978, Hayek came into conflict with the Liberal Party leader, David Steel, who claimed that liberty was possible only with "social justice and an equitable distribution of wealth and power, which in turn require a degree of active government intervention" and that the Conservative Party were more concerned with the connection between liberty and private enterprise than between liberty and democracy. Hayek claimed that a limited democracy might be better than other forms of limited government at protecting liberty but that an unlimited democracy was worse than other forms of unlimited government because "its government loses the power even to do what it thinks right if any group on which its majority depends thinks otherwise".
rewrite: During a 1978 dispute with Liberal Party head David Steel, Friedrich Hayek contested the view that freedom depends on social justice and fair wealth distribution, which Steel argued necessitates active governance. Steel also asserted that Conservatives prioritized linking liberty to private business over its connection to democratic principles. Hayek countered that while a democracy with constraints could safeguard freedom more effectively than other restricted governments, an unrestrained democracy posed a greater threat than other absolute regimes. He reasoned that in such a system, the government becomes unable to act on its own judgment if the majority’s supporting factions disagree.

input: Since the early history of the United States, Amerindians, African–Americans, and European Americans have been classified as belonging to different races. Efforts to track mixing between groups led to a proliferation of categories, such as mulatto and octoroon. The criteria for membership in these races diverged in the late 19th century. During Reconstruction, increasing numbers of Americans began to consider anyone with "one drop" of known "Black blood" to be Black, regardless of appearance.3 By the early 20th century, this notion was made statutory in many states.4 Amerindians continue to be defined by a certain percentage of "Indian blood" (called blood quantum). To be White one had to have perceived "pure" White ancestry. The one-drop rule or hypodescent rule refers to the convention of defining a person as racially black if he or she has any known African ancestry. This rule meant that those that were mixed race but with some discernible African ancestry were defined as black. The one-drop rule is specific to not only those with African ancestry but to the United States, making it a particularly African-American experience.
rewrite: From the nation's founding, groups such as Native Americans, African Americans, and European Americans were racially distinguished. Attempts to monitor intergroup unions resulted in many new labels like mulatto and octoroon. Standards for racial classification shifted notably in the late 1800s. Following the Civil War, a growing segment of the population adopted the "one-drop" principle, deeming any individual with any known African lineage as Black, no matter their physical traits. This concept was encoded into law across numerous states by the 1900s. For Native Americans, definitions often relied on a specific "blood quantum," or degree of indigenous ancestry. Conversely, being classified as White required ostensibly "pure" European descent. The one-drop rule, or hypodescent, specifically identifies a person as Black based on any traceable African heritage, thereby categorizing mixed-race individuals with discernible African roots as Black. This standard is unique to the U.S. context and is tied particularly to the African American community.

input: After the expulsion of the German population ethnic Russians, Belarusians, and Ukrainians were settled in the northern part. In the Soviet part of the region, a policy of eliminating all remnants of German history was pursued. All German place names were replaced by new Russian names. The exclave was a military zone, which was closed to foreigners; Soviet citizens could only enter with special permission. In 1967 the remnants of Königsberg Castle were demolished on the orders of Leonid Brezhnev to make way for a new "House of the Soviets".
rewrite: Following the removal of German inhabitants, ethnic Russians, Belarusians, and Ukrainians were moved into the northern territory. The Soviet administration systematically erased all traces of German heritage. Every geographical name of German origin was changed to a Russian alternative. This isolated area functioned as a restricted military district, inaccessible to outsiders and requiring special authorization for Soviet visitors. In 1967, by order of Leonid Brezhnev, the ruins of Königsberg Castle were cleared to construct the new "House of the Soviets."

input: The College of Arts and Letters was established as the university's first college in 1842 with the first degrees given in 1849. The university's first academic curriculum was modeled after the Jesuit Ratio Studiorum from Saint Louis University. Today the college, housed in O'Shaughnessy Hall, includes 20 departments in the areas of fine arts, humanities, and social sciences, and awards Bachelor of Arts (B.A.) degrees in 33 majors, making it the largest of the university's colleges. There are around 2,500 undergraduates and 750 graduates enrolled in the college.
rewrite: Founded in 1842 as the inaugural college of the university, the College of Arts and Letters conferred its initial degrees in 1849. Its original academic program was based on the Jesuit Ratio Studiorum from Saint Louis University. Currently located in O'Shaughnessy Hall, it comprises 20 departments spanning the fine arts, humanities, and social sciences. As the university's largest college, it offers Bachelor of Arts degrees across 33 majors to approximately 2,500 undergraduate and 750 graduate students.

input: Ann Arbor has a council-manager form of government. The City Council has 11 voting members: the mayor and 10 city council members. The mayor and city council members serve two-year terms: the mayor is elected every even-numbered year, while half of the city council members are up for election annually (five in even-numbered and five in odd-numbered years). Two council members are elected from each of the city's five wards. The mayor is elected citywide. The mayor is the presiding officer of the City Council and has the power to appoint all Council committee members as well as board and commission members, with the approval of the City Council. The current mayor of Ann Arbor is Christopher Taylor, a Democrat who was elected as mayor in 2014. Day-to-day city operations are managed by a city administrator chosen by the city council.
rewrite: Ann Arbor operates under a council-manager system. Its legislative body consists of eleven elected officials who vote: the mayor and ten council representatives. All serve two-year terms. Mayoral elections occur in even-numbered years. To ensure continuity, council elections are staggered, with five seats contested in even years and the other five in odd years. Each of the city's five wards elects two council members, whereas the mayor is chosen in a citywide vote. The mayor chairs the council and nominates individuals to all council committees and municipal boards, subject to council confirmation. Christopher Taylor, a Democrat first elected mayor in 2014, currently holds the office. Daily administrative functions are overseen by a city administrator appointed by the council.

input: During the Hundred Years' War, the army of the Duke of Burgundy and a force of about two hundred English soldiers occupied Paris from May 1420 until 1436. They repelled an attempt by Joan of Arc to liberate the city in 1429. A century later, during the French Wars of Religion, Paris was a stronghold of the Catholic League. On 24 August 1572, Paris was the site of the St. Bartholomew's Day massacre, when thousands of French Protestants were killed. The last of these wars, the eighth one, ended in 1594, after Henri IV had converted to Catholicism and was finally able to enter Paris as he supposedly declared Paris vaut bien une messe ("Paris is well worth a Mass"). The city had been neglected for decades; by the time of his assassination in 1610, Henry IV had rebuilt the Pont Neuf, the first Paris bridge with sidewalks and not lined with buildings, linked with a new wing the Louvre to the Tuileries Palace, and created the first Paris residential square, the Place Royale, now Place des Vosges.
rewrite: In the period of the Hundred Years' War, Paris fell under the control of the Burgundian army, supported by roughly two hundred English troops, from May 1420 through to 1436. This occupation force successfully defended the city against an assault led by Joan of Arc in 1429. A hundred years afterward, amid the French Wars of Religion, Paris served as a key bastion for the Catholic League. It was there, on August 24, 1572, that the St. Bartholomew's Day massacre occurred, resulting in the deaths of many thousands of Huguenots. The final conflict in this series concluded in 1594, following Henri IV's conversion to Catholicism, which allowed him to take the city—famously remarking that Paris was worth a mass. After years of decline, Henry IV initiated major improvements before his death in 1610. These included constructing the Pont Neuf, notable for its pedestrian paths and lack of buildings, connecting the Louvre to the Tuileries Palace with a new gallery, and establishing the initial planned residential square, the Place Royale, known today as the Place des Vosges.

input: The name Montana comes from the Spanish word Montaña, meaning "mountain", or more broadly, "mountainous country". Montaña del Norte was the name given by early Spanish explorers to the entire mountainous region of the west. The name Montana was added to a bill by the United States House Committee on Territories, which was chaired at the time by Rep. James Ashley of Ohio, for the territory that would become Idaho Territory. The name was successfully changed by Representatives Henry Wilson (Massachusetts) and Benjamin F. Harding (Oregon), who complained that Montana had "no meaning". When Ashley presented a bill to establish a temporary government in 1864 for a new territory to be carved out of Idaho, he again chose Montana Territory. This time Rep. Samuel Cox, also of Ohio, objected to the name. Cox complained that the name was a misnomer given that most of the territory was not mountainous and that a Native American name would be more appropriate than a Spanish one. Other names such as Shoshone were suggested, but it was eventually decided that the Committee on Territories could name it whatever they wanted, so the original name of Montana was adopted.
rewrite:
Derived from the Spanish term *Montaña*, which translates to "mountain" or "mountainous land," Montana's name has its roots in early Spanish exploration. Those explorers originally referred to the western mountain ranges as *Montaña del Norte*. The designation entered U.S. legislative history when Congressman James Ashley of Ohio, leading the House Committee on Territories, inserted it into a bill for what was then the Idaho Territory. However, colleagues Henry Wilson and Benjamin Harding argued the word was meaningless and managed to alter it temporarily.

When Ashley proposed another bill in 1864 to create a separate territory from Idaho, he once more suggested Montana. This prompted objection from fellow Ohio representative Samuel Cox, who called the name inaccurate, as much of the area was not actually mountainous. He believed a Native American name, like Shoshone, would be more fitting than a Spanish one. After debate, Congress concluded the Committee on Territories held the authority to select the name, leading to the formal adoption of Montana.

input: The Old Swiss Confederacy had acquired a reputation of invincibility during these earlier wars, but expansion of the federation suffered a setback in 1515 with the Swiss defeat in the Battle of Marignano. This ended the so-called "heroic" epoch of Swiss history. The success of Zwingli's Reformation in some cantons led to inter-cantonal religious conflicts in 1529 and 1531 (Wars of Kappel). It was not until more than one hundred years after these internal wars that, in 1648, under the Peace of Westphalia, European countries recognized Switzerland's independence from the Holy Roman Empire and its neutrality.
rewrite: Previously seen as unbeatable, the Old Swiss Confederacy faced a major reversal when it was defeated at Marignano in 1515, concluding a celebrated era in its history. Religious reforms led by Zwingli soon sparked civil wars between cantons in 1529 and 1531. Over a century later, the 1648 Peace of Westphalia finally brought formal recognition from European powers of Switzerland’s sovereignty and its neutral status, separating it from the Holy Roman Empire.

input: The period between the foundation of the Han dynasty and Wang Mang's reign is known as the Western Han dynasty (simplified Chinese: 西汉; traditional Chinese: 西漢; pinyin: Xī Hàn) or Former Han dynasty (simplified Chinese: 前汉; traditional Chinese: 前漢; pinyin: Qiánhàn) (206 BC – 9 AD). During this period the capital was at Chang'an (modern Xi'an). From the reign of Guangwu the capital was moved eastward to Luoyang. The era from his reign until the fall of Han is known as the Eastern Han dynasty (simplified Chinese: 东汉; traditional Chinese: 東漢; pinyin: Dōng Hàn) or the Later Han dynasty (simplified Chinese: 后汉; traditional Chinese: 後漢; pinyin: Hòu Hàn) (25–220 AD).
rewrite: The Western Han, also called the Former Han, lasted from 206 BC to 9 AD, beginning with the dynasty's establishment and ending with Wang Mang's rule. Its administrative center was located in Chang'an, present-day Xi'an. Following the rise of Emperor Guangwu, the capital was relocated east to Luoyang. The subsequent epoch, from 25 to 220 AD, is referred to as the Eastern Han or the Later Han dynasty, which continued until the Han empire's final collapse.

input: The sociology of culture grew from the intersection between sociology (as shaped by early theorists like Marx, Durkheim, and Weber) with the growing discipline of anthropology, where in researchers pioneered ethnographic strategies for describing and analyzing a variety of cultures around the world. Part of the legacy of the early development of the field lingers in the methods (much of cultural sociological research is qualitative), in the theories (a variety of critical approaches to sociology are central to current research communities), and in the substantive focus of the field. For instance, relationships between popular culture, political control, and social class were early and lasting concerns in the field.
rewrite: The field of cultural sociology emerged at the crossroads of sociology—influenced by foundational thinkers such as Marx, Durkheim, and Weber—and anthropology, which introduced detailed ethnographic studies of global societies. This formative period continues to influence the discipline today. Its enduring impact is evident in its predominant qualitative methodologies, its reliance on diverse critical theoretical frameworks, and its core subjects of study. Among these, the connections linking mass culture, social stratification, and mechanisms of power have remained central and persistent themes from the field's beginnings.

input: In October 2004, Sarah Forsyth claimed that she had been dismissed unfairly by Eton College and had been bullied by senior staff. She also claimed she was instructed to do some of Prince Harry's coursework to enable him to pass AS Art. As evidence, Forsyth provided secretly recorded conversations with both Prince Harry and her Head of Department, Ian Burke. An employment tribunal in July 2005 found that she had been unfairly dismissed and criticised Burke for bullying her and for repeatedly changing his story. It also criticised the school for failing to produce its capability procedures and criticised the Head Master for not reviewing the case independently.
rewrite: In October 2004, Sarah Forsyth alleged that Eton College terminated her employment without just cause and that she endured harassment from higher-ranking employees. She further asserted she was directed to complete portions of Prince Harry’s AS Art assignments to ensure his success. Forsyth submitted covertly taped discussions with the Prince and her department head, Ian Burke, as proof. A July 2005 tribunal ruled her dismissal was unjust, rebuked Burke for both intimidation and inconsistent testimony, and faulted the school for not providing its competency protocols. The Head Master was also censured for neglecting to conduct an autonomous assessment of the matter.

input: Because of its limited land area, Bermuda has had difficulty with over-population. In the first two centuries of settlement, it relied on steady human emigration to keep the population manageable.[citation needed] Before the American Revolution more than ten thousand Bermudians (over half of the total population through the years) gradually emigrated, primarily to the Southern United States. As Great Britain displaced Spain as the dominant European imperial power, it opened up more land for colonial development. A steady trickle of outward migration continued. With seafaring the only real industry in the early decades, by the end of the 18th century, at least a third of the island's manpower was at sea at any one time.
rewrite: Due to its small size, Bermuda has long struggled with overcrowding. For the initial 200 years after colonization, it depended on continuous outward migration to control its population numbers. Prior to the American Revolutionary War, over ten thousand residents—representing more than half of the cumulative population—slowly relocated, mainly to the American South. As British influence surpassed that of Spain, additional colonial territories became accessible. This sustained a pattern of people leaving the island. Since maritime work was the primary occupation early on, by the 1700s' close, one-third or more of Bermuda's able-bodied men were typically engaged in ocean-going roles at any given moment.

input: Although an alloy is technically an impure metal, when referring to alloys, the term "impurities" usually denotes those elements which are not desired. These impurities are often found in the base metals or the solutes, but they may also be introduced during the alloying process. For instance, sulfur is a common impurity in steel. Sulfur combines readily with iron to form iron sulfide, which is very brittle, creating weak spots in the steel. Lithium, sodium and calcium are common impurities in aluminium alloys, which can have adverse effects on the structural integrity of castings. Conversely, otherwise pure-metals that simply contain unwanted impurities are often called "impure metals" and are not usually referred to as alloys. Oxygen, present in the air, readily combines with most metals to form metal oxides; especially at higher temperatures encountered during alloying. Great care is often taken during the alloying process to remove excess impurities, using fluxes, chemical additives, or other methods of extractive metallurgy.
rewrite: While alloys are technically metals with added elements, the word "impurities" in this context specifically means undesired components. These unwanted elements can originate from the primary metals or the added materials, or they can enter during manufacturing. In steel, sulfur is a typical example, as it bonds with iron to create brittle iron sulfide, compromising the metal's strength. Similarly, elements like lithium, sodium, and calcium often appear in aluminum alloys, where they can weaken cast structures. On the other hand, metals that are essentially pure but contain such undesirable elements are typically labeled "impure metals" rather than alloys. Airborne oxygen, which easily forms oxides with many metals, especially under high alloying temperatures, is a common concern. Consequently, significant effort is made during production to eliminate these excess impurities through techniques like fluxes, chemical agents, or various refining processes.

input: According to the 2002 Census, 4.6% of the Chilean population, including the Rapanui (a Polynesian people) of Easter Island, was indigenous, although most show varying degrees of mixed heritage. Many are descendants of the Mapuche, and live in Santiago, Araucanía and the lake district. The Mapuche successfully fought off defeat in the first 300–350 years of Spanish rule during the Arauco War. Relations with the new Chilean Republic were good until the Chilean state decided to occupy their lands. During the Occupation of Araucanía the Mapuche surrendered to the country's army in the 1880s. Their land was opened to settlement by Chileans and Europeans. Conflict over Mapuche land rights continues to the present.
rewrite: Based on the 2002 Census, indigenous peoples, such as the Polynesian Rapanui from Easter Island, comprised 4.6% of Chile's inhabitants. The majority of this group has some mixed ancestry. A significant portion are Mapuche descendants, primarily residing in Santiago, Araucanía, and the lake region. The Mapuche notably resisted Spanish conquest for roughly three centuries in the Arauco War. Their relationship with the independent Chilean Republic remained peaceful until the state moved to seize their territories. Following their military defeat in the 1880s during the Occupation of Araucanía, their homelands were made available for Chilean and European colonists. Disputes regarding these land claims persist today.

input: Temperature extremes are moderated by the adjacent Puget Sound, greater Pacific Ocean, and Lake Washington. The region is largely shielded from Pacific storms by the Olympic Mountains and from Arctic air by the Cascade Range. Despite being on the margin of the rain shadow of the Olympic Mountains, the city has a reputation for frequent rain. This reputation stems from the frequency of light precipitation in the fall, winter, and spring. In an average year, at least 0.01 inches (0.25 mm) of precipitation falls on 150 days, more than nearly all U.S. cities east of the Rocky Mountains. It is cloudy 201 days out of the year and partly cloudy 93 days. Official weather and climatic data is collected at Seattle–Tacoma International Airport, located about 19 km (12 mi) south of downtown in the city of SeaTac, which is at a higher elevation, and records more cloudy days and fewer partly cloudy days per year.
rewrite: The nearby Puget Sound, Pacific Ocean, and Lake Washington help to temper severe hot and cold weather. The Olympic Mountains protect the area from many Pacific storm systems, while the Cascade Range blocks extremely cold Arctic air. Although situated on the edge of the Olympic rain shadow, Seattle is famously rainy. This perception arises from the common occurrence of light rainfall during autumn, winter, and spring. Typically, measurable precipitation of at least 0.01 inches occurs on roughly 150 days annually, a number exceeding most major cities east of the Rockies. Skies are completely overcast about 201 days per year and partly cloudy for around 93 days. The official weather station at Seattle–Tacoma International Airport, situated at a greater altitude in SeaTac approximately 12 miles south of the city center, experiences a higher number of overcast days and fewer partly cloudy days each year.

input: Norfolk Island is the only non-mainland Australian territory to have achieved self-governance. The Norfolk Island Act 1979, passed by the Parliament of Australia in 1979, is the Act under which the island was governed until the passing of the Norfolk Island Legislation Amendment Act 2015. The Australian government maintains authority on the island through an Administrator, currently Gary Hardgrave. From 1979 to 2015, a Legislative Assembly was elected by popular vote for terms of not more than three years, although legislation passed by the Australian Parliament could extend its laws to the territory at will, including the power to override any laws made by the assembly.
rewrite: Norfolk Island stands apart as the sole self-governing territory of Australia not located on the mainland. Its governance was established by the Norfolk Island Act of 1979, which remained in effect until amendments in 2015. The Australian government exercises oversight through an appointed Administrator. For over three decades, the island's residents elected their own Legislative Assembly. However, the federal parliament in Canberra always retained ultimate authority, possessing the right to impose its own laws or nullify those enacted locally.

input: Richard Owen showed that fossils of extinct species Darwin found in South America were allied to living species on the same continent. In March 1837, ornithologist John Gould announced that Darwin's rhea was a separate species from the previously described rhea (though their territories overlapped), that mockingbirds collected on the Galápagos Islands represented three separate species each unique to a particular island, and that several distinct birds from those islands were all classified as finches. Darwin began speculating, in a series of notebooks, on the possibility that "one species does change into another" to explain these findings, and around July sketched a genealogical branching of a single evolutionary tree, discarding Lamarck's independent lineages progressing to higher forms. Unconventionally, Darwin asked questions of fancy pigeon and animal breeders as well as established scientists. At the zoo he had his first sight of an ape, and was profoundly impressed by how human the orangutan seemed.
rewrite: Richard Owen identified that fossilized remains of vanished creatures discovered by Darwin in South America were closely related to contemporary animals inhabiting that region. In early 1837, the bird expert John Gould declared that the rhea Darwin encountered was a distinct species from the known variety, despite their ranges intersecting. He also noted that Galápagos mockingbirds comprised three different species, each confined to a single island, and that numerous birds gathered there were all varieties of finch. These revelations led Darwin to hypothesize in private journals that species might transform into new ones. By mid-year, he drew a diagram of a solitary ancestral tree with diverging branches, rejecting earlier concepts of separate lineages advancing toward complexity. In his research, Darwin consulted not only fellow scholars but also hobbyist breeders of pigeons and livestock. During a visit to the zoo, observing an orangutan for the first time, he was deeply struck by its remarkably human-like qualities.

input: Near-infrared is the region closest in wavelength to the radiation detectable by the human eye, mid- and far-infrared are progressively further from the visible spectrum. Other definitions follow different physical mechanisms (emission peaks, vs. bands, water absorption) and the newest follow technical reasons (the common silicon detectors are sensitive to about 1,050 nm, while InGaAs's sensitivity starts around 950 nm and ends between 1,700 and 2,600 nm, depending on the specific configuration). Unfortunately, international standards for these specifications are not currently available.
rewrite: The near-infrared band lies just beyond what our eyes can see, with mid- and far-infrared extending farther away. Various definitions rely on distinct physical properties, such as emission peaks or water absorption, while newer ones are based on detector technology. For instance, common silicon sensors work to roughly 1,050 nm, and InGaAs detectors operate from about 950 nm up to between 1,700 and 2,600 nm. Regrettably, no universal standards for these classifications yet exist.

input: The Allied disaster at Austerlitz significantly shook the faith of Emperor Francis in the British-led war effort. France and Austria agreed to an armistice immediately and the Treaty of Pressburg followed shortly after on 26 December. Pressburg took Austria out of both the war and the Coalition while reinforcing the earlier treaties of Campo Formio and of Lunéville between the two powers. The treaty confirmed the Austrian loss of lands to France in Italy and Bavaria, and lands in Germany to Napoleon's German allies. It also imposed an indemnity of 40 million francs on the defeated Habsburgs and allowed the fleeing Russian troops free passage through hostile territories and back to their home soil. Napoleon went on to say, "The battle of Austerlitz is the finest of all I have fought." Frank McLynn suggests that Napoleon was so successful at Austerlitz that he lost touch with reality, and what used to be French foreign policy became a "personal Napoleonic one". Vincent Cronin disagrees, stating that Napoleon was not overly ambitious for himself, "he embodied the ambitions of thirty million Frenchmen".
rewrite: The crushing defeat suffered by the Allies at Austerlitz profoundly undermined Emperor Francis's confidence in the British-directed conflict. This led to a swift ceasefire between France and Austria, culminating in the Treaty of Pressburg on December 26. This agreement formally removed Austria from both the war and the opposing Coalition, while also strengthening the prior terms established in the treaties of Campo Formio and Lunéville. Austria was forced to cede territories in Italy and Bavaria to France, and further lands in Germany to Napoleon's allied German states. The Habsburgs were also burdened with a war indemnity of 40 million francs, and the retreating Russian forces were granted safe conduct home through adversarial lands. Napoleon later declared Austerlitz his greatest military victory. Historian Frank McLynn argues that the scale of this triumph detached Napoleon from reality, transforming state diplomacy into a vehicle for his personal ambitions. Conversely, Vincent Cronin contends that Napoleon was not driven by excessive personal ambition, but rather that he personified the collective aspirations of the French people.

input: During the three years following its inception, the university bore three different names. The board first approved "Eliot Seminary," but William Eliot was uncomfortable with naming a university after himself and objected to the establishment of a seminary, which would implicitly be charged with teaching a religious faith. He favored a nonsectarian university. In 1854, the Board of Trustees changed the name to "Washington Institute" in honor of George Washington. Naming the University after the nation's first president, only seven years before the American Civil War and during a time of bitter national division, was no coincidence. During this time of conflict, Americans universally admired George Washington as the father of the United States and a symbol of national unity. The Board of Trustees believed that the university should be a force of unity in a strongly divided Missouri. In 1856, the University amended its name to "Washington University." The university amended its name once more in 1976, when the Board of Trustees voted to add the suffix "in St. Louis" to distinguish the university from the nearly two dozen other universities bearing Washington's name.
rewrite: In its initial three years, the institution operated under three distinct titles. Initially, the governing board selected "Eliot Seminary," yet William Eliot himself opposed this choice. He felt uneasy with the personal homage and rejected the term "seminary," as it suggested a focus on religious doctrine, preferring instead a secular establishment. By 1854, the trustees had adopted "Washington Institute" to pay tribute to George Washington. This decision, made on the eve of the Civil War amid deep national fractures, was deliberate. Washington was then revered by all Americans as a unifying founder, and the board aimed for the university to foster cohesion in a deeply split Missouri. In 1856, it was renamed simply "Washington University." A final change occurred in 1976, when the trustees appended "in St. Louis" to its name to differentiate it from the many other schools nationwide that also honor the first president.

input: According to the preamble in The Law of Treaties, treaties are a source of international law. If an act or lack thereof is condemned under international law, the act will not assume international legality even if approved by internal law. This means that in case of a conflict with domestic law, international law will always prevail.
rewrite: As stated in the preamble to The Law of Treaties, international law derives from treaties. Actions deemed unlawful internationally remain so, regardless of domestic legal approval. Consequently, international law takes precedence over any conflicting national legislation.

input: The Farmington Canal Trail is a rail trail that will eventually run continuously from downtown New Haven to Northampton, Massachusetts. The scenic trail follows the path of the historic New Haven and Northampton Company and the Farmington Canal. Currently, there is a continuous 14-mile (23 km) stretch of the trail from downtown, through Hamden and into Cheshire, making bicycle commuting between New Haven and those suburbs possible. The trail is part of the East Coast Greenway, a proposed 3,000-mile (4,800 km) bike path that would link every major city on the East Coast from Florida to Maine.
rewrite: Once completed, the Farmington Canal Trail will provide an unbroken route from New Haven, Connecticut, to Northampton, Massachusetts. This picturesque path traces the former course of the historic Farmington Canal and the New Haven and Northampton Company rail line. A present 14-mile (23 km) segment, extending from the city center through Hamden and into Cheshire, already enables bicycle travel between New Haven and these suburban areas.
