While some researchers sometimes use the concept of race to make distinctions among fuzzy sets of traits, others in the scientific community suggest that the idea of race often is used in a naive or simplistic way,[page needed] and argue that, among humans, race has no taxonomic significance by pointing out that all living humans belong to the same species, Homo sapiens, and subspecies, Homo sapiens sapiens.
rewrite: Despite widespread scientific consensus rejecting rigid, essentialist views of race, researchers globally still interpret the concept in varied and often contradictory manners, some of which inadvertently reinforce essentialist ideas. Certain experts employ racial categories to describe loosely defined trait groupings, while many others contend that its usage tends to be overly simplistic. They emphasize that race holds no biological classification value, noting that all modern humans are members of a single species and subspecies: Homo sapiens sapiens.

input: In Evita (1996), Madonna played the title role of Eva Perón. For a long time, Madonna had desired to play Perón and wrote to director Alan Parker to explain why she would be perfect for the part. She said later, "This is the role I was born to play. I put everything of me into this because it was much more than a role in a movie. It was exhilarating and intimidating at the same time..... And I am prouder of Evita than anything else I have done." After securing the role, she had vocal training and learned about the history of Argentina and Perón. During shooting she became ill several times due to the intense emotional effort required. However, as she told Oprah, she was also pregnant during the filming: "I was winded after every take. I had to lie on the couch every ten minutes so I could recover from dizzy spells, I was worried that I was shaking the baby around too much and that would injure it in some way." Madonna wrote in her personal diary at the time: "Ironically, this feeling of vulnerability and weakness is helping me in the movie. I'm sure Evita felt this way every day of her life once she discovered she was ill."
rewrite: In the 1996 film *Evita*, Madonna portrayed the central character, Eva Perón. She had long aspired to take on this part and personally contacted the film's director, Alan Parker, detailing her suitability for it. Reflecting afterward, she described it as the part she felt destined for, investing her entire self into the performance because it transcended a mere cinematic role. The experience was both thrilling and daunting for her, and she has since stated that *Evita* remains the achievement of which she is most proud. Once cast, she undertook voice lessons and studied Argentina's past and Perón's life. The production demanded considerable emotional depth, which led to Madonna falling ill on multiple occasions. Adding to the challenge, she was expecting a child during filming. She later explained to Oprah Winfrey that each scene left her breathless, requiring frequent rests on a couch to overcome lightheadedness. She also feared that the physical exertion might harm her unborn baby. In a diary entry from that period, Madonna noted the paradox that her own sense of fragility and exhaustion was aiding her portrayal, believing that Eva Perón herself likely felt similarly after learning of her sickness.

input: Brass, which is an alloy of copper and zinc, has been used since at least the 10th century BC in Judea and by the 7th century BC in Ancient Greece. Zinc metal was not produced on a large scale until the 12th century in India and was unknown to Europe until the end of the 16th century. The mines of Rajasthan have given definite evidence of zinc production going back to the 6th century BC. To date, the oldest evidence of pure zinc comes from Zawar, in Rajasthan, as early as the 9th century AD when a distillation process was employed to make pure zinc. Alchemists burned zinc in air to form what they called "philosopher's wool" or "white snow".
rewrite: An alloy of copper and zinc, brass was utilized as early as the 10th century BC in Judea and by the 7th century BC in Greece. However, metallic zinc was not manufactured in significant quantities until the 12th century in India, remaining unfamiliar in Europe until around the 1600s. Archaeological finds in Rajasthan confirm zinc extraction dating to the 6th century BC. The earliest known pure zinc, originating from Zawar in Rajasthan around the 9th century AD, was produced using distillation techniques. In experiments, alchemists would combust zinc to create a substance known as "philosopher's wool" or "white snow."

input: In their theoretical rules, the Cubist architects expressed the requirement of dynamism, which would surmount the matter and calm contained in it, through a creative idea, so that the result would evoke feelings of dynamism and expressive plasticity in the viewer. This should be achieved by shapes derived from pyramids, cubes and prisms, by arrangements and compositions of oblique surfaces, mainly triangular, sculpted facades in protruding crystal-like units, reminiscent of the so-called diamond cut, or even cavernous that are reminiscent of the late Gothic architecture. In this way, the entire surfaces of the facades including even the gables and dormers are sculpted. The grilles as well as other architectural ornaments attain a three-dimensional form. Thus, new forms of windows and doors were also created, e. g. hexagonal windows. Czech Cubist architects also designed Cubist furniture.
rewrite: According to the principles of Cubist architecture, a sense of energy and movement was essential, intended to transcend static material through inventive concepts. This aimed to instill in observers a powerful impression of dynamic force and sculptural expression. To realize this, designers employed geometric forms like pyramids, cubes, and prisms. They arranged slanting, often triangular planes and carved building fronts into projecting, crystalline segments similar to faceted gems, or into deep, recessed forms echoing Gothic styles. This extensive sculpting treatment covered all exterior surfaces, even roof elements. Decorative features, such as grilles, gained depth and volume. The approach also led to innovative window and door designs, including hexagonal shapes, and extended to the creation of fully Cubist furniture by Czech architects.

input: Raleigh is also served by Triangle Transit (known formerly as the Triangle Transit Authority, or TTA). Triangle Transit offers scheduled, fixed-route regional and commuter bus service between Raleigh and the region's other principal cities of Durham, Cary and Chapel Hill, as well as to and from the Raleigh-Durham International Airport, Research Triangle Park and several of the region's larger suburban communities. Triangle Transit also coordinates an extensive vanpool and rideshare program that serves the region's larger employers and commute destinations.
rewrite: Triangle Transit provides regional and commuter bus routes connecting Raleigh to Durham, Cary, Chapel Hill, and the airport, as well as Research Triangle Park and major suburbs. Additionally, it manages a wide-ranging vanpool and rideshare initiative tailored for the area's bigger employers and key commuter locations.

input: He invited a Roman Catholic priest, Father Anselm Strittmatter, O.S.B., to visit him for consultation. Von Neumann reportedly said in explanation that Pascal had a point, referring to Pascal's Wager. Father Strittmatter administered the last sacraments to him. Some of von Neumann's friends (such as Abraham Pais and Oskar Morgenstern) said they had always believed him to be "completely agnostic." "Of this deathbed conversion, Morgenstern told Heims, "He was of course completely agnostic all his life, and then he suddenly turned Catholic—it doesn't agree with anything whatsoever in his attitude, outlook and thinking when he was healthy." Father Strittmatter recalled that von Neumann did not receive much peace or comfort from it, as he still remained terrified of death.
rewrite: John von Neumann asked a Benedictine priest, Father Anselm Strittmatter, to come and speak with him. In doing so, he invoked Blaise Pascal's famous argument about belief. The priest performed the final rites. However, close associates, including Abraham Pais and Oskar Morgenstern, stated that von Neumann had lived as a total agnostic. Morgenstern expressed confusion to a biographer, noting this conversion starkly contradicted the scientist's lifelong perspectives. According to Father Strittmatter's memory, even after receiving the sacraments, von Neumann continued to be deeply afraid of dying, finding little solace.

input: A more elaborate form of urban AC is the rhythmic oldies format, which focuses primarily on "old school" R&B and soul hits from the 1960s to the 1990s, including Motown and disco hits. The format includes soul or disco artists such as ABBA, The Village People, The Jackson 5, Donna Summer, Tina Charles, Gloria Gaynor and the Bee Gees. Rhythmic oldies stations still exist today, but target African-Americans as opposed to a mass audience.
rewrite: A sophisticated version of urban adult contemporary radio is the rhythmic oldies genre, concentrating on classic R&B and soul tracks from the 1960s through the 1990s. This style features performers like ABBA, The Jackson 5, and Donna Summer, encompassing Motown and disco classics. While these stations continue to operate, they now primarily aim their programming at Black listeners rather than seeking a broad, general audience.

input: His opponents learned from Napoleon's innovations. The increased importance of artillery after 1807 stemmed from his creation of a highly mobile artillery force, the growth in artillery numbers, and changes in artillery practices. As a result of these factors, Napoleon, rather than relying on infantry to wear away the enemy's defenses, now could use massed artillery as a spearhead to pound a break in the enemy's line that was then exploited by supporting infantry and cavalry. McConachy rejects the alternative theory that growing reliance on artillery by the French army beginning in 1807 was an outgrowth of the declining quality of the French infantry and, later, France's inferiority in cavalry numbers. Weapons and other kinds of military technology remained largely static through the Revolutionary and Napoleonic eras, but 18th-century operational mobility underwent significant change.
rewrite: Napoleon's rivals adapted his military advances. After 1807, cannons became far more critical due to his development of a swift artillery corps, its expansion in size, and new tactical methods. Consequently, instead of depending on foot soldiers to gradually erode an adversary's position, he could concentrate cannon fire to rupture defensive lines, creating openings for infantry and cavalry to charge through. McConachy disputes the competing idea that the French turned to artillery from 1807 onward because their infantry was deteriorating and they later faced a shortage of cavalry. While arms and broader military technology changed little during this period, the strategic movement of forces evolved considerably from its 18th-century origins.

input: Balansiyya had a rebirth of sorts with the beginning of the Taifa of Valencia kingdom in the 11th century. The town grew, and during the reign of Abd al-Aziz a new city wall was built, remains of which are preserved throughout the Old City (Ciutat Vella) today. The Castilian nobleman Rodrigo Diaz de Vivar, known as El Cid, who was intent on possessing his own principality on the Mediterranean, entered the province in command of a combined Christian and Moorish army and besieged the city beginning in 1092. By the time the siege ended in May 1094, he had carved out his own fiefdom—which he ruled from 15 June 1094 to July 1099. This victory was immortalised in the Lay of the Cid. During his rule, he converted nine mosques into churches and installed the French monk Jérôme as bishop of the See of Valencia. El Cid was killed in July 1099 while defending the city from an Almoravid siege, whereupon his wife Ximena Díaz ruled in his place for two years.
rewrite: The city of Balansiyya experienced a revival in the 11th century with the establishment of the Taifa kingdom of Valencia. It expanded under Abd al-Aziz, who constructed a fresh defensive wall; sections of this structure can still be seen in the Ciutat Vella district. The Castilian lord Rodrigo Díaz de Vivar, called El Cid, sought to create a personal domain along the Mediterranean coast. Leading a mixed force of Christians and Moors, he invaded the region and initiated a blockade of the city in 1092. After the siege concluded in May 1094, he established his own territory, governing it from June 1094 until his death in 1099. His triumph was later celebrated in the epic poem *The Lay of the Cid*. As ruler, he transformed nine mosques into Christian places of worship and appointed the French cleric Jérôme as bishop. El Cid died in July 1099 during an Almoravid attack on the city, after which his wife, Ximena Díaz, assumed control for the next two years.

input: A local pioneer of folk song collection in the first half of the 19th century was Shakespearean scholar James Orchard Halliwell, but it was not until the second folk revival in the 20th century that the full range of song from the county, including industrial folk song, began to gain attention. The county produced one of the major figures of the revival in Ewan MacColl, but also a local champion in Harry Boardman, who from 1965 onwards probably did more than anyone to popularise and record the folk song of the county. Perhaps the most influential folk artists to emerge from the region in the late 20th century were Liverpool folk group The Spinners, and from Manchester folk troubadour Roy Harper and musician, comedian and broadcaster Mike Harding. The region is home to numerous folk clubs, many of them catering to Irish and Scottish folk music. Regular folk festivals include the Fylde Folk Festival at Fleetwood.
rewrite: In the early 1800s, James Orchard Halliwell, an expert on Shakespeare, became a local forerunner in gathering folk songs. However, the diverse musical traditions of the area, which encompassed industrial work songs, did not receive wider recognition until the folk revival of the 1900s. The region contributed significantly to this movement, producing renowned revivalist Ewan MacColl and a dedicated local advocate, Harry Boardman. Beginning in 1965, Boardman played a leading role in promoting and documenting the area's folk heritage. Later in the century, key influential figures included Liverpool's group The Spinners, alongside Manchester's singer-songwriter Roy Harper and the multi-talented Mike Harding. The area now hosts many folk clubs, often focusing on Irish and Scottish traditions, and annual events like the Fylde Folk Festival in Fleetwood.

input: The politics of Zhejiang is structured in a dual party-government system like all other governing institutions in Mainland China. The Governor of Zhejiang is the highest-ranking official in the People's Government of Zhejiang. However, in the province's dual party-government governing system, the Governor is subordinate to the Zhejiang Communist Party of China (CPC) Provincial Committee Secretary, colloquially termed the "Zhejiang CPC Party Chief".
rewrite: Zhejiang's political framework follows the dual party-government model common across mainland China. While the Governor leads the provincial government, this role is secondary to the Zhejiang Communist Party Provincial Committee Secretary, often called the "Zhejiang Party Chief," within the region's governing hierarchy.

input: In modern times, the Javanese are the largest ethnic group in Southeast Asia, with more than 100 million people, mostly concentrated in Java, Indonesia. In Burma, the Burmese account for more than two-thirds of the ethnic stock in this country, while ethnic Thais and Vietnamese account for about four-fifths of the respective populations of those countries. Indonesia is clearly dominated by the Javanese and Sundanese ethnic groups, while Malaysia is split between half Malays and one-quarter Chinese. Within the Philippines, the Tagalog, Cebuano, Ilocano, and Hiligaynon groups are significant.
rewrite: Today, the Javanese form Southeast Asia's most populous ethnic community, exceeding 100 million and primarily residing on Java in Indonesia. In Myanmar, the Burman majority constitutes over two-thirds of inhabitants. Similarly, Thais and Vietnamese comprise roughly four-fifths of their nations' people. Indonesia is largely Javanese and Sundanese, whereas Malaysia's population is half Malay and one-quarter Chinese. The Philippines features major groups like the Tagalog, Cebuano, Ilocano, and Hiligaynon.

input: With the end of the war with Japan, the Chinese Civil War resumed between the Chinese Communists and the Chinese Nationalists. While the Communists were struggling for supremacy in Manchuria, they were supported by the North Korean government with matériel and manpower. According to Chinese sources, the North Koreans donated 2,000 railway cars worth of matériel while thousands of Koreans served in the Chinese People's Liberation Army (PLA) during the war. North Korea also provided the Chinese Communists in Manchuria with a safe refuge for non-combatants and communications with the rest of China.
rewrite: Following the conclusion of World War II against Japan, conflict reignited in China between Communist and Nationalist forces. During the fight for control of Manchuria, the Communists received significant aid from North Korea in the form of supplies and personnel. Historical accounts from China note contributions including material equivalent to 2,000 freight cars, along with thousands of Korean soldiers joining the People's Liberation Army. Additionally, North Korea offered a secure sanctuary in Manchuria for civilian supporters and helped maintain logistical links.

input: In vertebrates, the part of the brain that plays the greatest role is the hypothalamus, a small region at the base of the forebrain whose size does not reflect its complexity or the importance of its function. The hypothalamus is a collection of small nuclei, most of which are involved in basic biological functions. Some of these functions relate to arousal or to social interactions such as sexuality, aggression, or maternal behaviors; but many of them relate to homeostasis. Several hypothalamic nuclei receive input from sensors located in the lining of blood vessels, conveying information about temperature, sodium level, glucose level, blood oxygen level, and other parameters. These hypothalamic nuclei send output signals to motor areas that can generate actions to rectify deficiencies. Some of the outputs also go to the pituitary gland, a tiny gland attached to the brain directly underneath the hypothalamus. The pituitary gland secretes hormones into the bloodstream, where they circulate throughout the body and induce changes in cellular activity.
rewrite: Among vertebrates, the hypothalamus stands out as the most influential brain component despite its modest dimensions. Situated near the bottom of the forebrain, this compact area is densely packed with numerous small clusters of neurons, each governing essential physiological processes. While it regulates arousal and social conduct—including sexual, aggressive, and nurturing actions—its primary responsibility lies in maintaining internal balance, or homeostasis. Specialized sensors within blood vessel walls relay data on factors like temperature, salt concentration, blood sugar, and oxygen levels to specific nuclei in the hypothalamus. In response, these nuclei direct commands to movement-control regions to correct any imbalances. Additionally, signals are sent to the adjacent pituitary gland, a minute structure just below the hypothalamus. This gland releases hormones into the circulation, which travel widely to alter how cells function throughout the organism.

input: In the 1940s, Detroit blues artist John Lee Hooker became a long-term resident in the city's southwest Delray neighborhood. Hooker, among other important blues musicians migrated from his home in Mississippi bringing the Delta blues to northern cities like Detroit. Hooker recorded for Fortune Records, the biggest pre-Motown blues/soul label. During the 1950s, the city became a center for jazz, with stars performing in the Black Bottom neighborhood. Prominent emerging Jazz musicians of the 1960s included: trumpet player Donald Byrd who attended Cass Tech and performed with Art Blakey and the Jazz Messengers early in his career and Saxophonist Pepper Adams who enjoyed a solo career and accompanied Byrd on several albums. The Graystone International Jazz Museum documents jazz in Detroit.
rewrite: During the 1940s, blues musician John Lee Hooker settled in Detroit's Delray area on the southwest side, making it his lasting home. Like many key blues artists, he moved north from Mississippi, introducing the Delta blues style to urban centers such as Detroit. He produced music with Fortune Records, the leading blues and soul label before Motown's rise. The 1950s saw Detroit grow into a jazz hub, with major acts playing in the Black Bottom district. Notable jazz talents emerging in the 1960s were trumpeter Donald Byrd—a Cass Tech graduate who started with Art Blakey's Jazz Messengers—and saxophonist Pepper Adams, who pursued a solo path and collaborated with Byrd on multiple recordings. Detroit's jazz history is preserved at the Graystone International Jazz Museum.

input: Red hair varies from a deep burgundy through burnt orange to bright copper. It is characterized by high levels of the reddish pigment pheomelanin (which also accounts for the red color of the lips) and relatively low levels of the dark pigment eumelanin. The term redhead (originally redd hede) has been in use since at least 1510. Cultural reactions have varied from ridicule to admiration; many common stereotypes exist regarding redheads and they are often portrayed as fiery-tempered. (See red hair).
rewrite: Red hair spans shades from dark burgundy to vibrant copper. This coloring results from elevated amounts of the red pigment pheomelanin—also found in lips—and lower quantities of the darker eumelanin. The label "redhead" dates to the early 1500s. Societal perceptions range from mockery to esteem, with numerous stereotypes persisting, frequently depicting redheads as having passionate or volatile personalities.

input: Several Islamic kingdoms (sultanates) under both foreign and, newly converted, Rajput rulers were established across the north western subcontinent (Afghanistan and Pakistan) over a period of a few centuries. From the 10th century, Sindh was ruled by the Rajput Soomra dynasty, and later, in the mid-13th century by the Rajput Samma dynasty. Additionally, Muslim trading communities flourished throughout coastal south India, particularly on the western coast where Muslim traders arrived in small numbers, mainly from the Arabian peninsula. This marked the introduction of a third Abrahamic Middle Eastern religion, following Judaism and Christianity, often in puritanical form. Mahmud of Ghazni in the early 11th century raided mainly the north-western parts of the Indian sub-continent 17 times, but he did not seek to establish "permanent dominion" in those areas.
rewrite: Over several centuries, a number of sultanates governed by foreign and recently Islamized Rajput leaders emerged in the northwestern regions of the subcontinent, encompassing areas now known as Afghanistan and Pakistan. Starting in the 10th century, the Rajput Soomra dynasty controlled Sindh, succeeded by the Rajput Samma dynasty around the mid-1200s. Meanwhile, along the southern coasts, especially in the west, small communities of Muslim merchants from Arabia prospered. Their presence signaled the arrival of a third major Middle Eastern faith, after Judaism and Christianity, frequently in a strict, reform-oriented interpretation. During the early 11th century, Mahmud of Ghazni launched seventeen raids primarily targeting the northwest of the subcontinent, though he never aimed to create lasting rule there.

input: The devotio was the most extreme offering a Roman general could make, promising to offer his own life in battle along with the enemy as an offering to the underworld gods. Livy offers a detailed account of the devotio carried out by Decius Mus; family tradition maintained that his son and grandson, all bearing the same name, also devoted themselves. Before the battle, Decius is granted a prescient dream that reveals his fate. When he offers sacrifice, the victim's liver appears "damaged where it refers to his own fortunes". Otherwise, the haruspex tells him, the sacrifice is entirely acceptable to the gods. In a prayer recorded by Livy, Decius commits himself and the enemy to the dii Manes and Tellus, charges alone and headlong into the enemy ranks, and is killed; his action cleanses the sacrificial offering. Had he failed to die, his sacrificial offering would have been tainted and therefore void, with possibly disastrous consequences. The act of devotio is a link between military ethics and those of the Roman gladiator.
rewrite: The ritual of devotio represented the ultimate sacrifice a Roman commander could perform, vowing to give his life alongside his foes to the gods of the underworld. Historical records, particularly from Livy, describe the ceremony undertaken by Decius Mus; it is said that both his son and grandson, who shared his name, later performed the same rite. Prior to combat, Decius experiences a prophetic dream foretelling his destiny. During a sacrificial rite, the animal's liver shows a flaw in the section pertaining to his own fate. The diviner assures him, however, that in all other respects the offering pleases the deities. In a prayer preserved by Livy, Decius consigns himself and the opposing army to the spirits of the dead and to Earth, then rides solo at full speed into the enemy lines to meet his death, thereby purifying the sacrifice. Had he survived, the offering would have been corrupted and invalid, risking catastrophe. This practice connects the moral code of the soldier to that of the gladiator in Roman culture.

input: A bare proton, H+, cannot exist in solution or in ionic crystals, because of its unstoppable attraction to other atoms or molecules with electrons. Except at the high temperatures associated with plasmas, such protons cannot be removed from the electron clouds of atoms and molecules, and will remain attached to them. However, the term 'proton' is sometimes used loosely and metaphorically to refer to positively charged or cationic hydrogen attached to other species in this fashion, and as such is denoted "H+" without any implication that any single protons exist freely as a species.
rewrite: A solitary proton, H+, cannot persist in liquid environments or ionic solids due to its powerful pull toward any atoms or molecules possessing electrons. Unless exposed to the extreme heat of plasma states, these protons stay bound within atomic or molecular electron clouds. Nonetheless, the word "proton" is often employed informally to describe positively charged hydrogen ions that are attached to other entities, symbolized as "H+", without suggesting that individual protons actually exist as independent particles.

input: The city's National Basketball Association teams are the Brooklyn Nets and the New York Knicks, while the New York Liberty is the city's Women's National Basketball Association. The first national college-level basketball championship, the National Invitation Tournament, was held in New York in 1938 and remains in the city. The city is well known for its links to basketball, which is played in nearly every park in the city by local youth, many of whom have gone on to play for major college programs and in the NBA.
rewrite: New York City hosts two NBA franchises: the Brooklyn Nets and the New York Knicks, alongside the WNBA's New York Liberty. It also has a historic connection to collegiate basketball, being the original and continuing home of the National Invitation Tournament since 1938. Basketball is deeply ingrained in the local culture, with youth games prevalent in parks across the boroughs, often serving as a pipeline to top university teams and professional leagues.

input: Another who contributed significantly to the spirituality of the order is Albertus Magnus, the only person of the period to be given the appellation "Great". His influence on the brotherhood permeated nearly every aspect of Dominican life. Albert was a scientist, philosopher, astrologer, theologian, spiritual writer, ecumenist, and diplomat. Under the auspices of Humbert of Romans, Albert molded the curriculum of studies for all Dominican students, introduced Aristotle to the classroom and probed the work of Neoplatonists, such as Plotinus. Indeed, it was the thirty years of work done by Thomas Aquinas and himself (1245–1274) that allowed for the inclusion of Aristotelian study in the curriculum of Dominican schools.
rewrite: Albertus Magnus, uniquely honored as "the Great" in his era, profoundly shaped the spiritual character of the Dominican order. His impact touched almost all facets of their communal life. A polymath, he excelled in fields ranging from science and philosophy to theology and diplomacy. With the support of Humbert of Romans, Albert redesigned the educational program for the order's students. He brought Aristotelian teachings into their studies and examined Neoplatonist thinkers like Plotinus. The collaborative efforts of Albert and Thomas Aquinas over three decades were ultimately responsible for integrating Aristotle's works into the Dominican academic framework.

input: The competition formed as the FA Premier League on 20 February 1992 following the decision of clubs in the Football League First Division to break away from the Football League, which was originally founded in 1888, and take advantage of a lucrative television rights deal. The deal was worth £1 billion a year domestically as of 2013–14, with BSkyB and BT Group securing the domestic rights to broadcast 116 and 38 games respectively. The league generates €2.2 billion per year in domestic and international television rights. In 2014/15, teams were apportioned revenues of £1.6 billion.
rewrite: The FA Premier League was established on February 20, 1992. This occurred when top-division Football League clubs chose to separate from the historic league, founded in 1888, to pursue a profitable broadcast contract. By the 2013–14 season, domestic TV rights were valued at £1 billion annually, with BSkyB and BT Group airing 116 and 38 matches each. Overall, yearly broadcasting income from global and domestic sources reaches €2.2 billion. Clubs shared £1.6 billion in revenues during the 2014/15 campaign.

input: After the Seleucid defeat at the Battle of Magnesia in 190 BC, the kings of Sophene and Greater Armenia revolted and declared their independence, with Artaxias becoming the first king of the Artaxiad dynasty of Armenia in 188. During the reign of the Artaxiads, Armenia went through a period of hellenization. Numismatic evidence shows Greek artistic styles and the use of the Greek language. Some coins describe the Armenian kings as "Philhellenes". During the reign of Tigranes the Great (95–55 BC), the kingdom of Armenia reached its greatest extent, containing many Greek cities including the entire Syrian tetrapolis. Cleopatra, the wife of Tigranes the Great, invited Greeks such as the rhetor Amphicrates and the historian Metrodorus of Scepsis to the Armenian court, and - according to Plutarch - when the Roman general Lucullus seized the Armenian capital Tigranocerta, he found a troupe of Greek actors who had arrived to perform plays for Tigranes. Tigranes' successor Artavasdes II even composed Greek tragedies himself.
rewrite: Following the Seleucid loss at Magnesia in 190 BC, the rulers of Sophene and Greater Armenia rose in rebellion, establishing their autonomy. By 188 BC, Artaxias had founded the Artaxiad royal line in Armenia. This dynasty oversaw a significant cultural shift toward Hellenistic influence within the region. Coinage from the era demonstrates this, featuring Greek artistic motifs and inscriptions, with some monarchs even labeled as "Philhellenes." Under King Tigranes the Great (ruling from 95 to 55 BC), the Armenian empire expanded to its peak, encompassing numerous Greek urban centers, such as the complete Syrian tetrapolis. His queen, Cleopatra, drew Greek intellectuals like the orator Amphicrates to the court. Historical accounts note that when Roman forces under Lucullus captured the capital, Tigranocerta, they discovered a company of Greek actors scheduled to perform for the king. Furthermore, Artavasdes II, who followed Tigranes, authored his own works in the form of Greek tragedies.

input: While most artists became established in other formats before moving to adult contemporary, Michael Bublé and Josh Groban started out as AC artists. Throughout this decade, artists such as Nick Lachey, James Blunt, John Mayer, Bruno Mars, Jason Mraz, Kelly Clarkson, Adele, Clay Aiken and Susan Boyle have become successful thanks to a ballad heavy sound. Much as some hot AC and modern rock artists have crossed over into each other, so too has soft AC crossed with country music in this decade. Country musicians such as Faith Hill, Shania Twain, LeAnn Rimes and Carrie Underwood have had success on both charts.
rewrite: Unlike many musicians who transition from other genres, Michael Bublé and Josh Groban launched their careers directly in adult contemporary. This period saw artists like Adele, Bruno Mars, and Kelly Clarkson rise to prominence largely through ballad-focused music. The decade also witnessed significant crossover, with soft adult contemporary blending with country. Performers including Carrie Underwood, Faith Hill, and Shania Twain achieved notable popularity on both the adult contemporary and country charts, mirroring the crossover trend between other formats like hot AC and modern rock.

input: Miami has one of the largest television markets in the nation and the second largest in the state of Florida. Miami has several major newspapers, the main and largest newspaper being The Miami Herald. El Nuevo Herald is the major and largest Spanish-language newspaper. The Miami Herald and El Nuevo Herald are Miami's and South Florida's main, major and largest newspapers. The papers left their longtime home in downtown Miami in 2013. The newspapers are now headquartered at the former home of U.S. Southern Command in Doral.
rewrite: Miami hosts one of the country's biggest TV markets and Florida's second largest. The city is served by several major papers, with The Miami Herald as the primary English-language publication and El Nuevo Herald as the leading Spanish one. Both are considered the foremost newspapers in Miami and South Florida. They relocated from their historic downtown offices in 2013, now operating from the ex-U.S. Southern Command facility in Doral.

input: Former members Heather and Gary Botting compare the cultural paradigms of the religion to George Orwell's Nineteen Eighty-four, and Alan Rogerson describes the religion's leadership as totalitarian. Other critics charge that by disparaging individual decision-making, the religion's leaders cultivate a system of unquestioning obedience in which Witnesses abrogate all responsibility and rights over their personal lives. Critics also accuse the religion's leaders of exercising "intellectual dominance" over Witnesses, controlling information and creating "mental isolation", which former Governing Body member Raymond Franz argued were all elements of mind control.
rewrite: Heather and Gary Botting, both ex-members, liken the religion's cultural frameworks to the dystopian world of Orwell's Nineteen Eighty-four. Alan Rogerson labels its governance as totalitarian. Detractors further claim its authorities undermine personal autonomy, fostering blind compliance where adherents surrender life choices and liberties. These leaders are also accused of imposing "intellectual dominance," managing knowledge to induce "mental isolation"—factors former insider Raymond Franz identified as components of thought control.

input:
The movie industry was born in Paris when Auguste and Louis Lumière projected the first motion picture for a paying audience at the Grand Café on 28 December 1895. Many of Paris' concert/dance halls were transformed into movie theatres when the media became popular beginning in the 1930s. Later, most of the largest cinemas were divided into multiple, smaller rooms. Paris' largest cinema room today is in Le Grand Rex theatre with 2,700 seats.
Big multiplex movie theaters have been built since the 1990s. UGC Ciné Cité Les Halles with 27 screens, MK2 Bibliothèque with 20 screens and UGC Ciné Cité Bercy with 18 screens are among the largest.
rewrite: Cinema originated in Paris with the Lumière brothers' first paid public film screening at the Grand Café on December 28, 1895. As movies grew popular from the 1930s onward, numerous local music and dance venues were converted into film theaters. Over time, the biggest single-screen cinemas were typically subdivided into several smaller auditoriums. The city's current largest single screen, seating 2,700, is at Le Grand Rex. Starting in the 1990s, large multiplexes emerged, including major venues like UGC Ciné Cité Les Halles (27 screens), MK2 Bibliothèque (20 screens), and UGC Ciné Cité Bercy (18 screens).

input: Since the 1988 Education Reform Act, parents have a right to choose which school their child should go to or whether to not send them to school at all and to home educate them instead. The concept of "school choice" introduces the idea of competition between state schools, a fundamental change to the original "neighbourhood comprehensive" model, and is partly intended as a means by which schools that are perceived to be inferior are forced either to improve or, if hardly anyone wants to go there, to close down. Government policy is currently promoting 'specialisation' whereby parents choose a secondary school appropriate for their child's interests and skills. Most initiatives focus on parental choice and information, implementing a pseudo-market incentive to encourage better schools. This logic has underpinned the controversial league tables of school performance.
rewrite: Since the 1988 Education Reform Act, families have been granted the authority to select their child's school or opt for homeschooling. This "school choice" principle fosters rivalry among public schools, marking a significant shift from the traditional local comprehensive system. One aim is to pressure underperforming institutions to enhance their quality or face closure due to lack of enrollment. Current policies encourage "specialisation," guiding parents toward secondary schools that match their child's aptitudes and passions. Efforts largely center on empowering parents with information and choice, creating a market-like dynamic to reward higher-performing institutions. This reasoning is the foundation for the debated school ranking systems.

input: The Partyja BPF (Belarusian Popular Front) was established in 1988 as a political party and cultural movement for democracy and independence, à la the Baltic republics’ popular fronts. The discovery of mass graves in Kurapaty outside Minsk by historian Zianon Pazniak, the Belarusian Popular Front’s first leader, gave additional momentum to the pro-democracy and pro-independence movement in Belarus. It claimed that the NKVD performed secret killings in Kurapaty. Initially the Front had significant visibility because its numerous public actions almost always ended in clashes with the police and the KGB.
rewrite: Founded in 1988, the Partyja BPF (Belarusian Popular Front) emerged as both a political force and a cultural initiative advocating for democratic governance and national sovereignty, similar to movements in the Baltic states. Its early prominence was fueled by historian and first leader Zianon Pazniak's uncovering of mass burial sites at Kurapaty near Minsk, which he attributed to covert executions by the NKVD. This revelation strengthened the independence campaign. The Front maintained a high public profile through frequent demonstrations, which often resulted in confrontations with police and KGB agents.

input: Plymouth is home to Plymouth Argyle F.C., who play in the fourth tier of English football league known as Football League Two. The team's home ground is called Home Park and is located in Central Park. It links itself with the group of English non-conformists that left Plymouth for the New World in 1620: its nickname is "The Pilgrims". The city also has four Non-League football clubs; Plymouth Parkway F.C. who play at Bolitho Park, Elburton Villa F.C. who play at Haye Road, Vospers Oak Villa F.C. who play at Weston Mill and Plymstock United F.C. who play at Deans Cross. All four clubs play in the South West Peninsula League.
rewrite: Plymouth Argyle F.C., a professional football club competing in England's Football League Two, is based in the city. The team hosts its matches at Home Park stadium within Central Park. Reflecting the historical departure of non-conformists to the New World in 1620, the club carries the nickname "The Pilgrims." Additionally, Plymouth is home to four Non-League football teams: Plymouth Parkway F.C. (Bolitho Park), Elburton Villa F.C. (Haye Road), Vospers Oak Villa F.C. (Weston Mill), and Plymstock United F.C. (Deans Cross). All four participate in the South West Peninsula League.

input: The Appalachian belt includes, with the ranges enumerated above, the plateaus sloping southward to the Atlantic Ocean in New England, and south-eastward to the border of the coastal plain through the central and southern Atlantic states; and on the north-west, the Allegheny and Cumberland plateaus declining toward the Great Lakes and the interior plains. A remarkable feature of the belt is the longitudinal chain of broad valleys, including The Great Appalachian Valley, which in the southerly sections divides the mountain system into two unequal portions, but in the northernmost lies west of all the ranges possessing typical Appalachian features, and separates them from the Adirondack group. The mountain system has no axis of dominating altitudes, but in every portion the summits rise to rather uniform heights, and, especially in the central section, the various ridges and intermontane valleys have the same trend as the system itself. None of the summits reaches the region of perpetual snow.
rewrite: The Appalachian region encompasses not only the named mountain ranges but also the elevated tablelands that descend southward toward the Atlantic in New England, and in a southeasterly direction to meet the coastal plain across the mid-Atlantic and southern states. To the northwest, the Allegheny and Cumberland plateaus gradually lower toward the Great Lakes and the expansive interior lowlands. A distinctive characteristic is the lengthy sequence of wide valleys, most notably the Great Appalachian Valley. In southern areas, this valley splits the mountains into two uneven sections, while farther north it sits to the west of all the ranges with classic Appalachian traits, dividing them from the Adirondacks. The system lacks a central crest of supreme elevation. Instead, peaks throughout achieve similar heights, and in the central part particularly, the numerous ridges and valleys between mountains align with the overall direction of the range. No peak is high enough to support permanent snow.

input: In a speech before the Organization of American States in November 2013, Kerry remarked that the era of the Monroe Doctrine was over. He went on to explain, "The relationship that we seek and that we have worked hard to foster is not about a United States declaration about how and when it will intervene in the affairs of other American states. It's about all of our countries viewing one another as equals, sharing responsibilities, cooperating on security issues, and adhering not to doctrine, but to the decisions that we make as partners to advance the values and the interests that we share."
rewrite: During an address to the Organization of American States in late 2013, John Kerry declared the conclusion of the Monroe Doctrine era. He elaborated that the U.S. goal is a partnership not defined by unilateral American pronouncements on involvement in hemispheric affairs. Instead, he advocated for a relationship grounded in mutual equality, shared duties, and collaborative security efforts. This partnership would move beyond rigid policy to joint choices made among allies, all focused on promoting common principles and shared goals.

input: There is a strong relationship between the properties of wood and the properties of the particular tree that yielded it. The density of wood varies with species. The density of a wood correlates with its strength (mechanical properties). For example, mahogany is a medium-dense hardwood that is excellent for fine furniture crafting, whereas balsa is light, making it useful for model building. One of the densest woods is black ironwood.
rewrite: The characteristics of wood are closely linked to those of the tree it comes from. Wood density differs by species and is directly connected to its strength. Mahogany, a moderately dense hardwood, is ideal for quality furniture, while lightweight balsa suits model construction. Among the heaviest woods is black ironwood.

input: The hypnotic electronic dance song "On and On", produced in 1984 by Chicago DJ Jesse Saunders and co-written by Vince Lawrence, had elements that became staples of the early house sound, such as the Roland TB-303 bass synthesizer and minimal vocals as well as a Roland (specifically TR-808) drum machine and Korg (specifically Poly-61) synthesizer. It also utilized the bassline from Player One's disco record "Space Invaders" (1979). "On and On" is sometimes cited as the 'first house record', though other examples from around that time, such as J.M. Silk's "Music is the Key" (1985), have also been cited.
rewrite: Released in 1984, the trance-inducing track "On and On" was created by Chicago DJ Jesse Saunders with Vince Lawrence. It helped define the emerging house genre by incorporating foundational elements like a Roland TB-303 bass synth, sparse vocals, a TR-808 drum machine, and a Korg Poly-61 synthesizer. The song also borrowed its bassline from Player One's 1979 disco single "Space Invaders." While often called the first house record, other contenders from the era, like J.M. Silk's 1985 "Music is the Key," also hold that distinction.

input: Rufinus relates a story that as Bishop Alexander stood by a window, he watched boys playing on the seashore below, imitating the ritual of Christian baptism. He sent for the children and discovered that one of the boys (Athanasius) had acted as bishop. After questioning Athanasius, Bishop Alexander informed him that the baptisms were genuine, as both the form and matter of the sacrament had been performed through the recitation of the correct words and the administration of water, and that he must not continue to do this as those baptized had not been properly catechized. He invited Athanasius and his playfellows to prepare for clerical careers.
rewrite: According to Rufinus, Bishop Alexander once observed from his window children playing by the sea, mimicking a baptismal ceremony. He summoned them and learned a boy named Athanasius had performed the role of a bishop. Alexander determined the baptisms were valid, as the essential words and use of water were correctly employed. However, he instructed Athanasius to stop, since the participants lacked proper religious instruction. The bishop then encouraged Athanasius and his friends to pursue formal training for service in the church.

input: Tensions between John and the barons had been growing for several years, as demonstrated by the 1212 plot against the king. Many of the disaffected barons came from the north of England; that faction was often labelled by contemporaries and historians as "the Northerners". The northern barons rarely had any personal stake in the conflict in France, and many of them owed large sums of money to John; the revolt has been characterised as "a rebellion of the king's debtors". Many of John's military household joined the rebels, particularly amongst those that John had appointed to administrative roles across England; their local links and loyalties outweighed their personal loyalty to John. Tension also grew across North Wales, where opposition to the 1211 treaty between John and Llywelyn was turning into open conflict. For some the appointment of Peter des Roches as justiciar was an important factor, as he was considered an "abrasive foreigner" by many of the barons. The failure of John's French military campaign in 1214 was probably the final straw that precipitated the baronial uprising during John's final years as king; James Holt describes the path to civil war as "direct, short and unavoidable" following the defeat at Bouvines.
rewrite: Hostilities between King John and his nobles had intensified over a number of years, evidenced by a conspiracy to overthrow him in 1212. A significant portion of the aggrieved nobility originated from the northern counties, a group commonly referred to by both modern scholars and people of the time as "the Northerners." These northern lords were largely detached from the king's wars in France, and a great number were deeply indebted to the crown, leading some to view the ensuing revolt as primarily an insurrection of royal debtors. Numerous members of the king's own military retinue defected to the rebel cause, especially those John had placed in regional administrative posts; their local ties and allegiances proved stronger than their duty to the monarch. Unrest also escalated in North Wales, where resistance to the 1211 agreement with Llywelyn escalated into outright warfare. For many barons, the naming of Peter des Roches as justiciar was a key grievance, as they perceived him as a harsh outsider. However, the decisive catalyst for open rebellion in the closing period of John's reign was likely the collapse of his French campaign in 1214. Historian James Holt notes that after the loss at Bouvines, the descent into civil war became "direct, short and unavoidable."

input: Incandescent light bulbs come in a range of shapes and sizes. The names of the shapes may be slightly different in some regions. Many of these shapes have a designation consisting of one or more letters followed by one or more numbers, e.g. A55 or PAR38. The letters represent the shape of the bulb. The numbers represent the maximum diameter, either in 1⁄8 of an inch, or in millimeters, depending on the shape and the region. For example, 63 mm reflectors are designated R63, but in the US, they are known as R20 (2.5 in). However, in both regions, a PAR38 reflector is known as PAR38.
rewrite: Incandescent bulbs are produced in various forms and dimensions. Designations for these forms can vary by location. Typically, a code with letters and numbers, like A55 or PAR38, identifies each type. The letters indicate the bulb's form, while the numbers show its widest measurement. This measurement is expressed in eighths of an inch or in millimeters, depending on the style and geographic area. As an illustration, a 63 mm reflector is called R63 in many places but labeled R20 in the United States. Notably, a PAR38 bulb carries the same name universally.

input: Between October 14–16, 1964, Leonid Brezhnev and a small cadre of high-ranking Communist Party officials, deposed Khrushchev as Soviet government leader a day after Voskhod 1 landed, in what was called the "Wednesday conspiracy". The new political leaders, along with Korolev, ended the technologically troublesome Voskhod program, cancelling Voskhod 3 and 4, which were in the planning stages, and started concentrating on the race to the Moon. Voskhod 2 would end up being Korolev's final achievement before his death on January 14, 1966, as it would become the last of the many space firsts that demonstrated the USSR's domination in spacecraft technology during the early 1960s. According to historian Asif Siddiqi, Korolev's accomplishments marked "the absolute zenith of the Soviet space program, one never, ever attained since." There would be a two-year pause in Soviet piloted space flights while Voskhod's replacement, the Soyuz spacecraft, was designed and developed.
rewrite: In mid-October 1964, shortly following the Voskhod 1 mission, Leonid Brezhnev and a group of party elites removed Khrushchev from power in a move later termed the "Wednesday conspiracy." This new leadership, in agreement with chief designer Sergei Korolev, terminated the problematic Voskhod initiative. Planned missions Voskhod 3 and 4 were scrapped, and focus shifted decisively to the lunar competition. Voskhod 2, which flew earlier in 1965, proved to be Korolev's last success before his death in early 1966. It also represented the final major space milestone that showcased the Soviet Union's clear technological supremacy in the earlier part of the decade. As noted by historian Asif Siddiqi, this period was the unmatched peak of the Soviet space effort. A subsequent two-year hiatus in human spaceflight occurred while the Soyuz vehicle, intended to succeed Voskhod, was being created.

input: In comparison to the other regions of Spain, the major economic benefit of Galicia is its fishing Industry. Galicia is a land of economic contrast. While the western coast, with its major population centers and its fishing and manufacturing industries, is prosperous and increasing in population, the rural hinterland — the provinces of Ourense and Lugo — is economically dependent on traditional agriculture, based on small landholdings called minifundios. However, the rise of tourism, sustainable forestry and organic and traditional agriculture are bringing other possibilities to the Galician economy without compromising the preservation of the natural resources and the local culture.
rewrite: Galicia's economy stands apart from the rest of Spain, primarily driven by its fishing sector. The region presents a stark economic divide. Its western coastline, densely populated and home to fishing and manufacturing, is thriving and growing. In contrast, the inland provinces of Ourense and Lugo rely on conventional farming, often practiced on small plots known as minifundios. New opportunities are emerging through tourism, sustainable forestry, and organic farming, diversifying the economy while protecting both the environment and cultural heritage.

input: Florida's nickname is the "Sunshine State", but severe weather is a common occurrence in the state. Central Florida is known as the lightning capital of the United States, as it experiences more lightning strikes than anywhere else in the country. Florida has one of the highest average precipitation levels of any state, in large part because afternoon thunderstorms are common in much of the state from late spring until early autumn. A narrow eastern part of the state including Orlando and Jacksonville receives between 2,400 and 2,800 hours of sunshine annually. The rest of the state, including Miami, receives between 2,800 and 3,200 hours annually.
rewrite: Despite its "Sunshine State" moniker, Florida frequently encounters intense weather. The central region leads the nation in lightning activity. The state also ranks among the wettest, primarily due to regular afternoon thunderstorms from late spring through early fall. Annually, a narrow eastern strip containing Orlando and Jacksonville sees 2,400 to 2,800 hours of sun. The remaining areas, such as Miami, enjoy more sunshine, with 2,800 to 3,200 hours each year.

input: By the 1860s the Kingdom of Prussia and the Austrian Empire were the two most powerful nations dominated by German-speaking elites. Both sought to expand their influence and territory. The Austrian Empire – like the Holy Roman Empire – was a multi-ethnic state, but German-speaking people there did not have an absolute numerical majority; the creation of the Austro-Hungarian Empire was one result of the growing nationalism of other ethnicities especially the Hungarians. Prussia under Otto von Bismarck would ride on the coat-tails of nationalism to unite all of modern-day Germany. The German Empire ("Second Reich") was created in 1871 following the proclamation of Wilhelm I as head of a union of German-speaking states, while disregarding millions of its non-German subjects who desired self-determination from German rule.
rewrite: During the 1860s, Prussian and Austrian power was paramount among German-led states, each aiming to extend its control and lands. Austria, a multi-ethnic realm similar to its Holy Roman predecessor, lacked a clear German-speaking majority; rising nationalist sentiments, particularly among Hungarians, later led to the formation of the Austro-Hungarian Empire. Meanwhile, Prussia, guided by Otto von Bismarck, harnessed nationalist fervor to consolidate the modern German nation. This culminated in the 1871 establishment of the German Empire, or Second Reich, with Wilhelm I declared emperor over a union of German states. This unification explicitly ignored the aspirations for self-determination among millions of non-German peoples within its borders.

input: The Atlantic coast of the United States is low, with minor exceptions. The Appalachian Highland owes its oblique northeast-southwest trend to crustal deformations which in very early geological time gave a beginning to what later came to be the Appalachian mountain system. This system had its climax of deformation so long ago (probably in Permian time) that it has since then been very generally reduced to moderate or low relief. It owes its present-day altitude either to renewed elevations along the earlier lines or to the survival of the most resistant rocks as residual mountains. The oblique trend of this coast would be even more pronounced but for a comparatively modern crustal movement, causing a depression in the northeast resulting in an encroachment of the sea upon the land. Additionally, the southeastern section has undergone an elevation resulting in the advance of the land upon the sea.
rewrite: The eastern shoreline of the United States is generally level, with few areas of significant height. The Appalachian region follows a diagonal path from the northeast to the southwest, a pattern established by ancient shifts in the earth's crust that eventually formed the Appalachian mountains. The major shaping of this range occurred in the distant geologic past, leaving it largely worn down to gentle hills and low elevations over time. Its current height is due either to recent uplift along its original structures or to the enduring presence of its hardest rock formations. This diagonal coastline would be even more distinct if not for recent geological activity that caused the land to sink in the northeast, allowing the ocean to intrude inland. Conversely, the southeast has experienced a rise in elevation, leading to the expansion of land outward into the sea.

input: Each of these four dialects was associated with an independent kingdom on the island. Of these, Northumbria south of the Tyne, and most of Mercia, were overrun by the Vikings during the 9th century. The portion of Mercia that was successfully defended, and all of Kent, were then integrated into Wessex under Alfred the Great. From that time on, the West Saxon dialect (then in the form now known as Early West Saxon) became standardised as the language of government, and as the basis for the many works of literature and religious materials produced or translated from Latin in that period.
rewrite: These four distinct dialects each originated in separate kingdoms across the region. During the 9th century, Viking invasions conquered Northumbria south of the Tyne and much of Mercia. However, the remaining part of Mercia and the entirety of Kent were later absorbed into the kingdom of Wessex by Alfred the Great. Consequently, the West Saxon dialect, specifically its Early West Saxon form, was established as the official administrative language. It also served as the foundation for numerous literary and religious texts, which were either newly composed or translated from Latin at that time.

input: Noted 19th-century mosaics include those by Edward Burne-Jones at St Pauls within the Walls in Rome. Another modern mosaic of note is the world's largest mosaic installation located at the Cathedral Basilica of St. Louis, located in St. Louis, Missouri. A modern example of mosaic is the Museum of Natural History station of the New York City Subway (there are many such works of art scattered throughout the New York City subway system, though many IND stations are usually designed with bland mosaics.) Another example of mosaics in ordinary surroundings is the use of locally themed mosaics in some restrooms in the rest areas along some Texas interstate highways.
rewrite: Significant mosaic works from the 1800s feature creations like those by Edward Burne-Jones in Rome's St. Pauls within the Walls. In contemporary times, the Cathedral Basilica of St. Louis in Missouri holds the planet's biggest mosaic artwork. Modern instances also encompass artistic pieces in everyday spaces, such as the mosaics at a Museum of Natural History subway stop in New York City. Similarly, certain Texas interstate highway rest stops incorporate restroom mosaics that reflect local themes.

input: British Somaliland became independent on 26 June 1960 as the State of Somaliland, and the Trust Territory of Somalia (the former Italian Somaliland) followed suit five days later. On 1 July 1960, the two territories united to form the Somali Republic, albeit within boundaries drawn up by Italy and Britain. A government was formed by Abdullahi Issa Mohamud and Muhammad Haji Ibrahim Egal other members of the trusteeship and protectorate governments, with Haji Bashir Ismail Yusuf as President of the Somali National Assembly, Aden Abdullah Osman Daar as the President of the Somali Republic and Abdirashid Ali Shermarke as Prime Minister (later to become President from 1967 to 1969). On 20 July 1961 and through a popular referendum, the people of Somalia ratified a new constitution, which was first drafted in 1960. In 1967, Muhammad Haji Ibrahim Egal became Prime Minister, a position to which he was appointed by Shermarke. Egal would later become the President of the autonomous Somaliland region in northwestern Somalia.
rewrite: On June 26, 1960, British Somaliland gained sovereignty, establishing itself as the State of Somaliland. Shortly after, on July 1, the former Italian-administered Trust Territory of Somalia also achieved independence. These two regions immediately merged to create the Somali Republic, though their borders were those previously established by the colonial powers. The new nation's leadership was drawn from both former administrations. Aden Abdullah Osman Daar assumed the presidency of the republic, with Abdirashid Ali Shermarke serving as Prime Minister; Shermarke would later become president. The legislature was led by Haji Bashir Ismail Yusuf. In a July 1961 referendum, a constitution originally prepared the prior year was officially approved by the populace. By 1967, Shermarke, as president, appointed Muhammad Haji Ibrahim Egal as Prime Minister. Egal would eventually lead the self-declared republic of Somaliland in the north.

input: Feathers are a feature characteristic of birds (though also present in some dinosaurs not currently considered to be true birds). They facilitate flight, provide insulation that aids in thermoregulation, and are used in display, camouflage, and signaling. There are several types of feathers, each serving its own set of purposes. Feathers are epidermal growths attached to the skin and arise only in specific tracts of skin called pterylae. The distribution pattern of these feather tracts (pterylosis) is used in taxonomy and systematics. The arrangement and appearance of feathers on the body, called plumage, may vary within species by age, social status, and sex.
rewrite: Feathers are unique structures primarily associated with birds, and they were also found in certain non-avian dinosaurs. Their functions include enabling flight, offering insulation for temperature control, and serving roles in communication and camouflage. These skin appendages develop in particular areas known as pterylae. The layout of these feather tracts, termed pterylosis, helps classify birds. Additionally, the overall feathering, or plumage, can differ among individuals of the same species based on factors like age, gender, and social standing.

input: Once the elevator arrives at the floor, it will park with its doors open and the car buttons will be disabled to prevent a passenger from taking control of the elevator. Medical personnel must then activate the code-blue key switch inside the car, select their floor and close the doors with the door close button. The elevator will then travel non-stop to the selected floor, and will remain in code-blue service until switched off in the car. Some hospital elevators will feature a 'hold' position on the code-blue key switch (similar to fire service) which allows the elevator to remain at a floor locked out of service until code blue is deactivated.
rewrite: When the elevator reaches its destination, it will stop and keep its doors open, with the interior controls deactivated to stop anyone from operating it. Healthcare staff need to turn on the emergency key switch inside, choose their desired floor, and use the button to shut the doors. The elevator will then proceed directly to that floor without stopping and will stay in emergency mode until the switch is turned off. Certain hospital elevators include a 'hold' setting on this switch, much like fire service operation, enabling the elevator to stay parked and out of regular use at a floor until the emergency mode is ended.

input: Myanmar's armed forces are known as the Tatmadaw, which numbers 488,000. The Tatmadaw comprises the Army, the Navy, and the Air Force. The country ranked twelfth in the world for its number of active troops in service. The military is very influential in Myanmar, with all top cabinet and ministry posts usually held by military officials. Official figures for military spending are not available. Estimates vary widely because of uncertain exchange rates, but Myanmar's military forces' expenses are high. Myanmar imports most of its weapons from Russia, Ukraine, China and India.
rewrite: Myanmar's military, called the Tatmadaw, has approximately 488,000 active personnel across its army, navy, and air force, placing it twelfth globally in troop count. The institution holds substantial political power, typically occupying all senior government positions. While no official budget is published, estimated defense expenditures are considerable, despite challenges in precise calculation due to fluctuating currency values. The nation primarily acquires its armaments from Russia, China, India, and Ukraine.

input: The Anglo-French hostilities were ended in 1763 by the Treaty of Paris, which involved a complex series of land exchanges, the most important being France's cession to Spain of Louisiana, and to Great Britain the rest of New France except for the islands of St. Pierre and Miquelon. Faced with the choice of retrieving either New France or its Caribbean island colonies of Guadeloupe and Martinique, France chose the latter to retain these lucrative sources of sugar, writing off New France as an unproductive, costly territory. France also returned Minorca to the British. Spain lost control of Florida to Great Britain, but it received from the French the Île d'Orléans and all of the former French holdings west of the Mississippi River. The exchanges suited the British as well, as their own Caribbean islands already supplied ample sugar, and, with the acquisition of New France and Florida, they now controlled all of North America east of the Mississippi.
rewrite: In 1763, the Treaty of Paris concluded the war between Britain and France. This agreement included several territorial transfers. Most significantly, France gave Louisiana to Spain and surrendered most of New France to Britain, keeping only St. Pierre and Miquelon. Confronted with the option of regaining New France or its valuable sugar-producing islands, Guadeloupe and Martinique, France selected the Caribbean colonies, deeming New France an expensive burden. France also restored Minorca to British control. While Spain ceded Florida to Britain, it gained French lands west of the Mississippi, including the Île d'Orléans. These terms benefited Britain, whose existing Caribbean possessions met its sugar needs. By gaining New France and Florida, Britain secured dominance over all North American territories east of the Mississippi.

input: The city had surrendered without a fight to the invading Moors (Berbers and Arabs) by 714 AD, and the cathedral of Saint Vincent was turned into a mosque. Abd al-Rahman I, the first emir of Cordoba, ordered the city destroyed in 755 during his wars against other nobility, but several years later his son, Abdullah, had a form of autonomous rule over the province of Valencia. Among his administrative acts he ordered the building of a luxurious palace, the Russafa, on the outskirts of the city in the neighbourhood of the same name. So far no remains have been found. Also at this time Valencia received the name Medina al-Turab (City of Sand). When Islamic culture settled in, Valencia, then called Balansiyya, prospered from the 10th century, due to a booming trade in paper, silk, leather, ceramics, glass and silver-work. The architectural legacy of this period is abundant in Valencia and can still be appreciated today in the remnants of the old walls, the Baños del Almirante bath house, Portal de Valldigna street and even the Cathedral and the tower, El Micalet (El Miguelete), which was the minaret of the old mosque.
rewrite:
By 714 AD, the city yielded peacefully to Moorish forces, comprising Berber and Arab groups, and its Cathedral of Saint Vincent was repurposed as a mosque. In 755, Abd al-Rahman I, Cordoba’s inaugural emir, commanded the city’s destruction amid conflicts with rival nobles. However, his son Abdullah later governed the Valencia region with a degree of independence. Under his administration, a lavish palace named Russafa was constructed on the city’s outskirts in a district sharing that name, though no traces of it have been discovered. During this era, Valencia was also designated Medina al-Turab, meaning “City of Sand.”

As Islamic influence took root, the city—known then as Balansiyya—began to thrive from the 10th century onward, fueled by vigorous commerce in goods like paper, silk, leather, ceramics, glass, and silverware. This period left a rich architectural heritage visible in modern Valencia, including surviving sections of the ancient fortifications, the Baños del Almirante bathhouse, Portal de Valldigna street, and structures such as the Cathedral and its tower, El Micalet (El Miguelete), originally the minaret of the former mosque.

input: Whereas SCIMs cannot turn a shaft faster than allowed by the power line frequency, universal motors can run at much higher speeds. This makes them useful for appliances such as blenders, vacuum cleaners, and hair dryers where high speed and light weight are desirable. They are also commonly used in portable power tools, such as drills, sanders, circular and jig saws, where the motor's characteristics work well. Many vacuum cleaner and weed trimmer motors exceed 10,000 rpm, while many similar miniature grinders exceed 30,000 rpm.
rewrite: Unlike SCIMs, which are limited by power line frequency, universal motors can achieve significantly higher rotational speeds. This advantage suits them for high-speed, lightweight devices like blenders, vacuums, and hair dryers. They are also ideal for portable power tools, including drills and saws, due to their performance traits. For instance, many vacuum and weed trimmer motors surpass 10,000 rpm, and some small grinders exceed 30,000 rpm.

input: To counter the trend towards low-density suburban residential growth, the government began a series of controversial public housing projects in the inner city by the Housing Commission of Victoria, which resulted in demolition of many neighbourhoods and a proliferation of high-rise towers. In later years, with the rapid rise of motor vehicle ownership, the investment in freeway and highway developments greatly accelerated the outward suburban sprawl and declining inner city population. The Bolte government sought to rapidly accelerate the modernisation of Melbourne. Major road projects including the remodelling of St Kilda Junction, the widening of Hoddle Street and then the extensive 1969 Melbourne Transportation Plan changed the face of the city into a car-dominated environment.
rewrite: In response to expanding suburban sprawl, authorities initiated disputed inner-city public housing developments through the Housing Commission of Victoria. This led to the clearance of numerous established areas and a surge in tall apartment buildings. Subsequently, as car ownership soared, heavy investment in freeways and major roads hastened the spread of suburbs and a drop in inner-city residents. The Bolte administration aggressively pushed to modernize Melbourne. Key initiatives like redesigning St Kilda Junction, broadening Hoddle Street, and the comprehensive 1969 transportation strategy transformed the urban landscape into one primarily designed for automobiles.

input: Her Majesty's Courts Service provide a Magistrates' Court and a Combined Crown and County Court in the city. The Plymouth Borough Police, formed in 1836, eventually became part of Devon and Cornwall Constabulary. There are police stations at Charles Cross and Crownhill (the Divisional HQ) and smaller stations at Plympton and Plymstock. The city has one of the Devon and Cornwall Area Crown Prosecution Service Divisional offices. Plymouth has five fire stations located in Camel's Head, Crownhill, Greenbank, Plympton and Plymstock which is part of Devon and Somerset Fire and Rescue Service. The Royal National Lifeboat Institution have an Atlantic 85 class lifeboat and Severn class lifeboat stationed at Millbay Docks.
rewrite: The city hosts a Magistrates' Court as well as a joint Crown and County Court under Her Majesty's Courts Service. The local Plymouth Borough Police, established in 1836, was later integrated into the Devon and Cornwall Constabulary. Primary police facilities are situated at Charles Cross and Crownhill, which serves as the Divisional Headquarters, with additional smaller stations in Plympton and Plymstock. A divisional office for the Devon and Cornwall Crown Prosecution Service is also located here. For fire services, five stations operate in Camel's Head, Crownhill, Greenbank, Plympton, and Plymstock, forming part of the Devon and Somerset Fire and Rescue Service. Additionally, the Royal National Lifeboat Institution bases both an Atlantic 85 and a Severn class lifeboat at Millbay Docks.

input: Wisdom, or the capacity for insight and judgment that is developed through experience, increases between the ages of fourteen and twenty-five, then levels off. Thus, it is during the adolescence-adulthood transition that individuals acquire the type of wisdom that is associated with age. Wisdom is not the same as intelligence: adolescents do not improve substantially on IQ tests since their scores are relative to others in their same age group, and relative standing usually does not change—everyone matures at approximately the same rate in this way.
rewrite: The ability to gain deep understanding and make sound decisions, which grows from life experience, rises from the mid-teens to around age twenty-five before stabilizing. This means the shift from youth to adulthood is when people gain the wisdom typically linked with growing older. Importantly, wisdom differs from intelligence. Teenagers do not show major IQ gains because these scores compare them to peers of the same age, and those relative positions generally remain fixed as everyone develops these cognitive abilities at a similar pace.

input: The Wayback Machine is a digital archive of the World Wide Web and other information on the Internet created by the Internet Archive, a nonprofit organization, based in San Francisco, California, United States. It was set up by Brewster Kahle and Bruce Gilliat, and is maintained with content from Alexa Internet. The service enables users to see archived versions of web pages across time, which the archive calls a "three dimensional index."
rewrite: The Wayback Machine is an online repository for internet content, including websites, established by the nonprofit Internet Archive in San Francisco. Founded by Brewster Kahle and Bruce Gilliat, it utilizes data from Alexa Internet. This tool allows people to view past versions of web pages, described by the archive as a three-dimensional index.

input: In mid-1944 Japan mobilized over 500,000 men  and launched a massive operation across China under the code name Operation Ichi-Go, their largest offensive of World War II, with the goal of connecting Japanese-controlled territory in China and French Indochina and capturing airbases in southeastern China where American bombers were based. During this time, many of the newest American-trained Chinese units and supplies were forcibly locked in the Burmese theater under Joseph Stilwell set by terms of the Lend-Lease Agreement. Though Japan suffered about 100,000 casualties, these attacks, the biggest in several years, gained much ground for Japan before Chinese forces stopped the incursions in Guangxi. Despite major tactical victories, the operation overall failed to provide Japan with any significant strategic gains. A great majority of the Chinese forces were able to retreat out of the area, and later come back to attack Japanese positions such as Battle of West Hunan. Japan was not any closer in defeating China after this operation, and the constant defeats the Japanese suffered in the Pacific meant that Japan never got the time and resources needed to achieve final victory over China. Operation Ichi-go created a great sense of social confusion in the areas of China that it affected. Chinese Communist guerrillas were able to exploit this confusion to gain influence and control of greater areas of the countryside in the aftermath of Ichi-go.
rewrite:
In the summer of 1944, Japan initiated its most extensive campaign of the war, designated Operation Ichi-Go. Mobilizing more than half a million troops, the offensive aimed to consolidate Japanese-held regions in China and French Indochina and seize Allied airfields in southeastern China used by American aircraft. Concurrently, a substantial portion of China's modernized, U.S.-equipped divisions and matériel were committed to the campaign in Burma under General Joseph Stilwell, as stipulated by Lend-Lease conditions.
