The Japanese advances, their largest in years, resulted in roughly 100,000 Japanese casualties but secured considerable territory before being halted in Guangxi. However, these tactical successes did not translate into strategic advantage. The bulk of Chinese forces withdrew in good order and later counterattacked, as seen in engagements like the Battle of West Hunan. The operation did not bring Japan nearer to subduing China, and mounting losses in the Pacific diverted the time and resources necessary for a conclusive victory.

Furthermore, the offensive caused widespread social disruption across affected regions. In the resulting chaos, Chinese Communist guerrilla forces effectively expanded their influence and control over vast rural areas, leveraging the instability for long-term political gain.

input: The aftermath of World War II saw an explosion in the discovery of new classes of antibacterial drugs including the cephalosporins (developed by Eli Lilly based on the seminal work of Giuseppe Brotzu and Edward Abraham), streptomycin (discovered during a Merck-funded research program in Selman Waksman's laboratory), the tetracyclines (discovered at Lederle Laboratories, now a part of Pfizer), erythromycin (discovered at Eli Lilly and Co.) and their extension to an increasingly wide range of bacterial pathogens. Streptomycin, discovered during a Merck-funded research program in Selman Waksman's laboratory at Rutgers in 1943, became the first effective treatment for tuberculosis. At the time of its discovery, sanitoriums for the isolation of tuberculosis-infected people were an ubiquitous feature of cities in developed countries, with 50% dying within 5 years of admission.
rewrite: Following World War II, numerous novel categories of antibiotic medications emerged. Key discoveries included cephalosporins, pioneered from earlier research by Giuseppe Brotzu and Edward Abraham and later advanced by Eli Lilly; streptomycin, identified in Selman Waksman's Rutgers University lab with Merck's support; tetracyclines, found at Lederle Laboratories; and erythromycin, developed by Eli Lilly. These drugs were subsequently applied to combat a growing spectrum of bacterial infections. Streptomycin, isolated in 1943, provided the first viable cure for tuberculosis. Before this breakthrough, isolating patients in sanitariums was common in urban areas across the developed world, and approximately half of those admitted succumbed to the disease within five years.

input: Prior to the second world war, birth control was prohibited in many countries, and in the United States even the discussion of contraceptive methods sometimes led to prosecution under Comstock laws. The history of the development of oral contraceptives is thus closely tied to the birth control movement and the efforts of activists Margaret Sanger, Mary Dennett, and Emma Goldman. Based on fundamental research performed by Gregory Pincus and synthetic methods for progesterone developed by Carl Djerassi at Syntex and by Frank Colton at G.D. Searle & Co., the first oral contraceptive, Enovid, was developed by E.D. Searle and Co. and approved by the FDA in 1960. The original formulation incorporated vastly excessive doses of hormones, and caused severe side effects. Nonetheless, by 1962, 1.2 million American women were on the pill, and by 1965 the number had increased to 6.5 million. The availability of a convenient form of temporary contraceptive led to dramatic changes in social mores including expanding the range of lifestyle options available to women, reducing the reliance of women on men for contraceptive practice, encouraging the delay of marriage, and increasing pre-marital co-habitation.
rewrite: Before World War II, numerous nations banned contraception, and in the U.S., merely talking about it could result in legal action under statutes like the Comstock Act. The creation of the birth control pill is deeply connected to advocacy for reproductive rights, championed by figures such as Margaret Sanger, Mary Dennett, and Emma Goldman. Building on essential studies by Gregory Pincus and key advances in progesterone synthesis from Carl Djerassi at Syntex and Frank Colton at G.D. Searle & Co., the inaugural oral contraceptive, Enovid, was produced by G.D. Searle and received FDA authorization in 1960. Early versions contained extremely high hormone levels, triggering serious adverse reactions. Despite this, usage surged rapidly, reaching 1.2 million American women by 1962 and climbing to 6.5 million by 1965. This easy-to-use, reversible contraceptive method spurred profound societal shifts. It broadened life choices for women, decreased their dependence on male partners for birth control, promoted later marriages, and made unmarried cohabitation more common.

input: According to Jan Nattier, the term Mahāyāna "Great Vehicle" was originally even an honorary synonym for Bodhisattvayāna "Bodhisattva Vehicle." The Aṣṭasāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, an early and important Mahayana text, contains a simple and brief definition for the term bodhisattva: "Because he has enlightenment as his aim, a bodhisattva-mahāsattva is so called."
rewrite: Jan Nattier notes that "Mahāyāna" initially served as an honorific alternative to "Bodhisattvayāna." An early key sutra defines a bodhisattva concisely: one who strives toward enlightenment.

input: In 550 BC, Cyrus the Great, son of Mandane and Cambyses I, took over the Median Empire, and founded the Achaemenid Empire by unifying other city states. The conquest of Media was a result of what is called the Persian Revolt. The brouhaha was initially triggered by the actions of the Median ruler Astyages, and was quickly spread to other provinces, as they allied with the Persians. Later conquests under Cyrus and his successors expanded the empire to include Lydia, Babylon, Egypt, parts of the Balkans and Eastern Europe proper, as well as the lands to the west of the Indus and Oxus rivers.
rewrite: In 550 BC, Cyrus the Great, whose parents were Cambyses I and Mandane, overthrew the Median Empire. This event, known as the Persian Revolt, began due to the Median king Astyages' conduct and rapidly gained momentum as neighboring regions joined the Persian cause. Through this, Cyrus established the Achaemenid Empire by merging various states. Subsequent campaigns by him and his heirs broadened its territory to encompass Lydia, Babylon, Egypt, sections of the Balkans and Eastern Europe, plus areas west of the Indus and Oxus rivers.

input: Leucothea was daughter of Orchamus and sister of Clytia. She fell in love with Apollo who disguised himself as Leucothea's mother to gain entrance to her chambers. Clytia, jealous of her sister because she wanted Apollo for herself, told Orchamus the truth, betraying her sister's trust and confidence in her. Enraged, Orchamus ordered Leucothea to be buried alive. Apollo refused to forgive Clytia for betraying his beloved, and a grieving Clytia wilted and slowly died. Apollo changed her into an incense plant, either heliotrope or sunflower, which follows the sun every day.
rewrite: Leucothea, offspring of Orchamus and sibling to Clytia, developed a passion for Apollo. The god entered her rooms by impersonating her mother. Clytia, coveting Apollo’s affection, informed their father of the deception. Orchamus, furious, commanded that Leucothea be entombed while living. Apollo would not pardon Clytia for her treachery, and she languished in sorrow until her death. Ultimately, he transformed her into a sun-tracking incense shrub, often considered a heliotrope or sunflower.

input: Karl Marx published the Communist Manifesto in February 1848, with little attention. However, a few days later the French Revolution of 1848 broke out, which replaced the monarchy of Louis Philippe with the Second French Republic. In June 1848, Paris workers, disenchanted with the new government, built barricades and raised red flags. The new government called in the French Army to put down the uprising, the first of many such confrontations between the army and the new worker's movements in Europe.
rewrite: In February 1848, Karl Marx released the Communist Manifesto to minimal notice. Shortly after, the 1848 French Revolution erupted, overthrowing King Louis Philippe and establishing the Second French Republic. By June, disillusioned Parisian laborers, protesting the republic, erected barricades under red banners. The state deployed the army to crush this revolt, marking the initial major clash between European military forces and emerging workers' movements.

input: Konbaung kings extended Restored Toungoo's administrative reforms, and achieved unprecedented levels of internal control and external expansion. For the first time in history, the Burmese language and culture came to predominate the entire Irrawaddy valley. The evolution and growth of Burmese literature and theatre continued, aided by an extremely high adult male literacy rate for the era (half of all males and 5% of females). Nonetheless, the extent and pace of reforms were uneven and ultimately proved insufficient to stem the advance of British colonialism.
rewrite: The rulers of the Konbaung dynasty furthered the governmental changes begun in the Restored Toungoo period, reaching new heights in both domestic authority and territorial growth. This era saw Burmese language and customs become dominant across the whole Irrawaddy region for the first time. Literary and theatrical traditions flourished, supported by exceptional male literacy rates for the period. However, the inconsistent scope and speed of these changes were inadequate to halt the encroachment of British colonial power.

input: There have been six instances as of 2009 in which the exemption process was initiated. Of these six, one was granted, one was partially granted, one was denied and three were withdrawn. Donald Baur, in The Endangered Species Act: law, policy, and perspectives, concluded," ... the exemption provision is basically a nonfactor in the administration of the ESA. A major reason, of course, is that so few consultations result in jeopardy opinions, and those that do almost always result in the identification of reasonable and prudent alternatives to avoid jeopardy."
rewrite: As of 2009, the exemption procedure had been started six times. Among these cases, one received full approval, one obtained partial approval, one was rejected, and three were retracted. According to Donald Baur's analysis in *The Endangered Species Act: Law, Policy, and Perspectives*, the exemption clause plays a negligible role in how the ESA is managed. This is largely because very few consultations lead to findings of jeopardy, and when they do, feasible alternatives are almost always found to prevent harm.

input: A common way in which emotions are conceptualized in sociology is in terms of the multidimensional characteristics including cultural or emotional labels (e.g., anger, pride, fear, happiness), physiological changes (e.g., increased perspiration, changes in pulse rate), expressive facial and body movements (e.g., smiling, frowning, baring teeth), and appraisals of situational cues. One comprehensive theory of emotional arousal in humans has been developed by Jonathan Turner (2007: 2009). Two of the key eliciting factors for the arousal of emotions within this theory are expectations states and sanctions. When people enter a situation or encounter with certain expectations for how the encounter should unfold, they will experience different emotions depending on the extent to which expectations for Self, other and situation are met or not met. People can also provide positive or negative sanctions directed at Self or other which also trigger different emotional experiences in individuals. Turner analyzed a wide range of emotion theories across different fields of research including sociology, psychology, evolutionary science, and neuroscience. Based on this analysis, he identified four emotions that all researchers consider being founded on human neurology including assertive-anger, aversion-fear, satisfaction-happiness, and disappointment-sadness. These four categories are called primary emotions and there is some agreement amongst researchers that these primary emotions become combined to produce more elaborate and complex emotional experiences. These more elaborate emotions are called first-order elaborations in Turner's theory and they include sentiments such as pride, triumph, and awe. Emotions can also be experienced at different levels of intensity so that feelings of concern are a low-intensity variation of the primary emotion aversion-fear whereas depression is a higher intensity variant.
rewrite:
In sociology, emotions are often understood through several interconnected dimensions. These aspects encompass the terms used within a culture to identify feelings, such as rage, joy, or anxiety; accompanying bodily shifts like a quickened heartbeat or sweating; outward displays through gestures or facial expressions; and the individual's interpretation of surrounding events. Scholar Jonathan Turner (2007; 2009) formulated an influential framework for understanding how emotions emerge. Central to his model are two triggers: the standards people hold and the feedback they receive. Individuals enter social settings with preconceived notions about what should occur, and their emotional response is shaped by whether their own actions, others' behaviors, and the situation itself align with or deviate from these anticipations. Similarly, receiving affirming or critical reactions—whether aimed at oneself or at another person—generates distinct emotional states.

Turner's synthesis drew from diverse academic domains like psychology, neuroscience, and evolutionary studies. From this review, he distilled four fundamental emotions that are universally recognized as rooted in human biology: assertiveness or anger, aversion or fear, contentment or happiness, and letdown or sadness. These core, or primary, emotions are widely seen as the basic components that blend to form more nuanced and complex feelings. Turner terms these complex derivatives first-order elaborations, which cover refined sentiments like pride, awe, and triumph. Furthermore, emotional experiences vary in their strength. For instance, worry represents a mild form of the primary emotion aversion-fear, while despair constitutes a much more severe expression of the same core feeling.

input: In Congregational and Presbyterian churches which profess a traditionally Calvinist or Reformed theology there are differing views regarding present-day continuation or cessation of the gifts (charismata) of the Spirit. Generally, however, Reformed charismatics distance themselves from renewal movements with tendencies which could be perceived as overemotional, such as Word of Faith, Toronto Blessing, Brownsville Revival and Lakeland Revival. Prominent Reformed charismatic denominations are the Sovereign Grace Churches and the Every Nation Churches in the USA, in Great Britain there is the Newfrontiers churches and movement, which leading figure is Terry Virgo.
rewrite: Within Congregational and Presbyterian churches that adhere to Reformed or Calvinist doctrine, opinions vary on whether the Holy Spirit's gifts continue today or have ceased. Typically, those who identify as Reformed charismatics distinguish themselves from more expressive renewal movements like the Toronto Blessing or Word of Faith. Notable denominations in this group include Sovereign Grace Churches and Every Nation Churches in the United States, along with Britain's Newfrontiers movement, led by Terry Virgo.

input: According to the 2010 Census, whites made up 51% of Houston's population; 26% of the total population were non-Hispanic whites. Blacks or African Americans made up 25% of Houston's population. American Indians made up 0.7% of the population. Asians made up 6% (1.7% Vietnamese, 1.3% Chinese, 1.3% Indian, 0.9% Pakistani, 0.4% Filipino, 0.3% Korean, 0.1% Japanese), while Pacific Islanders made up 0.1%. Individuals from some other race made up 15.2% of the city's population, of which 0.2% were non-Hispanic. Individuals from two or more races made up 3.3% of the city. At the 2000 Census, there were 1,953,631 people and the population density was 3,371.7 people per square mile (1,301.8/km²). The racial makeup of the city was 49.3% White, 25.3% African American, 5.3% Asian, 0.7% American Indian, 0.1% Pacific Islander, 16.5% from some other race, and 3.1% from two or more races. In addition, Hispanics made up 37.4% of Houston's population while non-Hispanic whites made up 30.8%, down from 62.4% in 1970.
rewrite: Based on the 2010 Census, Houston's demographic composition was majority white at 51%, with non-Hispanic whites accounting for 26%. The Black or African American community represented a quarter of residents. American Indians constituted 0.7%, and Asians comprised 6%, including significant Vietnamese, Chinese, and Indian groups. Pacific Islanders were 0.1%. People identifying with another race totaled 15.2%, with only 0.2% being non-Hispanic, and those of multiple races were 3.3%. In contrast, the 2000 Census recorded a population of nearly 1.95 million, with a density of about 3,372 per square mile. That year's racial distribution showed 49.3% White, 25.3% African American, 5.3% Asian, 0.7% American Indian, 0.1% Pacific Islander, 16.5% from other races, and 3.1% multiracial. Furthermore, Hispanic or Latino residents reached 37.4% in 2000, while non-Hispanic whites were 30.8%, a notable decline from 62.4% in 1970.

input: In the late 1980s, key breakthroughs in GaN epitaxial growth and p-type doping ushered in the modern era of GaN-based optoelectronic devices. Building upon this foundation, Dr. Moustakas at Boston University patented a method for producing high-brightness blue LEDs using a new two-step process. Two years later, in 1993, high-brightness blue LEDs were demonstrated again by Shuji Nakamura of Nichia Corporation using a gallium nitride growth process similar to Dr. Moustakas's. Both Dr. Moustakas and Mr. Nakamura were issued separate patents, which confused the issue of who was the original inventor (partly because although Dr. Moustakas invented his first, Dr. Nakamura filed first).[citation needed] This new development revolutionized LED lighting, making high-power blue light sources practical, leading to the development of technologies like BlueRay, as well as allowing the bright high resolution screens of modern tablets and phones.[citation needed]
rewrite: The late 1980s saw critical advances in growing gallium nitride layers and creating p-type material, which enabled the contemporary age of GaN light-emitting devices. Following this progress, Dr. Moustakas from Boston University received a patent for a novel two-stage technique to fabricate brilliant blue LEDs. Shortly thereafter in 1993, Shuji Nakamura at Nichia Corporation also successfully created high-brightness blue LEDs employing a comparable GaN fabrication method. Each inventor secured distinct patents, creating ambiguity over the true originator since Moustakas conceived his process earlier but Nakamura submitted his patent application first. This breakthrough transformed lighting by providing efficient, powerful blue emitters. It subsequently paved the way for innovations such as Blu-ray technology and facilitated the vibrant, detailed displays found in today's mobile phones and tablets.

input: Tennis player Marcos Baghdatis was ranked 8th in the world, was a finalist at the Australian Open, and reached the Wimbledon semi-final, all in 2006. High jumper Kyriakos Ioannou achieved a jump of 2.35 m at the 11th IAAF World Championships in Athletics in Osaka, Japan, in 2007, winning the bronze medal. He has been ranked third in the world. In motorsports, Tio Ellinas is a successful race car driver, currently racing in the GP3 Series for Marussia Manor Motorsport. There is also mixed martial artist Costas Philippou, who competes in the Ultimate Fighting Championship promotion's middleweight division. Costas holds a 6-3 record in UFC bouts, and recently defeated "The Monsoon" Lorenz Larkin with a Knockout in the 1st round.
rewrite: Marcos Baghdatis, a tennis professional, peaked at a world ranking of eighth in 2006, the same year he was the runner-up at the Australian Open and advanced to the semi-finals at Wimbledon. That same period saw high jumper Kyriakos Ioannou secure a bronze medal at the 2007 World Championships in Osaka by clearing 2.35 meters, earning him a global ranking of third. In auto racing, Tio Ellinas drives in the GP3 Series for Marussia Manor Motorsport. input: Most animals indirectly use the energy of sunlight by eating plants or plant-eating animals. Most plants use light to convert inorganic molecules in their environment into carbohydrates, fats, proteins and other biomolecules, characteristically containing reduced carbon in the form of carbon-hydrogen bonds. Starting with carbon dioxide (CO2) and water (H2O), photosynthesis converts the energy of sunlight into chemical energy in the form of simple sugars (e.g., glucose), with the release of molecular oxygen. These sugars are then used as the building blocks for plant growth, including the production of other biomolecules. When an animal eats plants (or eats other animals which have eaten plants), the reduced carbon compounds in the food become a source of energy and building materials for the animal. They are either used directly to help the animal grow, or broken down, releasing stored solar energy, and giving the animal the energy required for motion.
rewrite: Animals primarily obtain solar energy by consuming plants or other animals that have fed on plants. In contrast, plants directly harness light to transform inorganic substances into essential organic compounds like carbohydrates, fats, and proteins. These biomolecules are rich in reduced carbon, featuring carbon-hydrogen bonds. Through photosynthesis, plants utilize carbon dioxide and water, converting sunlight into chemical energy stored as simple sugars such as glucose, while releasing oxygen. These sugars form the foundation for plant development and the synthesis of other biological molecules. Upon consumption by animals, these carbon-based compounds serve as both an energy reserve and structural components. They are either assimilated directly for growth or metabolized to release the captured solar energy, powering the animal's movement and physiological functions.

input: Families throughout Han China made ritual sacrifices of animals and food to deities, spirits, and ancestors at temples and shrines, in the belief that these items could be utilized by those in the spiritual realm. It was thought that each person had a two-part soul: the spirit-soul (hun 魂) which journeyed to the afterlife paradise of immortals (xian), and the body-soul (po 魄) which remained in its grave or tomb on earth and was only reunited with the spirit-soul through a ritual ceremony. These tombs were commonly adorned with uniquely decorated hollow clay tiles that function also as a doorjamb to the tomb. Otherwise known as tomb tiles, these artifacts feature holes in the top and bottom of the tile allowing it to pivot. Similar tiles have been found in the Chengdu area of Sichuan province in south-central China.
rewrite: In Han-era China, households commonly offered animals and food in ceremonial rites to honor gods, spirits, and forebears at sacred sites. They believed these offerings could be accessed by beings in the spirit world. According to their beliefs, every individual possessed a dual soul: the hun, or spirit-soul, which traveled to an eternal paradise of immortals after death, and the po, or body-soul, which stayed within the earthly grave. Only a formal ritual could reunite these two aspects. Graves were often fitted with special hollow clay tiles, which served as both decorative elements and functional pivoting doorjambs. These objects, frequently called tomb tiles, include openings at their tops and bottoms to enable rotation. Comparable artifacts have been discovered in the Chengdu region of Sichuan in south-central China.

input: The first institute of madrasa education was at the estate of Hazrat Zaid bin Arkam near a hill called Safa, where Hazrat Muhammad was the teacher and the students were some of his followers.[citation needed] After Hijrah (migration) the madrasa of "Suffa" was established in Madina on the east side of the Al-Masjid an-Nabawi mosque. Hazrat 'Ubada bin Samit was appointed there by Hazrat Muhammad as teacher and among the students.[citation needed] In the curriculum of the madrasa, there were teachings of The Qur'an,The Hadith, fara'iz, tajweed, genealogy, treatises of first aid, etc. There were also trainings of horse-riding, art of war, handwriting and calligraphy, athletics and martial arts. The first part of madrasa based education is estimated from the first day of "nabuwwat" to the first portion of the "Umaiya" caliphate.[citation needed]
rewrite: The earliest madrasa was located on the property of Hazrat Zaid bin Arkam close to Safa hill, with Hazrat Muhammad instructing a group of his companions. Following the Hijrah, the "Suffa" madrasa was founded in Madina, adjacent to the Al-Masjid an-Nabawi's eastern wall. Hazrat Muhammad designated Hazrat 'Ubada bin Samit to serve as both educator and learner at this institution. The educational program encompassed subjects such as the Qur'an, Hadith, inheritance law, proper recitation, lineage studies, and basic medical care. Additionally, instruction was provided in military skills like horsemanship and combat, alongside penmanship, calligraphy, and various physical arts. This foundational period of formal Islamic schooling is generally considered to span from the beginning of prophethood through the early era of the Umayyad caliphate.

input: Though Brazilians of at least partial African heritage make up a large percentage of the population, few blacks have been elected as politicians. The city of Salvador, Bahia, for instance, is 80% people of color, but voters have not elected a mayor of color. Journalists like to say that US cities with black majorities, such as Detroit and New Orleans, have not elected white mayors since after the civil rights movement, when the Voting Rights Act of 1965 protected the franchise for minorities, and blacks in the South regained the power to vote for the first time since the turn of the 20th century. New Orleans elected its first black mayor in the 1970s. New Orleans elected a white mayor after the widescale disruption and damage of Hurricane Katrina in 2005.
rewrite: Despite a significant portion of Brazil's population having African ancestry, black individuals remain underrepresented in elected political offices. For example, Salvador, a city where 80% of residents are people of color, has never chosen a mayor from this demographic. Observers often contrast this with the United States, noting that majority-black cities like Detroit and New Orleans stopped electing white mayors following the civil rights era. This shift occurred after the 1965 Voting Rights Act secured electoral access for minorities, allowing Southern black communities to fully participate in elections again after decades of disenfranchisement. New Orleans selected its initial black mayor in the 1970s, but later elected a white mayor in the aftermath of Hurricane Katrina's devastation in 2005.

input: Gaddafi briefly studied History at the University of Libya in Benghazi, before dropping out to join the military. Despite his police record, in 1963 he began training at the Royal Military Academy, Benghazi, alongside several like-minded friends from Misrata. The armed forces offered the only opportunity for upward social mobility for underprivileged Libyans, and Gaddafi recognised it as a potential instrument of political change. Under Idris, Libya's armed forces were trained by the British military; this angered Gaddafi, who viewed the British as imperialists, and accordingly he refused to learn English and was rude to the British officers, ultimately failing his exams. British trainers reported him for insubordination and abusive behaviour, stating their suspicion that he was involved in the assassination of the military academy's commander in 1963. Such reports were ignored and Gaddafi quickly progressed through the course.
rewrite: Gaddafi initially pursued historical studies at the University of Libya in Benghazi but soon left to enlist in the army. Even with a prior police file, he entered the Royal Military Academy in Benghazi in 1963, training with a group of ideologically aligned companions from his hometown of Misrata. For many disadvantaged Libyans, the military represented the sole path to improving their social standing, and Gaddafi saw it as a viable means to drive political reform. Libya's military was then under British instruction during King Idris's rule, which Gaddafi resented due to his anti-imperialist stance against Britain. He deliberately avoided learning English and was hostile toward the British trainers, resulting in his examination failures. These officers accused him of disrespect and misconduct, even suggesting he might have been connected to the 1963 killing of the academy's leader. Their complaints were disregarded, however, and Gaddafi advanced swiftly through the program.

input: Most of the enlargement of the primate brain comes from a massive expansion of the cerebral cortex, especially the prefrontal cortex and the parts of the cortex involved in vision. The visual processing network of primates includes at least 30 distinguishable brain areas, with a complex web of interconnections. It has been estimated that visual processing areas occupy more than half of the total surface of the primate neocortex. The prefrontal cortex carries out functions that include planning, working memory, motivation, attention, and executive control. It takes up a much larger proportion of the brain for primates than for other species, and an especially large fraction of the human brain.
rewrite: The primate brain's growth is primarily due to a significant increase in the cerebral cortex, notably in the prefrontal and visual regions. Primate vision involves a network of over 30 distinct cortical areas, densely interconnected. These visual zones are thought to cover over 50% of the neocortex's total area. The prefrontal cortex manages tasks such as planning, attention, motivation, and executive function. It constitutes a substantially larger portion of the brain in primates compared to other animals, and is particularly expansive in humans.

input: Shortly after the unification of the region, the Western Jin dynasty collapsed. First the rebellions by eight Jin princes for the throne and later rebellions and invasion from Xiongnu and other nomadic peoples that destroyed the rule of the Jin dynasty in the north. In 317, remnants of the Jin court, as well as nobles and wealthy families, fled from the north to the south and reestablished the Jin court in Nanjing, which was then called Jiankang (建康), replacing Luoyang. It's the first time that the capital of the nation moved to southern part.
rewrite: Following the brief unification of the region, the Western Jin dynasty fell. This collapse was triggered by internal wars among royal princes and subsequent uprisings and incursions from northern nomadic groups, which ended Jin rule in the north. In 317, surviving members of the imperial family and elite households retreated southward. They re-founded the dynasty with a new capital at Jiankang, modern Nanjing, marking the nation’s first shift of its central seat of power to the south.

input: The experience of pain has many cultural dimensions. For instance, the way in which one experiences and responds to pain is related to sociocultural characteristics, such as gender, ethnicity, and age. An aging adult may not respond to pain in the way that a younger person would. Their ability to recognize pain may be blunted by illness or the use of multiple prescription drugs. Depression may also keep the older adult from reporting they are in pain. The older adult may also quit doing activities they love because it hurts too much. Decline in self-care activities (dressing, grooming, walking, etc.) may also be indicators that the older adult is experiencing pain. The older adult may refrain from reporting pain because they are afraid they will have to have surgery or will be put on a drug they might become addicted to. They may not want others to see them as weak, or may feel there is something impolite or shameful in complaining about pain, or they may feel the pain is deserved punishment for past transgressions.
rewrite: Pain is understood and expressed through a cultural lens. Factors like gender, ethnic background, and age shape how an individual both feels and communicates discomfort. An elderly person’s reaction to pain often differs from a younger individual’s. Illness or the side effects of various medications can dull their perception of discomfort. Depression might further prevent an older adult from acknowledging they are hurting. They may abandon cherished activities due to the severity of pain, and a noticeable reduction in daily routines—such as dressing or walking—can signal its presence. Often, seniors avoid mentioning pain due to fears of requiring surgery or developing a dependence on medication. Concerns about appearing frail, beliefs that complaining is improper, or feelings that the suffering is a justified penance for earlier mistakes can also lead to silence.

input: Valencia is also internationally famous for its football club, Valencia C.F., which won the Spanish league in 2002 and 2004 (the year it also won the UEFA Cup), for a total of six times, and was a UEFA Champions League runner-up in 2000 and 2001. The team's stadium is the Mestalla; its city rival Levante UD also plays in the highest division after gaining promotion in 2010, their stadium is Estadi Ciutat de València. From the year 2011 there has been a third team in the city, Huracán Valencia, who play their games in Municipal de Manises, in the Segunda División B.
rewrite: The city of Valencia is globally recognized for its prominent football team, Valencia C.F. This club has secured the national championship on six occasions, including victories in 2002 and 2004—the latter year also saw them win the UEFA Cup. They were also finalists in the UEFA Champions League in 2000 and 2001. Their home ground is Mestalla. A local rival, Levante UD, has competed in the top tier since earning promotion in 2010, playing at Estadi Ciutat de València. Since 2011, a third club, Huracán Valencia, has been based in the city, participating in Segunda División B at the Municipal de Manises stadium.

input: In his 1805 mandolin method, Anweisung die Mandoline von selbst zu erlernen nebst einigen Uebungsstucken von Bortolazzi, Bartolomeo Bortolazzi popularised the Cremonese mandolin, which had four single-strings and a fixed bridge, to which the strings were attached. Bortolazzi said in this book that the new wire strung mandolins were uncomfortable to play, when compared with the gut-string instruments. Also, he felt they had a "less pleasing...hard, zither-like tone" as compared to the gut string's "softer, full-singing tone." He favored the four single strings of the Cremonese instrument, which were tuned the same as the Neapolitan.
rewrite: In his 1805 instructional book for the mandolin, Bartolomeo Bortolazzi advocated for the Cremonese version of the instrument. This design featured four individual strings and a stationary bridge for attaching them. Bortolazzi expressed a clear preference for these gut-string mandolins, criticizing newer models strung with wire. He found the wire instruments harder to play and described their sound as harsh and reminiscent of a zither, lacking the softer, more resonant singing quality produced by gut strings. The Cremonese mandolin's tuning matched that of the Neapolitan type.

input: 155th Street starts on the West Side at Riverside Drive, crossing Broadway, Amsterdam Avenue and St. Nicholas Avenue. At St. Nicholas Place, the terrain drops off steeply, and 155th Street is carried on a 1,600-foot (490 m) long viaduct, a City Landmark constructed in 1893, that slopes down towards the Harlem River, continuing onto the Macombs Dam Bridge, crossing over (but not intersecting with) the Harlem River Drive. A separate, unconnected section of 155th Street runs under the viaduct, connecting Bradhurst Avenue and the Harlem River Drive.
rewrite: Beginning at Riverside Drive on the West Side, 155th Street extends across Broadway, Amsterdam Avenue, and St. Nicholas Avenue. Near St. Nicholas Place, the land declines sharply, requiring a sloping viaduct built in 1893. This 1,600-foot landmark structure descends toward the Harlem River and leads onto the Macombs Dam Bridge, passing above the Harlem River Drive. Below this elevated section, a separate segment of the street links Bradhurst Avenue with the Harlem River Drive.

input: Thousands of fonts exist on the market, but fewer than a dozen fonts—sometimes described as "pan-Unicode" fonts—attempt to support the majority of Unicode's character repertoire. Instead, Unicode-based fonts typically focus on supporting only basic ASCII and particular scripts or sets of characters or symbols. Several reasons justify this approach: applications and documents rarely need to render characters from more than one or two writing systems; fonts tend to demand resources in computing environments; and operating systems and applications show increasing intelligence in regard to obtaining glyph information from separate font files as needed, i.e., font substitution. Furthermore, designing a consistent set of rendering instructions for tens of thousands of glyphs constitutes a monumental task; such a venture passes the point of diminishing returns for most typefaces.
rewrite: While the market offers a vast array of typefaces, only a small number—often called "pan-Unicode" fonts—aim to cover most of Unicode's characters. Commonly, fonts built on Unicode concentrate on including just standard ASCII along with specific alphabets or symbol collections. This focused strategy is sensible for multiple causes: most software and files seldom require displaying text from numerous writing systems simultaneously; fonts consume memory and processing power; and modern systems and programs are increasingly adept at pulling necessary character shapes from different font files when required. Additionally, crafting a harmonious visual style and technical instructions for countless glyphs is an enormous undertaking, making it an impractical investment for the majority of font designs.

input: As of the first decade of the 21st century, contemporary neoclassical architecture is usually classed under the umbrella term of New Classical Architecture. Sometimes it is also referred to as Neo-Historicism/Revivalism, Traditionalism or simply neoclassical architecture like the historical style. For sincere traditional-style architecture that sticks to regional architecture, materials and craftsmanship, the term Traditional Architecture (or vernacular) is mostly used. The Driehaus Architecture Prize is awarded to major contributors in the field of 21st century traditional or classical architecture, and comes with a prize money twice as high as that of the modernist Pritzker Prize.
rewrite: In the early 2000s, modern neoclassical building design is often categorized as New Classical Architecture. Alternative labels include Neo-Historicism, Revivalism, or just neoclassical. The designation Traditional or vernacular architecture is generally reserved for authentic designs that faithfully employ local building methods, materials, and artisanal skill. A significant award in this domain is the Driehaus Architecture Prize, granted to leading figures in today's classical or traditional practice. Its monetary award is double the value of the modernist Pritzker Prize.

input: With Egypt and Macedonia weakened, the Seleucid Empire made increasingly aggressive and successful attempts to conquer the entire Greek world. Now not only Rome's allies against Philip, but even Philip himself, sought a Roman alliance against the Seleucids. The situation was made worse by the fact that Hannibal was now a chief military advisor to the Seleucid emperor, and the two were believed to be planning an outright conquest not just of Greece, but of Rome itself. The Seleucids were much stronger than the Macedonians had ever been, because they controlled much of the former Persian Empire, and by now had almost entirely reassembled Alexander the Great's former empire.
rewrite: As the power of Egypt and Macedonia declined, the Seleucid Empire pursued ever more forceful and effective campaigns to dominate Greece. This prompted both Rome's former allies in the conflict with Philip and Philip personally to seek Rome's support against the Seleucid threat. Compounding the crisis, Hannibal had become a leading military strategist for the Seleucid ruler, and they were suspected of plotting to invade not only Greece but Rome as well. The Seleucids possessed greater strength than Macedonia ever had, commanding large portions of the old Persian Empire and having nearly restored Alexander the Great's original domain.

input: One problem with these assignments is admixture. Many people have a highly varied ancestry. For example, in the United States, colonial and early federal history were periods of numerous interracial relationships, both outside and inside slavery. This has resulted in a majority of people who identify as African American having some European ancestors. Similarly, many people who identify as white have some African ancestors. In a survey in a northeastern U.S. university of college students who identified as "white", about 30% were estimated to have up to 10% African ancestry.
rewrite: A challenge in such categorizations stems from mixed heritage, as individuals often have diverse ancestral backgrounds. Historically, in the United States, the colonial and early national eras involved many interracial unions, within and outside the institution of slavery. Consequently, most self-identified African Americans possess European forebears, while many who consider themselves white have African ancestry. For instance, a study at a university in the Northeast found roughly 30% of students labeling themselves as "white" carried up to 10% African genetic lineage.

input: American Idol is broadcast to over 100 nations outside of the United States. In most nations these are not live broadcasts and may be tape delayed by several days or weeks. In Canada, the first thirteen seasons of American Idol were aired live by CTV and/or CTV Two, in simulcast with Fox. CTV dropped Idol after its thirteenth season and in August 2014, Yes TV announced that it had picked up Canadian rights to American Idol beginning in its 2015 season.
rewrite: The television show American Idol reaches an international audience, airing in more than 100 countries beyond the U.S. Typically, these international showings are not live and can be delayed by days or weeks. In Canada, CTV networks broadcast the first thirteen seasons simultaneously with Fox. Following that, CTV discontinued the program, and Yes TV later acquired the Canadian broadcast rights starting with the 2015 season.

input: Schwarzenegger signed another executive order on October 17, 2006 allowing California to work with the Northeast's Regional Greenhouse Gas Initiative. They plan to reduce carbon dioxide emissions by issuing a limited amount of carbon credits to each power plant in participating states. Any power plants that exceed emissions for the amount of carbon credits will have to purchase more credits to cover the difference. The plan took effect in 2009. In addition to using his political power to fight global warming, the governor has taken steps at his home to reduce his personal carbon footprint. Schwarzenegger has adapted one of his Hummers to run on hydrogen and another to run on biofuels. He has also installed solar panels to heat his home.
rewrite: On October 17, 2006, Governor Schwarzenegger issued a further directive enabling California to collaborate with the Northeastern Regional Greenhouse Gas Initiative. This strategy involves capping total emissions by distributing a set number of allowances to electricity generators in member states. Facilities that produce more carbon dioxide than their permits allow must buy additional credits to offset the excess. The program launched in 2009. Beyond these policy efforts to combat climate change, Schwarzenegger has made personal modifications to lessen his environmental impact. He converted one of his Hummer vehicles to operate using hydrogen fuel and another to use biofuels, and he has added solar panels to provide power for his residence.

input: In 1949, the city was chosen to be the seat of the Council of Europe with its European Court of Human Rights and European Pharmacopoeia. Since 1952, the European Parliament has met in Strasbourg, which was formally designated its official 'seat' at the Edinburgh meeting of the European Council of EU heads of state and government in December 1992. (This position was reconfirmed and given treaty status in the 1997 Treaty of Amsterdam). However, only the (four-day) plenary sessions of the Parliament are held in Strasbourg each month, with all other business being conducted in Brussels and Luxembourg. Those sessions take place in the Immeuble Louise Weiss, inaugurated in 1999, which houses the largest parliamentary assembly room in Europe and of any democratic institution in the world. Before that, the EP sessions had to take place in the main Council of Europe building, the Palace of Europe, whose unusual inner architecture had become a familiar sight to European TV audiences. In 1992, Strasbourg became the seat of the Franco-German TV channel and movie-production society Arte.
rewrite: In 1949, Strasbourg was selected as the location for the Council of Europe, including its associated institutions like the European Court of Human Rights and the European Pharmacopoeia. Starting in 1952, the European Parliament began convening in the city, and its status as the Parliament's official home was formally established during a European Council summit in Edinburgh in late 1992. This designation was later solidified under the Treaty of Amsterdam in 1997. Nonetheless, Strasbourg hosts only the Parliament's monthly plenary sessions, which last four days; all additional parliamentary activities occur in Brussels and Luxembourg. These plenary meetings are held in the Immeuble Louise Weiss, completed in 1999, which contains the biggest parliamentary chamber in Europe and globally among democratic bodies. Previously, parliamentary sessions occurred in the Palace of Europe, the main building of the Council of Europe, whose distinctive interior was widely recognized from television broadcasts. Additionally, 1992 saw Strasbourg become the base for the Franco-German television network and film producer Arte.

input: Parisian examples of European architecture date back more than a millennium; including the Romanesque church of the Abbey of Saint-Germain-des-Prés (1014-1163); the early Gothic Architecture of the Basilica of Saint-Denis (1144), the Notre Dame Cathedral (1163-1345), the Flamboyant Gothic of Saint Chapelle (1239-1248), the Baroque churches of Saint-Paul-Saint-Louis (1627-1641) and Les Invalides (1670-1708). The 19th century produced the neoclassical church of La Madeleine (1808-1842); the Palais Garnier Opera House (1875); the neo-Byzantine Basilica of Sacré-Cœur (1875-1919), and the exuberant Belle Époque modernism of the Eiffel Tower (1889). Striking examples of 20th century architecture include the Centre Georges Pompidou by Richard Rogers and Renzo Piano (1977), and the Louvre Pyramid by I.M. Pei (1989). Contemporary architecture includes the Musée du Quai Branly by Jean Nouvel (2006) and the new contemporary art museum of the Louis Vuitton Foundation by Frank Gehry (2014).
rewrite: Paris showcases over a thousand years of European architectural evolution. Early structures range from the Romanesque Abbey of Saint-Germain-des-Prés, begun in 1014, to Gothic landmarks like Saint-Denis Basilica and Notre-Dame. Later centuries introduced the Flamboyant Gothic of Sainte-Chapelle, Baroque designs such as Les Invalides, and 19th-century works like the neoclassical La Madeleine and the iconic Eiffel Tower. The twentieth century brought bold modern statements, including the Centre Pompidou's high-tech exterior and I.M. Pei's glass pyramid at the Louvre. Recent additions, like Jean Nouvel's Musée du Quai Branly and Frank Gehry's sculptural Louis Vuitton Foundation, continue this legacy of innovative design.

input: EU member countries have shown support for ambitious renewable energy goals. In 2010, Eurobarometer polled the twenty-seven EU member states about the target "to increase the share of renewable energy in the EU by 20 percent by 2020". Most people in all twenty-seven countries either approved of the target or called for it to go further. Across the EU, 57 percent thought the proposed goal was "about right" and 16 percent thought it was "too modest." In comparison, 19 percent said it was "too ambitious".
rewrite: Nations within the European Union have endorsed strong objectives for expanding renewable energy. A 2010 survey across the EU's 27 members asked about a 20% renewables target for 2020. A majority of citizens in every country supported or wanted an even higher goal. Overall, 57% considered the aim appropriate, while 16% viewed it as insufficient. Only 19% believed the proposed target was overly ambitious.

input: According to statute, Qing society was divided into relatively closed estates, of which in most general terms there were five. Apart from the estates of the officials, the comparatively minuscule aristocracy, and the degree-holding literati, there also existed a major division among ordinary Chinese between commoners and people with inferior status. They were divided into two categories: one of them, the good "commoner" people, the other "mean" people. The majority of the population belonged to the first category and were described as liangmin, a legal term meaning good people, as opposed to jianmin meaning the mean (or ignoble) people. Qing law explicitly stated that the traditional four occupational groups of scholars, farmers, artisans and merchants were "good", or having a status of commoners. On the other hand, slaves or bondservants, entertainers (including prostitutes and actors), and those low-level employees of government officials were the "mean people". Mean people were considered legally inferior to commoners and suffered unequal treatments, forbidden to take the imperial examination.
rewrite: Under legal provisions, Qing dynasty social structure was organized into largely separate hereditary classes, broadly categorized into five groups. Beyond the small ruling elite of nobles and bureaucrats, as well as educated individuals who held academic degrees, a fundamental distinction separated the general populace into ordinary citizens and those deemed of lower standing. This division created two primary classifications: the "good" commoners and the so-called "base" people. Most individuals fell into the first group, identified in legal terminology as *liangmin* (good people), in contrast to *jianmin* (mean or ignoble people). The law specifically recognized the classic four professions—scholars, peasants, craftsmen, and traders—as "good," granting them commoner status. Conversely, enslaved individuals, indentured servants, performers such as actors and prostitutes, and minor functionaries serving officials were classified as "mean people." This group held a subordinate legal position compared to commoners, facing systemic discrimination, including exclusion from the state civil service examinations.

input: A collector of film memorabilia, Spielberg purchased a balsa Rosebud sled from Citizen Kane (1941) in 1982. He bought Orson Welles's own directorial copy of the script for the radio broadcast The War of the Worlds (1938) in 1994. Spielberg has purchased Academy Award statuettes being sold on the open market and donated them to the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences, to prevent their further commercial exploitation. His donations include the Oscars that Bette Davis received for Dangerous (1935) and Jezebel (1938), and Clark Gable's Oscar for It Happened One Night (1934).
rewrite: As a film memorabilia enthusiast, Steven Spielberg acquired a Rosebud sled prop from the 1941 movie Citizen Kane in 1982. Later, in 1994, he obtained Orson Welles's personal script for the 1938 radio drama The War of the Worlds. To stop their commercial sale, he has also bought Oscar statuettes from the open market and given them to the Academy. Among these are awards originally presented to Bette Davis for her roles in Dangerous and Jezebel, and to Clark Gable for It Happened One Night.

input: In 1996, Comcast bought a controlling stake in Spectacor from the company's founder, Ed Snider. Comcast-Spectacor holdings now include the Philadelphia Flyers NHL hockey team, the Philadelphia 76ers National Basketball Association basketball team and two large multipurpose arenas in Philadelphia. Over a number of years, Comcast became majority owner of Comcast SportsNet, as well as Golf Channel and NBCSN (formerly the Outdoor Life Network, then Versus). In 2002, Comcast paid the University of Maryland $25 million for naming rights to the new basketball arena built on the College Park campus, the XFINITY Center. Before it was renamed for Comcast's cable subsidiary, XFINITY Center was called Comcast Center from its opening in 2002 through July 2014.
rewrite: In 1996, Comcast acquired a majority interest in Spectacor from its founder, Ed Snider. The combined entity, Comcast-Spectacor, possesses the Philadelphia Flyers NHL franchise, the Philadelphia 76ers NBA team, and two major Philadelphia venues. Gradually, Comcast also gained controlling stakes in Comcast SportsNet, the Golf Channel, and NBCSN, which was previously known as the Outdoor Life Network and later Versus. A 2002 agreement saw Comcast pay $25 million to the University of Maryland for the naming rights to its new campus basketball arena. Initially named the Comcast Center upon its 2002 opening, the facility was rebranded as the XFINITY Center in 2014 after Comcast's cable service.

input: Tourist hotspots in Portugal are Lisbon, Algarve, Madeira, Porto and the city of Coimbra, also, between 4-5 million religious pilgrims visit Fátima each year, where apparitions of the Blessed Virgin Mary to three shepherd children reportedly took place in 1917. The Sanctuary of Fátima is one of the largest Roman Catholic shrines in the world. The Portuguese government continues to promote and develop new tourist destinations, such as the Douro Valley, the island of Porto Santo, and Alentejo. Lisbon is the 16th European city which attracts the most tourists (with seven million tourists occupying the city's hotels in 2006, a number that grew 11.8% compared to previous year). Lisbon in recent years surpassed the Algarve as the leading tourist region in Portugal. Porto and Northern Portugal, especially the urban areas north of Douro River valley, was the tourist destination which grew most (11.9%) in 2006, surpassing Madeira (in 2010), as the third most visited destination.[citation needed]
rewrite: Portugal's most frequented travel locations include Lisbon, the Algarve, Madeira, Porto, and Coimbra. Additionally, Fátima draws roughly four to five million religious visitors annually, a site linked to reported 1917 visions of the Virgin Mary witnessed by three young shepherds. Its Sanctuary ranks among the globe's biggest Catholic pilgrimage sites. Efforts to diversify tourism focus on emerging areas like the Douro Valley, Porto Santo island, and Alentejo. Lisbon, now the country's top visitor region, ranks sixteenth in Europe for tourist appeal; its hotels hosted seven million guests in 2006, an 11.8% annual increase. The northern region around Porto experienced the highest growth that year at 11.9%, later overtaking Madeira to become the third most popular destination by 2010.

input: A novelty shop called Au Bon Marché had been founded in Paris in 1838 to sell lace, ribbons, sheets, mattresses, buttons, umbrellas and other assorted goods. It originally had four departments, twelve employees, and a floor space of three hundred meters. The entrepreneur Aristide Boucicaut became a partner in 1852, and changed the marketing plan, instituting fixed prices and guarantees that allowed exchanges and refunds, advertising, and a much wider variety of merchandise. The annual income of the store increased from 500,000 francs in 1852 to five million in 1860. In 1869 he built much larger building at 24 rue de Sèvres on the Left Bank, and enlarged the store again in 1872, with help from the engineering firm of Gustave Eiffel, creator of the Eiffel Tower. The income rose from twenty million francs in 1870 to 72 million at the time of the Boucicaut's death in 1877. The floor space had increased from three hundred square meters in 1838 to fifty thousand, and the number of employees had increased from twelve in 1838 to 1788 in 1879. Boucicaut was famous for his marketing innovations; a reading room for husbands while their wives shopped; extensive newspaper advertising; entertainment for children; and six million catalogs sent out to customers. By 1880 half the employees were women; unmarried women employees lived in dormitories on the upper floors.
rewrite:
In 1838, a Parisian store named Au Bon Marché opened, offering an array of items such as linens, haberdashery, and various household articles. Initially, it occupied a modest three-hundred-square-meter area, with just four sections and a dozen staff. In 1852, businessman Aristide Boucicaut joined as a partner and revolutionized its operations. He introduced set pricing, a policy ensuring returns and refunds, aggressive promotion, and a greatly expanded inventory. These changes propelled the shop’s yearly revenue from 500,000 francs in 1852 to five million by 1860.

A new, larger structure was erected at 24 rue de Sèvres on the Left Bank in 1869. With assistance from Gustave Eiffel’s engineering company, the store was further expanded in 1872. Earnings climbed dramatically, from twenty million francs in 1870 to seventy-two million upon Boucicaut’s passing in 1877. From its humble beginnings, the retail space grew to encompass fifty thousand square meters by 1879, and the workforce surged from the original twelve to 1,788.

Boucicaut pioneered numerous retail concepts: a lounge for waiting husbands, substantial advertising in periodicals, amusements for children, and the distribution of six million product catalogs. By 1880, women constituted half of all employees, with single female staff residing in dormitories located on the upper levels of the building.

input: In 1979, the committees began the redistribution of land in the Jefara plain, continuing through 1981. In May 1980, measures to redistribute and equalize wealth were implemented; anyone with over 1000 dinar in his bank account saw that extra money expropriated. The following year, the GPC announced that the government would take control of all import, export and distribution functions, with state supermarkets replacing privately owned businesses; this led to a decline in the availability of consumer goods and the development of a thriving black market.
rewrite: Starting in 1979 and lasting until 1981, authorities reallocated land in the Jefara plain. By May 1980, wealth equalization policies confiscated any bank savings exceeding 1000 dinars. In 1981, the GPC declared a state monopoly over all import, export, and distribution activities, substituting private shops with government-run stores. Consequently, consumer products became scarce, fueling the rapid growth of an underground market.

input: The Kakatiya dynasty was reduced to a vassal of the Khilji dynasty in 1310 after its defeat by Sultan Alauddin Khilji of the Delhi Sultanate. This lasted until 1321, when the Kakatiya dynasty was annexed by Malik Kafur, Allaudin Khilji's general. During this period, Alauddin Khilji took the Koh-i-Noor diamond, which is said to have been mined from the Kollur Mines of Golkonda, to Delhi. Muhammad bin Tughluq succeeded to the Delhi sultanate in 1325, bringing Warangal under the rule of the Tughlaq dynasty until 1347 when Ala-ud-Din Bahman Shah, a governor under bin Tughluq, rebelled against Delhi and established the Bahmani Sultanate in the Deccan Plateau, with Gulbarga, 200 km (124 mi) west of Hyderabad, as its capital. The Bahmani kings ruled the region until 1518 and were the first independent Muslim rulers of the Deccan.
rewrite: Following its loss to Sultan Alauddin Khilji of the Delhi Sultanate in 1310, the Kakatiya dynasty became subordinate to the Khiljis. This vassal status persisted until 1321, when Malik Kafur, a general serving Alauddin, fully absorbed the kingdom. It was during Khilji's dominance that the famed Koh-i-Noor diamond, reportedly originating from the Kollur Mines in Golkonda, was transported to Delhi. After Muhammad bin Tughluq ascended to power in 1325, Warangal fell under Tughlaq control. This lasted until 1347, when a provincial governor named Ala-ud-Din Bahman Shah revolted. He founded the Bahmani Sultanate on the Deccan Plateau, establishing its capital at Gulbarga, located approximately 200 kilometers west of Hyderabad. The Bahmani dynasty governed as the Deccan's inaugural sovereign Muslim rulers until 1518.

input: The earliest evidence of human inhabitants of modern day Chihuahua was discovered in the area of Samalayuca and Rancho Colorado. Clovis points have been found in northeastern Chihuahua that have been dated from 12,000 BC to 7000 BC. It is thought that these inhabitants were hunter gatherers. Inhabitants of the state later developed farming with the domestication of corn. An archeological site in northern Chihuahua known as Cerro Juanaqueña revealed squash cultivation, irrigation techniques, and ceramic artifacts dating to around 2000 BC.
rewrite: The first signs of people living in what is now Chihuahua come from the Samalayuca and Rancho Colorado regions. Discovered Clovis points in the northeast date from 12,000 to 7000 BC, indicating early hunter-gatherer societies. Over time, residents began farming, starting with the cultivation of corn. Excavations at Cerro Juanaqueña in the north show evidence of growing squash, early irrigation systems, and pottery from approximately 2000 BC.

input: Industries slowly brought the city and its inhabitants back to a renewed vitality and jobs attracted new residents. As the city's commerce improved, residents worked to restore or create community institutions. In 1865, the Avery Normal Institute was established by the American Missionary Association as the first free secondary school for Charleston's African American population. General William T. Sherman lent his support to the conversion of the United States Arsenal into the Porter Military Academy, an educational facility for former soldiers and boys left orphaned or destitute by the war. Porter Military Academy later joined with Gaud School and is now a university-preparatory school, Porter-Gaud School.
rewrite: The city gradually regained its energy as businesses provided employment and drew newcomers. With economic conditions improving, people focused on rebuilding civic foundations. In 1865, the Avery Normal Institute was founded by the American Missionary Association, offering Charleston's Black community its inaugural tuition-free high school. General William T. Sherman endorsed repurposing the U.S. Arsenal into the Porter Military Academy, which educated war veterans and boys impoverished or orphaned by the conflict. This academy eventually merged with Gaud School to form the college-preparatory institution known today as Porter-Gaud School.

input: Melbourne is often referred to as Australia's garden city, and the state of Victoria was once known as the garden state. There is an abundance of parks and gardens in Melbourne, many close to the CBD with a variety of common and rare plant species amid landscaped vistas, pedestrian pathways and tree-lined avenues. Melbourne's parks are often considered the best public parks in all of Australia's major cities. There are also many parks in the surrounding suburbs of Melbourne, such as in the municipalities of Stonnington, Boroondara and Port Phillip, south east of the central business district. The extensive area covered by urban Melbourne is formally divided into hundreds of suburbs (for addressing and postal purposes), and administered as local government areas 31 of which are located within the metropolitan area.
rewrite: Frequently called Australia's garden city, Melbourne is part of a state, Victoria, that historically held the title of garden state. The city boasts numerous parks and gardens, featuring a rich mix of both ordinary and exotic flora, along with designed landscapes, walking trails, and streets shaded by trees. Many of these green spaces lie near the central business district and are widely regarded as the finest public parks in any major Australian city. Additionally, the outer suburbs, including areas like Stonnington, Boroondara, and Port Phillip to the southeast, contain many parks. The broader urban region is officially split into hundreds of suburbs for mail and addressing, managed through local government authorities; thirty-one of these fall within the metropolitan zone.

input: In the case of the United States where a one-hour shift occurs at 02:00 local time, in spring the clock jumps forward from the last moment of 01:59 standard time to 03:00 DST and that day has 23 hours, whereas in autumn the clock jumps backward from the last moment of 01:59 DST to 01:00 standard time, repeating that hour, and that day has 25 hours. A digital display of local time does not read 02:00 exactly at the shift to summer time, but instead jumps from 01:59:59.9 forward to 03:00:00.0.
rewrite: In the United States, daylight saving time transitions happen at 2:00 AM. During the spring shift, clocks advance directly to 3:00 AM, shortening that day to 23 hours. Conversely, in the fall, they move back to 1:00 AM, causing that hour to repeat and extending the day to 25 hours. Consequently, a digital clock switching to summer time will never display 2:00 AM; it instantly changes from 1:59:59.9 to 3:00:00.0.

input: Several certification programs exist to support the professional aspirations of software testers and quality assurance specialists. No certification now offered actually requires the applicant to show their ability to test software. No certification is based on a widely accepted body of knowledge. This has led some to declare that the testing field is not ready for certification. Certification itself cannot measure an individual's productivity, their skill, or practical knowledge, and cannot guarantee their competence, or professionalism as a tester.
rewrite: Numerous credentials are available for software testing and QA professionals, yet none demand proof of practical testing skills or rely on a common knowledge standard. Consequently, some argue the field isn't prepared for certification. These credentials cannot assess a person's productivity, ability, hands-on expertise, or ensure their competence and professional standing as a tester.

input: Lighting or illumination is the deliberate use of light to achieve a practical or aesthetic effect. Lighting includes the use of both artificial light sources like lamps and light fixtures, as well as natural illumination by capturing daylight. Daylighting (using windows, skylights, or light shelves) is sometimes used as the main source of light during daytime in buildings. This can save energy in place of using artificial lighting, which represents a major component of energy consumption in buildings. Proper lighting can enhance task performance, improve the appearance of an area, or have positive psychological effects on occupants.
rewrite: Illumination involves the intentional application of light for functional or decorative purposes. It employs man-made sources such as lamps and fixtures, alongside natural light harnessed through windows or skylights. Utilizing daylight as a primary source in daytime structures can reduce energy use, since artificial lighting constitutes a significant part of a building's energy demands. Effective lighting boosts productivity in tasks, beautifies spaces, and can positively influence the mood of those within.

input: The Ministry of Foreign Affairs of the Republic of Greece conducts "bilateral relationships" with the countries of the "Mediterranean – Middle East Region" but has formulated no Near East Region. The Ministry of Foreign Affairs of the Republic of Turkey also does not use the term Near East. Its regions include the Middle East, the Balkans and others.
rewrite: Greece's foreign ministry manages diplomatic ties with Mediterranean and Middle Eastern nations, but does not formally recognize a "Near East" region. Similarly, Turkey's foreign affairs department avoids this term, organizing its work around areas like the Middle East and the Balkans instead.

input: The original Cubist architecture is very rare. There is only one country in the world where Cubism was really applied to architecture – namely Bohemia (today Czech Republic) and especially its capital, Prague. Czech architects were the first and only ones in the world to ever design original Cubist buildings. Cubist architecture flourished for the most part between 1910–1914, but the Cubist or Cubism-influenced buildings were also built after the World War I. After the war, the architectural style called Rondo-Cubism was developed in Prague fusing the Cubist architecture with round shapes.
rewrite: Authentic Cubist architecture is exceptionally uncommon, with Bohemia—now the Czech Republic—being the sole region where it was genuinely implemented in building design. Prague, its capital, holds particular significance. Czech architects uniquely pioneered original Cubist structures, primarily from 1910 to 1914. Construction of Cubist or Cubist-inspired edifices continued after World War I, leading to the emergence of Rondo-Cubism in Prague, which blended Cubist forms with circular elements.

input: Advertising is common in healthcare journals as well as through more mainstream media routes. In some countries, notably the US, they are allowed to advertise directly to the general public. Pharmaceutical companies generally employ sales people (often called 'drug reps' or, an older term, 'detail men') to market directly and personally to physicians and other healthcare providers. In some countries, notably the US, pharmaceutical companies also employ lobbyists to influence politicians. Marketing of prescription drugs in the US is regulated by the federal Prescription Drug Marketing Act of 1987.
rewrite: Healthcare journals and popular media both feature advertisements for medical products. In places like the United States, these promotions can target consumers directly. Companies typically use sales representatives, known as drug reps, to personally engage with doctors and clinicians. Additionally, in nations such as the U.S., the industry hires lobbyists to sway political figures. The promotion of prescription medications is governed by federal law, specifically the Prescription Drug Marketing Act established in 1987.

input: The loss of viewers continued into season seven. The premiere was down 11% among total viewers, and the results show in which Kristy Lee Cook was eliminated delivered its lowest-rated Wednesday show among the 18–34 demo since the first season in 2002. However, the ratings rebounded for the season seven finale with the excitement over the battle of the Davids, and improved over season six as the series' third most watched finale. The strong finish of season seven also helped Fox become the most watched TV network in the country for the first time since its inception, a first ever in American television history for a non-Big Three major broadcast network. Overall ratings for the season were down 10% from season six, which is in line with the fall in viewership across all networks due in part to the 2007–2008 Writers Guild of America strike.
rewrite: Season seven saw a further decline in audience numbers. The opening episode experienced an 11% drop in total viewership, and the episode featuring Kristy Lee Cook's elimination recorded the series' lowest Wednesday rating in the 18–34 age group since its 2002 debut. Despite this, the finale's ratings recovered significantly, fueled by the anticipated showdown between the two finalists named David. It became the third most-viewed finale for the series, outperforming the previous season's conclusion. This strong ending propelled Fox to become the nation's top-rated network for the first time in its history, marking an unprecedented achievement for a network outside the traditional major three. The season's overall ratings fell by 10% compared to season six, a trend consistent with broader industry declines partly attributed to the writers' strike during that period.

input: The standard connectors were designed to be robust. Because USB is hot-pluggable, the connectors would be used more frequently, and perhaps with less care, than other connectors. Many previous connector designs were fragile, specifying embedded component pins or other delicate parts that were vulnerable to bending or breaking. The electrical contacts in a USB connector are protected by an adjacent plastic tongue, and the entire connecting assembly is usually protected by an enclosing metal sheath.
rewrite: USB connectors were built to be durable, anticipating frequent and sometimes rough handling due to their hot-swap capability. Earlier designs often had fragile, exposed pins that could easily bend or snap. In contrast, USB features electrical contacts shielded by a plastic insert, with the whole connector further safeguarded by an outer metal shell.

input: Under ordinary conditions on Earth, elemental hydrogen exists as the diatomic gas, H2. However, hydrogen gas is very rare in the Earth's atmosphere (1 ppm by volume) because of its light weight, which enables it to escape from Earth's gravity more easily than heavier gases. However, hydrogen is the third most abundant element on the Earth's surface, mostly in the form of chemical compounds such as hydrocarbons and water. Hydrogen gas is produced by some bacteria and algae and is a natural component of flatus, as is methane, itself a hydrogen source of increasing importance.
rewrite: On our planet, hydrogen is typically found as a two-atom molecule, H2. Its extreme lightness allows it to drift away from Earth's gravitational pull, making it scarce in the air at just about one part per million. Despite this, hydrogen ranks as the third most common element on the planet's surface, primarily bound within substances like water and organic compounds. Certain microorganisms release hydrogen gas, and it occurs naturally in digestive gases, alongside methane, which is itself a significant and growing reservoir for hydrogen.

input: The English language has been official in the state of Oklahoma since 2010. The variety of North American English spoken is called Oklahoma English, and this dialect is quite diverse with its uneven blending of features of North Midland, South Midland, and Southern dialects. In 2000, 2,977,187 Oklahomans—92.6% of the resident population five years or older—spoke only English at home, a decrease from 95% in 1990. 238,732 Oklahoma residents reported speaking a language other than English in the 2000 census, about 7.4% of the total population of the state. Spanish is the second most commonly spoken language in the state, with 141,060 speakers counted in 2000. The next most commonly spoken language is Cherokee, with about 22,000 speakers living within the Cherokee Nation tribal jurisdiction area of eastern Oklahoma. Cherokee is an official language in the Cherokee Nation tribal jurisdiction area and in the United Keetoowah Band of Cherokee Indians.
rewrite: Oklahoma formally adopted English as its official language in 2010. The regional dialect, known as Oklahoma English, incorporates a distinct mix of linguistic traits from the North Midland, South Midland, and Southern American English varieties. Census data from 2000 indicates that approximately 2.98 million residents aged five and above, or 92.6%, spoke solely English at home, down from 95% a decade earlier. Around 238,732 people, representing 7.4% of the population, reported using another language. Spanish is the most prevalent of these, with over 141,000 speakers at that time. Following Spanish, Cherokee is spoken by roughly 22,000 individuals, primarily within the Cherokee Nation's territory in eastern Oklahoma. Cherokee holds official status within both the Cherokee Nation and the United Keetoowah Band of Cherokee Indians.

input: On December 30, 1922, with the creation of the Soviet Union, Russia became one of six republics within the federation of the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics. The final Soviet name for the republic, the Russian Soviet Federative Socialist Republic, was adopted in the Soviet Constitution of 1936. By that time, Soviet Russia had gained roughly the same borders of the old Tsardom of Russia before the Great Northern War of 1700.
rewrite: Following the establishment of the Soviet Union on the last day of 1922, Russia joined as a founding member state. Its official title, the Russian Soviet Federative Socialist Republic, was formally confirmed by the 1936 constitution. At this point, its territory closely mirrored that of the historic Tsardom of Russia prior to the 1700 Great Northern War.

input: In February 1918, he was appointed Officer in Charge of Boys at the Royal Naval Air Service's training establishment at Cranwell. With the establishment of the Royal Air Force two months later and the transfer of Cranwell from Navy to Air Force control, he transferred from the Royal Navy to the Royal Air Force. He was appointed Officer Commanding Number 4 Squadron of the Boys' Wing at Cranwell until August 1918, before reporting to the RAF's Cadet School at St Leonards-on-Sea where he completed a fortnight's training and took command of a squadron on the Cadet Wing. He was the first member of the royal family to be certified as a fully qualified pilot. During the closing weeks of the war, he served on the staff of the RAF's Independent Air Force at its headquarters in Nancy, France. Following the disbanding of the Independent Air Force in November 1918, he remained on the Continent for two months as a staff officer with the Royal Air Force until posted back to Britain. He accompanied the Belgian monarch King Albert on his triumphal reentry into Brussels on 22 November. Prince Albert qualified as an RAF pilot on 31 July 1919 and gained a promotion to squadron leader on the following day.
rewrite: In early 1918, he assumed responsibility for the boys' unit at the Royal Naval Air Service training base located in Cranwell.
