Just two months afterwards, the Royal Air Force was formed, and authority over Cranwell shifted from the Navy to this new service. Consequently, he moved from the Royal Navy into the Royal Air Force. Until August of that year, he led Number 4 Squadron within the Boys' Wing at Cranwell. Subsequently, he attended a two-week course at the RAF Cadet School in St Leonards-on-Sea, after which he took charge of a squadron on the Cadet Wing. He holds the distinction of being the initial royal family member to earn official certification as a fully trained pilot. In the final stages of the First World War, he was assigned to the headquarters staff of the RAF's Independent Air Force in Nancy, France. After this force was dissolved in November 1918, he stayed in Europe for an additional two months, serving as a Royal Air Force staff officer before receiving orders to return to Britain. He was present alongside Belgium's King Albert during the king's celebratory return to Brussels on November 22. Having officially qualified as an RAF pilot on July 31, 1919, Prince Albert was elevated to the rank of squadron leader the very next day.

input: Commercial credit and agricultural consumer loans were the main types of loans. The trade credit was usually extended by temples in order to finance trade expeditions and was nominated in silver. The interest rate was set at 1/60 a month (one shekel per mina) some time before 2000 BC and it remained at that level for about two thousand years. Rural loans commonly arose as a result of unpaid obligations due to an institution (such as a temple), in this case the arrears were considered to be lent to the debtor. They were denominated in barley or other crops and the interest rate was typically much higher than for commercial loans and could amount to 1/3 to 1/2 of the loan principal.
rewrite: The primary forms of lending were business credit and farm loans for individuals. Temples often provided trade financing, with silver as the specified currency, to support commercial ventures. A monthly interest rate of one shekel per mina, established prior to 2000 BC, remained unchanged for roughly two millennia. Agricultural debts typically originated from unpaid dues to entities like temples, where the overdue sum was treated as a new loan to the borrower. These were valued in barley or similar produce and carried significantly higher interest rates than commercial credit, sometimes reaching between a third and half of the original amount borrowed.

input: Although there is some evidence of earlier inhabitation in the region of Utrecht, dating back to the Stone Age (app. 2200 BCE) and settling in the Bronze Age (app. 1800–800 BCE), the founding date of the city is usually related to the construction of a Roman fortification (castellum), probably built in around 50 CE. A series of such fortresses was built after the Roman emperor Claudius decided the empire should not expand north. To consolidate the border the limes Germanicus defense line was constructed  along the main branch of the river Rhine, which at that time flowed through a more northern bed compared to today (what is now the Kromme Rijn). These fortresses were designed to house a cohort of about 500 Roman soldiers. Near the fort settlements would grow housing artisans, traders and soldiers' wives and children.
rewrite: While traces of human activity in the Utrecht area extend to the Stone Age (circa 2200 BCE), with more established Bronze Age communities (around 1800–800 BCE), the city's official origin is typically linked to Roman times. Around 50 CE, a Roman fort was erected there. This construction followed Emperor Claudius's decision to halt northern expansion, leading to the establishment of the *limes Germanicus* frontier. This defensive line followed the main channel of the Rhine, which then ran north of its present course along what is now the Kromme Rijn. Such forts were built to garrison approximately 500 troops. Communities of craftspeople, merchants, and soldiers' families often developed adjacent to these military posts.

input: Within a species not all populations may be migratory; this is known as "partial migration". Partial migration is very common in the southern continents; in Australia, 44% of non-passerine birds and 32% of passerine species are partially migratory. In some species, the population at higher latitudes tends to be migratory and will often winter at lower latitude. The migrating birds bypass the latitudes where other populations may be sedentary, where suitable wintering habitats may already be occupied. This is an example of leap-frog migration. Many fully migratory species show leap-frog migration (birds that nest at higher latitudes spend the winter at lower latitudes), and many show the alternative, chain migration, where populations 'slide' more evenly north and south without reversing order.
rewrite: Not all members of a species undertake seasonal journeys; this phenomenon is termed partial migration. It occurs frequently across southern landmasses, such as in Australia, where 44% of non-passerine and nearly a third of passerine bird species exhibit this pattern. Often, groups living farther north or south will migrate seasonally to milder regions, while their counterparts in intermediate areas remain resident year-round. Consequently, the travelers skip over these settled middle latitudes, a strategy called leap-frog migration. Numerous wholly migratory species display this leap-frog pattern, while others practice chain migration, in which populations shift more uniformly north and south, maintaining their relative latitudinal positions.

input: Israel has a three-tier court system. At the lowest level are magistrate courts, situated in most cities across the country. Above them are district courts, serving as both appellate courts and courts of first instance; they are situated in five of Israel's six districts. The third and highest tier is the Supreme Court, located in Jerusalem; it serves a dual role as the highest court of appeals and the High Court of Justice. In the latter role, the Supreme Court rules as a court of first instance, allowing individuals, both citizens and non-citizens, to petition against the decisions of state authorities. Although Israel supports the goals of the International Criminal Court, it has not ratified the Rome Statute, citing concerns about the ability of the court to remain free from political impartiality.
rewrite: Israel's judicial structure consists of three levels. The base is formed by magistrate courts, found in numerous cities nationwide. The intermediate level comprises district courts, which hear both initial trials and appeals; these are located in five out of the country's six districts. At the apex is the Supreme Court in Jerusalem. It functions as the final appellate body and also operates as the High Court of Justice. In this unique capacity, it accepts direct petitions from anyone, including non-citizens, challenging government authorities' actions. While Israel endorses the aims of the International Criminal Court, it has not joined its founding treaty, the Rome Statute, due to reservations about the court's potential for political bias.

input: The town experienced major expansion during the Victorian era. The Southampton Docks company had been formed in 1835. In October 1838 the foundation stone of the docks was laid and the first dock opened in 1842. The structural and economic development of docks continued for the next few decades. The railway link to London was fully opened in May 1840. Southampton subsequently became known as The Gateway to the Empire.
rewrite: Southampton grew significantly in the Victorian period. Its docks were established by a company founded in 1835, with construction starting in 1838 and the first dock operational by 1842. Development of the port infrastructure and its economy progressed for years afterward. A complete rail connection to London launched in 1840, leading to the city's designation as The Gateway to the Empire.

input: Upon graduating in September 1785, Bonaparte was commissioned a second lieutenant in La Fère artillery regiment.[note 4] He served in Valence and Auxonne until after the outbreak of the Revolution in 1789, and took nearly two years' leave in Corsica and Paris during this period. At this time, he was a fervent Corsican nationalist, and wrote to Corsican leader Pasquale Paoli in May 1789, "As the nation was perishing I was born. Thirty thousand Frenchmen were vomited on to our shores, drowning the throne of liberty in waves of blood. Such was the odious sight which was the first to strike me."
rewrite: After completing his studies in September 1785, Bonaparte received a commission as a second lieutenant in the La Fère artillery regiment. He was stationed in Valence and Auxonne until shortly after the Revolution began in 1789, also spending close to two years on leave in Corsica and Paris. During these years, he was a passionate supporter of Corsican independence. In a letter to the Corsican leader Pasquale Paoli in May 1789, he declared that his birth coincided with his homeland's subjugation, describing the arrival of French troops as a bloody deluge that crushed liberty.

input: Though it was known in the nineteenth century that bacteria are the cause of many diseases, no effective antibacterial treatments were available. In 1910, Paul Ehrlich developed the first antibiotic, by changing dyes that selectively stained Treponema pallidum — the spirochaete that causes syphilis — into compounds that selectively killed the pathogen. Ehrlich had been awarded a 1908 Nobel Prize for his work on immunology, and pioneered the use of stains to detect and identify bacteria, with his work being the basis of the Gram stain and the Ziehl–Neelsen stain.
rewrite: During the 1800s, it was understood that bacteria led to numerous illnesses, yet no successful cures existed. The initial antimicrobial remedy emerged in 1910, created by Paul Ehrlich. He modified dyes that specifically colored the syphilis-causing Treponema pallidum, turning them into agents that destroyed this bacterium. Ehrlich, a 1908 Nobel laureate in immunology, also led the way in applying dyes to reveal and classify bacteria, forming the foundation for techniques like the Gram and Ziehl–Neelsen stains.

input: A permanent European presence in New Netherland began in 1624 – making New York the 12th oldest continuously occupied European-established settlement in the continental United States  – with the founding of a Dutch fur trading settlement on Governors Island. In 1625, construction was started on a citadel and a Fort Amsterdam on Manhattan Island, later called New Amsterdam (Nieuw Amsterdam). The colony of New Amsterdam was centered at the site which would eventually become Lower Manhattan. The Dutch colonial Director-General Peter Minuit purchased the island of Manhattan from the Canarsie, a small band of the Lenape, in 1626 for a value of 60 guilders (about $1000 in 2006); a disproved legend says that Manhattan was purchased for $24 worth of glass beads.
rewrite: European settlement in New Netherland was permanently established in 1624, marking the start of what would become the twelfth longest-running European-founded community in the continental United States. This began with a Dutch trading post for furs on Governors Island. The following year, work commenced on a fortress and Fort Amsterdam on Manhattan Island, a site later named New Amsterdam. This colony was focused on the area known today as Lower Manhattan. In 1626, Peter Minuit, the Dutch colonial leader, acquired Manhattan from the Canarsie group of the Lenape people for 60 guilders, equivalent to roughly $1,000 in modern value. A famous but inaccurate story claims the price was merely $24 in glass beads.

input: The first post-Classical published classification of humans into distinct races seems to be François Bernier's Nouvelle division de la terre par les différents espèces ou races qui l'habitent ("New division of Earth by the different species or races which inhabit it"), published in 1684. In the 18th century the differences among human groups became a focus of scientific investigation. But the scientific classification of phenotypic variation was frequently coupled with racist ideas about innate predispositions of different groups, always attributing the most desirable features to the White, European race and arranging the other races along a continuum of progressively undesirable attributes. The 1735 classification of Carl Linnaeus, inventor of zoological taxonomy, divided the human race Homo sapiens into continental varieties of europaeus, asiaticus, americanus, and afer, each associated with a different humour: sanguine, melancholic, choleric, and phlegmatic, respectively. Homo sapiens europaeus was described as active, acute, and adventurous, whereas Homo sapiens afer was said to be crafty, lazy, and careless.
rewrite: The earliest known attempt to categorize humanity into separate races after the Classical era appears in François Bernier's 1684 work, which proposed a new global division based on different species or races. During the 1700s, the study of variations between human populations emerged as a formal scientific pursuit. However, this effort to systematically classify physical traits was often intertwined with prejudiced beliefs about inherent group qualities. These frameworks consistently assigned the most favored characteristics to Europeans of white descent, while ranking other groups according to a descending scale of increasingly negative traits. Carl Linnaeus, who established zoological taxonomy, exemplified this in 1735 by classifying humans into continental types—European, Asian, American, and African—linking each to a classical temperament: sanguine, melancholic, choleric, and phlegmatic. His description characterized the European type as energetic, sharp, and daring, while labeling the African type as sly, indolent, and negligent.

input: The Oklahoma City Thunder of the National Basketball Association (NBA) has called Oklahoma City home since the 2008–09 season, when owner Clayton Bennett relocated the franchise from Seattle, Washington. The Thunder plays home games at the Chesapeake Energy Arena in downtown Oklahoma City, known affectionately in the national media as 'the Peake' and 'Loud City'. The Thunder is known by several nicknames, including "OKC Thunder" and simply "OKC", and its mascot is Rumble the Bison.
rewrite: Since the 2008–09 NBA season, the Oklahoma City Thunder have been based in Oklahoma City, following owner Clayton Bennett's move of the team from Seattle. Their home court is the Chesapeake Energy Arena downtown, a venue often referred to as 'the Peake' or 'Loud City'. The team is commonly called "OKC" or "OKC Thunder," and its mascot is Rumble the Bison.

input: Zhejiang, as the heartland of the Jiangnan (Yangtze River Delta), remained the wealthiest area during the Six Dynasties (220 or 222–589), Sui, and Tang. After being incorporated into the Sui dynasty, its economic richness was used for the Sui dynasty's ambitions to expand north and south, particularly into Korea and Vietnam. The plan led the Sui dynasty to restore and expand the network which became the Grand Canal of China. The Canal regularly transported grains and resources from Zhejiang, through its metropolitan center Hangzhou (and its hinterland along both the Zhe River and the shores of Hangzhou Bay), and from Suzhou, and thence to the North China Plain. The débâcle of the Korean war led to Sui's overthrow by the Tang, who then presided over a centuries-long golden age for the country. Zhejiang was an important economic center of the empire's Jiangnan East Circuit and was considered particularly prosperous. Throughout the Tang dynasty, The Grand Canal had remained effective, transporting grains and material resources to North China plain and metropolitan centers of the empire. As the Tang Dynasty disintegrated, Zhejiang constituted most of the territory of the regional kingdom of Wuyue.
rewrite: During the Six Dynasties period and continuing through the Sui and Tang eras, the Jiangnan region, with Zhejiang at its core, was China's most prosperous area. Following its integration into the Sui empire, the region's substantial wealth financed imperial campaigns to the north and south, including ventures into Korea and Vietnam. To support these ambitions, the Sui government renovated and enlarged the waterway network, ultimately forming the Grand Canal. This vital artery continuously moved grain and supplies collected from Zhejiang—specifically from the capital Hangzhou, its surrounding areas along the Zhe River and Hangzhou Bay, and from Suzhou—northward to the political heartland. The Sui dynasty's collapse, precipitated by its disastrous war in Korea, gave way to the Tang, which ushered in a prolonged golden age. Zhejiang served as a key economic hub within the empire's Jiangnan East Circuit, renowned for its affluence. The Grand Canal remained fully operational throughout the Tang period, efficiently channeling food and goods to the northern plains and major cities. When the Tang empire eventually fragmented, the territory of Zhejiang largely formed the basis of the regional state of Wuyue.

input: Portuguese cuisine is diverse. The Portuguese consume a lot of dry cod (bacalhau in Portuguese), for which there are hundreds of recipes. There are more than enough bacalhau dishes for each day of the year. Two other popular fish recipes are grilled sardines and caldeirada, a potato-based stew that can be made from several types of fish. Typical Portuguese meat recipes, that may be made out of beef, pork, lamb, or chicken, include cozido à portuguesa, feijoada, frango de churrasco, leitão (roast suckling pig) and carne de porco à alentejana. A very popular northern dish is the arroz de sarrabulho (rice stewed in pigs blood) or the arroz de cabidela (rice and chickens meat stewed in chickens blood).
rewrite: The food of Portugal offers a wide variety of flavors. A staple ingredient is dried cod, known locally as bacalhau, which features in countless preparations. In fact, one could eat a different cod dish every day. Other common seafood choices include sardines cooked on a grill and caldeirada, a fish stew with potatoes. Meat dishes are also central, utilizing beef, pork, lamb, or chicken in classics like cozido à portuguesa, feijoada, and roast suckling pig. From the north come unique specialties such as arroz de sarrabulho and arroz de cabidela, which are rice dishes cooked with blood.

input: The use of uranium in its natural oxide form dates back to at least the year 79 CE, when it was used to add a yellow color to ceramic glazes. Yellow glass with 1% uranium oxide was found in a Roman villa on Cape Posillipo in the Bay of Naples, Italy, by R. T. Gunther of the University of Oxford in 1912. Starting in the late Middle Ages, pitchblende was extracted from the Habsburg silver mines in Joachimsthal, Bohemia (now Jáchymov in the Czech Republic), and was used as a coloring agent in the local glassmaking industry. In the early 19th century, the world's only known sources of uranium ore were these mines.
rewrite: The application of natural uranium oxide can be traced to 79 CE or earlier, serving as a yellow pigment for pottery glazes. In 1912, Oxford researcher R. T. Gunther discovered Roman-era glass at a villa on Italy’s Cape Posillipo containing one percent uranium oxide. By the late medieval period, the mineral pitchblende was being mined from silver deposits in Joachimsthal, Bohemia (present-day Jáchymov, Czech Republic), and utilized to color glass locally. Throughout the early 1800s, these same mines remained the sole global source for uranium ore.

input: On June 16, 1911, their four companies were consolidated in New York State by Charles Ranlett Flint to form the Computing-Tabulating-Recording Company (CTR). CTR's business office was in Endicott. The individual companies owned by CTR continued to operate using their established names until the businesses were integrated in 1933 and the holding company eliminated. The four companies had 1,300 employees and offices and plants in Endicott and Binghamton, New York; Dayton, Ohio; Detroit, Michigan; Washington, D.C.; and Toronto. They manufactured machinery for sale and lease, ranging from commercial scales and industrial time recorders, meat and cheese slicers, to tabulators and punched cards.
rewrite: On June 16, 1911, Charles Ranlett Flint merged four separate firms in New York, creating the Computing-Tabulating-Recording Company (CTR). Headquartered in Endicott, CTR allowed its acquired companies to keep their original names and operate independently until a full consolidation in 1933 dissolved the holding company structure. With 1,300 staff, the combined entity had facilities in several cities including Endicott, Binghamton, Dayton, Detroit, Washington, D.C., and Toronto. Their product line encompassed a wide array of equipment for purchase or rental, from tabulators and punched cards to scales, time clocks, and food slicers.

input: The Nigerian government has commissioned the overseas production and launch of four satellites. The Nigeriasat-1 was the first satellite to be built under the Nigerian government sponsorship. The satellite was launched from Russia on 27 September 2003. Nigeriasat-1 was part of the world-wide Disaster Monitoring Constellation System. The primary objectives of the Nigeriasat-1 were: to give early warning signals of environmental disaster; to help detect and control desertification in the northern part of Nigeria; to assist in demographic planning; to establish the relationship between malaria vectors and the environment that breeds malaria and to give early warning signals on future outbreaks of meningitis using remote sensing technology; to provide the technology needed to bring education to all parts of the country through distant learning; and to aid in conflict resolution and border disputes by mapping out state and International borders.
rewrite: Nigeria has initiated a program to develop and deploy four satellites from abroad. The inaugural satellite, Nigeriasat-1, funded by the government, was sent into orbit from a Russian facility on September 27, 2003. This spacecraft joined an international network designed for disaster monitoring. Its key missions included issuing environmental disaster alerts, monitoring desert encroachment in Nigeria's north, and supporting population planning. It also aimed to study the environmental conditions linked to malaria carriers, forecast meningitis outbreaks via remote sensing, and enable nationwide educational access through distance learning technologies. Additionally, the satellite was intended to help clarify boundaries and resolve disputes by accurately mapping domestic and international borders.

input: The French breech-loading rifle, the Chassepot, had a far longer range than the German needle gun; 1,500 yards (1,400 m) compared to 600 yd (550 m). The French also had an early machine-gun type weapon, the mitrailleuse, which could fire its thirty-seven barrels at a range of around 1,200 yd (1,100 m). It was developed in such secrecy, that little training with the weapon had occurred, leaving French gunners with no experience; the gun was treated like artillery and in this role it was ineffective. Worse still, once the small number of soldiers who had been trained how to use the new weapon became casualties, there were no replacements who knew how to operate the mitrailleuse.
rewrite: The Chassepot, a French rifle that loaded at the breech, significantly outranged the German needle gun, reaching distances of roughly 1,400 meters versus about 550 meters. France also possessed the mitrailleuse, an early rapid-fire weapon capable of discharging rounds from its many barrels over approximately 1,100 meters. However, its development was so clandestine that troops received minimal instruction, resulting in a lack of skilled operators. Deployed incorrectly as conventional artillery, it proved largely useless. Furthermore, when the few trained crew members were wounded or killed, no other soldiers knew how to work the gun.

input: Other radio stations based in Mogadishu include Mustaqbal Media corporation and the Shabelle Media Network, the latter of which was in 2010 awarded the Media of the Year prize by the Paris-based journalism organisation, Reporters Without Borders (RSF). In total, about one short-wave and ten private FM radio stations broadcast from the capital, with several radio stations broadcasting from the central and southern regions.
rewrite: In Mogadishu, additional broadcasters are Mustaqbal Media and Shabelle Media Network. Reporters Without Borders, an international journalism group, named Shabelle its Media of the Year in 2010. The capital hosts roughly ten private FM stations and one short-wave outlet, while several more operate from central and southern Somalia.

input: Strasbourg features a number of prominent parks, of which several are of cultural and historical interest: the Parc de l'Orangerie, laid out as a French garden by André le Nôtre and remodeled as an English garden on behalf of Joséphine de Beauharnais, now displaying noteworthy French gardens, a neo-classical castle and a small zoo; the Parc de la Citadelle, built around impressive remains of the 17th-century fortress erected close to the Rhine by Vauban; the Parc de Pourtalès, laid out in English style around a baroque castle (heavily restored in the 19th century) that now houses a small three-star hotel, and featuring an open-air museum of international contemporary sculpture. The Jardin botanique de l'Université de Strasbourg (botanical garden) was created under the German administration next to the Observatory of Strasbourg, built in 1881, and still owns some greenhouses of those times. The Parc des Contades, although the oldest park of the city, was completely remodeled after World War II. The futuristic Parc des Poteries is an example of European park-conception in the late 1990s. The Jardin des deux Rives, spread over Strasbourg and Kehl on both sides of the Rhine opened in 2004 and is the most extended (60-hectare) park of the agglomeration. The most recent park is Parc du Heyritz (8,7 ha), opened in 2014 along a canal facing the hôpital civil.
rewrite:
Strasbourg boasts numerous significant parks, many with cultural and historical value. The Parc de l'Orangerie was originally designed as a formal French garden by André le Nôtre, later transformed into an English landscape garden for Joséphine de Beauharnais. Today it contains elegant French gardens, a neoclassical château, and a modest zoo. The Parc de la Citadelle surrounds substantial ruins of a 17th-century fortress constructed near the Rhine by the military engineer Vauban. Encircling a baroque château—extensively renovated in the 1800s and now a three-star hotel—the Parc de Pourtalès is arranged in the English manner and includes an outdoor museum for modern international sculpture.

Founded during the period of German administration adjacent to the 1881 Observatory, the University of Strasbourg’s Botanical Garden retains several original greenhouses. Parc des Contades, despite being the city’s oldest, was entirely redesigned following the Second World War. In contrast, the futuristic Parc des Poteries exemplifies European park design from the late 1990s. Spanning both Strasbourg and Kehl across the Rhine, the Jardin des deux Rives opened in 2004 and is the largest park in the metropolitan area at 60 hectares. The newest is the Parc du Heyritz (8.7 hectares), inaugurated in 2014 alongside a canal near the city’s civil hospital.

input: Buddhism first entered China during the Eastern Han and was first mentioned in 65 AD. Liu Ying (d. 71 AD), a half-brother to Emperor Ming of Han (r. 57–75 AD), was one of its earliest Chinese adherents, although Chinese Buddhism at this point was heavily associated with Huang-Lao Daoism. China's first known Buddhist temple, the White Horse Temple, was erected during Ming's reign. Important Buddhist canons were translated into Chinese during the 2nd century AD, including the Sutra of Forty-two Chapters, Perfection of Wisdom, Shurangama Sutra, and Pratyutpanna Sutra.
rewrite: Buddhism initially arrived in China in the Eastern Han era, with records dating back to 65 AD. An early Chinese follower was Liu Ying, who died in 71 AD and was a half-brother of Emperor Ming. At this time, Buddhist practices were deeply intertwined with Huang-Lao Daoist traditions. The inaugural recognized Buddhist temple in China, the White Horse Temple, was constructed under Emperor Ming. Key scriptures, such as the Sutra of Forty-two Chapters and several Perfection of Wisdom texts, were translated into Chinese in the second century AD.

input: In the Church of England, the ecclesiastical courts that formerly decided many matters such as disputes relating to marriage, divorce, wills, and defamation, still have jurisdiction of certain church-related matters (e.g. discipline of clergy, alteration of church property, and issues related to churchyards). Their separate status dates back to the 12th century when the Normans split them off from the mixed secular/religious county and local courts used by the Saxons. In contrast to the other courts of England the law used in ecclesiastical matters is at least partially a civil law system, not common law, although heavily governed by parliamentary statutes. Since the Reformation, ecclesiastical courts in England have been royal courts. The teaching of canon law at the Universities of Oxford and Cambridge was abrogated by Henry VIII; thereafter practitioners in the ecclesiastical courts were trained in civil law, receiving a Doctor of Civil Law (D.C.L.) degree from Oxford, or a Doctor of Laws (LL.D.) degree from Cambridge. Such lawyers (called "doctors" and "civilians") were centered at "Doctors Commons", a few streets south of St Paul's Cathedral in London, where they monopolized probate, matrimonial, and admiralty cases until their jurisdiction was removed to the common law courts in the mid-19th century.
rewrite: Within the Church of England, the specialized tribunals that once adjudicated a wide array of cases—including those concerning marriage, divorce, estates, and slander—continue to hold authority over specific ecclesiastical affairs. These encompass clergy discipline, modifications to church buildings, and matters involving consecrated burial grounds. Their distinct existence originated in the 12th century under Norman rule, which separated them from the earlier Saxon courts that blended secular and religious authority. Unlike England's other judicial bodies, these courts operate under a framework that is partly based on civil law rather than common law, though they are now heavily regulated by acts of Parliament. Post-Reformation, these tribunals have functioned as crown courts. Instruction in canon law was discontinued at Oxford and Cambridge by Henry VIII; subsequently, advocates practicing in these courts were educated in civil law, earning a Doctor of Civil Law degree from Oxford or a Doctor of Laws from Cambridge. These practitioners, known as "doctors" or "civilians," were based at Doctors' Commons in London, near St. Paul's Cathedral. There, they held exclusive authority over wills, marriage, and maritime cases until the mid-1800s, when such matters were transferred to the common law courts.

input: Buddhism began to spread throughout Japan during the Heian period, primarily through two major esoteric sects, Tendai and Shingon. Tendai originated in China and is based on the Lotus Sutra, one of the most important sutras of Mahayana Buddhism; Saichō was key to its transmission to Japan. Shingon is the Japanese transmission of the Chinese Chen Yen school. Shingon, brought to Japan by the monk Kūkai, emphasizes Esoteric Buddhism. Both Kūkai and Saichō aimed to connect state and religion and establish support from the aristocracy, leading to the notion of 'aristocratic Buddhism'. An important element of Tendai doctrine was the suggestion that enlightenment was accessible to "every creature". Saichō also sought independent ordination for Tendai monks. A close relationship developed between the Tendai monastery complex on Mount Hiei and the imperial court in its new capital at the foot of the mountain. As a result, Tendai emphasized great reverence for the emperor and the nation. Kammu himself was a notable patron of the otherworldly Tendai sect, which rose to great power over the ensuing centuries. Kūkai greatly impressed the emperors who succeeded Emperor Kammu, and also generations of Japanese, not only with his holiness but also with his poetry, calligraphy, painting, and sculpture. Shingon, through its use of "rich symbols, rituals and mandalas" held a wide-ranging appeal.
rewrite:
During Japan's Heian era, Buddhism became widely established, largely due to the influence of two principal esoteric schools: Tendai and Shingon. The Tendai tradition, which finds its roots in China and centers on the teachings of the Lotus Sutra, was introduced by the monk Saichō. Shingon represents the Japanese lineage of the Chinese Chen Yen school, brought to the country by Kūkai and focused on esoteric practices. Both founders worked to intertwine religious and governmental authority, securing backing from the elite and fostering what is termed 'aristocratic Buddhism.'

A core Tendai belief proposed that awakening was possible for all beings. Saichō further advocated for autonomous ordination for its monks. The sect's main temple on Mount Hiei maintained strong ties with the imperial court situated nearby, fostering a doctrine of deep loyalty to the emperor and state. Emperor Kammu himself was a significant supporter of the transcendent Tendai school, which grew immensely powerful in later centuries. Kūkai earned high esteem from subsequent emperors and the populace not just for his piety, but also for his artistic mastery in verse, calligraphy, painting, and sculpture. Meanwhile, Shingon attracted a broad following through its elaborate employment of symbolic imagery, ceremonies, and mandalas.

input: When used with a load that has a torque curve that increases with speed, the motor will operate at the speed where the torque developed by the motor is equal to the load torque. Reducing the load will cause the motor to speed up, and increasing the load will cause the motor to slow down until the load and motor torque are equal. Operated in this manner, the slip losses are dissipated in the secondary resistors and can be very significant. The speed regulation and net efficiency is also very poor.
rewrite: A motor paired with a load requiring more torque at higher speeds will settle at the point where both torque values match. If the load lessens, the motor accelerates; a heavier load slows it down until balance is restored. In this setup, substantial energy is lost as heat in the secondary resistors due to slip. Consequently, both speed control and overall efficiency become notably inadequate.

input: In 1988, Apple sued Microsoft and Hewlett-Packard on the grounds that they infringed Apple's copyrighted GUI, citing (among other things) the use of rectangular, overlapping, and resizable windows. After four years, the case was decided against Apple, as were later appeals. Apple's actions were criticized by some in the software community, including the Free Software Foundation (FSF), who felt Apple was trying to monopolize on GUIs in general, and boycotted GNU software for the Macintosh platform for seven years.
rewrite: In 1988, Apple initiated legal action against Microsoft and Hewlett-Packard, claiming they violated Apple's graphical user interface copyrights by employing features like overlapping, resizable rectangular windows. After a four-year trial and subsequent unsuccessful appeals, the ruling favored the defendants. This lawsuit drew criticism from segments of the software industry, such as the Free Software Foundation, which accused Apple of seeking a GUI monopoly and subsequently avoided supporting GNU software on Macintosh computers for seven years.

input: On the other hand, changes through the Phanerozoic correlate much better with the hyperbolic model (widely used in population biology, demography and macrosociology, as well as fossil biodiversity) than with exponential and logistic models. The latter models imply that changes in diversity are guided by a first-order positive feedback (more ancestors, more descendants) and/or a negative feedback arising from resource limitation. Hyperbolic model implies a second-order positive feedback. The hyperbolic pattern of the world population growth arises from a second-order positive feedback between the population size and the rate of technological growth. The hyperbolic character of biodiversity growth can be similarly accounted for by a feedback between diversity and community structure complexity. The similarity between the curves of biodiversity and human population probably comes from the fact that both are derived from the interference of the hyperbolic trend with cyclical and stochastic dynamics.
rewrite: In contrast, shifts observed during the Phanerozoic era align more closely with a hyperbolic framework—common in fields like population biology and demography, as well as studies of fossil biodiversity—than with exponential or logistic patterns. These latter models suggest diversity changes are driven either by a primary positive feedback loop, where greater numbers of ancestors lead to more descendants, or by a limiting negative feedback due to scarce resources. The hyperbolic approach, however, involves a secondary positive feedback mechanism. This pattern in global population expansion results from an interconnected feedback where population size accelerates technological progress, which in turn fuels further growth. Biodiversity’s hyperbolic increase can be explained analogously through a reciprocal relationship between species variety and the complexity of ecological communities. The parallel seen in biodiversity and human population trends likely stems from both being shaped by hyperbolic forces interacting with cyclical and random fluctuations.

input: Portugal has considerable resources of wind and river power, the two most cost-effective renewable sources. Since the turn of the 21st century, there has been a trend towards the development of a renewable resource industry and reduction of both consumption and use of fossil fuel resources. In 2006, the world's largest solar power plant at that date, the Moura Photovoltaic Power Station, began operating near Moura, in the south, while the world's first commercial wave power farm, the Aguçadoura Wave Farm, opened in the Norte region (2008). By the end of 2006, 66% of the country's electrical production was from coal and fuel power plants, while 29% were derived from hydroelectric dams, and 6% by wind energy.
rewrite: Portugal possesses significant potential for wind and hydroelectric power, which are among the most economical renewable options. The start of this century has seen a national shift toward growing a renewable energy sector while decreasing reliance on fossil fuels. In the mid-2000s, the country launched pioneering projects: the Moura Photovoltaic Power Station, then the globe's largest solar facility in the south, and the first commercial wave energy installation, the Aguçadoura Wave Farm, in the north. At the close of 2006, conventional coal and fuel plants still generated 66% of electricity, with hydroelectric sources providing 29% and wind contributing 6%.

input: The theories developed in the 1930s and 1940s to integrate molecular genetics with Darwinian evolution are called the modern evolutionary synthesis, a term introduced by Julian Huxley. Evolutionary biologists subsequently refined this concept, such as George C. Williams' gene-centric view of evolution. He proposed an evolutionary concept of the gene as a unit of natural selection with the definition: "that which segregates and recombines with appreciable frequency.":24 In this view, the molecular gene transcribes as a unit, and the evolutionary gene inherits as a unit. Related ideas emphasizing the centrality of genes in evolution were popularized by Richard Dawkins.
rewrite: The modern evolutionary synthesis, a name coined by Julian Huxley, refers to the mid-20th-century frameworks that merged molecular genetics and Darwinian theory. Later thinkers like George C. Williams refined this, advancing a gene-focused perspective. He defined an evolutionary gene as an entity that frequently undergoes segregation and recombination, acting as a unit of selection. According to this model, while a molecular gene is transcribed as one piece, an evolutionary gene is inherited as one. Richard Dawkins further disseminated these core concepts highlighting genes' primary role.

input: In the 10th century the establishment of churches and monasteries led to the development of stone architecture that elaborated vernacular Roman forms, from which the term "Romanesque" is derived. Where available, Roman brick and stone buildings were recycled for their materials. From the tentative beginnings known as the First Romanesque, the style flourished and spread across Europe in a remarkably homogeneous form. Just before 1000 there was a great wave of building stone churches all over Europe. Romanesque buildings have massive stone walls, openings topped by semi-circular arches, small windows, and, particularly in France, arched stone vaults. The large portal with coloured sculpture in high relief became a central feature of façades, especially in France, and the capitals of columns were often carved with narrative scenes of imaginative monsters and animals. According to art historian C. R. Dodwell, "virtually all the churches in the West were decorated with wall-paintings", of which few survive. Simultaneous with the development in church architecture, the distinctive European form of the castle was developed, and became crucial to politics and warfare.
rewrite: During the 900s, the founding of new churches and monastic communities spurred advances in stone construction. This architecture adapted local Roman building traditions, giving rise to the label "Romanesque." Builders frequently repurposed materials from existing Roman structures when possible. Evolving from its early, experimental phase (often called First Romanesque), the style matured and expanded throughout Europe, maintaining a consistent character. A significant surge in constructing stone churches occurred just prior to the year 1000. Typical Romanesque structures feature thick stone walls, doorways and windows crowned with rounded arches, and relatively narrow openings. In France, stone barrel vaults were common. Elaborately sculpted main doorways, often with deeply carved figures, became a focal point of church fronts, especially in France. Column tops were frequently adorned with carvings depicting stories and fantastical creatures. Art historian C. R. Dodwell notes that wall paintings once adorned nearly all Western churches, though few examples remain today. In the same period, the classic European castle emerged as a distinct form, playing a vital role in political and military affairs.

input: Nasser's involvement in political activity increased throughout his school years, such that he only attended 45 days of classes during his last year of secondary school. Despite it having the almost unanimous backing of Egypt's political forces, Nasser strongly objected to the 1936 Anglo-Egyptian Treaty because it stipulated the continued presence of British military bases in the country. Nonetheless, political unrest in Egypt declined significantly and Nasser resumed his studies at al-Nahda, where he received his leaving certificate later that year.
rewrite: Nasser became increasingly politically engaged during his education, missing all but 45 days of his final secondary school year. He vehemently opposed the 1936 Anglo-Egyptian Treaty, which ensured British troops remained in Egypt, even though most domestic political groups supported it. As the country's turmoil subsided, he returned to his studies at al-Nahda and earned his graduation certificate that same year.

input: Other sports clubs include Plymouth Albion R.F.C. and the Plymouth Raiders basketball club. Plymouth Albion Rugby Football Club is a rugby union club that was founded in 1875 and are currently competing in the third tier of Professional English Rugby . They play at the Brickfields. Plymouth Raiders play in the British Basketball League – the top tier of British basketball. They play at the Plymouth Pavilions entertainment arena and were founded in 1983. Plymouth cricket club was formed in 1843, the current 1st XI play in the Devon Premier League. Plymouth Devils are a speedway team in the British Premier League. Plymouth was home to an American football club, the Plymouth Admirals until 2010. Plymouth is also home to Plymouth Marjons Hockey Club, with their 1st XI playing in the National League last season.
rewrite: In addition to the city's well-known teams, Plymouth hosts several other athletic organizations. Among these is Plymouth Albion R.F.C., a rugby union side established in 1875, which now participates in England's third professional division and hosts matches at Brickfields. The Plymouth Raiders, a basketball franchise founded in 1983, competes in the premier British Basketball League, with games held at the Plymouth Pavilions. Cricket has been represented since 1843 by a club whose leading team is in the Devon Premier League. The Plymouth Devils are a speedway squad in the British Premier League. Previously, the city was home to the Plymouth Admirals American football team until 2010. Furthermore, Plymouth Marjons Hockey Club fields a first team that recently played in the National League.

input: Meanwhile, Le Verrier by letter urged Berlin Observatory astronomer Johann Gottfried Galle to search with the observatory's refractor. Heinrich d'Arrest, a student at the observatory, suggested to Galle that they could compare a recently drawn chart of the sky in the region of Le Verrier's predicted location with the current sky to seek the displacement characteristic of a planet, as opposed to a fixed star. On the evening of 23 September 1846, the day Galle received the letter, he discovered Neptune within 1° of where Le Verrier had predicted it to be, about 12° from Adams' prediction. Challis later realised that he had observed the planet twice, on 4 and 12 August, but did not recognise it as a planet because he lacked an up-to-date star map and was distracted by his concurrent work on comet observations.
rewrite: Le Verrier contacted Johann Gottfried Galle at the Berlin Observatory via mail, encouraging him to examine the heavens using their telescope. Heinrich d'Arrest, an observatory student, proposed a method to Galle: they could use a new celestial map of the area Le Verrier indicated, checking it against the actual night sky to spot the telltale motion of a planet among the stars. That very night, September 23, 1846, after getting the letter, Galle found Neptune. It was remarkably close to Le Verrier's calculated position, though far from where Adams had estimated. Elsewhere, Challis later understood he had seen the planet on two occasions in August but failed to identify it, as he was without a current star chart and preoccupied with studying comets.

input: According to the latest nationwide census, Roman Catholics constituted 30.8% of the total population of Germany, followed by the Evangelical Protestants at 30.3%. Other religions, atheists or not specified constituted 38.8% of the population at the time. Among "others" are Protestants not included in Evangelical Church of Germany, and other Christians such as the Restorationist New Apostolic Church. Protestantism was more common among the citizens of Germany. The North and East Germany is predominantly Protestant, the South and West rather Catholic. Nowadays there is a non-religious majority in Hamburg and the East German states.
rewrite: Recent census data shows Roman Catholics make up 30.8% of Germany's population, with Evangelical Protestants at 30.3%. The remaining 38.8% includes various other faiths, atheists, and unspecified affiliations. This "other" category encompasses Protestant groups outside the national Evangelical Church and other Christian denominations. Historically, Protestantism has been more widespread across the country. Regional differences persist, with Protestantism dominant in the north and east, while the south and west are more Catholic. Presently, Hamburg and eastern states have largely non-religious populations.

input: Many regions in Russia were affected by the Soviet famine of 1932–1933: Volga; Central Black Soil Region; North Caucasus; the Urals; the Crimea; part of Western Siberia; and the Kazak ASSR. With the adoption of the 1936 Soviet Constitution on December 5, 1936, the size of the RSFSR was significantly reduced. The Kazakh ASSR and Kirghiz ASSR were transformed into the Kazakh and Kirghiz Soviet Socialist Republics. The Karakalpak Autonomous Socialist Soviet Republic was transferred to the Uzbek SSR.
rewrite: The Soviet famine from 1932 to 1933 impacted numerous areas across Russia, including the Volga, North Caucasus, Urals, Crimea, Western Siberia, and the Kazakh ASSR. Following the new constitution in December 1936, the Russian republic's borders were greatly diminished. This change elevated the Kazakh and Kirghiz regions to full republics, while the Karakalpak area was incorporated into Uzbekistan.

input: On August 1, 2012, Windows 8 (build 9200) was released to manufacturing with the build number 6.2.9200.16384 . Microsoft planned to hold a launch event on October 25, 2012 and release Windows 8 for general availability on the next day. However, only a day after its release to manufacturing, a copy of the final version of Windows 8 Enterprise N (a version for European markets lacking bundled media players to comply with a court ruling) leaked online, followed by leaks of the final versions of Windows 8 Pro and Enterprise a few days later. On August 15, 2012, Windows 8 was made available to download for MSDN and TechNet subscribers. Windows 8 was made available to Software Assurance customers on August 16, 2012. Windows 8 was made available for students with a DreamSpark Premium subscription on August 22, 2012, earlier than advertised.
rewrite: Windows 8 reached its manufacturing release stage on August 1, 2012, identified as build 6.2.9200.16384. Microsoft scheduled a public launch for October 25, with broad retail availability starting the following day. Shortly after the manufacturing milestone, however, the completed Windows 8 Enterprise N edition—a variant for Europe without media players due to legal requirements—was illicitly published online. Leaks of the Pro and Enterprise editions soon followed. Ahead of the public launch, Microsoft provided early access: subscribers to MSDN and TechNet could download the OS starting August 15, Software Assurance customers gained access on August 16, and students enrolled in DreamSpark Premium received it on August 22, which was sooner than initially planned.

input: Bath Rugby play at the Recreation Ground in Bath, and the Somerset County Cricket Club are based at the County Ground in Taunton. The county gained its first Football League club in 2003, when Yeovil Town won promotion to Division Three as Football Conference champions. They had achieved numerous FA Cup victories over football League sides in the past 50 years, and since joining the elite they have won promotion again—as League Two champions in 2005. They came close to yet another promotion in 2007, when they reached the League One playoff final, but lost to Blackpool at the newly reopened Wembley Stadium. Yeovil achieved promotion to the Championship in 2013 after beating Brentford in the playoff final. Horse racing courses are at Taunton and Wincanton.
rewrite: The Recreation Ground in Bath is home to Bath Rugby, while Somerset County Cricket Club plays at the County Ground in Taunton. Somerset welcomed its inaugural Football League club in 2003, following Yeovil Town's ascent to Division Three after topping the Football Conference. Prior to this, Yeovil had secured several FA Cup wins against League opponents over five decades. After entering the League, they earned another promotion by winning the League Two title in 2005. They nearly advanced again in 2007, reaching the League One playoff final at the rebuilt Wembley Stadium, but fell to Blackpool. Yeovil later reached the Championship in 2013 by defeating Brentford in the playoff final. The county also features horse racing venues in Taunton and Wincanton.

input: Despite this, the Austrians, under the command of General Laudon, captured Glatz (now Kłodzko, Poland) in Silesia. In the Battle of Liegnitz Frederick scored a strong victory despite being outnumbered three to one. The Russians under General Saltykov and Austrians under General Lacy briefly occupied his capital, Berlin, in October, but could not hold it for long. The end of that year saw Frederick once more victorious, defeating the able Daun in the Battle of Torgau; but he suffered very heavy casualties, and the Austrians retreated in good order.
rewrite: Nevertheless, Austrian forces led by General Laudon seized Glatz (present-day Kłodzko, Poland) in Silesia. Frederick then achieved a decisive triumph at the Battle of Liegnitz, overcoming odds of three to one. Later, a combined Russian-Austrian army briefly took Berlin in October but could not maintain control. By year's end, Frederick emerged victorious again at Torgau, though with severe losses, while the Austrian troops withdrew in disciplined formation.

input: Polarization is predictable from an antenna's geometry, although in some cases it is not at all obvious (such as for the quad antenna). An antenna's linear polarization is generally along the direction (as viewed from the receiving location) of the antenna's currents when such a direction can be defined. For instance, a vertical whip antenna or Wi-Fi antenna vertically oriented will transmit and receive in the vertical polarization. Antennas with horizontal elements, such as most rooftop TV antennas in the United States, are horizontally polarized (broadcast TV in the U.S. usually uses horizontal polarization). Even when the antenna system has a vertical orientation, such as an array of horizontal dipole antennas, the polarization is in the horizontal direction corresponding to the current flow. The polarization of a commercial antenna is an essential specification.
rewrite: The polarization of an antenna can typically be deduced from its physical structure, though this may not be immediately apparent in designs like the quad antenna. Generally, linear polarization aligns with the orientation of the antenna's electrical currents from the receiver's viewpoint, whenever such a direction is discernible. For example, a vertical whip or a similarly oriented Wi-Fi antenna operates with vertical polarization. Conversely, antennas featuring horizontal components, like many U.S. rooftop TV antennas, are horizontally polarized—a standard for American broadcast television. Even in systems with a vertical layout, such as an array of horizontal dipoles, polarization remains horizontal, following the direction of current. This characteristic is a crucial technical detail for any commercial antenna.

input: Bal Gangadhar Tilak, an Indian nationalist leader, declared Swaraj as the destiny of the nation. His popular sentence "Swaraj is my birthright, and I shall have it" became the source of inspiration for Indians. Tilak was backed by rising public leaders like Bipin Chandra Pal and Lala Lajpat Rai, who held the same point of view. Under them, India's three big provinces – Maharashtra, Bengal and Punjab, India shaped the demand of the people and India's nationalism. In 1907, the Congress was split into two factions: The radicals, led by Tilak, advocated civil agitation and direct revolution to overthrow the British Empire and the abandonment of all things British. The moderates, led by leaders like Dadabhai Naoroji and Gopal Krishna Gokhale, on the other hand wanted reform within the framework of British rule.
rewrite: Bal Gangadhar Tilak, a prominent figure in India's independence movement, asserted that self-rule was the nation's ultimate fate. His famous declaration, "Swaraj is my birthright, and I shall have it," deeply motivated his fellow citizens. He found strong support in contemporaries such as Bipin Chandra Pal and Lala Lajpat Rai, who shared his convictions. Together, their influence in key regions—Maharashtra, Bengal, and Punjab—helped mold popular sentiment and fuel national identity. A major division occurred in the Indian National Congress in 1907. The extremist faction, under Tilak's leadership, promoted mass protest and outright rebellion to end British control, rejecting British institutions entirely. Conversely, the moderate wing, represented by figures including Dadabhai Naoroji and Gopal Krishna Gokhale, sought progressive changes while remaining under British governance.

input: Swaziland derives its name from a later king named Mswati II. KaNgwane, named for Ngwane III, is an alternative name for Swaziland the surname of whose royal house remains Nkhosi Dlamini. Nkhosi literally means "king". Mswati II was the greatest of the fighting kings of Swaziland, and he greatly extended the area of the country to twice its current size. The Emakhandzambili clans were initially incorporated into the kingdom with wide autonomy, often including grants of special ritual and political status. The extent of their autonomy however was drastically curtailed by Mswati, who attacked and subdued some of them in the 1850s.
rewrite: The nation of Swaziland takes its title from King Mswati II. Another term for the country, KaNgwane, references Ngwane III, while its monarchy retains the name Nkhosi Dlamini, with "Nkhosi" translating to "king." Mswati II, the most formidable warrior king, expanded the realm to double its present territory. Early Emakhandzambili groups were integrated with considerable self-rule and privileged ceremonial roles. This independence was severely reduced when Mswati conquered several of these clans during the 1850s.

input: Many Sanskrit dramas also indicate that the language coexisted with Prakrits, spoken by multilingual speakers with a more extensive education. Sanskrit speakers were almost always multilingual. In the medieval era, Sanskrit continued to be spoken and written, particularly by learned Brahmins for scholarly communication. This was a thin layer of Indian society, but covered a wide geography. Centres like Varanasi, Paithan, Pune and Kanchipuram had a strong presence of teaching and debating institutions, and high classical Sanskrit was maintained until British times.
rewrite: Sanskrit theatrical works reveal that the language existed alongside Prakrits, used by educated individuals fluent in multiple tongues. Throughout the medieval period, it remained a living language, chiefly among scholarly Brahmins for intellectual exchange. Though this group represented a small segment of society, its influence was geographically widespread. Major hubs such as Varanasi, Paithan, Pune, and Kanchipuram featured vibrant academic institutions that preserved refined Sanskrit scholarship well into the colonial era.

input: By the end of the 5th century the western section of the empire was divided into smaller political units, ruled by the tribes that had invaded in the early part of the century. The deposition of the last emperor of the west, Romulus Augustus, in 476 has traditionally marked the end of the Western Roman Empire.[E] The Eastern Roman Empire, often referred to as the Byzantine Empire after the fall of its western counterpart, had little ability to assert control over the lost western territories. The Byzantine emperors maintained a claim over the territory, but none of the new kings in the west dared to elevate himself to the position of emperor of the west, Byzantine control of most of the Western Empire could not be sustained; the reconquest of the Italian peninsula and Mediterranean periphery by Justinian (r. 527–565) was the sole, and temporary, exception.
rewrite: By the close of the 400s, the western territories of the Roman Empire had fragmented into various kingdoms governed by invading tribal groups. The year 476, when the final western emperor Romulus Augustus was removed from power, is commonly viewed as the terminus of the Western Roman Empire. Meanwhile, the Eastern Roman Empire—later known as the Byzantine Empire—possessed very limited power to reclaim the western lands it had lost. Although Byzantine rulers continued to assert sovereignty over these regions, none of the new monarchs in the west assumed the title of western emperor. Sustained dominion over the former western provinces proved impossible for Byzantium. The only significant, though brief, reversal of this trend occurred under Emperor Justinian, who reigned from 527 to 565 and managed to retake parts of Italy and other Mediterranean areas.

input: St. John's (/ˌseɪntˈdʒɒnz/, local /ˌseɪntˈdʒɑːnz/) is the capital and largest city in Newfoundland and Labrador, Canada. St. John's was incorporated as a city in 1888, yet is considered by some to be the oldest English-founded city in North America. It is located on the eastern tip of the Avalon Peninsula on the island of Newfoundland. With a population of 214,285 as of July 1, 2015, the St. John's Metropolitan Area is the second largest Census Metropolitan Area (CMA) in Atlantic Canada after Halifax and the 20th largest metropolitan area in Canada. It is one of the world's top ten oceanside destinations, according to National Geographic Magazine. Its name has been attributed to the feast day of John the Baptist, when John Cabot was believed to have sailed into the harbour in 1497, and also to a Basque fishing town with the same name.
rewrite: St. John's serves as the capital and most populous city in Canada's Newfoundland and Labrador. Although officially incorporated in 1888, it is often regarded as the oldest city in North America established by the English. Situated on the far east of the Avalon Peninsula on Newfoundland island, its metropolitan region had 214,285 residents in mid-2015. This makes it the second largest CMA in Atlantic Canada, following Halifax, and the country's 20th biggest metro area. National Geographic Magazine ranks it among the top ten coastal destinations globally. The city's name is thought to derive either from the feast day of John the Baptist, coinciding with John Cabot's 1497 harbor arrival, or from an identically named Basque fishing settlement.

input: Chemical communications in animals rely on a variety of aspects including taste and smell. Chemoreception is the physiological response of a sense organ (i.e. taste or smell) to a chemical stimulus where the chemicals act as signals to regulate the state or activity of a cell. A semiochemical is a message-carrying chemical that is meant to attract, repel, and convey information. Types of semiochemicals include pheromones and kairomones. One example is the butterfly Phengaris arion which uses chemical signals as a form of mimicry to aid in predation.
rewrite: Animals use chemical signals like taste and smell to communicate. This process, called chemoreception, involves sensory organs detecting chemical cues that influence cellular behavior. These message-carrying compounds, known as semiochemicals, can attract, deter, or share information. Common types are pheromones and kairomones. For instance, the Phengaris arion butterfly employs such chemical cues to mimicry, helping it hunt more effectively.

input: Distinctive and self-identified black communities have been reported in countries such as Iraq, with a reported 1.2 million black people, and they attest to a history of discrimination. African-Iraquis have sought minority status from the government, which would reserve some seats in Parliament for representatives of their population. According to Alamin M. Mazrui et al., generally in the Arabian Peninsula and neighboring countries, most of those of visible African descent are still classified and identify as Arab, not black.
rewrite: Black communities that recognize their own identity exist in nations like Iraq, where approximately 1.2 million individuals report facing a legacy of prejudice. These African-descended Iraqis have requested official minority recognition to secure parliamentary representation. As noted by scholars including Alamin M. Mazrui, across the Arabian Peninsula and adjacent regions, people of clear African ancestry are predominantly categorized and view themselves as Arab rather than black.

input: Darwin's barnacle studies convinced him that variation arose constantly and not just in response to changed circumstances. In 1854, he completed the last part of his Beagle-related writing and began working full-time on evolution. His thinking changed from the view that species formed in isolated populations only, as on islands, to an emphasis on speciation without isolation; that is, he saw increasing specialisation within large stable populations as continuously exploiting new ecological niches. He conducted empirical research focusing on difficulties with his theory. He studied the developmental and anatomical differences between different breeds of many domestic animals, became actively involved in fancy pigeon breeding, and experimented (with the help of his son Francis) on ways that plant seeds and animals might disperse across oceans to colonise distant islands. By 1856, his theory was much more sophisticated, with a mass of supporting evidence.
rewrite: Darwin's examination of barnacles led him to conclude that new variations emerge continuously, rather than solely as reactions to environmental shifts. Finishing his final writings from the Beagle voyage in 1854, he dedicated himself entirely to developing his evolutionary ideas. His perspective shifted from believing new species only develop in separated groups, like on islands, to recognizing that speciation can also occur widely within large, settled populations. Here, increasing specialization allows organisms to persistently occupy new environmental opportunities. He engaged in hands-on research to address challenges to his theory. This included analyzing physical differences among domesticated animal breeds, participating in pigeon breeding, and testing with his son Francis how seeds and creatures could travel over seas to reach remote islands. By 1856, his theory had grown far more detailed and was backed by substantial evidence.

input: On the whole, Eisenhower's support of the nation's fledgling space program was officially modest until the Soviet launch of Sputnik in 1957, gaining the Cold War enemy enormous prestige around the world. He then launched a national campaign that funded not just space exploration but a major strengthening of science and higher education. His Open Skies Policy attempted to legitimize illegal Lockheed U-2 flyovers and Project Genetrix while paving the way for spy satellite technology to orbit over sovereign territory, created NASA as a civilian space agency, signed a landmark science education law, and fostered improved relations with American scientists.
rewrite: Initially, President Eisenhower provided only limited public backing for America's nascent space initiatives. This changed after the 1957 Sputnik launch, which significantly boosted Soviet global standing during the Cold War. In response, Eisenhower initiated a comprehensive national effort that substantially increased investment in space, scientific research, and universities. His actions included establishing NASA as a civilian agency, enacting important legislation for science education, and seeking to authorize aerial surveillance through the Open Skies Policy, which also facilitated the development of reconnaissance satellites. He also worked to mend ties with the scientific community.

input: The Alps are split into five climatic zones, each with different vegetation. The climate, plant life and animal life vary among the different sections or zones of the mountains. The lowest zone is the colline zone, which exists between 500 and 1,000 m (1,640 and 3,281 ft), depending on the location. The montane zone extends from 800 to 1,700 m (2,625 to 5,577 ft), followed by the sub-Alpine zone from 1,600 to 2,400 m (5,249 to 7,874 ft). The Alpine zone, extending from tree line to snow line, is followed by the glacial zone, which covers the glaciated areas of the mountain. Climatic conditions show variances within the same zones; for example, weather conditions at the head of a mountain valley, extending directly from the peaks, are colder and more severe than those at the mouth of a valley which tend to be less severe and receive less snowfall.
rewrite: The Alps feature five distinct climate regions, each supporting unique plant communities. Environmental conditions, flora, and fauna differ across these mountain sections. The lowest area, known as the colline zone, ranges from 500 to 1,000 meters in elevation, varying by locality. Above it lies the montane zone, spanning 800 to 1,700 meters, then the sub-Alpine zone from 1,600 to 2,400 meters. Next is the Alpine zone, reaching from the tree limit to the snow line, and finally the glacial zone, which includes all ice-covered terrain. Climate can also differ inside a single zone; conditions are harsher and colder near valley heads beneath the peaks, while valley openings experience milder weather with reduced snow.

input: Han Chinese Banners were made up of Han Chinese who defected to the Qing up to 1644 and joined the Eight Banners, giving them social and legal privileges in addition to being acculturated to Manchu culture. So many Han defected to the Qing and swelled the ranks of the Eight Banners that ethnic Manchus became a minority, making up only 16% in 1648, with Han Bannermen dominating at 75% and Mongol Bannermen making up the rest. This multi-ethnic force in which Manchus were only a minority conquered China for the Qing.
rewrite: Han Bannermen of Chinese ethnicity were those who aligned with the Qing dynasty before its 1644 conquest, entering the Eight Banners system. This integration granted them preferential status under the law and required adoption of Manchu customs. Their numbers grew so substantially that, by 1648, ethnic Manchus comprised a mere 16% of the banners, while Han Bannermen formed a 75% majority, the remainder being Mongols. This predominantly non-Manchu military force was instrumental in securing China for the Qing.

input: BBC Television is a service of the British Broadcasting Corporation. The corporation, which has operated in the United Kingdom under the terms of a Royal charter since 1927, has produced television programmes from its own since 1932, although the start of its regular service of television broadcasts is dated to 2 November 1936.
rewrite: BBC Television is operated by the British Broadcasting Corporation. This organization has been governed by a Royal charter in the UK since 1927. It began creating TV programs in 1932, but its regular broadcasting service officially commenced on November 2, 1936.

input: The word madrasah derives from the triconsonantal Semitic root د-ر-س D-R-S 'to learn, study', through the wazn (form/stem) مفعل(ة)‎; mafʻal(ah), meaning "a place where something is done". Therefore, madrasah literally means "a place where learning and studying take place". The word is also present as a loanword with the same innocuous meaning in many Arabic-influenced languages, such as: Urdu, Bengali, Hindi, Persian, Turkish, Azeri, Kurdish, Indonesian, Malay and Bosnian / Croatian. In the Arabic language, the word مدرسة madrasah simply means the same as school does in the English language, whether that is private, public or parochial school, as well as for any primary or secondary school whether Muslim, non-Muslim, or secular. Unlike the use of the word school in British English, the word madrasah more closely resembles the term school in American English, in that it can refer to a university-level or post-graduate school as well as to a primary or secondary school. For example, in the Ottoman Empire during the Early Modern Period, madaris had lower schools and specialised schools where the students became known as danişmends. The usual Arabic word for a university, however, is جامعة (jāmiʻah). The Hebrew cognate midrasha also connotes the meaning of a place of learning; the related term midrash literally refers to study or learning, but has acquired mystical and religious connotations.
rewrite: The term madrasah originates from the Semitic root D-R-S, which conveys the idea of learning or studying. It is structured using a specific grammatical pattern that denotes a location where an activity occurs, thus giving madrasah the direct interpretation of "a place where study happens." This word has been adopted into numerous languages influenced by Arabic, including Urdu, Bengali, Persian, Turkish, and several others, where it retains the same neutral sense. In Arabic, madrasah broadly corresponds to the English word "school," encompassing all types—private, public, religious, or secular—and covering both primary and secondary education. In contrast to British English usage, it aligns more closely with American English, as it can also refer to institutions of higher learning or postgraduate studies. Historically, in the Ottoman Empire, madaris included basic schools and advanced specialized institutions, with students in the latter often called danişmends. It is important to note that the standard Arabic term for a university is jāmiʻah. A related Hebrew word, midrasha, similarly signifies a place of learning, while midrash, though fundamentally about study, has developed deeper spiritual and interpretive meanings.

input: In 2010, a number of workers committed suicide at a Foxconn operations in China. Apple, HP, and others stated that they were investigating the situation. Foxconn guards have been videotaped beating employees. Another employee killed himself in 2009 when an Apple prototype went missing, and claimed in messages to friends, that he had been beaten and interrogated.
rewrite: During 2010, several Foxconn employees in China took their own lives. Apple and HP announced inquiries into the matter. Security personnel were recorded assaulting workers. In a 2009 incident, a worker died by suicide after losing an Apple prototype, alleging beatings and questioning in messages to friends.

input: Vietnam: The event was held in Ho Chi Minh City on April 29. Some 60 torchbearers carried the torch from the downtown Opera House to the Military Zone 7 Competition Hall stadium near Tan Son Nhat International Airport along an undisclosed route. Vietnam is involved in a territorial dispute with China (and other countries) for sovereignty of the Spratly and Paracel Islands; tensions have risen recently[when?] following reports that the Chinese government had established a county-level city named Sansha in the disputed territories, resulting in anti-Chinese demonstrations in December 2007 in Hanoi and Ho Chi Minh City. However to sustain its relationship with China the Vietnamese government has actively sought to head off protests during the torch relay, with Prime Minister Nguyễn Tấn Dũng warning government agencies that "hostile forces" may try to disrupt the torch relay.
rewrite: On April 29 in Ho Chi Minh City, approximately sixty individuals participated in a torch relay. The flame traveled from the central Opera House to a stadium near Tan Son Nhat International Airport, with the specific path kept confidential. This occurred amid ongoing regional strains, as Vietnam asserts its claims over the Spratly and Paracel Islands, territories also contested by China and others. Frictions escalated after China created the Sansha administrative district in the area, which previously sparked protests in Vietnamese cities. To maintain diplomatic ties with China, Vietnamese authorities worked to prevent demonstrations during the relay. Prime Minister Nguyễn Tấn Dũng cautioned that adversarial groups might attempt to interfere with the event.

input: Han Chinese make up the vast majority of the population, and the largest Han subgroup are the speakers of Wu varieties of Chinese. There are also 400,000 members of ethnic minorities, including approximately 200,000 She people and approximately 20,000 Hui Chinese[citation needed]. Jingning She Autonomous County in Lishui is the only She autonomous county in China.
rewrite: The Han Chinese constitute most inhabitants, with Wu dialect speakers being the largest subgroup. Ethnic minorities number around 400,000, including roughly 200,000 She and 20,000 Hui people. China's sole She autonomous county is Jingning, located within Lishui.

input: The sensitivity of Earth-based infrared telescopes is significantly limited by water vapor in the atmosphere, which absorbs a portion of the infrared radiation arriving from space outside of selected atmospheric windows. This limitation can be partially alleviated by placing the telescope observatory at a high altitude, or by carrying the telescope aloft with a balloon or an aircraft. Space telescopes do not suffer from this handicap, and so outer space is considered the ideal location for infrared astronomy.
rewrite: Infrared telescopes on Earth face major constraints due to atmospheric water vapor, which blocks much of the incoming infrared light except within specific wavelength bands. To reduce this interference, observatories can be built at high elevations or mounted on balloons or airplanes. However, telescopes in orbit experience no such atmospheric obstruction, making space the optimal environment for conducting infrared astronomical observations.

input: Dogs bear their litters roughly 58 to 68 days after fertilization, with an average of 63 days, although the length of gestation can vary. An average litter consists of about six puppies, though this number may vary widely based on the breed of dog. In general, toy dogs produce from one to four puppies in each litter, while much larger breeds may average as many as twelve.
rewrite: The gestation period for dogs typically lasts between 58 and 68 days, averaging 63 days. Litter sizes vary significantly by breed, with an average of six puppies. Smaller toy breeds often have one to four offspring per litter, whereas larger breeds can commonly have around twelve puppies.

input: A UCLA research study published in the June 2006 issue of the American Journal of Geriatric Psychiatry found that people can improve cognitive function and brain efficiency through simple lifestyle changes such as incorporating memory exercises, healthy eating, physical fitness and stress reduction into their daily lives. This study examined 17 subjects, (average age 53) with normal memory performance. Eight subjects were asked to follow a "brain healthy" diet, relaxation, physical, and mental exercise (brain teasers and verbal memory training techniques). After 14 days, they showed greater word fluency (not memory) compared to their baseline performance.
