They live together in large well-organized colonies that may be so tightly integrated and genetically similar that the colonies of some species are sometimes considered superorganisms. It is sometimes argued that the various species of honey bee are the only invertebrates (and indeed one of the few non-human groups) to have evolved a system of abstract symbolic communication where a behavior is used to represent and convey specific information about something in the environment. In this communication system, called dance language, the angle at which a bee dances represents a direction relative to the sun, and the length of the dance represents the distance to be flown.:309–311 Though perhaps not as advanced as honey bees, bumblebees also potentially have some social communication behaviors. Bombus terrestris, for example, exhibit a faster learning curve for visiting unfamiliar, yet rewarding flowers, when they can see a conspecific foraging on the same species.
rewrite: Social insects like ants, termites, and numerous bees and wasps represent the best-known eusocial creatures. They reside in sizable, highly structured communities that can be so cohesive and alike genetically that certain colonies are often viewed as single superorganisms. Some posit that honey bees stand alone among invertebrates—and are rare even beyond humans—in developing an abstract, symbolic method of exchanging information. This system involves a dance whose orientation indicates a direction using the sun's position, while the dance's duration communicates flight distance. Bumblebees may also possess simpler social communication. For instance, *Bombus terrestris* learns more rapidly to approach novel but beneficial flowers if observing another bumblebee already collecting nectar from them.

input: In 1902, the Siemens company developed a tantalum lamp filament. These lamps were more efficient than even graphitized carbon filaments and could operate at higher temperatures. Since tantalum metal has a lower resistivity than carbon, the tantalum lamp filament was quite long and required multiple internal supports. The metal filament had the property of gradually shortening in use; the filaments were installed with large loops that tightened in use. This made lamps in use for several hundred hours quite fragile. Metal filaments had the property of breaking and re-welding, though this would usually decrease resistance and shorten the life of the filament. General Electric bought the rights to use tantalum filaments and produced them in the US until 1913.
rewrite: In 1902, Siemens introduced a lamp filament made from tantalum. This innovation surpassed the efficiency of even graphitized carbon filaments and could withstand greater heat. Due to tantalum's reduced electrical resistance compared to carbon, the filament needed to be lengthy and was held in place by several supports inside the bulb. During operation, these metal filaments would slowly shrink; they were initially mounted with generous loops that contracted over time. Consequently, after several hundred hours of use, the lamps became very delicate. Additionally, the filaments could fracture and then fuse back together, a process that typically lowered resistance and reduced their overall lifespan. General Electric acquired the licensing rights and manufactured these filaments in the United States until 1913.

input: Silicon Alley, centered in Manhattan, has evolved into a metonym for the sphere encompassing the New York City metropolitan region's high technology industries involving the Internet, new media, telecommunications, digital media, software development, biotechnology, game design, financial technology ("fintech"), and other fields within information technology that are supported by its entrepreneurship ecosystem and venture capital investments. In the first half of 2015, Silicon Alley generated over US$3.7 billion in venture capital investment across a broad spectrum of high technology enterprises, most based in Manhattan, with others in Brooklyn, Queens, and elsewhere in the region. High technology startup companies and employment are growing in New York City and the region, bolstered by the city's position in North America as the leading Internet hub and telecommunications center, including its vicinity to several transatlantic fiber optic trunk lines, New York's intellectual capital, and its extensive outdoor wireless connectivity. Verizon Communications, headquartered at 140 West Street in Lower Manhattan, was at the final stages in 2014 of completing a US$3 billion fiberoptic telecommunications upgrade throughout New York City. As of 2014, New York City hosted 300,000 employees in the tech sector.
rewrite:
Centered in Manhattan, Silicon Alley has become a shorthand term for the broader New York City area's vibrant cluster of tech-related industries. This includes internet services, new media, telecom, digital content, software, biotech, gaming, fintech, and various other IT sectors, all thriving within a dynamic environment of entrepreneurial activity and venture capital funding. In just the initial six months of 2015, venture funding for these diverse tech firms surpassed $3.7 billion. While Manhattan is the primary base, many companies also operate in Brooklyn, Queens, and other parts of the region.

The city and surrounding area are experiencing significant growth in tech startups and jobs. This expansion is fueled by New York's status as North America's premier internet and telecommunications nexus, its proximity to key transatlantic fiber-optic cables, its deep pool of intellectual talent, and its widespread public wireless networks. By 2014, Verizon, based in Lower Manhattan, was finishing a massive $3 billion citywide upgrade to fiber-optic infrastructure. That same year, the technology sector within New York City employed approximately 300,000 people.

input: Having sold more than 300 million records worldwide, Madonna is recognized as the best-selling female recording artist of all time by Guinness World Records. The Recording Industry Association of America (RIAA) listed her as the best-selling female rock artist of the 20th century and the second best-selling female artist in the United States, with 64.5 million certified albums. According to Billboard, Madonna is the highest-grossing solo touring artist of all time, earning US $1.31 billion from her concerts since 1990. She was ranked at number two, behind only The Beatles, on the Billboard Hot 100 All-Time Top Artists, making her the most successful solo artist in the history of American singles chart. Madonna became one of the five founding members of the UK Music Hall of Fame and was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in her first year of eligibility.
rewrite: Madonna holds the Guinness World Record for the top-selling female musician in history, with global record sales exceeding 300 million copies. In the United States, the RIAA certifies her as the leading female rock artist of the 1900s and the second highest-selling female artist overall, based on 64.5 million certified album units. Her concert revenue since 1990 totals $1.31 billion, positioning her as the highest-earning solo touring act ever, per Billboard. That publication also places her as the second-greatest artist of all time on its Hot 100 chart, trailing only The Beatles, which makes her the most accomplished solo performer in the chart's history. Furthermore, she was a charter inductee into the UK Music Hall of Fame and was admitted to the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in her initial eligible year.

input: On 6 April 2011, after his proposed "Plan for Stability and Growth IV" (PEC IV) was rejected by the Parliament, Prime Minister José Sócrates announced on national television that the country would request financial assistance from the IMF and the European Financial Stability Facility, as Greece and the Republic of Ireland had done previously. It was the third time that the Portuguese government had requested external financial aid from the IMF—the first occasion occurred in the late 1970s following the Carnation's Revolution. In October 2011, Moody's Investor Services downgraded nine Portuguese banks due to financial weakness.
rewrite: Following the parliamentary defeat of his "Plan for Stability and Growth IV" on April 6, 2011, Prime Minister José Sócrates publicly declared that Portugal would seek a financial rescue. The country turned to the International Monetary Fund and the European Financial Stability Facility, following the precedents set by Greece and Ireland. This marked Portugal's third appeal to the IMF for such support, the first having been made in the aftermath of the 1970s Carnation Revolution. Later that year, in October, Moody's downgraded nine Portuguese banks, citing their fragile finances.

input: During the 20th century Valencia remained the third most populous city of Spain as its population tripled, rising from 213,550 inhabitants in 1900 to 739,014 in 2000. Valencia was also third in industrial and economic development; notable milestones include urban expansion of the city in the latter 1800s, the creation of the Banco de Valencia in 1900, construction of the Central and Columbus markets, and the construction of the Gare du Nord railway station, completed in 1921. The new century was marked in Valencia with a major event, the Valencian regional exhibition of 1909 (La Exposición Regional Valenciana de 1909), which emulated the national and universal expositions held in other cities. This production was promoted by the Ateneo Mercantil de Valencia (Mercantile Athenaeum of Valencia), especially by its chairman, Tomás Trénor y Palavicino, and had the support of the Government and the Crown; it was officially inaugurated by King Alfonso XIII himself.
rewrite: Throughout the 1900s, Valencia consistently held its position as Spain's third largest city. Its number of residents grew threefold, climbing from roughly 214,000 at the start of the century to nearly 740,000 by its conclusion. Economically and industrially, it also ranked third nationally. Key developments featured the city's outward growth in the late nineteenth century, the founding of the Banco de Valencia in 1900, and the building of several major public structures like the Central and Columbus markets, along with the Gare du Nord train station, finished in 1921. A defining occurrence for Valencia in the new century was the 1909 Valencian Regional Exhibition. Modeled on larger international fairs, this undertaking was championed by the Mercantile Athenaeum of Valencia, particularly its president, Tomás Trénor y Palavicino. It received backing from the state and monarchy, with King Alfonso XIII presiding over the official opening.

input: On the basis of the expansion and development of Yerevan State University a number of higher educational independent Institutions were formed including Medical Institute separated in 1930 which was set up on the basis of medical faculty. In 1980 Yerevan State Medical University was awarded one of the main rewards of the former USSR – the Order of Labor red Banner for training qualified specialists in health care and valuable service in the development of Medical Science. In 1995 YSMI was renamed to YSMU and since 1989 it has been named after Mkhitar Heratsi, the famous medieval doctor. Mkhitar Heratsi was the founder of Armenian Medical school in Cilician Armenia. The great doctor played the same role in Armenian Medical Science as Hippocrates in Western, Galen in Roman, Ibn Sīnā in Arabic medicine.
rewrite: Several independent colleges emerged from the growth of Yerevan State University. Among these was a Medical Institute, established in 1930 from the original university medical department. In recognition of its excellence in educating healthcare professionals and advancing medical research, the institute received a major Soviet honor in 1980: the Order of the Red Banner of Labor. It was renamed Yerevan State Medical University (YSMU) in 1995. Since 1989, the university has borne the name of Mkhitar Heratsi, a celebrated medieval physician who founded Armenia's medical tradition. His foundational influence on Armenian medicine is compared to that of Hippocrates in Greek, Galen in Roman, and Ibn Sīnā in Arabic medical history.

input: Public policy determines the extent to which renewable energy (RE) is to be incorporated into a developed or developing country's generation mix. Energy sector regulators implement that policy—thus affecting the pace and pattern of RE investments and connections to the grid. Energy regulators often have authority to carry out a number of functions that have implications for the financial feasibility of renewable energy projects. Such functions include issuing licenses, setting performance standards, monitoring the performance of regulated firms, determining the price level and structure of tariffs, establishing uniform systems of accounts, arbitrating stakeholder disputes (like interconnection cost allocations), performing management audits, developing agency human resources (expertise), reporting sector and commission activities to government authorities, and coordinating decisions with other government agencies. Thus, regulators make a wide range of decisions that affect the financial outcomes associated with RE investments. In addition, the sector regulator is in a position to give advice to the government regarding the full implications of focusing on climate change or energy security. The energy sector regulator is the natural advocate for efficiency and cost-containment throughout the process of designing and implementing RE policies. Since policies are not self-implementing, energy sector regulators become a key facilitator (or blocker) of renewable energy investments.
rewrite: The integration of renewable energy into a nation's power supply, whether in advanced or emerging economies, is fundamentally shaped by public policy. It falls to energy regulatory bodies to execute this policy, thereby directly influencing the rate and manner of investments in renewables and their linkage to the electricity network. These regulators typically hold powers that critically impact the economic viability of such projects. Their responsibilities span granting operational permits, defining and enforcing quality benchmarks, overseeing utility companies, and establishing both the amount and design of consumer rates. They also implement standardized accounting, resolve conflicts among parties—such as disputes over grid connection expenses—conduct audits, cultivate internal expertise, report to higher government levels, and align actions with other agencies. Consequently, their broad decision-making authority significantly sways the financial returns from renewable ventures. Furthermore, the regulator is uniquely placed to counsel the government on the comprehensive consequences of prioritizing climate goals or energy independence. Acting as a natural proponent for efficiency and controlling expenses, the regulator plays a central role throughout the creation and application of renewable energy strategies. Given that policies do not enact themselves, these regulatory institutions emerge as essential enablers, or potential obstacles, for investments in renewable energy.

input: Uranium is a chemical element with symbol U and atomic number 92. It is a silvery-white metal in the actinide series of the periodic table. A uranium atom has 92 protons and 92 electrons, of which 6 are valence electrons. Uranium is weakly radioactive because all its isotopes are unstable (with half-lives of the six naturally known isotopes, uranium-233 to uranium-238, varying between 69 years and 4.5 billion years). The most common isotopes of uranium are uranium-238 (which has 146 neutrons and accounts for almost 99.3% of the uranium found in nature) and uranium-235 (which has 143 neutrons, accounting for 0.7% of the element found naturally). Uranium has the second highest atomic weight of the primordially occurring elements, lighter only than plutonium. Its density is about 70% higher than that of lead, but slightly lower than that of gold or tungsten. It occurs naturally in low concentrations of a few parts per million in soil, rock and water, and is commercially extracted from uranium-bearing minerals such as uraninite.
rewrite: With the chemical symbol U and atomic number 92, uranium is a silvery-white metallic member of the actinide group. Each atom contains 92 protons and 92 electrons, including six valence electrons. All forms of uranium are slightly radioactive due to the instability of its isotopes; the half-lives for its six natural variants range from 69 years to 4.5 billion years. Predominantly, natural uranium consists of uranium-238, making up roughly 99.3% and containing 146 neutrons, while uranium-235, with 143 neutrons, constitutes about 0.7%. Among the original elements present since Earth's formation, uranium possesses the second greatest atomic mass, surpassed only by plutonium. It is approximately 70% denser than lead, though not as dense as gold or tungsten. Found in trace amounts of a few parts per million within soil, rock, and water, it is industrially obtained from minerals like uraninite.

input: The Logic and Metaphysics have been extensively reprinted, the latter, e.g., at Venice in 1493, 1495, and 1546. Some of his shorter essays on medicine, logic, etc., take a poetical form (the poem on logic was published by Schmoelders in 1836).[citation needed] Two encyclopaedic treatises, dealing with philosophy, are often mentioned. The larger, Al-Shifa' (Sanatio), exists nearly complete in manuscript in the Bodleian Library and elsewhere; part of it on the De Anima appeared at Pavia (1490) as the Liber Sextus Naturalium, and the long account of Ibn Sina's philosophy given by Muhammad al-Shahrastani seems to be mainly an analysis, and in many places a reproduction, of the Al-Shifa'. A shorter form of the work is known as the An-najat (Liberatio). The Latin editions of part of these works have been modified by the corrections which the monastic editors confess that they applied. There is also a حكمت مشرقيه (hikmat-al-mashriqqiyya, in Latin Philosophia Orientalis), mentioned by Roger Bacon, the majority of which is lost in antiquity, which according to Averroes was pantheistic in tone.
rewrite: The works on Logic and Metaphysics have seen numerous reprints, with the Metaphysics, for instance, published in Venice in 1493, 1495, and 1546. Several of his brief medical and logical writings are composed in verse; the logical poem was issued by Schmoelders in 1836. Two comprehensive philosophical compendiums are frequently cited. The more extensive one, Al-Shifa' (Healing), survives almost in full across manuscripts, including at the Bodleian Library. A segment concerning the soul was printed in Pavia (1490) as the Liber Sextus Naturalium. Muhammad al-Shahrastani's detailed summary of Ibn Sina's thought largely examines and frequently replicates the Al-Shifa'. A condensed version is titled An-najat (Deliverance). Latin translations of portions of these texts were altered by the monkish editors, who admitted to making revisions. Another work, the Hikmat-al-mashriqqiyya (Oriental Philosophy), referenced by Roger Bacon, is mostly lost to time. Averroes noted that it leaned toward pantheism.

input: In addition to the call buttons, elevators usually have floor indicators (often illuminated by LED) and direction lanterns. The former are almost universal in cab interiors with more than two stops and may be found outside the elevators as well on one or more of the floors. Floor indicators can consist of a dial with a rotating needle, but the most common types are those with successively illuminated floor indications or LCDs. Likewise, a change of floors or an arrival at a floor is indicated by a sound, depending on the elevator.
rewrite: Elevators typically include floor displays and directional signals alongside call buttons. These interior indicators are nearly standard in cabs serving multiple floors and may also appear outside on certain levels. Common displays feature lights that illuminate each floor in sequence or use LCD screens, rather than older dial-and-needle designs. Additionally, an audible signal often sounds when the elevator reaches or passes a floor, varying by model.

input: An intellectual revitalization of Europe started with the birth of medieval universities in the 12th century. The contact with the Islamic world in Spain and Sicily, and during the Reconquista and the Crusades, allowed Europeans access to scientific Greek and Arabic texts, including the works of Aristotle, Ptolemy, Jābir ibn Hayyān, al-Khwarizmi, Alhazen, Avicenna, and Averroes. European scholars had access to the translation programs of Raymond of Toledo, who sponsored the 12th century Toledo School of Translators from Arabic to Latin. Later translators like Michael Scotus would learn Arabic in order to study these texts directly. The European universities aided materially in the translation and propagation of these texts and started a new infrastructure which was needed for scientific communities. In fact, European university put many works about the natural world and the study of nature at the center of its curriculum, with the result that the "medieval university laid far greater emphasis on science than does its modern counterpart and descendent."
rewrite: A resurgence of intellectual life in Europe commenced during the 12th century with the establishment of the first medieval universities. Through interactions with Islamic societies in regions like Spain and Sicily, as well as via the Crusades and Reconquista, Europeans rediscovered a wealth of ancient Greek and Arabic scholarly writings. These included pivotal works by figures such as Aristotle, Ptolemy, and numerous Islamic scientists and philosophers like Avicenna and Alhazen. Translation efforts, notably those sponsored by Raymond of Toledo, converted these texts from Arabic into Latin. Subsequent scholars, including Michael Scotus, acquired Arabic to engage with the originals directly. These emerging academic institutions provided crucial support for translating and disseminating such knowledge, creating an essential foundation for scientific discourse. By placing the study of the natural world at the heart of education, the medieval university arguably fostered a greater focus on science than many contemporary academic institutions do.

input: J. Edgar Hoover served as Director from 1924 to 1972, a combined 48 years with the BOI, DOI, and FBI. He was chiefly responsible for creating the Scientific Crime Detection Laboratory, or the FBI Laboratory, which officially opened in 1932, as part of his work to professionalize investigations by the government. Hoover was substantially involved in most major cases and projects that the FBI handled during his tenure. After Hoover's death, Congress passed legislation that limited the tenure of future FBI Directors to ten years.
rewrite: J. Edgar Hoover led the Bureau of Investigation and its successor, the FBI, for 48 years beginning in 1924. A key part of his drive to modernize federal investigations was founding the FBI Laboratory, established in 1932. He played a central role in the Bureau's significant operations throughout his lengthy service. Following his death in 1972, lawmakers enacted a ten-year term limit for all subsequent Directors.

input: New York is a global hub of international business and commerce. In 2012, New York City topped the first Global Economic Power Index, published by The Atlantic (to be differentiated from a namesake list published by the Martin Prosperity Institute), with cities ranked according to criteria reflecting their presence on similar lists as published by other entities. The city is a major center for banking and finance, retailing, world trade, transportation, tourism, real estate, new media as well as traditional media, advertising, legal services, accountancy, insurance, theater, fashion, and the arts in the United States; while Silicon Alley, metonymous for New York's broad-spectrum high technology sphere, continues to expand. The Port of New York and New Jersey is also a major economic engine, handling record cargo volume in the first half of 2014.
rewrite: New York stands as a worldwide center for trade and finance. In 2012, it led the inaugural Global Economic Power Index by The Atlantic, which rated urban areas based on their frequent appearance on various influential rankings from different organizations. The metropolis is a key hub for numerous sectors including finance, retail, international commerce, logistics, hospitality, property, both digital and conventional media, marketing, law, accounting, insurance, theater, fashion, and arts. Silicon Alley, representing the city's diverse tech industry, keeps growing. Additionally, the Port of New York and New Jersey remains a vital economic force, moving unprecedented amounts of goods in early 2014.

input: More complex inflection is still found in certain lexicalized expressions like de heer des huizes (literally, the man of the house), etc. These are usually remnants of cases (in this instance, the genitive case which is still used in German, cf. Der Herr des Hauses) and other inflections no longer in general use today. In such lexicalized expressions remnants of strong and weak nouns can be found too, e.g. in het jaar des Heren (Anno Domini), where "-en" is actually the genitive ending of the weak noun. Also in this case, German retains this feature. Though the genitive is widely avoided in speech.
rewrite: Certain fixed phrases retain more intricate inflection patterns, such as "de heer des huizes" (the man of the house). These are typically surviving fragments of grammatical cases, like the genitive, which has otherwise fallen out of common usage. Similar traces of older strong and weak noun inflections appear, for example, in "het jaar des Heren" (Anno Domini), where the "-en" ending derives from a weak noun's genitive form. German still commonly employs such constructions, whereas the genitive case is largely omitted in everyday spoken language.

input: In North America, especially the first half of this period, people experienced considerable prosperity in the Roaring Twenties. The social and societal upheaval known as the Roaring Twenties began in North America and spread to Europe in the aftermath of World War I. The Roaring Twenties, often called "The Jazz Age", saw an exposition of social, artistic, and cultural dynamism. 'Normalcy' returned to politics, jazz music blossomed, the flapper redefined modern womanhood, Art Deco peaked. The spirit of the Roaring Twenties was marked by a general feeling of discontinuity associated with modernity, a break with traditions. Everything seemed to be feasible through modern technology. New technologies, especially automobiles, movies and radio proliferated 'modernity' to a large part of the population. The 1920s saw the general favor of practicality, in architecture as well as in daily life. The 1920s was further distinguished by several inventions and discoveries, extensive industrial growth and the rise in consumer demand and aspirations, and significant changes in lifestyle.
rewrite: The 1920s, particularly in North America, were a time of widespread economic well-being and profound social change. This era, frequently termed the Jazz Age, originated in the aftermath of the First World War and was characterized by immense cultural and creative energy. A sense of returning to political stability coincided with the flourishing of jazz, the emergence of the flapper as a new feminine ideal, and the height of Art Deco style. The period's ethos involved a distinct rupture with past conventions, embracing a modern sense that anything was possible with advancing technology. Innovations like the automobile, radio, and cinema brought this contemporary feeling to the masses. There was a growing emphasis on functional design in both buildings and everyday objects. This decade was also defined by rapid industrial expansion, numerous technological advances, increasing consumer desires, and dramatic shifts in how people lived.

input: In October 2008, Tom Benson announced that the New Orleans VooDoo were ceasing operations and folding "based on circumstances currently affecting the league and the team". Shortly thereafter, an article in Sports Business Journal announced that the AFL had a tentative agreement to sell a $100 million stake in the league to Platinum Equity; in exchange, Platinum Equity would create a centralized, single-entity business model that would streamline league and team operations and allow the league to be more profitable. Benson's move to shut down the VooDoo came during the Platinum Equity conference call, leading to speculation that he had folded because of the deal.
rewrite: In October 2008, Tom Benson declared that the New Orleans VooDoo would be closing down, citing conditions impacting both the franchise and the Arena Football League. Around the same time, a report indicated the AFL had provisionally agreed to sell a $100 million share to Platinum Equity. This investment was to fund a consolidated league structure designed to increase efficiency and profits. Benson’s decision to terminate the team occurred during discussions about this deal, fueling rumors that the agreement directly influenced his choice.

input: By 1900, 7,531 people lived in the city. The population increased gradually to 13,913 in 1910. At about this time, the U.S. Veterans Administration had begun construction on the present Veterans Hospital. Many veterans who had been gassed in World War I and were in need of respiratory therapy began coming to Tucson after the war, due to the clean dry air. Over the following years the city continued to grow, with the population increasing to 20,292 in 1920 and 36,818 in 1940. In 2006 the population of Pima County, in which Tucson is located, passed one million while the City of Tucson's population was 535,000.
rewrite: At the dawn of the twentieth century, the city was home to 7,531 residents. This number rose steadily to 13,913 by 1910. Around that period, construction commenced on what is now the Veterans Hospital. Following World War I, numerous veterans suffering from gas exposure and requiring treatment for their lungs were drawn to Tucson for its arid, pure atmosphere. Subsequent decades saw ongoing expansion, with inhabitants numbering 20,292 in 1920 and 36,818 by 1940. By 2006, Pima County, containing Tucson, exceeded one million people, while the city itself had 535,000 residents.

input: According to the same study, even though digital piracy inflicts additional costs on the production side of media, it also offers the main access to media goods in developing countries. The strong tradeoffs that favor using digital piracy in developing economies dictate the current neglected law enforcements toward digital piracy. In China, the issue of digital infringement is not merely legal, but social – originating from the high demand for cheap and affordable goods as well as the governmental connections of the businesses which produce such goods.
rewrite: The research indicates that while media producers face extra expenses due to digital piracy, it remains the primary way people in developing nations access media. This significant benefit explains why anti-piracy laws are often weakly enforced there. In China, digital infringement is a social problem as much as a legal one, driven by widespread demand for low-cost goods and the close ties between government and the businesses supplying them.

input: Some of the most important surviving works of Old English literature are Beowulf, an epic poem; the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle, a record of early English history; the Franks Casket, an inscribed early whalebone artefact; and Cædmon's Hymn, a Christian religious poem. There are also a number of extant prose works, such as sermons and saints' lives, biblical translations, and translated Latin works of the early Church Fathers, legal documents, such as laws and wills, and practical works on grammar, medicine, and geography. Still, poetry is considered the heart of Old English literature. Nearly all Anglo-Saxon authors are anonymous, with a few exceptions, such as Bede and Cædmon. Cædmon, the earliest English poet we know by name, served as a lay brother in the monastery at Whitby.
rewrite: Key works from the Old English period include the epic poem Beowulf, the historical Anglo-Saxon Chronicle, the carved whalebone Franks Casket, and the religious verse of Cædmon's Hymn. Prose writings also survive, encompassing sermons, biographies of saints, Bible translations, and works by early Church Fathers rendered into English, alongside legal records and instructional texts on topics like grammar and science. However, poetic works form the core of this literary tradition. Most writers from this era are unknown, with notable exceptions like the scholar Bede and the poet Cædmon, who was a lay brother at Whitby Abbey and is the first English poet known by name.

input: However, during this period, major figures and artists in the scene began leaning away from underground aesthetics. In the music press, the increasingly esoteric writing of post-punk publications soon began to alienate their readerships; it is estimated that within several years, NME suffered the loss of half its circulation. Writers like Paul Morley began advocating "overground brightness" instead of the experimental sensibilities promoted in early years. Morley's own musical collaboration with engineer Gary Langan and programmer J. J. Jeczalik, the Art of Noise, would attempt to bring sampled and electronic sounds to the pop mainstream. A variety of more pop-oriented groups, including ABC, the Associates, Adam and the Ants and Bow Wow Wow (the latter two managed by former Sex Pistols manager Malcolm McLaren) emerged in tandem with the development of the New Romantic subcultural scene. Emphasizing glamour, fashion, and escapism in distinction to the experimental seriousness of earlier post-punk groups, the club-oriented scene drew some suspicion from denizens of the movement.
rewrite: During this time, key influencers and musicians started moving from underground styles toward more accessible approaches. Music journalism reflected this shift, as the obscure language favored by post-punk magazines gradually pushed readers away; reports suggest that publications like NME saw their readership drop by half in just a few years. Critics such as Paul Morley championed a turn toward mainstream appeal, rejecting the earlier emphasis on avant-garde experimentation. Morley himself helped form the Art of Noise with Gary Langan and J. J. Jeczalik, a project aimed at introducing sampled and electronic music to wider pop audiences. Concurrently, the rise of the New Romantic subculture brought forth pop-focused acts like ABC, the Associates, Adam and the Ants, and Bow Wow Wow—the latter two guided by former Sex Pistols manager Malcolm McLaren. This club-centered movement, which stressed glamour, fashion, and fantasy over the rigorous experimentalism of prior post-punk, was met with some skepticism from those within the original scene.

input: Notably, a statute does not disappear automatically merely because it has been found unconstitutional; it must be deleted by a subsequent statute. Many federal and state statutes have remained on the books for decades after they were ruled to be unconstitutional. However, under the principle of stare decisis, no sensible lower court will enforce an unconstitutional statute, and any court that does so will be reversed by the Supreme Court. Conversely, any court that refuses to enforce a constitutional statute (where such constitutionality has been expressly established in prior cases) will risk reversal by the Supreme Court.
rewrite: A law does not simply vanish once declared unconstitutional; it must be formally repealed by later legislation. Consequently, numerous federal and state laws have stayed officially recorded for years after such rulings. Yet, following stare decisis, no reasonable lower court will apply a statute known to be invalid, and doing so guarantees reversal by the Supreme Court. Similarly, if a court declines to enforce a statute whose constitutionality is clearly settled by precedent, it also faces likely reversal by the higher court.

input: Since life began on Earth, five major mass extinctions and several minor events have led to large and sudden drops in biodiversity. The Phanerozoic eon (the last 540 million years) marked a rapid growth in biodiversity via the Cambrian explosion—a period during which the majority of multicellular phyla first appeared. The next 400 million years included repeated, massive biodiversity losses classified as mass extinction events. In the Carboniferous, rainforest collapse led to a great loss of plant and animal life. The Permian–Triassic extinction event, 251 million years ago, was the worst; vertebrate recovery took 30 million years. The most recent, the Cretaceous–Paleogene extinction event, occurred 65 million years ago and has often attracted more attention than others because it resulted in the extinction of the dinosaurs.
rewrite: Throughout Earth's history, biodiversity has experienced numerous sharp declines due to catastrophic events. The Phanerozoic eon, spanning the past 540 million years, began with a swift surge in life forms known as the Cambrian explosion, when most complex animal groups originated. However, the subsequent eras were punctuated by severe die-offs. Among these, the disintegration of Carboniferous rainforests caused tremendous reductions in flora and fauna. The most devastating crisis occurred roughly 251 million years ago at the Permian-Triassic boundary, after which vertebrates required tens of millions of years to reestablish themselves. More familiar is the Cretaceous-Paleogene event 65 million years ago, which ended the age of dinosaurs and continues to capture significant public and scientific interest.

input: San Diego was ranked as the 20th-safest city in America in 2013 by Business Insider. According to Forbes magazine, San Diego was the ninth-safest city in the top 10 list of safest cities in the U.S. in 2010. Like most major cities, San Diego had a declining crime rate from 1990 to 2000. Crime in San Diego increased in the early 2000s. In 2004, San Diego had the sixth lowest crime rate of any U.S. city with over half a million residents. From 2002 to 2006, the crime rate overall dropped 0.8%, though not evenly by category. While violent crime decreased 12.4% during this period, property crime increased 1.1%. Total property crimes per 100,000 people were lower than the national average in 2008.
rewrite: In 2013, Business Insider placed San Diego as America's 20th safest city. Earlier, Forbes had listed it as the ninth safest among U.S. cities in 2010. Mirroring a broader national trend, the city saw crime fall from 1990 through 2000, before a rise in the early 2000s. By 2004, it held the sixth lowest crime rate among U.S. cities with populations exceeding 500,000. Between 2002 and 2006, the overall crime rate declined slightly by 0.8%, but this change was not uniform. Violent crime fell by 12.4%, whereas property crime rose by 1.1%. In 2008, the rate of property crimes per 100,000 residents remained below the national average.

input: Absolute idealism is G. W. F. Hegel's account of how existence is comprehensible as an all-inclusive whole. Hegel called his philosophy "absolute" idealism in contrast to the "subjective idealism" of Berkeley and the "transcendental idealism" of Kant and Fichte, which were not based on a critique of the finite and a dialectical philosophy of history as Hegel's idealism was. The exercise of reason and intellect enables the philosopher to know ultimate historical reality, the phenomenological constitution of self-determination, the dialectical development of self-awareness and personality in the realm of History.
rewrite: Hegel's system of absolute idealism presents reality as a fully coherent and integrated totality. He distinguished his approach from the subjective idealism of Berkeley and the transcendental idealism of Kant and Fichte. Hegel's framework is unique for its critique of finite limitations and its dialectical interpretation of history. Through rational thought, one can comprehend the fundamental nature of historical reality, the structure of self-determination, and the dialectical progression of self-consciousness and individuality within History.

input: Her fourth studio album 4 was released on June 28, 2011 in the US. 4 sold 310,000 copies in its first week and debuted atop the Billboard 200 chart, giving Beyoncé her fourth consecutive number-one album in the US. The album was preceded by two of its singles "Run the World (Girls)" and "Best Thing I Never Had", which both attained moderate success. The fourth single "Love on Top" was a commercial success in the US. 4 also produced four other singles; "Party", "Countdown", "I Care" and "End of Time". "Eat, Play, Love", a cover story written by Beyoncé for Essence that detailed her 2010 career break, won her a writing award from the New York Association of Black Journalists. In late 2011, she took the stage at New York's Roseland Ballroom for four nights of special performances: the 4 Intimate Nights with Beyoncé concerts saw the performance of her 4 album to a standing room only.
rewrite: Beyoncé's fourth studio album, titled *4*, arrived in the United States on June 28, 2011. It achieved immediate commercial success, moving 310,000 units in its opening week and landing at number one on the Billboard 200. This marked her fourth US chart-topping album in a row. The project was promoted by several singles. The earlier releases "Run the World (Girls)" and "Best Thing I Never Had" saw modest performance, while the later track "Love on Top" became a significant hit. Other singles from the album included "Party," "Countdown," "I Care," and "End of Time." That same year, Beyoncé earned a writing prize from the New York Association of Black Journalists for her Essence magazine essay "Eat, Play, Love," which recounted her decision to step back from work in 2010. Later in 2011, she held a series of exclusive concerts at New York's Roseland Ballroom. These four sold-out shows, billed as *4 Intimate Nights with Beyoncé*, featured live renditions of the entire album.

input: Presbyterians distinguish themselves from other denominations by doctrine, institutional organization (or "church order") and worship; often using a "Book of Order" to regulate common practice and order. The origins of the Presbyterian churches are in Calvinism. Many branches of Presbyterianism are remnants of previous splits from larger groups. Some of the splits have been due to doctrinal controversy, while some have been caused by disagreement concerning the degree to which those ordained to church office should be required to agree with the Westminster Confession of Faith, which historically serves as an important confessional document – second only to the Bible, yet directing particularities in the standardization and translation of the Bible – in Presbyterian churches.
rewrite: Presbyterian churches set themselves apart through their theological beliefs, structural governance, and forms of worship, frequently guided by an official manual. Their roots are found in the Calvinist tradition. Numerous Presbyterian groups emerged from historical divisions within broader movements. These separations sometimes resulted from theological disputes, and other times from conflicts over how strictly ordained leaders must adhere to the Westminster Confession of Faith. This historic statement is a foundational creed for Presbyterians, subordinate only to Scripture itself, and it also provides specific guidance for standardizing and interpreting the Bible.

input: In 2004 the Central African Republic Bush War began as forces opposed to Bozizé took up arms against his government. In May 2005 Bozizé won a presidential election that excluded Patassé and in 2006 fighting continued between the government and the rebels. In November 2006, Bozizé's government requested French military support to help them repel rebels who had taken control of towns in the country's northern regions. Though the initially public details of the agreement pertained to logistics and intelligence, the French assistance eventually included strikes by Mirage jets against rebel positions.
rewrite: The Central African Republic's Bush War commenced in 2004 with armed opposition to President Bozizé. After winning a 2005 election that barred former leader Patassé, Bozizé continued to face rebel conflict into 2006. That November, his administration sought French aid to retake northern towns captured by insurgents. While early terms of the deal focused on logistical and intelligence support, France later escalated its involvement to include aerial attacks by Mirage fighter planes on rebel strongholds.

input: Kerry's paternal grandparents, shoe businessman Frederick A. "Fred" Kerry and musician Ida Lowe, were immigrants from the Austro-Hungarian Empire. Fred was born as "Fritz Kohn" before he and Ida took on the "Kerry" name and moved to the United States. Fred and Ida were born Jewish, and converted to Catholicism together in Austria. His maternal ancestors were of Scottish and English descent, and his maternal grandfather James Grant Forbes II was a member of the Forbes family, while his maternal grandmother Margaret Tyndal Winthrop was a member of the Dudley–Winthrop family. Margaret's paternal grandfather Robert Charles Winthrop served as the 22nd Speaker of the U.S. House of Representatives. Robert's father was Governor Thomas Lindall Winthrop. Thomas' father John Still Winthrop was a great-great-grandson of Massachusetts Bay Colony Governor John Winthrop and great-grandson of Governor Thomas Dudley. Through his mother, John is a first cousin once removed of French politician Brice Lalonde.
rewrite: Kerry's grandparents on his father's side, Frederick A. "Fred" Kerry and Ida Lowe, emigrated from the Austro-Hungarian Empire. Fred, originally named Fritz Kohn, adopted the surname Kerry with Ida prior to their relocation to America. Both were born into Jewish families and jointly converted to Catholicism while still in Austria. On his mother's side, his forebears were Scottish and English. His maternal grandfather, James Grant Forbes II, belonged to the Forbes family, and his maternal grandmother, Margaret Tyndal Winthrop, was part of the Dudley–Winthrop lineage. Margaret's grandfather, Robert Charles Winthrop, was the 22nd Speaker of the U.S. House. Robert's father, Thomas Lindall Winthrop, served as a governor. Thomas' father, John Still Winthrop, was a direct descendant of Massachusetts Bay Colony Governor John Winthrop and Governor Thomas Dudley. Through this maternal line, John is a first cousin once removed of the French political figure Brice Lalonde.

input: In 680 Ibn al-Zubayr fled Medina for Mecca. Hearing about Husayn's opposition to Yazid I, the people of Kufa sent to Husayn asking him to take over with their support. Al-Husayn sent his cousin Muslim bin Agail to verify if they would rally behind him. When the news reached Yazid I, he sent Ubayd-Allah bin Ziyad, ruler of Basrah, with the instruction to prevent the people of Kufa rallying behind Al-Husayn. Ubayd-Allah bin Ziyad managed to disperse the crowd that gathered around Muslim bin Agail and captured him. Realizing Ubayd-Allah bin Ziyad had been instructed to prevent Husayn from establishing support in Kufa, Muslim bin Agail requested a message to be sent to Husayn to prevent his immigration to Kufa. The request was denied and Ubayd-Allah bin Ziyad killed Muslim bin Agail. While Ibn al-Zubayr would stay in Mecca until his death, Husayn decided to travel on to Kufa with his family, unaware of the lack of support there. Husayn and his family were intercepted by Yazid I's forces led by Amru bin Saad, Shamar bin Thi Al-Joshan, and Hussain bin Tamim, who fought Al-Husayn and his male family members until they were killed. There were 200 people in Husayn's caravan, many of whom were women, including his sisters, wives, daughters and their children. The women and children from Husayn's camp were taken as prisoners of war and led back to Damascus to be presented to Yazid I. They remained imprisoned until public opinion turned against him as word of Husayn's death and his family's capture spread. They were then granted passage back to Medina. The sole adult male survivor from the caravan was Ali ibn Husayn who was with fever too ill to fight when the caravan was attacked.
rewrite:
In the year 680, Ibn al-Zubayr escaped from Medina to Mecca. Learning of Husayn ibn Ali’s refusal to pledge allegiance to the caliph Yazid I, residents of Kufa dispatched messengers urging Husayn to assume leadership, promising their backing. To confirm their commitment, Husayn directed his cousin, Muslim ibn Aqil, to assess the situation in Kufa. Upon discovering these developments, Yazid I ordered Ubayd Allah ibn Ziyad, the governor of Basra, to stop the Kufans from aligning with Husayn. Ibn Ziyad successfully broke up the assembly supporting Muslim ibn Aqil and took him prisoner. Recognizing that Ibn Ziyad’s mission was to block any base for Husayn in Kufa, Muslim sought to send a warning to Husayn, advising him not to come. This appeal was refused, and Muslim was executed.

Meanwhile, Ibn al-Zubayr remained in Mecca, where he would later perish. Unaware that support in Kufa had collapsed and that no safe haven awaited, Husayn journeyed toward the city with his household. En route, his caravan was confronted by Yazid’s army, commanded by figures such as Umar ibn Sa’d and Shimr ibn Dhil-Jawshan. In the ensuing conflict, Husayn and the adult males with him were slain. The traveling party numbered around two hundred, a majority being women and children from his immediate family. Following the battle, these surviving women and children were seized as captives and transported to Damascus to be displayed before Yazid I. They were held in captivity until growing public outrage over Husayn’s killing and the imprisonment of his family forced their release. They were eventually allowed to return to Medina. The only grown man to survive the ordeal was Ali ibn Husayn, who was spared because he lay gravely ill and unable to fight when the attack occurred.

input: Between 1963 and 1965, there was a "downtown boom" that led to the construction of more than 700 buildings in the city. In 1968, Virginia Commonwealth University was created by the merger of the Medical College of Virginia with the Richmond Professional Institute. In 1970, Richmond's borders expanded by an additional 27 square miles (70 km2) on the south. After several years of court cases in which Chesterfield County fought annexation, more than 47,000 people who once were Chesterfield County residents found themselves within the city's perimeters on January 1, 1970. In 1996, still-sore tensions arose amid controversy involved in placing a statue of African American Richmond native and tennis star Arthur Ashe to the famed series of statues of Confederate heroes of the Civil War on Monument Avenue. After several months of controversy, the bronze statue of Ashe was finally completed on Monument Avenue facing the opposite direction from the Confederate Heroes on July 10, 1996.
rewrite: From 1963 to 1965, a surge of development in the city center resulted in over seven hundred new structures being erected. Virginia Commonwealth University was formed in 1968 through the combination of the Richmond Professional Institute and the Medical College of Virginia. The city's area grew significantly in 1970, extending its southern boundary by roughly seventy square kilometers. This followed protracted legal disputes with Chesterfield County over the annexation, which ultimately brought over forty-seven thousand former county inhabitants into Richmond at the start of that year. In 1996, a contentious debate emerged regarding the installation of a monument honoring Arthur Ashe, a renowned African American tennis player from Richmond, alongside statues commemorating Confederate figures on Monument Avenue. Following months of public dispute, a bronze sculpture of Ashe was unveiled on the avenue on July 10, 1996, positioned to face away from the earlier monuments.

input: Kathmandu is a center for art in Nepal, displaying the work of contemporary artists in the country and also collections of historical artists. Patan in particular is an ancient city noted for its fine arts and crafts. Art in Kathmandu is vibrant, demonstrating a fusion of traditionalism and modern art, derived from a great number of national, Asian, and global influences. Nepali art is commonly divided into two areas: the idealistic traditional painting known as Paubhas in Nepal and perhaps more commonly known as Thangkas in Tibet, closely linked to the country's religious history and on the other hand the contemporary western-style painting, including nature-based compositions or abstract artwork based on Tantric elements and social themes of which painters in Nepal are well noted for. Internationally, the British-based charity, the Kathmandu Contemporary Art Centre is involved with promoting arts in Kathmandu.
rewrite: Kathmandu serves as Nepal's artistic hub, showcasing both modern creations and historical collections. The ancient city of Patan is especially renowned for its exquisite arts and crafts. The art scene here is dynamic, blending traditional forms with contemporary styles, influenced by local, Asian, and worldwide trends. Nepali art is typically categorized into two main streams. One is the idealized traditional Paubha painting, also called Thangka in Tibet, deeply connected to religious heritage. The other is modern painting in a Western style, featuring nature scenes, abstract works with Tantric motifs, and social commentary, for which Nepali artists are widely recognized. Globally, institutions like the UK charity, the Kathmandu Contemporary Art Centre, work to advance the city's arts.

input: The Faraday constant F is the charge of one mole of electrons, equal to the Avogadro constant NA multiplied by the elementary charge e. It can be determined by careful electrolysis experiments, measuring the amount of silver dissolved from an electrode in a given time and for a given electric current. In practice, it is measured in conventional electrical units, and so given the symbol F90. Substituting the definitions of NA and e, and converting from conventional electrical units to SI units, gives the relation to the Planck constant.
rewrite: The Faraday constant, denoted as F, represents the total electric charge carried by one mole of electrons. It is calculated by multiplying the Avogadro number by the charge of a single electron. This value is often determined through precise electrolysis, observing the mass of silver removed from an electrode by a known current over time. When expressed in standard electrical units as F90, and using the definitions of its components converted to SI units, it establishes a direct link to the Planck constant.

input: Most MIs occur due to coronary artery disease. Risk factors include high blood pressure, smoking, diabetes, lack of exercise, obesity, high blood cholesterol, poor diet, and excessive alcohol intake, among others. The mechanism of an MI often involves the complete blockage of a coronary artery caused by a rupture of an atherosclerotic plaque. MIs are less commonly caused by coronary artery spasms, which may be due to cocaine, significant emotional stress, and extreme cold, among others. A number of tests are useful to help with diagnosis, including electrocardiograms (ECGs), blood tests, and coronary angiography. An ECG may confirm an ST elevation MI if ST elevation is present. Commonly used blood tests include troponin and less often creatine kinase MB.
rewrite: Most heart attacks are triggered by coronary artery disease. Contributing conditions such as hypertension, tobacco use, diabetes, physical inactivity, excess body weight, elevated cholesterol, unhealthy eating, and heavy drinking can increase risk. Typically, a heart attack happens when an unstable plaque in a coronary artery ruptures, leading to a total obstruction. In rarer instances, severe spasms in these arteries—potentially induced by substances like cocaine, intense emotional distress, or exposure to severe cold—are the cause. Diagnosis relies on various assessments. Electrocardiograms can identify a specific type of heart attack if certain elevations are detected. Blood tests, primarily checking troponin levels and occasionally creatine kinase MB, along with coronary angiography, are also key diagnostic tools.

input: The body’s capability to react to antigen depends on a person's age, antigen type, maternal factors and the area where the antigen is presented. Neonates are said to be in a state of physiological immunodeficiency, because both their innate and adaptive immunological responses are greatly suppressed. Once born, a child’s immune system responds favorably to protein antigens while not as well to glycoproteins and polysaccharides. In fact, many of the infections acquired by neonates are caused by low virulence organisms like Staphylococcus and Pseudomonas. In neonates, opsonic activity and the ability to activate the complement cascade is very limited. For example, the mean level of C3 in a newborn is approximately 65% of that found in the adult. Phagocytic activity is also greatly impaired in newborns. This is due to lower opsonic activity, as well as diminished up-regulation of integrin and selectin receptors, which limit the ability of neutrophils to interact with adhesion molecules in the endothelium. Their monocytes are slow and have a reduced ATP production, which also limits the newborn's phagocytic activity. Although, the number of total lymphocytes is significantly higher than in adults, the cellular and humoral immunity is also impaired. Antigen-presenting cells in newborns have a reduced capability to activate T cells. Also, T cells of a newborn proliferate poorly and produce very small amounts of cytokines like IL-2, IL-4, IL-5, IL-12, and IFN-g which limits their capacity to activate the humoral response as well as the phagocitic activity of macrophage. B cells develop early during gestation but are not fully active.
rewrite: The effectiveness of an individual's immune response to an antigen is influenced by several factors, including age, the nature of the antigen itself, influences from the mother, and the specific site of exposure. Newborns experience a condition of natural immune deficiency, as both their immediate and learned defense mechanisms are not fully developed. After birth, an infant's immune defenses react more robustly to protein-based antigens compared to those composed of sugars or complex carbohydrates. Consequently, infections in newborns are often caused by typically less aggressive pathogens, such as certain bacteria. Key immune functions like opsonization and complement activation are notably deficient; for instance, a critical complement protein is present at only about two-thirds of adult levels. Phagocytosis, the process by which cells engulf invaders, is also significantly hindered. This results from weak opsonization and inadequate expression of certain surface receptors, impairing white blood cells' ability to adhere to and migrate through blood vessel walls. Furthermore, their monocytes are sluggish and generate less energy, further reducing phagocytic efficiency. While newborns possess a higher total count of lymphocytes, both cell-mediated and antibody-based immunity are functionally limited. Their antigen-presenting cells are less effective at stimulating T cells, and those T cells exhibit poor multiplication and produce minimal signaling proteins, which curtails the activation of antibody responses and macrophage activity. Although B cells emerge early in fetal development, they remain largely inactive at birth.

input: Federalism in the United States is the evolving relationship between state governments and the federal government of the United States. American government has evolved from a system of dual federalism to one of associative federalism. In "Federalist No. 46," James Madison asserted that the states and national government "are in fact but different agents and trustees of the people, constituted with different powers." Alexander Hamilton, writing in "Federalist No. 28," suggested that both levels of government would exercise authority to the citizens' benefit: "If their [the peoples'] rights are invaded by either, they can make use of the other as the instrument of redress." (1)
rewrite: The structure of federalism in America describes the changing dynamic between national and state authorities. Over time, the U.S. system has shifted from a model of distinct dual powers to one of cooperative association. James Madison, in the Federalist Papers, described both state and federal governments as separate representatives of the populace, each granted unique responsibilities. Similarly, Alexander Hamilton argued that citizens could seek protection from one governing level if the other overstepped, utilizing each as a check and a means to defend their liberties.

input: Of the approximately 850 municipalities of Thuringia, 126 are classed as towns (within a district) or cities (forming their own urban district). Most of the towns are small with a population of less than 10,000; only the ten biggest ones have a population greater than 30,000. The first towns emerged during the 12th century, whereas the latest ones received town status only in the 20th century. Today, all municipalities within districts are equal in law, whether they are towns or villages. Independent cities (i.e. urban districts) have greater powers (the same as any district) than towns within a district.
rewrite: Thuringia contains around 850 municipalities, of which 126 hold the designation of town or city. The majority are small, with fewer than 10,000 residents, and only its ten largest exceed 30,000 inhabitants. The earliest towns appeared in the 1100s, with the most recent gaining their status in the 1900s. Legally, all municipalities inside a district are equal, be they towns or villages. However, independent cities that form their own urban districts possess broader authority, equivalent to that of an entire district.

input: In 1976 Montini became the first pontiff in modern history to deny the accusation of homosexuality. Published by his order in January 1976 was a homily Persona Humana: Declaration on Certain Questions concerning Sexual Ethics, which outlawed pre or extra-marital sex, condemned homosexuality, and forbade masturbation. It provoked French author and former diplomat Roger Peyrefitte, in an interview published by the magazine Tempo, to accuse Montini of hypocrisy, and of having a longtime lover who was a movie actor. According to rumors prevalent both inside the Curia and in Italian society, this was Paolo Carlini, who had a bit part as a hairdresser in the Audrey Hepburn film Roman Holiday. Peyrefitte had previously published the accusation in two books, but the interview (previously published in a French gay magazine) brought the rumors to a wider public and caused an uproar. In a brief address to a crowd of approximately 20,000 in St. Peters Square on April 18, Montini called the charges "horrible and slanderous insinuations" and appealed for prayers on his behalf. Special prayers for Montini were said in all Italian Roman Catholic churches in "a day of consolation". In 1984 a New York Times correspondent repeated the allegations.
rewrite: In 1976, Pope Paul VI (born Giovanni Battista Montini) made history as the first modern pope to publicly refute claims of being homosexual. That January, under his directive, the Vatican issued the declaration "Persona Humana," addressing sexual ethics. This document prohibited sexual activity outside of marriage, denounced homosexual acts, and banned masturbation. This stance prompted French writer and ex-diplomat Roger Peyrefitte to publicly charge the pope with hypocrisy during an interview with Tempo magazine, alleging Montini had a long-term relationship with a film actor. Widespread gossip within the Vatican and Italian circles identified this man as Paolo Carlini, an actor with a minor role in "Roman Holiday." While Peyrefitte had written about this in earlier books, the magazine interview, which had first appeared in a French publication for gay readers, spread the scandal to a broader audience and created a major controversy. Addressing roughly 20,000 people in St. Peter's Square on April 18, Montini denounced the allegations as "horrible and slanderous insinuations" and asked for prayers. All Catholic churches across Italy subsequently held a "day of consolation," offering special prayers for the pontiff. The claims resurfaced in 1984 when a correspondent for The New York Times reported them again.

input: In November 2008, 720p HD support was added. At the time of the 720p launch, the YouTube player was changed from a 4:3 aspect ratio to a widescreen 16:9. With this new feature, YouTube began a switchover to H.264/MPEG-4 AVC as its default video compression format. In November 2009, 1080p HD support was added. In July 2010, YouTube announced that it had launched a range of videos in 4K format, which allows a resolution of up to 4096×3072 pixels. In June 2015, support for 8K resolution was added, with the videos playing at 7680×4320 pixels.
rewrite: In late 2008, YouTube introduced 720p high-definition playback, simultaneously updating its video player to a 16:9 widescreen format from the older 4:3 shape. This shift also marked the platform's adoption of H.264/MPEG-4 AVC as its primary compression standard. The following year brought 1080p HD capability. By mid-2010, the service began offering select 4K content, supporting resolutions as high as 4096x3072 pixels. Finally, in the summer of 2015, YouTube expanded its offerings to include 8K resolution videos, which display at 7680x4320 pixels.

input: In the controversial elections in 2002, Sassou won with almost 90% of the vote cast. His two main rivals, Lissouba and Bernard Kolelas, were prevented from competing and the only remaining credible rival, Andre Milongo, advised his supporters to boycott the elections and then withdrew from the race. A new constitution, agreed upon by referendum in January 2002, granted the president new powers, extended his term to seven years, and introduced a new bicameral assembly. International observers took issue with the organization of the presidential election and the constitutional referendum, both of which were reminiscent in their organization of Congo's era of the one-party state. Following the presidential elections, fighting restarted in the Pool region between government forces and rebels led by Pastor Ntumi; a peace treaty to end the conflict was signed in April 2003.
rewrite: During the disputed 2002 polls, Denis Sassou Nguesso secured a victory with nearly ninety percent of the ballots. His primary opponents, Pascal Lissouba and Bernard Kolelas, were barred from participation, while the sole other significant candidate, Andre Milongo, urged a boycott before exiting the contest. Earlier that year, a January referendum had approved a revised constitution, which amplified presidential authority, established a two-chamber parliament, and lengthened the presidential term to seven years. International monitors criticized the conduct of both the referendum and the election, noting their resemblance to the electoral practices of the nation's former single-party system. After the vote, combat resumed in the Pool area between official troops and insurgents under Pastor Ntumi, until a peace agreement was reached in April 2003.

input: Track lighting, invented by Lightolier, was popular at one period of time because it was much easier to install than recessed lighting, and individual fixtures are decorative and can be easily aimed at a wall. It has regained some popularity recently in low-voltage tracks, which often look nothing like their predecessors because they do not have the safety issues that line-voltage systems have, and are therefore less bulky and more ornamental in themselves. A master transformer feeds all of the fixtures on the track or rod with 12 or 24 volts, instead of each light fixture having its own line-to-low voltage transformer. There are traditional spots and floods, as well as other small hanging fixtures. A modified version of this is cable lighting, where lights are hung from or clipped to bare metal cables under tension.
rewrite: Originally developed by Lightolier, track lighting experienced a period of widespread use due to its simple installation compared to inset ceiling lights, along with the adjustable and decorative nature of its individual lamps. It is seeing renewed interest today, particularly in low-voltage designs that bear little resemblance to earlier models. These modern systems avoid the safety concerns and bulky hardware of traditional line-voltage tracks, resulting in a more streamlined and decorative appearance. A single central transformer supplies 12 or 24 volts to every fixture on the track, eliminating the need for a transformer in each lamp. Available styles include conventional spotlights and floodlights, plus various small suspended designs. A related approach is cable lighting, where fixtures are attached to taut, exposed metal cables.

input: where  is the maximum possible exposure that does not lead to a clipped or bloomed camera output. Typically, the lower limit of the saturation speed is determined by the sensor itself, but with the gain of the amplifier between the sensor and the analog-to-digital converter, the saturation speed can be increased. The factor 78 is chosen such that exposure settings based on a standard light meter and an 18-percent reflective surface will result in an image with a grey level of 18%/√2 = 12.7% of saturation. The factor √2 indicates that there is half a stop of headroom to deal with specular reflections that would appear brighter than a 100% reflecting white surface.
rewrite: The maximum exposure level that avoids overexposure or sensor blooming defines the upper limit. While the sensor's inherent properties set the minimum saturation threshold, this level can be raised using the amplifier's gain before the analog-to-digital conversion. The constant 78 is selected so that, under lighting conditions measured by a conventional light meter from an 18% gray card, the resulting image brightness reaches 12.7% of the saturation point (calculated as 18% divided by √2). The inclusion of √2 provides a half-stop buffer to accommodate intense highlights that exceed the brightness of a pure white reference.

input: Gorbachev also radically expanded the scope of Glasnost, stating that no subject was off-limits for open discussion in the media. Even so, the cautious Soviet intelligentsia took almost a year to begin pushing the boundaries to see if he meant what he said. For the first time, the Communist Party leader had appealed over the heads of Central Committee members for the people's support in exchange for expansion of liberties. The tactic proved successful: Within two years political reform could no longer be sidetracked by Party "conservatives." An unintended consequence was that having saved reform, Gorbachev's move ultimately killed the very system it was designed to save.
rewrite: Gorbachev significantly widened Glasnost, declaring all topics open for media debate. Yet the wary Soviet intellectual class hesitated nearly a year before testing his sincerity. For the first time, a Party chief bypassed the Central Committee to seek public backing by promising greater freedoms. This strategy worked: in under two years, Party traditionalists could no longer derail political change. Ironically, while this action rescued the reform process, it also led to the collapse of the system it aimed to preserve.

input: Tiberius Gracchus was elected tribune in 133 BC. He attempted to enact a law which would have limited the amount of land that any individual could own. The aristocrats, who stood to lose an enormous amount of money, were bitterly opposed to this proposal. Tiberius submitted this law to the Plebeian Council, but the law was vetoed by a tribune named Marcus Octavius. Tiberius then used the Plebeian Council to impeach Octavius. The theory, that a representative of the people ceases to be one when he acts against the wishes of the people, was counter to Roman constitutional theory. If carried to its logical end, this theory would remove all constitutional restraints on the popular will, and put the state under the absolute control of a temporary popular majority. His law was enacted, but Tiberius was murdered with 300 of his associates when he stood for reelection to the tribunate.
rewrite: In 133 BC, Tiberius Gracchus assumed the role of tribune. He sought to pass legislation capping private land ownership, a move fiercely resisted by wealthy nobles facing significant financial loss. When he presented the measure to the Plebeian Council, another tribune, Marcus Octavius, blocked it with a veto. Gracchus responded by having the council remove Octavius from office. This action relied on a principle—that an official who defies the public’s desires forfeits his mandate—which contradicted established Roman governance. Such a doctrine, if fully applied, would erase all legal checks on majority rule, granting a fleeting popular majority total authority over the state. Although his land reform ultimately passed, Tiberius and about 300 followers were killed during his campaign for a second term as tribune.

input: The city is also home to two large colleges. The City College Plymouth provides courses from the most basic to Foundation degrees for approximately 26,000 students. Plymouth College of Art offers a selection of courses including media. It was started 153 years ago and is now one of only four independent colleges of art and design in the UK.
rewrite: Plymouth hosts two major colleges. City College Plymouth serves around 26,000 students with courses ranging from introductory to Foundation degree levels. Meanwhile, Plymouth College of Art, established 153 years ago, provides programs in areas like media and is among just four independent UK art and design institutions.

input: Between 1853 and 1870, the Emperor Napoleon III and the city's first director of parks and gardens, Jean-Charles Alphand, created the Bois de Boulogne, the Bois de Vincennes, Parc Montsouris and the Parc des Buttes-Chaumont, located at the four points of the compass around the city, as well as many smaller parks, squares and gardens in the Paris' quarters. Since 1977, the city has created 166 new parks, most notably the Parc de la Villette (1987), Parc André Citroën (1992), and Parc de Bercy (1997). One of the newest parks, the Promenade des Berges de la Seine (2013), built on a former highway on the Left Bank of the Seine between the Pont de l'Alma and the Musée d'Orsay, has floating gardens and gives a view of the city's landmarks.
rewrite: From 1853 to 1870, under the direction of Emperor Napoleon III and chief landscape architect Jean-Charles Alphand, four major green spaces were established at the cardinal directions surrounding Paris: the Bois de Boulogne, Bois de Vincennes, Parc Montsouris, and Parc des Buttes-Chaumont. This period also saw the addition of numerous smaller gardens and squares throughout the city's neighborhoods. In a more recent wave of development beginning in 1977, municipal authorities have added 166 parks. Notable among these are the Parc de la Villette, Parc André Citroën, and Parc de Bercy. A contemporary example is the Promenade des Berges de la Seine, which opened in 2013 on a repurposed roadway along the river's Left Bank. This park features gardens on the water and offers vistas of famous Parisian monuments.

input: PlayStation Network is the unified online multiplayer gaming and digital media delivery service provided by Sony Computer Entertainment for PlayStation 3 and PlayStation Portable, announced during the 2006 PlayStation Business Briefing meeting in Tokyo. The service is always connected, free, and includes multiplayer support. The network enables online gaming, the PlayStation Store, PlayStation Home and other services. PlayStation Network uses real currency and PlayStation Network Cards as seen with the PlayStation Store and PlayStation Home.
rewrite: Sony Computer Entertainment's PlayStation Network is an integrated online platform for multiplayer gaming and digital content distribution. Initially revealed at Tokyo's 2006 PlayStation Business Briefing, it supports PlayStation 3 and PlayStation Portable. This free, continuously active service facilitates online play, access to the PlayStation Store, and features like PlayStation Home. Transactions are conducted using actual money or specific network cards.

input: The Community Tool Box is a public service of the University maintained by the Work Group for Community Health and Development. It is a free, online resource that contains more than 7,000 pages of practical information for promoting community health and development, and is a global resource for both professionals and grassroots groups engaged in the work of community health and development.
rewrite: The Community Tool Box is a free, web-based public service from the University's Work Group for Community Health and Development. With over 7,000 pages of guidance, it offers practical support for advancing community health and development worldwide, serving both experts and local organizations involved in this field.

input: According to the writer of Luke, Mary was a relative of Elizabeth, wife of the priest Zechariah of the priestly division of Abijah, who was herself part of the lineage of Aaron and so of the tribe of Levi.[Luke 1:5;1:36] Some of those who consider that the relationship with Elizabeth was on the maternal side, consider that Mary, like Joseph, to whom she was betrothed, was of the House of David and so of the Tribe of Judah, and that the genealogy of Jesus presented in Luke 3 from Nathan, third son of David and Bathsheba, is in fact the genealogy of Mary,[need quotation to verify] while the genealogy from Solomon given in Matthew 1 is that of Joseph. (Aaron's wife Elisheba was of the tribe of Judah, so all their descendants are from both Levi and Judah.)[Num.1:7 & Ex.6:23]
rewrite: The Gospel of Luke describes Mary as a kinswoman of Elizabeth. Elizabeth was married to Zechariah, a priest from the line of Abijah, and she herself was descended from Aaron, placing her within the Levite tribe. Certain scholars, interpreting this familial link as being through Mary's mother, propose that Mary belonged to the House of David and the Tribe of Judah, just as her husband Joseph did. From this perspective, the lineage of Jesus recorded in Luke, which traces back to David's son Nathan, would actually be Mary's ancestry. Conversely, the genealogy in Matthew, which follows David's line through Solomon, would be that of Joseph.
