It also received a Best Picture nomination and began his repeated work with actor Richard Dreyfuss.

input: In sheer numbers, Kerry had fewer endorsements than Howard Dean, who was far ahead in the superdelegate race going into the Iowa caucuses in January 2004, although Kerry led the endorsement race in Iowa, New Hampshire, Arizona, South Carolina, New Mexico and Nevada. Kerry's main perceived weakness was in his neighboring state of New Hampshire and nearly all national polls. Most other states did not have updated polling numbers to give an accurate placing for the Kerry campaign before Iowa. Heading into the primaries, Kerry's campaign was largely seen as in trouble, particularly after he fired campaign manager Jim Jordan. The key factors enabling it to survive were when fellow Massachusetts Senator Ted Kennedy assigned Mary Beth Cahill to be the campaign manager, as well as Kerry's mortgaging his own home to lend the money to his campaign (while his wife was a billionaire, campaign finance rules prohibited using one's personal fortune). He also brought on the "magical" Michael Whouley who would be credited with helping bring home the Iowa victory the same as he did in New Hampshire for Al Gore in 2000 against Bill Bradley.
rewrite:
Entering the 2004 Democratic primaries, John Kerry trailed significantly behind Howard Dean in securing superdelegate support nationally. However, Kerry held an advantage in delegate endorsements within several key early states, including Iowa, New Hampshire, and a handful of others. His campaign was widely considered to be struggling, especially following the dismissal of his campaign manager. Public polling, largely stagnant outside of a few states, offered little encouraging data for Kerry, with surveys in New Hampshire and national polls highlighting particular vulnerability.

The campaign's fortunes turned due to several crucial developments. Senator Ted Kennedy of Massachusetts intervened by appointing Mary Beth Cahill to lead the effort. Additionally, Kerry personally secured a loan for his campaign by taking a mortgage on his home—a necessary step despite his wife's wealth, due to legal restrictions on directly using personal fortunes. A further pivotal move was enlisting strategist Michael Whouley, renowned for his effective grassroots organizing. Whouley, who had previously helped secure Al Gore's 2000 New Hampshire primary win, was instrumental in orchestrating Kerry's eventual victory in the Iowa caucuses.

input: On the other hand, certain financial techniques can reduce the impact of such purchases on the currency. One is sterilisation, in which highly valued assets are sold at the same time that the weaker assets are purchased, which keeps the money supply neutral. Another technique is simply to accept the bad assets as long-term collateral (as opposed to short-term repo swaps) to be held until their market value stabilises. This would imply, as a quid pro quo, adjustments in taxation and expenditure in the economies of the weaker states to improve the perceived value of the assets.
rewrite: Conversely, some monetary strategies can lessen the effect of these acquisitions on exchange rates. Sterilisation, for instance, involves selling strong assets while buying weaker ones to maintain a stable money supply. Alternatively, authorities might hold devalued assets as long-term collateral until markets recover, rather than using short-term swaps. This approach would require, in exchange, that struggling economies modify their tax and spending policies to enhance the assets' market credibility.

input: The Government of National Capital Territory of Delhi does not release any economic figures specifically for New Delhi but publishes an official economic report on the whole of Delhi annually. According to the Economic Survey of Delhi, the metropolis has a net State Domestic Product (SDP) of Rs. 83,085 crores (for the year 2004–05) and a per capita income of Rs. 53,976($1,200). In the year 2008–09 New Delhi had a Per Capita Income of Rs.1,16,886 ($2,595).It grew by 16.2% to reach Rs.1,35,814 ($3,018) in 2009–10 fiscal. New Delhi's Per Capita GDP (at PPP) was at $6,860 during 2009–10 fiscal, making it one of the richest cities in India. The tertiary sector contributes 78.4% of Delhi's gross SDP followed by secondary and primary sectors with 20.2% and 1.4% contribution respectively.
rewrite: The Delhi government issues yearly economic data for the entire capital territory, as separate statistics for New Delhi alone are not provided. The report indicates that Delhi's overall net State Domestic Product was ₹83,085 crore in 2004–05, with per capita earnings of ₹53,976 ($1,200). By 2008–09, New Delhi's individual per capita income rose to ₹1,16,886 ($2,595), then increased 16.2% to ₹1,35,814 ($3,018) in 2009–10. That year, the city's per capita GDP measured by purchasing power parity reached $6,860, ranking it among India's wealthiest urban centers. Services dominate Delhi's economy, accounting for 78.4% of its gross SDP, while industry and agriculture contribute 20.2% and 1.4%, respectively.

input: On October 17, 1987, about 3,000 Armenians demonstrated in Yerevan complaining about the condition of Lake Sevan, the Nairit chemicals plant, and the Metsamor Nuclear Power Plant, and air pollution in Yerevan. Police tried to prevent the protest but took no action to stop it once the march was underway. The demonstration was led by Armenian writers such as Silva Kaputikian, Zori Balayan, and Maro Margarian and leaders from the National Survival organization. The march originated at the Opera Plaza after speakers, mainly intellectuals, addressed the crowd.
rewrite: On October 17, 1987, roughly 3,000 people gathered in Yerevan to protest environmental issues, including the state of Lake Sevan, pollution from the Nairit and Metsamor facilities, and city air quality. Although police initially attempted to block the event, they did not intervene after the procession began. Organized by the National Survival group and prominent authors including Silva Kaputikian, Zori Balayan, and Maro Margarian, the rally started at Opera Plaza following speeches by various intellectuals.

input: An advantage of the universal motor is that AC supplies may be used on motors which have some characteristics more common in DC motors, specifically high starting torque and very compact design if high running speeds are used. The negative aspect is the maintenance and short life problems caused by the commutator. Such motors are used in devices such as food mixers and power tools which are used only intermittently, and often have high starting-torque demands. Multiple taps on the field coil provide (imprecise) stepped speed control. Household blenders that advertise many speeds frequently combine a field coil with several taps and a diode that can be inserted in series with the motor (causing the motor to run on half-wave rectified AC). Universal motors also lend themselves to electronic speed control and, as such, are an ideal choice for devices like domestic washing machines. The motor can be used to agitate the drum (both forwards and in reverse) by switching the field winding with respect to the armature.
rewrite: A key benefit of universal motors is their ability to operate on alternating current while maintaining direct current motor traits, notably strong initial torque and a small, dense form factor at elevated operational speeds. Their primary drawback involves the wear and limited lifespan associated with the commutator assembly. These motors are well-suited for intermittent-use appliances like kitchen mixers and handheld tools, which frequently require high starting torque. Basic speed adjustment is achieved through multiple connections on the field coil, offering rough, incremental control. Many multi-speed kitchen blenders utilize this tapped coil setup along with a diode, enabling operation on half-wave rectified current for lower speeds. Furthermore, these motors adapt readily to electronic speed regulation, making them a preferred option for home appliances such as washing machines. Reversing the drum’s agitation direction is accomplished by altering the electrical relationship between the field winding and the armature.

input: While the largest European-American population in Montana overall is German, pockets of significant Scandinavian ancestry are prevalent in some of the farming-dominated northern and eastern prairie regions, parallel to nearby regions of North Dakota and Minnesota. Farmers of Irish, Scots, and English roots also settled in Montana. The historically mining-oriented communities of western Montana such as Butte have a wider range of European-American ethnicity; Finns, Eastern Europeans and especially Irish settlers left an indelible mark on the area, as well as people originally from British mining regions such as Cornwall, Devon and Wales. The nearby city of Helena, also founded as a mining camp, had a similar mix in addition to a small Chinatown. Many of Montana's historic logging communities originally attracted people of Scottish, Scandinavian, Slavic, English and Scots-Irish descent.[citation needed]
rewrite: Montana's population reflects varied European ancestries tied to its economic history. Though German heritage is most common statewide, many in the northern and eastern farmlands have Scandinavian roots, similar to adjacent parts of North Dakota and Minnesota. Settlers of Irish, Scottish, and English background also established agricultural communities. In the west, mining towns like Butte drew a diverse array of Europeans, including Finns, Eastern Europeans, and a strong Irish influence, along with people from British mining areas like Cornwall. Helena, another mining center, had a comparable ethnic blend and once included a small Chinese district. Additionally, the state's early logging camps attracted workers of Scottish, Scandinavian, Slavic, English, and Scots-Irish descent.

input: There are three primary shopping centers in the Bronx: The Hub, Gateway Center and Southern Boulevard. The Hub–Third Avenue Business Improvement District (B.I.D.), in The Hub, is the retail heart of the South Bronx, located where four roads converge: East 149th Street, Willis, Melrose and Third Avenues. It is primarily located inside the neighborhood of Melrose but also lines the northern border of Mott Haven. The Hub has been called "the Broadway of the Bronx", being likened to the real Broadway in Manhattan and the northwestern Bronx. It is the site of both maximum traffic and architectural density. In configuration, it resembles a miniature Times Square, a spatial "bow-tie" created by the geometry of the street. The Hub is part of Bronx Community Board 1.
rewrite: Three main retail areas serve the Bronx: The Hub, Gateway Center, and Southern Boulevard. The Hub, formally known as the Hub–Third Avenue Business Improvement District, acts as the central commercial zone for the South Bronx. It sits at the junction of East 149th Street, Willis, Melrose, and Third Avenues. While its core is in Melrose, it extends to the edge of Mott Haven. Often termed "the Broadway of the Bronx," it draws comparison to Manhattan's famous thoroughfare in its role as a bustling focal point. This area experiences the highest concentration of both pedestrian activity and buildings. Its layout, shaped by the intersecting streets, forms a compact, bow-tie design reminiscent of a smaller Times Square. The Hub falls within the jurisdiction of Bronx Community Board 1.

input: The economy has been growing quickly in recent years. In both 2010 and 2011, the metro area's gross domestic product (GDP) led 27 other metropolitan areas in the country, according to the Conference Board of Canada, recording growth of 6.6 per cent and 5.8 per cent respectively. At $52,000 the city's per capita GDP is the second highest out of all major Canadian cities. Economic forecasts suggest that the city will continue its strong economic growth in the coming years not only in the "oceanic" industries mentioned above, but also in tourism and new home construction as the population continues to grow. In May 2011, the city's unemployment rate fell to 5.6 per cent, the second lowest unemployment rate for a major city in Canada.
rewrite: In recent years, the region has experienced rapid economic expansion. Data from the Conference Board of Canada shows the metropolitan area's GDP growth outpaced that of 27 other major Canadian metro areas in both 2010 and 2011, with increases of 6.6% and 5.8% in those consecutive years. Its per capita GDP stands at $52,000, ranking second among the nation's large urban centers. Projections indicate this robust performance will persist, fueled not just by established maritime sectors but also by expanding tourism and residential building to accommodate a rising population. As of May 2011, the local jobless rate dropped to 5.6%, the second lowest figure for any major Canadian city.

input: The last three years of Eisenhower's second term in office were ones of relatively good health. Eventually after leaving the White House, he suffered several additional and ultimately crippling heart attacks. A severe heart attack in August 1965 largely ended his participation in public affairs. In August 1966 he began to show symptoms of cholecystitis, for which he underwent surgery on December 12, 1966, when his gallbladder was removed, containing 16 gallstones. After Eisenhower's death in 1969 (see below), an autopsy unexpectedly revealed an adrenal pheochromocytoma, a benign adrenaline-secreting tumor that may have made the President more vulnerable to heart disease. Eisenhower suffered seven heart attacks in total from 1955 until his death.
rewrite: During the final three years of his presidency, Dwight Eisenhower remained in fairly sound health. However, upon concluding his time in office, he experienced a series of increasingly debilitating heart attacks. A major cardiac event in August 1965 effectively halted his public engagements. The following year, signs of gallbladder inflammation emerged, leading to surgery in December 1966 to remove an organ holding sixteen gallstones. Following his passing in 1969, a postmortem examination surprisingly identified a benign adrenal tumor. This growth secreted adrenaline and might have heightened his susceptibility to cardiac conditions. Ultimately, Eisenhower endured seven heart attacks between 1955 and the end of his life.

input: Qutb Shahi architecture of the 16th and early 17th centuries followed classical Persian architecture featuring domes and colossal arches. The oldest surviving Qutb Shahi structure in Hyderabad is the ruins of Golconda fort built in the 16th century. The Charminar, Mecca Masjid, Charkaman and Qutb Shahi tombs are other existing structures of this period. Among these the Charminar has become an icon of the city; located in the centre of old Hyderabad, it is a square structure with sides 20 m (66 ft) long and four grand arches each facing a road. At each corner stands a 56 m (184 ft)-high minaret. Most of the historical bazaars that still exist were constructed on the street north of Charminar towards Golconda fort. The Charminar, Qutb Shahi tombs and Golconda fort are considered to be monuments of national importance in India; in 2010 the Indian government proposed that the sites be listed for UNESCO World Heritage status.:11–18
rewrite: The architectural style of the Qutb Shahi dynasty during the 1500s and early 1600s drew heavily from Persian traditions, characterized by immense arches and prominent domes. The earliest example still standing in Hyderabad is the 16th-century Golconda fort, now in ruins. Other constructions from this era include the Mecca Masjid, Charkaman, and the royal tombs. The most famous is the Charminar, a landmark at the heart of the historic city. This edifice is square, each side measuring 20 meters, with a towering arch on every face oriented toward a major thoroughfare. Four minarets rise approximately 56 meters from each corner. Many traditional marketplaces that remain today line the thoroughfare extending north from the Charminar to the fort. Along with the Qutb Shahi tombs and Golconda fort, the Charminar is recognized as a nationally significant monument. In 2010, India nominated these sites for inclusion on the UNESCO World Heritage list.

input: In addition to limiting the total average power used by the device, the USB specification limits the inrush current (i.e., that used to charge decoupling and filter capacitors) when the device is first connected. Otherwise, connecting a device could cause problems with the host's internal power. USB devices are also required to automatically enter ultra low-power suspend mode when the USB host is suspended. Nevertheless, many USB host interfaces do not cut off the power supply to USB devices when they are suspended.
rewrite: The USB standard not only restricts the overall average power consumption of a device but also caps the initial surge of current needed to energize internal capacitors upon connection. This prevents potential disruptions to the host's power system. Furthermore, devices must switch to a minimal-power suspend state when the host is inactive. However, it is common for hosts to continue supplying power to USB devices even during suspension.

input: The Western powers, largely unsatisfied with the Treaty of Nanjing, gave grudging support to the Qing government during the Taiping and Nian Rebellions. China's income fell sharply during the wars as vast areas of farmland were destroyed, millions of lives were lost, and countless armies were raised and equipped to fight the rebels. In 1854, Britain tried to re-negotiate the Treaty of Nanjing, inserting clauses allowing British commercial access to Chinese rivers and the creation of a permanent British embassy at Beijing.
rewrite: Unhappy with the terms of the Treaty of Nanjing, Western nations offered reluctant aid to the Qing dynasty against major internal uprisings. The conflicts devastated China's economy, ruining agricultural regions, causing immense loss of life, and consuming vast resources to sustain military campaigns. In 1854, Britain sought to revise the treaty, demanding new terms for navigational rights on inland waterways and establishing a lasting diplomatic mission in the capital.

input: The introduction of new or equivalent deities coincided with Rome's most significant aggressive and defensive military forays. In 206 BC the Sibylline books commended the introduction of cult to the aniconic Magna Mater (Great Mother) from Pessinus, installed on the Palatine in 191 BC. The mystery cult to Bacchus followed; it was suppressed as subversive and unruly by decree of the Senate in 186 BC. Greek deities were brought within the sacred pomerium: temples were dedicated to Juventas (Hebe) in 191 BC, Diana (Artemis) in 179 BC, Mars (Ares) in 138 BC), and to Bona Dea, equivalent to Fauna, the female counterpart of the rural Faunus, supplemented by the Greek goddess Damia. Further Greek influences on cult images and types represented the Roman Penates as forms of the Greek Dioscuri. The military-political adventurers of the Later Republic introduced the Phrygian goddess Ma (identified with Roman Bellona, the Egyptian mystery-goddess Isis and Persian Mithras.)
rewrite: Rome's major military campaigns, both offensive and defensive, were accompanied by the adoption of new or comparable gods. In 206 BC, following a directive from the Sibylline texts, the worship of the formless Magna Mater was brought from Pessinus; her temple was established on the Palatine by 191 BC. Subsequently, the secretive Bacchic rites emerged, only to be banned by the Senate in 186 BC for being disruptive. Hellenic divinities were formally welcomed inside the city's religious boundary: shrines were consecrated to Juventas (191 BC), Diana (179 BC), Mars (138 BC), and to Bona Dea—a counterpart to Fauna—joined by the Greek deity Damia. Additional Greek sway was seen in representing the Roman Penates as versions of the Dioscuri. Later Republic-era commanders promoting their own agendas introduced foreign figures like the Phrygian Ma, equated with Bellona, as well as Isis and Mithras.

input: These statistics point to the complexities surrounding the lack of health/nutrition literacy and reveal the degree to which they are embedded in the social structure and interconnected with other problems. Among these problems are the lack of information about food choices, a lack of understanding of nutritional information and its application to individual circumstances, limited or difficult access to healthful foods, and a range of cultural influences and socioeconomic constraints such as low levels of education and high levels of poverty that decrease opportunities for healthful eating and living.
rewrite: These figures highlight the intricate nature of inadequate health and nutrition awareness, showing how deeply it is woven into societal frameworks and linked to various issues. These include insufficient knowledge for making food decisions, difficulty interpreting and personalizing dietary guidelines, barriers to obtaining nutritious food, and cultural and economic factors like limited education and widespread poverty. These combined elements restrict possibilities for maintaining a healthy diet and lifestyle.

input: By the end of May, drafts were formally presented. In mid-June, the main Tripartite negotiations started. The discussion was focused on potential guarantees to central and east European countries should a German aggression arise. The USSR proposed to consider that a political turn towards Germany by the Baltic states would constitute an "indirect aggression" towards the Soviet Union. Britain opposed such proposals, because they feared the Soviets' proposed language could justify a Soviet intervention in Finland and the Baltic states, or push those countries to seek closer relations with Germany. The discussion about a definition of "indirect aggression" became one of the sticking points between the parties, and by mid-July, the tripartite political negotiations effectively stalled, while the parties agreed to start negotiations on a military agreement, which the Soviets insisted must be entered into simultaneously with any political agreement.
rewrite: Formal drafts were submitted near the close of May. Principal talks among the three powers commenced in the middle of June. These conversations centered on possible security assurances for nations in central and eastern Europe in the event of German hostility. The Soviet position included a clause that would label any Baltic state's political alignment with Germany as an act of "indirect aggression" against the USSR. British delegates resisted these terms, concerned the wording might be used to legitimize Soviet interference in Finland and the Baltic region or drive those nations toward Germany. Debating the meaning of "indirect aggression" emerged as a key obstacle. By mid-July, the political discussions had largely reached an impasse. The participants then consented to begin talks on a military pact, a step the Soviet side demanded occur concurrently with any political accord.

input: The pagan Slavic populations were Christianized between the 6th and 10th centuries. Orthodox Christianity is predominant in the East and South Slavs, while Roman Catholicism is predominant in West Slavs and the western South Slavs. The religious borders are largely comparable to the East–West Schism which began in the 11th century. The majority of contemporary Slavic populations who profess a religion are Orthodox, followed by Catholic, while a small minority are Protestant. There are minor Slavic Muslim groups. Religious delineations by nationality can be very sharp; usually in the Slavic ethnic groups the vast majority of religious people share the same religion. Some Slavs are atheist or agnostic: only 19% of Czechs professed belief in god/s in the 2005 Eurobarometer survey.
rewrite: Between the sixth and tenth centuries, the Slavic peoples who practiced paganism gradually adopted Christianity. Today, Eastern and Southern Slavs primarily follow Orthodox Christianity, whereas Western Slavs and some Southern Slavs are chiefly Roman Catholic. This division in faith closely mirrors the historical split between Eastern and Western churches in the eleventh century. Among modern Slavs who adhere to a religion, most are Orthodox, with Catholics forming the next largest group; Protestants and Muslims constitute smaller minorities. Religious affiliation often aligns strongly with national identity, with most adherents within a given Slavic group sharing the same faith. However, not all Slavs are religious; for instance, a 2005 survey found merely 19% of Czechs expressed belief in any deity.

input: Among all cities in the Mediterranean part of the European Union, Limassol has one of the warmest winters, in the period January – February average temperature is 17–18 °C (63–64 °F) during the day and 7–8 °C (45–46 °F) at night, in other coastal locations in Cyprus is generally 16–17 °C (61–63 °F) during the day and 6–8 °C (43–46 °F) at night. During March, Limassol has average temperatures of 19–20 °C (66–68 °F) during the day and 9–11 °C (48–52 °F) at night, in other coastal locations in Cyprus is generally 17–19 °C (63–66 °F) during the day and 8–10 °C (46–50 °F) at night.
rewrite: Limassol experiences some of the mildest winter conditions of any city along the EU's Mediterranean coast. From January through February, daytime highs average 17–18 °C (63–64 °F), with nighttime lows of 7–8 °C (45–46 °F). This is slightly warmer than other Cypriot coastal areas, which typically see daytime temperatures of 16–17 °C (61–63 °F) and nighttime readings of 6–8 °C (43–46 °F). In March, Limassol's averages rise to 19–20 °C (66–68 °F) during the day and 9–11 °C (48–52 °F) after dark, again exceeding the common coastal range of 17–19 °C (63–66 °F) and 8–10 °C (46–50 °F).

input: The Ottoman Empire, believed to be about to collapse, was portrayed in the press as the sick man of Europe". The Balkan states, with the partial exception of Bosnia and Albania, were primarily Christian. Starting in 1894 the Ottomans struck at the Armenians on the explicit grounds that they were a non-Muslim people and as such were a potential threat to the Muslim empire within which they resided. The Hamidian Massacres aroused the indignation of the entire Christian world. In the United States the now aging Julia Ward Howe, author of the Battle Hymn of the Republic, leaped into the war of words and joined the Red Cross. Relations of minorities within the Ottoman Empire and the disposition of former Ottoman lands became known as the "Eastern Question," as the Ottomans were on the east of Europe.
rewrite: Often described in European media as the "sick man of Europe," the Ottoman Empire was widely perceived to be nearing its end. Most Balkan regions, excluding Bosnia and Albania to some degree, were predominantly Christian. From 1894 onward, Ottoman forces targeted Armenian communities, justifying this persecution on the basis that their non-Muslim faith posed a possible danger to the Muslim state. These killings, known as the Hamidian Massacres, provoked outrage throughout Christian nations. In America, the elderly poet Julia Ward Howe, famous for writing "The Battle Hymn of the Republic," vigorously entered the public debate and enlisted with the Red Cross. The issues surrounding minority populations in the empire and the fate of its former territories were collectively termed the "Eastern Question," referencing the empire's geographic position relative to Europe.

input: On 23 November 1991, in a prepared statement made on his deathbed, Mercury confirmed that he had AIDS. Within 24 hours of the statement, he died of bronchial pneumonia, which was brought on as a complication of AIDS. His funeral service on 27 November in Kensal Green, West London was private, and held in accordance with the Zoroastrian religious faith of his family. "Bohemian Rhapsody" was re-released as a single shortly after Mercury's death, with "These Are the Days of Our Lives" as the double A-side. The music video for "These Are the Days of Our Lives" contains Mercury's final scenes in front of the camera. The single went to number one in the UK, remaining there for five weeks – the only recording to top the Christmas chart twice and the only one to be number one in four different years (1975, 1976, 1991, and 1992). Initial proceeds from the single – approximately £1,000,000 – were donated to the Terrence Higgins Trust.
rewrite: On his deathbed, Freddie Mercury issued a prepared statement dated 23 November 1991, publicly acknowledging he had AIDS. He passed away less than a day later from bronchial pneumonia, a condition resulting from the disease. A private funeral, adhering to his family's Zoroastrian beliefs, was conducted in Kensal Green, West London, on 27 November. Soon after his death, "Bohemian Rhapsody" was reissued as a single, paired with "These Are the Days of Our Lives." The video for the latter song features Mercury's final filmed performance. This release reached the top of the UK charts for five consecutive weeks, achieving the unique distinction of being the Christmas number one on two separate occasions and charting at number one across four different calendar years (1975, 1976, 1991, and 1992). Around one million pounds from the single's early sales were directed to the Terrence Higgins Trust.

input: This article covers numbered east-west streets in Manhattan, New York City. Major streets have their own linked articles; minor streets are discussed here. The streets do not run exactly east–west, because the grid plan is aligned with the Hudson River rather than with the cardinal directions. "West" is approximately 29 degrees north of true west.
rewrite: This piece details Manhattan's numbered east-west roads. While main avenues have separate entries, lesser ones are addressed here. Their orientation isn't precisely east-west, as the grid follows the Hudson River's course. "West" aligns roughly 29 degrees north of true west.

input: Other important Venetian mosaics can be found in the Cathedral of Santa Maria Assunta in Torcello from the 12th century, and in the Basilical of Santi Maria e Donato in Murano with a restored apse mosaic from the 12th century and a beautiful mosaic pavement (1140). The apse of the San Cipriano Church in Murano was decorated with an impressive golden mosaic from the early 13th century showing Christ enthroned with Mary, St John and the two patron saints, Cipriano and Cipriana. When the church was demolished in the 19th century, the mosaic was bought by Frederick William IV of Prussia. It was reassembled in the Friedenskirche of Potsdam in the 1840s.
rewrite: Significant Venetian mosaics also exist in Torcello's Cathedral of Santa Maria Assunta, dating to the 1100s, and Murano's Basilica of Santi Maria e Donato, featuring a redone 12th-century apse mosaic and an intricate floor from 1140. Another notable work was the early 13th-century golden apse mosaic in Murano's San Cipriano Church, depicting Christ enthroned with Mary, John, and the saints Cipriano and Cipriana. After the church's demolition in the 1800s, King Frederick William IV of Prussia purchased the artwork. It was later reconstructed during the 1840s within Potsdam's Friedenskirche.

input: According to the Quran, God communicated with man and made his will known through signs and revelations. Prophets, or 'Messengers of God', received revelations and delivered them to humanity. The message has been identical and for all humankind. "Nothing is said to you that was not said to the messengers before you, that your lord has at his Command forgiveness as well as a most Grievous Penalty." The revelation does not come directly from God to the prophets. Angels acting as God's messengers deliver the divine revelation to them. This comes out in Quran 42:51, in which it is stated: "It is not for any mortal that God should speak to them, except by revelation, or from behind a veil, or by sending a messenger to reveal by his permission whatsoever He will."
rewrite: The Quran teaches that God conveys His intentions to humanity via signs and revelations. These divine communications are received by prophets, termed God's messengers, who then share them with people. The core message remains consistent and universal across time. As expressed in the scripture, the themes of divine mercy and severe punishment have been reiterated to all previous messengers. This revelation reaches prophets indirectly; angels serve as intermediaries, delivering God's word. This process is clarified in a verse stating that God does not speak directly to humans, but rather through inspiration, from behind a barrier, or by dispatching a celestial messenger to disclose what He wills.

input: The first visible institution to run into trouble in the United States was the Southern California–based IndyMac, a spin-off of Countrywide Financial. Before its failure, IndyMac Bank was the largest savings and loan association in the Los Angeles market and the seventh largest mortgage originator in the United States. The failure of IndyMac Bank on July 11, 2008, was the fourth largest bank failure in United States history up until the crisis precipitated even larger failures, and the second largest failure of a regulated thrift. IndyMac Bank's parent corporation was IndyMac Bancorp until the FDIC seized IndyMac Bank. IndyMac Bancorp filed for Chapter 7 bankruptcy in July 2008.
rewrite: IndyMac, originally part of Countrywide Financial and based in Southern California, was the initial major U.S. institution to show signs of collapse. Prior to its downfall, it served as the biggest savings and loan association in the Los Angeles region and ranked as the nation's seventh largest home loan provider. Its closure on July 11, 2008, stood as the fourth biggest bank collapse in American history at that time, later surpassed by subsequent crisis-related failures, and was the second largest thrift failure. The FDIC took control of the bank from its parent company, IndyMac Bancorp, which then declared Chapter 7 bankruptcy.

input: In 1896, Patrick and Gilbert observed that during a prolonged period of sleep deprivation, sleepiness increases and decreases with a period of approximately 24 hours. In 1918, J.S. Szymanski showed that animals are capable of maintaining 24-hour activity patterns in the absence of external cues such as light and changes in temperature. In the early 20th century, circadian rhythms were noticed in the rhythmic feeding times of bees. Extensive experiments were done by Auguste Forel, Ingeborg Beling, and Oskar Wahl to see whether this rhythm was due to an endogenous clock.[citation needed] Ron Konopka and Seymour Benzer isolated the first clock mutant in Drosophila in the early 1970s and mapped the "period" gene, the first discovered genetic determinant of behavioral rhythmicity. Joseph Takahashi discovered the first mammalian circadian clock mutation (clockΔ19) using mice in 1994. However, recent studies show that deletion of clock does not lead to a behavioral phenotype (the animals still have normal circadian rhythms), which questions its importance in rhythm generation.
rewrite: In 1896, researchers Patrick and Gilbert noted that when individuals are deprived of sleep for extended durations, their drowsiness fluctuates on a roughly daily cycle. By 1918, J.S. Szymanski demonstrated that creatures can sustain daily cycles of activity even without environmental signals like light or temperature variations. Around the same era, scientists observed daily patterns in the feeding behaviors of bees. Auguste Forel, Ingeborg Beling, and Oskar Wahl conducted numerous tests to determine if this pattern originated from an internal biological timer. Later, in the 1970s, Ron Konopka and Seymour Benzer identified the initial clock-related mutation in fruit flies, pinpointing the "period" gene as the first known genetic influence on daily behavioral cycles. In 1994, Joseph Takahashi found the first such mutation in mammals, termed clockΔ19, using mice. Yet, current research indicates that removing this gene does not alter circadian behavior, casting doubt on its essential role in creating these rhythms.

input: In September 1982, Prime minister Margaret Thatcher travelled to Beijing to negotiate with the Chinese government on the future of Britain's last major and most populous overseas territory, Hong Kong. Under the terms of the 1842 Treaty of Nanking, Hong Kong Island itself had been ceded to Britain in perpetuity, but the vast majority of the colony was constituted by the New Territories, which had been acquired under a 99-year lease in 1898, due to expire in 1997. Thatcher, seeing parallels with the Falkland Islands, initially wished to hold Hong Kong and proposed British administration with Chinese sovereignty, though this was rejected by China. A deal was reached in 1984—under the terms of the Sino-British Joint Declaration, Hong Kong would become a special administrative region of the People's Republic of China, maintaining its way of life for at least 50 years. The handover ceremony in 1997 marked for many, including Charles, Prince of Wales, who was in attendance, "the end of Empire".
rewrite: In September 1982, British Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher visited Beijing for talks concerning Hong Kong, the final significant and densely populated colonial holding of the United Kingdom. The core of the issue lay in its dual legal status. While Hong Kong Island had been permanently granted to Britain via the 1842 Treaty of Nanking, the adjoining New Territories, which formed the bulk of the colony, were held under a 99-year lease from 1898, set to lapse in 1997. Drawing a comparison to the Falklands, Thatcher's opening position favored continued British control under nominal Chinese authority, a plan China refused. Negotiations concluded in 1984 with the Sino-British Joint Declaration, stipulating Hong Kong's return as a Chinese Special Administrative Region, guaranteed to preserve its existing social systems for fifty years. The 1997 transfer ceremony was witnessed by Prince Charles and widely perceived as the conclusive chapter of the British Empire.

input: The relationship between genes can be measured by comparing the sequence alignment of their DNA.:7.6 The degree of sequence similarity between homologous genes is called conserved sequence. Most changes to a gene's sequence do not affect its function and so genes accumulate mutations over time by neutral molecular evolution. Additionally, any selection on a gene will cause its sequence to diverge at a different rate. Genes under stabilizing selection are constrained and so change more slowly whereas genes under directional selection change sequence more rapidly. The sequence differences between genes can be used for phylogenetic analyses to study how those genes have evolved and how the organisms they come from are related.
rewrite: Genetic connections can be assessed by examining how closely DNA sequences align. This similarity in homologous genes is termed sequence conservation. Typically, many alterations in a gene's code do not impact its role, allowing mutations to gather gradually through neutral evolution. Selective pressures also influence divergence rates; genes experiencing stabilizing selection evolve slowly due to constraints, while those under directional selection adapt more quickly. These genetic variations serve as a basis for phylogenetic studies, helping trace the evolution of the genes and the evolutionary relationships among their originating species.

input: The CBS Records Group was led very successfully by Clive Davis until his dismissal in 1972, after it was discovered that Davis has used CBS funds to finance his personal life, including an expensive bar mitzvah party for his son. He was replaced first by former head Goddard Lieberson, then in 1975 by the colourful and controversial lawyer Walter Yetnikoff, who led the company until 1990.
rewrite: Clive Davis effectively managed the CBS Records Group until his 1972 termination for misusing company money on personal expenses, such as his son's lavish bar mitzvah. Goddard Lieberson, a previous leader, initially succeeded him. Then in 1975, the flamboyant and divisive attorney Walter Yetnikoff took over, remaining in charge until 1990.

input: According to filings to the Canadian Radio-television and Telecommunications Commission (CRTC) by Thunder Bay Electronics (owner of CBC's Thunder Bay affiliate CKPR-DT) and Bell Media (owner of CBC affiliates CFTK-TV in Terrace and CJDC-TV in Dawson Creek),[citation needed] the CBC informed them that it will not extend its association with any of its private affiliates beyond August 31, 2011. Incidentally, that was also the date for analogue to digital transition in Canada. Given recent practice and the CBC's decision not to convert any retransmitters to digital, even in markets with populations in the hundreds in thousands, it is not expected that the CBC will open new transmitters to replace its affiliates, and indeed may pare back its existing transmitter network. However, in March 2011, CKPR announced that it had come to a programming agreement with the CBC, in which the station will continue to provide CBC programming in Thunder Bay for a period of five years. On March 16, 2012, Astral Media announced the sale of its assets to Bell Media, owners of CTV and CTV Two, for $3.38 billion with CFTK and CJDC included in the acquisition. Whether the stations will remain CBC affiliates or become owned-and-operated stations of CTV or CTV Two following the completion of the merger is undetermined.
rewrite: Documents submitted to Canada's CRTC by Thunder Bay Electronics and Bell Media indicate that the CBC notified these companies it would end its partnerships with privately held affiliate stations after August 31, 2011. This date coincided with the nation's switch from analog to digital broadcasting. Based on the CBC's recent approach of not upgrading its retransmitters to digital—even in areas with substantial populations—industry observers anticipate the public broadcaster will not establish new transmitters to take the place of these affiliates and might instead reduce its current transmission infrastructure. Nevertheless, in March 2011, CKPR disclosed a five-year arrangement with the CBC to keep airing its programs in Thunder Bay. Separately, on March 16, 2012, Astral Media revealed it would sell its holdings, including stations CFTK and CJDC, to Bell Media for $3.38 billion. Bell Media also controls the CTV and CTV Two networks. It remains unclear whether these acquired stations will continue as CBC affiliates or be converted into CTV-owned outlets after the merger concludes.

input: Most samurai were bound by a code of honor and were expected to set an example for those below them. A notable part of their code is seppuku (切腹, seppuku?) or hara kiri, which allowed a disgraced samurai to regain his honor by passing into death, where samurai were still beholden to social rules. Whilst there are many romanticized characterizations of samurai behavior such as the writing of Bushido (武士道, Bushidō?) in 1905, studies of Kobudo and traditional Budō indicate that the samurai were as practical on the battlefield as were any other warrior.
rewrite: Samurai warriors typically adhered to a strict ethical code and were seen as role models for lower social classes. A key element was seppuku, a ritual suicide permitting a dishonored warrior to restore his status through death, demonstrating how these rules extended beyond life. Although modern portrayals, like the 1905 text *Bushido*, often idealize their conduct, historical practices from Kobudo and Budō reveal that samurai approached combat with the same pragmatism as other fighters.

input: In January 1920, Tito and his wife made a long and difficult journey home to Yugoslavia where he arrived in September. Upon his return, Broz joined the Communist Party of Yugoslavia. The CPY's influence on the political life of the Kingdom of Yugoslavia was growing rapidly. In the 1920 elections the Communists won 59 seats in the parliament and became the third strongest party. Winning numerous local elections, they gained a stronghold in the second largest city of Zagreb, electing Svetozar Delić for mayor. After the assassination of Milorad Drašković, the Yugoslav Minister of the Interior, by a young communist on 2 August 1921, the CPY was declared illegal under the Yugoslav State Security Act of 1921. During 1920 and 1921 all Communist-won mandates were nullified. Broz continued his work underground despite pressure on Communists from the government. As 1921 began he moved to Veliko Trojstvo near Bjelovar and found work as a machinist. In 1925, Broz moved to Kraljevica where he started working at a shipyard. He was elected as a union leader and a year later he led a shipyard strike. He was fired and moved to Belgrade, where he worked in a train coach factory in Smederevska Palanka. He was elected as Workers' Commissary but was fired as soon as his CPY membership was revealed. Broz then moved to Zagreb, where he was appointed secretary of Metal Workers' Union of Croatia. In 1928, he became the Zagreb Branch Secretary of the CPY. In the same year he was arrested, tried in court for his illegal communist activities, and sent to jail. During his five years at Lepoglava prison he met Moša Pijade, who became his ideological mentor. After his release, he lived incognito and assumed numerous noms de guerre, among them "Walter" and "Tito".
rewrite: In early 1920, Josip Broz, later known as Tito, and his spouse undertook an arduous trip back to their homeland, finally reaching Yugoslavia that September. Shortly after arriving, Broz became a member of the Communist Party of Yugoslavia (CPY). The party was swiftly expanding its role within the political sphere of the Kingdom of Yugoslavia. That same year, in parliamentary elections, communist candidates secured 59 seats, elevating them to the position of the third most powerful political group. Their success extended to municipal contests, where they established a significant base of support in Zagreb, the nation's second major urban center, and succeeded in making Svetozar Delić its mayor. However, following the killing of Interior Minister Milorad Drašković by a communist youth in August 1921, authorities used the State Security Act to ban the CPY. Throughout 1920 and 1921, all electoral victories by communists were invalidated. Broz persisted in his political efforts in secret, resisting state persecution. At the start of 1921, he relocated to Veliko Trojstvo, close to Bjelovar, securing employment as a machinist. By 1925, he had moved again to Kraljevica, working at a shipyard. There, his fellow workers chose him as a union official, and in 1926 he organized a strike, which led to his dismissal. He then found work at a railway carriage plant in Smederevska Palanka, near Belgrade. Although elected as a Workers' Commissary, he was quickly terminated once his party affiliation was discovered. Broz subsequently went to Zagreb, where he was named secretary of the Metal Workers' Union for Croatia. In 1928, he rose to become the Zagreb branch secretary for the then-outlawed CPY. That year, he was taken into custody, prosecuted for his clandestine political work, and imprisoned. While serving a five-year sentence at Lepoglava, he encountered Moša Pijade, who guided his political thought. After being freed, Broz lived undercover, adopting several aliases including "Walter" and the now-famous "Tito."

input: With financial support from Sanders and Hubbard, Bell hired Thomas Watson as his assistant,[N 15] and the two of them experimented with acoustic telegraphy. On June 2, 1875, Watson accidentally plucked one of the reeds and Bell, at the receiving end of the wire, heard the overtones of the reed; overtones that would be necessary for transmitting speech. That demonstrated to Bell that only one reed or armature was necessary, not multiple reeds. This led to the "gallows" sound-powered telephone, which could transmit indistinct, voice-like sounds, but not clear speech.
rewrite: Funded by Sanders and Hubbard, Bell brought Thomas Watson on as his aide, and together they worked on acoustic telegraphy experiments. In June 1875, Watson unintentionally tweaked a reed. Bell, listening at the other end, detected its complex overtones, which he recognized as essential for conveying spoken words. This proved to him that a single reed, rather than several, was sufficient. Their subsequent invention, the "gallows" telephone, used sound power to send muffled vocal noises, though intelligible speech remained out of reach.

input: On August 18, 1970, the NAACP filed suit against Michigan state officials, including Governor William Milliken, charging de facto public school segregation. The NAACP argued that although schools were not legally segregated, the city of Detroit and its surrounding counties had enacted policies to maintain racial segregation in public schools. The NAACP also suggested a direct relationship between unfair housing practices and educational segregation, which followed segregated neighborhoods. The District Court held all levels of government accountable for the segregation in its ruling. The Sixth Circuit Court affirmed some of the decision, holding that it was the state's responsibility to integrate across the segregated metropolitan area. The U.S. Supreme Court took up the case February 27, 1974. The subsequent Milliken v. Bradley decision had wide national influence. In a narrow decision, the Court found that schools were a subject of local control and that suburbs could not be forced to solve problems in the city's school district.
rewrite: On August 18, 1970, the NAACP initiated legal action against the state of Michigan and Governor William Milliken, alleging racial separation in public schools existed in practice. The suit contended that officials in Detroit and adjacent areas had implemented measures preserving segregated education, despite an absence of laws mandating it. It further asserted that discriminatory housing policies, which created divided residential areas, were directly linked to this school segregation. A federal District Court determined that government entities at multiple levels were responsible for this condition. While upholding portions of this ruling, the Sixth Circuit Court of Appeals placed the duty for achieving integration across the wider metropolitan region on the state. The U.S. Supreme Court heard arguments beginning February 27, 1974. Its eventual ruling in Milliken v. Bradley proved nationally significant. By a close margin, the Court decided that education was primarily under local authority, and surrounding suburban districts could not be compelled to participate in remedying segregation within the city's schools.

input: During his brief majority reign, Murad IV (1612–1640) reasserted central authority and recaptured Iraq (1639) from the Safavids. The resulting Treaty of Zuhab of that same year decisively parted the Caucasus and adjacent regions between the two neighbouring empires as it had already been defined in the 1555 Peace of Amasya. The Sultanate of women (1648–1656) was a period in which the mothers of young sultans exercised power on behalf of their sons. The most prominent women of this period were Kösem Sultan and her daughter-in-law Turhan Hatice, whose political rivalry culminated in Kösem's murder in 1651. During the Köprülü Era (1656–1703), effective control of the Empire was exercised by a sequence of Grand Viziers from the Köprülü family. The Köprülü Vizierate saw renewed military success with authority restored in Transylvania, the conquest of Crete completed in 1669, and expansion into Polish southern Ukraine, with the strongholds of Khotyn and Kamianets-Podilskyi and the territory of Podolia ceding to Ottoman control in 1676.
rewrite: In his short time as an adult ruler, Sultan Murad IV restored strong imperial control and reclaimed Iraq from Safavid Persia in 1639. The subsequent Treaty of Zuhab that year formally confirmed the division of the Caucasus and nearby areas between the rival empires, reaffirming borders originally established by the 1555 Peace of Amasya. A later phase known as the Sultanate of Women saw the mothers of underage sultans governing as regents. Key figures included Kösem Sultan and Turhan Hatice, whose intense competition for influence ended with Kösem's assassination. Following this, the Köprülü Era began, marked by a series of capable grand viziers from the same family who directed the state. This period brought military revitalization: Ottoman power was reasserted in Transylvania, Crete was fully taken in 1669, and territories were gained in southern Ukraine from Poland, including the fortresses of Khotyn and Kamianets-Podilskyi, with the region of Podolia coming under Ottoman rule by 1676.

input: The two nations planned a joint mission to dock the last US Apollo craft with a Soyuz, known as the Apollo-Soyuz Test Project (ASTP). To prepare, the US designed a docking module for the Apollo that was compatible with the Soviet docking system, which allowed any of their craft to dock with any other (e.g. Soyuz/Soyuz as well as Soyuz/Salyut). The module was also necessary as an airlock to allow the men to visit each other's craft, which had incompatible cabin atmospheres. The USSR used the Soyuz 16 mission in December 1974 to prepare for ASTP.
rewrite: In a collaborative effort, the United States and Soviet Union organized a mission to connect the final Apollo spacecraft with a Soyuz vehicle, called the Apollo-Soyuz Test Project. For this endeavor, American engineers created a special docking module for Apollo that would fit the Soviet universal docking interface, enabling connections between various spacecraft types. This component also served as a vital airlock, permitting crew transfers despite differing cabin atmospheres. The Soviets conducted the Soyuz 16 flight in late 1974 as a rehearsal for the joint mission.

input: In Canada, the largest Presbyterian denomination – and indeed the largest Protestant denomination – was the Presbyterian Church in Canada, formed in 1875 with the merger of four regional groups. In 1925, the United Church of Canada was formed by the majority of Presbyterians combining with the Methodist Church, Canada, and the Congregational Union of Canada. A sizable minority of Canadian Presbyterians, primarily in southern Ontario but also throughout the entire nation, withdrew, and reconstituted themselves as a non-concurring continuing Presbyterian body. They regained use of the original name in 1939.
rewrite: Canada's biggest Presbyterian and Protestant group was originally the Presbyterian Church in Canada, established in 1875 from four regional bodies. In 1925, most Presbyterians united with Methodist and Congregational churches to create the United Church of Canada. However, a significant minority across the country, especially in southern Ontario, chose to separate and continue as a distinct Presbyterian church. This group reclaimed the original Presbyterian Church in Canada name in 1939.

input: Mexico City remains the only Latin American city to host the Olympic Games, having held the Summer Olympics in 1968, winning bids against Buenos Aires, Lyon and Detroit. (This too will change thanks to Rio, 2016 Summer Games host). The city hosted the 1955 and 1975 Pan American Games, the last after Santiago and São Paulo withdrew. The ICF Flatwater Racing World Championships were hosted here in 1974 and 1994. Lucha libre is a Mexican style of wrestling, and is one of the more popular sports throughout the country. The main venues in the city are Arena México and Arena Coliseo.
rewrite: Mexico City is unique in Latin America for having organized the Olympic Games, serving as host for the 1968 Summer Olympics after outbidding Detroit, Lyon, and Buenos Aires. (Rio de Janeiro's 2016 Games will end this distinction.) It also staged the Pan American Games in 1955 and 1975, the latter after Santiago and São Paulo pulled out. The city held the ICF Flatwater Racing World Championships in 1974 and 1994. A major national sport is lucha libre, the distinctive Mexican wrestling style, with its primary venues being Arena México and Arena Coliseo.

input: The Vietnam War is often regarded as a low point for the U.S. Army due to the use of drafted personnel, the unpopularity of the war with the American public, and frustrating restrictions placed on the military by American political leaders. While American forces had been stationed in the Republic of Vietnam since 1959, in intelligence & advising/training roles, they did not deploy in large numbers until 1965, after the Gulf of Tonkin Incident. American forces effectively established and maintained control of the "traditional" battlefield, however they struggled to counter the guerrilla hit and run tactics of the communist Viet Cong and the North Vietnamese Army. On a tactical level, American soldiers (and the U.S. military as a whole) did not lose a sizable battle.
rewrite: The U.S. military's experience in the Vietnam War is frequently seen as one of its most difficult periods. This stemmed from employing conscripted troops, widespread domestic opposition to the conflict, and limiting rules imposed by political leadership. Although U.S. personnel had been present in South Vietnam since 1959 in support capacities, a major buildup only commenced in 1965 following the Gulf of Tonkin events. Militarily, U.S. forces consistently dominated conventional engagements but found it challenging to combat the irregular warfare and elusive strategies of Viet Cong and North Vietnamese Army units. Consequently, while American troops did not suffer a major tactical defeat in any significant battle, the overall war effort proved deeply problematic.

input: A second New Haven gastronomical claim to fame is Louis' Lunch, which is located in a small brick building on Crown Street and has been serving fast food since 1895. Though fiercely debated, the restaurant's founder Louis Lassen is credited by the Library of Congress with inventing the hamburger and steak sandwich. Louis' Lunch broils hamburgers, steak sandwiches and hot dogs vertically in original antique 1898 cast iron stoves using gridirons, patented by local resident Luigi Pieragostini in 1939, that hold the meat in place while it cooks.
rewrite: Another notable culinary landmark in New Haven is Louis' Lunch, a Crown Street eatery housed in a modest brick structure. Operating since 1895, it is recognized by the Library of Congress as the birthplace of the hamburger and steak sandwich, an attribution credited to founder Louis Lassen despite some dispute. The establishment prepares its burgers, steak sandwiches, and hot dogs in historic 1898 stoves, using specialized 1939 gridirons designed by Luigi Pieragostini to secure the meat during vertical broiling.

input: Some examples of social and religious transition ceremonies that can be found in the U.S., as well as in other cultures around the world, are Confirmation, Bar and Bat Mitzvahs, Quinceañeras, sweet sixteens, cotillions, and débutante balls. In other countries, initiation ceremonies play an important role, marking the transition into adulthood or the entrance into adolescence. This transition may be accompanied by obvious physical changes, which can vary from a change in clothing to tattoos and scarification. Furthermore, transitions into adulthood may also vary by gender, and specific rituals may be more common for males or for females. This illuminates the extent to which adolescence is, at least in part, a social construction; it takes shape differently depending on the cultural context, and may be enforced more by cultural practices or transitions than by universal chemical or biological physical changes.
rewrite: Various cultures, including that of the United States, observe rites of passage that signify social and spiritual change. These include events like Confirmation, Bar and Bat Mitzvahs, Quinceañeras, sweet sixteen parties, cotillions, and débutante balls. Globally, many societies hold significant initiation rituals to denote entry into adolescence or adulthood. Such passages are sometimes highlighted by visible bodily alterations, ranging from new attire to permanent marks like tattoos or scarification. These ceremonies also frequently differ by gender, with certain customs being predominantly for boys or girls. This diversity demonstrates that adolescence is largely a social concept, molded more by local traditions and symbolic milestones than by inevitable biological development.

input: At Maecenas' insistence (according to the tradition) Virgil spent the ensuing years (perhaps 37–29 BC) on the long didactic hexameter poem called the Georgics (from Greek, "On Working the Earth") which he dedicated to Maecenas. The ostensible theme of the Georgics is instruction in the methods of running a farm. In handling this theme, Virgil follows in the didactic ("how to") tradition of the Greek poet Hesiod's Works and Days and several works of the later Hellenistic poets. The four books of the Georgics focus respectively on raising crops and trees (1 and 2), livestock and horses (3), and beekeeping and the qualities of bees (4). Well-known passages include the beloved Laus Italiae of Book 2, the prologue description of the temple in Book 3, and the description of the plague at the end of Book 3. Book 4 concludes with a long mythological narrative, in the form of an epyllion which describes vividly the discovery of beekeeping by Aristaeus and the story of Orpheus' journey to the underworld. Ancient scholars, such as Servius, conjectured that the Aristaeus episode replaced, at the emperor's request, a long section in praise of Virgil's friend, the poet Gallus, who was disgraced by Augustus, and who committed suicide in 26 BC.
rewrite: At the urging of his patron Maecenas, as the established account holds, Virgil composed the *Georgics* over a period of years, likely from 37 to 29 BC. This extensive instructional work in hexameter verse, whose title derives from a Greek term for agriculture, is formally addressed to Maecenas. Its surface purpose is to offer practical guidance on farm management. In adopting this didactic approach, Virgil places himself within a lineage extending from Hesiod's *Works and Days* to later Greek poets of the Hellenistic period. The poem is divided into four parts: the first two deal with cultivating crops and orchards, the third with cattle and horses, and the fourth with beekeeping and the nature of bees. Notable sections encompass the celebrated praise of Italy in Book 2, the opening depiction of a temple in Book 3, and the account of a devastating plague concluding that same book. The final book ends with an extended myth, a short epic narrating Aristaeus's development of beekeeping and the tragic descent of Orpheus into the underworld. Commentators from antiquity, like Servius, speculated that this Aristaeus story was inserted on Augustus's orders, replacing original verses lauding the poet Gallus, a friend of Virgil's who fell from imperial favor and took his own life in 26 BC.

input: At times when a death sentence is affirmed on direct review, it is considered final. Yet, supplemental methods to attack the judgment, though less familiar than a typical appeal, do remain. These supplemental remedies are considered collateral review, that is, an avenue for upsetting judgments that have become otherwise final. Where the prisoner received his death sentence in a state-level trial, as is usually the case, the first step in collateral review is state collateral review. (If the case is a federal death penalty case, it proceeds immediately from direct review to federal habeas corpus.) Although all states have some type of collateral review, the process varies widely from state to state. Generally, the purpose of these collateral proceedings is to permit the prisoner to challenge his sentence on grounds that could not have been raised reasonably at trial or on direct review. Most often these are claims, such as ineffective assistance of counsel, which requires the court to consider new evidence outside the original trial record, something courts may not do in an ordinary appeal. State collateral review, though an important step in that it helps define the scope of subsequent review through federal habeas corpus, is rarely successful in and of itself. Only around 6 percent of death sentences are overturned on state collateral review. In 2010, the death sentences of 53 inmates were overturned as a result of legal appeals or high court reversals.
rewrite: When a capital sentence is upheld through initial appeals, it achieves finality. However, additional legal avenues exist to contest such a judgment, distinct from the standard appellate process. These subsequent mechanisms are known as collateral review, which serves as a means to challenge rulings that are otherwise considered conclusive. For individuals sentenced to death in state courts, which is the common scenario, the initial phase of this collateral challenge occurs at the state level. (In federal capital cases, the process moves directly from initial appeals to federal habeas corpus proceedings.) While every state provides some form of collateral review, their specific procedures differ significantly. Typically, these proceedings allow a condemned person to contest their sentence based on issues that could not reasonably have been presented during the trial or in earlier appeals. Frequently, these involve assertions like inadequate legal representation, which necessitate examining evidence outside the original trial record—an action not permitted in a conventional appeal. Although state collateral review plays a crucial role in shaping the boundaries for later federal habeas corpus review, it seldom results in overturning a sentence on its own. Approximately six percent of death sentences are reversed at this stage. For instance, in 2010, the sentences of 53 inmates were set aside due to successful legal challenges or reversals by higher courts.

input: Among the vast varieties of microorganisms, relatively few cause disease in otherwise healthy individuals. Infectious disease results from the interplay between those few pathogens and the defenses of the hosts they infect. The appearance and severity of disease resulting from any pathogen, depends upon the ability of that pathogen to damage the host as well as the ability of the host to resist the pathogen. However a host's immune system can also cause damage to the host itself in an attempt to control the infection. Clinicians therefore classify infectious microorganisms or microbes according to the status of host defenses - either as primary pathogens or as opportunistic pathogens:
rewrite: Only a small fraction of microbes lead to illness in people with robust health. Sickness arises from the interaction between these infectious agents and a host's protective responses. The intensity and nature of an illness hinge on both the microbe's capacity to inflict harm and the host's capability to counteract it. Notably, the immune response itself can sometimes injure the host while fighting the infection. Consequently, medical professionals categorize microbes based on the host's condition—as either primary pathogens or opportunistic ones.

input: The Somali Telecommunication Association (STA), a watchdog organization that oversees the policy development and regulatory framework of Somalia's ICT sector, reported in 2006 that there were over half a million users of internet services within the territory. There were also 22 established ISPs and 234 cyber cafes, with an annual growth rate of 15.6%.
rewrite: In 2006, the STA, a regulatory body for Somalia's ICT policies, noted more than 500,000 internet users nationwide. The sector included 22 internet service providers and 234 internet cafes, expanding annually at a rate of 15.6%.

input: The major settlements in the ceremonial county are concentrated on the Fylde coast (the Blackpool Urban Area), and a belt of towns running west-east along the M65: Preston, Blackburn, Accrington, Burnley, Nelson and Colne. South of Preston are the towns of Leyland and Chorley; the three formed part of the Central Lancashire New Town designated in 1970. The north of the county is predominantly rural and sparsely populated, except for the towns of Lancaster and Morecambe which form a large conurbation of almost 100,000 people. Lancashire is home to a significant Asian population, numbering over 70,000 and 6% of the county's population, and concentrated largely in the former cotton mill towns in the south east.
rewrite: The ceremonial county's primary population centers are found along the Fylde coast, including the Blackpool region, and in a series of towns aligned with the M65 corridor from Preston eastward to Colne, encompassing Blackburn, Accrington, Burnley, and Nelson. South of Preston lie Leyland and Chorley; these three settlements were included in the 1970 Central Lancashire New Town plan. The northern area is mostly countryside with low density, with the notable exception of the combined Lancaster and Morecambe area, a substantial urban center of roughly 100,000 residents. Over 70,000 individuals of Asian descent, constituting about six percent of Lancashire's population, reside primarily in the historic textile manufacturing towns of the southeast.

input: Romulus was credited with several religious institutions. He founded the Consualia festival, inviting the neighbouring Sabines to participate; the ensuing rape of the Sabine women by Romulus's men further embedded both violence and cultural assimilation in Rome's myth of origins. As a successful general, Romulus is also supposed to have founded Rome's first temple to Jupiter Feretrius and offered the spolia opima, the prime spoils taken in war, in the celebration of the first Roman triumph. Spared a mortal's death, Romulus was mysteriously spirited away and deified.
rewrite: Romulus established various religious practices, creating the Consualia festival to draw nearby Sabines. This event led to the abduction of Sabine women, intertwining force and integration into Rome's founding story. A victorious commander, he is also believed to have built the initial temple for Jupiter Feretrius and dedicated the finest war trophies, the spolia opima, during Rome's inaugural triumph. Rather than dying, he vanished and was later worshipped as a god.

input: According to the Federal Bureau of Investigation's Uniform Crime Reports, in 2010 the Raleigh Police Department and other agencies in the city reported 1,740 incidents of violent crime and 12,995 incidents of property crime – far below both the national average and the North Carolina average. Of the violent crimes reported, 14 were murders, 99 were forcible rapes and 643 were robberies. Aggravated assault accounted for 984 of the total violent crimes. Property crimes included burglaries which accounted for 3,021, larcenies for 9,104 and arson for 63 of the total number of incidents. Motor vehicle theft accounted for 870 incidents out of the total.
rewrite: Based on FBI crime statistics from 2010, Raleigh law enforcement documented significantly fewer criminal incidents than both the state and national norms. The city recorded 1,740 violent crimes, which included 14 homicides, 99 rapes, 643 robberies, and 984 serious assaults. Additionally, there were 12,995 property crimes, comprising 3,021 burglaries, 9,104 thefts, 63 cases of arson, and 870 stolen vehicles.

input: The earliest Greek philosophers, known as the pre-Socratics, provided competing answers to the question found in the myths of their neighbors: "How did the ordered cosmos in which we live come to be?" The pre-Socratic philosopher Thales (640-546 BC), dubbed the "father of science", was the first to postulate non-supernatural explanations for natural phenomena, for example, that land floats on water and that earthquakes are caused by the agitation of the water upon which the land floats, rather than the god Poseidon. Thales' student Pythagoras of Samos founded the Pythagorean school, which investigated mathematics for its own sake, and was the first to postulate that the Earth is spherical in shape. Leucippus (5th century BC) introduced atomism, the theory that all matter is made of indivisible, imperishable units called atoms. This was greatly expanded by his pupil Democritus.
rewrite: The initial Greek thinkers, often called the pre-Socratics, sought to explain how the universe's structured reality originated, a question also present in surrounding mythologies. Thales (640-546 BC), frequently called the first scientist, broke from tradition by proposing natural causes for events. He suggested, for instance, that the earth rests on water and that disturbances in this water cause earthquakes, not a deity. His follower, Pythagoras, established a school dedicated to mathematical study for its own sake and was the first to propose a spherical Earth. Later, Leucippus developed atomism, the idea that everything consists of indestructible, fundamental particles termed atoms, a theory his student Democritus later elaborated.

input: The final chapter reviews points from earlier chapters, and Darwin concludes by hoping that his theory might produce revolutionary changes in many fields of natural history. Although he avoids the controversial topic of human origins in the rest of the book so as not to prejudice readers against his theory, here he ventures a cautious hint that psychology would be put on a new foundation and that "Light will be thrown on the origin of man". Darwin ends with a passage that became well known and much quoted:
rewrite: In the closing section, Darwin revisits key arguments from the book. He expresses hope that his ideas will fundamentally transform natural history. While deliberately avoiding human evolution earlier to prevent bias, he now carefully suggests that psychology will be newly grounded and that understanding of mankind's beginnings will emerge. The work concludes with a passage that later gained significant fame and frequent citation.

input: Apple was initially reluctant to embrace mice with multiple buttons and scroll wheels. Macs did not natively support pointing devices that featured multiple buttons, even from third parties, until Mac OS X arrived in 2001. Apple continued to offer only single button mice, in both wired and Bluetooth wireless versions, until August 2005, when it introduced the Mighty Mouse. While it looked like a traditional one-button mouse, it actually had four buttons and a scroll ball, capable of independent x- and y-axis movement. A Bluetooth version followed in July 2006. In October 2009, Apple introduced the Magic Mouse, which uses multi-touch gesture recognition (similar to that of the iPhone) instead of a physical scroll wheel or ball. It is available only in a wireless configuration, but the wired Mighty Mouse (re-branded as "Apple Mouse") is still available as an alternative. Since 2010, Apple has also offered the Magic Trackpad as a means to control Macintosh desktop computers in a way similar to laptops.
rewrite: For many years, Apple resisted incorporating multi-button and scrolling features into its mice. Even with external devices, Mac computers lacked built-in support for more than a single button until the launch of Mac OS X in 2001. The company persisted in providing only single-button designs, both corded and wireless, until August 2005. At that time, it released the Mighty Mouse. This device maintained a classic single-button appearance but concealed four buttons and a unique scroll ball that could move independently on two axes. A wireless Bluetooth model was introduced in July 2006. Succeeding this, the Magic Mouse arrived in October 2009, replacing mechanical scrolling with a multi-touch surface for gestures, akin to iPhone technology. It is exclusively wireless, though a corded version of the older model, renamed the "Apple Mouse," remains an option. Additionally, since 2010, Apple has provided the Magic Trackpad, allowing desktop Macs to be controlled with laptop-style gestures.

input: The year 1789 brought the French Revolution and with it the first division of Alsace into the départements of Haut- and Bas-Rhin. Alsatians played an active role in the French Revolution. On 21 July 1789, after receiving news of the Storming of the Bastille in Paris, a crowd of people stormed the Strasbourg city hall, forcing the city administrators to flee and putting symbolically an end to the feudal system in Alsace. In 1792, Rouget de Lisle composed in Strasbourg the Revolutionary marching song "La Marseillaise" (as Marching song for the Army of the Rhine), which later became the anthem of France. "La Marseillaise" was played for the first time in April of that year in front of the mayor of Strasbourg Philippe-Frédéric de Dietrich. Some of the most famous generals of the French Revolution also came from Alsace, notably Kellermann, the victor of Valmy, Kléber, who led the armies of the French Republic in Vendée and Westermann, who also fought in the Vendée.
rewrite: In 1789, the French Revolution led to the initial separation of Alsace into the départements of Haut-Rhin and Bas-Rhin. The people of this region were deeply engaged in the revolutionary events. Following reports of the Bastille's fall in Paris, a group stormed Strasbourg's city hall on July 21, 1789, causing the officials to escape and marking the symbolic collapse of feudal power in the area. During 1792, in Strasbourg, Rouget de Lisle wrote the rousing tune "La Marseillaise," originally intended as a marching song for the Army of the Rhine, which later gained status as the French national anthem. Its inaugural performance took place that April at the residence of Strasbourg's mayor, Philippe-Frédéric de Dietrich. Furthermore, several distinguished military leaders of the revolution hailed from Alsace, including Kellermann, celebrated for his triumph at Valmy; Kléber, who commanded republican forces in the Vendée; and Westermann, who also saw action there.

input: As with most ancient civilizations, Rome's military served the triple purposes of securing its borders, exploiting peripheral areas through measures such as imposing tribute on conquered peoples, and maintaining internal order. From the outset, Rome's military typified this pattern and the majority of Rome's wars were characterized by one of two types. The first is the foreign war, normally begun as a counter-offensive or defense of an ally. The second is the civil war, which plagued the Roman Republic in its final century. Roman armies were not invincible, despite their formidable reputation and host of victories. Over the centuries the Romans "produced their share of incompetents" who led Roman armies into catastrophic defeats. Nevertheless, it was generally the fate of the greatest of Rome's enemies, such as Pyrrhus and Hannibal, to win early battles but lose the war. The history of Rome's campaigning is, if nothing else, a history of obstinate persistence overcoming appalling losses.
