rewrite: Like many early societies, Rome’s armed forces fulfilled three main roles: protecting its frontiers, extracting resources from neighboring regions—often by demanding payment from subdued populations—and upholding stability within its own territory. From its earliest days, Rome’s military followed this model, and most of its conflicts fell into one of two categories. The first was external warfare, typically launched either in response to an attack or in defense of an allied state. The second was internal strife, which troubled the Roman Republic intensely during its last hundred years. Despite their fearsome image and numerous triumphs, Roman legions were not unbeatable. Across the ages, Rome “had its fair share of incapable leaders” who guided their forces to disastrous losses. Still, even Rome’s most powerful adversaries, including figures like Pyrrhus and Hannibal, commonly saw early successes only to be defeated in the longer conflict. Ultimately, the record of Rome’s military endeavors is a testament to relentless endurance prevailing over devastating setbacks.

input: The large magnitude of solar energy available makes it a highly appealing source of electricity. The United Nations Development Programme in its 2000 World Energy Assessment found that the annual potential of solar energy was 1,575–49,837 exajoules (EJ). This is several times larger than the total world energy consumption, which was 559.8 EJ in 2012.
rewrite: Solar power is an attractive electricity source due to its vast potential. A 2000 UN assessment estimated its yearly capacity at 1,575–49,837 exajoules, greatly exceeding global energy use of about 560 exajoules in 2012.

input: A working group consisting of Leon van de Kerkhof (The Netherlands), Gerhard Stoll (Germany), Leonardo Chiariglione (Italy), Yves-François Dehery (France), Karlheinz Brandenburg (Germany) and James D. Johnston (USA) took ideas from ASPEC, integrated the filter bank from Layer 2, added some of their own ideas and created MP3, which was designed to achieve the same quality at 128 kbit/s as MP2 at 192 kbit/s.
rewrite: An international team, including experts from several nations, developed MP3 by combining concepts from ASPEC with Layer 2's filter bank and introducing new innovations. The format was engineered to match the audio quality of MP2 at 192 kbit/s while operating at only 128 kbit/s.

input: Chanakya, 4th Century BC Indian political philosopher. The Arthashastra provides an account of the science of politics for a wise ruler, policies for foreign affairs and wars, the system of a spy state and surveillance and economic stability of the state. Chanakya quotes several authorities including Bruhaspati, Ushanas, Prachetasa Manu, Parasara, and Ambi, and described himself as a descendant of a lineage of political philosophers, with his father Chanaka being his immediate predecessor. Another influential extant Indian treatise on political philosophy is the Sukra Neeti. An example of a code of law in ancient India is the Manusmṛti or Laws of Manu.
rewrite: Chanakya was an ancient Indian thinker from the 4th century BC who specialized in statecraft. His work, the Arthashastra, outlines principles for effective governance, covering areas such as international relations, military strategy, espionage networks, and fiscal health. He references earlier scholars like Bruhaspati and Manu, noting his own father, Chanaka, as part of this intellectual tradition. Other significant texts from classical India include the Sukra Neeti and the legal code known as the Manusmṛti.

input: Sessions for West's sixth solo effort begin to take shape in early 2013 in his own personal loft's living room at a Paris hotel. Determined to "undermine the commercial", he once again brought together close collaborators and attempted to incorporate Chicago drill, dancehall, acid house, and industrial music. Primarily inspired by architecture, West's perfectionist tendencies led him to contact producer Rick Rubin fifteen days shy of its due date to strip down the record's sound in favor of a more minimalist approach. Initial promotion of his sixth album included worldwide video projections of the album's music and live television performances. Yeezus, West's sixth album, was released June 18, 2013 to rave reviews from critics. It became the rapper's sixth consecutive number one debut, but also marked his lowest solo opening week sales. Def Jam issued "Black Skinhead" to radio in July 2013 as the album's lead single. On September 6, 2013, Kanye West announced he would be headlining his first solo tour in five years, to support Yeezus, with fellow American rapper Kendrick Lamar accompanying him along the way.
rewrite: In early 2013, Kanye West started crafting his sixth solo album from a living room in his private Paris hotel suite. Aiming to subvert mainstream expectations, he reunited with trusted associates and experimented with blending genres like Chicago drill, dancehall, acid house, and industrial. His architectural influences and relentless perfectionism prompted him, just two weeks before the deadline, to enlist producer Rick Rubin to radically simplify the production toward a sparser aesthetic. The album’s early promotion featured global video projections of its content and televised live acts. Titled *Yeezus*, the record launched on June 18, 2013, to widespread critical acclaim. It achieved West’s sixth straight chart-topping debut, yet also represented his weakest first-week sales for a solo project. That July, Def Jam released “Black Skinhead” as the primary radio single. On September 6, 2013, West revealed plans for his first solo tour in half a decade to promote *Yeezus*, with rapper Kendrick Lamar joining as the supporting act.

input: In addition to the Jazz Festival (described above), New Haven serves as the home city of the annual International Festival of Arts and Ideas. New Haven's Saint Patrick's Day parade, which began in 1842, is New England's oldest St. Patty's Day parade and draws the largest crowds of any one-day spectator event in Connecticut. The St. Andrew the Apostle Italian Festival has taken place in the historic Wooster Square neighborhood every year since 1900. Other parishes in the city celebrate the Feast of Saint Anthony of Padua and a carnival in honor of St. Bernadette Soubirous. New Haven celebrates Powder House Day every April on the New Haven Green to commemorate the city's entrance into the Revolutionary War. The annual Wooster Square Cherry Blossom Festival commemorates the 1973 planting of 72 Yoshino Japanese Cherry Blossom trees by the New Haven Historic Commission in collaboration with the New Haven Parks Department and residents of the neighborhood. The Festival now draws well over 5,000 visitors. The Film Fest New Haven has been held annually since 1995.
rewrite: Beyond the Jazz Festival, New Haven also hosts the yearly International Festival of Arts and Ideas. The city's Saint Patrick's Day parade, established in 1842, is the longest-running event of its kind in New England and attracts Connecticut's biggest single-day audience. Since 1900, the historic Wooster Square area has been home to the annual St. Andrew the Apostle Italian Festival. Additional church communities observe the Feast of Saint Anthony of Padua and hold a carnival for St. Bernadette Soubirous. Each April, Powder House Day is marked on the New Haven Green to honor the city's role in the American Revolution. The Wooster Square Cherry Blossom Festival remembers the 1973 planting of 72 Japanese cherry trees, a joint effort by local historians, city parks staff, and area citizens. This event now attracts more than five thousand attendees annually. Furthermore, the city has presented the Film Fest New Haven every year since 1995.

input: The Palacio Taranco is located in front of the Plaza Zabala, in the heart of Ciudad Vieja. It was erected in the early 20th century as the residence of the Ortiz Taranco brothers on the ruins of Montevideo's first theatre (of 1793), during a period in which the architectural style was influenced by French architecture. The palace was designed by French architects Charles Louis Girault and Jules Chifflot León who also designed the Petit Palais and the Arc de Triomphe in Paris. It passed to the city from the heirs of the Tarancos in 1943, along with its precious collection of Uruguayan furniture and draperies and was deemed by the city as an ideal place for a museum; in 1972 it became the Museum of Decorative Arts of Montevideo and in 1975 it became a National Heritage Site. The Decorative Arts Museum has an important collection of European paintings and decorative arts, ancient Greek and Roman art and Islamic ceramics of the 10th–18th century from the area of present-day Iran. The palace is often used as a meeting place by the Uruguayan government.
rewrite: Situated facing Zabala Plaza in Montevideo's historic Old City, the Palacio Taranco was built in the early 1900s. It served as the home for the Ortiz Taranco siblings, constructed over the remains of the city's inaugural theater from 1793. This era saw a strong French architectural influence, reflected in the palace's design by Charles Louis Girault and Jules Chifflot León, the same minds behind Paris's Petit Palais and Arc de Triomphe. The Taranco family's descendants transferred the property, along with its valuable assortment of Uruguayan furnishings and textiles, to the city in 1943. Officials considered it a perfect setting for a museum, leading to its establishment as the Museum of Decorative Arts in 1972 and its designation as a National Heritage Site three years later. The museum holds significant European paintings and decorative objects, classical Greco-Roman artifacts, and Islamic pottery from the 10th to 18th centuries originating in modern-day Iran. The Uruguayan government also frequently utilizes the palace for official functions.

input: Mexico City offers an immense and varied consumer retail market, ranging from basic foods to ultra high-end luxury goods. Consumers may buy in fixed indoor markets, mobile markets (tianguis), from street vendors, from downtown shops in a street dedicated to a certain type of good, in convenience stores and traditional neighborhood stores, in modern supermarkets, in warehouse and membership stores and the shopping centers that they anchor, in department stores, big-box stores and in modern shopping malls.
rewrite: Mexico City presents a vast and diverse retail landscape, catering to all needs from everyday essentials to exclusive luxury items. Shoppers can purchase goods in numerous settings, including permanent indoor markets, traveling street markets, independent vendors, specialized commercial streets, local corner shops, contemporary supermarkets, wholesale clubs, large department stores, expansive big-box retailers, and modern enclosed shopping complexes.

input: The territory now contained within Bronx County was originally part of Westchester County, one of the 12 original counties of the English Province of New York. The present Bronx County was contained in the town of Westchester and parts of the towns of Yonkers, Eastchester, and Pelham. In 1846, a new town, West Farms, was created by division of Westchester; in turn, in 1855, the town of Morrisania was created from West Farms. In 1873, the town of Kingsbridge (roughly corresponding to the modern Bronx neighborhoods of Kingsbridge, Riverdale, and Woodlawn) was established within the former borders of Yonkers.
rewrite: The area now known as Bronx County was initially a section of Westchester County, among the first twelve counties established in the English Province of New York. It lay within the old town of Westchester and sections of Yonkers, Eastchester, and Pelham. West Farms was formed from Westchester in 1846, and Morrisania later separated from West Farms in 1855. Finally, in 1873, the town of Kingsbridge was set up from a part of Yonkers, covering areas similar to today's Kingsbridge, Riverdale, and Woodlawn neighborhoods.

input: The cuisine of Switzerland is multifaceted. While some dishes such as fondue, raclette or rösti are omnipresent through the country, each region developed its own gastronomy according to the differences of climate and languages.  Traditional Swiss cuisine uses ingredients similar to those in other European countries, as well as unique dairy products and cheeses such as Gruyère or Emmental, produced in the valleys of Gruyères and Emmental. The number of fine-dining establishments is high, particularly in western Switzerland.
rewrite: Swiss food culture is diverse. Although certain meals like fondue and rösti are common nationwide, local culinary traditions vary with climate and language. Ingredients often resemble those found elsewhere in Europe, alongside distinctive local cheeses like Gruyère. The country, especially its western part, also boasts a significant concentration of upscale restaurants.

input: Extensive and diverse public spending is, in itself, inherently at risk of cronyism, kickbacks, and embezzlement. Complicated regulations and arbitrary, unsupervised official conduct exacerbate the problem. This is one argument for privatization and deregulation. Opponents of privatization see the argument as ideological. The argument that corruption necessarily follows from the opportunity is weakened by the existence of countries with low to non-existent corruption but large public sectors, like the Nordic countries. These countries score high on the Ease of Doing Business Index, due to good and often simple regulations, and have rule of law firmly established. Therefore, due to their lack of corruption in the first place, they can run large public sectors without inducing political corruption. Recent evidence that takes both the size of expenditures and regulatory complexity into account has found that high-income democracies with more expansive state sectors do indeed have higher levels of corruption.
rewrite: When government spending is vast and varied, it naturally creates openings for favoritism, bribery, and the misuse of funds. This danger is intensified by convoluted rules and the unchecked power of officials. Such concerns are often cited to justify transferring public services to private hands and reducing regulations. Critics of this approach view it as driven by belief rather than fact. The claim that corruption is an inevitable result of such opportunities is challenged by nations, such as those in Scandinavia, which maintain substantial public sectors yet exhibit little to no corruption. These countries rank well on business climate indices because of their clear, effective laws and strong legal frameworks. Their existing integrity allows for large-scale public operations without sparking graft. However, newer studies considering both spending volume and regulatory intricacy indicate that among wealthy democracies, those with broader government involvement tend to experience more corruption.

input: Notre Dame's conference affiliations for all of its sports except football and fencing changed in July 2013 as a result of major conference realignment, and its fencing affiliation will change in July 2014. The Irish left the Big East for the ACC during a prolonged period of instability in the Big East; while they maintain their football independence, they have committed to play five games per season against ACC opponents. In ice hockey, the Irish were forced to find a new conference home after the Big Ten Conference's decision to add the sport in 2013–14 led to a cascade of conference moves that culminated in the dissolution of the school's former hockey home, the Central Collegiate Hockey Association, after the 2012–13 season. Notre Dame moved its hockey team to Hockey East. After Notre Dame joined the ACC, the conference announced it would add fencing as a sponsored sport beginning in the 2014–15 school year. There are many theories behind the adoption of the athletics moniker but it is known that the Fighting Irish name was used in the early 1920s with respect to the football team and was popularized by alumnus Francis Wallace in his New York Daily News columns. The official colors of Notre Dame are Navy Blue and Gold Rush which are worn in competition by its athletic teams. In addition, the color green is often worn because of the Fighting Irish nickname. The Notre Dame Leprechaun is the mascot of the athletic teams. Created by Theodore W. Drake in 1964, the leprechaun was first used on the football pocket schedule and later on the football program covers. The leprechaun was featured on the cover of Time in November 1964 and gained national exposure.
rewrite:
In July 2013, the University of Notre Dame shifted the conference alignment for most of its athletic programs, excluding football and fencing, due to widespread restructuring among major collegiate leagues. This move was followed by a planned change for its fencing team in July 2014. The institution departed the Big East Conference for the Atlantic Coast Conference, a transition prompted by ongoing instability within the Big East. While Notre Dame continues to operate its football program independently, it has agreed to schedule five annual games against ACC members. For ice hockey, the university needed to secure a new conference after the Big Ten's announcement to sponsor the sport starting in the 2013–14 season triggered a series of realignments. This ultimately resulted in the disbanding of the Central Collegiate Hockey Association, Notre Dame's former league, following the 2012–13 season. Consequently, the hockey team relocated to Hockey East. Following Notre Dame's entry into the ACC, the conference declared it would begin sponsoring fencing as an official sport in the 2014–15 academic year.

The origin of the "Fighting Irish" nickname is attributed to several accounts, though it is documented that the term was applied to the football squad in the early 1920s. Alumnus Francis Wallace helped cement its popularity through his columns in the New York Daily News. The official colors representing the university are Navy Blue and Gold Rush, which its teams wear in official competitions. Reflecting the Irish heritage implied by the nickname, the color green is also frequently incorporated into athletic uniforms. Serving as the official mascot for all sports teams is the Notre Dame Leprechaun. Designed by Theodore W. Drake in 1964, the leprechaun first appeared on printed football schedules and later on program covers. This symbol achieved national recognition when it was featured on the cover of *Time* magazine in November of that same year.

input: During colonial times, Edenton served as the state capital beginning in 1722, and New Bern was selected as the capital in 1766. Construction of Tryon Palace, which served as the residence and offices of the provincial governor William Tryon, began in 1767 and was completed in 1771. In 1788 Raleigh was chosen as the site of the new capital, as its central location protected it from attacks from the coast. Officially established in 1792 as both county seat and state capital, the city was named after Sir Walter Raleigh, sponsor of Roanoke, the "lost colony" on Roanoke Island.
rewrite: Edenton functioned as North Carolina's capital starting in 1722, followed by New Bern in 1766. The building of Tryon Palace, the governor's official home and workplace, started a year later and finished in 1771. Raleigh became the chosen capital in 1788, partly for its inland safety from coastal raids. Formally founded in 1792 to serve as both state capital and county seat, the city honors Sir Walter Raleigh, who backed the Roanoke Island settlement that later vanished.

input: Carnivore and herbivore diets are contrasting, with basic nitrogen and carbon proportions vary for their particular foods. "The nitrogen content of plant tissues averages about 2%, while in fungi, animals, and bacteria it averages about 5% to 10%." Many herbivores rely on bacterial fermentation to create digestible nutrients from indigestible plant cellulose, while obligate carnivores must eat animal meats to obtain certain vitamins or nutrients their bodies cannot otherwise synthesize. All animals' diets must provide sufficient amounts of the basic building blocks they need, up to the point where their particular biology can synthesize the rest. Animal tissue contains chemical compounds, such as water, carbohydrates (sugar, starch, and fiber), amino acids (in proteins), fatty acids (in lipids), and nucleic acids (DNA and RNA). These compounds in turn consist of elements such as carbon, hydrogen, oxygen, nitrogen, phosphorus, calcium, iron, zinc, magnesium, manganese, and so on. All of these chemical compounds and elements occur in various forms and combinations (e.g. hormones, vitamins, phospholipids, hydroxyapatite).
rewrite: The diets of meat-eaters and plant-eaters differ fundamentally, reflected in the distinct nitrogen and carbon ratios found in their respective food sources. Plant matter generally contains around 2% nitrogen, whereas fungi, animals, and bacteria average between 5% and 10%. To access nutrients locked in tough plant cellulose, numerous herbivores depend on symbiotic bacteria for fermentation. In contrast, true carnivores require meat to acquire specific vitamins and nutrients they are unable to produce internally. Every animal's nutrition must supply the essential raw materials its own physiology cannot manufacture. Tissues from animals are composed of substances like water, carbohydrates, proteins with amino acids, lipids with fatty acids, and nucleic acids. These are built from elemental components including carbon, hydrogen, oxygen, nitrogen, phosphorus, calcium, and trace metals. Such compounds and elements exist in diverse arrangements, forming structures like vitamins, hormones, and phospholipids.

input: The Theater District is a 17-block area in the center of downtown Houston that is home to the Bayou Place entertainment complex, restaurants, movies, plazas, and parks. Bayou Place is a large multilevel building containing full-service restaurants, bars, live music, billiards, and Sundance Cinema. The Bayou Music Center stages live concerts, stage plays, and stand-up comedy. Space Center Houston is the official visitors' center of NASA's Lyndon B. Johnson Space Center. The Space Center has many interactive exhibits including moon rocks, a shuttle simulator, and presentations about the history of NASA's manned space flight program. Other tourist attractions include the Galleria (Texas's largest shopping mall, located in the Uptown District), Old Market Square, the Downtown Aquarium, and Sam Houston Race Park.
rewrite: Centered in downtown Houston, the Theater District spans seventeen blocks and features the Bayou Place entertainment venue alongside various dining options, theaters, and green spaces. Bayou Place itself is a sizable, multi-story structure offering restaurants, bars, musical performances, pool tables, and a movie theater. Live concerts, theatrical productions, and comedy shows are hosted at the Bayou Music Center. Serving as the public gateway to NASA's Johnson Space Center, Space Center Houston displays interactive items such as lunar samples and a shuttle simulator, while detailing the story of human spaceflight. Further notable sites comprise the massive Galleria mall in Uptown, Old Market Square, the Downtown Aquarium, and Sam Houston Race Park.

input: During the Age of Enlightenment, philosophers such as John Locke advocated the principle in their writings, whereas others, such as Thomas Hobbes, strongly opposed it. Montesquieu was one of the foremost supporters of separating the legislature, the executive, and the judiciary. His writings considerably influenced the opinions of the framers of the United States Constitution.
rewrite: In the Enlightenment era, thinkers like John Locke endorsed the concept in their works, while others, including Thomas Hobbes, firmly rejected it. Montesquieu, a leading proponent of dividing government into legislative, executive, and judicial branches, greatly shaped the views of America's founding document's authors.

input: The strength of the Viking influence on Old English appears from the fact that the indispensable elements of the language - pronouns, modals, comparatives, pronominal adverbs (like "hence" and "together"), conjunctions and prepositions - show the most marked Danish influence; the best evidence of Scandinavian influence appears in the extensive word borrowings for, as Jespersen indicates, no texts exist in either Scandinavia or in Northern England from this time to give certain evidence of an influence on syntax. The change to Old English from Old Norse was substantive, pervasive, and of a democratic character. Old Norse and Old English resembled each other closely like cousins and with some words in common, they roughly understood each other; in time the inflections melted away and the analytic pattern emerged. It is most “important to recognize that in many words the English and Scandinavian language differed chiefly in their inflectional elements. The body of the word was so nearly the same in the two languages that only the endings would put obstacles in the way of mutual understanding. In the mixed population which existed in the Danelaw these endings must have led to much confusion, tending gradually to become obscured and finally lost.” This blending of peoples and languages happily resulted in “simplifying English grammar.”
rewrite:
The impact of Norse languages on Old English was profound, as seen in how core linguistic components—including pronouns, auxiliary verbs, comparative forms, adverbs such as "hence," along with conjunctions and prepositions—bear strong traces of Danish origins. The most visible sign of this Scandinavian effect is the large number of borrowed terms. Since no surviving records from Scandinavia or Northern England during this period provide clear proof of syntactic changes, vocabulary adoption serves as key evidence. The shift from Old Norse to Old English was significant, widespread, and reflected everyday usage among common speakers.

Old Norse and Old English were akin to close relatives, sharing similarities that allowed basic mutual comprehension. Over time, the complex grammatical endings faded, giving way to a more straightforward analytical structure. Crucially, many terms in both languages differed mainly in their inflectional suffixes. The core of these words was often nearly identical, so only the endings hindered understanding. In the culturally mixed region of the Danelaw, these varying inflections likely caused considerable confusion, gradually becoming less distinct until they disappeared entirely. This fusion of populations and tongues fortunately contributed to a noticeable simplification of English grammar.

input: The teachings on the Four Noble Truths are regarded as central to the teachings of Buddhism, and are said to provide a conceptual framework for Buddhist thought. These four truths explain the nature of dukkha (suffering, anxiety, unsatisfactoriness), its causes, and how it can be overcome. The four truths are:[note 4]
rewrite: The Four Noble Truths form the core of Buddhist doctrine, offering a structure for its philosophy. They describe the essence of suffering, its origins, and the path to its cessation.

input: Another study of dogs' roles in families showed many dogs have set tasks or routines undertaken as family members, the most common of which was helping with the washing-up by licking the plates in the dishwasher, and bringing in the newspaper from the lawn. Increasingly, human family members are engaging in activities centered on the perceived needs and interests of the dog, or in which the dog is an integral partner, such as dog dancing and dog yoga.
rewrite: Research into canine family contributions reveals that dogs often have regular duties, like cleaning dishes by licking them in the dishwasher or fetching the paper from outside. Families are also more frequently participating in activities designed around their dog's assumed preferences, or where the pet is a key participant, including pursuits like canine-focused dance and yoga.

input: The Ismailis differ from Twelvers because they had living imams for centuries after the last Twelver Imam went into concealment. They followed Isma'il ibn Jafar, elder brother of Musa al-Kadhim, as the rightful Imam after his father Ja'far al-Sadiq. The Ismailis believe that whether Imam Ismail did or did not die before Imam Ja'far, he had passed on the mantle of the imamate to his son Muḥammad ibn Ismail as the next imam. Thus, their line of imams is as follows (the years of their individual imamats during the Common Era are given in brackets):
rewrite: Ismaili Shiism diverges from the Twelver tradition by maintaining a continuous line of living imams long after the Twelvers' final imam entered occultation. They uphold Isma'il ibn Jafar, the older sibling of Musa al-Kadhim, as the legitimate successor to Imam Ja'far al-Sadiq. Ismailis hold that the imamate was transmitted from Imam Ismail to his son Muḥammad ibn Ismail, regardless of Ismail's precise timing of death. Their succession of imams, with CE dates of leadership provided, follows from this lineage.

input: Chopin's qualities as a pianist and composer were recognized by many of his fellow musicians. Schumann named a piece for him in his suite Carnaval, and Chopin later dedicated his Ballade No. 2 in F major to Schumann. Elements of Chopin's music can be traced in many of Liszt's later works. Liszt later transcribed for piano six of Chopin's Polish songs. A less fraught friendship was with Alkan, with whom he discussed elements of folk music, and who was deeply affected by Chopin's death.
rewrite: Numerous contemporaries acknowledged Chopin's dual talents in performance and composition. Schumann honored him with a piece in "Carnaval," and Chopin reciprocated by dedicating his F major Ballade No. 2 to Schumann. Liszt's later pieces show Chopin's influence, and he arranged six of Chopin's Polish songs for piano. Chopin also shared a cordial relationship with Alkan, conversing on folk music; Alkan was profoundly moved when Chopin died.

input: Whilst filming in Mexico City, speculation in the media claimed that the script had been altered to accommodate the demands of Mexican authorities—reportedly influencing details of the scene and characters, casting choices, and modifying the script in order to portray the country in a "positive light"—in order to secure tax concessions and financial support worth up to $20 million for the film. This was denied by producer Michael G. Wilson, who stated that the scene had always been intended to be shot in Mexico as production had been attracted to the imagery of the Day of the Dead, and that the script had been developed from there. Production of Skyfall had previously faced similar problems while attempting to secure permits to shoot the film's pre-title sequence in India before moving to Istanbul.
rewrite: During production in Mexico City, media reports suggested that the screenplay was revised to meet the requests of local officials, allegedly to depict the nation favorably. These changes were said to involve specific plot and character elements, as well as casting decisions, with the aim of obtaining tax incentives and funding totaling around $20 million. Producer Michael G. Wilson refuted these claims, explaining that the setting was always planned to be Mexico due to the visual appeal of the Day of the Dead celebration, and the story was built around that location. The film's crew had encountered comparable difficulties earlier when trying to get approval to film the opening sequence in India, which ultimately led them to shoot in Istanbul instead.

input: Brood parasitism, in which an egg-layer leaves her eggs with another individual's brood, is more common among birds than any other type of organism. After a parasitic bird lays her eggs in another bird's nest, they are often accepted and raised by the host at the expense of the host's own brood. Brood parasites may be either obligate brood parasites, which must lay their eggs in the nests of other species because they are incapable of raising their own young, or non-obligate brood parasites, which sometimes lay eggs in the nests of conspecifics to increase their reproductive output even though they could have raised their own young. One hundred bird species, including honeyguides, icterids, and ducks, are obligate parasites, though the most famous are the cuckoos. Some brood parasites are adapted to hatch before their host's young, which allows them to destroy the host's eggs by pushing them out of the nest or to kill the host's chicks; this ensures that all food brought to the nest will be fed to the parasitic chicks.
rewrite: Brood parasitism occurs when a bird deposits its eggs in another bird's nest, a behavior more frequently observed in avian species than in any other animal group. Typically, the host bird incubates and rears these foreign offspring, often to the detriment of its own young. This strategy divides into two categories. Obligate brood parasites, such as cuckoos, honeyguides, and certain ducks—totaling around one hundred species—rely entirely on other birds to raise their chicks, being unable to do so themselves. In contrast, non-obligate parasites, which may include members of the same species, occasionally use others' nests to boost their reproductive success, even though they are capable of parenting their own offspring. Additionally, some parasitic chicks hatch earlier than the host's, enabling them to eliminate competing eggs or nestlings, thereby monopolizing all the food delivered by the host parents.

input: The area near the border with Cameroon close to the coast is rich rainforest and part of the Cross-Sanaga-Bioko coastal forests ecoregion, an important centre for biodiversity. It is habitat for the drill monkey, which is found in the wild only in this area and across the border in Cameroon. The areas surrounding Calabar, Cross River State, also in this forest, are believed to contain the world's largest diversity of butterflies. The area of southern Nigeria between the Niger and the Cross Rivers has lost most of its forest because of development and harvesting by increased population, with it being replaced by grassland (see Cross-Niger transition forests).
rewrite: The coastal region bordering Cameroon consists of dense rainforests within the Cross-Sanaga-Bioko ecoregion, recognized as a significant biodiversity hotspot. This environment serves as the exclusive natural habitat for the drill monkey, which lives solely here and in adjacent parts of Cameroon. Additionally, the forests around Calabar in Cross River State are thought to host the greatest variety of butterfly species on Earth. Further west, the terrain between the Niger and Cross Rivers has largely been deforested due to human activity and population growth, transforming much of the landscape into grasslands.

input: Lactase is an enzyme that breaks down the disaccharide lactose to its component parts, glucose and galactose. Glucose and galactose can be absorbed by the small intestine. Approximately 65 percent of the adult population produce only small amounts of lactase and are unable to eat unfermented milk-based foods. This is commonly known as lactose intolerance. Lactose intolerance varies widely by ethnic heritage; more than 90 percent of peoples of east Asian descent are lactose intolerant, in contrast to about 5 percent of people of northern European descent.
rewrite: The enzyme lactase helps digest lactose by splitting it into the simpler sugars glucose and galactose, which the small intestine can then absorb. Many adults—around 65%—produce very little lactase, making them unable to properly digest most dairy products, a condition called lactose intolerance. Its prevalence differs significantly among ethnic groups; for example, over 90% of people of East Asian ancestry are affected, compared to just roughly 5% of those with Northern European roots.

input: On August 24, 2006, Apple and Creative announced a broad settlement to end their legal disputes. Apple will pay Creative US$100 million for a paid-up license, to use Creative's awarded patent in all Apple products. As part of the agreement, Apple will recoup part of its payment, if Creative is successful in licensing the patent. Creative then announced its intention to produce iPod accessories by joining the Made for iPod program.
rewrite: On August 24, 2006, Apple and Creative Technology resolved their litigation through a comprehensive agreement. Apple agreed to provide Creative with a $100 million payment for a complete license to utilize its patented technology across all devices. A portion of this sum may be returned to Apple should Creative license the patent to others. Concurrently, Creative revealed plans to develop iPod-compatible products by enrolling in Apple's accessory certification program.

input: Next, Spielberg teamed with Star Wars creator and friend George Lucas on an action adventure film, Raiders of the Lost Ark, the first of the Indiana Jones films. The archaeologist and adventurer hero Indiana Jones was played by Harrison Ford (whom Lucas had previously cast in his Star Wars films as Han Solo). The film was considered an homage to the cliffhanger serials of the Golden Age of Hollywood. It became the biggest film at the box office in 1981, and the recipient of numerous Oscar nominations including Best Director (Spielberg's second nomination) and Best Picture (the second Spielberg film to be nominated for Best Picture). Raiders is still considered a landmark example of the action-adventure genre. The film also led to Ford's casting in Ridley Scott's Blade Runner.
rewrite: Following this, Spielberg collaborated with his close associate George Lucas, the mind behind Star Wars, on the action-adventure movie *Raiders of the Lost Ark*, launching the Indiana Jones series. Harrison Ford, who Lucas had earlier featured as Han Solo in his Star Wars movies, took on the role of the archaeologist and daring protagonist, Indiana Jones. The movie served as a tribute to the suspenseful serials from Hollywood's classic era. It emerged as the highest-grossing film of 1981 and earned many Academy Award nominations, such as Best Picture (marking Spielberg's second film to receive this honor) and Best Director (Spielberg's second nomination in that category). *Raiders* remains a definitive benchmark for action-adventure cinema. Additionally, this role contributed to Ford being selected for Ridley Scott's *Blade Runner*.

input: The indirect method of applying tesserae is often used for very large projects, projects with repetitive elements or for areas needing site specific shapes. Tiles are applied face-down to a backing paper using an adhesive, and later transferred onto walls, floors or craft projects. This method is most useful for extremely large projects as it gives the maker time to rework areas, allows the cementing of the tiles to the backing panel to be carried out quickly in one operation and helps ensure that the front surfaces of the mosaic tiles and mosaic pieces are flat and in the same plane on the front, even when using tiles and pieces of differing thicknesses. Mosaic murals, benches and tabletops are some of the items usually made using the indirect method, as it results in a smoother and more even surface.
rewrite: The indirect tesserae technique is commonly chosen for extensive installations, designs with repeating patterns, or sections requiring custom-cut shapes. In this process, individual pieces are adhered face-down onto a temporary paper backing. Once arranged, the entire assembly is transferred as a single unit to its final location, such as a wall, floor, or art object. This approach is particularly advantageous for sizable works because it permits adjustments during the layout phase and enables the permanent adhesive application to be completed efficiently in one step. It also guarantees a uniformly flat front surface, even when incorporating materials of varying depths. Consequently, projects like mosaic murals, benches, and tabletops frequently employ this method to achieve a seamless and level finish.

input: Strict separation of powers did not operate in The United Kingdom, the political structure of which served in most instances[citation needed] as a model for the government created by the U.S. Constitution.[citation needed] Under the UK Westminster system, based on parliamentary sovereignty and responsible government, Parliament (consisting of the Sovereign (King-in-Parliament), House of Lords and House of Commons) was the supreme lawmaking authority. The executive branch acted in the name of the King ("His Majesty's Government"), as did the judiciary. The King's Ministers were in most cases members of one of the two Houses of Parliament, and the Government needed to sustain the support of a majority in the House of Commons. One minister, the Lord Chancellor, was at the same time the sole judge in the Court of Chancery and the presiding officer in the House of Lords. Therefore, it may be seen that the three branches of British government often violated the strict principle of separation of powers, even though there were many occasions when the different branches of the government disagreed with each other. Some U.S. states did not observe a strict separation of powers in the 18th century. In New Jersey, the Governor also functioned as a member of the state's highest court and as the presiding officer of one house of the New Jersey Legislature. The President of Delaware was a member of the Court of Appeals; the presiding officers of the two houses of the state legislature also served in the executive department as Vice Presidents. In both Delaware and Pennsylvania, members of the executive council served at the same time as judges. On the other hand, many southern states explicitly required separation of powers. Maryland, Virginia, North Carolina and Georgia all kept the branches of government "separate and distinct."
rewrite:
The United Kingdom's political framework, which frequently provided a template for the U.S. Constitution, did not maintain a rigid division of governmental functions. The British Westminster model rests on the principles of parliamentary supremacy and accountable governance, where the ultimate legislative power resides with Parliament—comprising the monarch, the House of Lords, and the House of Commons. Both the executive and judicial branches operated under the authority of the Crown. Typically, the King's ministers were drawn from Parliament, and the ruling administration had to maintain majority backing in the Commons. Notably, the Lord Chancellor embodied the blending of roles, serving simultaneously as the chief judge in the Court of Chancery and the speaker of the House of Lords. Consequently, while conflicts between government branches did occur, the British system regularly departed from a strict separation of powers.

Similarly, several early American states in the 18th century did not adhere to a complete separation. In New Jersey, the governor also sat on the highest court and presided over one legislative chamber. Delaware’s president was a member of the Court of Appeals, and the leaders of its legislative houses acted as vice presidents in the executive branch. Both Delaware and Pennsylvania allowed executive councilors to serve as judges concurrently. In contrast, numerous southern states expressly mandated a clear division. Maryland, Virginia, North Carolina, and Georgia each enshrined in their constitutions that the governmental branches must remain "separate and distinct."

input: The settlement of Plympton, further up the River Plym than the current Plymouth, was also an early trading port, but the river silted up in the early 11th century and forced the mariners and merchants to settle at the current day Barbican near the river mouth. At the time this village was called Sutton, meaning south town in Old English. The name Plym Mouth, meaning "mouth of the River Plym" was first mentioned in a Pipe Roll of 1211. The name Plymouth first officially replaced Sutton in a charter of King Henry VI in 1440. See Plympton for the derivation of the name Plym.
rewrite: Originally located farther inland along the River Plym, the trading post of Plympton declined when its waterway became clogged with silt during the 1000s. This prompted sailors and traders to move downstream to a site then known as Sutton, an Old English term for "south town," situated near the river's outlet. The designation "Plym Mouth," referring to the river's estuary, appears in records dating to 1211. "Plymouth" was formally adopted in place of Sutton by a royal charter issued in 1440.

input: Through his actions and speeches, and because he was able to symbolize the popular Arab will, Nasser inspired several nationalist revolutions in the Arab world. He defined the politics of his generation and communicated directly with the public masses of the Arab world, bypassing the various heads of states of those countries—an accomplishment not repeated by other Arab leaders. The extent of Nasser's centrality in the region made it a priority for incoming Arab nationalist heads of state to seek good relations with Egypt, in order to gain popular legitimacy from their own citizens.
rewrite: Nasser became a powerful symbol of Arab aspirations, motivating numerous nationalist movements across the region. His direct connection with the people, rather than their governments, uniquely shaped the era's political landscape. This influence made his approval essential; subsequent nationalist leaders prioritized strong ties with Egypt to secure validation and support from their own populations. No other Arab figure has since matched this level of popular engagement and regional centrality.

input: Conversely, most heat-treatable alloys are precipitation hardening alloys, which produce the opposite effects that steel does. When heated to form a solution and then cooled quickly, these alloys become much softer than normal, during the diffusionless transformation, and then harden as they age. The solutes in these alloys will precipitate over time, forming intermetallic phases, which are difficult to discern from the base metal. Unlike steel, in which the solid solution separates to form different crystal phases, precipitation hardening alloys separate to form different phases within the same crystal. These intermetallic alloys appear homogeneous in crystal structure, but tend to behave heterogeneous, becoming hard and somewhat brittle.
rewrite: In contrast, many alloys that can be heat-treated gain strength through precipitation hardening, a process with outcomes opposite to those in steel. Initially, these alloys are heated to create a uniform solution and rapidly cooled, resulting in a soft state following a diffusionless change. They subsequently strengthen during aging. Over time, dissolved elements separate out, creating intermetallic compounds that blend into the base material. Unlike the distinct crystalline phases formed in steel, these alloys develop different phases inside a single crystal lattice. Although they seem uniform in structure, such alloys often act as non-uniform materials, turning hard and relatively brittle.

input: When the Frankish rulers established the system of feudalism, the Bishops of Utrecht came to exercise worldly power as prince-bishops. The territory of the bishopric not only included the modern province of Utrecht (Nedersticht, 'lower Sticht'), but also extended to the northeast. The feudal conflict of the Middle Ages heavily affected Utrecht. The prince-bishopric was involved in almost continuous conflicts with the Counts of Holland and the Dukes of Guelders. The Veluwe region was seized by Guelders, but large areas in the modern province of Overijssel remained as the Oversticht.
rewrite: Upon the Frankish implementation of feudal governance, the Bishops of Utrecht gained secular authority, becoming prince-bishops. Their domain encompassed more than today's Utrecht province, reaching toward the northeast. Medieval feudal struggles deeply impacted this region. The prince-bishopric found itself persistently at odds with the Counts of Holland and the Dukes of Guelders. While Guelders took control of the Veluwe area, extensive lands in what is now Overijssel were retained as the Oversticht.

input: Under the Qing dynasty (1644–1911), the Nanjing area was known as Jiangning (江寧) and served as the seat of government for the Viceroy of Liangjiang. It had been visited by the Kangxi and Qianlong emperors a number of times on their tours of the southern provinces. Nanjing was invaded by British troops during the close of the First Opium War, which was ended by the Treaty of Nanjing in 1842. As the capital of the brief-lived rebel Taiping Heavenly Kingdom (founded by the Taiping rebels in the mid-19th century, Nanjing was known as Tianjing (天京, "Heavenly Capital" or "Capital of Heaven").
rewrite: During the Qing era from 1644 to 1911, the region of Nanjing was called Jiangning and functioned as the administrative center for the Liangjiang Viceroy. Emperors Kangxi and Qianlong repeatedly stopped there during their journeys to the south. Near the conclusion of the First Opium War, British forces occupied the city, leading to the 1842 Treaty of Nanjing. In the mid-1800s, it was renamed Tianjing, or "Heavenly Capital," when it became the center of the short-lived Taiping Heavenly Kingdom rebellion.

input: General Ridgway was appointed Supreme Commander, Korea; he regrouped the UN forces for successful counterattacks, while General James Van Fleet assumed command of the U.S. Eighth Army. Further attacks slowly depleted the PVA and KPA forces; Operations Courageous (23–28 March 1951) and Tomahawk (23 March 1951) were a joint ground and airborne infilltration meant to trap Chinese forces between Kaesong and Seoul. UN forces advanced to "Line Kansas", north of the 38th parallel. The 187th Airborne Regimental Combat Team's ("Rakkasans") second of two combat jumps was on Easter Sunday, 1951, at Munsan-ni, South Korea, codenamed Operation Tomahawk. The mission was to get behind Chinese forces and block their movement north. The 60th Indian Parachute Field Ambulance provided the medical cover for the operations, dropping an ADS and a surgical team and treating over 400 battle casualties apart from the civilian casualties that formed the core of their objective as the unit was on a humanitarian mission.
rewrite:
General Ridgway took over as the top UN commander in Korea, reorganizing the coalition's troops to mount effective offensives. At the same time, General James Van Fleet began leading the U.S. Eighth Army. Sustained assaults gradually reduced the strength of the Chinese and North Korean armies. In late March 1951, Operations Courageous and Tomahawk were launched as a combined maneuver using ground and paratrooper units. The goal was to encircle opposing troops in the area between Kaesong and Seoul. This push allowed UN soldiers to reach "Line Kansas," a position just above the 38th parallel.

As part of Operation Tomahawk on Easter Sunday, the 187th Airborne Regimental Combat Team, known as the "Rakkasans," made a combat parachute drop at Munsan-ni. Their objective was to cut off the retreat routes of Chinese forces. Medical support was provided by the 60th Indian Parachute Field Ambulance, which deployed an advanced surgical team. While their primary role was humanitarian, the unit cared for more than 400 military wounded in addition to many civilians.

input: The European Revolutions of 1848, known in some countries as the Spring of Nations or the Year of Revolution, were a series of political upheavals throughout the European continent. Described as a revolutionary wave, the period of unrest began in France and then, further propelled by the French Revolution of 1848, soon spread to the rest of Europe. Although most of the revolutions were quickly put down, there was a significant amount of violence in many areas, with tens of thousands of people tortured and killed. While the immediate political effects of the revolutions were reversed, the long-term reverberations of the events were far-reaching.
rewrite: In 1848, a wave of political revolts swept across Europe, also called the Springtime of Nations. This period of widespread turmoil started in France, and the momentum from its revolution quickly ignited similar uprisings elsewhere on the continent. Most of these rebellions were suppressed swiftly, yet they involved considerable bloodshed, leading to the torture and death of many thousands. The immediate conservative restoration could not erase the profound and lasting historical impact these revolutions ultimately achieved.

input: The term "Late Middle Ages" refers to one of the three periods of the Middle Ages, along with the Early Middle Ages and the High Middle Ages. Leonardo Bruni was the first historian to use tripartite periodization in his History of the Florentine People (1442). Flavio Biondo used a similar framework in Decades of History from the Deterioration of the Roman Empire (1439–1453). Tripartite periodization became standard after the German historian Christoph Cellarius published Universal History Divided into an Ancient, Medieval, and New Period (1683).
rewrite: The "Late Middle Ages" denotes the final segment of the medieval era, following the Early and High Middle Ages. Historian Leonardo Bruni initially established this three-part division in his 1442 work on Florentine history. Flavio Biondo adopted a comparable model shortly thereafter. This tripartite framework was later solidified and gained widespread acceptance following Christoph Cellarius's publication of a universal history in 1683, which formally separated history into ancient, medieval, and modern periods.

input: The main industries are mineral based, agriculture based, and textile based. Rajasthan is the second largest producer of polyester fibre in India. The Pali and Bhilwara District produces more cloth than Bhiwandi, Maharashtra and the bhilwara is the largest city in suitings production and export and Pali is largest city in cotton and polyster in blouse pieces and rubia production and export. Several prominent chemical and engineering companies are located in the city of Kota, in southern Rajasthan. Rajasthan is pre-eminent in quarrying and mining in India. The Taj Mahal was built from the white marble which was mined from a town called Makrana. The state is the second largest source of cement in India. It has rich salt deposits at Sambhar, copper mines at Khetri, Jhunjhunu, and zinc mines at Dariba, Zawar mines and Rampura Aghucha (opencast) near Bhilwara. Dimensional stone mining is also undertaken in Rajasthan. Jodhpur sandstone is mostly used in monuments, important buildings and residential buildings. This stone is termed as "chittar patthar". Jodhpur leads in Handicraft and Guar Gum industry. Rajasthan is also a part of the Mumbai-Delhi Industrial corridor is set to benefit economically. The State gets 39% of the DMIC, with major districts of Jaipur, Alwar, Kota and Bhilwara benefiting.
rewrite: Rajasthan's economy is anchored by three core sectors: minerals, agriculture, and textiles. It ranks as India's second-largest generator of polyester fiber. In textile manufacturing, the districts of Pali and Bhilwara outproduce Bhiwandi in Maharashtra in cloth output. Bhilwara is the leading center for creating and exporting suitings, while Pali dominates in producing and exporting cotton and polyester blouse pieces, along with rubia. Southern Rajasthan's city of Kota hosts a number of significant chemical and engineering firms. The state holds a leading position in India's quarrying and mining sector. Notably, the white marble extracted from Makrana was used to construct the Taj Mahal. Rajasthan is the country's second biggest cement supplier. Its natural resources include substantial salt reserves in Sambhar, copper mines in Khetri and Jhunjhunu, and zinc operations in Dariba, Zawar, and the open-pit site at Rampura Aghucha near Bhilwara. The state also engages in dimensional stone mining; Jodhpur sandstone, locally known as "chittar patthar," is widely used in monuments, significant structures, and homes. Jodhpur is a frontrunner in the handicraft and guar gum sectors. Furthermore, Rajasthan's inclusion in the Mumbai-Delhi Industrial Corridor promises economic advantages, with the state allocated 39% of the corridor's area. Key beneficiary districts include Jaipur, Alwar, Kota, and Bhilwara.

input: Valerian's first religious edict singled out Christianity as a particularly self-interested and subversive foreign cult, outlawed its assemblies and urged Christians to sacrifice to Rome's traditional gods. His second edict acknowledged a Christian threat to the Imperial system – not yet at its heart but close to it, among Rome’s equites and Senators. Christian apologists interpreted his disgraceful capture and death as divine judgement. The next forty years were peaceful; the Christian church grew stronger and its literature and theology gained a higher social and intellectual profile, due in part to its own search for political toleration and theological coherence. Origen discussed theological issues with traditionalist elites in a common Neoplatonist frame of reference – he had written to Decius' predecessor Philip the Arab in similar vein – and Hippolytus recognised a “pagan” basis in Christian heresies. The Christian churches were disunited; Paul of Samosata, Bishop of Antioch was deposed by a synod of 268 for "dogmatic reasons – his doctrine on the human nature of Christ was rejected – and for his lifestyle, which reminded his brethren of the habits of the administrative elite". The reasons for his deposition were widely circulated among the churches. Meanwhile, Aurelian (270-75) appealed for harmony among his soldiers (concordia militum), stabilised the Empire and its borders and successfully established an official, Hellenic form of unitary cult to the Palmyrene Sol Invictus in Rome's Campus Martius.
rewrite: The initial decree from Valerian specifically condemned Christianity as an alien and disruptive sect driven by selfish motives, banning its gatherings and demanding adherents make offerings to the conventional Roman deities. A subsequent proclamation recognized the danger Christians posed to the Imperial structure—not within its core yet, but emerging among the influential equestrian and senatorial orders. Defenders of the faith later viewed his humiliating defeat and demise as punishment from God. A four-decade period of calm followed, during which the Church expanded in strength. Its writings and doctrinal systems achieved greater prominence in society and intellectual circles, partly because of its efforts to secure official acceptance and develop consistent theology. Figures like Origen engaged with conservative upper classes on spiritual matters, using shared Neoplatonic concepts—he had earlier addressed Philip the Arab in like manner—while Hippolytus identified traces of pagan thought within Christian deviations. The faith was internally divided; for instance, Paul of Samosata was removed as Antioch’s bishop by a council in 268 due to both theological disagreements over Christ’s humanity and a personal conduct that echoed the excesses of governing officials. This rationale was broadly shared across congregations. Concurrently, Emperor Aurelian emphasized military unity, consolidated the realm and its frontiers, and effectively instituted an organized, Hellenized version of a singular sun-god cult in Rome’s Campus Martius.

input: The United Kingdom has traditionally been governed as a unitary state by the Westminster Parliament in London. Instead of adopting a federal model, the UK has relied on gradual devolution to decentralise political power. Devolution in the UK began with the Government of Ireland Act 1914 which granted home rule to Ireland as a constituent country of the former United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland. Following the partition of Ireland in 1921 which saw the creation of the sovereign Irish Free State (which eventually evolved into the modern day Republic of Ireland), Northern Ireland retained its devolved government through the Parliament of Northern Ireland, the only part of the UK to have such a body at this time. This body was suspended in 1972 and Northern Ireland was governed by direct rule during the period of conflict known as The Troubles.
rewrite: The United Kingdom has historically operated as a unified entity under the central authority of Parliament in London. Rather than implementing a federal structure, it has pursued a stepwise transfer of authority to its constituent nations. This process of devolution commenced with the 1914 Government of Ireland Act, providing self-government to Ireland within the then-existing union. After Ireland's division in 1921, which led to the independent Irish Free State (later the Republic of Ireland), Northern Ireland maintained its own legislative assembly, uniquely possessing this status within the UK at the time. That parliament was suspended in 1972, leading to direct administration from London throughout the era of strife referred to as The Troubles.

input: During up-peak mode (also called moderate incoming traffic), elevator cars in a group are recalled to the lobby to provide expeditious service to passengers arriving at the building, most typically in the morning as people arrive for work or at the conclusion of a lunch-time period. Elevators are dispatched one-by-one when they reach a pre-determined passenger load, or when they have had their doors opened for a certain period of time. The next elevator to be dispatched usually has its hall lantern or a "this car leaving next" sign illuminated to encourage passengers to make maximum use of the available elevator system capacity. Some elevator banks are programmed so that at least one car will always return to the lobby floor and park whenever it becomes free.
rewrite: During periods of high incoming traffic, such as morning arrivals or after lunch, elevator groups are managed to prioritize the main lobby. This operational mode, known as up-peak, concentrates cars at the ground floor to quickly accommodate entering passengers. Each elevator departs either after reaching a set occupancy or once its doors have remained open for a specific duration. To guide waiting passengers, a signal or indicator light on the next car scheduled for departure is activated, promoting efficient use of space. Additionally, many systems are configured to ensure that whenever an elevator is unoccupied, it automatically returns and waits at the lobby level.

input: In 1922, Egypt, which had been declared a British protectorate at the outbreak of the First World War, was granted formal independence, though it continued to be a British client state until 1954. British troops remained stationed in Egypt until the signing of the Anglo-Egyptian Treaty in 1936, under which it was agreed that the troops would withdraw but continue to occupy and defend the Suez Canal zone. In return, Egypt was assisted to join the League of Nations. Iraq, a British mandate since 1920, also gained membership of the League in its own right after achieving independence from Britain in 1932. In Palestine, Britain was presented with the problem of mediating between the Arab and Jewish communities. The 1917 Balfour Declaration, which had been incorporated into the terms of the mandate, stated that a national home for the Jewish people would be established in Palestine, and Jewish immigration allowed up to a limit that would be determined by the mandatory power. This led to increasing conflict with the Arab population, who openly revolted in 1936. As the threat of war with Germany increased during the 1930s, Britain judged the support of the Arab population in the Middle East as more important than the establishment of a Jewish homeland, and shifted to a pro-Arab stance, limiting Jewish immigration and in turn triggering a Jewish insurgency.
rewrite:
Egypt was formally recognized as an independent nation in 1922, having been under British protection since the start of World War I. However, it effectively remained under British influence until 1954. A military presence was maintained there until the 1936 Anglo-Egyptian Treaty, which stipulated a withdrawal of forces except from the Suez Canal area, which Britain would continue to hold and protect. As part of this arrangement, Britain supported Egypt's entry into the League of Nations. Similarly, Iraq, under British administration since 1920, became an independent state in 1932 and subsequently joined the League.

In Palestine, Britain faced the growing challenge of balancing Arab and Jewish interests. The mandate's terms included the 1917 Balfour Declaration, which endorsed creating a Jewish national home and permitted immigration, with levels to be set by British authorities. This policy fueled tensions, culminating in an Arab revolt in 1936. With the rising danger of conflict with Germany in the 1930s, British priorities shifted. Perceiving Arab backing in the region as crucial for impending war, Britain adopted a position more favorable to Arabs. This involved restricting Jewish immigration, a move that ultimately provoked an armed Jewish rebellion.

input: Modern morphology recognizes a continuum between the major morphological categories of root, stem (caulome), leaf (phyllome) and trichome. Furthermore, it emphasizes structural dynamics. Modern systematics aims to reflect and discover phylogenetic relationships between plants. Modern Molecular phylogenetics largely ignores morphological characters, relying on DNA sequences as data. Molecular analysis of DNA sequences from most families of flowering plants enabled the Angiosperm Phylogeny Group to publish in 1998 a phylogeny of flowering plants, answering many of the questions about relationships among angiosperm families and species. The theoretical possibility of a practical method for identification of plant species and commercial varieties by DNA barcoding is the subject of active current research.
rewrite: Contemporary morphology views the primary forms of roots, stems, leaves, and trichomes as existing along a connected spectrum, with a focus on their changing structures. In classification, modern systematics seeks to reveal and represent the evolutionary connections among plants. Today's molecular phylogenetics predominantly uses DNA data over physical traits. By examining DNA across numerous flowering plant families, the Angiosperm Phylogeny Group produced a 1998 evolutionary tree that clarified many connections between angiosperm families and species. Active research now explores the potential for using DNA barcoding to identify plant species and commercial cultivars.

input: Many television shows and films have been produced which portray in-character professional wrestlers as protagonists, such as Ready to Rumble, ¡Mucha Lucha!, Nacho Libre, and the Santo film series. In the wildly popular Rocky series of films about the fictional boxer Rocky Balboa, Rocky III saw its hero fighting a "boxer vs. wrestler" exhibition match against the enormous and villainous wrestler "Thunderlips", portrayed by real-life soon-to-be wrestling icon Hulk Hogan. At least two stage plays set in the world of pro wrestling have been produced: The Baron is a comedy that retells the life of an actual performer known as Baron von Raschke. From Parts Unknown... is an award-nominated Canadian drama about the rise and fall of a fictional wrestler. The 2009 South Park episode "W.T.F." played on the soap operatic elements of professional wrestling. One of the lead characters on the Disney Channel series Kim Possible was a huge fan of pro wrestling and actually featured it on an episode (with two former WWE wrestlers voicing the two fictitious wrestlers featured in the episode). The 2008 film The Wrestler, about a washed-up professional wrestler, garnered several Oscar nominations.
rewrite: Numerous movies and TV programs have depicted professional wrestlers as central figures, including titles like *Ready to Rumble*, *¡Mucha Lucha!*, *Nacho Libre*, and the Santo movies. In the acclaimed *Rocky* film franchise, the installment *Rocky III* featured a special bout pitting the boxer hero against a menacing, oversized wrestler called "Thunderlips," played by the future legend Hulk Hogan. The theater has also explored this realm: the comedy *The Baron* dramatizes the story of a real-life grappler, Baron von Raschke, while the Canadian play *From Parts Unknown...*—which received award recognition—traces the career of an imaginary performer's ascent and decline. Television has engaged with wrestling's dramatic flair as well, such as in the *South Park* episode "W.T.F.," which exaggerated its soap-opera style. On the Disney show *Kim Possible*, a main character was an avid fan, and one episode spotlighted the sport, with ex-WWE stars providing voices for invented wrestlers. Additionally, the 2008 movie *The Wrestler*, focusing on a past-his-prime fighter, earned multiple Academy Award nominations.

input: Some types of energy are a varying mix of both potential and kinetic energy. An example is mechanical energy which is the sum of (usually macroscopic) kinetic and potential energy in a system. Elastic energy in materials is also dependent upon electrical potential energy (among atoms and molecules), as is chemical energy, which is stored and released from a reservoir of electrical potential energy between electrons, and the molecules or atomic nuclei that attract them.[need quotation to verify].The list is also not necessarily complete. Whenever physical scientists discover that a certain phenomenon appears to violate the law of energy conservation, new forms are typically added that account for the discrepancy.
rewrite: Certain forms of energy represent a blend of stored and active energy. Mechanical energy, for instance, combines the kinetic and potential energy within a physical system. Similarly, the energy stored in elastic materials or chemical bonds fundamentally arises from electrical potential energy at the atomic and molecular level. This list of energy types remains open-ended. When observations seem to contradict energy conservation, scientists often propose new forms to explain the difference.

input: Bern was the site of the 1954 Football (Soccer) World Cup Final, a huge upset for the Hungarian Golden Team, who were beaten 3–2 by West Germany. The football team BSC Young Boys is based in Bern at the Stade de Suisse Wankdorf, which also was one of the venues for the European football championship 2008 in which it hosted 3 matches.
rewrite: In 1954, Bern hosted the FIFA World Cup Final, where West Germany's surprising 3–2 victory ended the Hungarian Golden Team's dominance. The city is also home to BSC Young Boys, who play at the Stade de Suisse Wankdorf. This stadium was a venue for UEFA Euro 2008, staging three matches.

input: Since the start of the 1994–95 season, the FA Cup has been sponsored. However, to protect the identity of the competition, the sponsored name has always included 'The FA Cup' in addition to the sponsor's name, unlike sponsorship deals for the League Cup where the word 'cup' is preceded by only the sponsor's name. Sponsorship deals run for four years, though – as in the case of E.ON – one-year extensions may be agreed. Emirates airline is the sponsor from 2015 to 2018, renaming the competition as 'The Emirates FA Cup', unlike previous editions, which included 'The FA Cup in association with E.ON' and 'The FA Cup with Budweiser'.
rewrite: Beginning with the 1994–95 season, the FA Cup has carried sponsor titles. To maintain the tournament's distinct character, these titles always incorporate "The FA Cup" alongside the sponsor, contrasting with the League Cup where the sponsor's name alone precedes "Cup." Sponsorship terms typically last four years, with occasional one-year renewals, as seen with E.ON. Since 2015, Emirates has been the sponsor, using "The Emirates FA Cup," a format differing from earlier partnerships that used wordier constructions like "in association with" or "with."

input: In July 2013, there were 41,000 non-Germans by citizenship living in Thuringia (1.9% of the population − among the smallest proportions of any state in Germany). Nevertheless, the number rose from 33,000 in July 2011, an increase of 24% in only two years. About 4% of the population are migrants (including persons that already received the German citizenship). The biggest groups of foreigners by citizenship are (as of 2012): Russians (3,100), Poles (3,000), Vietnamese (2,800), Turks (2,100) and Ukrainians (2,000). The amount of foreigners varies between regions: the college towns Erfurt, Jena, Weimar and Ilmenau have the highest rates, whereas there are almost no migrants living in the most rural smaller municipalities.
rewrite: In July 2013, Thuringia was home to 41,000 foreign nationals, representing 1.9% of its population—one of the lowest shares nationwide. This figure had grown significantly from 33,000 just two years earlier in 2011, marking a 24% rise. Including those who have since gained German citizenship, migrants constitute roughly 4% of residents. The largest foreign nationalities as of 2012 were Russian, Polish, Vietnamese, Turkish, and Ukrainian. Distribution is uneven: university cities like Erfurt, Jena, Weimar, and Ilmenau have the highest concentrations, while remote rural areas have very few foreign inhabitants.

input: By the early 1970s, softer songs by artists like The Carpenters, Anne Murray, John Denver, Barry Manilow, and even Streisand, began to be played more often on "Top 40" radio and others were added to the mix on many AC stations. Also, some of these stations even played softer songs by Elvis Presley, Linda Ronstadt, Elton John, Rod Stewart, Billy Joel, and other rock-based artists.
rewrite: In the early 1970s, gentler music from performers such as The Carpenters and John Denver gained increased airplay on Top 40 and Adult Contemporary stations. Additionally, many of these outlets started featuring mellower tracks by rock-influenced acts like Elton John, Linda Ronstadt, and Billy Joel.

input: While no other Timely character would achieve the success of these "big three", some notable heroes—many of which continue to appear in modern-day retcon appearances and flashbacks—include the Whizzer, Miss America, the Destroyer, the original Vision, and the Angel. Timely also published one of humor cartoonist Basil Wolverton's best-known features, "Powerhouse Pepper", as well as a line of children's funny-animal comics featuring popular characters like Super Rabbit and the duo Ziggy Pig and Silly Seal.
rewrite: Although Timely's other heroes never matched the popularity of its top three, several—such as the Whizzer, Miss America, and the original Vision—still surface in contemporary stories and memories. The publisher also released Basil Wolverton's famous "Powerhouse Pepper" and a series of humorous animal comics starring characters like Super Rabbit, Ziggy Pig, and Silly Seal.

input: The Second Aliyah (1904–14), began after the Kishinev pogrom; some 40,000 Jews settled in Palestine, although nearly half of them left eventually. Both the first and second waves of migrants were mainly Orthodox Jews, although the Second Aliyah included socialist groups who established the kibbutz movement. During World War I, British Foreign Secretary Arthur Balfour sent the Balfour Declaration of 1917 to Baron Rothschild (Walter Rothschild, 2nd Baron Rothschild), a leader of the British Jewish community, that stated that Britain intended for the creation of a Jewish "national home" within the Palestinian Mandate.
rewrite: The Second Aliyah commenced in 1904 following the Kishinev pogrom, bringing roughly 40,000 Jewish immigrants to Palestine, though close to half later departed. While both this and the earlier wave consisted largely of Orthodox individuals, the second influx also featured socialists who founded the first kibbutzim. Subsequently, in 1917 during the First World War, British Foreign Secretary Arthur Balfour addressed a declaration to Baron Walter Rothschild, a prominent UK Jewish figure, expressing official British support for establishing a Jewish national homeland in Palestine.

input: Samuel Adelstein described the Lombardi mandolin in 1893 as wider and shorter than the Neapolitan mandolin, with a shallower back and a shorter and wider neck, with six single strings to the regular mandolin's set of 4. The Lombardi was tuned C, D, A, E, B, G. The strings were fastened to the bridge like a guitar's. There were 20 frets, covering three octaves, with an additional 5 notes. When Adelstein wrote, there were no nylon strings, and the gut and single strings "do not vibrate so clearly and sweetly as the double steel string of the Neapolitan."
rewrite: In 1893, Samuel Adelstein noted the Lombardi mandolin differed from the Neapolitan style. It was broader, shorter in length and depth, and had a wider, shorter neck. Instead of four pairs, it used six individual strings tuned to C, D, A, E, B, and G, anchored at the bridge like a guitar. Its twenty frets spanned three octaves plus five extra notes. At the time, gut strings were used, which Adelstein felt lacked the clear, sweet resonance of the Neapolitan's double steel strings.

input: More detail was given in Darwin's 1868 book on The Variation of Animals and Plants under Domestication, which tried to explain heredity through his hypothesis of pangenesis. Although Darwin had privately questioned blending inheritance, he struggled with the theoretical difficulty that novel individual variations would tend to blend into a population. However, inherited variation could be seen, and Darwin's concept of selection working on a population with a range of small variations was workable. It was not until the modern evolutionary synthesis in the 1930s and 1940s that a model of heredity became completely integrated with a model of variation. This modern evolutionary synthesis had been dubbed Neo Darwinian Evolution because it encompasses Charles Darwin's theories of evolution with Gregor Mendel's theories of genetic inheritance.
rewrite: In his 1868 work, *The Variation of Animals and Plants under Domestication*, Charles Darwin elaborated further, proposing pangenesis as a mechanism for heredity. He was aware of the problem that new traits might dilute within a population if inheritance simply blended together, even though he observed that variation persists. His core idea—that natural selection acts upon numerous slight differences in a group—remained viable. A fully unified theory combining models of inheritance and variation only emerged decades later with the modern evolutionary synthesis during the 1930s and 1940s. This framework, often called Neo-Darwinian Evolution, successfully merged Darwin’s principles of natural selection with Gregor Mendel’s laws of genetics.

input: An alloy of aluminium and gallium in pellet form added to water can be used to generate hydrogen. The process also produces alumina, but the expensive gallium, which prevents the formation of an oxide skin on the pellets, can be re-used.
