Japanese leadership considered the defense of Saipan absolutely essential. Achieving this objective required the elimination of the formidable U.S. Fifth Fleet, a force comprising fifteen aircraft carriers with over 950 aircraft, seven battleships, twenty-eight submarines, sixty-nine destroyers, and numerous cruisers. In response, Vice Admiral Jisaburo Ozawa committed nearly the entire Imperial Japanese Navy to battle. His task force included nine carriers bearing 473 planes, five battleships, multiple cruisers, and twenty-eight destroyers. His aviators were both outnumbered two-to-one and equipped with largely outdated aircraft. While Japanese ships possessed strong antiaircraft guns, they were hindered by inferior radar and the absence of proximity fuzes.

Facing these disadvantages, Ozawa formulated a tactical plan to leverage his few advantages. Japanese planes, lacking protective armor, enjoyed a significantly longer operational range. They could strike from approximately 480 kilometers and conduct reconnaissance over a radius of 900 kilometers. By contrast, American Hellcat fighters were limited to roughly 320 kilometers for attack and 525 kilometers for search missions. Ozawa intended to station his fleet beyond U.S. fighter range. His aircraft would assault the American carriers, proceed to airfields on Guam to refuel and rearm, attack once more on their return flight, and finally recover aboard their own ships. This strategy was further supported by an expected contribution of some 500 additional aircraft based on Guam and neighboring islands.

input: Corey Clark was disqualified during the finals for having an undisclosed police record; however, he later alleged that he and Paula Abdul had an affair while on the show and that this contributed to his expulsion. Clark also claimed that Abdul gave him preferential treatment on the show due to their affair. The allegations were dismissed by Fox after an independent investigation. Two semi-finalists were also disqualified that year – Jaered Andrews for an arrest on an assault charge, and Frenchie Davis for having previously modelled for an adult website.
rewrite: Corey Clark was removed from the finals for failing to reveal a prior arrest. He subsequently asserted that a romantic involvement with judge Paula Abdul led to both special favoritism during the competition and his eventual dismissal. Fox rejected these claims following a separate inquiry. That same season, two other semi-finalists were eliminated: Jaered Andrews due to an assault arrest and Frenchie Davis for past adult website modeling.

input: Furthermore, despite the novel's thematic focus on racial injustice, its black characters are not fully examined. In its use of racial epithets, stereotyped depictions of superstitious blacks, and Calpurnia, who to some critics is an updated version of the "contented slave" motif and to others simply unexplored, the book is viewed as marginalizing black characters. One writer asserts that the use of Scout's narration serves as a convenient mechanism for readers to be innocent and detached from the racial conflict. Scout's voice "functions as the not-me which allows the rest of us—black and white, male and female—to find our relative position in society". A teaching guide for the novel published by The English Journal cautions, "what seems wonderful or powerful to one group of students may seem degrading to another". A Canadian language arts consultant found that the novel resonated well with white students, but that black students found it "demoralizing". Another criticism, articulated by Michael Lind, is that the novel indulges in classist stereotyping and demonization of poor rural "white trash".
rewrite: While the book centers on racial prejudice, its African American characters remain underdeveloped. Critics note that through repeated racial slurs, portrayals of superstitious Black individuals, and the figure of Calpurnia—seen by some as a modern "happy slave" trope and by others as simply lacking depth—the narrative sidelines these roles. One analysis suggests that employing Scout as the narrator offers readers an easy way to remain naive and removed from the tensions of racism. Her perspective "acts as the other, enabling everyone else—regardless of race or gender—to locate their own social standing." An instructional resource in The English Journal warns that "elements one set of students finds inspiring might feel insulting to a different group." An educator in Canada observed that while white pupils responded positively to the story, Black students often felt disheartened by it. Additional critique, voiced by commentator Michael Lind, contends that the story also engages in class-based bias, negatively stereotyping and vilifying impoverished rural whites.

input: With the death of Zhengde and ascension of Jiajing, the politics at court shifted in favor of the Neo-Confucian establishment which not only rejected the Portuguese embassy of Fernão Pires de Andrade (d. 1523), but had a predisposed animosity towards Tibetan Buddhism and lamas. Evelyn S. Rawski, a professor in the Department of History of the University of Pittsburgh, writes that the Ming's unique relationship with Tibetan prelates essentially ended with Jiajing's reign while Ming influence in the Amdo region was supplanted by the Mongols.
rewrite: Following the reign of Zhengde and the rise of Jiajing, imperial politics realigned with orthodox Neo-Confucian interests. This faction dismissed the Portuguese diplomatic mission led by Fernão Pires de Andrade and held a deep-seated hostility toward Tibetan Buddhism. Historian Evelyn S. Rawski notes that the Ming dynasty's distinctive patronage of Tibetan clerics concluded under Jiajing, as Mongol power replaced Ming authority in the Amdo region.

input: St. John's served as the capital city of the Colony of Newfoundland and the Dominion of Newfoundland before Newfoundland became Canada's tenth province in 1949. The city now serves as the capital of Newfoundland and Labrador, therefore the provincial legislature is located in the city. The Confederation Building, located on Confederation Hill, is home to the House of Assembly along with the offices for the Members of the House of Assembly (MHAs) and Ministers. The city is represented by ten MHAs, four who are members of the governing Progressive Conservative Party, three that belong to the New Democratic Party (NDP), and three that belong to the Liberal Party. Lorraine Michael, leader of the NDP since 2006, represents the district of Signal Hill-Quidi Vidi.
rewrite: Before Newfoundland joined Canada as its tenth province in 1949, St. John's was the capital for both its colonial and dominion periods. Today, it remains the capital of the province of Newfoundland and Labrador, hosting the provincial legislature. The House of Assembly, along with the offices for Ministers and Members of the House of Assembly (MHAs), is situated in the Confederation Building on Confederation Hill. The city's population is represented by ten MHAs: four from the governing Progressive Conservative Party, three from the New Democratic Party (NDP), and three from the Liberal Party. Since 2006, the NDP has been led by Lorraine Michael, who serves as the MHA for the Signal Hill-Quidi Vidi district.

input: The Crimean War was a military conflict fought between October 1853 – March 1856 in which Russia lost to an alliance of France, the United Kingdom, the Ottoman Empire, and Sardinia. The immediate cause involved the rights of Christian minorities in the Holy Land, which was controlled by the Ottoman Empire. The French promoted the rights of Catholics, while Russia promoted those of the Eastern Orthodox Christians. The longer-term causes involved the decline of the Ottoman Empire and the unwillingness of the United Kingdom and France to allow Russia to gain territory and power at Ottoman expense. It has widely been noted that the causes, in one case involving an argument over a key, have never revealed a "greater confusion of purpose", yet led to a war noted for its "notoriously incompetent international butchery."
rewrite: From 1853 to 1856, the Crimean War saw Russia defeated by a coalition comprising France, Britain, the Ottoman Empire, and Sardinia. The triggering dispute centered on privileges for Christian groups within the Ottoman-controlled Holy Land, with France backing Catholic interests and Russia supporting Eastern Orthodox adherents. Underlying this was the broader geopolitical struggle stemming from the Ottoman Empire's weakening state, coupled with British and French determination to block Russian expansion and growing influence in the region. Historians frequently observe that the motivations for the conflict, at times stemming from trivial disagreements, displayed profound disarray in strategic aims. Nevertheless, the war is remembered for its widespread and severe military mismanagement.

input: Private CBC affiliates are not as common as they were in the past, as many such stations have been purchased either by the CBC itself or by Canwest Global or CHUM Limited, respectively becoming E! or A-Channel (later A, now CTV Two) stations. One private CBC affiliate, CHBC-TV in Kelowna, joined E! (then known as CH) on February 27, 2006. When a private CBC affiliate reaffiliates with another network, the CBC has normally added a retransmitter of its nearest O&O station to ensure that CBC service is continued. However, due to an agreement between CHBC and CFJC-TV in Kamloops, CFJC also disaffiliated from the CBC on February 27, 2006, but no retransmitters were installed in the licence area. Former private CBC affiliates CKPG-TV Prince George and CHAT-TV Medicine Hat disaffiliated on August 31, 2008 and joined E!, but the CBC announced it will not add new retransmitters to these areas. Incidentally, CFJC, CKPG and CHAT are all owned by an independent media company, Jim Pattison Group. With the closure of E! and other changes in the media landscape, several former CBC affiliates have since joined City or Global, or closed altogether.
rewrite: The number of privately owned stations affiliated with the CBC has diminished over time. Many have been acquired by larger broadcasters, such as the CBC directly, Canwest Global, or CHUM Limited, with the latter converting them into stations under the E! or A-Channel (later renamed A and then CTV Two) banners. For instance, the private affiliate CHBC-TV in Kelowna switched to the E! network (at the time called CH) on February 27, 2006. Typically, when a private station ends its CBC affiliation, the public broadcaster installs a rebroadcaster of its nearest owned-and-operated station to maintain service. Yet, when CHBC and Kamloops' CFJC-TV both disaffiliated on that same date under a mutual agreement, no such retransmitters were established for that region. Similarly, stations CKPG-TV in Prince George and CHAT-TV in Medicine Hat left the CBC on August 31, 2008, to join E!, with the CBC stating it would not add new rebroadcasters there. Notably, CFJC, CKPG, and CHAT are all part of the independent Jim Pattison Group. Following the shutdown of E! and broader industry shifts, numerous former CBC affiliates have since aligned with City or Global, or have ceased operations entirely.

input: Available web browsers range in features from minimal, text-based user interfaces with bare-bones support for HTML to rich user interfaces supporting a wide variety of file formats and protocols. Browsers which include additional components to support e-mail, Usenet news, and Internet Relay Chat (IRC), are sometimes referred to as "Internet suites" rather than merely "web browsers".
rewrite: Web browsers vary from simple text-only interfaces with basic HTML to feature-rich ones handling diverse formats. Some also incorporate email, newsgroups, and chat functions, earning them the broader label of "Internet suites" instead of just browsers.

input: While West had encountered controversy a year prior when he stormed out of the American Music Awards of 2004 after losing Best New Artist, the rapper's first large-scale controversy came just days following Late Registration's release, during a benefit concert for Hurricane Katrina victims. In September 2005, NBC broadcast A Concert for Hurricane Relief, and West was a featured speaker. When West was presenting alongside actor Mike Myers, he deviated from the prepared script. Myers spoke next and continued to read the script. Once it was West's turn to speak again, he said, "George Bush doesn't care about black people." West's comment reached much of the United States, leading to mixed reactions; President Bush would later call it one of the most "disgusting moments" of his presidency. West raised further controversy in January 2006 when he posed on the cover of Rolling Stone wearing a crown of thorns.
rewrite: Although West had already caused a stir by abruptly leaving the 2004 American Music Awards after not winning Best New Artist, his major public controversy erupted shortly after Late Registration debuted. This occurred during a televised charity event for Hurricane Katrina survivors in September 2005. While co-presenting with actor Mike Myers on the NBC special, West departed from the approved remarks. After Myers adhered to the script, West used his next speaking turn to declare, “George Bush doesn’t care about black people.” The statement quickly spread nationwide, provoking divided responses; President Bush later described it as among the most offensive incidents during his time in office. West stirred additional debate several months later, in January 2006, by appearing on the cover of Rolling Stone magazine adorned with a thorny crown.

input: Where old disc recordings are considered to be of artistic or historic interest, from before the era of tape or where no tape master exists, archivists play back the disc on suitable equipment and record the result, typically onto a digital format, which can be copied and manipulated to remove analog flaws without any further damage to the source recording. For example, Nimbus Records uses a specially built horn record player to transfer 78s. Anyone can do this using a standard record player with a suitable pickup, a phono-preamp (pre-amplifier) and a typical personal computer. However, for accurate transfer, professional archivists carefully choose the correct stylus shape and diameter, tracking weight, equalisation curve and other playback parameters and use high-quality analogue-to-digital converters.
rewrite: When older disc recordings hold artistic or historical value, particularly from periods predating magnetic tape or when no master tape is available, archivists use appropriate playback devices to capture the audio. This output is usually converted into a digital file, allowing for duplication and the correction of analog imperfections without harming the original source. Nimbus Records, for instance, employs a custom horn phonograph for 78 RPM transfers. While a basic setup with a standard turntable, proper cartridge, preamp, and computer can accomplish this, professionals ensure precision by selecting the exact stylus type and size, adjusting tracking force and equalization, and utilizing superior analog-to-digital conversion equipment.

input: During her childhood, Madonna was inspired by actors, later saying, "I loved Carole Lombard and Judy Holliday and Marilyn Monroe. They were all incredibly funny ... and I saw myself in them ... my girlishness, my knowingness and my innocence." Her "Material Girl" music video recreated Monroe's look in the song "Diamonds Are a Girl's Best Friend", from the film Gentlemen Prefer Blondes (1953). She studied the screwball comedies of the 1930s, particularly those of Lombard, in preparation for the film Who's That Girl. The video for "Express Yourself" (1989) was inspired by Fritz Lang's silent film Metropolis (1927). The video for "Vogue" recreated the style of Hollywood glamour photographs, in particular those by Horst P. Horst, and imitated the poses of Marlene Dietrich, Carole Lombard, and Rita Hayworth, while the lyrics referred to many of the stars who had inspired her, including Bette Davis, described by Madonna as an idol. However, Madonna's film career has been largely received negatively by the film critic community. Stephanie Zacharek, critic for Time magazine, stated that, "[Madonna] seems wooden and unnatural as an actress, and it's tough to watch, because she's clearly trying her damnedest." According to biographer Andrew Morton, "Madonna puts a brave face on the criticism, but privately she is deeply hurt." After the box office bomb Swept Away (2002), Madonna vowed that she would never again act in a film, hoping her repertoire as a bad actress would never be discussed again.
rewrite:
In her youth, Madonna found inspiration in various film stars, recalling, “I admired Carole Lombard, Judy Holliday, and Marilyn Monroe tremendously. Each possessed a sharp wit … and I recognized aspects of myself in them—my playful femininity, my awareness, and my naivete.” Her iconic “Material Girl” video paid direct homage to Monroe’s performance of “Diamonds Are a Girl’s Best Friend” from the movie *Gentlemen Prefer Blondes*. To prepare for her role in *Who’s That Girl*, she immersed herself in 1930s screwball comedies, focusing on Lombard’s work. The 1989 “Express Yourself” video drew visual cues from Fritz Lang’s silent classic *Metropolis*. Similarly, the “Vogue” video emulated the aesthetic of classic Hollywood glamour photography, especially the work of Horst P. Horst, and mimicked poses struck by Marlene Dietrich, Carole Lombard, and Rita Hayworth. The song’s lyrics also paid tribute to other inspirations, like Bette Davis, whom she called an idol.

Despite these creative influences, Madonna’s own acting has generally been panned by critics. *Time* magazine reviewer Stephanie Zacharek noted that Madonna appears stiff and artificial on screen, despite evident effort. Biographer Andrew Morton wrote that while she publicly brushes off such critiques, they wound her privately. Following the commercial and critical failure of *Swept Away* in 2002, she resolved to abandon film acting, wishing to leave her reputation as a poor actress behind.

input: Another common application is the control of the throttle of an internal combustion engine in conjunction with an electronic governor. In this usage, the motor works against a return spring to move the throttle in accordance with the output of the governor. The latter monitors engine speed by counting electrical pulses from the ignition system or from a magnetic pickup and, depending on the speed, makes small adjustments to the amount of current applied to the motor. If the engine starts to slow down relative to the desired speed, the current will be increased, the motor will develop more torque, pulling against the return spring and opening the throttle. Should the engine run too fast, the governor will reduce the current being applied to the motor, causing the return spring to pull back and close the throttle.
rewrite: A frequent use for these motors involves managing the throttle of a combustion engine alongside an electronic regulator. Here, the actuator opposes a restoring spring to adjust the throttle based on the regulator's signal. The governor tracks rotational speed by sensing pulses from the ignition or a magnetic sensor, then slightly alters the current sent to the motor accordingly. When engine RPM drops below the set point, current rises, boosting motor torque to overcome the spring and open the throttle. Conversely, if RPM climbs too high, the governor decreases current, allowing the spring to retract and close the throttle.

input: Sometimes people of mixed African-American and Native American descent report having had elder family members withholding pertinent genealogical information. Tracing the genealogy of African Americans can be a very difficult process, as censuses did not identify slaves by name before the American Civil War, meaning that most African Americans did not appear by name in those records. In addition, many white fathers who used slave women sexually, even those in long-term relationships like Thomas Jefferson's with Sally Hemings, did not acknowledge their mixed-race slave children in records, so paternity was lost.
rewrite: Individuals with both African-American and Native American heritage often recount that older relatives concealed key family history details. For African Americans, genealogical research is particularly challenging because pre-Civil War censuses omitted the names of enslaved individuals, leaving most ancestors unrecorded. Furthermore, white fathers, including those in sustained partnerships such as Thomas Jefferson and Sally Hemings, frequently failed to legally recognize their children born to enslaved women, resulting in lost paternal lineages.

input: Minute Maid Park (home of the Astros) and Toyota Center (home of the Rockets), are located in downtown Houston. Houston has the NFL's first retractable-roof stadium with natural grass, NRG Stadium (home of the Texans). Minute Maid Park is also a retractable-roof stadium. Toyota Center also has the largest screen for an indoor arena in the United States built to coincide with the arena's hosting of the 2013 NBA All-Star Game. BBVA Compass Stadium is a soccer-specific stadium for the Dynamo, the Texas Southern University football team, and Dash, located in East Downtown. In addition, NRG Astrodome was the first indoor stadium in the world, built in 1965. Other sports facilities include Hofheinz Pavilion (Houston Cougars basketball), Rice Stadium (Rice Owls football), and Reliant Arena. TDECU Stadium is where the University of Houston Houston Cougars football team plays. Houston has hosted several major sports events: the 1968, 1986 and 2004 Major League Baseball All-Star Games; the 1989, 2006 and 2013 NBA All-Star Games; Super Bowl VIII and Super Bowl XXXVIII, as well as hosting the 2005 World Series and 1981, 1986, 1994 and 1995 NBA Finals, winning the latter two. Super Bowl LI is currently slated to be hosted in NRG Stadium in 2017.
rewrite:
Houston's downtown area features several prominent sports venues. The Astros play baseball at Minute Maid Park, which is equipped with a retractable roof. Nearby, the Toyota Center, home to the Rockets, contains the biggest indoor arena screen in the nation, an installation timed for the 2013 NBA All-Star Game. The city also boasts NRG Stadium, the NFL's inaugural retractable-roof facility with a natural grass field, where the Texans compete. Soccer-specific BBVA Compass Stadium, situated in East Downtown, hosts the Dynamo and Dash, along with the Texas Southern University football team.

Historically, the NRG Astrodome, constructed in 1965, was the world's first indoor stadium. Additional local facilities encompass Hofheinz Pavilion for University of Houston basketball, Rice Stadium for Rice University football, Reliant Arena, and TDECU Stadium, the football home for the Houston Cougars.

The city has a rich history of hosting major events, including MLB All-Star Games in 1968, 1986, and 2004; NBA All-Star Games in 1989, 2006, and 2013; Super Bowls VIII and XXXVIII; the 2005 World Series; and the NBA Finals in 1981, 1986, 1994, and 1995, with Houston teams winning the last two. Super Bowl LI is scheduled for NRG Stadium in 2017.

input: Numerous major American cultural movements began in the city, such as the Harlem Renaissance, which established the African-American literary canon in the United States. The city was a center of jazz in the 1940s, abstract expressionism in the 1950s, and the birthplace of hip hop in the 1970s. The city's punk and hardcore scenes were influential in the 1970s and 1980s. New York has long had a flourishing scene for Jewish American literature.
rewrite: This city served as the origin for many significant cultural shifts in America. It launched the Harlem Renaissance, defining African-American literature nationally. New York was the epicenter of 1940s jazz, 1950s abstract expressionism, and 1970s hip hop. Its punk and hardcore movements were pivotal in the following decades, and it has consistently sustained a vibrant Jewish American literary community.

input: Richard Phillips Feynman was born on May 11, 1918, in Queens, New York City, the son of Lucille (née Phillips), a homemaker, and Melville Arthur Feynman, a sales manager. His family originated from Russia and Poland; both of his parents were Ashkenazi Jews. They were not religious, and by his youth Feynman described himself as an "avowed atheist". He also stated "To select, for approbation the peculiar elements that come from some supposedly Jewish heredity is to open the door to all kinds of nonsense on racial theory," and adding "... at thirteen I was not only converted to other religious views, but I also stopped believing that the Jewish people are in any way 'the chosen people'." Later in his life, during a visit to the Jewish Theological Seminary, he encountered the Talmud for the first time, and remarked that he found it a "wonderful book" and "valuable".
rewrite: Richard Phillips Feynman entered the world on May 11, 1918, in the Queens borough of New York. His mother, Lucille Phillips, managed the home, while his father, Melville Arthur Feynman, worked in sales. The family's roots lay in Russia and Poland, and his parents were both of Ashkenazi Jewish descent, though they practiced no religion. From a young age, Feynman firmly identified as an atheist. He rejected the notion of selecting admirable traits and attributing them to a specific Jewish lineage, seeing it as a gateway to irrational racial ideologies. By the time he was thirteen, he had abandoned not only religious belief but also the idea that Jewish people held a divinely chosen status. Decades later, while visiting the Jewish Theological Seminary, he first examined the Talmud. He later expressed great admiration for the text, calling it a marvelous and worthwhile volume.

input: In 118 BC, King Micipsa of Numidia (current-day Algeria and Tunisia) died. He was succeeded by two legitimate sons, Adherbal and Hiempsal, and an illegitimate son, Jugurtha. Micipsa divided his kingdom between these three sons. Jugurtha, however, turned on his brothers, killing Hiempsal and driving Adherbal out of Numidia. Adherbal fled to Rome for assistance, and initially Rome mediated a division of the country between the two brothers. Eventually, Jugurtha renewed his offensive, leading to a long and inconclusive war with Rome. He also bribed several Roman commanders, and at least two tribunes, before and during the war. His nemesis, Gaius Marius, a legate from a virtually unknown provincial family, returned from the war in Numidia and was elected consul in 107 BC over the objections of the aristocratic senators. Marius invaded Numidia and brought the war to a quick end, capturing Jugurtha in the process. The apparent incompetence of the Senate, and the brilliance of Marius, had been put on full display. The populares party took full advantage of this opportunity by allying itself with Marius.
rewrite: Upon the death of Numidian King Micipsa in 118 BC, his realm, located in what is now Algeria and Tunisia, passed to his two rightful heirs, Adherbal and Hiempsal, as well as an illegitimate son named Jugurtha. The kingdom was partitioned among the three. Jugurtha soon betrayed his siblings, murdering Hiempsal and forcing Adherbal into exile. Adherbal sought refuge and aid in Rome. Roman intervention initially resulted in a negotiated settlement to split Numidia between the surviving brothers, but Jugurtha resumed hostilities, sparking a protracted and indecisive conflict with Rome. Throughout this period, he secured favor by bribing multiple Roman military leaders and at least two tribunes. The war was ultimately concluded by Gaius Marius, a legate from an obscure provincial background. After returning from Numidia, Marius overcame senatorial opposition to be elected consul in 107 BC. He launched a swift and effective campaign into Numidia, capturing Jugurtha. This episode clearly revealed the Senate's ineffectiveness and Marius's capability, a contrast exploited by the populares faction, which formed a political alliance with the victorious general.

input: The sixty-one year reign of the Kangxi Emperor was the longest of any Chinese emperor. Kangxi's reign is also celebrated as the beginning of an era known as the "High Qing", during which the dynasty reached the zenith of its social, economic and military power. Kangxi's long reign started when he was eight years old upon the untimely demise of his father. To prevent a repeat of Dorgon's dictatorial monopolizing of power during the regency, the Shunzhi Emperor, on his deathbed, hastily appointed four senior cabinet ministers to govern on behalf of his young son. The four ministers — Sonin, Ebilun, Suksaha, and Oboi — were chosen for their long service, but also to counteract each other's influences. Most important, the four were not closely related to the imperial family and laid no claim to the throne. However, as time passed, through chance and machination, Oboi, the most junior of the four, achieved such political dominance as to be a potential threat. Even though Oboi's loyalty was never an issue, his personal arrogance and political conservatism led him into an escalating conflict with the young emperor. In 1669 Kangxi, through trickery, disarmed and imprisoned Oboi — a significant victory for a fifteen-year-old emperor over a wily politician and experienced commander.
rewrite: The Kangxi Emperor ruled China for sixty-one years, a longer span than any other monarch in the nation's history. His time in power is widely regarded as the start of the "High Qing" period, a peak in the dynasty's societal, financial, and martial strength. Kangxi ascended to the throne at the age of eight following his father's sudden death. To avoid a recurrence of the autocratic control seen under the regent Dorgon, the dying Shunzhi Emperor quickly selected four senior advisors to rule as a regency council for his child successor. These men—Sonin, Ebilun, Suksaha, and Oboi—were picked for their extensive experience and to balance one another's authority. Crucially, none had direct familial ties to the imperial house or any legitimate royal ambition. Over the years, however, Oboi, originally the lowest-ranked of the quartet, skillfully maneuvered to become overwhelmingly powerful, emerging as a possible danger. While his devotion to the throne was not in doubt, his overbearing demeanor and rigid traditionalism increasingly clashed with the adolescent emperor. In 1669, the fifteen-year-old Kangxi successfully outwitted Oboi, having him captured and jailed—a major triumph for a young ruler against a cunning and battle-hardened statesman.

input: The FAA gradually assumed additional functions. The hijacking epidemic of the 1960s had already brought the agency into the field of civil aviation security. In response to the hijackings on September 11, 2001, this responsibility is now primarily taken by the Department of Homeland Security. The FAA became more involved with the environmental aspects of aviation in 1968 when it received the power to set aircraft noise standards. Legislation in 1970 gave the agency management of a new airport aid program and certain added responsibilities for airport safety. During the 1960s and 1970s, the FAA also started to regulate high altitude (over 500 feet) kite and balloon flying.
rewrite: Over time, the FAA took on more roles. It first entered civil aviation security during the hijacking surge of the 1960s. Following the 9/11 attacks, this duty shifted mainly to the Department of Homeland Security. Starting in 1968, the agency began addressing environmental issues by gaining authority to establish noise limits for aircraft. A 1970 law placed it in charge of a new program for airport funding and expanded its oversight of airport safety. Additionally, throughout the 1960s and 1970s, the FAA extended its regulations to include kites and balloons operating above 500 feet.

input: In 1654, Otto von Guericke invented the first vacuum pump and conducted his famous Magdeburg hemispheres experiment, showing that teams of horses could not separate two hemispheres from which the air had been partially evacuated. Robert Boyle improved Guericke's design and with the help of Robert Hooke further developed vacuum pump technology. Thereafter, research into the partial vacuum lapsed until 1850 when August Toepler invented the Toepler Pump and Heinrich Geissler invented the mercury displacement pump in 1855, achieving a partial vacuum of about 10 Pa (0.1 Torr). A number of electrical properties become observable at this vacuum level, which renewed interest in further research.
rewrite: In 1654, Otto von Guericke created the initial vacuum pump and performed his renowned demonstration with the Magdeburg hemispheres. This proved that even horses could not pull apart two sealed hemispheres once some air was removed. Robert Boyle later enhanced this apparatus, and alongside Robert Hooke, advanced the technology. Interest in partial vacuums then faded until the mid-19th century, when August Toepler introduced his pump in 1850 and Heinrich Geissler developed a mercury displacement pump by 1855, reaching a vacuum near 10 Pa. This level allowed various electrical phenomena to be seen, reigniting scientific investigation.

input: The Han-era family was patrilineal and typically had four to five nuclear family members living in one household. Multiple generations of extended family members did not occupy the same house, unlike families of later dynasties. According to Confucian family norms, various family members were treated with different levels of respect and intimacy. For example, there were different accepted time frames for mourning the death of a father versus a paternal uncle. Arranged marriages were normal, with the father's input on his offspring's spouse being considered more important than the mother's. Monogamous marriages were also normal, although nobles and high officials were wealthy enough to afford and support concubines as additional lovers. Under certain conditions dictated by custom, not law, both men and women were able to divorce their spouses and remarry.
rewrite: During the Han dynasty, families were organized along paternal lines, with an average household containing a core unit of four or five individuals. It was uncommon for several generations of relatives to share a residence, a practice that would become more typical in subsequent eras. Guided by Confucian principles, distinct degrees of reverence and closeness were expected toward different relatives. This was reflected in customs like the prescribed mourning periods for a father, which differed from those for an uncle. Marriages were generally arranged, with the father's opinion on the match holding greater weight than the mother's. While monogamy was standard, affluent nobles and officials often maintained concubines. Custom, rather than legal statute, permitted both husbands and wives to end their marriages and marry again under specific social conditions.

input: Part of the Russian resistance was credited[by whom?] to the deployment of newly invented blockade mines. Perhaps the most influential contributor to the development of naval mining was a Swede resident in Russia, the inventor and civil engineer Immanuel Nobel (the father of Alfred Nobel). Immanuel Nobel helped the Russian war effort by applying his knowledge of industrial explosives, such as nitroglycerin and gunpowder. One account dates modern naval mining from the Crimean War: "Torpedo mines, if I may use this name given by Fulton to self-acting mines underwater, were among the novelties attempted by the Russians in their defences about Cronstadt and Sevastopol", as one American officer put it in 1860.
rewrite: A portion of the Russian defensive success was attributed to the use of innovative sea mines. A key figure in advancing this naval technology was Immanuel Nobel, a Swedish inventor and engineer living in Russia, who was also Alfred Nobel's father. He supported the Russian military by leveraging his expertise with explosives like nitroglycerin and gunpowder. Some histories trace contemporary naval mining to the Crimean War, noting that the Russians employed what were then called "torpedo mines" in protecting Kronstadt and Sevastopol, a point referenced by an American naval officer in 1860.

input: In 1838, Claridge obtained patents in Scotland on 27 March, and Ireland on 23 April, and in 1851 extensions were sought for all three patents, by the trustees of a company previously formed by Claridge. This was Claridge's Patent Asphalte Company, formed in 1838 for the purpose of introducing to Britain "Asphalte in its natural state from the mine at Pyrimont Seysell in France", and "laid one of the first asphalt pavements in Whitehall". Trials were made of the pavement in 1838 on the footway in Whitehall, the stable at Knightsbridge Barracks, "and subsequently on the space at the bottom of the steps leading from Waterloo Place to St. James Park". "The formation in 1838 of Claridge's Patent Asphalte Company (with a distinguished list of aristocratic patrons, and Marc and Isambard Brunel as, respectively, a trustee and consulting engineer), gave an enormous impetus to the development of a British asphalt industry". "By the end of 1838, at least two other companies, Robinson's and the Bastenne company, were in production", with asphalt being laid as paving at Brighton, Herne Bay, Canterbury, Kensington, the Strand, and a large floor area in Bunhill-row, while meantime Claridge's Whitehall paving "continue(d) in good order".
rewrite:
In March and April of 1838, Claridge secured patent rights in Scotland and Ireland. Later, in 1851, extensions for these patents were pursued by the trustees of a firm he had earlier established. This enterprise, named Claridge's Patent Asphalte Company and founded in 1838, aimed to bring naturally occurring asphalt from the Pyrimont Seysell quarry in France to Great Britain. It was responsible for installing some of the initial asphalt surfaces on Whitehall. Initial tests of this pavement occurred that same year on a Whitehall walkway, the stables of Knightsbridge Barracks, and later on the area below the stairs connecting Waterloo Place to St. James's Park.

The 1838 establishment of Claridge's company, which boasted a notable roster of aristocratic supporters and included Marc and Isambard Brunel as a trustee and advisor, significantly accelerated the growth of an asphalt industry in Britain. Before the close of 1838, at least two additional firms, Robinson's and the Bastenne company, were also manufacturing asphalt. This material was used for paving in locations such as Brighton, Herne Bay, Canterbury, Kensington, the Strand, and a substantial floor space in Bunhill-row. During this period, Claridge's original Whitehall pavement remained in excellent condition.

input: In South Australia, initially a Liberal and Country Party affiliated party, the Liberal and Country League (LCL), mostly led by Premier of South Australia Tom Playford, was in power from the 1933 election to the 1965 election, though with assistance from an electoral malapportionment, or gerrymander, known as the Playmander. The LCL's Steele Hall governed for one term from the 1968 election to the 1970 election and during this time began the process of dismantling the Playmander. David Tonkin, as leader of the South Australian Division of the Liberal Party of Australia, became Premier at the 1979 election for one term, losing office at the 1982 election. The Liberals returned to power at the 1993 election, led by Premiers Dean Brown, John Olsen and Rob Kerin through two terms, until their defeat at the 2002 election. They have since remained in opposition under a record five Opposition Leaders.
rewrite: In South Australia, the Liberal and Country League (LCL), which was originally aligned with the Liberal and Country Party, held government from 1933 to 1965. This lengthy tenure, primarily under Premier Tom Playford, was partly sustained by a biased electoral system called the Playmander. Following this, the LCL's Steele Hall served a single term starting in 1968 and initiated reforms to eliminate that unfair districting. Later, David Tonkin, heading the state's Liberal Party, won the premiership in 1979 but lost it in the 1982 election. The Liberals regained office in 1993, with Dean Brown, John Olsen, and Rob Kerin serving as Premiers over two terms until losing in 2002. Since that defeat, they have continuously been in opposition, led by a historic total of five Opposition Leaders.

input: The phrase "in whole or in part" has been subject to much discussion by scholars of international humanitarian law. The International Criminal Tribunal for the Former Yugoslavia found in Prosecutor v. Radislav Krstic – Trial Chamber I – Judgment – IT-98-33 (2001) ICTY8 (2 August 2001) that Genocide had been committed. In Prosecutor v. Radislav Krstic – Appeals Chamber – Judgment – IT-98-33 (2004) ICTY 7 (19 April 2004) paragraphs 8, 9, 10, and 11 addressed the issue of in part and found that "the part must be a substantial part of that group. The aim of the Genocide Convention is to prevent the intentional destruction of entire human groups, and the part targeted must be significant enough to have an impact on the group as a whole." The Appeals Chamber goes into details of other cases and the opinions of respected commentators on the Genocide Convention to explain how they came to this conclusion.
rewrite: The expression "in whole or in part" has generated considerable debate among experts in international humanitarian law. In the Radislav Krstic case, the initial trial judgment from the International Criminal Tribunal for the Former Yugoslavia in 2001 established that genocide occurred. Subsequently, the 2004 Appeals Chamber judgment examined the meaning of "in part" in several paragraphs. It determined that the targeted segment must constitute a substantial portion of the larger group. This interpretation aligns with the Genocide Convention's fundamental purpose of prohibiting the deliberate annihilation of complete human collectives. Therefore, the targeted part must be sufficiently significant that its destruction affects the overall viability of the group. To support this reasoning, the Appeals Chamber delves into prior legal precedents and considers the analyses of prominent scholars specializing in the Genocide Convention.

input: Iran received access to the Internet in 1993. According to 2014 census, around 40% of the population of Iran are Internet users. Iran ranks 24th among countries by number of Internet users. According to the statistics provided by the web information company of Alexa, Google Search and Yahoo! are the most used search engines in Iran. Over 80% of the users of Telegram, a cloud-based instant messaging service, are from Iran. Instagram is the most popular online social networking service in Iran. Direct access to Facebook has been blocked in Iran since the 2009 Iranian presidential election protests, due to organization of the opposition movements on the website; but however, Facebook has around 12 to 17 million users in Iran who are using virtual private networks and proxy servers to access the website. Around 90% of Iran's e-commerce takes place on the Iranian online store of Digikala, which has around 750,000 visitors per day and more than 2.3 million subscribers. Digikala is the most visited online store in the Middle East, and ranks 4th among the most visited websites in Iran.
rewrite: Internet connectivity first became available in Iran during 1993. Census figures from 2014 indicate that approximately four out of every ten Iranians use the Internet, placing the nation 24th globally in terms of total users. Data from Alexa shows that Google Search and Yahoo! are the predominant search engines there. The cloud messaging service Telegram counts more than 80% of its user base as Iranian. Instagram is the leading social platform in the country. While Facebook has been officially inaccessible since the 2009 election protests, due to its use by opposition groups, an estimated 12 to 17 million Iranians still reach the site via VPNs or proxy servers. Domestically, about 90% of all online shopping occurs through Digikala, an Iranian marketplace. This site attracts roughly 750,000 daily visitors and has over 2.3 million subscribers, making it the top online store in the Middle East and the fourth most-visited website within Iran.

input: A large number of Bell's writings, personal correspondence, notebooks, papers and other documents reside at both the United States Library of Congress Manuscript Division (as the Alexander Graham Bell Family Papers), and at the Alexander Graham Bell Institute, Cape Breton University, Nova Scotia; major portions of which are available for online viewing.

input: Several Muslim countries like Turkey and Iran exhibit high scientific publication. Some countries have tried to encourage scientific research. In Pakistan, establishment of the Higher Education Commission in 2002, resulted in a 5-fold increase in the number of PhDs and a 10-fold increase in the number of scientific research papers in 10 years with the total number of universities increasing from 115 in 2001 to over 400 in 2012.[citation needed] Saudi Arabia has established the King Abdullah University of Science and Technology. United Arab Emirates has invested in Zayed University, United Arab Emirates University, and Masdar Institute of Science and Technology[clarification needed]
rewrite: Nations with significant Muslim populations, including Turkey and Iran, are producing substantial scientific research. Efforts to boost academic inquiry have been implemented in various regions. For instance, Pakistan's creation of the Higher Education Commission in 2002 led to a fivefold rise in doctoral graduates and a tenfold surge in research publications within a decade, while universities grew from 115 to over 400. Similarly, Saudi Arabia founded the King Abdullah University of Science and Technology, and the United Arab Emirates has directed resources into institutions like Zayed University and the Masdar Institute.

input: The term "Kievan Rus'" (Ки́евская Русь Kievskaya Rus’) was coined in the 19th century in Russian historiography to refer to the period when the centre was in Kiev. In English, the term was introduced in the early 20th century, when it was found in the 1913 English translation of Vasily Klyuchevsky's A History of Russia, to distinguish the early polity from successor states, which were also named Rus. Later, the Russian term was rendered into Belarusian and Ukrainian as Кіеўская Русь Kijeŭskaja Rus’ and Ки́ївська Русь Kyivs'ka Rus’, respectively.
rewrite: The phrase "Kievan Rus'" originated in 19th-century Russian historical writing, denoting the era during which Kiev served as the political heartland. It entered English usage in the early 1900s, appearing in a translated history to differentiate that early state from later entities also called Rus. Subsequently, the original Russian expression was adapted into Belarusian and Ukrainian, each with its own linguistic rendering.

input: The Melbourne rail network has its origins in privately built lines from the 1850s gold rush era, and today the suburban network consists of 209 suburban stations on 16 lines which radiate from the City Loop, a partially underground metro section of the network beneath the Central Business District (Hoddle Grid). Flinders Street Station is Melbourne's busiest railway station, and was the world's busiest passenger station in 1926. It remains a prominent Melbourne landmark and meeting place. The city has rail connections with regional Victorian cities, as well as direct interstate rail services to Sydney and Adelaide and beyond which depart from Melbourne's other major rail terminus, Southern Cross Station in Spencer Street. In the 2013–2014 financial year, the Melbourne rail network recorded 232.0 million passenger trips, the highest in its history. Many rail lines, along with dedicated lines and rail yards are also used for freight. The Overland to Adelaide departs Southern Cross twice a week, while the XPT to Sydney departs twice a day.
rewrite: Melbourne's railway system began with private lines constructed during the 1850s gold rush. Its present suburban setup includes 16 routes emanating from the City Loop, an underground metro segment under the central business district, serving 209 stations. Flinders Street Station, the network's most active hub, was once the globe's busiest passenger station in 1926 and continues to be a major city icon and gathering spot. The system links to regional Victorian centers and provides direct interstate services to Sydney and Adelaide, primarily departing from Southern Cross Station on Spencer Street. Passenger journeys reached a record 232 million in the 2013–2014 fiscal year. Numerous tracks and specialized infrastructure also support freight operations. The Overland service to Adelaide runs twice weekly from Southern Cross, and the XPT to Sydney departs two times daily.

input: The Universal Film Manufacturing Company was incorporated in New York on April 30, 1912. Laemmle, who emerged as president in July 1912, was the primary figure in the partnership with Dintenfass, Baumann, Kessel, Powers, Swanson, Horsley, and Brulatour. Eventually all would be bought out by Laemmle. The new Universal studio was a vertically integrated company, with movie production, distribution and exhibition venues all linked in the same corporate entity, the central element of the Studio system era.
rewrite: The Universal Film Manufacturing Company was founded in New York on April 30, 1912. Carl Laemmle became its president that July, leading a coalition with several partners. He later acquired their shares to gain full control. This vertically integrated studio combined film creation, distribution, and theater operations under one corporation, a defining structure of the classic Hollywood studio system.

input: Besides Prince William and Prince Harry, members of the extended British Royal Family who have attended Eton include Prince Richard, Duke of Gloucester and his son Alexander Windsor, Earl of Ulster; Prince Edward, Duke of Kent, his eldest son George Windsor, Earl of St Andrews and grandson Edward Windsor, Lord Downpatrick and his youngest son Lord Nicholas Windsor; Prince Michael of Kent and his son Lord Frederick Windsor; James Ogilvy, son of Princess Alexandra and the Right Honourable Angus Ogilvy, himself an Eton alumnus. Prince William of Gloucester (1942-1972) also attended Eton, as did George Lascelles, 7th Earl of Harewood, son of Princess Mary, Princess Royal.
rewrite: Beyond the well-known princes William and Harry, numerous other relatives within the British monarchy have studied at Eton College. This list includes the Duke of Gloucester, Prince Richard, and his son Alexander, the Earl of Ulster. Also educated there were Prince Edward, Duke of Kent, along with his son George, Earl of St Andrews, and his grandson Edward, Lord Downpatrick, plus his other son Lord Nicholas.
