Radar fire control meant they could hit targets from a much greater distance than the Japanese. The battleship Yamashiro, a cruiser and a destroyer were crippled by 16-inch (406 mm) shells; Yamashiro sank at 04:19. Only one of Nishimura's force of seven ships survived the engagement. At 04:25 Shima's force of two cruisers and eight destroyers reached the battle. Seeing Fusō and believing her to be the wrecks of two battleships, Shima ordered a retreat, ending the last battleship-vs-battleship action in history.
rewrite:
Nishimura commanded a group of seven warships: two battleships, a cruiser, and four destroyers. Maintaining radio silence prevented him from coordinating with Shima and Kurita’s fleets. Moreover, due to a longstanding personal rivalry, Nishimura and Shima had not collaborated on any strategy prior to the operation. Around 2:00 a.m., as Nishimura moved into the constricted waters of Surigao Strait, Shima trailed roughly 22 miles behind, while Kurita remained far off in the Sibuyan Sea, hours away from Leyte. Shortly after passing Panaon Island, Nishimura’s squadron encountered a carefully prepared ambush by the Allied 7th Fleet Support Force, under Rear Admiral Jesse Oldendorf. Oldendorf’s substantial command included six battleships, eight cruisers of various classes, 29 destroyers, and 39 torpedo boats. To proceed through the strait toward the invasion beaches, Nishimura was forced into a perilous gauntlet.

Approximately at 3:00 a.m., torpedoes struck the battleship Fusō and three destroyers; Fusō was ripped apart and split into two sections. By 3:50 a.m., American battleships commenced their main bombardment. Their advanced radar-directed aiming systems allowed them to strike accurately from ranges far beyond Japanese capabilities. Under a barrage of heavy 16-inch shells, the battleship Yamashiro, along with a cruiser and a destroyer, were severely damaged. Yamashiro went down at 4:19 a.m. Of Nishimura’s original seven vessels, only one managed to escape destruction. Shima’s force—two cruisers and eight destroyers—arrived at the scene around 4:25 a.m. Observing the burning halves of Fusō, which he mistook for two separate wrecked battleships, Shima decided to withdraw. This retreat concluded the final direct engagement between opposing battleships in naval warfare.

input: 187th Street crosses Washington Heights and running from Laurel Hill Terrace in the east to Chittenden Avenue in the west near the George Washington Bridge and Hudson River. The street is interrupted by a long set of stairs east of Fort Washington Avenue leading to the Broadway valley. West of there, it is mostly lined with store fronts and serves as a main shopping district for the Hudson Heights neighborhood.
rewrite: 187th Street extends across Washington Heights, connecting Laurel Hill Terrace on its eastern end to Chittenden Avenue near the George Washington Bridge and Hudson River to the west. A lengthy staircase east of Fort Washington Avenue breaks its path, descending toward the Broadway valley. The segment west of this point features numerous shops, functioning as a primary commercial area for Hudson Heights.

input: The strongest contribution of the French Academies to the public sphere comes from the concours académiques (roughly translated as 'academic contests') they sponsored throughout France. These academic contests were perhaps the most public of any institution during the Enlightenment. The practice of contests dated back to the Middle Ages, and was revived in the mid-17th century. The subject matter had previously been generally religious and/or monarchical, featuring essays, poetry, and painting. By roughly 1725, however, this subject matter had radically expanded and diversified, including "royal propaganda, philosophical battles, and critical ruminations on the social and political institutions of the Old Regime." Topics of public controversy were also discussed such as the theories of Newton and Descartes, the slave trade, women's education, and justice in France.
rewrite: The French Academies made their most significant public impact through the academic competitions they organized across the country. These contests stood out as among the most visible institutional activities of the Enlightenment era. Revived in the mid-1600s, the tradition of such competitions originated in medieval times. Initially, the content focused largely on religion and monarchy, expressed through poetry, essays, and art. But starting around 1725, the themes broadened dramatically to encompass royalist messaging, philosophical disputes, and critiques of the period's social and political structures. The contests also engaged with contentious issues of the day, including the ideas of Newton and Descartes, the ethics of slavery, the schooling of women, and the state of the French judicial system.

input: The Jamahiriya's radical direction earned the government many enemies. In February 1978, Gaddafi discovered that his head of military intelligence was plotting to kill him, and began to increasingly entrust security to his Qaddadfa tribe. Many who had seen their wealth and property confiscated turned against the administration, and a number of western-funded opposition groups were founded by exiles. Most prominent was the National Front for the Salvation of Libya (NFSL), founded in 1981 by Mohammed Magariaf, which orchestrated militant attacks against Libya's government, while another, al-Borkan, began killing Libyan diplomats abroad. Following Gaddafi's command to kill these "stray dogs", under Colonel Younis Bilgasim's leadership, the Revolutionary Committees set up overseas branches to suppress counter-revolutionary activity, assassinating various dissidents. Although nearby nations like Syria also used hit squads, Gaddafi was unusual in publicly bragging about his administration's use of them; in June 1980, he ordered all dissidents to return home or be "liquidated wherever you are."
rewrite: The Jamahiriya's extreme policies generated widespread hostility toward the regime. Early in 1978, learning that his military intelligence chief was planning his assassination, Gaddafi increasingly relied on his own Qaddadfa tribe for protection. Numerous citizens, having lost their assets through confiscation, became opposed to the government. Several opposition organizations, backed by Western sources, were also established abroad. The most notable was the National Front for the Salvation of Libya (NFSL), started in 1981 by Mohammed Magariaf, which conducted armed assaults within Libya. Another group, al-Borkan, targeted Libyan diplomats overseas. In response, Gaddafi issued orders to eliminate these "stray dogs." Under Colonel Younis Bilgasim, the Revolutionary Committees formed international units to crush opposition, executing several exiles. While states such as Syria employed similar covert squads, Gaddafi was distinctive in openly boasting about these tactics. In mid-1980, he commanded all opponents to return or face being "liquidated" anywhere in the world.

input: The state of California was admitted to the United States in 1850. That same year San Diego was designated the seat of the newly established San Diego County and was incorporated as a city. Joshua H. Bean, the last alcalde of San Diego, was elected the first mayor. Two years later the city was bankrupt; the California legislature revoked the city's charter and placed it under control of a board of trustees, where it remained until 1889. A city charter was re-established in 1889 and today's city charter was adopted in 1931.
rewrite: California joined the United States in 1850. In that year, San Diego also became both the county seat for its newly formed county and an official city. Joshua H. Bean, who had served as the final alcalde, became its inaugural mayor. By 1852, the city faced insolvency, leading the state legislature to dissolve its charter and install a trustee board for management. This governance lasted until 1889, when a city charter was reinstated. The current charter was put into effect in 1931.

input: The vast majority of visitors in Greece in 2007 came from the European continent, numbering 12.7 million, while the most visitors from a single nationality were those from the United Kingdom, (2.6 million), followed closely by those from Germany (2.3 million). In 2010, the most visited region of Greece was that of Central Macedonia, with 18% of the country's total tourist flow (amounting to 3.6 million tourists), followed by Attica with 2.6 million and the Peloponnese with 1.8 million. Northern Greece is the country's most-visited geographical region, with 6.5 million tourists, while Central Greece is second with 6.3 million.
rewrite: In 2007, most tourists to Greece arrived from Europe, totaling 12.7 million. The largest national group was from the UK at 2.6 million, with Germany second at 2.3 million. By 2010, Central Macedonia was the top region, drawing 18% of all visitors, or 3.6 million tourists. Attica followed with 2.6 million, then the Peloponnese with 1.8 million. Overall, Northern Greece received 6.5 million tourists, making it the most popular area, while Central Greece ranked second with 6.3 million.

input: They maintained that the potassium tartrate used in his treatment prevented his stomach from expelling these compounds and that his thirst was a symptom of the poison. Their hypothesis was that the calomel given to Napoleon became an overdose, which killed him and left extensive tissue damage behind. According to a 2007 article, the type of arsenic found in Napoleon's hair shafts was mineral, the most toxic, and according to toxicologist Patrick Kintz, this supported the conclusion that he was murdered.
rewrite: Experts argued that the potassium tartrate administered hindered his stomach from eliminating these substances, with his thirst indicating poisoning. They proposed that Napoleon received a fatal excess of calomel, causing his death and significant tissue harm. A 2007 paper noted that arsenic detected in his hair was mineral-based, the most lethal form. Toxicologist Patrick Kintz stated this evidence reinforced the murder theory.

input: The digital data on a CD begins at the center of the disc and proceeds toward the edge, which allows adaptation to the different size formats available. Standard CDs are available in two sizes. By far, the most common is 120 millimetres (4.7 in) in diameter, with a 74- or 80-minute audio capacity and a 650 or 700 MiB (737,280,000-byte) data capacity. This capacity was reportedly specified by Sony executive Norio Ohga in May 1980 so as to be able to contain the entirety of the London Philharmonic Orchestra's recording of Beethoven's Ninth Symphony on one disc. This is a myth according to Kees Immink, as the code format had not yet been decided in May 1980. The adoption of EFM one month later would have allowed a playing time of 97 minutes for 120 mm diameter or 74 minutes for a disc as small as 100 mm. The 120 mm diameter has been adopted by subsequent formats, including Super Audio CD, DVD, HD DVD, and Blu-ray Disc. Eighty-millimeter discs ("Mini CDs") were originally designed for CD singles and can hold up to 24 minutes of music or 210 MiB of data but never became popular.[citation needed] Today, nearly every single is released on a 120 mm CD, called a Maxi single.[citation needed]
rewrite: On compact discs, digital information is stored starting from the innermost part and spiraling outward to the rim. This design accommodates discs of various dimensions. Typically, CDs come in two primary sizes. The predominant version measures 120 millimeters across, offering either 74 or 80 minutes of audio, equivalent to roughly 650 or 700 MiB of data. A popular anecdote suggests this capacity was chosen by Sony's Norio Ohga to fit a complete recording of Beethoven’s Ninth Symphony by the London Philharmonic Orchestra. However, engineer Kees Immink has refuted this story, noting that the technical encoding standard was not finalized at the time. Shortly after, the selection of EFM modulation enabled a potential 97 minutes of playback for a 120 mm disc, or about 74 minutes for a 100 mm alternative. The 120 mm size became the basis for later optical media like DVD, Super Audio CD, and Blu-ray. A smaller 80 mm variant, often called a Mini CD, was created for singles with a capacity near 24 minutes of audio, but it saw limited adoption. Currently, most music singles are issued as full-size 120 mm discs, commonly referred to as Maxi singles.

input: Beyoncé has received praise for her stage presence and voice during live performances. Jarett Wieselman of the New York Post placed her at number one on her list of the Five Best Singer/Dancers. According to Barbara Ellen of The Guardian Beyoncé is the most in-charge female artist she's seen onstage, while Alice Jones of The Independent wrote she "takes her role as entertainer so seriously she's almost too good." The ex-President of Def Jam L.A. Reid has described Beyoncé as the greatest entertainer alive. Jim Farber of the Daily News and Stephanie Classen of Star Phoenix both praised her strong voice and her stage presence.
rewrite: Beyoncé is widely acclaimed for her dynamic live shows and vocal talent. Critics consistently highlight her commanding performances; one review ranks her as the top vocalist-dancer, while another notes her unparalleled authority onstage. Observers remark that her dedication to performance borders on perfection. A prominent music executive has called her the premier entertainer of our time. Additional reviewers have specifically commended the power of her voice and her captivating energy during concerts.

input: The eastern shoreline of Funafuti Lagoon was modified during World War II when the airfield (what is now Funafuti International Airport) was constructed. The coral base of the atoll was used as fill to create the runway. The resulting borrow pits impacted the fresh-water aquifer. In the low areas of Funafuti the sea water can be seen bubbling up through the porous coral rock to form pools with each high tide. Since 1994 a project has been in development to assess the environmental impact of transporting sand from the lagoon to fill all the borrow pits and low-lying areas on Fongafale. In 2014 the Tuvalu Borrow Pits Remediation (BPR) project was approved in order to fill 10 borrow pits, leaving Tafua Pond, which is a natural pond. The New Zealand Government funded the BPR project. The project was carried out in 2015 with 365,000 sqm of sand being dredged from the lagoon to fill the holes and improve living conditions on the island. This project increase the usable land space on Fongafale by eight per cent.
rewrite:
During World War II, the construction of an airfield on Funafuti Atoll—now the site of Funafuti International Airport—significantly altered the lagoon’s eastern coast. Builders used coral material excavated from the atoll to form the runway, which left behind a series of excavated areas known as borrow pits. These depressions damaged the island’s freshwater supply by allowing seawater to infiltrate. In lower sections of Funafuti, ocean water visibly rises through the permeable coral during high tide, forming tidal pools.

Starting in 1994, plans were made to study the effects of using sand dredged from the lagoon to refill these pits and other low zones on Fongafale islet. Approval for the Tuvalu Borrow Pits Remediation project came in 2014, aiming to fill ten borrow pits while preserving the natural Tafua Pond. Funded by New Zealand, the work was completed in 2015. It involved moving 365,000 square meters of sand from the lagoon to reclaim the land, enhancing local habitability and expanding Fongafale’s usable area by eight percent.

input: Rebirth refers to a process whereby beings go through a succession of lifetimes as one of many possible forms of sentient life, each running from conception to death. The doctrine of anattā (Sanskrit anātman) rejects the concepts of a permanent self or an unchanging, eternal soul, as it is called in Hinduism and Christianity. According to Buddhism there ultimately is no such thing as a self independent from the rest of the universe. Buddhists also refer to themselves as the believers of the anatta doctrine—Nairatmyavadin or Anattavadin. Rebirth in subsequent existences must be understood as the continuation of a dynamic, ever-changing process of pratītyasamutpāda ("dependent arising") determined by the laws of cause and effect (karma) rather than that of one being, reincarnating from one existence to the next.
rewrite: Rebirth describes the cyclical journey of conscious beings through multiple lives, each spanning from birth to death. In contrast to faiths like Hinduism and Christianity, Buddhism denies the existence of a fixed soul or permanent self, a principle known as anattā. This teaching asserts that no independent, enduring identity exists separate from the wider cosmos. Followers of this view are called Anattavadin. Crucially, rebirth is not the transmigration of an unchanging entity. Instead, it represents the persistent flow of a conditioned process—dependent origination—where each new existence is shaped by the causal chain of karma, not by a migrating self.

input: New York City is situated in the Northeastern United States, in southeastern New York State, approximately halfway between Washington, D.C. and Boston. The location at the mouth of the Hudson River, which feeds into a naturally sheltered harbor and then into the Atlantic Ocean, has helped the city grow in significance as a trading port. Most of New York City is built on the three islands of Long Island, Manhattan, and Staten Island.
rewrite: Located in the northeastern U.S., New York City lies in the southeast of its namesake state, roughly midway from Boston to Washington, D.C. Its position where the Hudson River meets a protected bay and the Atlantic Ocean fostered its historical development as a major commercial harbor. The city's urban area primarily occupies three islands: Manhattan, Long Island, and Staten Island.

input: In winter, the Piedmont is colder than the coast, with temperatures usually averaging in the upper 40s–lower 50s °F (8–12 °C) during the day and often dropping below the freezing point at night. The region averages around 3–5 in (8–13 cm) of snowfall annually in the Charlotte area, and slightly more north toward the Virginia border. The Piedmont is especially notorious for sleet and freezing rain. Freezing rain can be heavy enough to snarl traffic and break down trees and power lines. Annual precipitation and humidity are lower in the Piedmont than in the mountains or the coast, but even at its lowest, the average is 40 in (1,020 mm) per year.
rewrite: During winter, the Piedmont region experiences lower temperatures compared to coastal areas. Daytime highs typically range from the upper 40s to lower 50s Fahrenheit (8–12°C), while nighttime lows frequently fall below freezing. Annual snowfall averages 3–5 inches (8–13 cm) near Charlotte, increasing somewhat farther north. The area is particularly prone to sleet and freezing rain, which can accumulate severely, disrupting travel and damaging trees and utility lines. Although yearly rainfall and humidity are less here than in the mountains or along the coast, the Piedmont still receives an average minimum of 40 inches (1,020 mm) of precipitation annually.

input: The Neolithic 2 (PPNB) began around 8,800 BCE according to the ASPRO chronology in the Levant (Jericho, Israel). As with the PPNA dates, there are two versions from the same laboratories noted above. This system of terminology, however, is not convenient for southeast Anatolia and settlements of the middle Anatolia basin. This era was before the Mesolithic era.[citation needed] A settlement of 3,000 inhabitants was found in the outskirts of Amman, Jordan. Considered to be one of the largest prehistoric settlements in the Near East, called 'Ain Ghazal, it was continuously inhabited from approximately 7,250 – 5,000 B.
rewrite: According to the ASPRO timeline, the Pre-Pottery Neolithic B (PPNB) period commenced about 8,800 BCE in the Levant region, such as at Jericho. As with the prior PPNA phase, two dating interpretations exist from the previously mentioned labs. This chronological framework is less applicable to southeast Anatolia and central Anatolian basin sites. Preceding the Mesolithic, this era included substantial settlements like 'Ain Ghazal near Amman, a major Near Eastern prehistoric site occupied from roughly 7,250 to 5,000 BCE.

input: The American Civil War boosted the local economy with wartime purchases of industrial goods, including that of the New Haven Arms Company, which would later become the Winchester Repeating Arms Company. (Winchester would continue to produce arms in New Haven until 2006, and many of the buildings that were a part of the Winchester plant are now a part of the Winchester Repeating Arms Company Historic District.) After the war, population grew and doubled by the start of the 20th century, most notably due to the influx of immigrants from southern Europe, particularly Italy. Today, roughly half the populations of East Haven, West Haven, and North Haven are Italian-American. Jewish immigration to New Haven has left an enduring mark on the city. Westville was the center of Jewish life in New Haven, though today many have fanned out to suburban communities such as Woodbridge and Cheshire.
rewrite: The economy of the region was significantly stimulated by the American Civil War, as military procurement created demand for manufactured products. This benefited firms like the New Haven Arms Company, the precursor to the Winchester Repeating Arms Company. Winchester maintained its manufacturing operations in the city for many decades. Following the conflict, the area experienced substantial demographic expansion, with its resident count doubling by 1900. This surge was largely driven by new arrivals from Southern Europe, especially Italy. Consequently, Italian-Americans now constitute about half the inhabitants of several neighboring towns. Additionally, Jewish migration has profoundly influenced the city's character. While the Westville area was historically the hub for this community, many families have since relocated to nearby suburbs.

input: Most bacteria have a single circular chromosome that can range in size from only 160,000 base pairs in the endosymbiotic bacteria Candidatus Carsonella ruddii, to 12,200,000 base pairs in the soil-dwelling bacteria Sorangium cellulosum. Spirochaetes of the genus Borrelia are a notable exception to this arrangement, with bacteria such as Borrelia burgdorferi, the cause of Lyme disease, containing a single linear chromosome. The genes in bacterial genomes are usually a single continuous stretch of DNA and although several different types of introns do exist in bacteria, these are much rarer than in eukaryotes.
rewrite: Bacterial chromosomes are typically circular and vary greatly in size, from as small as 160,000 base pairs in some endosymbionts to over 12 million in certain soil bacteria. An exception is found in Borrelia spirochaetes, like the Lyme disease agent, which possess a linear chromosome. Generally, bacterial genes form an uninterrupted DNA sequence, and while introns can occur, they are far less common than in organisms with complex cells.

input: Daniel Gralath was the first to combine several jars in parallel into a "battery" to increase the charge storage capacity. Benjamin Franklin investigated the Leyden jar and came to the conclusion that the charge was stored on the glass, not in the water as others had assumed. He also adopted the term "battery", (denoting the increasing of power with a row of similar units as in a battery of cannon), subsequently applied to clusters of electrochemical cells. Leyden jars were later made by coating the inside and outside of jars with metal foil, leaving a space at the mouth to prevent arcing between the foils.[citation needed] The earliest unit of capacitance was the jar, equivalent to about 1.11 nanofarads.
rewrite: Daniel Gralath pioneered the connection of multiple Leyden jars in parallel, creating a "battery" to boost overall charge capacity. Benjamin Franklin studied the device and determined the charge resided in the glass itself, contrary to the belief it was held in the water. He also popularized the word "battery," drawing from military terminology for grouped artillery, later used for electrochemical cell arrays. Later designs involved lining both the interior and exterior of jars with metal foil, with a gap left at the top to avoid electrical discharge between the layers. The original unit for measuring capacitance, the jar, approximated 1.11 nanofarads.

input: Cara Cusumano, director of the Tribeca Film Festival, stated in April 2014: "Piracy is less about people not wanting to pay and more about just wanting the immediacy – people saying, 'I want to watch Spiderman right now' and downloading it". The statement occurred during the third year that the festival used the Internet to present its content, while it was the first year that it featured a showcase of content producers who work exclusively online. Cusumano further explained that downloading behavior is not merely conducted by people who merely want to obtain content for free:
rewrite: In April 2014, Tribeca Film Festival director Cara Cusumano remarked that piracy often stems from a demand for instant access rather than an unwillingness to pay. She illustrated this by noting how individuals might immediately download a film like "Spiderman" out of a desire to watch it at once. This comment was made as the festival entered its third year of online streaming and first year highlighting digital-native creators. Cusumano added that such downloading is frequently motivated by this urgency, not simply by a wish to avoid costs.

input: As of the early 21st century, Christianity has approximately 2.4 billion adherents. The faith represents about a third of the world's population and is the largest religion in the world. Christians have composed about 33 percent of the world's population for around 100 years. The largest Christian denomination is the Roman Catholic Church, with 1.17 billion adherents, representing half of all Christians.
rewrite: At the start of this century, around 2.4 billion people follow Christianity, making it the globe's biggest religion. This accounts for roughly one-third of humanity, a proportion maintained for a century. The Roman Catholic Church is the largest single group, comprising 1.17 billion members, or half of all Christians.

input: In this respect, the counterpart of Ashkenazi is Sephardic, since most non-Ashkenazi Orthodox Jews follow Sephardic rabbinical authorities, whether or not they are ethnically Sephardic. By tradition, a Sephardic or Mizrahi woman who marries into an Orthodox or Haredi Ashkenazi Jewish family raises her children to be Ashkenazi Jews; conversely an Ashkenazi woman who marries a Sephardi or Mizrahi man is expected to take on Sephardic practice and the children inherit a Sephardic identity, though in practice many families compromise. A convert generally follows the practice of the beth din that converted him or her. With the integration of Jews from around the world in Israel, North America, and other places, the religious definition of an Ashkenazi Jew is blurring, especially outside Orthodox Judaism.
rewrite: In this context, Sephardic tradition serves as the parallel to Ashkenazi, as the majority of Orthodox Jews who are not Ashkenazi adhere to Sephardic religious leadership, regardless of their actual ethnic descent. Customarily, if a woman of Sephardic or Mizrahi background marries into an Ashkenazi Orthodox family, her children are brought up within the Ashkenazi tradition. The reverse is also traditionally expected: an Ashkenazi woman marrying a Sephardi or Mizrahi man adopts Sephardic customs, with the children assuming a Sephardic identity, although families often find a middle ground. Converts typically adopt the customs of the rabbinical court that oversaw their conversion. However, as Jewish communities globally become more interconnected, particularly in Israel and North America, the distinct religious boundaries defining an Ashkenazi Jew are becoming less clear, most notably beyond Orthodox circles.

input: Somerset is a rural county of rolling hills such as the Blackdown Hills, Mendip Hills, Quantock Hills and Exmoor National Park, and large flat expanses of land including the Somerset Levels. There is evidence of human occupation from Paleolithic times, and of subsequent settlement in the Roman and Anglo-Saxon periods. The county played a significant part in the consolidation of power and rise of King Alfred the Great, and later in the English Civil War and the Monmouth Rebellion. The city of Bath is famous for its substantial Georgian architecture and is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
rewrite: Somerset features a varied landscape of undulating hills like the Blackdowns, Mendips, Quantocks, and Exmoor, alongside broad lowlands such as the Somerset Levels. Human activity dates to the Paleolithic era, with continued habitation through Roman and Anglo-Saxon times. The region was important during King Alfred's reign and in conflicts like the Civil War and Monmouth Rebellion. Bath, renowned for its extensive Georgian buildings, holds UNESCO World Heritage status.

input: Having initially announced a new album entitled So Help Me God slated for a 2014 release, in March 2015 West announced that the album would instead be tentatively called SWISH. Later that month, West was awarded an honorary doctorate by the School of the Art Institute of Chicago for his contributions to music, fashion, and popular culture, officially making him an honorary DFA. The next month, West headlined at the Glastonbury Festival in the UK, despite a petition signed by almost 135,000 people against his appearance. At one point, he told the audience: "You are now watching the greatest living rock star on the planet." Media outlets, including social media sites such as Twitter, were sharply divided on his performance. NME stated, "The decision to book West for the slot has proved controversial since its announcement, and the show itself appeared to polarise both Glastonbury goers and those who tuned in to watch on their TVs." The publication added that "he's letting his music speak for and prove itself." The Guardian said that "his set has a potent ferocity – but there are gaps and stutters, and he cuts a strangely lone figure in front of the vast crowd."
rewrite: Kanye West first revealed plans for an album named *So Help Me God*, intended for 2014. However, by March 2015, he changed the working title to *SWISH*. That same month, he received an honorary doctorate from the School of the Art Institute of Chicago, recognizing his impact across music, fashion, and pop culture, which formally granted him the honorary DFA distinction. In the following month, he topped the bill at the UK's Glastonbury Festival, even though a petition against his booking had gathered nearly 135,000 signatures. During the set, he declared to the crowd, "You are now watching the greatest living rock star on the planet." Reaction to his show was deeply split, particularly on platforms like Twitter. NME noted that his booking had been contentious from the start and that the performance further divided festival attendees and television viewers alike. The outlet also commented that he allowed his work to stand on its own merits. According to The Guardian, his performance carried a powerful intensity, yet it was marked by pauses and hesitations, and he seemed an isolated presence before the enormous audience.

input: Crystal Bowersox, who has Type-I diabetes, fell ill due to diabetic ketoacidosis on the morning of the girls performance night for the top 20 week and was hospitalized. The schedule was rearranged so the boys performed first and she could perform the following night instead; she later revealed that Ken Warwick, the show producer, wanted to disqualify her but she begged to be allowed to stay on the show.
rewrite: Crystal Bowersox, a contestant with Type-I diabetes, became sick with diabetic ketoacidosis on the day her group was set to perform. This led to her hospitalization. The show's schedule was adjusted, having the boys perform first so she could appear the next evening. She later shared that producer Ken Warwick considered removing her, but she persuaded him to let her remain in the competition.

input: During the Eastern Han, conscription could be avoided if one paid a commutable tax. The Eastern Han court favored the recruitment of a volunteer army. The volunteer army comprised the Southern Army (Nanjun 南軍), while the standing army stationed in and near the capital was the Northern Army (Beijun 北軍). Led by Colonels (Xiaowei 校尉), the Northern Army consisted of five regiments, each composed of several thousand soldiers. When central authority collapsed after 189 AD, wealthy landowners, members of the aristocracy/nobility, and regional military-governors relied upon their retainers to act as their own personal troops (buqu 部曲).
rewrite: In the Eastern Han era, individuals could pay a tax to be exempt from mandatory military service. The imperial administration preferred to enlist voluntary forces. These volunteers formed the Southern Army, whereas the permanent Northern Army was garrisoned in the capital region. Commanded by Colonels, the Northern Army was organized into five regiments, each containing thousands of troops. Following the disintegration of central power after 189 AD, powerful elites such as landowners, nobles, and provincial governors utilized their private retainers as personal armies.

input: On 12 February 1912, after rounds of negotiations, Longyu issued an imperial edict bringing about the abdication of the child emperor Puyi. This brought an end to over 2,000 years of Imperial China and began an extended period of instability of warlord factionalism. The unorganized political and economic systems combined with a widespread criticism of Chinese culture led to questioning and doubt about the future. In the 1930s, the Empire of Japan invaded Northeast China and founded Manchukuo in 1932, with Puyi, as the emperor. After the invasion by the Soviet Union, Manchukuo collapsed in 1945.
rewrite: Following negotiations, Empress Dowager Longyu declared the child emperor Puyi's abdication on February 12, 1912. This act concluded more than two millennia of imperial rule in China, ushering in a prolonged era of fragmentation dominated by regional warlords. The resulting disorder in governance and the economy, along with broad cultural disillusionment, fostered deep uncertainty about the nation's path. Japan's occupation of northeastern China in the 1930s led to the establishment of Manchukuo in 1932, installing Puyi as its figurehead. This puppet state dissolved in 1945 following Soviet military intervention.

input: Valencia's port is the biggest on the Mediterranean western coast, the first of Spain in container traffic as of 2008 and the second of Spain in total traffic, handling 20% of Spain's exports. The main exports are foodstuffs and beverages. Other exports include oranges, furniture, ceramic tiles, fans, textiles and iron products. Valencia's manufacturing sector focuses on metallurgy, chemicals, textiles, shipbuilding and brewing. Small and medium-sized industries are an important part of the local economy, and before the current crisis unemployment was lower than the Spanish average.
rewrite: Situated on the western Mediterranean, Valencia's port is the region's largest. Since 2008, it has led Spain in container volume and ranks second in overall cargo, managing one-fifth of the nation's exports. Primary goods shipped are food and drink, supplemented by items like citrus fruit, furniture, tiles, and textiles. Local manufacturing emphasizes metals, chemicals, textiles, ship construction, and beer. Small to mid-size businesses are economically vital, and historically, joblessness here stayed below the national level.

input: When a tree is very young it is covered with limbs almost, if not entirely, to the ground, but as it grows older some or all of them will eventually die and are either broken off or fall off. Subsequent growth of wood may completely conceal the stubs which will however remain as knots. No matter how smooth and clear a log is on the outside, it is more or less knotty near the middle. Consequently, the sapwood of an old tree, and particularly of a forest-grown tree, will be freer from knots than the inner heartwood. Since in most uses of wood, knots are defects that weaken the timber and interfere with its ease of working and other properties, it follows that a given piece of sapwood, because of its position in the tree, may well be stronger than a piece of heartwood from the same tree.
rewrite: In its early years, a tree typically has branches extending nearly to the base. As it matures, many lower limbs die and detach. New wood growth often envelops the remaining stubs, yet these persist internally as knots. Even if a log's exterior appears flawless, its core is usually knotty. Therefore, the outer sapwood of a mature tree, especially one grown in a forest, tends to contain fewer knots than the inner heartwood. Knots generally impair timber by reducing strength and complicating woodworking. Consequently, due to its location, a section of sapwood can be stronger and more workable than a piece of heartwood from the identical tree.

input: Puritans were blocked from changing the established church from within, and were severely restricted in England by laws controlling the practice of religion. Their beliefs, however, were transported by the emigration of congregations to the Netherlands (and later to New England), and by evangelical clergy to Ireland (and later into Wales), and were spread into lay society and parts of the educational system, particularly certain colleges of the University of Cambridge. They took on distinctive beliefs about clerical dress and in opposition to the episcopal system, particularly after the 1619 conclusions of the Synod of Dort they were resisted by the English bishops. They largely adopted Sabbatarianism in the 17th century, and were influenced by millennialism.
rewrite: Unable to reform England's official church internally, Puritans faced legal constraints on their religious activities. Their doctrines spread as entire congregations relocated to the Netherlands and later New England, while preachers carried them to Ireland and Wales. These ideas permeated lay communities and educational institutions, including some colleges at Cambridge University. Puritans developed unique views on ministerial garments and opposed the hierarchical church structure, facing pushback from bishops especially after the Synod of Dort in 1619. During the 1600s, they commonly embraced strict Sabbath observance and were shaped by millennial beliefs.

input: Not all boys who pass the College election examination choose to become King's Scholars. If they choose instead to belong to one of the 24 Oppidan Houses, they are known as Oppidan Scholars. Oppidan scholarships may also be awarded for consistently performing with distinction in School and external examinations. To gain an Oppidan Scholarship, a boy must have either three distinctions in a row or four throughout his career. Within the school, an Oppidan Scholar is entitled to use the letters OS after his name.
rewrite: Not every student who succeeds on the College's entrance exam opts to be a King's Scholar. Those selecting one of the 24 Oppidan Houses become Oppidan Scholars. This honor can also be earned through sustained academic excellence in both internal and external assessments. Qualification requires either three consecutive distinctions or four total over a student's tenure. An Oppidan Scholar is permitted to append the initials OS following his surname.

input: Some critiqued Paul VI's decision; the newly created Synod of Bishops had an advisory role only and could not make decisions on their own, although the Council decided exactly that. During the pontificate of Paul VI, five such synods took place, and he is on record of implementing all their decisions. Related questions were raised about the new National Bishop Conferences, which became mandatory after Vatican II. Others questioned his Ostpolitik and contacts with Communism and the deals he engaged in for the faithful.
rewrite: Paul VI faced criticism for establishing the Synod of Bishops with merely consultative power, despite the Council's directive. He did, however, enact all proposals from the five synods held under his leadership. Further scrutiny targeted the now-compulsory National Bishop Conferences and his Ostpolitik, which involved negotiating with Communist regimes to protect believers.

input: By the late Middle Ages, Buddhism had become virtually extinct in India, although it continued to exist in surrounding countries. It is now again gaining strength worldwide. China and India are now starting to fund Buddhist shrines in various Asian countries as they compete for influence in the region.[web 20]
rewrite: Buddhism largely disappeared from India by the late medieval period, surviving only in neighboring nations. Today, it is experiencing a global resurgence. To expand their regional sway, China and India are financing Buddhist temples across Asia.

input: The university's first chancellor was Joseph Gibson Hoyt. Crow secured the university charter from the Missouri General Assembly in 1853, and Eliot was named President of the Board of Trustees. Early on, Eliot solicited support from members of the local business community, including John O'Fallon, but Eliot failed to secure a permanent endowment. Washington University is unusual among major American universities in not having had a prior financial endowment. The institution had no backing of a religious organization, single wealthy patron, or earmarked government support.
rewrite: Joseph Gibson Hoyt served as the inaugural chancellor. After obtaining the university's charter from Missouri's legislature in 1853, Crow saw Eliot appointed to lead the Board of Trustees. Eliot initially sought funding from area businessmen like John O'Fallon, yet could not establish a lasting endowment. Unlike most prominent U.S. universities, Washington University began without any initial financial reserve, religious affiliation, generous benefactor, or dedicated public funds.

input: European Dutch remained the literary language until the start of the 1920s, when under pressure of Afrikaner nationalism the local "African" Dutch was preferred over the written, European-based standard. In 1925, section 137 of the 1909 constitution of the Union of South Africa was amended by Act 8 of 1925, stating "the word Dutch in article 137 [...] is hereby declared to include Afrikaans". The constitution of 1983 only listed English and Afrikaans as official languages. It is estimated that between 90% to 95% of Afrikaans vocabulary is ultimately of Dutch origin.
rewrite: Until the 1920s, the Dutch used in literature across South Africa followed European standards. However, rising Afrikaner nationalist sentiment then shifted preference toward the local vernacular, known as Afrikaans. This change was formally recognized in 1925, when a constitutional amendment clarified that the term "Dutch" legally encompassed Afrikaans. By the 1983 constitution, only English and Afrikaans held official status. Linguistically, approximately 90 to 95 percent of Afrikaans words trace their roots back to Dutch.

input: Unarmed fox hunting on horseback with hounds is the type of hunting most closely associated with the United Kingdom; in fact, "hunting" without qualification implies fox hunting. What in other countries is called "hunting" is called "shooting" (birds) or "stalking" (deer) in Britain. Originally a form of vermin control to protect livestock, fox hunting became a popular social activity for newly wealthy upper classes in Victorian times and a traditional rural activity for riders and foot followers alike. Similar to fox hunting in many ways is the chasing of hares with hounds. Pairs of Sight hounds (or long-dogs), such as greyhounds, may be used to pursue a hare in coursing, where the greyhounds are marked as to their skill in coursing the hare (but are not intended to actually catch it), or the hare may be pursued with scent hounds such as beagles or harriers. Other sorts of foxhounds may also be used for hunting stags (deer) or mink. Deer stalking with rifles is carried out on foot without hounds, using stealth.
rewrite: In the United Kingdom, the term "hunting" typically refers to the pursuit of foxes on horseback using packs of hounds, without firearms. This contrasts with other nations, where "hunting" is a broader term; in Britain, shooting birds or stalking deer are distinct activities. Initially practiced to control pests and safeguard farm animals, fox hunting evolved during the Victorian era into a fashionable pastime for the affluent and a customary pursuit for country communities. A comparable practice is hare coursing, which employs hounds. In formal coursing, sight hounds like greyhounds are judged on their ability to chase, not capture, a hare, while scent hounds such as beagles may also be used in the pursuit. Certain foxhound breeds can also track deer or mink. Separately, deer stalking involves hunters stealthily approaching on foot to shoot with rifles, without the aid of hounds.

input: However questions still remain, as some of the corrupt government officials have still not been brought to justice, while the many families who lost their only child, are still seeking compensation and justice to what had happened. According to the Times, many parents were warned by the government not to stage a protest under the threat of arrest.
rewrite: Yet unresolved issues persist, as certain corrupt officials evade accountability, and numerous families who lost their sole child continue to pursue redress. The Times reports that authorities cautioned many parents against protesting, warning they could face arrest.

input: The restoration of power to the patriciate was only temporary. After a period of unrest with repeated violent clashes such as the Züriputsch of 1839, civil war (the Sonderbundskrieg) broke out in 1847 when some Catholic cantons tried to set up a separate alliance (the Sonderbund). The war lasted for less than a month, causing fewer than 100 casualties, most of which were through friendly fire. Yet however minor the Sonderbundskrieg appears compared with other European riots and wars in the 19th century, it nevertheless had a major impact on both the psychology and the society of the Swiss and of Switzerland.
rewrite: The patrician class briefly regained authority, but this did not last. Following turmoil marked by events like the 1839 Züriputsch, a civil war erupted in 1847. Several Catholic cantons had formed a breakaway league, known as the Sonderbund, triggering the conflict. It concluded in under a month with fewer than 100 lives lost, many by accidental fire from their own side. Although minor relative to other 19th-century European upheavals, the Sonderbund War profoundly shaped Swiss national consciousness and social structures.

input: A common application of a torque motor would be the supply- and take-up reel motors in a tape drive. In this application, driven from a low voltage, the characteristics of these motors allow a relatively constant light tension to be applied to the tape whether or not the capstan is feeding tape past the tape heads. Driven from a higher voltage, (and so delivering a higher torque), the torque motors can also achieve fast-forward and rewind operation without requiring any additional mechanics such as gears or clutches. In the computer gaming world, torque motors are used in force feedback steering wheels.
rewrite: Torque motors are frequently employed in tape drives to operate the reels that hold the media. When powered by a low voltage, their design maintains a steady, gentle pull on the tape as it moves past the heads, regardless of the capstan's motion. Applying a higher voltage increases the torque, enabling rapid winding or rewinding functions without needing extra mechanical components like gears. Beyond data storage, these motors are also integral to creating realistic force feedback in simulation devices, such as racing wheels for video games.

input: The Korean War was a conflict between the United States and its United Nations allies and the communist powers under influence of the Soviet Union (also a UN member nation) and the People's Republic of China (which later also gained UN membership). The principal combatants were North and South Korea. Principal allies of South Korea included the United States, Canada, Australia, the United Kingdom, although many other nations sent troops under the aegis of the United Nations. Allies of North Korea included the People's Republic of China, which supplied military forces, and the Soviet Union, which supplied combat advisors and aircraft pilots, as well as arms, for the Chinese and North Korean troops.
rewrite: The Korean War saw North and South Korea as the primary opposing forces. The South was backed by a United Nations coalition led by the United States, with significant contributions from nations like Canada, Australia, and the United Kingdom. Conversely, North Korea received substantial support from communist allies. The People's Republic of China deployed its own military forces to the conflict, while the Soviet Union provided weaponry, strategic advisors, and even pilots for aerial combat, aiding both Chinese and North Korean soldiers.

input: On 3 December, Chopin complained about his bad health and the incompetence of the doctors in Majorca: "Three doctors have visited me ... The first said I was dead; the second said I was dying; and the third said I was about to die." He also had problems having his Pleyel piano sent to him. It finally arrived from Paris in December. Chopin wrote to Pleyel in January 1839: "I am sending you my Preludes [(Op. 28)]. I finished them on your little piano, which arrived in the best possible condition in spite of the sea, the bad weather and the Palma customs." Chopin was also able to undertake work on his Ballade No. 2, Op. 38; two Polonaises, Op. 40; and the Scherzo No. 3, Op. 39.
rewrite: On December 3, Chopin expressed frustration over his poor condition and the inadequacy of physicians in Majorca, noting that three medical men had examined him with grim and varying prognoses. Additionally, he faced difficulties in receiving his Pleyel piano, which ultimately reached him from Paris that same month. By January 1839, Chopin informed Pleyel that he was dispatching his completed Preludes, composed on that instrument, which had survived the voyage, sea conditions, and local customs in good order. During this period, he also progressed on several compositions, including his second Ballade, two Polonaises, and his third Scherzo.

input: In the 1960s, Downtown Houston consisted of a collection of mid-rise office structures. Downtown was on the threshold of an energy industry–led boom in 1970. A succession of skyscrapers were built throughout the 1970s—many by real estate developer Gerald D. Hines—culminating with Houston's tallest skyscraper, the 75-floor, 1,002-foot (305 m)-tall JPMorgan Chase Tower (formerly the Texas Commerce Tower), completed in 1982. It is the tallest structure in Texas, 15th tallest building in the United States, and the 85th tallest skyscraper in the world, based on highest architectural feature. In 1983, the 71-floor, 992-foot (302 m)-tall Wells Fargo Plaza (formerly Allied Bank Plaza) was completed, becoming the second-tallest building in Houston and Texas. Based on highest architectural feature, it is the 17th tallest in the United States and the 95th tallest in the world. In 2007, downtown Houston had over 43 million square feet (4,000,000 m²) of office space.
rewrite: During the 1960s, Houston's city center was characterized by a group of moderately tall office buildings. By 1970, it stood at the brink of a major expansion driven by the energy sector. The following decade saw a wave of high-rise construction, often led by property magnate Gerald D. Hines. This period peaked in 1982 with the opening of the JPMorgan Chase Tower, originally named the Texas Commerce Tower. Reaching 75 stories and 1,002 feet (305 meters), it remains the highest building in Texas. It ranks as the 15th tallest in the U.S. and 85th globally when measured by its pinnacle. The 71-story Wells Fargo Plaza, finished in 1983 at 992 feet (302 meters), became the state's second-tallest structure. It holds the position of 17th tallest nationally and 95th tallest worldwide by the same metric. By 2007, the downtown area contained more than 43 million square feet of office space.

input: Symmetry groups are groups consisting of symmetries of given mathematical objects—be they of geometric nature, such as the introductory symmetry group of the square, or of algebraic nature, such as polynomial equations and their solutions. Conceptually, group theory can be thought of as the study of symmetry.t[›] Symmetries in mathematics greatly simplify the study of geometrical or analytical objects. A group is said to act on another mathematical object X if every group element performs some operation on X compatibly to the group law. In the rightmost example below, an element of order 7 of the (2,3,7) triangle group acts on the tiling by permuting the highlighted warped triangles (and the other ones, too). By a group action, the group pattern is connected to the structure of the object being acted on.
rewrite: Symmetry groups are collections of transformations that preserve the structure of specific mathematical entities, whether geometric shapes like a square or algebraic systems like polynomial equations. Essentially, group theory explores the nature of these symmetries. The presence of symmetry allows mathematicians to analyze geometric or analytical systems in a more streamlined manner. A group acts on an object X when each of its elements applies an operation to X in a way consistent with the group's internal rules. For instance, in a depicted tiling pattern, an element from the (2,3,7) triangle group rearranges the distorted colored triangles. Such actions link the group's inherent pattern to the underlying architecture of the object it influences.

input: Currently, the Regular Force component of the Army consists of three field-ready brigade groups: 1 Canadian Mechanized Brigade Group, at CFB Edmonton and CFB Shilo; 2 Canadian Mechanized Brigade Group, at CFB Petawawa and CFB Gagetown; and 5 Canadian Mechanized Brigade Group, at CFB Valcartier and Quebec City. Each contains one regiment each of artillery, armour, and combat engineers, three battalions of infantry (all scaled in the British fashion), one battalion for logistics, a squadron for headquarters/signals, and several smaller support organizations. A tactical helicopter squadron and a field ambulance are co-located with each brigade, but do not form part of the brigade's command structure.
rewrite: The Army's Regular Force presently fields three operational brigade groups. The 1st is based at CFB Edmonton and CFB Shilo, the 2nd at CFB Petawawa and CFB Gagetown, and the 5th at CFB Valcartier and Quebec City. Every brigade includes an artillery, armour, and engineer regiment, three infantry battalions organized on the British model, a service battalion, a headquarters and signals squadron, and other minor units. A tactical helicopter squadron and a field ambulance unit are stationed with each brigade but operate under separate command.

input: The kingdom is mentioned in the Periplus of the Erythraean Sea as an important market place for ivory, which was exported throughout the ancient world. Aksum was at the time ruled by Zoskales, who also governed the port of Adulis. The Aksumite rulers facilitated trade by minting their own Aksumite currency. The state also established its hegemony over the declining Kingdom of Kush and regularly entered the politics of the kingdoms on the Arabian peninsula, eventually extending its rule over the region with the conquest of the Himyarite Kingdom.
rewrite: According to the Periplus of the Erythraean Sea, this realm was a key ivory trading center, supplying the ancient globe. Under King Zoskales, who controlled Adulis port, Aksum issued its own coins to promote commerce. The kingdom also asserted dominance over the fading Kushite state and frequently intervened in Arabian affairs, ultimately conquering the Himyarite Kingdom to control that area.

input: The abbey was restored to the Benedictines under the Catholic Mary I of England, but they were again ejected under Elizabeth I in 1559. In 1560, Elizabeth re-established Westminster as a "Royal Peculiar" – a church of the Church of England responsible directly to the Sovereign, rather than to a diocesan bishop – and made it the Collegiate Church of St Peter (that is, a non-cathedral church with an attached chapter of canons, headed by a dean.) The last of Mary's abbots was made the first dean.
rewrite: Under Queen Mary I, the Benedictine order regained control of the abbey, only to be removed once more after Elizabeth I ascended the throne. In 1560, Elizabeth designated Westminster a "Royal Peculiar," placing it under the monarch's direct authority instead of a local bishop. It was also reconstituted as the Collegiate Church of St Peter, featuring a dean leading a chapter of canons. The inaugural dean was the final abbot appointed during Mary's reign.

input: This new approach liberated scientific speculation from the dogmatic restraints of Aristotelian science, and paved the way for new approaches. Particularly within the field of theories of motion great advances were made, when such scholars as Jean Buridan, Nicole Oresme and the Oxford Calculators challenged the work of Aristotle. Buridan developed the theory of impetus as the cause of the motion of projectiles, which was an important step towards the modern concept of inertia. The works of these scholars anticipated the heliocentric worldview of Nicolaus Copernicus.
rewrite: This innovative method freed scientific thought from the rigid doctrines of Aristotle, enabling fresh perspectives. Significant progress occurred in motion theory, as thinkers like Jean Buridan, Nicole Oresme, and the Oxford Calculators contested Aristotelian ideas. Buridan's impetus theory, explaining projectile movement, was a key precursor to inertia. Their contributions laid essential groundwork for the later heliocentric model developed by Nicolaus Copernicus.

input: Nasser remains an iconic figure in the Arab world, particularly for his strides towards social justice and Arab unity, modernization policies, and anti-imperialist efforts. His presidency also encouraged and coincided with an Egyptian cultural boom, and launched large industrial projects, including the Aswan Dam and Helwan City. Nasser's detractors criticize his authoritarianism, his government's human rights violations, his populist relationship with the citizenry, and his failure to establish civil institutions, blaming his legacy for future dictatorial governance in Egypt. Historians describe Nasser as a towering political figure of the Middle East in the 20th century.
rewrite: Nasser is still a revered symbol across Arab nations, celebrated for advancing social equity, promoting pan-Arab solidarity, pursuing modernization, and resisting imperialism. His era saw a flourishing of Egyptian culture and major industrial initiatives like the Aswan High Dam and Helwan. Critics, however, point to his autocratic rule, human rights abuses, reliance on populist appeal, and lack of strong civic foundations, arguing this paved the way for later dictatorships. Scholars regard him as a dominant Middle Eastern leader of the 1900s.

input: Motorsport racecourses and events were banned in Switzerland following the 1955 Le Mans disaster with exception to events such as Hillclimbing. During this period, the country still produced successful racing drivers such as Clay Regazzoni, Sebastian Buemi, Jo Siffert, Dominique Aegerter, successful World Touring Car Championship driver Alain Menu, 2014 24 Hours of Le Mans winner Marcel Fässler and 2015 24 Hours Nürburgring winner Nico Müller. Switzerland also won the A1GP World Cup of Motorsport in 2007–08 with driver Neel Jani. Swiss motorcycle racer Thomas Lüthi won the 2005 MotoGP World Championship in the 125cc category. In June 2007 the Swiss National Council, one house of the Federal Assembly of Switzerland, voted to overturn the ban, however the other house, the Swiss Council of States rejected the change and the ban remains in place.
rewrite: Following a tragic accident at Le Mans in 1955, Switzerland prohibited motorsport circuits and races, though hillclimb competitions were still permitted. Despite this restriction, the nation cultivated many accomplished competitors. These included Formula One driver Clay Regazzoni, Sebastian Buemi, Jo Siffert, motorcyclist Dominique Aegerter, touring car champion Alain Menu, Le Mans victor Marcel Fässler, and Nico Müller, who triumphed at the Nürburgring. The Swiss team also secured the A1GP World Cup in 2008 with Neel Jani, and Thomas Lüthi claimed a 125cc motorcycle world title in 2005. An attempt to repeal the prohibition was initiated by the National Council in 2007 but was overturned by the Council of States, leaving the ban effectively unchanged.

input: While outer space provides the most rarefied example of a naturally occurring partial vacuum, the heavens were originally thought to be seamlessly filled by a rigid indestructible material called aether. Borrowing somewhat from the pneuma of Stoic physics, aether came to be regarded as the rarefied air from which it took its name, (see Aether (mythology)). Early theories of light posited a ubiquitous terrestrial and celestial medium through which light propagated. Additionally, the concept informed Isaac Newton's explanations of both refraction and of radiant heat. 19th century experiments into this luminiferous aether attempted to detect a minute drag on the Earth's orbit. While the Earth does, in fact, move through a relatively dense medium in comparison to that of interstellar space, the drag is so minuscule that it could not be detected. In 1912, astronomer Henry Pickering commented: "While the interstellar absorbing medium may be simply the ether, [it] is characteristic of a gas, and free gaseous molecules are certainly there".
rewrite: Although naturally occurring partial vacuums are most extreme in outer space, ancient beliefs held that the cosmos was completely occupied by an unyielding, eternal substance known as aether. This idea drew inspiration from the Stoic notion of pneuma, with aether being seen as an extremely thin form of air, as reflected in its etymological roots. Initial models describing light proposed that it traveled through this pervasive medium, present both on Earth and in the sky. This framework also supported Isaac Newton's theories on the bending of light and thermal radiation. Later, in the 1800s, scientific efforts focused on detecting the luminiferous aether tried to measure a slight resistance affecting Earth's path through space. Even though our planet does travel through a medium denser than the void between stars, any resulting drag is too insignificant to measure. Astronomer Henry Pickering noted in 1912 that while this interstellar material might be the aether, it behaves like a gas, and independent gas molecules are undoubtedly present.

input: However, some scholars contest the idea of a Proto-Euphratean language or one substrate language. It has been suggested by them and others, that the Sumerian language was originally that of the hunter and fisher peoples, who lived in the marshland and the Eastern Arabia littoral region, and were part of the Arabian bifacial culture. Reliable historical records begin much later; there are none in Sumer of any kind that have been dated before Enmebaragesi (c. 26th century BC). Professor Juris Zarins believes the Sumerians were settled along the coast of Eastern Arabia, today's Persian Gulf region, before it flooded at the end of the Ice Age.
rewrite: Some academics challenge the concept of a single Proto-Euphratean or underlying language. Instead, they propose Sumerian originated with hunter-gatherer and fishing communities inhabiting the marshlands and eastern Arabian coast, who belonged to the broader Arabian bifacial culture. Substantiated historical documentation starts far later; no Sumerian records exist prior to Enmebaragesi (circa 2600 BCE). Scholar Juris Zarins posits that these Sumerian populations were first established along the eastern Arabian shoreline, in what is now the Persian Gulf, prior to its inundation following the Ice Age.

input: In Arabic-speaking cultures, two words are commonly used for Christians: Naṣrānī (نصراني), plural Naṣārā (نصارى) is generally understood to be derived from Nazareth through the Syriac (Aramaic); Masīḥī (مسيحي) means followers of the Messiah. The term Nasara rose to prominence in July 2014, after the Fall of Mosul to the terrorist organization Islamic State of Iraq and the Levant. The nun or ن— the first letter of Nasara—was spray-painted on the property of Christians ejected from the city.
rewrite: In Arabic cultures, Christians are referred to by two main terms. Naṣrānī, originating from Nazareth via Syriac, and Masīḥī, meaning "follower of the Messiah." The word Nasara gained widespread attention in mid-2014 following ISIS's capture of Mosul. The group marked properties from which Christians were expelled by painting the Arabic letter "nūn," standing for Nasara, on their homes.

input: Yet the most impressive aesthetic works were done among the scholars and urban elite. Calligraphy and painting remained a central interest to both court painters and scholar-gentry who considered the Four Arts part of their cultural identity and social standing. The painting of the early years of the dynasty included such painters as the orthodox Four Wangs and the individualists Bada Shanren (1626–1705) and Shitao (1641–1707). The nineteenth century saw such innovations as the Shanghai School and the Lingnan School which used the technical skills of tradition to set the stage for modern painting.
rewrite: The most artistically significant creations emerged from educated circles and city-dwelling elites. For court artists and the scholarly class alike, calligraphy and painting were essential pursuits, integral to their cultural self-image and status. Early dynastic works featured masters like the conventional Four Wangs and the distinctive artists Bada Shanren and Shitao. Later, the 1800s brought new movements such as the Shanghai and Lingnan Schools, which applied classical techniques to pave the way for contemporary art.

input: Many solar photovoltaic power stations have been built, mainly in Europe. As of July 2012, the largest photovoltaic (PV) power plants in the world are the Agua Caliente Solar Project (USA, 247 MW), Charanka Solar Park (India, 214 MW), Golmud Solar Park (China, 200 MW), Perovo Solar Park (Russia 100 MW), Sarnia Photovoltaic Power Plant (Canada, 97 MW), Brandenburg-Briest Solarpark (Germany 91 MW), Solarpark Finow Tower (Germany 84.7 MW), Montalto di Castro Photovoltaic Power Station (Italy, 84.2 MW), Eggebek Solar Park (Germany 83.6 MW), Senftenberg Solarpark (Germany 82 MW), Finsterwalde Solar Park (Germany, 80.7 MW), Okhotnykovo Solar Park (Russia, 80 MW), Lopburi Solar Farm (Thailand 73.16 MW), Rovigo Photovoltaic Power Plant (Italy, 72 MW), and the Lieberose Photovoltaic Park (Germany, 71.8 MW).
rewrite: Numerous large-scale solar power facilities have been constructed globally, with a significant concentration in Europe. By mid-2012, the leading installations by capacity included the Agua Caliente Solar Project in the United States at 247 megawatts, Charanka Solar Park in India at 214 MW, and China's Golmud Solar Park at 200 MW. Other major plants were located in Russia, Canada, Italy, and Thailand. Germany hosted several substantial sites, such as the Brandenburg-Briest Solarpark, Finow Tower, Eggebek, Senftenberg, Finsterwalde, and Lieberose facilities, with capacities ranging from approximately 72 to 91 megawatts.

input: Under a banner of "reducing public drunkenness" the Beer Act of 1830 introduced a new lower tier of premises permitted to sell alcohol, the Beer Houses. At the time beer was viewed as harmless, nutritious and even healthy. Young children were often given what was described as small beer, which was brewed to have a low alcohol content, as the local water was often unsafe. Even the evangelical church and temperance movements of the day viewed the drinking of beer very much as a secondary evil and a normal accompaniment to a meal. The freely available beer was thus intended to wean the drinkers off the evils of gin, or so the thinking went.
rewrite: The Beer Act of 1830 was framed as a measure to decrease drunkenness. It created a new class of licensed outlets called Beer Houses, where alcohol could be sold. During this era, beer was considered a safe, nourishing beverage, often given to children in a diluted form known as small beer because water supplies were frequently contaminated. Both religious reformers and temperance groups primarily saw beer as a minor vice and a customary part of dining. The widespread availability of beer was therefore meant to steer consumers away from the perceived greater dangers of gin, according to the prevailing logic.

input: Gagarin became a national hero of the Soviet Union and the Eastern Bloc, and a worldwide celebrity. Moscow and other cities in the USSR held mass demonstrations, the scale of which was second only to the World War II Victory Parade of 1945. April 12 was declared Cosmonautics Day in the USSR, and is celebrated today in Russia as one of the official "Commemorative Dates of Russia." In 2011, it was declared the International Day of Human Space Flight by the United Nations.
rewrite: Gagarin emerged as a celebrated hero across the Soviet Union, its allied nations, and the globe. Major Soviet cities witnessed enormous public gatherings, rivaled only by the 1945 victory celebrations. The anniversary of his flight, April 12, was established as Cosmonautics Day, a Russian commemorative date. Later, the United Nations designated it the International Day of Human Space Flight.

input: In June 1718 Blackbeard, aka Edward Teach, ran his flagship, the Queen Anne's Revenge, aground at Beaufort Inlet, North Carolina, in present-day Carteret County. After the grounding her crew and supplies were transferred to smaller ships. In 1996 Intersal, Inc., a private firm, discovered the remains of a vessel likely to be the Queen Anne's Revenge, which was added to the US National Register of Historic Places. In November, after losing his ship and appealing to the governor of North Carolina who promised safe-haven and a pardon, the notorious pirate, Blackbeard (Edward Teach) was killed in an ambush by troops from Virginia.
rewrite: In June of 1718, the infamous pirate Blackbeard, also known as Edward Teach, deliberately stranded his primary vessel, the *Queen Anne's Revenge*, near Beaufort Inlet in what is now Carteret County, North Carolina. His men moved their cargo onto smaller ships. A private company called Intersal, Inc., located what is believed to be this shipwreck in 1996, leading to its listing on the US National Register of Historic Places. Later that November, after losing his flagship and seeking a promised pardon from North Carolina's governor, Blackbeard was ambushed and slain by forces from Virginia.

input: QED vacuum has interesting and complex properties. In QED vacuum, the electric and magnetic fields have zero average values, but their variances are not zero. As a result, QED vacuum contains vacuum fluctuations (virtual particles that hop into and out of existence), and a finite energy called vacuum energy. Vacuum fluctuations are an essential and ubiquitous part of quantum field theory. Some experimentally verified effects of vacuum fluctuations include spontaneous emission and the Lamb shift. Coulomb's law and the electric potential in vacuum near an electric charge are modified.
rewrite: The quantum vacuum in quantum electrodynamics exhibits intricate characteristics. While average electric and magnetic field strengths are zero, their statistical variations are nonzero. This leads to quantum fluctuations—virtual particles appearing and disappearing—and a measurable vacuum energy. Such fluctuations are fundamental to quantum field theory. Verified phenomena like spontaneous emission and the Lamb shift arise from these effects. Additionally, Coulomb's law and the electric potential near a charge are altered in this vacuum.

input: Transformation, unlike transduction or conjugation, depends on numerous bacterial gene products that specifically interact to perform this complex process, and thus transformation is clearly a bacterial adaptation for DNA transfer. In order for a bacterium to bind, take up and recombine donor DNA into its own chromosome, it must first enter a special physiological state termed competence (see Natural competence). In Bacillus subtilis, about 40 genes are required for the development of competence. The length of DNA transferred during B. subtilis transformation can be between a third of a chromosome up to the whole chromosome. Transformation appears to be common among bacterial species, and thus far at least 60 species are known to have the natural ability to become competent for transformation. The development of competence in nature is usually associated with stressful environmental conditions, and seems to be an adaptation for facilitating repair of DNA damage in recipient cells.
rewrite: Unlike transduction or conjugation, transformation involves many specialized bacterial proteins working together to transfer DNA, indicating it is an evolved trait. For a bacterial cell to absorb and integrate external DNA into its genome, it must achieve a distinct state called competence. In *Bacillus subtilis*, roughly 40 genes are involved in reaching this state. During transformation in this species, the amount of DNA acquired can range from a third of a chromosome to an entire chromosome. This mechanism is widespread, with over 60 bacterial species identified as naturally capable of developing competence. Typically triggered by environmental stress, natural competence likely serves as a mechanism to help cells repair damaged DNA.

input: On 1 July 1967, BBC Two became the first television channel in Europe to broadcast regularly in colour, using the West German PAL system that is still in use today although being gradually superseded by digital systems. (BBC One and ITV began 625-line colour broadcasts simultaneously on 15 November 1969). Unlike other terrestrial channels, BBC Two does not have soap opera or standard news programming, but a range of programmes intended to be eclectic and diverse (although if a programme has high audience ratings it is often eventually repositioned to BBC One). The different remit of BBC2 allowed its first controller, Sir David Attenborough to commission the first heavyweight documentaries and documentary series such as Civilisation, The Ascent of Man and Horizon.
rewrite: On 1 July 1967, BBC Two launched Europe's inaugural regular colour television service. It employed the West German PAL format, a standard that remains active but is now slowly being replaced by digital broadcasting. While BBC One and ITV commenced their own colour transmissions on 15 November 1969, BBC Two has always maintained a distinct schedule. It deliberately avoids conventional soap operas and daily news bulletins, instead offering an intentionally varied mix of content. However, popular shows often transfer to BBC One. This unique purpose enabled its inaugural head, Sir David Attenborough, to pioneer serious documentary works like *Civilisation*, *The Ascent of Man*, and *Horizon*.

input: On August 9, 2015, ESPN reported that the New Orleans VooDoo and Las Vegas Outlaws had ceased operations, effective immediately, a claim which was subsequently validated on the AFL website. On September 1, 2015, the Spokane Shock officially left the AFL and joined the IFL under the new name Spokane Empire, becoming the fifth active AFL/af2 franchise to leave for the IFL since bankruptcy (Iowa Barnstormers, Tri-Cities Fever, Green Bay Blizzard and Arkansas Twisters—now the Texas Revolution—left previously).
rewrite: On August 9, 2015, ESPN announced the immediate shutdown of the New Orleans VooDoo and Las Vegas Outlaws, a report later confirmed by the AFL. That September 1, the Spokane Shock departed the AFL for the IFL, rebranding as the Spokane Empire. This move marked them as the fifth team from the AFL or its developmental league to transition to the IFL following the league's financial collapse, joining several prior defectors.

input: Thousands more employees work in Midtown, north of the central business district. Midtown's anchors are the city's largest single employer Detroit Medical Center, Wayne State University, and the Henry Ford Health System in New Center. Midtown is also home to watchmaker Shinola and an array of small and/or startup companies. New Center bases TechTown, a research and business incubator hub that’s part of the WSU system. Like downtown and Corktown, Midtown also has a fast-growing retailing and restaurant scene.
rewrite: Midtown, located just north of the downtown core, employs thousands of additional workers. Its major institutions include the Detroit Medical Center, Wayne State University, and the Henry Ford Health System, which are among the city's biggest employers. The area also hosts Shinola and numerous small or emerging businesses. TechTown, a WSU-affiliated innovation center, operates in New Center. Similar to other districts, Midtown features a rapidly expanding array of shops and dining establishments.

input: The name Anabaptist, meaning "one who baptizes again", was given them by their persecutors in reference to the practice of re-baptizing converts who already had been baptized as infants. Anabaptists required that baptismal candidates be able to make their own confessions of faith and so rejected baptism of infants. The early members of this movement did not accept the name Anabaptist, claiming that since infant baptism was unscriptural and null and void, the baptizing of believers was not a re-baptism but in fact their first real baptism. As a result of their views on the nature of baptism and other issues, Anabaptists were heavily persecuted during the 16th century and into the 17th by both Magisterial Protestants and Roman Catholics.[aa] While most Anabaptists adhered to a literal interpretation of the Sermon on the Mount, which precluded taking oaths, participating in military actions, and participating in civil government, some who practiced re-baptism felt otherwise.[ab] They were thus technically Anabaptists, even though conservative Amish, Mennonites, and Hutterites and some historians tend to consider them as outside of true Anabaptism.
