Anabaptist reformers of the Radical Reformation are diveded into Radical and the so-called Second Front. Some important Radical Reformation theologians were John of Leiden, Thomas Müntzer, Kaspar Schwenkfeld, Sebastian Franck, Menno Simons. Second Front Reformers included Hans Denck, Conrad Grebel, Balthasar Hubmaier and Felix Manz.
rewrite:
The term Anabaptist, translating to "rebaptizer," was applied to them by opponents, criticizing their custom of baptizing anew those who had undergone infant christening. They held that only individuals capable of professing personal faith could receive baptism, thereby dismissing infant baptism as invalid. Founding followers of this tradition refused the label, arguing that because infant baptism lacked biblical foundation and was ineffective, their rite constituted an initial, genuine baptism rather than a repetition. Due to these stances on baptism and other doctrines, Anabaptists faced severe oppression throughout the 1500s and 1600s from both established Protestant churches and Catholicism.

Many Anabaptists followed a strict reading of the Sermon on the Mount, refusing vows, military service, and involvement in state affairs. However, certain groups that performed believer's baptism dissented from these principles. Although these dissenters are accurately categorized as Anabaptists, traditional communities like the Amish, Mennonites, and Hutterites, along with various scholars, often exclude them from authentic Anabaptist lineage. Figures of the Radical Reformation are categorized into Radical and Second Front movements. Prominent Radical theologians included John of Leiden, Thomas Müntzer, Kaspar Schwenkfeld, Sebastian Franck, and Menno Simons. The Second Front featured reformers such as Hans Denck, Conrad Grebel, Balthasar Hubmaier, and Felix Manz.

input: The design architecture of USB is asymmetrical in its topology, consisting of a host, a multitude of downstream USB ports, and multiple peripheral devices connected in a tiered-star topology. Additional USB hubs may be included in the tiers, allowing branching into a tree structure with up to five tier levels. A USB host may implement multiple host controllers and each host controller may provide one or more USB ports. Up to 127 devices, including hub devices if present, may be connected to a single host controller. USB devices are linked in series through hubs. One hub—built into the host controller—is the root hub.
rewrite: USB employs an unbalanced design where a central host connects to numerous peripheral devices through a tiered-star arrangement. This structure can incorporate extra hubs, forming a branching tree that supports up to five layers. A single host can house several controllers, each offering one or more ports. As many as 127 devices, counting any hubs, may attach to one controller. All devices are daisy-chained via these hubs, beginning with the root hub integrated into the host controller.

input: Ozawa's "Northern Force" had four aircraft carriers, two obsolete battleships partly converted to carriers, three cruisers and nine destroyers. The carriers had only 108 planes. The force was not spotted by the Allies until 16:40 on 24 October. At 20:00 Toyoda ordered all remaining Japanese forces to attack. Halsey saw an opportunity to destroy the remnants of the Japanese carrier force. The U.S. Third Fleet was formidable – nine large carriers, eight light carriers, six battleships, 17 cruisers, 63 destroyers and 1,000 planes – and completely outgunned Ozawa's force. Halsey's ships set out in pursuit of Ozawa just after midnight. U.S. commanders ignored reports that Kurita had turned back towards San Bernardino Strait. They had taken the bait set by Ozawa. On the morning of 25 October Ozawa launched 75 planes. Most were shot down by U.S. fighter patrols. By 08:00 U.S. fighters had destroyed the screen of Japanese fighters and were hitting ships. By evening, they had sunk the carriers Zuikaku, Zuihō, and Chiyoda, and a destroyer. The fourth carrier, Chitose, and a cruiser were disabled and later sank.
rewrite: Ozawa’s “Northern Force” comprised four aircraft carriers, two older battleships partially refitted as carriers, three cruisers, and nine destroyers. The carriers held a mere 108 aircraft. Allied forces did not detect this group until late afternoon on October 24. That evening, Toyoda commanded all available Japanese units to commence an assault. Recognizing a chance to eliminate the remaining enemy carrier strength, Halsey gave chase with the powerful U.S. Third Fleet shortly after midnight. His fleet vastly outmatched Ozawa’s, boasting nine fleet carriers, eight light carriers, six battleships, seventeen cruisers, sixty-three destroyers, and about one thousand planes. American leaders disregarded intelligence indicating Kurita had reversed course toward San Bernardino Strait; they had fully accepted Ozawa’s decoy. On October 25, Ozawa sent seventy-five planes aloft, most of which U.S. patrol fighters eliminated. By 8:00 a.m., American air attacks had overwhelmed the Japanese defensive screen and were striking naval vessels directly. By day’s end, they had sunk the carriers Zuikaku, Zuihō, and Chiyoda, along with a destroyer. A fourth carrier, Chitose, and a cruiser were crippled and later foundered.
